Process Details:
## Overview
Identify and Refine Performance Indicators is the process of defining, updating, and retiring the measures used to assess the performance of products and services across their life cycle. It ensures that the organization’s Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), Service Level Indicators/Objectives (SLIs/SLOs), and supporting metrics remain aligned to strategy, reflect the current portfolio (including newly introduced offerings and retired ones), and enable fact-based decisions.

This process:
- Translates strategy and customer expectations into measurable outcomes.
- Provides a standardized, governed measurement framework across products/services.
- Ensures changes from Introduce new products/services [10077] and Retire outdated products/services [10078] are reflected in dashboards, targets, SLAs/OLAs, and reporting.
- Improves product/service success by enabling timely detection of issues, validating value hypotheses, and guiding investments or retirements.

## Key Activities
- Capture triggers: portfolio changes, strategic updates, regulatory changes, customer feedback.
- Inventory current indicators; assess gaps and redundancies versus the revamped portfolio.
- Define measurement objectives using a structured method (e.g., Goal-Question-Metric).
- Design candidate indicators (definitions, formulas, dimensions, targets, thresholds).
- Validate feasibility: data availability, instrumentation needs, privacy/compliance.
- Align and approve through governance (product, service, data, finance stakeholders).
- Implement changes: data pipelines, telemetry, dashboards, reports, SLAs/OLAs.
- Communicate and train stakeholders; update process and reporting documentation.
- Monitor indicator performance and data quality; iterate and retire obsolete metrics.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Portfolio changes: introductions/retirements, roadmaps, business cases.
  - Strategy and objectives (OKRs), value propositions, pricing and margin targets.
  - Customer/market insights: NPS/CSAT, churn, usage analytics, voice-of-customer.
  - Operational performance: incident data, SLAs/OLAs, MTTR/MTBF, capacity, uptime.
  - Financial data: revenue, cost-to-serve, CAC, LTV, margins.
  - Regulatory/compliance requirements (e.g., GDPR, CCPA, sector-specific SLAs).
  - Existing KPI catalog, definitions, and dashboard inventories.
  - Data architecture: source systems, lineage, quality profiles, telemetry capabilities.

- Prerequisites:
  - Defined product/service taxonomy and ownership (product owners, service owners).
  - Data governance framework (roles, policies, approval workflows).
  - Access to data platforms (warehouse/lake), analytics, and observability tools.
  - Change management and release processes for analytics/BI and service catalogs.

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - 2.1.2.1 Introduce new products/services [10077] (triggers new indicators).
  - 2.1.2.3 Retire outdated products/services [10078] (triggers indicator retirement).
  - Product/service change management and master data management.
  - Data governance and BI/reporting development lifecycle.
  - Incident/problem management (for SLI/SLO targets).
  - Compliance management and audit.

## Process Steps
1. Trigger and intake
   - Capture triggers from new/retired offerings, strategic shifts, regulatory updates.
   - Log change request in the KPI backlog with context, business objectives, timelines.

2. Stakeholder mapping and governance setup
   - Identify product/service owners, data owners/stewards, finance, CX, operations, compliance, analytics/BI.
   - Confirm decision rights, approval thresholds, and review cadence.

3. Current-state assessment
   - Inventory current indicators relevant to impacted offerings.
   - Map metrics to objectives; identify duplicates, conflicts, gaps, and vanity metrics.
   - Assess data quality and latency of existing sources.

4. Define measurement objectives
   - Use Goal-Question-Metric (GQM) or OKR alignment to specify:
     - Goals (e.g., accelerate adoption, improve reliability, expand margin).
     - Questions to answer (e.g., “Are new users achieving activation within 7 days?”).
     - Candidate metrics (e.g., Activation rate, Time-to-First-Value).

5. Design candidate indicators
   - For each indicator define:
     - Name, business purpose, type (KPI/SLI/diagnostic), scope (products, segments).
     - Owner and steward; calculation formula with numerator/denominator; time grain.
     - Dimensions (region, cohort, plan), filters, inclusion/exclusion rules.
     - Data sources and lineage; latency expectations; data quality rules.
     - Targets, thresholds, and guardrails (leading/lagging metrics).
     - Privacy classification and retention; regulatory mapping.
   - Draft acceptance criteria for each indicator (what “good” looks like).

6. Feasibility and impact analysis
   - Validate data availability; identify instrumentation gaps (event tracking, logs).
   - Estimate effort/cost for pipelines, dashboards, and telemetry changes.
   - Assess impacts on SLAs/OLAs, contracts, and customer reporting.
   - Conduct privacy/compliance review; complete DPIA if required.

7. Prioritize and plan
   - Score indicators on business value, risk reduction, effort, and urgency.
   - Build an implementation plan with sprints/releases, owners, and dependencies.

8. Governance review and approval
   - Present definitions, targets, and impact analysis to the governance board.
   - Resolve conflicts (e.g., revenue recognition, financial definitions).
   - Secure approvals; capture decisions and version the KPI catalog.

9. Implement data collection and transformation
   - Update event schemas and telemetry (engineering/ops).
   - Build/modify ETL/ELT pipelines and data models (analytics engineering).
   - Configure data quality checks, lineage, and monitoring.

10. Build and update reporting
    - Develop or update dashboards and reports (self-serve and executive).
    - Implement alerting thresholds for SLIs/SLOs and key KPIs.
    - Update API feeds and customer-facing reports if applicable.

11. Update targets and contracts
    - Align internal targets and external SLAs/OLAs; update service catalogs.
    - Coordinate with legal/commercial teams for contractual changes if required.

12. Change management and enablement
    - Communicate changes, rationale, and go-live dates to stakeholders.
    - Provide training and usage guidance; update documentation and playbooks.

13. Pilot and validate
    - Run limited pilot; validate calculations, visualizations, and alerts.
    - Compare against benchmarks and historical baselines.
    - Collect feedback; iterate before full rollout.

14. Go-live and monitor
    - Deploy to production; monitor adoption, data quality, and alert noise.
    - Track metric utility (used in decisions) and unintended consequences.
    - Schedule periodic reviews; retire obsolete indicators with controlled deprecation.

15. Retire or revise indicators
    - When products retire or strategy shifts, follow a deprecation plan:
      - Communicate deprecation; remove from dashboards by set date.
      - Archive historical data and definitions; update the KPI catalog.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- KPI and Indicator Catalog with standardized definitions and metadata.
- Measurement framework documents (KPI trees, leading/lagging map, guardrails).
- Data requirements and lineage documentation; ETL/ELT specifications.
- Instrumentation backlog items and implementation plan.
- Updated dashboards, reports, alerts, and API outputs.
- Updated targets, SLAs/OLAs, and service catalog entries.
- Training materials, communication packs, and updated SOPs.
- Change log and governance approvals; audit trail and version history.

Success criteria:
- 100% of in-scope products/services have approved KPIs/SLIs within agreed time.
- Indicators are trusted (meet data quality thresholds) and actively used in decisions.
- Obsolete indicators retired on schedule with no reporting breaks.
- No compliance/privacy violations; clean audit results.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product Manager / Service Owner: Define objectives, own KPI set and targets, approve trade-offs; ensure instrumentation in backlog.
- Portfolio Manager / PMO: Coordinate cross-portfolio alignment, prioritization, and timelines.
- Data Product Owner / BI Lead: Translate definitions into data models, dashboards, and ensure data quality.
- Data Steward / Governance Lead: Maintain KPI catalog, enforce standards, manage approvals and versioning.
- Analytics Engineer / Data Engineer: Build pipelines, models, and quality checks; maintain lineage.
- Observability/Telemetry Engineer: Implement event tracking, SLIs, and alerting.
- Finance Business Partner: Validate financial definitions, targets, and impacts.
- Customer Insights/Research: Provide VOC/NPS and interpret customer-facing metrics.
- Operations/Service Delivery: Define reliability and support metrics; ensure SLA feasibility.
- Compliance/Legal/Privacy: Review compliance, retention, and consent; approve external reporting.
- ITSM/Support Lead: Align incident, request, and satisfaction metrics.
- Executive Sponsor / Governance Board: Approve KPI sets, resolve conflicts, ensure strategic alignment.

## Best Practices
- Align to strategy and lifecycle stage: define stage-specific KPIs (e.g., adoption, engagement, retention, profitability).
- Use a balanced set: leading and lagging, outcome and output, value and risk (guardrails).
- Standardize definitions: one source of truth with clear formulas, dimensions, and ownership.
- Apply SMART targets and statistical thresholds; use baselines and seasonality adjustments.
- Adopt GQM or OKR mapping to avoid vanity metrics and ensure traceability.
- Instrument by design: include metric requirements in product/service design and DoD.
- Govern changes: formal approvals, versioning, and deprecation policies.
- Ensure data quality: automated checks, anomaly detection, and lineage visibility.
- Respect privacy and ethics: minimize data, apply consent, differential privacy where needed.
- Cohorts and segmentation: measure by segment for actionable insight (region, plan, persona).
- Benchmark externally where possible; calibrate targets to market and SLAs.
- Document assumptions and exclusions; include sensitivity analysis.

## Common Challenges
- Metric sprawl and conflicting definitions
  - Solution: Central catalog, tight governance, harmonization workshops, golden definitions.
- Data availability or quality gaps
  - Solution: Data quality SLAs, instrumentation backlog, interim proxies with sunset date.
- Misaligned incentives or gaming
  - Solution: Balanced scorecards with guardrails; avoid purely volume-based targets; audit usage.
- Lagging insights and latency
  - Solution: Upgrade pipelines, near-real-time telemetry for critical SLIs, caching strategies.
- Low adoption of dashboards
  - Solution: Train users, embed metrics in rituals (QBRs, ops reviews), tailor to personas.
- Compliance risks
  - Solution: Privacy-by-design reviews, retention rules, PII minimization, access controls.
- Change fatigue
  - Solution: Clear change calendar, impact analysis, phased rollouts, strong communication.

## Performance Metrics (for this process)
- Portfolio coverage: % products/services with approved KPI sets within X days of launch/retirement.
- Lead time: Average time from trigger to KPI go-live.
- Data quality: % indicators meeting quality thresholds (completeness, accuracy, timeliness).
- Adoption: Monthly active users of KPI dashboards; usage in decision logs.
- Actionability: % metrics tied to decisions or experiments in last quarter.
- Redundancy reduction: Net change in total metrics vs. prior period (with maintained coverage).
- Alert efficacy: Signal-to-noise ratio; % alerts acknowledged and acted upon.
- Compliance: Number of audit findings; % indicators with completed privacy assessment.
- Maintenance: % obsolete indicators retired on schedule.

## Technology and Tools
- Data platforms: Data warehouse/lake (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift), lakehouse (Databricks).
- ETL/ELT and orchestration: dbt, Airflow, Fivetran/Stitch, Kafka/Kinesis for streams.
- BI and visualization: Tableau, Power BI, Looker, Superset; embedded analytics.
- Product analytics and experimentation: Amplitude, Mixpanel, Heap; Optimizely/LaunchDarkly for A/B and feature flags.
- Observability and SLIs: Datadog, New Relic, Grafana/Prometheus, OpenTelemetry.
- Customer feedback: Qualtrics, Medallia; NPS/CSAT tools; social listening.
- ITSM and support: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, Zendesk, Salesforce Service Cloud.
- CRM and revenue: Salesforce, HubSpot; financial systems/ERP for margin and cost.
- Data governance and catalog: Collibra, Alation, Atlan; data quality tools (Great Expectations).
- Privacy and access: Consent management platforms, DLP, IAM/role-based access.
- Documentation and change: Confluence/Notion for SOPs, Jira/Azure DevOps for backlog, Git for versioning KPI definitions.

Example indicator categories to consider:
- Financial: revenue growth, ARPU, gross margin, CAC payback.
- Customer: NPS, CSAT, churn/retention, activation rate, adoption/engagement (DAU/MAU, stickiness).
- Reliability/Service: availability, MTTR/MTBF, SLA attainment, change failure rate.
- Quality: defect density, escape rate, returns/refunds, support contact rate.
- Time-to-value: time-to-first-value, onboarding completion time.
- Operational: cost-to-serve, utilization, backlog age, cycle time.
- Compliance/Sustainability: audit pass rate, data privacy incidents, carbon intensity (where applicable).

## Overview
Conduct mandatory and elective reviews is the recurring process that verifies whether the organization’s policies, controls, and day-to-day practices effectively protect intellectual property (IP) and meet applicable regulatory and contractual requirements across the product/service lifecycle. It ensures that patents, copyrights, trade secrets, trademarks, licensing, export controls, open-source usage, and product regulatory obligations are being managed as designed, and that gaps are identified, remediated, and prevented from recurring.

Purpose:
- Confirm compliance with mandated regulations, standards, and contracts.
- Validate that IP protection and regulatory controls are designed well and operating effectively.
- Provide evidence and assurance to leadership, regulators, auditors, and partners.
- Drive continuous improvement via corrective and preventive actions (CAPA).

Role in the organization:
- Acts as the assurance and improvement mechanism within the Govern and manage product/service development program.
- Connects policy intent to frontline execution, enabling risk-based decision-making at portfolio, program, and product levels.
- Integrates with product stage-gates to ensure compliance before market entries, releases, and lifecycle changes.

## Key Activities
- Establish annual review plan: scope, cadence, mandatory vs elective, risk-based prioritization.
- Define review criteria and checklists mapped to policies, controls, and external obligations.
- Prepare and execute reviews (document walkthroughs, control design/effectiveness testing, sampling).
- Rate findings and risks; perform root cause analysis.
- Develop, approve, and track CAPA with owners and due dates.
- Report to governance bodies; maintain evidence and audit trail.
- Update policies/SOPs, training, and systems based on lessons learned.
- Continuously monitor key controls and adjust the program.

- Product development pipeline and release calendar; stage-gate criteria.
- Regulatory inventory applicable to products/regions (e.g., ISO 13485, ISO 27001, SOC 2, MDR, FDA design controls, export controls).

- Prior audit/review results, CAPA backlog, exception waivers.

- Governance forum (e.g., IP/Compliance Steering Committee) and escalation paths.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Identify, register, and maintain IP assets.
- Manage licensing and third-party IP usage.
- Monitor regulatory changes and update controls.
- Conduct training and awareness.
- Product lifecycle management and stage-gate governance.
- Vendor risk management and secure software development lifecycle (SSDL).
- Records management and legal hold.

## Process Steps
1) Plan the review program
- Compile regulatory and contractual obligations to determine mandatory reviews (e.g., scheduled ISO audits, SOX control testing, royalty audits).
- Propose elective reviews based on risk indicators (e.g., new market entry, high OSS usage, trade secret reliance, acquisitions).
- Prioritize using a risk heatmap (impact x likelihood) and coverage targets for high-risk areas.
- Build an annual calendar with quarterly refresh; align with product milestones.
- Obtain approval from the IP/Compliance Steering Committee.

2) Define scope, criteria, and methods
- For each review, define objectives, in-scope entities (business units, products, geographies), and time period.
- Map policy and control objectives to external requirements and contracts.
- Create review checklists and test procedures (design and operating effectiveness).
- Define sampling approach (e.g., 25 transactions across regions; 2 releases per product).
- Confirm independence of reviewers and segregation from control owners.

3) Prepare logistics and notifications
- Assign lead reviewer, SMEs, and observers; confirm resource availability.
- Issue data/evidence request lists; define secure evidence transfer method.
- Set kickoff meeting, engagement timeline, and communication plan.
- Validate system access, NDAs, and confidentiality requirements.

4) Execute the review
- Conduct kickoff: scope, timeline, roles, ground rules.
- Perform document walkthroughs (policies, SOPs, process maps, training, change records).
- Assess control design: adequacy vs. requirements; coverage; alignment to risks.
- Test operating effectiveness: sampling, re-performance, observation, tool configuration checks, audit trail validation.
- Validate data integrity in source systems (IPMS, CLM, QMS, GRC).
- Assess third-party and OSS controls (license compliance, attribution, approvals).
- Capture evidence, observations, and potential nonconformities in a central tool.

5) Analyze results and rate findings
- Categorize findings: nonconformity, deficiency, improvement opportunity.
- Rate severity (e.g., Critical/Major/Minor) and residual risk; assess regulatory impact and deadline sensitivity.
- Perform root cause analysis (e.g., 5 Whys, fishbone).
- Draft preliminary recommendations and proposed actions.

6) Reporting and stakeholder validation
- Issue draft report; conduct management review for factual accuracy.
- Finalize report with: executive summary, scope, methods, findings with evidence, heatmap, recommendations, and agreed actions with owners/dates.
- Log actions into CAPA tracker; update risk register and exceptions (with expiry dates).

7) Remediation and CAPA management
- Owners implement corrective actions (process/SOP updates, tooling changes, training, contracts updates, rework evidence).
- Define preventive actions to address systemic causes.
- Verify closure (evidence review or re-test) and formally close CAPA.
- Escalate overdue critical actions; apply temporary compensating controls as needed.

8) Retrospective and continuous improvement
- Conduct lessons learned; update checklists, templates, and training.
- Adjust risk ratings and next cycle priorities based on trends and incidents.
- Provide performance dashboards to governance and business leadership.

9) Evidence retention and audit readiness
- Archive reports, evidence, workpapers, and approvals per retention policy and legal hold requirements.
- Maintain traceability from findings to CAPA and closure evidence.

10) Ongoing monitoring and spot checks
- Track key indicators (e.g., missed docket deadlines, OSS noncompliance rates).
- Run targeted spot checks between formal reviews in high-risk areas.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Annual/quarterly review plan and calendar.
- Review scopes, checklists, and test scripts.
- Evidence logs and workpapers with traceability.
- Review reports with findings, risk ratings, and recommendations.
- CAPA register with owners, due dates, and status.
- Updated policies, SOPs, training materials, and control library.
- Exception/waiver register with approvals and expiry dates.
- Management dashboards and KPIs.
- Updated risk register entries and regulatory mapping.

Success criteria:
- 100% completion of mandatory reviews by due dates.
- ≥95% on-time CAPA closure for critical/major findings; declining repeat findings.
- Reduced high-severity incidents (e.g., missed IP deadlines, license breaches).
- No material regulatory nonconformities or penalties; clean external audits.
- Increased process maturity scores and review coverage of high-risk areas.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- IP Counsel/Head of IP: Owns IP policy; sponsors reviews; approves remediation impacting IP strategy.
- Compliance Officer/Program Manager: Owns review program; plans, coordinates, and reports; maintains risk register and calendar.
- Regulatory Affairs/QA: Ensures alignment with product regulatory obligations; co-leads regulated-product reviews; manages nonconformities in QMS.
- Patent Operations/Docketing Manager: Provides docket data, deadlines, and evidence; remediates docketing control gaps.
- Product/Engineering Leaders: Provide process and release evidence; implement CAPA in development and release workflows.
- OSS Compliance/DevSecOps: Provides SBOMs and scan results; remediates OSS license issues.
- Contracts/CLM Manager: Supplies contracts, audit rights, and royalty schedules; supports findings on licensing compliance.
- Information Security/Data Protection Officer: Advises on trade secret controls, access, DLP; supports privacy/regulatory intersections.
- Internal Audit (optional/independent): Performs or validates reviews; ensures independence and rigor.
- Procurement/Vendor Risk: Provides third-party IP/compliance assessments and evidence.
- Finance/Tax: Supports SOX-related IP capitalization controls and royalty accounting.
- Training/L&D: Updates curricula based on findings; tracks completion.
- Business Unit Leadership: Accepts risk, approves exceptions, funds remediation, ensures timely CAPA.

## Best Practices
- Use a risk-based review plan emphasizing high-impact assets, geographies, suppliers, and releases.
- Separate duties: reviewers independent from control owners; apply Three Lines model.
- Standardize templates, severity criteria, and evidence requirements for consistency.
- Integrate with stage-gates: make passing key compliance checks a release prerequisite.
- Maintain a living regulatory inventory and map controls to requirements and contracts.
- Automate evidence collection where possible (system logs, dashboards, SBOMs).
- Leverage GRC/IPMS/QMS integration for single source of truth and traceability.
- Manage third-party risks: ensure IP indemnities, OSS license vetting, and export screening are enforced.
- Establish a clear exception process with risk acceptance and expiry dates.
- Conduct periodic mock inspections and tabletop exercises for readiness.
- Focus on root cause and prevention; avoid purely cosmetic fixes.
- Communicate findings and improvements transparently to build a culture of compliance.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Fragmented data and systems: Integrate IPMS, CLM, QMS, and GRC; use data catalogs and ETL where needed.
- Unclear ownership: Define RACI for each control; publish owners and alternates.
- Reviewer independence: Create an internal audit pool or use cross-BU reviewers; rotate assignments.
- Rapid regulatory changes: Implement horizon scanning and regulatory change management; update mappings promptly.
- Resource constraints: Prioritize using risk; timebox elective reviews; leverage automation and sampling.
- Documentation gaps: Maintain current SOPs/process maps; require documentation as part of CAPA closure.
- Third-party/OSS risks: Enforce pre-approval workflows; include audit rights; monitor with SBOM and scanning tools.
- Global complexity: Localize requirements; appoint regional compliance champions; provide translations.
- CAPA fatigue and delays: Limit open actions; track with dashboards; escalate and tie to performance objectives.

## Performance Metrics
- Review completion rate (mandatory vs elective) and on-time percentage.
- Coverage of high-risk areas (%) and depth (design vs operating effectiveness).
- Findings per review and severity distribution; repeat finding rate.
- Average time to CAPA closure; CAPA backlog and overdue actions.
- Docketing accuracy and missed deadline rate (office actions, annuities, maintenance).
- OSS license noncompliance rate per release; percent of releases with clean SBOM.
- Number of policy exceptions and average age; compensating controls in place.
- Training completion rates for targeted populations post-findings.
- External audit/regulatory outcomes (nonconformities, observations).
- Cost of compliance vs cost of noncompliance (penalties, rework, delays).

## Technology and Tools
- IP Management/Docketing: Anaqua, Clarivate FoundationIP, PATTSY WAVE, CPA Global. 
- GRC/IRM Platforms: ServiceNow GRC, RSA Archer, MetricStream for control libraries, testing, and CAPA.
- QMS/eQMS: MasterControl, Veeva, Greenlight Guru for nonconformances and regulated product controls.
- Contract Lifecycle Management: Icertis, DocuSign CLM for license terms, royalties, audit rights.
- OSS and Component Scanning: Synopsys Black Duck, Snyk, FOSSA; SBOM tooling (CycloneDX, SPDX).
- Regulatory/Privacy Management: OneTrust, TrustArc; export control screening (e2open Amber Road).
- Document/Records Management: SharePoint, OpenText; legal hold and eDiscovery tools.
- BI/Dashboards: Power BI, Tableau for KPIs and trends.
- Workflow/BPM and Ticketing: ServiceNow, Jira, Camunda, Nintex for reviews and CAPA workflows.
- Security/Trade Secret Protection: DLP/CASB, IAM, encryption, secure repositories and data rooms.
- Collaboration and Evidence Collection: Confluence, secure file transfer and evidence vaults.

Process Details:
# [2.1.3.2] Review Infringement of Patents and Copyrights

## Overview
This process ensures that products and services do not infringe third-party intellectual property (IP) rights—specifically patents and copyrights—and that open-source software (OSS) usage is compliant with licensing obligations. It provides a systematic, repeatable approach to identify, assess, mitigate, and document infringement risks throughout the product lifecycle.

Purpose:
- Enable safe commercialization with freedom to operate (FTO) in target markets
- Prevent costly litigation, rework, delays, and brand damage
- Ensure OSS license compliance and ethical community engagement
- Provide evidence and documentation for audits, customer diligence, and release gates

Role in the organization:
- Integral to product development stage gates and release readiness
- Supports IP strategy (defensive and offensive), procurement, and vendor risk management
- Interfaces with legal, engineering, product management, security/compliance, and open-source program office (OSPO) or equivalent

Scope:
- Patent FTO assessments and infringement reviews for features, processes, and designs
- Copyright provenance and license compliance for software, UI assets, documentation, and multimedia
- OSS compliance (license identification, compatibility, obligations, notices) and upstream community considerations
- Ongoing monitoring and re-reviews for design changes, new geographies, and third-party updates

Note: This is a business process and not legal advice; legal counsel should provide formal legal opinions and litigation strategy.

## Key Activities
- Intake and scoping: identify features, jurisdictions, distribution models, and third-party components
- IP landscape and prior art search; patent claim mapping and FTO analysis
- Copyright provenance review and license compliance assessment
- OSS SBOM creation/validation; automated scanning and manual audit
- Risk assessment and classification (likelihood, impact, jurisdiction)
- Mitigation planning (design-around, licensing, alternative components, usage restrictions)
- Review and approvals tied to stage gates/release readiness
- Documentation creation (FTO reports, claim charts, notices, OSS attributions)
- Monitoring and re-review triggers management
- Training and continuous improvement based on findings

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Product concept and requirements; architecture and design docs
- Feature list by release; target markets (countries/regions)
- Distribution and deployment model (cloud/SaaS, on-prem, embedded, mobile app stores)
- Source code access; initial SBOM (including transitive dependencies)
- List of third-party assets: SDKs, APIs, libraries, models, datasets, fonts, images, audio/video, documentation
- Vendor contracts and license terms; OSS license inventory
- Known standards/SEPs (standard-essential patents) implicated by features
- Prior internal FTO analyses and IP strategy documents

Prerequisites:
- IP/OSS policies and guidelines published and trained
- Approved tools for code scanning, SBOM generation, and patent search
- Defined jurisdictional scope and intended release date(s)
- Stage-gate criteria established (e.g., FTO review required at design freeze and before GA)

Dependencies on other processes:
- 2.1.3.1 Identify and register IP assets (coordination with patent filing strategy)
- 2.1.2 Product development stage-gate governance
- Vendor management and procurement (contract/license intake and negotiation)
- Secure development lifecycle and CI/CD governance (gates for OSS compliance)
- Records management and audit readiness

## Process Steps
1) Trigger and Intake
- Triggers: new feature or major design change; addition of third-party components; target market expansion; pre-release gate; M&A/IP acquisition; customer diligence request
- Create review ticket; define scope, timeline, and jurisdictions
- Assign IP counsel and OSS compliance lead

2) Collect and Normalize Artifacts
- Gather architecture diagrams, feature specs, user flows, and distribution model
- Export/assemble SBOM (format: SPDX or CycloneDX) including versions and licenses
- List all third-party assets (code and non-code) and their provenance
- Capture vendor licenses and restrictions (usage, territory, sublicensing, attribution)

3) Automated Scanning and Initial Screening
- Run code scanning for license detection and policy violations
- Identify copyleft and strong reciprocity risks (e.g., GPL, AGPL, SSPL)
- Flag cryptography, codecs, media, fonts, and content for special review
- Generate initial OSS compliance report and alert on incompatible licenses

4) Patent Landscape and Search Strategy
- Define keywords, CPC/IPC classes, and competitors
- Search global databases (USPTO, EPO, WIPO) and paid tools for relevant patents/applications
- Include standard-essential patents if applicable; note FRAND commitments
- Document search methodology for reproducibility

5) FTO and Claim Charting
- Shortlist patents by relevance and status (granted, pending) in target jurisdictions
- Create claim charts mapping product features/process steps to patent claim elements
- Evaluate literal and doctrine-of-equivalents exposure; assess non-infringement arguments
- Consider design-around possibilities and feasibility

6) Copyright and Provenance Review
- Verify ownership of internal code and assets; confirm contributor agreements
- Check third-party content licenses (code, UI/UX, fonts, icons, media, datasets)
- Validate license obligations (attribution, source offer, copyleft triggers, share-alike)
- Assess AI-generated code/content provenance and license implications; ensure policy compliance for code suggestions and training data claims

7) OSS License Compatibility and Obligations
- Review license compatibility matrix relative to distribution model (e.g., SaaS vs. on-prem)
- Determine downstream obligations (NOTICE files, license texts, copyright headers)
- For copyleft components, enforce separation strategies (process isolation, network APIs, no static linking if required) or choose alternatives
- Plan fulfillment: source code offers, published modifications, attribution pages

8) Risk Assessment and Classification
- Score risks by likelihood and impact (litigation probability, injunction risk, revenue exposure, remediation cost)
- Tag by geography and release
- Identify SEP exposure and FRAND licensing needs
- Decide mitigation path: design change, remove/replace component, seek license, usage restrictions, proceed with documented risk acceptance

9) Mitigation Execution
- Implement design-arounds; replace components; adjust usage or architecture
- Negotiate licenses (patent, content, or OSS exceptions) and update contracts
- Update SBOM and codebase; add compliance artifacts (NOTICE, LICENSES)
- Validate changes via rescans and updated claim charts as needed

10) Review, Decision, and Approvals
- Present findings to product leadership and legal: FTO summary, claim charts, compliance report, mitigation plan, residual risks
- Approvals: Legal/IP Counsel approves FTO posture; OSS Compliance approves license compliance; Product/Engineering approve execution feasibility and timelines
- Gate outcomes: approve, approve with conditions, defer, or block release

11) Documentation and Records
- Archive FTO report, claim charts, search logs, OSS compliance report, SBOM, licenses, approvals, and exceptions in the IP repository
- Update risk register and compliance obligations register
- Generate customer-facing third-party notices package if required

12) Monitoring and Re-Review
- Establish monitoring for competitor patents, continuation filings, and OSS license changes
- Set re-review triggers: code changes to core features, dependency updates, new geographies, material license updates, major releases
- Track and meet takedown requests or infringement notices; execute notice-and-takedown procedures promptly

13) Feedback and Training
- Feed recurring issues into training curriculum and coding guidelines
- Update policy and tooling based on post-mortems and audit findings

## Outputs and Deliverables
- FTO report (by jurisdiction) with search methodology and conclusions
- Patent claim charts and design-around analyses
- OSS compliance report and attestation for the release
- SBOM (SPDX/CycloneDX) and third-party notices package (NOTICE.txt, licenses directory, attribution page)
- Risk register entries with ratings and mitigation status
- Approvals and exceptions/waivers with expiry dates and conditions
- Updated contracts or license addenda if applicable
- Release gate decision record

Success criteria:
- No release proceeds without documented FTO posture and OSS compliance
- All mandatory obligations (attribution, source offers) are fulfilled prior to distribution
- Residual risks formally accepted at appropriate authority levels
- Records are audit-ready and easily retrievable

## Roles and Responsibilities
- IP Counsel (Internal)
  - Lead FTO analysis; review patent searches and claim charts
  - Advise on infringement risk, SEP/FRAND issues, and licensing strategies
  - Approve legal posture and residual risk acceptance thresholds
- External IP Counsel (as needed)
  - Provide formal opinions; support complex jurisdictions and litigation-sensitive matters
- OSS Compliance Lead / OSPO
  - Own OSS policy, scanning, license compatibility, notices, and SBOM integrity
  - Approve OSS usage and exceptions; manage upstream engagement policies (CLA/DCO)
- Product Manager
  - Provide scope, target markets, and release plans; ensure stage-gate adherence
  - Prioritize mitigations in roadmap
- Engineering Lead / Architect
  - Supply design and code artifacts; execute design-arounds and component changes
  - Ensure CI/CD gates enforce compliance checks
- Procurement/Vendor Management
  - Source and negotiate third-party licenses; maintain contracts and usage rights
- Build/Release Manager
  - Integrate scans into pipelines; package compliance artifacts into builds
- Security/Compliance
  - Align with broader compliance frameworks and audit requirements
- Community/Developer Relations (if contributing upstream)
  - Ensure compliance with community governance, CLAs/DCO, and responsible disclosure
- PMO/Stage-Gate Governance
  - Enforce gates and ensure documentation completeness

## Best Practices
- Shift-left IP reviews: initiate at concept and architecture phases; update at design freeze and pre-GA
- Maintain a single source of truth for SBOMs; automate generation on every build
- Use both automated scanning and manual review for high-risk components/features
- Standardize claim chart templates, risk rating scales, and approval checklists
- Pre-approve a curated component catalog with vetted licenses and versions
- Define clear policies for copyleft, AGPL/SaaS, SSPL, and CLA/DCO requirements
- Separate proprietary code from copyleft code (process, network isolation, or plugin architectures) where needed
- Track SEPs relevant to adopted standards; plan FRAND negotiations early
- Establish re-review triggers and expiry dates for exceptions
- Train developers regularly on IP hygiene, license basics, and attribution practices
- Keep thorough, time-stamped records to support audits and customer diligence

## Common Challenges
- Incomplete or inaccurate SBOMs (transitive dependencies missed)
  - Solution: enforce dependency lockfiles, CI SBOM generation, and periodic manual audits
- License incompatibilities discovered late in the cycle
  - Solution: CI gates on pull requests; curated component catalog; early OSS review
- Ambiguous patent claims or evolving continuation filings
  - Solution: ongoing monitoring; seek external opinions; conservative design choices
- Global differences in IP law and enforcement
  - Solution: jurisdiction-specific review; prioritize high-risk markets; local counsel
- Copyleft obligations conflicting with business model
  - Solution: architectural isolation, alternative components, or dual licensing arrangements
- Third-party vendor license restrictions not aligned with product use
  - Solution: involve procurement early; negotiate rights; consider alternative vendors
- AI-generated code/content provenance uncertainty
  - Solution: approved tooling, logging of prompts/suggestions, mandatory code review and license verification
- Time pressure and resource constraints
  - Solution: risk tiering, SLAs, reusable playbooks, and dedicated review sprints

## Performance Metrics
- FTO review cycle time (median days) by risk tier and release phase
- Percentage of releases with complete SBOM and OSS notices at GA
- Number and severity of potential infringements identified per release
- Percentage of risks mitigated pre-GA vs. accepted with conditions
- Post-release IP incidents (infringement claims, takedowns) per quarter
- Rework rate due to IP issues after design freeze
- OSS policy violations caught pre-merge vs. post-merge
- Accuracy of SBOMs (variance between scan and manual audit)
- Time to resolve infringement notices or takedown requests
- Training coverage: % of engineers completing IP/OSS training within period

Targets should be set by product risk tier (e.g., critical features, regulated markets).

## Technology and Tools
Patent and prior art search:
- Public: USPTO, EPO Espacenet, WIPO PATENTSCOPE, Google Patents
- Commercial: Derwent Innovation, Questel Orbit, PatSnap, LexisNexis TotalPatent One
- Claim charting and analytics: internal templates; analytics features in above tools

OSS and license compliance:
- Scanners: Synopsys Black Duck, Mend (WhiteSource), Snyk Open Source, FOSSA, FOSSology
- SBOM: SPDX/CycloneDX tooling; Syft, Anchore; CI integrations for SBOM attestation
- Policy enforcement: CI/CD plugins, pre-commit hooks, repository scanning (e.g., GitHub Advanced Security, GitLab)

Build and release:
- CI/CD: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps
- Package managers: npm/yarn, Maven/Gradle, pip/poetry, Cargo; configured with internal registries and approved lists

Records and workflow:
- Issue tracking: Jira/Azure Boards
- Document and records management: Confluence, SharePoint, iManage
- Contract lifecycle management: Icertis, Agiloft
- IP docketing: Anaqua, CPA Global/Clarivate

Monitoring and notices:
- Patent watch services; alerts from PTOs and vendor tools
- Takedown management workflows and contact points documented (DMCA, platform-specific)

# [2.1.3.3] Determine Patent and Copyright Needs

## Overview
This process evaluates whether new or changed products, services, technologies, content, and software require patent or copyright protection, and if so, what kind, where, and when. It ensures the organization:
- Protects valuable intellectual assets and competitive advantage
- Minimizes IP risk (e.g., loss of rights due to premature disclosure, infringement claims)
- Aligns IP investments with business strategy, market timing, and budgets
- Prepares clear decisions and handoffs to the downstream process “Manage copyrights and patents [11062]” for execution (e.g., filings, registrations, licensing)

It operates closely with innovation, R&D, product management, engineering, marketing, and legal teams within the overall product/service development program.

## Key Activities
- Intake and triage of potential IP (invention disclosures, creative works, software/code, documentation)
- Asset classification (patent candidate, copyright work, trade secret, defensive publication, open source contribution)
- Patentability and novelty assessment, including targeted prior art search
- Preliminary freedom-to-operate (FTO) risk scan to flag blocking third-party rights
- Business and strategic value assessment (market potential, detectability, lifecycle, competitiveness)
- Protection-path decisioning (patent vs trade secret vs copyright vs defensive publication vs open source)
- Jurisdiction and timing strategy (where to protect, filing/registration deadlines, public disclosure control)
- Budgeting and prioritization
- Approvals and handoff to filing/registration execution
- Documentation, docketing, and periodic re-evaluation

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Invention Disclosure Forms (IDFs), technical specs, prototypes, lab notebooks, architecture/design docs
  - Source code repositories and commit history; BOMs and SBOMs
  - Marketing and UI/UX assets; manuals, training materials, multimedia; website/app content
  - Product roadmap, release timelines, go-to-market plans
  - Competitive intelligence; standards participation details
  - Contractual obligations: NDAs, employee IP assignment, contractor/work-for-hire, joint development, grant/funding terms
  - Prior IP: existing patents/applications, copyrights, trade secrets

- Prerequisites:
  - Approved IP policy and decision criteria (patent, trade secret, copyright, open source)
  - Publication/release control policy and review gates
  - NDAs and IP assignment agreements in place for staff and contributors
  - Access to IP search tools and an IP management system (IPMS/docketing)
  - Defined approval authority and budget guardrails

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Innovation management and invention harvesting
  - Manage patents and copyrights [11062] (for execution of filings/registrations and ongoing management)
  - Open source governance/compliance
  - Vendor and partner management (IP terms)
  - Regulatory and export control review (where applicable)
  - Product development stage-gates and risk management

## Process Steps
1. Trigger and intake
   - Triggered by invention disclosure, code completion milestone, design freeze, new marketing content, or planned external disclosure (publication, conference, press).
   - Log item in IPMS; assign unique ID and preliminary classification.

2. Assemble evaluation team
   - IP counsel/agent (lead), inventor/author, product manager, engineering lead, OSS/compliance, and portfolio manager. Include marketing for content/UI assets.

3. Asset classification and scoping
   - Identify asset type(s): technology feature, algorithm, hardware design, UI, code, content, data selection/arrangement.
   - Define scope and key dates (conception/prototype, first public disclosure risk, release target).

4. Evidence collection
   - Gather enabling documentation (diagrams, test results, code diffs), inventorship/author lists, contractual encumbrances, and related prior filings.

5. Novelty and patentability triage
   - Quick assessment of novelty, non-obviousness, and utility; outline potential claimable features.
   - Identify any prior public disclosures within the team/company.

6. Prior art search (targeted)
   - Conduct structured searches using patent and non-patent literature; summarize top references.
   - Capture search queries and findings in IPMS.

7. Preliminary FTO scan
   - Identify high-risk third-party patents relevant to planned product claims; document potential blockers for escalation.

8. Business value and strategy assessment
   - Score each asset on:
     - Business impact/revenue enablement
     - Detectability/enforceability (can infringement be proven?)
     - Reverse engineering risk; longevity vs product lifecycle
     - Competitive differentiation; standard-essential potential
     - Geographic market importance and competitors’ footprint
     - Cost-to-protect and maintenance obligations
   - Map to portfolio strategy (offense, defense, cross-licensing, deterrence).

9. Protection path decision
   - Patent: If novel, valuable, enforceable, and time-sensitive.
   - Trade secret: If secrecy is maintainable, long-lived, and hard to reverse engineer.
   - Copyright: For software code, UI, documentation, multimedia, databases (selection/arrangement); determine if registration is warranted in key jurisdictions.
   - Defensive publication: When preventing others from patenting is beneficial but patenting is not.
   - Open source contribution: If strategic and compliant with license obligations; define scope and license.

10. Jurisdiction and timing strategy
    - Select jurisdictions based on market, manufacturing, enforcement likelihood, and budget (e.g., provisional/priority filing, PCT, national phases).
    - Set deadlines: priority date, 12-month Paris window, public disclosure control, marketing release gates.

11. Budgeting and prioritization
    - Estimate near-term and lifecycle costs; rank items vs budget and portfolio targets.
    - Decide defer, accelerate, or stage (e.g., provisional now, full later).

12. Approvals
    - Route decision package to approval authority (e.g., IP Steering Committee, General Counsel, BU leader).
    - Capture approvals and conditions in IPMS.

13. Interim protections and compliance
    - Implement NDAs, access controls, trade secret protocols; apply copyright notices and version control.
    - Hold or sequence external disclosures until filings/registrations complete.
    - Address OSS license obligations; remediate conflicts before release.

14. Handoff to Manage copyrights and patents [11062]
    - Provide complete dossier: claims/feature list, drawings, inventors, prior art, jurisdiction/timing plan, budgets, approvals, and counsel assignments.

15. Recordkeeping and docketing
    - Update IPMS with decisions, deadlines, and ownership/assignment records; link to product SKUs/releases.

16. Review and revisit
    - Reassess at major milestones (beta, GA, feature pivots, market changes) and after competitor intelligence updates.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- IP assessment report per asset (findings, searches, FTO flags, business rationale)
- Decision log and approved protection strategy (patent/trade secret/copyright/defensive/open source)
- Jurisdiction and timing plan with docketed deadlines
- Budget estimates and prioritization list
- Handoff package to filing/registration execution
- Interim protection measures implemented (NDAs, access controls, notices)
- Updated risk register entries (e.g., potential infringement, disclosure risks)

Success criteria:
- Decisions made before any public disclosure that could forfeit rights
- Alignment with business strategy and portfolio objectives
- No preventable loss of rights; reduction of infringement risk
- On-time handoff with complete, high-quality dossiers
- Adherence to budget and prioritization guidelines

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Inventor/Engineer/Author: Submit disclosures; provide technical detail and enablement; validate accuracy; identify contributors/inventors/authors.
- Product Manager: Articulate business value, market timing, and roadmap dependencies; coordinate release gates.
- IP Counsel/Patent Agent (Lead): Guide assessment; conduct patentability analysis; supervise searches; recommend strategy; manage approvals and handoff.
- Copyright/IP Specialist: Determine copyrightability and registration needs; ensure notices; address ownership/assignments and work-for-hire issues.
- OSS Compliance Officer: Scan codebases; assess license implications; approve/reject open source use or contributions.
- Portfolio Manager/Head of IP: Ensure alignment to portfolio strategy; budget oversight; prioritization.
- Engineering Lead/Architect: Clarify implementation details; assess reverse engineering and detectability.
- Marketing/Communications: Manage publication plans; route materials through IP review before external release.
- Finance/PMO: Validate budgets; track costs; enforce gating in project plans.
- Outside Counsel (as needed): Deep prior art/FTO, complex jurisdictional advice, drafting input post-decision.
- Compliance/Regulatory/Export Control (as needed): Flag standards, export, or regulated tech constraints.

## Best Practices
- Engage early: Tie IP intake to design reviews and sprint milestones; don’t wait for release.
- Enforce publication gates: No external disclosures before IP review; maintain conference/press review workflows.
- Use a decision matrix: Standard criteria for patent vs trade secret vs copyright vs defensive publication.
- Right-size searches: Quick triage first; escalate to comprehensive searches for top candidates.
- Focus on enforceability: Prioritize inventions that can be detected in the market and proven in evidence.
- Maintain rigorous documentation: Lab notebooks, code history, contributor records, and dates.
- Determine inventorship/authorship carefully: Follow legal standards; resolve disputes early.
- Trade secret hygiene: Access controls, need-to-know, encryption, and training for designated secrets.
- OSS governance: Continuous scanning in CI/CD; SBOMs; approved license list; contribution review board.
- Portfolio alignment: Balance offensive, defensive, and cross-licensing goals; prune low-value assets.
- Leverage defensive publications: Use when deterrence is desired without prosecution costs.
- Educate teams: Ongoing training on IP basics and disclosure timing risks.
- Docket discipline: Track all key dates; set reminders well ahead of deadlines.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Premature public disclosure
  - Solution: Mandatory IP review gate; training; integrate with marketing/PR and academic collaborations.
- Weak invention quality or insufficient enablement
  - Solution: Invention harvesting workshops; coaching; require enabling documentation before approval.
- Budget constraints
  - Solution: Prioritization framework; stage filings (provisional/PCT); focus on high-detectability, high-value features.
- Inventorship/authorship disputes
  - Solution: Clear criteria and neutral review by IP counsel; maintain contemporaneous contribution records.
- Infringement risks discovered late
  - Solution: Earlier FTO scanning; integrate with design decisions; mitigation plans (design-around, licensing).
- Open source license conflicts
  - Solution: Automated scanning; pre-approved component lists; legal review for copyleft; contributor license agreements for inbound contributions.
- Jurisdiction complexity and maintenance burdens
  - Solution: Tiered country strategy linked to revenue/competition; periodic pruning.
- Partner and contractor IP ownership gaps
  - Solution: Standard IP terms and assignments; verify before engagement; audit deliverables for rights.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs)
- Cycle time: Average days from intake to decision
- On-time rate: Percent decided before public disclosure/release gate
- Coverage: Percent of strategic features with defined IP protection path
- Conversion: Percent of assessed patent candidates approved for filing
- Cost per decision and cost adherence vs budget
- Prior art/FTO hit rate and mitigation lead time
- Public disclosure incidents (count/trend)
- OSS compliance incidents and mean time to remediate
- Portfolio alignment score (share of assets meeting strategy criteria)
- Stakeholder satisfaction (inventor and product team feedback)
- Backlog health (age and volume of undecided disclosures)

## Technology and Tools
- IP Management System (IPMS) and docketing: Anaqua, CPA Global/Clarivate, Dennemeyer, PatSnap
- Patent search and analytics: Derwent Innovation, PatSeer, Orbit, Google Patents, Lens.org
- Prior art and literature databases: IEEE, ACM, arXiv, Standards databases
- FTO/risk tools and legal analytics: Unified Patents, Lex Machina, litigation databases
- OSS scanning/compliance: Black Duck, Snyk, FOSSA, WhiteSource, OSLC; SBOM generators (CycloneDX, SPDX)
- Document and evidence management: Confluence/SharePoint, ELNs (Benchling, LabArchives), secure repositories
- Source control and CI/CD: GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket with integrated scanning and approval gates
- Workflow and approvals: Jira/ServiceNow/Asana; e-signature (DocuSign, Adobe Sign)
- Competitive intelligence and patent landscaping: PatSnap, Questel, Innography
- Budget and portfolio dashboards: BI tools (Power BI, Tableau) integrated with IPMS

Process Details:
## Overview
Eliminate Quality and Reliability Problems is the closed-loop process of identifying, analyzing, prioritizing, and removing defects, failure modes, and sources of variability from a prototype so that it meets defined quality and reliability targets before broader validation and market launch. It sits within Design and Prototype Products and Services and ensures the prototype can withstand expected usage, environments, and lifecycle demands.

Purpose:
- Protect customer experience by ensuring the product/service remains usable, safe, and consistent over its intended lifetime.
- Achieve compliance with internal standards and external regulations.
- Reduce cost of poor quality (rework, scrap, returns, warranty) and accelerate reliability growth before scaling.

Role in the organization:
- Provides the bridge between early design intent and validation readiness.
- Feeds back learnings into requirements, design standards, test plans, and supplier/process controls.
- Enables go/no-go decisions for design gates by demonstrating issue closure and reliability maturity.

## Key Activities
- Aggregate and triage issues: Collect defects, failures, and reliability risks from tests, simulations, reviews, and field analogs. Prioritize using risk metrics (e.g., RPN, severity x occurrence x detectability).
- Root cause analysis (RCA): Use structured methods (5 Whys, Ishikawa, Fault Tree, 8D) to find systemic causes.
- Corrective and preventive actions (CAPA): Define, implement, and validate design, process, software, supplier, or documentation changes that remove causes and prevent recurrence.
- Reliability engineering and growth: Model reliability, allocate targets, plan and execute reliability growth activities (e.g., HALT, ALT, ESS), and track improvements.
- Design optimization: Apply design-for-reliability (DfR), derating, tolerancing, robust design (DOE/Taguchi), and error-proofing to eliminate failure modes.
- Verification and regression testing: Re-test fixes under normal, edge, and accelerated conditions; ensure no regressions.
- Configuration and change control: Manage engineering change orders (ECOs), versioning, and traceability via PLM/ALM.
- Update risk and quality artifacts: Maintain DFMEA/PFMEA/SFMEA, FRACAS logs, test plans (DVP&R), control plans, and standards.
- Readiness and gate reviews: Demonstrate closure of high-risk items against acceptance criteria; decide on next prototype build or validation.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Prototype(s), service blueprint/process maps, and supporting materials (BOM/BOP, drawings, code, runbooks).
- Quality and reliability targets (e.g., MTBF/MTTF, DPPM, uptime/SLA, safety margins, standards).
- Test results: Verification, environmental, stress, reliability, usability, and performance data.
- Issue/defect backlog and FRACAS entries with evidence (logs, traces, photos, telemetry).
- Risk analyses: DFMEA/PFMEA/SFMEA, hazard analyses, fault trees, RBDs.
- Applicable regulations/standards (e.g., ISO 9001, IATF 16949, ISO 13485, IEC 61508, ISO/IEC 25010, Telcordia SR-332, MIL-HDBK-217).

Prerequisites:
- Baseline design and prototype build complete and controlled in PLM/ALM.
- Defined acceptance criteria and reliability growth plan.
- Test environments, fixtures, and monitoring in place; data capture calibrated.
- Cross-functional team (design, test, quality, reliability, manufacturing/service, supplier quality, compliance) mobilized.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Upstream: Define quality/reliability requirements, risk assessment, initial design and prototyping, defect identification.
- Parallel: Supplier qualification, manufacturing process development, service design.
- Downstream: Prototype validation, pilot build, launch readiness, warranty planning.

## Process Steps
1. Plan and mobilize
   - Confirm scope, targets, gate criteria, and risk priorities.
   - Establish cross-functional Problem Elimination Team with a cadence, RACI, and toolchain (FRACAS, PLM/ALM).
   - Freeze a configuration baseline for analysis; define containment vs permanent corrective action strategy.

2. Aggregate and triage issues
   - Ingest issues from tests, simulations, inspections, code analysis, telemetry, and supplier feedback.
   - Normalize data (taxonomy, severity/occurrence/detectability). Remove duplicates and clarify problem statements.
   - Prioritize via risk scoring (e.g., RPN, safety-critical), customer impact, and effort/lead time.

3. Reproduce and characterize failures
   - Establish repeatable test protocols to reproduce issues; capture detailed conditions.
   - Instrument prototypes/services to enhance observability (sensors, logging, tracing, error codes).
   - For services/software: create minimal repro cases, chaos/fault injection, soak tests.

4. Root cause analysis (RCA)
   - Perform structured RCA appropriate to failure type:
     - Mechanical/EE: 5 Whys, Ishikawa, Fault Tree, FEA, DFMEA linkage, teardown, microscopy, EDA simulations, worst-case analysis.
     - Software/Service: incident postmortem (blameless), log/trace analysis, code review, dependency analysis, SFMEA.
   - Validate root cause via experiments or simulation; avoid symptom-level fixes.

5. Define corrective and preventive actions (CAPA)
   - Brainstorm options; use DOE/Taguchi for robust settings; apply derating, tolerance changes, material changes, architectural refactors, error-proofing.
   - Decide permanent corrective action(s) and preventive changes (e.g., inspection/test, design standard updates, supplier controls).
   - Assess impacts (performance, cost, safety, compliance, manufacturability, serviceability); run trade-off analysis.

6. Approve and control changes
   - Raise ECO/ECN with full documentation (problem statement, root cause, alternatives, verification plan).
   - Run change through CCB (change control board) including quality, reliability, safety, compliance, supplier.
   - Update drawings, CAD, code, specifications, requirements, BOM/BOP, control plans, and service documentation.

7. Implement changes and update prototype
   - Build updated prototypes or deploy service changes in controlled environments.
   - For supplier-caused issues: coordinate PPAP/APQP updates and verification at supplier; qualify new components/materials.
   - For processes: update work instructions, fixtures, test programs; train personnel.

8. Verify fixes and regressions
   - Execute targeted verification per DVP&R, plus regression to ensure no new issues.
   - Conduct reliability testing as applicable:
     - HALT/HASS, ESS, ALT/accelerated life, thermal cycling, vibration, humidity, power cycling, EMC.
     - Soak/long-duration stability tests, fuzzing/chaos engineering, failover drills, disaster recovery for services.
   - Analyze results statistically (Weibull, growth models like Duane/AMSAA). Compare to targets.

9. Update risk and quality artifacts
   - Close FRACAS items with evidence. Update DFMEA/PFMEA/SFMEA with new S/O/D ratings and residual risk.
   - Update verification plans, control plans, and monitoring requirements.
   - Create lessons learned and update design standards/checklists.

10. Decide readiness and iterate
    - Review against acceptance criteria (e.g., zero open severity-1 safety issues, RPN thresholds, reliability targets).
    - If not met, re-prioritize remaining issues and iterate steps 3–9.
    - If met, proceed to next gate (validation testing/pilot build) with a documented residual risk and monitoring plan.

11. Post-change monitoring (as applicable)
    - Implement enhanced monitoring/telemetry for early detection of recurrences.
    - Define lead indicators (drift in parametrics, error rates) and triggers for rapid response.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Updated prototype(s) and configurations meeting quality/reliability targets.
- Approved change documentation: ECO/ECN packages, updated designs/specs/BOMs/code, revised service blueprints/runbooks.
- Closed-loop FRACAS and CAPA records with evidence and verification results.
- Updated DFMEA/PFMEA/SFMEA, fault trees, reliability models, and control plans.
- Test plans and reports (DVP&R, reliability test reports, regression results, statistical analyses).
- Lessons learned and updated standards/checklists.
- Go/no-go decision records and residual risk register.

Success criteria:
- All critical/safety issues closed; no open severity-1 items.
- RPNs reduced to threshold; recurrence rate near zero.
- Reliability metrics (e.g., MTBF/MTTF, FIT, uptime/SLA) meet or exceed targets with confidence.
- No significant regressions introduced by changes.
- Compliance requirements satisfied and documented.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product Development Lead: Owns process outcomes; prioritizes scope; facilitates gate decisions.
- Quality Engineer: Manages FRACAS/CAPA; ensures QMS compliance; tracks metrics.
- Reliability Engineer: Defines targets; plans/executes reliability testing and modeling; drives reliability growth.
- Design Engineers (Mechanical/Electrical/Software): Perform RCA; implement design changes; support verification.
- Test/Validation Engineer: Develops and runs tests; ensures reproducibility; manages test data.
- Manufacturing/Process Engineer: Addresses process-induced defects; updates control plans and work instructions.
- Supplier Quality/Procurement: Engages suppliers; manages PPAP/APQP; verifies supplier changes.
- Service Operations/SRE: For services/software—implements reliability fixes, runbooks, observability, incident response improvements.
- Compliance/Regulatory: Reviews changes for standard/regulatory adherence; maintains documentation.
- Project Manager: Schedules, risk manages, tracks progress, escalates constraints.
- Data/Failure Analyst: Builds dashboards; conducts statistical and Weibull analyses; monitors reliability trends.

## Best Practices
- Establish a robust FRACAS for closed-loop issue management with clear taxonomy and evidence standards.
- Use FMEA early and continuously; link issues back to FMEA to update S/O/D and controls.
- Apply Design for Reliability: derating, margin analysis, worst-case/tolerance analysis, RBD/FTA, robust design via DOE.
- Accelerate learning with HALT/ALT and environmental stress screening; test to failure to expose margins.
- Strengthen observability: design-in sensors, logs, traceability, self-diagnostics; for services, centralized logging and distributed tracing.
- Control changes rigorously via PLM/ALM with configuration baselines and CCBs.
- Use reliability growth planning and track via Duane/AMSAA; iterate rapidly with timeboxed sprints.
- Cross-functional reviews including suppliers; integrate APQP/PPAP where applicable.
- Document blameless postmortems; convert lessons into standards and checklists.
- Shift-left: run static analysis, simulation, and unit/integration tests early; conduct DfX reviews before builds.
- Validate at extremes: environmental, usage, and mis-use cases; include variability (component tolerances, operator differences).
- For services: implement chaos engineering, SLOs/SLA management, error budgets, and game days.
- Protect safety first; apply functional safety practices (e.g., ISO 26262/IEC 61508) and independent review for safety-related changes.

## Common Challenges
- Intermittent or non-reproducible failures: Increase instrumentation; run long-duration or stress tests; use design of experiments to isolate factors; collect richer telemetry.
- Schedule and cost pressure: Use risk-based prioritization; focus on severity- and occurrence-heavy issues; employ reliability growth curves to justify iterations.
- Inadequate data for reliability estimation: Use accelerated testing; pool prior data; apply Bayesian methods; expand sample sizes incrementally.
- Supplier-related defects: Tighten incoming inspection; engage suppliers with joint RCA; update specifications; require PPAP re-approval.
- Regression introduction: Implement strong regression suites; automated testing; configuration baselines; staged rollouts/canary for software.
- Complex interactions/hidden couplings: Use system-level FTA/RBD and DOE; perform interface reviews and architectural simplification.
- Change fatigue and poor traceability: Enforce ECO discipline; maintain a single source of truth in PLM/ALM; regular configuration audits.
- Service variability (people/process): Standardize work; error-proof processes; training; service FMEA; monitor adherence.
- Conflicting requirements (cost, performance, reliability): Apply trade-off analysis and value engineering; align on CTQs and customer value.

## Performance Metrics
- Issue metrics: Count open/closed by severity; FRACAS cycle time; average/median time-to-close; recurrence rate; regression rate.
- Risk reduction: RPN reduction; number/percent of high-risk failure modes mitigated; residual risk index.
- Reliability metrics: MTBF/MTTF/FIT vs targets; reliability growth slope (Duane/AMSAA); Weibull beta/eta changes; uptime/SLA adherence; mean time to recovery (MTTR) for services.
- Test coverage: Percent of critical functions covered by stress/reliability tests; pass rates; environmental envelope coverage.
- Quality cost: Estimated reduction in warranty/return costs; scrap/rework on prototypes; cost of non-quality avoided.
- Process health: On-time completion to gate; CAPA effectiveness (no-repeat rate after 3 months/3 cycles); percent changes with full traceability.

## Technology and Tools
- PLM/ALM and change control: PTC Windchill, Siemens Teamcenter, Dassault ENOVIA, Jira/Azure DevOps/Git for software.
- FRACAS/CAPA/QMS: EtQ, TrackWise, Arena QMS, Greenlight Guru, custom FRACAS in Jira/ServiceNow; ISO 9001-compliant workflows.
- Reliability engineering: ReliaSoft Weibull++/BlockSim, Minitab, JMP, R/Python for statistical analysis; RAM Command; FTA tools.
- Simulation and analysis: FEA (ANSYS, Abaqus), CFD, SPICE, thermal analysis, worst-case circuit analysis tools, model-based systems engineering (MBSE) tools.
- Test systems: Environmental chambers, vibration/shock tables, power cycling rigs, burn-in, EMC test equipment; automated test frameworks.
- Observability and monitoring: For services/software—Prometheus/Grafana, ELK/Opensearch, Splunk, OpenTelemetry; chaos tools (Gremlin, Litmus).
- Code and quality tools: Static/dynamic analysis (SonarQube, Coverity), fuzzers, unit/integration test frameworks, performance profilers.
- Supplier quality: APQP/PPAP documentation systems, incoming inspection SPC, measurement systems analysis (MSA) tools.
- Collaboration and knowledge: Confluence, SharePoint, design standards repositories, lessons-learned databases.
