Process Details:
## Overview
Collaborate demand with customers is the structured, recurring process of jointly creating and maintaining a demand signal with customers (e.g., retailers, distributors, B2B clients) to improve forecast accuracy, service levels, and inventory efficiency. It translates market and customer intelligence—such as point-of-sale (POS) data, promotion calendars, inventory positions, and pipeline—into a consensus demand plan at the product-location-time level. This process is a core component of demand management within supply chain planning and typically operates within CPFR (Collaborative Planning, Forecasting, and Replenishment), Joint Business Planning (JBP), or VMI (Vendor-Managed Inventory) frameworks.

Its purpose is to:
- Reduce forecast error and bias by incorporating customer insights and causal factors.
- Improve service (OTIF/OSA), reduce stockouts and excess, and stabilize supply planning.
- Align commercial plans (pricing, trade, promotions) with operational plans (capacity, inventory, logistics).
- Create a single, governed demand signal that feeds S&OP/IBP, MPS, procurement, and logistics.

## Key Activities
- Customer segmentation for collaboration (strategic vs. standard accounts; CPFR/VMI/JBP tiers).
- Governance and data-sharing setup (NDAs, SLAs, calendars, decision rights).
- Data integration and validation (POS, orders, inventory, promotions, returns, digital signals).
- Baseline forecast preparation and versioning.
- Exception identification and root-cause analysis (variance vs. baseline/last plan/targets).
- Joint demand review sessions and scenario planning (price/promo, cannibalization, substitution).
- Consensus demand creation and approval (frozen/time-fenced windows).
- Publication of the collaborative forecast and integration into planning systems.
- Continuous monitoring, performance measurement, and improvement loops.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Historical shipments and baseline statistical forecast (from Manage demand for products).
- Customer-provided data: POS sales by SKU/location, on-hand/on-order inventory, open orders/backlog, returns, planograms, store/DC changes.
- Commercial plans: promotions/trade events, pricing, new product introductions (NPI), end-of-life (EOL), account targets.
- External/market signals: holidays, macroeconomic indicators, competitive events.
- Master data: product hierarchies (SKU/GTIN), customer/location hierarchies (ship-to/store/DC), units of measure, calendars (ISO week), lead times.

Prerequisites:
- Data sharing agreements and governance (NDA, usage, privacy).
- Technical connectivity (EDI, API, portal access) and data quality thresholds.
- Aligned master data and calendars between parties.
- Defined collaboration cadence, meeting routines, and escalation paths.
- Role assignments with decision rights and RACI.
- Documented metrics and targets (MAPE/WAPE, bias, service).

Dependencies on other processes:
- 4.1.2 Manage demand for products: Provides baseline forecast, receives collaborative updates, performs accuracy analysis.
- S&OP/IBP: Consumes consensus demand; provides constraint feedback and scenario guidance.
- 4.1 Plan and align supply chain resources: Aligns capacity and inventory strategies to demand.
- 4.2 Procure materials and services, 4.3 Manage logistics: Use demand signal for sourcing, replenishment, and transportation planning.
- Trade marketing/pricing: Supplies promotion plans and price changes; receives forecasted uplift feedback.

## Process Steps
1. Define collaboration scope and segmentation
   - Identify target customers and channels by revenue/variability/strategic importance.
   - Select collaboration model per tier (CPFR, VMI, portal-based review).
   - Set horizons and time buckets (e.g., weekly 0–13 weeks, monthly 3–18 months).

2. Establish governance and agreements
   - Execute NDAs, data usage, and confidentiality terms.
   - Define roles, decision rights (who approves final consensus), KPIs, and SLAs (e.g., data delivery by Day -2, exception closure within 2 business days).
   - Build a collaboration calendar (data cut date, exception review, consensus meeting, forecast publish).

3. Set up connectivity and master data alignment
   - Implement EDI/API/portal integrations (e.g., EDI 852 POS, 867 product transfer/sales, 846 inventory, 830 planning schedule).
   - Align SKU and customer hierarchies; standardize UoM and pack sizes; map locations to DCs.
   - Validate calendars and time zones; set conversion rules (eaches, cases, pallets).

4. Prepare the baseline and data ingestion
   - Generate baseline statistical forecast at agreed granularity.
   - Ingest customer data (POS, on-hand/on-order, promo plans, open POs).
   - Apply automated data quality checks (completeness, duplication, spikes, latency).

5. Reconcile and cleanse data
   - Resolve anomalies with customers (e.g., POS gaps, phantom inventory).
   - Normalize promotions and price events (event library, uplift factors).
   - Align sell-in vs sell-out with lead-time offsets; reconcile shipments vs POS.

6. Identify exceptions and drivers
   - Run exception rules: variance thresholds (e.g., >20% vs baseline), OSA dips, weeks-of-supply outliers.
   - Classify drivers: price changes, display features, cannibalization, distribution gains/losses, seasonality.
   - Prepare exception list and analytics for joint review.

7. Conduct joint demand review
   - Review exceptions, proposed uplifts/deltas, and causal assumptions.
   - Share scenario simulations (e.g., promo depth x duration, price elasticity, cross-elasticities).
   - Agree on NPI launch curves, pipeline seeding, and exit plans for EOL.

8. Form consensus demand
   - Lock short-term frozen window (e.g., weeks 1–4) where changes require escalation.
   - Approve consensus forecast for medium/long term; capture version and timestamp.
   - Document assumptions and rationale for auditability.

9. Publish and integrate
   - Publish consensus forecast to demand planning system and downstream (S&OP, MPS, replenishment).
   - For VMI: generate planned orders and replenishment recommendations per customer/DC.
   - Notify stakeholders; update allocation plans if supply is constrained.

10. Monitor execution and exceptions
   - Track POS vs forecast, shipment adherence, OSA, and weeks-of-supply.
   - Trigger alerts for deviations beyond thresholds; collaborate on corrective actions (pull-in/push-out, substitution, safety stock adjustments).

11. Performance review and continuous improvement
   - Monthly/quarterly scorecards by customer/SKU: MAPE, bias, FVA, promo uplift accuracy.
   - Post-event reviews for promotions and NPIs; update uplift libraries and parameters.
   - Review and refine collaboration tiers, SLAs, and process cadence.

12. Governance and compliance
   - Maintain change logs, meeting minutes, and approvals.
   - Ensure data privacy/security and retention policies are followed.
   - Conduct periodic audits of assumptions and overrides.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Consensus demand plan by SKU-customer/location-time horizon with version control.
- Locked/frozen demand windows and exception list with closure status.
- Assumptions and drivers file (events, elasticities, distribution changes).
- Customer-specific replenishment plans (for VMI/CPFR), capacity reservations/allocation guidance.
- Collaboration scorecards and post-event analyses.
- Meeting minutes and action trackers.

Deliverables produced:
- Published demand signal integrated into planning systems.
- Data quality and reconciliation reports.
- Scenario analyses and what-if results for key events.

Success criteria:
- Improved forecast accuracy and reduced bias versus baseline.
- Higher OTIF/OSA for collaborating customers.
- Reduced inventory (DOS), fewer stockouts and obsolescence.
- Timely adherence to collaboration calendar and SLA closure rates.
- Positive customer satisfaction/NPS and increased revenue reliability.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Demand Planning Lead: Owns process, prepares baseline, runs exceptions, consolidates consensus, publishes signal.
- Customer Collaboration Manager/CPFR Analyst: Manages day-to-day collaboration, data exchanges, joint reviews, and scorecards.
- Key Account Manager/Sales: Provides commercial plans, negotiates event details, aligns with customer; validates assumptions.
- Trade/Shopper Marketing: Supplies promotion calendar and expected uplift; conducts post-event analysis.
- Supply Planner/S&OP Leader: Communicates constraints, evaluates feasibility, aligns capacity and inventory; arbitrates trade-offs.
- Data Engineering/IT Integration: Builds and maintains EDI/API/portal data flows; ensures data quality and master data alignment.
- Category/Channel Management: Shares market insights, assortment changes, and planogram impacts.
- Finance: Aligns demand with revenue targets; tracks forecast value add and impacts on working capital.
- Legal/Compliance: Oversees data sharing agreements, privacy, and audit requirements.
- Customer Roles (e.g., Retail Replenishment Planner, Buyer): Provides data and event plans; participates in joint reviews and commits to consensus.

## Best Practices
- Collaborate where it matters: tier strategic/high-variance accounts for deeper collaboration; automate the rest.
- Single-number philosophy: one governed demand signal across functions with documented assumptions.
- Standardize data and calendars: GS1 identifiers, ISO weeks, consistent hierarchies, and UoM.
- Exception-driven cadence: focus meetings on variances and high-impact events, not all SKUs.
- Event libraries and elasticity: maintain and refresh uplift and price elasticity models by SKU/channel.
- Frozen windows and guardrails: stabilize near-term plans; require approvals for late changes.
- Transparent scorecards: share accuracy, bias, service, and FVA with customers; align incentives.
- Post-event learning: run promo/NPI retrospectives to refine parameters; avoid repeating poor events.
- Automation first: build pipelines for ingestion, validation, and reconciliation; minimize manual steps.
- Change management and training: onboard stakeholders, publish SOPs, and coach on data interpretation.

## Common Challenges
- Data quality and latency: Incomplete POS, misaligned hierarchies, delayed feeds.
  - Solutions: Data quality checks, master data governance, SLAs, fallback proxies (shipment-to-POS ratios).
- Misaligned calendars and units: Week definitions, pack sizes, store/DC mappings.
  - Solutions: Calendar and UoM harmonization, conversion rules, reference mapping tables.
- Bias and gaming: Overstated demand to secure inventory.
  - Solutions: Bias monitoring, FVA, allocation policies tied to accuracy, governed overrides.
- Promo noise and cannibalization: Hard-to-predict uplift and cross-effects.
  - Solutions: Causal models, event libraries, post-event calibration, assortment cannibalization matrices.
- NPI with little history: Uncertain launch curves.
  - Solutions: Analog modeling, attribute-based forecasting, phased distribution plans.
- Reluctance to share data: Trust and competitive concerns.
  - Solutions: NDAs, role-based access, clear value articulation, start with pilot scope.
- System fragmentation: Multiple tools and manual spreadsheets.
  - Solutions: Integrate to a central demand platform; use APIs; retire shadow systems.
- Capacity constraints overshadow demand: Supply dictates what can ship.
  - Solutions: Early visibility and scenario planning; allocate based on customer priority and accuracy scorecards; communicate constraints.

## Performance Metrics
- Forecast Accuracy: MAPE/WAPE by customer/SKU and horizon; Promo uplift accuracy.
- Forecast Bias: Mean percentage error with bias direction; target within ±5%.
- Forecast Value Add (FVA): Accuracy improvement vs. naive/statistical baseline from collaboration.
- Demand Plan Stability: Week-over-week changes outside frozen window.
- Service Metrics: OTIF to collaborating customers; OSA at shelf; fill rate.
- Inventory Health: Days of supply, stockouts, backorders, and obsolescence for collaborating accounts.
- Data Timeliness and Quality: % feeds on time, completeness, exception closure SLA adherence.
- Collaboration Coverage: % revenue/SKUs under active collaboration; cadence adherence.
- Financial Impact: Revenue plan attainment, waste reduction (for perishables), working capital improvement.

## Technology and Tools
- Demand Planning Platforms: SAP IBP, Kinaxis RapidResponse, Blue Yonder, o9 Solutions, Anaplan.
- CPFR/VMI Portals: Retailer portals or supplier-hosted collaboration hubs.
- Integration and Data Exchange:
  - EDI: 852 (Product Activity/POS), 867 (Product Transfer and Resale), 846 (Inventory), 830 (Planning Schedule), 850/855/856/860 (PO flows).
  - APIs and SFTP for near-real-time POS and inventory.
- Master Data Management: GS1/GTIN, GDSN, product and customer hierarchy tools; data cataloging.
- Analytics and Visualization: Power BI, Tableau, ThoughtSpot; notebooks for elasticity and causal modeling.
- Scenario and Optimization: What-if engines within planning suites; price/promo elasticity models; event libraries.
- Workflow and Collaboration: Teams/Slack for communication; ServiceNow/Jira for exception management and approvals; e-signature for governance.
- Data Platforms: Data lake/warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Azure Synapse) for storage and analytics.
- Security and Compliance: Role-based access control, encryption, audit logs; privacy compliance for any customer data.

# [4.1.2.3] Develop Demand Consensus Forecast

## Overview
Develop Demand Consensus Forecast is the cross-functional process of reconciling the statistical baseline forecast with inputs from Sales, Marketing, Customer/Channel partners, and Finance to produce a single, documented demand plan. The consensus forecast aligns volume, mix, timing, and assumptions across the organization and serves as the demand input to S&OP/IBP, supply planning, procurement, and financial planning.

Purpose:
- Improve forecast accuracy, reduce bias, and enable proactive balancing of demand and supply.
- Create a single-number plan tied to documented assumptions and scenarios.
- Synchronize commercial plans (promotions, launches) with supply and financial objectives.

Role in the organization:
- Acts as the Demand Review in the S&OP/IBP cycle.
- Drives downstream planning (Aggregate and detailed supply plans, capacity, inventory, logistics).
- Provides an auditable, version-controlled forecast for performance management and continuous improvement.

Cadence/horizon:
- Monthly cycle (typical), with weekly refresh for near-term exceptions.
- Planning horizon: 3–24 months (industry-dependent); time buckets: weekly 0–13 weeks, monthly thereafter.

## Key Activities
- Prepare and validate the statistical baseline forecast and history.
- Gather and incorporate market intelligence and customer collaboration inputs (e.g., CPFR, POS data).
- Apply event overlays (promotions, trade, marketing campaigns) and NPI/NPD plans.
- Conduct exception-based reviews (variance thresholds) by product, customer, and region.
- Run scenario analysis and reconcile with financial targets and strategic guidance.
- Facilitate pre-consensus reviews (BU/Region) and a formal consensus meeting.
- Resolve conflicts, document assumptions, decisions, risks/opportunities, and confidence ranges.
- Finalize, approve, publish, and version-control the consensus forecast.
- Measure performance (MAPE, bias, FVA) and capture learnings to improve future cycles.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Baseline statistical forecast at agreed hierarchy and horizons.
- Historical shipments, orders, and preferably sell-out/POS data.
- Sales intelligence: pipeline, customer forecasts, committed orders, churn risks.
- Marketing/trade calendars: promotions, price changes, media plans.
- Product portfolio data: lifecycle status, NPIs, end-of-life, cannibalization assumptions.
- External signals: macro indicators, seasonality drivers, competitor moves, supply disruptions.
- Financial targets: revenue, margin guidance.
- Master data: product, customer, channel hierarchies; calendars; units of measure.

Prerequisites:
- Defined forecast hierarchy and planning calendar (e.g., 4-4-5) with cut-off dates.
- Governance and RACI for roles, override thresholds, and approval levels.
- Data quality standards and data stewardship in place.
- Consensus meeting charter, agenda, and decision rights.
- Tooling configured for collaboration, versioning, and audit trails.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [4.1.2.1] Develop baseline forecast.
- [4.1.2.2] Collect market/customer intelligence.
- [4.1.2.4] Measure forecast accuracy and improve approach (feeds continuous improvement).
- [4.1.3] Plan supply (downstream consumer of the consensus output).
- Trade/Promotion Management, NPI Stage-Gate, Financial Planning and Analysis (alignment).

## Process Steps
1) Plan the cycle
- Publish calendar, submission deadlines, and approval windows.
- Confirm forecast hierarchy, time buckets, and freeze rules.

2) Prepare the demand package
- Extract and validate baseline forecast and clean history.
- Roll up/down to required hierarchies (SKU-location, product-family, customer/channel).
- Pre-load known events (promotions, NPIs, price changes) with initial lifts/decays.

3) Solicit cross-functional inputs (workflow-driven)
- Sales submits account-level adjustments, customer forecasts, and pipeline impacts.
- Marketing provides promotion/event uplifts and media impact assumptions.
- Product/Category provides NPI demand profiles and cannibalization assumptions.
- Finance provides revenue/margin targets and guardrails.

4) Validate and standardize inputs
- Check unit consistency (units, revenue, currency), date alignment, and duplication.
- Reconcile sell-in vs sell-out; adjust for channel inventory changes if applicable.
- Flag exceptions: large deviations vs baseline, history, or targets.

5) Exception-based review and scenario building
- Analyze high-impact items by ABC/XYZ segmentation and variance thresholds.
- Build scenarios (base, upside, downside; demand-shaping options).
- Quantify risks/opportunities with probabilities and confidence intervals.

6) Pre-consensus reviews (regional/BU)
- Discuss exceptions, resolve local issues, converge on preliminary figures.
- Document assumptions and rationale for overrides (with owner and expiry date).

7) Financial and supply alignment checks
- Reconcile units-to-revenue with pricing/promotions; highlight gaps to financial targets.
- Identify potential supply constraints from supply planning for visibility (demand remains unconstrained unless governance dictates otherwise).
- Prepare gap-closure options and trade-offs.

8) Demand Consensus Meeting
- Participants: Demand planner (facilitator), Sales, Marketing, Finance, Supply planning, Product/Category, S&OP lead.
- Review by exception: largest value drivers and contentious items.
- Decide on final adjustments, agree on risks/opportunities, confidence ranges, and actions.
- Record decisions, owners, and due dates.

9) Finalize and approve
- Apply approved overrides; lock the consensus forecast version.
- Obtain required approvals per governance (e.g., BU lead or S&OP chair).

10) Publish and communicate
- Distribute the consensus forecast to supply planning, procurement, logistics, and FP&A.
- Publish assumption log, risk/opportunity register, and variance analysis.
- Archive all versions and supporting documentation for audit.

11) Post-cycle review and improvement
- Calculate accuracy (MAPE, bias), FVA by contributor and hierarchy.
- Capture lessons learned, update event libraries, and refine algorithms/profiles.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Final consensus demand forecast (single-number plan) by agreed hierarchy and horizon, with version ID and freeze dates.
- Assumption log detailing overrides, events, drivers, and validity windows.
- Risk and opportunity register with quantified ranges and owners.
- Variance reconciliation: baseline vs inputs vs final; units-to-revenue reconciliation.
- Consensus deck/minutes and action tracker.

Success criteria:
- Forecast published on time per calendar with required approvals.
- Accuracy and bias within agreed thresholds by segment/horizon.
- Documented assumptions and FVA demonstrating value over baseline.
- High adoption by downstream functions and minimal last-minute changes.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Demand Planner (Process owner/facilitator): Orchestrates cycle, prepares baseline and demand package, runs exceptions and scenarios, manages meeting, finalizes/publishes forecast, maintains versioning and KPIs.
- Sales/Account Managers: Provide customer forecasts, pipeline impacts, confirm promotions/assortment changes, validate feasibility, own account-level assumptions.
- Marketing/Trade/Category Managers: Provide promotion/event calendars, expected lifts, media plans, and post-event learnings; maintain event library.
- Product/Category Management/NPI Lead: Supply NPI demand profiles, phase-in/out timing, cannibalization and substitution assumptions.
- Finance Business Partner: Reconcile to revenue/margin targets, validate price/cost assumptions, ensure alignment to financial plan and scenarios.
- Supply Planning Representative: Provide visibility to potential constraints, lead-times, and feasibility for awareness (does not constrain demand unless agreed).
- S&OP/IBP Leader: Chair consensus, resolve escalations, ensure cross-functional alignment and decision-making discipline.
- Data Steward/IT: Ensure data quality, master data governance, tool availability, and integrations.
- Customer Collaboration Lead (if applicable): Coordinate CPFR inputs, POS data, and joint business planning inputs.

## Best Practices
- Maintain a single-number plan: ensure one authoritative forecast with controlled versions.
- Use hierarchical and segmented forecasting: ABC/XYZ and by channel/customer; forecast at the demand signal source (sell-out where possible).
- Run exception-based reviews: focus meetings on high-impact variances and contributors.
- Govern overrides: set thresholds, require documented assumptions, and time-bound validity.
- Integrate event modeling: structured promotion/NPI profiles; maintain a learnings library.
- Leverage Forecast Value Added (FVA): measure contributor impact; minimize unhelpful overrides.
- Align with finance early: reconcile units-to-revenue; agree on exchange rates and pricing.
- Document and share assumptions: transparency builds trust and accelerates decisions.
- Version control and freeze windows: lock published forecasts; manage changes via formal change control.
- Enable customer collaboration (CPFR): incorporate customer forecasts and POS where feasible.
- Continuous improvement loop: track MAPE/bias by horizon/segment; update models and processes regularly.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Inconsistent data and master data issues: Implement stewardship, automate validations, and align calendars/UoM across systems.
- Excessive manual overrides and bias: Enforce thresholds, train on bias awareness, use FVA to hold contributors accountable.
- Late or low-quality inputs: Set SLAs, automated reminders, and escalate via governance; provide templates and self-service analytics.
- Misalignment with financial targets: Early reconciliation checkpoints; scenario planning and clear decision rights for trade-offs.
- NPI uncertainty and cannibalization: Use analogous product modeling, phased ranges, and rapid post-launch learning updates.
- Sell-in vs sell-out disconnect: Incorporate POS and channel inventory models; reconcile via inventory flow logic.
- Meeting inefficiency: Pre-reads, exception lists, time-boxed agenda, decision logs, and clear ownership of actions.
- Tool fragmentation: Move to an integrated planning platform with workflow, collaboration, and audit trails.

## Performance Metrics
Effectiveness and quality:
- MAPE and WMAPE by segment and horizon (e.g., 0–3, 4–6, 7–12 months).
- Forecast Bias (Mean Error %) and Tracking Signal.
- Forecast Value Added (by function and overall).
- Promotion/NPI forecast accuracy and uplift accuracy.
- Percent forecast overridden and size of overrides.

Timeliness and adoption:
- Cycle time to consensus; on-time publication rate.
- Percent of portfolio covered by consensus (volume coverage).
- Forecast stability (week-over-week/month-over-month change).
- Change requests after freeze (count and value); adherence to change control.

Business impact:
- Service level/fill rate improvement attributable to forecast.
- Inventory turns and excess/obsolete trends linked to forecast error.
- Revenue attainment vs plan attributable to forecast accuracy improvements.

## Technology and Tools
- Demand planning platforms: SAP IBP, Oracle Demand Management/Demantra, Kinaxis RapidResponse, o9, Blue Yonder, Anaplan.
- Collaboration and CPFR: Customer portals, EDI for customer forecasts, POS data ingestion, joint planning tools.
- Advanced analytics/ML: Time-series and causal models, promotion analytics, NPI analog modeling; Python/R for custom models.
- Data management: MDM solutions, data lakes/warehouses, ETL pipelines; calendar and UoM harmonization.
- Workflow and governance: Built-in planning workflows, approval hierarchies, audit trails; task orchestration tools.
- Visualization and reporting: BI dashboards (Power BI, Tableau) for exceptions, FVA, and KPI tracking.
- Meeting and documentation: Agenda/minutes templates, assumption logs, risk registers, and version repositories.

Process Details:
# [4.1.2.4] Determine Available to Promise (ATP)

## Overview
Determine Available to Promise (ATP) is the process of calculating and committing the quantity and timing of products/services that can be promised to customers based on projected supply, existing commitments, policies, and constraints. It bridges demand planning and order fulfillment by translating supply plans and inventory into reliable customer promise dates and quantities.

Purpose:
- Provide fast, reliable order promise answers to customers and channels.
- Protect inventory and capacity through rules and allocations that align with business priorities (customer tiers, channels, geographies).
- Minimize backorders, de-commitments, and expedites by ensuring commitments reflect realistic supply.
- Improve customer experience and on-time delivery performance.

Role in the organization:
- Central to Order Management and Customer Service for confirming orders.
- Relies on Supply Planning (MPS/MRP/DRP), Procurement, Production, and Logistics for upstream supply and lead times.
- Feeds Sales, Finance, and S&OP through promise performance visibility (e.g., OTDP).

Scope:
- Time-phased promise computation across the planning horizon (near-term daily buckets, longer-term weekly).
- Multi-node network support (plants, DCs, drop-ship, 3PL, consignment).
- Configurable rules: allocations, substitutions, partial shipments, split lines, order priority, time fences.

## Key Activities
- Collect and validate available supply: on-hand, WIP, inbound POs/ASNs, planned orders, inter-site transfers, returns.
- Net out constraints: existing customer reservations, safety stock, quality holds, lot attributes, shelf-life, regulatory/customer restrictions.
- Time-phase supply and demand to compute ATP by bucket (e.g., daily/weekly).
- Apply policy rules:
  - Customer/channel allocations and protections.
  - Order priority and promise stratification (VIP, standard).
  - Time fences (firm, planning, speculative).
  - Substitution and alternate source rules.
- Execute order promising:
  - Match demand line to source(s), check ATP, propose commit date/qty.
  - Evaluate split shipments, alternate products, alternate locations, partial commits.
- Manage exceptions:
  - Insufficient ATP, propose backorder date, escalate for expedite or CTP (capable-to-promise) check.
  - Re-ATP/backorder processing due to supply changes.
- Record and communicate commitments:
  - Create or update reservations.
  - Send confirmations to customers/channels.
  - Update forecast consumption and allocations.
- Monitor and improve:
  - Track KPIs, analyze de-commit/root causes, tune rules and parameters.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Inventory and supply:
  - On-hand inventory by location and lot/batch with statuses (available, QA hold, damaged).
  - WIP and confirmed production orders with due dates and yields.
  - Inbound POs/ASNs with dates and confirmed quantities.
  - Planned supply (MPS/MRP/DRP), approved capacity-based plans.
  - Intercompany transfer orders and expected receipts.
  - Returns/RMA estimates if considered usable.
- Demand and reservations:
  - Confirmed sales orders, reservations, and backorders.
  - Allocations by customer/channel/program.
  - Forecasts and forecast consumption logic.
  - Safety stock targets and service levels.
- Master data and policy:
  - Item master, UOM, pack sizes, substitution lists, supersessions.
  - Sourcing matrix and ATP rule sets by product/customer/channel.
  - Calendars and cut-off times (order acceptance, shipping).
  - Lead times (manufacturing, procurement, transportation), time fences.
  - Lot/serial and shelf-life rules; customer-specific attribute requirements.
- Network and costs (optional):
  - Distribution network topology, transit times.
  - Priority, penalty/expedite costs (for optimization scenarios).

Prerequisites:
- Data quality thresholds met (inventory accuracy, confirmed supply dates).
- Integration between OMS/ERP, WMS, TMS, and planning system is operational.
- Governance for allocations and de-commit approvals in place.
- Products released for sale (saleable status) with valid sourcing rules.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 4.1.2 Manage demand for products (forecasts, forecast consumption).
- 4.1 Plan for and align supply chain resources (MPS/MRP outputs, capacity plans).
- 4.2 Procure materials and services (supplier confirmations).
- 4.3 Manage production (production schedule adherence).
- 4.4 Manage logistics (carrier capacity, cut-offs, transit times).
- Master data management and quality control processes.

## Process Steps
1. Define ATP horizon and buckets
   - Set planning horizon (e.g., 0–13 weeks) with near-term daily buckets and mid/long-term weekly buckets.
   - Configure time fences:
     - Firm zone (e.g., 0–7 days): only consider on-hand and confirmed supply; no reliance on planned orders.
     - Planning zone (e.g., 8–28 days): include planned supply with risk-adjusted yields.
     - Forecast zone (beyond planning): restrict promising or require management approval.

2. Collect and cleanse supply data
   - Pull on-hand balances by location/lot/attribute; exclude non-saleable stock.
   - Import confirmed supply (production, POs, transfer orders, drop-ship confirmations).
   - Include planned orders if within acceptable certainty window; apply readiness checks.
   - Apply adjustments for scrap/yield factors and known downtime.

3. Net out non-ATP quantities
   - Subtract:
     - Existing customer reservations and allocated inventory.
     - Safety stock (either full exclusion or partial availability by policy).
     - Quality holds, customer-specific holds, regulatory holds.
     - In-transit shrink or risk buffers.
   - Result: Projected Available Balance (PAB) per time bucket before new orders.

4. Apply allocation and segmentation rules
   - Reserve protected inventory for strategic customers, channels, geographies, or programs.
   - Set max/min caps per segment to prevent over-consumption.
   - Enable substitution policies at segment level (e.g., allow downgrade/upgrade by customer).

5. Compute time-phased ATP
   - For each bucket, ATP = (PAB beginning + receipts in bucket) − (committed demand in bucket) − protections.
   - Maintain both gross ATP and net ATP per segment and per location.
   - Consider attribute- and lot-specific ATP for regulated/perishable products.

6. Execute order promising for incoming demand lines
   - Identify source set using rules:
     - Preferred ship-from hierarchy (DC → alternate DC → plant → drop-ship).
     - Check geographic eligibility and transport lead times vs. customer requested date (CRD).
   - Check product-level rules:
     - Allow partial shipment? Line-split allowed? Alternate product or kit components?
     - Lot attributes or shelf-life minimums.
   - Evaluate ATP at candidate sources:
     - If sufficient ATP on/before CRD, commit quantity/date.
     - If insufficient, propose:
       - Split: commit available now + backorder remainder.
       - Alternative ship-from with earlier availability.
       - Substitute product with customer consent.
       - Later date aligned with next available bucket.
   - If still insufficient, trigger escalation:
     - CTP check for manufacturing capacity and materials.
     - Expedite options for procurement or interplant transfer.
     - Management approval workflow for borrow-from allocations.

7. Reserve and record commitment
   - Create hard reservation for committed quantities and dates in ERP/OMS.
   - Update allocation consumption and forecast consumption to avoid double-counting.
   - Generate confirmation to customer/channel (e.g., EDI 855, portal/API).

8. Handle exceptions and re-ATP
   - Monitor supply changes (delays, yield drops) and demand changes (cancellations, priority upgrades).
   - Run scheduled and event-driven backorder processing to re-promise impacted lines.
   - Apply de-commit policy hierarchy; notify stakeholders and customers proactively with revised dates.

9. Audit, monitor, and improve
   - Capture promise decision logs (source, rule used, reason codes).
   - Review KPIs, identify root causes (data accuracy, plan adherence, rule misalignment).
   - Tune buffers, time fences, and allocations; update lead times and substitution lists.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Confirmed order commitments (quantity, promised ship and/or delivery date, source location).
- Reservations in ERP/OMS against inventory and inbound supply.
- ATP snapshots by product-location-time bucket (gross and net, by segment).
- Backorder and exception lists with suggested actions.
- Customer communications (order acknowledgements, changes).
- Analytics and audit logs for promise decisions and rule application.

Success criteria:
- High on-time-to-promise (OTTP) and on-time-to-customer-request (OTCR) rates.
- Low de-commitment and backorder rates.
- Fast response time for promise decisions.
- Alignment with allocation policies and minimal policy overrides.
- Positive customer satisfaction (CSAT/NPS) for order reliability.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Order Management/Customer Service Representative:
  - Enter orders, review system proposals, obtain customer approvals for substitutes/splits.
  - Communicate confirmations and changes.
- Demand Planner:
  - Ensure forecast consumption rules are correct; align demand signals with ATP.
- Supply Planner/Master Scheduler:
  - Provide reliable supply plan inputs; approve use of planned orders in ATP.
  - Coordinate expedites or CTP checks for escalations.
- Inventory Control/Logistics:
  - Maintain inventory accuracy and status; manage holds and cycle counts.
  - Provide cut-off times, carrier capacity, and shipping calendars.
- Sales/Key Account Manager:
  - Manage allocations, customer priorities, and exceptions/de-commit approvals.
- Master Data/MDM:
  - Maintain item, sourcing, lead times, substitutions, and policy parameters.
- Quality/Regulatory:
  - Manage QA holds, lot releases, shelf-life rules, and attribute requirements.
- IT/Systems Analyst:
  - Maintain integrations, performance, and rule configurations; monitor re-ATP jobs.
- S&OP Lead:
  - Align ATP policies with business strategy and service-level targets.

## Best Practices
- Use global ATP (G-ATP) across the network to optimize source selection and reduce split shipments.
- Segment ATP by customer/channel and protect inventory for strategic segments via allocations.
- Implement time fences with differentiated confidence (on-hand only in short horizon).
- Maintain attribute- and lot-specific ATP for regulated or perishable items (shelf-life, certifications).
- Incorporate forecast consumption so real orders consume forecast and avoid double-selling.
- Enable substitutions with governance; maintain substitution chains and customer preferences.
- Automate backorder re-ATP on supply/demand changes with clear de-commit policies.
- Use CTP for make-to-order or constrained environments to check materials and capacity.
- Keep real-time integration with WMS/OMS to reduce latency; target sub-second ATP for e-commerce.
- Align ATP with logistics constraints: cut-off times, ship days, carrier capacity, blackout dates.
- Regularly calibrate lead times and yields using actuals; tighten buffers where possible.
- Establish strong data quality controls: inventory accuracy, status codes, and location master.
- Simulate impacts of promotions and new product launches; pre-allocate as needed.
- Provide decision transparency with audit trails to support continuous improvement.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Inaccurate or stale data → Implement data latency SLAs, real-time feeds where needed, and inventory cycle counting.
- Overpromising due to planned orders with low reliability → Restrict planned orders to planning zone; require confirmations; apply readiness scores.
- Allocation conflicts between channels → Governance and automated allocation engines; escalation rules and cap management.
- High de-commit rates → Root-cause on supply reliability and data issues; apply risk buffers; enhance supplier confirmations; use CTP.
- Latency in promise response for high-velocity channels → Cache ATP snapshots, optimize queries, and scale infrastructure.
- Complex product attributes (lot, shelf-life, certifications) → Attribute-based ATP and strict lot selection rules.
- Unplanned demand spikes (promotions not modeled) → Event monitoring, rapid re-allocation, temporary buffers, and promotion governance.
- Multi-node inventory visibility gaps (3PL, drop-ship) → Integrate 3PL and vendor feeds; VMI/consignment visibility; ASN compliance enforcement.
- Capacity constraints not reflected in ATP → Use capacity-aware CTP and align production scheduling with promising rules.

## Performance Metrics
- On-Time-to-Promise (OTTP): % of orders shipped on or before promised date.
- On-Time-to-Request (OTR/OTCR): % of orders meeting customer requested date.
- First-commit accuracy: % of commitments that did not change (no de-commit).
- De-commit rate: % of lines with revised promise after initial confirmation.
- Backorder rate: % of demand lines backordered at any time.
- Fill rate at order line and order level; perfect order rate.
- Promise lead time: Average days between order date and promised ship/delivery date.
- ATP response time: Average time to return promise for an order line.
- Allocation adherence: % of protected inventory consumed by intended segments.
- Expedite incidence/cost due to ATP errors.
- Inventory reservation accuracy: % of reservations tied to actual fulfillment.
- Forecast consumption accuracy: Degree to which actual orders consume forecast as intended.

Targets should be set by segment (e.g., e-commerce vs. wholesale) and monitored over time, with thresholds for alerts.

## Technology and Tools
- ERP/OMS with ATP modules:
  - SAP S/4HANA Advanced ATP (aATP), SAP APO/IBP gATP
  - Oracle Cloud Order Management GOP/ATP, Oracle E-Business Suite ATP
  - Microsoft Dynamics 365 SCM ATP
  - Manhattan OM/DOM, Blue Yonder Luminate, Kinaxis RapidResponse, o9, ToolsGroup
- WMS/TMS for real-time inventory and logistics calendars.
- Planning systems (MPS/MRP/DRP, IBP/S&OP) for supply inputs.
- Allocation and rules engines for segmentation, priorities, and substitutions.
- CTP engines integrated with production scheduling and finite capacity.
- Integration middleware/APIs/EDI for inbound/outbound confirmations (e.g., EDI 855, 856).
- Data quality and MDM tools for product, location, and policy master data.
- Analytics/monitoring:
  - Dashboards for ATP KPIs, exceptions, and re-ATP outcomes.
  - Audit logging and decision tracing.

Implementation notes:
- Start with a minimal viable rule set (on-hand only in firm zone) and iterate.
- Pilot with a subset of SKUs/customers; validate KPIs and adjust buffers and rules.
- Establish change control for ATP parameters; version and document rule changes.

Process Details:
## Overview
Monitor activity against demand forecast and revise forecast is the closed-loop process that compares actual demand signals to the approved consensus forecast, identifies significant deviations, determines root causes, and updates the forecast in a controlled, timely manner. Its purpose is to keep demand plans current and reliable so that supply, procurement, and logistics decisions stay aligned with market reality.

This process sits at the heart of Sales & Operations Execution (S&OE) and feeds the broader Sales & Operations Planning (S&OP/IBP) cycle. It reduces stockouts and excess inventory, stabilizes operations, and improves customer service by translating near-real-time market signals into actionable forecast revisions.

Scope includes all levels of the demand hierarchy (SKU–location–channel–customer, aggregated product categories, etc.) across multiple time horizons: near-term demand sensing (days–weeks) and medium-term consensus updates (monthly–quarterly).

## Key Activities
- Continuous monitoring of demand signals:
  - Compare actuals (sell-in, sell-out/POS, orders, shipments) vs forecast at defined intervals.
  - Track KPIs (MAPE/WAPE, bias, tracking signal, service levels).
- Exception detection and prioritization:
  - Automatically flag items outside tolerance thresholds.
  - Prioritize by impact (A/B/C, margin, critical customers).
- Root cause analysis:
  - Investigate drivers (promotions, price changes, competitor actions, supply constraints, OOS).
- Forecast revision:
  - Adjust near-term and medium-term forecasts within guardrails.
  - Apply hierarchy reconciliation and version control.
- Consensus and approval:
  - Review proposed changes with Sales, Marketing, Supply Planning, and Finance as needed.
  - Approve per delegation thresholds.
- Publication and communication:
  - Publish revised forecast to planning systems and notify stakeholders.
- Post-change monitoring and continuous improvement:
  - Measure outcome vs expectations; refine thresholds, models, and rules.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Approved consensus forecast by item–location–time bucket (baseline and overlays such as promotions).
  - Actual demand signals: confirmed orders, POS/sell-out, shipments, consumption, returns, cancellations, backorders, lost sales estimates.
  - Inventory and availability: on-hand, in-transit, ATP, OOS events, service level.
  - Commercial drivers: promotion calendar, pricing changes, media spend, product lifecycle status, customer events, trade terms.
  - External signals (as applicable): weather, holidays, local events, macro indicators, competitor actions, online search trends.
  - Master data and hierarchies: product, location, customer/channel, calendars, units of measure.
- Prerequisites:
  - Data integration pipelines with defined latency SLAs (e.g., POS daily, orders hourly, shipments daily).
  - Clean and synchronized master data across systems.
  - Defined exception thresholds and segmentation policies (e.g., tighter tolerances for A items).
  - A demand planning platform that supports versioning, audit trail, and hierarchy reconciliation.
  - Clear governance for approvals, change control, and communication.
  - Trained personnel with access to required tools.
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Upstream: Create statistical/causal forecast; Build consensus forecast; Manage promotions and pricing; Maintain master data.
  - Downstream: Supply planning and MRP; Procurement and supplier scheduling; Logistics and allocation; S&OE/S&OP meetings.

## Process Steps
1. Define cadence and scope
   - Establish monitoring frequency (e.g., daily near-term sensing, weekly S&OE review).
   - Segment items (ABC/XYZ) and set item-specific thresholds and freeze windows.

2. Ingest and align data
   - Pull latest signals (orders, POS, shipments, inventory, returns) and commercial drivers.
   - Align to common hierarchies and time buckets matching the forecast.

3. Validate and cleanse data
   - Run automated checks for completeness, duplicates, outliers, and calendar alignment.
   - Correct or flag anomalies; annotate known events (promotion, OOS) to prevent misinterpretation.

4. Calculate variances and health metrics
   - Compute deviations by item–location–time: absolute variance, percent error, bias, tracking signal (CFE/MAD), stability vs last forecast, service levels.
   - Identify variance types: volume, mix, timing (demand shift), and channel migration.

5. Detect and prioritize exceptions
   - Apply rules such as:
     - Percent error > X% and volume > Y units for Z periods.
     - Tracking signal outside [-4, +4] or other agreed bounds.
     - Service level below target for 2 consecutive periods.
   - Rank by financial and service impact (revenue, margin, critical customers).

6. Diagnose root causes
   - Collaborate with Sales/Marketing on promotions, pricing, account events.
   - Check supply-related confounds (substitutions, OOS, allocations) to distinguish unconstrained demand from constrained shipments.
   - Review external signals (weather, competitor actions).
   - Document findings and evidence.

7. Formulate forecast adjustments
   - Near-term (0–8 weeks): apply demand sensing rules and constrained/unconstrained logic; adjust at the lowest practical level and reconcile up/down the hierarchy.
   - Medium-term (2–6 months): update baselines considering structural changes, lifecycle stage, and causal drivers.
   - Use prediction intervals and guardrails to avoid overreacting to noise.

8. Run simulations and impact assessment
   - Evaluate impact on service, inventory, capacity, procurement, and logistics.
   - Compare scenarios (e.g., best case/base/worst case; promo uplift ranges).

9. Review and approval
   - Prepare change set with rationale, data, and expected impact.
   - Route for approval per thresholds (e.g., >10% change at category level requires manager approval; high-value customers require Sales sign-off).

10. Publish and integrate
    - Create a new forecast version with effective date, horizon, and change log.
    - Publish to demand planning, supply planning/MRP, allocation, and replenishment systems.
    - Trigger safety stock recalculation if appropriate.

11. Communicate changes
    - Notify stakeholders (Supply Planning, Procurement, Logistics, Sales, Finance, Customer Service) with summary and actions.
    - Update S&OE dashboard and meeting packs.

12. Monitor outcomes and learn
    - Track post-change performance vs expectations.
    - Adjust thresholds, models, and business rules; capture lessons learned.
    - Feed insights into S&OP and continuous improvement backlog.

Decision guardrails and examples:
- Freeze windows: do not change the next 1–2 weeks unless service risk is high or a documented event occurs.
- Maximum delta per cycle: cap week-over-week changes for A items to avoid supply disruption, unless approved.
- Bias management: target near-zero bias over rolling windows; initiate corrective actions when persistent bias is detected.

Artifacts generated each cycle:
- Exception list with prioritization scores.
- Root cause notes with supporting data.
- Forecast change set with version, rationale, approver, and effective dates.
- Impact assessment and scenario results.
- Communication summary and action items.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Revised demand forecast:
  - New version(s) by item–location–time with overlays (promotions, events) and prediction intervals.
- Exception and change logs:
  - Documented deviations, root causes, decisions, approvals, and timestamps.
- Updated dashboards and reports:
  - KPI updates, variance analysis, stability charts, service risk heatmaps.
- Downstream triggers:
  - Signals to supply planning/MRP, procurement, allocation, replenishment, and customer commitments.
- Success criteria:
  - Improved accuracy and reduced bias in monitored horizons.
  - Faster exception resolution and fewer service failures.
  - Stable, explainable changes with measurable business benefit (service level, inventory turns, cost).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Demand Planner:
  - Own daily/weekly monitoring, exception analysis, forecast adjustments, and documentation.
- Demand Planning Manager:
  - Set policy, thresholds, and guardrails; approve high-impact changes; coach and escalate.
- Sales/Account Managers:
  - Provide customer intelligence; validate demand changes; confirm event and pipeline impacts.
- Marketing/Trade:
  - Maintain promo calendar and uplift assumptions; confirm media spend and timing; update changes.
- Supply Planner:
  - Evaluate feasibility; translate forecast changes into supply plans; flag constraints.
- Finance/FP&A:
  - Assess revenue/margin impacts; align with budget/LE; support consensus reconciliation.
- Data Analyst/Data Scientist:
  - Maintain models, demand sensing logic, anomaly detection; analyze structural shifts.
- IT/Data Engineering/MDM:
  - Operate data pipelines, integrations, master data quality, access controls.
- S&OE Lead/IBP Manager:
  - Facilitate reviews; ensure alignment and timely decisions; track actions.
- Customer Service/Order Management:
  - Provide order pattern insight; capture cancellations/backorders; communicate to customers.
- Product Management:
  - Advise on lifecycle changes, substitutions, cannibalization, and rationalization.

## Best Practices
- Multi-horizon approach:
  - Use demand sensing for the near term; statistical/ML models for medium term; apply hierarchy reconciliation.
- Segmentation-driven thresholds:
  - Tighter controls for A/high-variability items; simplified handling for C items to focus effort.
- Use unconstrained demand:
  - Correct shipment-based actuals for OOS and allocations; incorporate POS/sell-out where available.
- Robust exception management:
  - Automate detection; triage by impact; limit overrides to where they add value.
- Guardrails to prevent overreaction:
  - Freeze windows, max change limits, prediction intervals, and tracking signal monitoring.
- Promotion and price elasticity:
  - Model uplift and halo/cannibalization; maintain promo calendars and link actual outcomes to refine assumptions.
- Intermittent demand handling:
  - Use appropriate methods (e.g., Croston/SBA) and review by exception.
- Data quality by design:
  - Automated validation, event tagging, and clear stewardship ownership.
- Closed-loop learning:
  - Measure Forecast Value Add (FVA) of overrides and processes; retire non-value-adding steps.
- Governance and auditability:
  - Version control, rationale capture, approvals, and accessible logs for compliance and traceability.
- Collaboration:
  - Shared dashboards, standard templates, and structured S&OE cadences with clear roles.
- External signals:
  - Integrate weather, events, web trends, and competitive intel; test and adopt those with proven lift.

## Common Challenges
- Data latency and inconsistency:
  - Solution: define SLAs; use streaming or near-real-time feeds; harmonize calendars and hierarchies; implement data quality checks.
- Misinterpreting constrained shipments as low demand:
  - Solution: use POS/orders; estimate lost sales; adjust for OOS; coordinate with Supply Planning.
- Overriding models due to noise or bias:
  - Solution: guardrails, bias tracking, override justification, and FVA measurement.
- Poor visibility to promotions and price changes:
  - Solution: enforce promo governance; integrate calendars; require pre/post analysis.
- Structural breaks (NPIs, delistings, regulation, macro shocks):
  - Solution: change-point detection, rapid re-baselining, analog item methods, scenario planning.
- Cannibalization and channel shifts:
  - Solution: model cross-effects; monitor mix and channel migration; adjust hierarchies and targets.
- Intermittent and long-tail demand:
  - Solution: specialized methods, broader aggregation for planning, flexible service policies.
- Organizational misalignment and slow approvals:
  - Solution: clear RACI, delegation thresholds, S&OE cadence, standard decision templates.

## Performance Metrics
- Forecast accuracy and error:
  - MAPE/WAPE by horizon and segment; MASE for comparability; absolute error in units and value.
- Bias and tracking:
  - Mean bias percent; tracking signal (CFE/MAD); percent of items within tolerance.
- Forecast stability:
  - Week-over-week change magnitude; percent within guardrails.
- Service outcomes:
  - Fill rate, on-time in-full (OTIF), on-shelf availability (OSA), stockout incidents, backorder rate.
- Inventory health:
  - Days of supply, inventory turns, excess/obsolete value attributable to forecast error.
- Process efficiency:
  - Exception closure lead time; percent of exceptions addressed; cycle-time from signal to publication; automation coverage.
- Financial impact:
  - Revenue/margin variance due to forecast changes; expediting and premium freight costs avoided; FVA of overrides and process steps.
- Adoption and governance:
  - Percent of forecast with documented rationale; approval SLA adherence; audit issues.

## Technology and Tools
- Demand planning and IBP platforms:
  - SAP IBP, Oracle Demantra, Kinaxis RapidResponse, o9 Solutions, Anaplan, Blue Yonder, etc., supporting versioning, reconciliation, and workflows.
- Analytics and visualization:
  - Power BI, Tableau, Qlik; embedded dashboards for KPIs, exception heatmaps, and variance drilldowns.
- Data integration and storage:
  - Data lakes/warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Azure Synapse); ETL/ELT tools (Informatica, dbt, Fivetran); event streaming (Kafka) for near-real-time signals.
- Advanced analytics/ML:
  - Python/R notebooks; AutoML platforms; anomaly detection; demand sensing models; price/promo elasticity; change-point detection.
- Collaboration and workflow:
  - Slack/Teams integration, email notifications; workflow engines (ServiceNow, Jira) for approval and action tracking.
- Master data and governance:
  - MDM tools; role-based access control; audit logging; data quality monitoring.
- Integration with operational systems:
  - ERP (SAP, Oracle), OMS, WMS, TMS, CRM, e-commerce platforms, and POS aggregators.

Practical configuration suggestions:
- Set horizon-specific tolerances (e.g., near-term ±15% for A items; mid-term ±25%).
- Define approval thresholds by financial impact and level of aggregation.
- Maintain a canonical change log with fields: item, location, time bucket, old/new forecast, reason code, evidence link, requester, approver, timestamp.
- Establish S&OE cadence: daily automated monitoring; weekly cross-functional review; monthly feed into S&OP.

This documented process enables timely, evidence-based forecast revisions, ensuring the supply chain stays aligned with dynamic market demand while maintaining governance, efficiency, and measurable business outcomes.

Process Details:
## Overview
Evaluate and revise demand forecasting approach is a recurring process that assesses how well current demand forecasting methods, parameters, and governance are performing, then refines them to align with current market realities and business objectives. It ensures forecasts are accurate, unbiased, explainable, and valuable for downstream planning (S&OP/IBP, master production scheduling, procurement, logistics).

This process:
- Diagnoses forecast performance by product/channel/region/time horizon.
- Identifies drivers of error (data quality, structural change, promotions/price, lifecycle shifts).
- Tests alternative models/methods, parameters, features, and governance rules.
- Implements controlled improvements and monitors results.
- Documents changes and trains stakeholders.

It is typically executed on a quarterly or semiannual cycle, with expedited reviews when major disruptions or product portfolio changes occur.

## Key Activities
- Define objectives and scope (segments, horizons, KPIs, target improvements).
- Collect and prepare data (historical demand, forecasts, events, external factors).
- Performance assessment (accuracy, bias, stability, value-add vs benchmarks).
- Root cause analysis (data, method, process, market).
- Methodology review and selection (statistical, ML, causal, hierarchical reconciliation).
- Parameter tuning and feature engineering.
- Backtesting and rolling-origin cross-validation.
- Champion–challenger evaluation and risk assessment.
- Stakeholder review and governance sign-off.
- Implementation (system configuration, automation, documentation).
- Change management and training.
- Post-implementation monitoring and continuous improvement.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Historical demand at required granularities (SKU, channel, region, customer; units and value).
  - Prior forecasts and planners’ overrides, with timestamps and rationale.
  - Event calendars: promotions, price changes, launches, cannibalization, stockouts/shortages, holidays.
  - Product master data: hierarchy, lifecycle phase, substitutions, pack changes.
  - External drivers: macro indicators, weather, mobility, competitive actions (if used).
  - Service-level targets, lead times, safety stock policies.
  - Current forecasting methods, parameters, and governance documentation.
  - Data quality reports (missingness, outliers, latency) and system performance logs.

- Prerequisites:
  - Defined forecast hierarchy and aggregation/disaggregation rules.
  - Agreed KPIs and acceptance thresholds (e.g., WAPE reduction ≥3%, bias within ±3%).
  - Data access and security permissions; sandbox/test environment.
  - Version control and experiment tracking in place.
  - Calendar alignment with S&OP/IBP cycle and downstream cutoffs.

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - 4.1.2 Manage demand for products (upstream data/forecasts and overrides).
  - Promotion and price planning (to supply event calendars and uplift assumptions).
  - New product introduction/lifecycle management (analog selection, phase-in/out rules).
  - Master data management (product/channel hierarchy accuracy).
  - S&OP/IBP (for targets, scenarios, and governance).
  - IT/Analytics platform management (for deployment and monitoring).

## Process Steps
1. Initiate review and define scope
   - Trigger: scheduled cadence (e.g., quarterly) or event-driven (e.g., persistent bias >5%).
   - Select segments to review (e.g., top 80% volume, high-variability SKUs, new launches).
   - Set objectives, KPIs, and success criteria; confirm timelines and resources.

2. Gather and validate data
   - Extract historical actuals, forecasts, overrides, drivers, and external data for the lookback window.
   - Run data quality checks (completeness, anomalies, out-of-stock masking, calendar alignment).
   - Impute/adjust: correct for stockouts/lost sales where measurable; cap/transform outliers.

3. Baseline performance assessment
   - Compute accuracy and bias by segment and horizon (e.g., 1–13 weeks or months).
   - Compare against benchmarks (naive, seasonal naive, simple exponential smoothing).
   - Assess forecast value add (FVA): planner/system overrides vs baseline methods.
   - Evaluate stability (month-over-month forecast change), timeliness, and adoption.

4. Diagnose root causes
   - Analyze error patterns: trend/seasonality misfit, promotion/price effects, lifecycle shifts, structural breaks, intermittency.
   - Review override effectiveness; identify where judgment helps or hurts.
   - Engage commercial, marketing, and supply teams to validate hypotheses.

5. Design candidate improvements
   - Segmentation: ABC-XYZ (value vs variability), lifecycle stage, intermittency.
   - Method options by segment:
     - Stable/continuous demand: ETS/ARIMA, Theta, ensemble of statistical models.
     - Trend/seasonal with events: ETS+regressors, Prophet, TBATS.
     - Promotion/price-driven: causal uplift models, gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM), elasticities.
     - Intermittent/spiky: Croston, SBA, TSB, ADIDA, zero-inflated models.
     - New products: analogs, attribute-based models, Bayesian hierarchical models.
   - Hierarchical forecasting and reconciliation (top-down, bottom-up, MinT).
   - Feature engineering: holidays, promo intensity, price gaps, distribution, weather.
   - Parameter tuning and regularization to prevent overfitting.
   - Override policy adjustments (limits, required rationale, cooling-off rules).

6. Backtesting and validation
   - Use rolling-origin cross-validation; mirror operational horizons and freeze calendars.
   - Measure KPIs (WAPE, sMAPE, MAE/RMSE, MPE/BIAS, MASE), FVA, stability.
   - Conduct change-point analysis and stress tests for shocks (e.g., price jumps, stockouts).
   - Document model cards (assumptions, data, performance, risks).

7. Select champion(s) and define governance
   - Choose approach per segment based on performance and explainability.
   - Define thresholds for when to switch methods or re-tune automatically.
   - Update reconciliation strategy and override governance.
   - Prepare rollback plan.

8. Stakeholder review and sign-off
   - Socialize findings, trade-offs, and expected impacts with Demand Planning, Sales, Marketing, Finance, S&OP.
   - Obtain approvals per change control policy.

9. Implement changes
   - Configure in planning system (methods, parameters, hierarchies, calendars).
   - Update pipelines, schedules, and monitoring alerts.
   - Migrate in phases (pilot → scale), using A/B or shadow mode where feasible.

10. Train and communicate
    - Train planners on changes, interpretation, and override policy.
    - Publish documentation and FAQs.

11. Monitor post-implementation
    - Track KPIs vs baseline; alert on drift/bias.
    - Review override behavior and effectiveness.
    - Capture lessons learned; schedule next review cycle.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Updated forecasting methodology by segment, with documented assumptions.
- Model cards and validation reports (backtest results, KPI comparison, risks).
- Revised system configurations and parameter sets.
- Updated governance and override policies.
- Training materials and communications.
- Monitoring dashboards and alert thresholds.
- Change log and rollback plan.

Success criteria:
- Statistically and practically significant improvement in accuracy and/or bias.
- Positive forecast value add versus naive and prior approach.
- Stable, explainable results and improved planner adoption.
- No adverse downstream impact (e.g., service levels, inventory turns).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Demand Planning Lead: Owns process, scope, KPIs, stakeholder alignment, approvals.
- Demand Planners (Category/Region): Provide business context, evaluate results, apply and justify overrides, adopt new methods.
- Data Scientist/Forecaster: Designs experiments, develops models, backtests, documents model cards.
- Data Engineer/Analytics Engineer: Data pipelines, quality checks, feature store, deployment.
- IT/Systems Administrator: Configures planning tools, manages environments, access, and performance.
- S&OP/IBP Lead: Ensures alignment with cycle, mediates trade-offs, integrates with supply/financial plans.
- Sales/Marketing/Trade Promotion: Supply event data, validate uplift assumptions, review outcomes.
- Finance: Validates value impact (e.g., inventory, revenue forecast accuracy), supports KPI targets.
- Change Manager/Trainer: Coordinates training, communications, adoption measurement.
- Governance/Model Risk (if applicable): Reviews compliance, monitors model risk and drift.

## Best Practices
- Segment-first approach: Choose methods by demand pattern, value, and lifecycle; avoid one-size-fits-all.
- Rolling-origin evaluation: Mimic operational forecasting conditions for robust validation.
- Use multiple benchmarks: Always compare to naive/seasonal naive and last-year methods.
- Control bias: Track and correct systematic over/under-forecasting; set bias guardrails.
- Hierarchical reconciliation: Ensure consistency across SKU/channel/region/total using proven methods (e.g., MinT).
- Treat events explicitly: Model promotions, price, holidays as features; maintain accurate event calendars.
- Intermittent demand methods: Apply Croston variants or ADIDA where appropriate; avoid MAPE for sparse series.
- Override governance: Limit overrides to cases with documented rationale; measure override effectiveness.
- Data quality discipline: Detect and correct stockout-masked demand, outliers, and calendar misalignments.
- Champion–challenger: Continuously test alternatives in shadow mode; adopt only with evidence.
- Documentation and transparency: Maintain model cards, assumptions, and decision logs.
- MLOps for forecasting: Version data, code, and models; automate monitoring and retraining; enable rollback.
- Ethical/use constraints: Avoid using prohibited or privacy-sensitive data; comply with data governance.

## Common Challenges
- Poor data quality and latency
  - Solution: Automated checks, lost sales estimation, standard lag handling, collaboration with MDM.
- Structural breaks (e.g., channel shifts, market shocks)
  - Solution: Change-point detection, shorter training windows, regime-switching or ensemble models, scenario overlays.
- Promotion and price effects mis-modeled
  - Solution: Maintain accurate promo metadata, uplift/price elasticity models, post-event decay features.
- Intermittent/sporadic demand
  - Solution: Croston/SBA/TSB, aggregation/disaggregation (ADIDA), focus on inventory-oriented KPIs.
- New product forecasting
  - Solution: Analog and attribute-based models, Bayesian pooling, structured ramp assumptions.
- Hierarchy inconsistency
  - Solution: Reconciliation, governance of aggregation rules, align calendars and time buckets.
- Overfitting and complexity
  - Solution: Regularization, simple baselines, cross-validation, penalize complexity, explainability requirements.
- Stakeholder resistance
  - Solution: Involve users early, show FVA and service impact, phased rollout, training.
- Tool limitations/performance
  - Solution: Hybrid architecture (planning system + external modeling), optimize pipelines, batch scheduling.

## Performance Metrics
- Accuracy and bias:
  - WAPE/MAE/ RMSE by segment and horizon.
  - sMAPE or MASE for comparability across series.
  - Bias (ME, MPE) with guardrails (e.g., ±3%).
- Forecast value add:
  - FVA vs naive and prior approach; override effectiveness (% of overrides that improved forecast).
- Stability and usability:
  - Forecast volatility (period-over-period change), planner adoption rate, % SKUs within error thresholds.
- Process metrics:
  - Cycle time to evaluate and implement changes.
  - % of portfolio covered by revised approach; refresh frequency adherence.
  - Model drift alerts per month and time to resolution.
- Business impact proxies:
  - Service level change attributable to forecast improvement.
  - Inventory turns, expedites, and obsolescence trends.

## Technology and Tools
- Demand planning platforms: SAP IBP, Oracle Demantra, Kinaxis RapidResponse, Blue Yonder, o9.
- Time-series/statistical libraries: Statsmodels (ARIMA/ETS), Prophet, Nixtla StatsForecast, Darts, Kats.
- Machine learning frameworks: scikit-learn, XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost, PyTorch/TF for deep learning if applicable.
- Hierarchical reconciliation: hts/forecast reconciliation packages or built-in platform features (e.g., MinT).
- Data engineering and quality: dbt, Apache Airflow, Azure Data Factory; Great Expectations for data tests.
- MLOps and experiment tracking: MLflow, DVC, Git, feature stores.
- Visualization and monitoring: Power BI, Tableau, Grafana; custom dashboards with alerting.
- Data platforms: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks.
