## Overview
Generate detailed schedule is the short- to mid-term finite-capacity scheduling process that translates the line-level production plan and firm/firm-planned orders into a feasible, time-phased, resource-constrained execution schedule. It specifies every production operation, timing, duration, sequence, material staging, tooling, labor, and maintenance windows so that shop floor teams can execute with clarity and deviations can be tracked and managed.

Purpose:
- Convert the master schedule or line-level plan into a working, realistic schedule at the operation/work-center level.
- Balance demand priorities with constraints (capacity, materials, tooling, labor, maintenance).
- Minimize changeovers, overtime, and WIP while maximizing on-time completion and resource utilization.
- Provide a baseline to dispatch work, stage materials, and monitor schedule adherence.

Role in the organization:
- Core link between planning (S&OP/MPS/MRP) and execution (MES/Shop Floor).
- Drives procurement and warehouse kitting timing, maintenance coordination, and logistics commitments.
- Enables proactive exception management and continuous improvement through schedule performance analytics.

## Key Activities
- Consolidate inputs: demand, orders, routings, BOMs, calendars, constraints, and maintenance.
- Finite-capacity scheduling at work center/resource level, including sequence-dependent setups.
- Material availability check and pegging; reserve/allocate critical components.
- Optimization of sequences around bottlenecks; changeover reduction and campaign planning.
- Labor scheduling and skill-to-task matching; shift and overtime planning.
- Integration of planned maintenance and known downtime; buffers for unplanned events.
- Generation of dispatch lists, Gantt schedules, kitting/pick lists, and staging timetables.
- What-if simulation (e.g., rush orders, delays, outages) and decision support.
- Publication of the frozen/firm schedule and cadence for rolling reschedules.
- Exception management: alerts for infeasibilities, shortages, quality holds, or delays.
- Versioning, approvals, and audit trail for schedule changes.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Demand and orders: customer orders, transfer orders, MPS, forecast (if applicable).
- Production orders/lots: firmed or convertible planned orders with quantities and due dates.
- Master data: routings/operations, standard times (setup/run/queue/move), BOMs, scrap/yield, alternates.
- Resource data: work centers/capacity, machine calendars, labor shifts/skills, tooling and fixture availability.
- Constraints: maintenance windows (planned/unplanned blocks), quality inspection steps, cleaning/CIP/SIP.
- Inventory and supply: on-hand/WIP, open POs, lead times, supplier commits, substitutions.
- Policies: lot-sizing rules, time fences, priority rules, overtime thresholds, setup matrices/families.
- Compliance: regulatory constraints (campaign limits, cleaning requirements, sterile zones).
- Facility constraints: storage/staging space, utilities/energy limits, hazardous material rules.

Prerequisites:
- Accurate and current master data (routings, BOMs, calendars).
- Line-level plan and MPS agreed in S&OP; frozen and slushy time fences defined.
- Integration with ERP/MRP, CMMS, MES, and WMS is functioning.
- Roles and authorities for schedule release and change control established.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 4.3.1.1/4.3.1.2 upstream schedule planning and order creation.
- 4.2 Procure materials and services for component availability.
- Maintenance scheduling (planned/unplanned) for capacity constraints.
- 4.3.2 Execute production and 4.3.3 Test/QA for feedback and holds.
- Logistics/warehousing for kitting, staging, and shipment commitments.

## Process Steps
1. Define scope and horizon
   - Set scheduling horizon (e.g., 1–6 weeks) and granularity (minutes/hours).
   - Apply time fences: frozen (no changes), slushy (limited changes), liquid (flexible).
   - Confirm objective function priorities (on-time completion, minimal changeovers, cost, throughput).

2. Load and validate data
   - Import latest orders, MPS, and firm planned orders.
   - Validate routings, BOMs, standard times, setup matrices, and alternates.
   - Load resource calendars, maintenance blocks, labor skills and shift patterns.
   - Sync inventories, open POs, and expected receipts; perform data quality checks and flag anomalies.

3. Prepare constraints and rules
   - Define bottleneck resources, queue/transfer times, WIP limits, and buffers (Drum-Buffer-Rope).
   - Set sequence rules per line (e.g., light-to-dark colors, allergen sequences, product family campaigns).
   - Establish labor and tooling constraints, including tool life and calibration windows.
   - Set scheduling policies: lot splitting/overlap, co/alternate routing, substitutions.

4. Material availability check and pegging
   - Explode BOMs for all orders in horizon; peg components to orders.
   - Identify shortages, late supplies, or quality holds; propose substitutes where allowed.
   - Reserve/allocate constrained parts to priority orders; generate exception list for shortages.

5. Finite-capacity scheduling and sequencing
   - Schedule bottlenecks first using finite capacity and objective function; apply changeover matrices.
   - Sequence operations within work centers considering setup families and campaign sizes.
   - Allocate labor skills to operations; plan overtime only when rules allow.
   - Incorporate maintenance windows; insert buffers for changeover and cleaning (CIP/SIP).
   - Use lot split/overlap to reduce lead time where beneficial; respect WIP and space limits.

6. Generate preliminary schedule
   - Produce Gantt and dispatch lists with start/finish times for each operation.
   - Create material staging and kitting schedule aligned to operation starts.
   - Calculate expected completion dates and compare to due dates; flag tardy items.

7. Simulate what-if scenarios and optimize
   - Evaluate scenarios: expedite critical orders, delay/cancel orders, alternative routings, supplier delays, equipment outage.
   - Measure trade-offs (overtime, changeover cost, tardiness) and select best scenario.
   - Re-run optimizer/heuristics as needed; validate feasibility with SMEs.

8. Review and align cross-functionally
   - Conduct daily/weekly scheduling huddle with Production, Materials, Maintenance, QA, and Customer Service.
   - Resolve exceptions: shortages, quality holds, tool availability, labor gaps.
   - Confirm frozen-zone commitments; agree on escalations and customer communications.

9. Freeze, version, and publish
   - Freeze near-term portion; assign version ID and store change log.
   - Publish to MES and shop floor: work-to lists, sequencing, setup instructions, quality checkpoints.
   - Send pick lists and staging tasks to WMS; update CMMS with schedule implications.

10. Execute monitoring and deviation management
    - Track schedule adherence in MES; capture reasons for variance (downtime, changeover overruns, rework).
    - Trigger alerts for jeopardized orders; enact predefined expedite/resequence rules.
    - Update allocations if materials arrive early/late; re-publish revised dispatch lists as needed.

11. Close and improve
    - After-action review: compare plan vs actual for cycle times, setup times, yields, and adherence.
    - Calibrate standard times, setup matrices, and capacities; update policies and master data.
    - Feed insights to S&OP and continuous improvement (SMED, TPM, bottleneck debottlenecking).

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Finite, feasible schedule with start/finish times per operation and resource.
- Sequencing plans with setup/changeover instructions.
- Dispatch lists by work center/shift.
- Material kitting and staging schedule and pick lists.
- Labor and overtime plan; tooling/fixture reservations.
- Exception reports (shortages, late orders, capacity overloads).
- Schedule version and change log; frozen-zone baseline.
- What-if scenario results and decisions.

Deliverables produced:
- Published schedule package to MES/Shop Floor, WMS, CMMS, QA.
- Communication to Customer Service for confirmed commits and delays.

Success criteria:
- On-time completion for frozen-zone orders meets target (e.g., ≥95%).
- No infeasible schedules (zero capacity or material violations).
- Changeovers and overtime within thresholds; schedule stability maintained.
- Timely and accurate publication; adherence to change control.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Master Scheduler / Production Planner
  - Owns schedule creation, optimization, and publication; manages time fences and priorities.
- Production/Shop Floor Supervisor
  - Validates feasibility; manages day-of execution and updates; approves resequencing within authority.
- Materials Planner / Buyer
  - Confirms component availability; manages allocations and expedites; updates supply commits.
- Maintenance Planner
  - Provides maintenance windows; adjusts PM/CM plans; coordinates outages with schedulers.
- Quality/QA Lead
  - Confirms inspection steps, hold times, and release sequences; communicates holds/deviations.
- Process/Manufacturing Engineer
  - Maintains routings, standard times, changeover matrices; supports alternates and improvements.
- Tooling/Fixture Coordinator
  - Ensures tool availability, calibration, and setup readiness.
- Warehouse/Kitting Supervisor
  - Executes kitting and staging aligned to the schedule; manages space and sequencing.
- IT/APS Administrator
  - Maintains scheduling system, integrations, and data governance; ensures performance and backups.
- Customer Service/Order Management
  - Aligns customer priorities, communicates revised commits, manages rush/cancel changes.
- EHS/Compliance (as applicable)
  - Ensures scheduled campaigns adhere to safety and regulatory constraints.

## Best Practices
- Use finite-capacity APS with sequence-dependent setup modeling and objective functions aligned to business goals.
- Calibrate master data monthly using actuals; include realistic queue/move times, yields, and scrap factors.
- Define clear time fences and a schedule stability policy; minimize changes inside the frozen zone.
- Schedule bottlenecks first; apply TOC/Drum-Buffer-Rope with protective buffers at constraints.
- Standardize setup families and apply SMED to systematically reduce changeovers.
- Maintain alternate routings/resources and component substitutions to increase flexibility.
- Integrate maintenance planning; align PMs with natural changeovers/campaign ends.
- Implement daily tiered huddles for rapid exception resolution; empower limited resequencing at the line.
- Keep kitting/staging time-phased with starts; respect staging space and FIFO/FEFO where required.
- Use scenario planning for rush orders/outages; predefine escalation and expedite rules.
- Track root causes for schedule misses; feed into continuous improvement and S&OP.
- Consider energy-aware scheduling to avoid peak tariffs where feasible.

## Common Challenges
- Data quality issues (inaccurate routings, setup times)
  - Solution: governance, periodic time studies, automatic feedback from MES to update standards.
- Frequent unplanned downtime
  - Solution: TPM, predictive maintenance, protective buffers at bottlenecks, alternate routing readiness.
- Material shortages or late supplies
  - Solution: tighter supplier collaboration, VMI/consignment, safety stocks at decoupling points, dynamic allocation.
- High changeover burden
  - Solution: family/campaign scheduling, SMED, product wheels, sequence rules baked into APS.
- Labor/skill gaps or absenteeism
  - Solution: cross-training matrix, flexible staffing pools, skill-based scheduling, contingent labor plans.
- Rush orders disrupting stability
  - Solution: expedite policy with cost/impact visibility, reserved capacity buffers, premium freight guidelines.
- Quality holds/rework variability
  - Solution: design-in quality gates in schedule, rework routings and capacity plans, SPC to reduce variability.
- Space and staging constraints
  - Solution: limit WIP, pull systems, staggered kitting, visual controls for staging capacity.
- Over-reliance on manual scheduling
  - Solution: implement APS/MES integration, train planners, automate rules/alerts.

## Performance Metrics
- Schedule adherence
  - Start/finish adherence (%) by work center and by frozen zone.
- On-time order completion (OTD/OTIF) within horizon.
- Throughput vs plan and bottleneck utilization.
- Changeover performance: number, time variance vs standard.
- Overtime hours vs target and cost impact.
- Schedule stability: number of changes inside frozen zone; reschedule frequency.
- Material readiness: percent orders with full kit at T-Buffer; shortages per 100 orders.
- Planning cycle time: time to generate and publish schedule.
- Queue and WIP metrics: average queue time, WIP turns, aging WIP.
- Exception rate: alerts per day and mean time to resolution.
- Data quality KPIs: percent routings complete/accurate; delta plan vs actual times.

## Technology and Tools
- ERP/MRP: SAP S/4HANA PP, Oracle Fusion Cloud, Microsoft D365, Infor, Epicor for orders, BOMs, routings.
- APS/FCS: SAP PP/DS, Siemens Opcenter APS (Preactor), DELMIA Ortems, PlanetTogether, Blue Yonder, Kinaxis, OMP, AspenTech for finite scheduling and optimization.
- MES: Siemens Opcenter Execution, Rockwell FactoryTalk, AVEVA, Ignition, Plex for dispatching and feedback.
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo for maintenance windows and outages.
- WMS: Manhattan, Blue Yonder, SAP EWM for kitting and staging execution.
- Analytics/BI: Power BI, Tableau for KPI dashboards; schedule adherence monitoring.
- Supporting capabilities: Gantt visualizers, constraint-based optimizers (MILP/heuristics), simulation/what-if engines, IoT integrations for real-time machine status, document control for setup instructions.

Process Details:
# 4.3.1.4 Schedule production orders and create lots

## Overview
This process translates planned demand into executable, capacity-feasible production orders and logical production lots/batches. It defines when and where each product will be made, how operations will sequence across resources, and how items are grouped into lots to optimize changeovers, compliance, and traceability. The process connects demand and materials plans (MRP/MPS) with shop-floor execution, ensuring orders are firmed and scheduled with consideration of resource availability, material readiness, maintenance windows, quality requirements, and regulatory constraints.

Primary objectives:
- Create firm production orders and production lots that meet due dates within capacity and material constraints.
- Sequence and load operations on work centers/lines for efficient throughput and minimal changeover time.
- Provide a clear, communicated dispatch schedule to operations, warehouse, quality, and maintenance.

Organizational role:
- Serves as the gate between planning and execution, balancing service, cost, and asset utilization.
- Drives daily/weekly production stability, traceability (via lot control), and compliance (e.g., cleaning campaigns, allergens, GMP).

## Key Activities
- Convert planned orders into firmed production orders.
- Determine lot sizes and create production lots/batches (including campaigns/family groupings).
- Allocate and reserve materials; perform availability checks (ATP/CTP).
- Perform finite/constraint-based capacity scheduling and sequencing of operations.
- Coordinate with maintenance for downtime and with quality for sampling/hold requirements.
- Resolve capacity and material conflicts (split/merge orders, alternate resources, overtime, subcontracting).
- Approve and communicate the production schedule and dispatch lists.
- Replan/resequence in response to changes (demand updates, supply delays, breakdowns).

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Firmed MPS, planned orders from MRP, and/or sales/customer orders (due dates, quantities, priorities).
  - Item master data: BOMs, production versions/alternate BOMs, routings/operations (setup/run/labor standards), yields/scrap, lot control/serialization rules, shelf life.
  - Resource data: work centers/lines, calendars and shifts, capacities, tooling/fixture availability, changeover matrix, setup families, cleaning requirements.
  - Inventory and supply: on-hand and reserved stock, open purchase orders/expected receipts with confirmed dates, safety stocks, quality status (released/on hold).
  - Maintenance data: planned downtime, maintenance work orders, constraints.
  - Quality/compliance: sampling plans, inspection points, regulatory batch size ranges, genealogy requirements, allergen/campaign rules.
  - Constraints and policies: lot sizing rules (fixed lot, minimum/maximum, period order quantity), time fences, frozen zones, lead-time offsets, overtime policies, subcontract options.
- Prerequisites:
  - Master data validated and current (BOM/routing/revision effectivity, calendars).
  - Agreed planning horizons and time fences (frozen, slushy, flexible).
  - Approved change notices/ECNs incorporated or time-phased.
  - Integrated system connectivity among ERP/MES/WMS/CMMS/QA systems.
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Demand planning and MPS finalization (4.1/4.2).
  - Procurement and inbound material scheduling (4.2).
  - Maintenance planning and scheduling (4.3.1.x).
  - Quality planning and release processes (4.3.x).
  - Engineering change management.

## Process Steps
1. Trigger and scope
   - Receive scheduling trigger (end-of-day MRP run, weekly cycle, urgent order).
   - Confirm scheduling horizon (e.g., 2 weeks frozen, 4 weeks slushy, 8 weeks forecast).

2. Consolidate demand and candidate orders
   - Review planned orders, customer orders, and safety stock replenishments.
   - Filter by make-to-order vs make-to-stock policies; identify orders needing firming.

3. Validate master data and constraints
   - Check BOM/routing versions and effectivity dates.
   - Confirm work center calendars, shifts, and maintenance windows.
   - Load changeover matrices and campaign rules (e.g., allergen → non-allergen only).

4. Determine lot sizing strategy
   - Apply policy by item/family: fixed lot size, EOQ, MOQ/MPQ, period order quantity, dynamic lot sizing (Wagner-Whitin/least unit cost), regulatory min/max batch sizes.
   - Consider demand variability, shelf life, yields, and storage limits.
   - Decide on lot splitting/merging for capacity balance and due date adherence.

5. Create production lots/batches
   - Group orders into lots by product family, formulation, color, or tooling to minimize changeovers.
   - For process/campaign planning, define campaign length, sequence, and cleaning cycles.
   - Assign unique lot/batch IDs with traceability attributes (SLED, genealogy requirements).

6. Material availability check and allocation
   - Run ATP/CTP/CTM checks for all components and packaging.
   - Allocate/reserve materials to planned lots; identify shortages and alternatives (substitute parts, expedite, split lots).
   - Validate quality release status and sampling/inspection needs.

7. Capacity and sequencing
   - Choose scheduling direction: backward (to meet due date) or forward (from earliest start).
   - Run finite capacity scheduling with operation-level constraints (setup/run/queue/transfer times, overlaps).
   - Apply sequencing rules (earliest due date, minimum changeover, campaign-first, critical ratio).
   - Evaluate alternate routings/resources; check tooling and operator skill constraints.

8. Resolve conflicts and optimize
   - If overcapacity or material shortfalls: split/merge lots, resequence, move to alternate resource, schedule overtime, subcontract, adjust due dates with customer agreement, add protective capacity.
   - Iterate with what-if scenarios; choose best schedule per objectives (OTIF, utilization, changeover cost, WIP limits).

9. Firm and approve orders
   - Convert planned orders to firm production orders with assigned lots, quantities, and dates.
   - Route for approval where required (production, materials, quality, maintenance).
   - Lock frozen-zone orders; apply schedule stability rules.

10. Communicate and publish the schedule
   - Generate and distribute dispatch lists by work center/line.
   - Publish Gantt views, load charts, and changeover plans.
   - Issue pick lists/material staging requests to warehouse; reserve tooling/fixtures.
   - Communicate sampling/inspection points and holds to QA.

11. Prepare for execution
   - Create shop packets/travelers, barcodes/labels, and electronic work instructions.
   - Update MES with operation sequences, parameters, and lot genealogy settings.
   - Confirm maintenance and cleaning tasks aligned with schedule.

12. Monitor and replan
   - Conduct daily stand-ups to review adherence, shortages, and exceptions.
   - Re-sequence within slushy/flexible horizons for breakdowns, rush orders, or late supplies.
   - Track deviations and capture reasons for continuous improvement.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Firmed production orders with:
  - Assigned work centers/resources, start/finish dates, operation sequences, and priorities.
  - Lot/batch IDs, sizes, and campaign grouping.
- Material reservations and pick/staging requests with timing.
- Dispatch lists, Gantt schedules, capacity/load reports, changeover/cleaning plans.
- Tooling/fixture and labor allocations; maintenance/cleaning reservations.
- QA sampling/inspection plan aligned to lots.
- Exception list (shortages, overcapacity, risks).
- Success criteria:
  - Feasible schedule within capacity and material constraints; on-time completion projected ≥ target.
  - Minimal reschedules within frozen zone; agreed service-level attainment.
  - Compliance with regulatory lot sizing, traceability, and cleaning requirements.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Master Scheduler: Owns finite schedule, sequencing rules, and approval; manages time fences and plan stability.
- Production Planner/MRP Controller: Converts planned to firm orders; sets lot sizes; coordinates materials availability.
- Production Supervisor/Line Lead: Validates resource feasibility; executes dispatch lists; provides feedback on constraints.
- Materials/Warehouse: Stages components; confirms reservations; manages kitting and returns.
- Quality Assurance/Control: Defines sampling/inspection requirements; releases/holds lots; ensures compliance rules.
- Maintenance Planner: Communicates downtime; aligns PM/CM with schedule; reserves technicians/tools.
- Process/Manufacturing Engineer: Maintains routings, standards, changeover matrices; validates alternate routings.
- Procurement/Supplier Scheduler: Confirms inbound dates; expedites shortages; manages vendor capacity for subcontracting.
- IT/Systems Admin: Ensures ERP/MES/APS integration, data accuracy, and reporting.
- Customer Service/S&OP: Communicates customer priorities; approves due date changes.

## Best Practices
- Maintain high-quality master data (BOMs, routings, yields, calendars) with governance and effective dating.
- Use finite, constraint-based scheduling and align with true constraints (materials, capacity, tooling, skills).
- Apply time fences and a frozen schedule window to stabilize operations.
- Implement campaign planning for high-changeover environments; use changeover matrices and SMED to reduce setup time.
- Align schedule with maintenance and cleaning; plan micro-downtime windows proactively.
- Integrate ATP/CTP with scheduling to avoid infeasible commitments; coordinate closely with procurement for critical parts.
- Employ scenario planning/sandboxes to evaluate alternatives before committing.
- Right-size lots considering demand variability, shelf life, storage, and regulatory min/max batch sizes.
- Communicate visually (dispatch boards, Gantt charts, Andon) and run daily tiered meetings.
- Track reasons for reschedules and misses; drive continuous improvement actions.
- Ensure robust lot genealogy and traceability, including rework/scrap handling.
- Standardize sequencing rules but allow controlled overrides with documented rationales.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Inaccurate master data → Establish master data governance, audits, and change control; tie KPI penalties to data defects.
- Frequent demand changes → Use time fences and ATP rules; maintain protective capacity; deploy fast re-planning cadence.
- Material shortages → Implement supplier collaboration and visibility; safety lead times for risk parts; qualified substitutes.
- Long changeovers/high mix → Campaign planning, SMED, product family sequencing, pre-staging/quick-change tooling.
- Resource conflicts and skill constraints → Cross-train operators; maintain skills matrix in scheduler; define alternates.
- Unplanned downtime → Integrate CMMS with APS; predictive maintenance; buffer critical resources.
- Quality holds/rework → Plan QA capacity; incorporate inspection steps in schedule; pre-approve rework routings.
- Regulatory constraints (GMP, allergens) → Enforce cleaning sequences; validated batch sizes; electronic batch records.
- Multi-site coordination → Use global ATP/CTP; shared capacity visibility; clear make/buy/transfer rules.
- Plan instability → Freeze windows; limit overrides; measure schedule adherence and reschedule counts.

## Performance Metrics
- Schedule adherence:
  - Adherence to planned start/finish times (%).
  - Orders started/completed on or before due date (% OTIF).
  - Number of reschedules per order per week.
- Capacity/utilization:
  - Load vs capacity by resource (%), overtime hours, bottleneck utilization.
  - Changeover time as % of available time; average changeover duration.
- Flow and efficiency:
  - Average queue time per operation, WIP levels, cycle time vs standard.
  - Throughput and line takt attainment.
- Material readiness:
  - Shortages at start (% orders with full kit), expedites count, component-related delays.
- Lot quality/compliance:
  - First-pass yield, scrap/rework rate vs plan.
  - Lot genealogy completeness, EBR right-first-time.
- Stability and predictability:
  - Frozen zone violations, schedule stability index.
  - Forecast error impact on schedule (orders moved due to demand change).
- Cost and service:
  - Premium freight/expedite cost due to schedule; subcontracting cost.
  - Customer service level for make-to-order lines.

Targets should be tiered (daily/weekly) and tied to tiered accountability.

## Technology and Tools
- ERP/MRP: SAP S/4HANA PP/PP-DS, SAP ECC PP, Oracle Fusion/Cloud SCM, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Supply Chain.
- APS/Scheduling: Siemens Opcenter APS (Preactor), Asprova, Blue Yonder, Kinaxis, AspenTech (process industries), PlanetTogether.
- MES: Siemens Opcenter Execution, Rockwell FactoryTalk ProductionCentre, Aveva/MES, Ignition MES modules.
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Infor EAM for maintenance integration.
- WMS/Kanban: SAP EWM, Manhattan, Blue Yonder WMS, eKanban systems for staging.
- QA/LIMS/EBR: LabVantage, LabWare, MasterControl, Werum PAS-X for regulated batch records.
- IIoT/Data: Machine connectivity (OPC UA), OEE dashboards, digital twins for what-if scenarios.
- Visualization/Reporting: Gantt boards, load charts, Power BI/Tableau dashboards for schedule KPIs.
- Shop-floor enablement: Barcode/RFID for lot tracking, electronic work instructions, label management (NiceLabel/Loftware).

These tools enable integrated, real-time scheduling that is material- and capacity-aware, supports regulatory traceability, and provides the visibility needed to execute reliably and improve continuously.

Process Details:
## Overview
Request Unplanned Maintenance is the rapid-response process used to capture, triage, prioritize, and schedule urgent maintenance work needed to address unexpected equipment failures or safety-critical conditions during production. Its purpose is to minimize production downtime, protect people and assets, and restore equipment to safe, compliant operation as quickly as possible—while maintaining control, documentation, and coordination with production scheduling.

This process sits within Schedule Production and ensures that emergency/urgent maintenance is integrated into the production plan, that specialized personnel are mobilized, and that safety and quality requirements are met. It feeds accurate data to the CMMS/EAM for traceability, reliability analysis, and continuous improvement.

## Key Activities
- Detect and notify: Identify breakdown or imminent failure, create an unplanned maintenance request in CMMS, and alert responsible parties.
- Triage and prioritize: Assess severity, safety risk, production impact, and assign a priority code with target response/repair times.
- Approve and authorize: Validate the request, confirm emergency classification, and secure approvals per authority matrix.
- Coordinate with production: Align on equipment isolation, downtime window, and production schedule impact.
- Plan-at-speed: Rapidly define scope, required skills, permits, parts, tools, and access conditions; check warranty or vendor support.
- Assign and schedule: Route to specialized personnel, assign an on-call/standby team, and schedule the job start within SLA.
- Prepare logistics: Reserve parts, arrange permits (e.g., LOTO, hot work), mobilize test equipment and tools, and secure access.
- Communicate and escalate: Provide status updates, manage escalations, and document decisions.
- Handover to execution: Release the approved and ready work order to the maintenance supervisor/technicians for execution; coordinate functional testing and return-to-service with quality and production.
- Closeout and learn: Capture failure codes, downtime, materials, costs; trigger RCA if thresholds are met; update preventive strategies and spares.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs
  - Breakdown signal: operator report, SCADA/IIoT alarm, QA hold, vibration/thermal anomaly, or inspection finding.
  - Asset master data: equipment ID, location, criticality, BOM, maintenance history, warranty status.
  - Production context: current job/lot, takt rate, planned changeovers, batch integrity requirements.
  - Safety context: known hazards, energy sources, MSDS, isolation points.
  - Resource availability: on-call roster, skill matrix, vendor contracts, MRO inventory status.

- Prerequisites
  - CMMS/EAM configured for unplanned work types, priority codes, failure codes, SLAs, routing rules.
  - Defined authority matrix for emergency approvals and spending thresholds.
  - EHS procedures for emergency response and permits (LOTO, confined space, hot work).
  - Communication channels (andon, radio, paging/escalation lists) and a single point of contact.
  - Trained personnel on rapid triage, safe isolation, and incident reporting.

- Dependencies on other processes
  - Production scheduling and control (to secure downtime windows and update the master schedule).
  - MRO inventory management and procurement (to source critical spares).
  - EHS/Permit-to-Work management.
  - Quality control (post-repair verification, product release/hold).
  - Vendor/contractor management (for OEM callouts).
  - Finance/costing (capture of maintenance costs).
  - Reliability engineering/RCM (RCA and preventive strategy adjustments).

## Process Steps
1. Detect and stabilize
   - Operator observes failure or alarm triggers; immediately perform safe-stop/containment actions per SOP.
   - Activate andon/emergency maintenance call; notify production supervisor and maintenance coordinator.

2. Create request in CMMS
   - Record asset, symptoms, when/frequency, error codes, impact, and immediate safety concerns.
   - Attach photos/condition data; classify as Unplanned–Emergency or Unplanned–Urgent.

3. Triage and risk assessment
   - Maintenance coordinator reviews within defined response time (e.g., ≤5 minutes for emergency).
   - Conduct a quick risk assessment (safety, environmental, compliance, product quality) and operational impact.
   - Determine preliminary cause and whether continued operation is possible at reduced capacity.

4. Prioritize and set targets
   - Assign priority code with SLA (e.g., P1 respond ≤15 min, restore ≤2 hours; P2 respond ≤1 hour, restore ≤8 hours).
   - Confirm with production supervisor; if misclassified, downgrade/upgrade with rationale.

5. Approve and authorize
   - Obtain authorization per authority matrix (maintenance supervisor or duty manager).
   - Pre-authorize overtime/callout and spending thresholds as needed.

6. Check constraints and options
   - Verify safety requirements and need for permits; identify isolation points (LOTO).
   - Check warranty/OEM obligations, service contracts, and vendor availability.
   - Assess spares/tools/test equipment availability; propose workarounds or temporary repairs if needed.

7. Rapid plan (fit-for-purpose)
   - Define scope of work, skill requirements, crew size, estimated duration, and acceptance criteria.
   - Identify necessary parts from asset BOM; reserve/issue from stores or trigger urgent procurement.
   - Prepare permits (electrical isolation, hot work, confined space), JSA, and method statement.
   - Determine testing/validation steps with quality (e.g., calibration, functional checks).

8. Coordinate production impact
   - Agree downtime window, isolate equipment, and remove WIP if required to protect product integrity.
   - Update production schedule and notify stakeholders (scheduler, shift lead, logistics).

9. Assign and schedule work order
   - Create/convert request to work order with clear priority, scope, and attachments.
   - Route to specialized personnel based on skill matrix; dispatch on-call team if after-hours.
   - Place work order in “Ready to Execute” and schedule immediate start within SLA.

10. Mobilize and permit
   - Issue permits and complete LOTO; confirm job briefing and toolbox talk.
   - Stage parts, tools, and access equipment at point of use; confirm all safety controls in place.

11. Execute handover and monitor
   - Handover to maintenance supervisor/lead tech to begin repair.
   - Coordinator tracks progress, communicates ETA and blockers to production; escalates if SLA at risk.

12. Verification and return-to-service
   - On completion, perform functional testing; involve quality if required.
   - Remove LOTO per procedure; restore equipment; perform trial run and monitor.

13. Document and close
   - Record failure codes, root cause hypothesis, actual time, materials, and costs in CMMS.
   - Capture downtime start/stop, affected orders/batches, and scrap impact.
   - Close work order or convert to follow-up planned work if permanent fix deferred.

14. Learn and improve
   - Trigger RCA when thresholds met (repeat failures, high cost/downtime, safety incidents).
   - Update PM/PdM tasks, SOPs, spare min/max, and job plans; feed insights to reliability program.
   - Communicate lessons learned in shift handover and weekly review.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Outputs
  - Logged and approved unplanned maintenance request and work order with priority and SLA.
  - Agreed downtime plan integrated into production schedule.
  - Issued permits and safety documentation; LOTO records.
  - Assigned specialized personnel; mobilization plan; reserved/issued parts.
  - Status updates and escalation records; communication to stakeholders.

- Deliverables
  - Completed repair or interim safe state; equipment returned to service.
  - CMMS record with failure codes, labor hours, materials, and costs.
  - Post-repair verification results and quality release (if applicable).
  - RCA report or improvement actions (when triggered).

- Success criteria
  - Response and restoration within SLA; minimized downtime impact on customer orders.
  - Zero safety or environmental incidents; full compliance with permits.
  - Accurate, timely documentation enabling reliability analysis.
  - First-time fix or effective temporary mitigation leading to stable operations.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Operator/Requester: Detect issue, perform safe stop, create request with clear details, support triage.
- Production Supervisor/Scheduler: Approve downtime, align schedule, communicate impact, authorize priority changes.
- Maintenance Coordinator/Dispatcher: Triage, prioritize, approve per matrix, plan-at-speed, assign, communicate, escalate.
- Maintenance Planner/Scheduler: Rapid parts check, job plan retrieval, permit coordination, schedule integration.
- Maintenance Supervisor/Lead Technician: Accept work, ensure safe execution readiness, brief team, coordinate with EHS/quality.
- Specialized Technicians (electrical, mechanical, instrumentation, controls): Execute repair; document findings.
- EHS Officer: Assess risk, issue permits, verify controls, oversee compliance.
- Quality Engineer/Inspector: Define/perform verification tests; release equipment/product holds as needed.
- Stores/MRO: Confirm availability, issue/kit spares and tools, trigger urgent buys.
- Procurement/Vendor Manager: Expedite critical spares/services; manage OEM callouts and warranties.
- Reliability Engineer: Analyze failure data, lead RCA, update maintenance strategies and spares policies.
- IT/CMMS Administrator: Ensure system availability, mobile access, notification/escalation rules.
- Plant/Shift Manager: Resolve conflicts, approve overtime/costs, support escalations.

## Best Practices
- Safety first: Enforce strict LOTO and permit-to-work; require toolbox talks for all emergency jobs.
- Clear priority schema: Standardize priority codes with response/repair SLAs and apply consistently; audit for misuse.
- Single point of contact: Use a dispatcher model to coordinate requests and reduce communication gaps.
- Skill-based routing and on-call rosters: Maintain up-to-date skill matrices and ensure 24/7 specialized coverage.
- Rapid planning discipline: Maintain ready-to-use job plans for common failures; pre-kit critical spares and tools.
- Criticality-driven decisions: Use asset criticality to guide prioritization, spares stocking, and escalation paths.
- Data quality: Mandate completion of failure codes, cause/remedy, and parts used; use mobile CMMS to capture at source.
- Vendor readiness: Keep OEM service agreements current; pre-authorize callout procedures and NDAs/site access.
- Integrated communications: Link andon/SCADA alerts to CMMS tickets; use automated paging/escalation for P1 events.
- Post-incident learning: Conduct quick after-action reviews; trigger RCA for repeat/high-impact failures; implement countermeasures.
- Protect product integrity: Define QA checks and hold/release protocols post-maintenance; document any deviations.
- Control emergency work ratio: Set targets for emergency vs. total maintenance hours; drive reduction through PdM/RCM.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Overuse of “emergency” classification: Implement gating criteria and supervisor approval; review weekly and coach.
- Parts unavailability: Maintain critical spares list and min/max; use vendor stocking agreements and consignment; enable 24/7 parts access.
- Permit delays: Pre-authorize templates and digital permit workflows; train cross-functional approvers; stage LOTO kits.
- Communication lapses: Use standard status updates (e.g., every 30–60 minutes), escalation matrix, and incident channels.
- Vendor/OEM delays: Keep multiple qualified vendors; remote diagnostics enablement; contract SLAs with penalties.
- Incomplete requests: Provide operator checklists and mobile forms with mandatory fields and photos.
- Conflicting production priorities: Use a formal decision matrix with plant manager arbitration; quantify cost-of-delay.
- Repeat failures: Trigger RCA after N occurrences or downtime threshold; implement design changes and PM updates.
- Documentation gaps at night/weekends: Enforce mobile CMMS use; brief shift leads on minimum documentation standards.
- Safety shortcuts under pressure: Visible leadership reinforcement; stop-work authority; audit emergency jobs.

## Performance Metrics
- Response time (request to triage start; request to technician arrival) by priority.
- Mean time to repair (MTTR) for unplanned events; distribution by asset and failure mode.
- Downtime hours and production impact (lost units, OEE hit) attributable to unplanned maintenance.
- SLA compliance rate for P1/P2 jobs.
- First-time fix rate; rework/rollback rate within 72 hours of repair.
- Ratio of emergency hours to total maintenance hours.
- Parts availability rate (critical spares fill rate); urgent procurement lead time.
- Safety and compliance metrics (permit adherence, LOTO violations, incidents).
- Data quality completeness (failure codes, cause/remedy, time and materials captured).
- Repeat failure rate for top assets; time between failures (MTBF) trend.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Oracle eAM, Infor EAM for requests, work orders, parts, costs, and KPIs.
- Mobile maintenance apps: For on-the-spot request creation, attachments, time/materials capture, digital signatures.
- IIoT/SCADA/Condition monitoring: Automated alerts and diagnostics; vibration, thermal, oil analysis integrations to trigger requests.
- Andon/Alarm systems: Visual and audible alerts integrated with dispatching workflows.
- Permit-to-Work and LOTO systems: Digital permits, isolation point libraries, e-signatures.
- Scheduling/APS: Integration with production planning to reflect downtime and reschedule orders.
- MRO inventory systems: Real-time stock, reservations, kitting, and urgent PO creation.
- Communication and escalation: Paging, radios, MS Teams/Slack, automated call trees.
- Knowledge base: Digital job plans, SOPs, troubleshooting guides, and past failure remedies.
- Test and diagnostic equipment: Calibrated multimeters, analyzers, portable vibration/thermal cameras.
- Access/security systems: Badge access for vendors, visitor management, contractor induction modules.

This process, executed with rigor and speed, ensures unplanned maintenance is safely controlled, rapidly scheduled, and effectively coordinated with production to protect throughput, quality, and asset health.

[5.1.2.1] Define service delivery goals
Level: 4

Process Details:
## Overview
Define service delivery goals is the process of translating customer needs, business strategy, and operational realities into a concise set of SMARTER goals that guide how services are delivered. These goals describe the outcomes the organization will achieve for customers (experience, quality, timeliness, accessibility), for the business (cost, revenue, risk, compliance), and for operations (capacity, productivity, reliability).

Purpose:
- Align service delivery with customer expectations and corporate strategy.
- Provide a clear north star for service owners, resource planning, and improvement initiatives.
- Establish measurable targets that drive prioritization, funding, and accountability.

Role in the organization:
- Sits within Develop service delivery strategies and informs policies, SLAs/OLAs/SLOs, service design, capacity planning, budgeting, training, and performance management.
- Feeds governance by defining what success looks like and how it is measured and reviewed.

## Key Activities
- Synthesize inputs: customer insights (VoC), market benchmarks, historical performance, regulatory requirements, and strategic priorities.
- Segment customers and map journeys to identify critical-to-quality (CTQ) attributes.
- Define goal themes (e.g., experience, reliability, speed, cost-to-serve, accessibility, compliance, sustainability).
- Draft SMARTER goals and OKRs/KPIs with baselines and targets.
- Assess feasibility, risks, and trade-offs; align with capacity and budget.
- Socialize, refine, and secure governance approval.
- Cascade goals into SLAs/OLAs/SLOs and team-level objectives, with a review cadence.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Corporate strategy, mission/vision, risk appetite, and financial targets.
- Service portfolio/catalog and current service blueprints.
- Voice-of-Customer data: CSAT/NPS/CES, complaints, churn, usage analytics, sentiment.
- Historical performance: SLA attainment, response/resolve times, first-contact resolution, uptime, backlog, error/defect rates, MTTR.
- Market/competitor benchmarks and industry standards.
- Regulatory/compliance requirements (e.g., privacy, accessibility, sector regulations).
- Resource and capacity data: staffing, skills, tooling, budget, technology roadmap.
- Risk register and known constraints.

Prerequisites:
- Service delivery governance model defined (decision rights, approval forums, review cadence).
- Agreed measurement framework and data availability (definitions, data sources, quality).
- Identified customer segments and priority personas.
- Designated service owners and accountability structures.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 5.1 Establish service delivery governance and strategies (provides governance, policies).
- 5.1.2 Develop service delivery strategies (parent process; this is an early output feeding policies and procedures).
- 5.2 Manage service resources (capacity and budget constraints).
- 5.3 Plan service delivery and 5.4 Measure service performance (use the goals to plan and measure).
- Risk management/compliance processes (to validate feasibility and controls).

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and scope
- Confirm purpose, timelines, services in scope, and decision-makers.
- Define success criteria for the goal-setting cycle.

2) Gather and validate inputs
- Compile strategy, VoC, performance data, regulatory requirements, and benchmarks.
- Validate data quality and resolve gaps; create a baseline snapshot.

3) Segment and map customer journeys
- Identify priority customer segments and journeys.
- Extract pain points and desired outcomes; define CTQs (e.g., “on-time,” “first-time-right”).

4) Identify goal themes and value drivers
- Group needs into themes: experience, speed, reliability, quality, cost-to-serve, accessibility/inclusion, safety/privacy, sustainability, innovation.
- Link each theme to business value levers (retention, conversion, margin, risk).

5) Draft candidate goals
- Write SMARTER goal statements for each theme.
- For each goal, specify baseline, target, time horizon, owner, and assumptions.
- Use both outcome and operational/behavioral indicators.

6) Define measurement and data plan
- Select KPIs/OKRs; define formulas, data sources, collection frequency, and segmentation.
- Establish leading and lagging indicators and set thresholds/SLAs/SLOs with error budgets where relevant.

7) Feasibility and impact analysis
- Assess capacity, technology, process, and change impacts; identify dependencies.
- Quantify expected benefits and costs (simple business case); run scenario/bandwidth checks.
- Review regulatory and risk implications; define controls.

8) Prioritize and resolve trade-offs
- Apply a prioritization method (e.g., weighted scoring against impact, effort, risk, strategic fit).
- Resolve conflicts (e.g., speed vs. cost) and set guardrails (minimum compliance/SLOs).

9) Stakeholder socialization and refinement
- Conduct workshops with service owners, operations, finance, CX, compliance, and IT.
- Incorporate feedback; refine targets and definitions.

10) Formalize goal charters
- For each approved goal: document purpose, scope, KPI definitions, targets, owner, initiatives, dependencies, risks, and review cadence.

11) Governance review and approval
- Present the goal set and charters to the designated forum; capture decisions and conditions.

12) Cascade and align
- Translate enterprise/service-level goals into team-level OKRs/initiatives.
- Align SLAs/OLAs/SLOs and update service catalogs/blueprints accordingly.

13) Communication and enablement
- Publish goals, definitions, and dashboards; brief teams.
- Align incentives/training and integrate into performance management.

14) Instrumentation and dashboard setup
- Implement data pipelines, tagging, and dashboards with near real-time visibility.
- Validate data accuracy and alerting thresholds.

15) Review cadence and continuous improvement
- Establish quarterly/monthly reviews; track progress and assumptions.
- Adjust goals as needed due to market, regulatory, or operational changes; maintain version control.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Approved service delivery goal set (3–7 goals) with SMARTER definitions.
- Goal charters per goal (owner, KPI definitions, baseline/targets, initiatives, risks, cadence).
- KPI/OKR dictionary and measurement plan (formulas, sources, frequency, segmentation).
- Updated SLAs/OLAs/SLOs and service catalog entries.
- Prioritization rationale and business case summaries.
- Communication pack: one-pagers, FAQs, town hall materials.
- Dashboard requirements and initial dashboards.
- Risk/dependency log and change record.

Success criteria:
- Goals are specific, measurable, feasible, and approved by governance.
- Baselines and targets are documented and traceable to data sources.
- Goals are cascaded to teams and reflected in SLAs/OLAs/SLOs.
- Dashboards are live; stakeholders can self-serve performance views.
- Early progress aligns with plan; no critical compliance gaps.

Example goal statements:
- Improve First Contact Resolution from 68% to 80% for Tier-1 incidents by Q4 FY2025, reducing average handle time variance by 20% without decreasing CSAT below 4.4/5.
- Achieve 99.9% service uptime for the Customer Portal with MTTR below 60 minutes and change failure rate under 10% by end of FY2025.
- Reduce cost-to-serve per case by 12% YoY while maintaining CSAT ≥ 4.5/5 and agent engagement ≥ 75% by Q3 FY2026.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Sets strategic direction, resolves trade-offs, approves final goals.
- Service Strategy Lead (Process Owner): Orchestrates the process, ensures alignment, manages governance and timelines.
- Service Owners: Provide service-specific insights, draft and own goals, define SLAs/OLAs/SLOs.
- Customer Experience/Success Lead: Brings VoC, journey insights, CTQs, and customer impact analysis.
- Data/Analytics Lead: Baselines, defines KPIs, validates data quality, builds dashboards.
- Operations Manager: Validates feasibility and operational impacts; identifies initiatives and capacity needs.
- Finance Business Partner: Quantifies benefits/costs and ensures alignment with budgets.
- Risk/Compliance Officer: Ensures goals and measures comply with regulatory and policy requirements.
- IT/Platform Architect: Confirms tooling and data feasibility; plans instrumentation.
- PMO/Change Manager: Plans communication, training, and change adoption; tracks delivery of enabling initiatives.
- HR/Performance Management: Aligns incentives with goals and cascades to performance plans.

## Best Practices
- Use SMARTER and OKR frameworks; keep the set focused (3–7 goals) to maintain clarity and execution.
- Balance outcome, quality, speed, cost, and risk/compliance; include both leading and lagging indicators.
- Anchor on VoC and journey maps; translate customer pain points into CTQs and goals.
- Set targets from baselines and benchmarks; avoid target-only goals without data underpinnings.
- Define unambiguous KPI formulas and data lineage; maintain a KPI dictionary.
- Establish guardrails (e.g., minimum CSAT/compliance thresholds) to prevent gaming and harmful trade-offs.
- Pilot where possible to validate feasibility and refine targets.
- Make goals visible and traceable; link to initiatives, budgets, and owners in one system of record.
- Review and adapt regularly; use quarterly business reviews to recalibrate as conditions change.
- Bake in accessibility, privacy, and security considerations from inception.

## Common Challenges
- Conflicting priorities across functions: Use a clear prioritization framework and executive arbitration.
- Data quality and availability issues: Invest early in data definitions, sources, and quality checks; document assumptions.
- Overly ambitious or vague goals: Require baselines and feasibility checks; enforce SMARTER criteria at governance gates.
- Misaligned incentives: Align performance management and rewards to the approved goals and guardrails.
- Scope creep and goal proliferation: Cap the number of goals; require business case justification for additions.
- Lack of stakeholder buy-in: Co-create goals via workshops, share customer evidence, and communicate trade-offs transparently.
- Regulatory or risk blind spots: Involve compliance early; include minimum control targets and audits.
- Change fatigue: Sequence rollouts, provide training, and celebrate wins to maintain momentum.

## Performance Metrics
Process effectiveness KPIs:
- Cycle time to define and approve goals (start to governance sign-off).
- Percentage of goals meeting SMARTER criteria at first review.
- Stakeholder satisfaction with clarity and feasibility of goals (survey score).
- Percentage of goals with baselines, targets, and owners documented.
- Time to live dashboards after goal approval.
- Number of rework iterations per goal; root causes.
- Cascade rate: percentage of teams with aligned OKRs within 30/60/90 days.
- Audit conformance to KPI definitions and data quality thresholds.

Outcome linkage KPIs (used to validate that defined goals drive performance):
- SLA/SLO attainment rate after goal implementation.
- Improvement deltas vs. baseline on targeted KPIs (e.g., CSAT, FCR, MTTR).
- Cost-to-serve trend vs. target while maintaining guardrail metrics (e.g., CSAT, quality).
- Compliance incident rate and severity related to service delivery.
- Employee engagement/productivity indices within impacted teams.

## Technology and Tools
- VoC and survey platforms: Qualtrics, Medallia, SurveyMonkey; social/listening tools.
- Analytics and dashboards: Power BI, Tableau, Looker; statistical tools (R, Python) for baselining and forecasting.
- ITSM/ESM platforms: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management for SLAs/OLAs, incident and change data.
- CRM/CDP: Salesforce, Dynamics, Adobe Experience Platform for customer segments and outcomes.
- Monitoring/observability: Datadog, New Relic, Splunk, Prometheus/Grafana for uptime, MTTR, error budgets.
- OKR/goal management: WorkBoard, Perdoo, Gtmhub, Ally.io for cascades and visibility.
- Collaboration and documentation: Confluence, SharePoint, Notion; whiteboarding with Miro/Mural.
- Project/portfolio management: Jira, Azure DevOps, Asana, Monday for initiative linkage and capacity.
- Data catalog and governance: Collibra, Alation for KPI definitions and lineage.
- Benchmark sources and standards: Industry benchmarks (e.g., HDI, ITIL-based measures), regulatory libraries.
- Accessibility/privacy compliance tools: Axe, WAVE, OneTrust.

Process Details:
## Overview
[5.1.2.6] Review and validate service delivery procedures is the structured process used to evaluate whether current service delivery procedures meet defined performance parameters, regulatory obligations, and customer expectations. When gaps are identified, procedures are revised, validated through pilots or controlled tests, and formally approved for adoption.

Purpose:
- Ensure procedures consistently enable SLA attainment, quality, safety, compliance, and customer satisfaction.
- Reduce defects, rework, and variability in service delivery.
- Provide a governed mechanism to adjust procedures based on data, feedback, and strategic changes.

Role in the organization:
- Operates within the “Develop service delivery strategies” domain, closing the loop between strategy and operational execution.
- Feeds continuous improvement and compliance management.
- Interfaces with change management, training, knowledge management, risk, and audit functions to ensure safe, controlled rollout of procedural changes.

## Key Activities
- Trigger and scoping: Detect underperformance or change drivers; define scope and objectives of review.
- Evidence gathering: Collect KPIs, SLA results, customer feedback, incident/problem trends, audit findings, and regulatory updates.
- Gap analysis: Compare “as-is” procedures against target performance, standards, and best practices.
- Risk and impact assessment: Evaluate operational, compliance, customer, and technology impacts; prioritize changes.
- Procedure redesign: Draft improved procedures, process maps, and controls; align with policies and standards.
- Validation planning: Define test criteria, pilot scope, environments, and success thresholds.
- Pilot execution and evaluation: Run controlled tests; measure against entry/exit criteria; capture lessons.
- Governance and approval: Obtain required reviews and sign-offs (e.g., CAB, compliance, service owners).
- Implementation planning: Prepare rollout plans, communications, training, cutover and rollback strategies.
- Deployment and adoption: Execute controlled rollout; monitor stabilization; resolve issues.
- Documentation and knowledge updates: Update SOPs, work instructions, KB articles, and version logs.
- Post-implementation review: Confirm benefits realization; close audit and risk items; schedule next review.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Performance data: SLA/OLA/KPI reports, control charts, capacity and utilization reports.
- Operational insights: Incident/problem records, change failure reports, major incident postmortems.
- Customer and employee feedback: CSAT/NPS/VoC, frontline suggestions, complaints.
- Compliance and risk: Audit findings, regulatory/contractual requirements, risk registers.
- Current documentation: Procedure manuals, process maps, service blueprints, RACI charts.
- Standards and policies: Quality policies (e.g., ISO 9001), ITIL/COBIT guidance, safety standards.
- Tooling data: Workflow logs, process mining outputs, monitoring dashboards.

Prerequisites:
- Defined governance model (roles, approval authorities, change thresholds).
- Document control standards and repositories (versioning, templates, metadata).
- KPI definitions, thresholds, and data quality controls.
- Access to required systems for data extraction and testing.
- Trained reviewers with relevant domain and compliance knowledge.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [5.1.2] Develop service delivery strategies (upstream alignment).
- Change management (CAB approvals, release windows).
- Risk management (assessment, mitigation, acceptance).
- Quality management and internal audit (findings, validation).
- Training and enablement (content creation, delivery).
- Knowledge management (KB updates, publication).
- Vendor/supplier management if third-party procedures are impacted.

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and Scope
- Identify trigger: KPI breach, recurring incidents, audit nonconformance, regulatory change, customer escalations, strategic shifts.
- Define scope, objectives, and success criteria; classify criticality (critical/high/medium/low).
- Register the review in the improvement/change backlog with a unique ID.

Gate 0: Scope and objectives approved by Service Delivery Manager and Process Owner.

2) Assemble Team and Plan
- Assign roles: Process Owner, QA/Compliance, Data Analyst, Operations SME, Customer Success representative, Change Manager.
- Develop a review plan: timelines, data sources, stakeholders, pilot strategy, communication approach.
- Confirm data availability and access; raise data quality issues if needed.

3) Baseline “As-Is”
- Map the current procedure: steps, roles, systems, controls, handoffs, pain points.
- Extract 3–6 months of performance and operational data; create trend and control charts.
- Identify variation sources (special vs. common cause).

4) Gap and Root-Cause Analysis
- Compare against targets, standards, and customer expectations.
- Conduct root-cause analysis (5 Whys, fishbone, Pareto, process mining).
- Document findings and hypotheses; quantify impact (frequency, severity, cost, customer impact).

Gate 1: Problem statement and target outcomes endorsed by Process Owner and QA.

5) Redesign and Risk Assessment
- Draft revised procedure, process map, control points, and acceptance criteria.
- Assess risks and controls (FMEA scoring severity/occurrence/detection; define mitigations).
- Validate compliance and privacy requirements with Compliance Officer.
- Confirm tool/system feasibility with IT/Platform teams.

Gate 2: Draft procedure and risk plan reviewed by CAB/SteerCo for pilot approval.

6) Validation Planning
- Define pilot scope and cohort, environments, and duration.
- Establish entry/exit criteria, measurement plan, and data capture methods.
- Prepare training/job aids for pilot participants; create rollback plan.

7) Pilot Execution
- Conduct pilot; monitor in near real-time via dashboards.
- Capture qualitative feedback from frontline staff and customers (if applicable).
- Log deviations, defects, and issues; implement quick fixes where low risk.

8) Evaluate Pilot and Iterate
- Analyze outcomes vs. exit criteria; compare to baseline.
- Decide: proceed, iterate, or stop/rollback based on data and risk.
- Update procedure and artifacts accordingly.

Gate 3: Pilot exit review; approval to proceed to full rollout.

9) Approval and Change Control
- Compile validation report with evidence, updated risks, and mitigations.
- Submit changes for formal approval (CAB, QA, Compliance, Information Security as needed).
- Record approvals, conditions, and effective dates in the document control system.

10) Implementation and Adoption
- Execute rollout plan (phased/big-bang as approved), honoring change windows and communication plans.
- Deliver training; ensure access to updated SOPs/KBs; track training completion.
- Monitor stabilization metrics; provide hypercare support.

11) Post-Implementation Review and Closure
- Verify performance uplift against success criteria over a defined observation period.
- Close related audit and risk items; document lessons learned.
- Update review cadence and next scheduled review date.

Gate 4: Benefits realization confirmed; process closed and archived.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Updated procedures: Approved SOPs, process maps, work instructions with new version numbers and effective dates.
- Validation artifacts: Pilot plan and results, test evidence, acceptance criteria outcomes, validation report.
- Governance records: Approval logs, change records (RFCs), risk assessments (FMEA), compliance sign-offs.
- Enablement materials: Training content, job aids, communications, updated KB articles.
- Monitoring assets: Updated KPIs/SLAs if changed, dashboards, control charts.
- Success criteria met:
  - Target KPIs achieved/stabilized within agreed tolerance.
  - Compliance requirements demonstrably satisfied.
  - Training and adoption thresholds met (e.g., 95% completion within 2 weeks).
  - No high-severity incidents attributable to the change post-implementation window.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Process Owner: Sponsors review, defines objectives, approves scope and final procedure, accountable for outcomes.
- Service Delivery Manager: Coordinates execution, resources, and stakeholder engagement; ensures operational feasibility.
- Quality/Compliance Officer: Ensures alignment with standards, regulations, and internal policies; approves compliance.
- Data Analyst/BI: Extracts and analyzes data; builds baseline and pilot performance reports.
- Operations SMEs/Team Leads: Provide frontline insights; execute pilots; validate practicality.
- Customer Success/Account Manager: Represents customer expectations; collects VoC; communicates externally as needed.
- Change Manager/CAB: Manages change control, risk evaluation, scheduling, and approvals.
- IT/Platform Owner: Assesses system impacts; implements tool/workflow changes.
- Knowledge Manager/Technical Writer: Updates documentation, KBs, and ensures version control.
- Training/L&D: Develops and delivers training; tracks completion and competency.
- Internal Audit (as required): Reviews evidence for closure of findings; provides independent assurance.
- Project/Program Manager (for complex changes): Oversees plan, RAID management, and reporting.

## Best Practices
- Anchor decisions in data; use control charts and statistical tests for before/after comparisons.
- Involve frontline staff and, where appropriate, customers in co-design and validation.
- Apply lean/Six Sigma principles: remove waste, simplify handoffs, mistake-proof critical steps.
- Use a risk-based approach: prioritize reviews for high-impact, high-risk procedures; tailor rigor accordingly.
- Pilot changes in controlled environments; maintain clear entry/exit criteria and rollback plans.
- Maintain a single source of truth for procedures with strict version control and change history.
- Standardize templates for SOPs, process maps, risk assessments, and validation reports.
- Enforce segregation of duties in reviews and approvals for objectivity.
- Schedule periodic reviews (e.g., annual for critical, biennial for non-critical) even without triggers.
- Ensure accessibility and usability of procedures; apply human factors and service blueprinting.
- Automate monitoring and alerts; integrate KPIs directly into dashboards with thresholds.

## Common Challenges
- Poor data quality or availability: Mitigate with defined data owners, quality checks, and standardized extracts.
- Stakeholder resistance to change: Use early engagement, clear rationale, benefits framing, and change champions.
- Scope creep: Enforce documented scope and gates; use a backlog for out-of-scope improvements.
- Conflicting requirements (operations vs. compliance vs. customer experience): Facilitate trade-off decisions with a decision matrix and executive sponsorship.
- Hidden workarounds and tribal knowledge: Conduct gemba walks/shadowing; incorporate insights into formal procedures.
- Tool limitations: Involve platform teams early; consider configuration vs. customization; plan interim controls.
- Training gaps: Provide concise job aids, microlearning, and on-the-job coaching; measure competency, not just completion.
- Documentation sprawl: Archive superseded content; use metadata and controlled vocabularies; deprecate duplicates.

## Performance Metrics
Effectiveness and outcomes:
- % of revised procedures meeting KPIs within X weeks of rollout.
- SLA attainment rate before vs. after change; variance to target.
- Defect/rework rate and first-time-right rate post-implementation.
- Customer satisfaction (CSAT/NPS) movement for impacted services.
- Compliance metrics: number/time to close audit findings; zero critical nonconformities.

Efficiency and timeliness:
- Cycle time from trigger to approved procedure.
- Lead time for pilot execution and analysis.
- On-time completion of scheduled reviews (%).
- Change failure rate (CFR) and mean time to recover (MTTR) for related changes.

Adoption and quality:
- Training completion rate and time-to-competency.
- Procedure adherence rate (via QA checks or process mining).
- Number of high-severity incidents linked to the changed procedure within stabilization window.
- Documentation quality score (readability, completeness, usability via stakeholder survey).

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM and workflow: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, BMC Helix for incident/problem/change linkage and approvals.
- BPM and process modeling: BPMN tools (Signavio, Bizagi, Visio) for maps and simulations.
- Analytics and BI: Power BI, Tableau, Looker; statistical tools (Minitab, R/Python) for analysis.
- Process mining: Celonis, UiPath Process Mining to identify real execution patterns and bottlenecks.
- Document and knowledge management: SharePoint, Confluence, ISO-compliant DMS; e-signature tools (DocuSign, Adobe Sign).
- Test and validation: TestRail, Zephyr; feature flagging and A/B testing (LaunchDarkly, Optimizely) where applicable.
- Monitoring and observability: Grafana, Prometheus, Splunk, ELK for real-time KPIs and alerts.
- Survey and VoC: Qualtrics, Medallia, Typeform for customer and employee feedback.
- Training and LMS: SAP SuccessFactors, Workday Learning, Docebo for training delivery and tracking.
- Collaboration and communication: MS Teams, Slack, email campaign tools for stakeholder updates.
- Risk and audit: Archer, ZenGRC, or equivalent for risk assessments and audit evidence tracking.
