# Process [7.7.7.5] Gather workforce data

## Overview
Gather workforce data is the process of collecting, validating, and provisioning internal and external workforce data to support workforce analytics and reporting. It ensures analysts have timely, high-quality, compliant datasets to answer questions on headcount, turnover, DEI, compensation, skills, talent, engagement, workforce planning, and compliance.

The process bridges source systems (HRIS, ATS, Payroll, Time & Attendance, LMS, Benefits, Engagement, VMS, ERP, facilities/badging, identity systems) and the analytics environment (data lake/warehouse/marts) through governed, secure data pipelines. It underpins downstream processes such as developing workforce analytics, generating HR metrics, and executive reporting.

## Key Activities
- Intake and scoping of data needs from stakeholders
- Source identification and evaluation (internal and external)
- Compliance, privacy, and security assessment and approvals
- Data access provisioning and vendor/partner data-sharing agreements
- Integration design (frequency, extraction method, schema, keys)
- Data extraction, landing, and incremental ingestion
- Transformation, standardization, and master data alignment
- Data quality checks, reconciliation, and issue resolution
- De-identification, masking, and aggregation as required
- Metadata, lineage, and documentation
- Scheduling/orchestration and monitoring of refresh cycles
- Access provisioning to curated datasets and ongoing support

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Documented analytics requirements (purpose, questions, time horizon, refresh cadence)
  - Target data model definitions and data dictionary (standard HR entities and fields)
  - Source system list and data catalog entries (owners, schemas, APIs, file specs)
  - Legal basis/consent for processing; privacy impact assessment (as applicable)
  - Data-sharing agreements/DPAs and vendor file specifications (for external sources)
  - IAM credentials/service accounts and network connectivity details
  - Master identifiers (global person ID, position ID, org IDs) and mapping tables
  - Retention schedule and classification policy (PII/PHI, sensitive attributes)
- Prerequisites:
  - Governance approval to process relevant data domains
  - Provisioned environments (dev/test/prod), storage, and tooling
  - Security controls: encryption at rest/in transit, key management, secret storage
  - Defined SLAs/SLOs for freshness and availability
  - Team training on privacy, data handling, and tools
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Define workforce analytics requirements (7.7.7.x)
  - Manage HR information systems and data governance
  - Access provisioning and IAM
  - Vendor onboarding and contract management
  - Master data management and metadata management
  - Incident/change management

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and scope
   - Receive intake form capturing business questions, required fields, population scope, timeframe, refresh cadence, legal basis, and consumers.
   - Assign a data owner, data engineer, and project lead.

2. Assess compliance and risk
   - Classify data (PII/sensitive) and conduct a privacy impact assessment if required.
   - Define minimization approach, de-identification/aggregation strategy, and retention.

3. Identify and evaluate sources
   - Map needs to internal systems (HRIS, ATS, Payroll, LMS, T&A, Benefits, Engagement, VMS, ERP) and external sources (benchmark/comp surveys, labor market data, background/assessment vendors, government stats).
   - Evaluate data coverage, quality, access methods, and cost.

4. Establish agreements and access
   - For external sources: finalize data-sharing agreements/DPAs including schema, cadence, SLAs, security controls, and change notification.
   - For internal sources: obtain data owner approvals; raise IAM and network access requests; create service accounts with least privilege.

5. Design the integration
   - Choose extraction method (API, webhook, ODBC/JDBC, SFTP file feed, CDC, message bus).
   - Define frequency (real-time, daily, weekly), backfill needs, and data partitioning.
   - Specify target schema aligned to standard HR data model; define keys and SCD/effective-dating approach; handle time zone/currency normalization.

6. Build extraction and landing
   - Implement connectors/API calls/queries or configure vendor file feeds.
   - Ingest to a secure landing zone; validate file formats and schema; quarantine nonconforming drops.

7. Transform and standardize
   - Apply source-to-target mappings, code translations (job families, locations, reasons), and unit conversions.
   - Resolve identifiers using MDM; deduplicate and merge.
   - Implement business rules (e.g., employee status logic, tenure calculation) and history management (SCD Type 2/effective dates).

8. Data quality and reconciliation
   - Run automated checks (completeness, conformity, validity, uniqueness, integrity).
   - Reconcile counts/totals with source systems (e.g., headcount by org, payroll totals).
   - Investigate and remediate issues; create feedback loops with source owners.

9. Privacy controls
   - Apply masking, tokenization, or aggregation as designed; segregate PII from analytical views where feasible.
   - Enforce row/column-level security policies.

10. Load curated datasets
    - Publish cleansed, conformed datasets to the analytics store (lakehouse/warehouse/marts).
    - Register datasets, schemas, and lineage in the data catalog.

11. Orchestrate and monitor
    - Schedule refresh pipelines; configure alerts for delays, failures, or DQ breaches.
    - Define SLAs and incident response runbooks.

12. Provision access
    - Grant access based on RBAC/ABAC with approvals; enable data usage logging.

13. User acceptance and sign-off
    - Conduct stakeholder UAT; validate key metrics; obtain formal sign-off.

14. Operationalize and improve
    - Transition to steady-state operations; maintain documentation; review metrics and optimize cost/performance.
    - Implement change management for source schema or contract changes.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Curated datasets ready for analysis (e.g., employee master, org hierarchy, job/position, compensation, headcount snapshots, hires/exits, time/attendance, learning, engagement, skills)
- Source-to-target mapping documentation and transformation logic
- Data dictionary and business definitions
- Data quality scorecards and reconciliation reports
- Metadata and data lineage records (catalog entries)
- Integration schedules, SLAs, and runbooks
- Access control records and approvals
- Contracts/DPAs and vendor feed specifications
- Audit-ready logs (access, processing, incident records)
- Success criteria:
  - Meets defined completeness/accuracy thresholds and freshness SLAs
  - Privacy and security controls verified; no critical audit findings
  - Stakeholder UAT sign-off; documented and cataloged datasets
  - Stable operations with monitored pipelines and low incident rates

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Business Requestor/Stakeholder: Defines questions, scope, and acceptance criteria; participates in UAT.
- HR Analytics Lead: Translates requirements; prioritizes requests; ensures analytical fitness-for-purpose.
- HR Data Engineer/Integration Engineer: Designs/builds/operates pipelines; implements transformations and DQ checks.
- HRIS Analyst/System Owner: Provides source expertise; approves access; supports reconciliation.
- Data Steward (HR Data): Maintains definitions, standards, and DQ rules; triages data issues.
- Data Architect: Defines target models and integration patterns; ensures scalability and alignment to enterprise architecture.
- Privacy Officer/Legal: Reviews DPIA/DPAs; approves processing purposes and controls.
- Information Security: Assesses security posture; enforces encryption, access, and monitoring standards.
- Vendor Manager/Procurement: Manages external data contracts, SLAs, and change notices.
- IAM Administrator: Provisions identities, roles, and access controls.
- Data Quality Analyst: Designs and monitors DQ checks; reports scorecards.
- PM/Scrum Master: Plans and tracks delivery; manages risks and communications.
- Operations/Support (SRE): Monitors jobs; handles incidents; maintains runbooks and on-call.

## Best Practices
- Align to a standard HR data model with global identifiers for person, position, org, and location.
- Implement effective-dated and slowly changing dimensions to preserve history.
- Minimize PII; prefer aggregated or pseudonymized datasets for analytics.
- Use data contracts and a schema registry for internal and vendor feeds; test for schema drift.
- Automate pipelines with CI/CD, infrastructure-as-code, and versioned configurations.
- Establish robust DQ and reconciliation frameworks with automated alerts.
- Separate landing, raw, curated, and presentation layers; enforce environment isolation.
- Handle global nuances: time zones, calendars, currencies, and local code mappings.
- Maintain comprehensive metadata, lineage, and business definitions in a catalog.
- Define clear SLAs/SLOs for freshness and availability; monitor and report.
- Pilot integrations and backfill with sampling before full-scale loads.
- Enforce least-privilege access with row/column-level security and detailed logging.
- Implement retention and deletion schedules; support data subject rights processes.
- Build change management: upstream change notifications, backward compatibility, and rollback plans.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Inconsistent definitions across systems: Establish canonical definitions and stewardship; maintain mapping tables.
- Missing or duplicate identifiers: Introduce global IDs; use MDM and survivorship rules.
- Poor data quality and gaps: Define DQ rules; implement escalation paths with source owners; monitor scorecards.
- Access and approval delays: Standardize intake and pre-approved data domains; maintain reusable service accounts.
- Vendor feed volatility or schema drift: Contractual change notice periods; schema registry; contract testing.
- Manual files and ad hoc extracts: Move to scheduled, validated feeds; provide validation portals and templates.
- Privacy constraints limiting data use: Apply de-identification/aggregation; obtain documented legal basis; limit access.
- Organizational hierarchy complexity and frequent reorgs: Use effective dating; compute as-of hierarchies with loop checks.
- Global/local variations (e.g., legal entities, holidays): Maintain localization metadata and normalization rules.
- Refresh reliability and latency: Design for idempotency and retries; adopt CDC where available; monitor end-to-end latency.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs)
- Time-to-first-data: days from approved request to initial delivery
- Freshness lag: time between source update and availability in analytics
- Completeness: percentage of required fields populated; population coverage
- Accuracy/Validity: rule pass rate; reconciliation variance vs. source (e.g., headcount ±0.5%)
- Pipeline reliability: success rate, failure rate, MTTR, on-time runs (% SLA met)
- Incident rate: DQ or pipeline incidents per period; severity distribution
- Change responsiveness: time to adapt to source/schema changes
- Stakeholder satisfaction: CSAT/NPS for delivered datasets
- Compliance: number of audit findings, privacy incidents, and access violations
- Metadata coverage: percentage of datasets with complete catalog entries and lineage
- Cost efficiency: run cost per refresh/integration; storage utilization efficiency

## Technology and Tools
- Source systems (examples): Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle HCM; ATS (Greenhouse, Taleo, Workday); Payroll (ADP, Workday, SAP); Time & Attendance (UKG/Kronos); LMS (Cornerstone, Degreed); Engagement (Qualtrics, Glint); VMS (Beeline, Fieldglass); ERP/Finance; IAM (Okta, Azure AD); Facilities/Badging.
- Integration and orchestration: ETL/ELT (Informatica, Talend, Fivetran, Stitch), transformation (dbt), orchestration (Airflow, Prefect), APIs (API gateways), messaging (Kafka), SFTP.
- Storage and compute: Data lake/warehouse/lakehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks), object storage (S3, ADLS, GCS).
- Data quality and testing: Great Expectations, Amazon Deequ, unit/integration tests, contract testing.
- Governance and catalog: Collibra, Alation, Apache Atlas; schema registry.
- Security and privacy: KMS encryption, HashiCorp Vault/Secrets Manager, DLP (Microsoft Purview, Symantec), privacy management (OneTrust, BigID).
- Monitoring and logging: CloudWatch, Datadog, Splunk, ELK; job monitoring dashboards.
- DevOps: Git/GitHub/GitLab, CI/CD (GitHub Actions, Jenkins), IaC (Terraform).
- Ticketing and documentation: ServiceNow/Jira; Confluence/Wiki.

Process Details:
## Overview
The “Develop insights into workforce analytics outcomes” process synthesizes quantitative and qualitative workforce data into clear, actionable insights that inform decisions across HR and the business (e.g., hiring plans, retention strategies, skills development, pay equity, DEI, productivity). It sits within Implement Workforce Analytics and bridges analytical output (dashboards, models, reports) and decision-making by translating patterns, trends, and drivers into prioritized recommendations, implications, and action plans.

Purpose:
- Identify what is happening (descriptive), why it is happening (diagnostic), what might happen (predictive), and what to do about it (prescriptive) in the workforce.
- Triangulate analytics with business context to avoid misinterpretation.
- Communicate insights in a decision-ready format and catalyze actions with estimated impact and risk.

Role in the organization:
- Serves HR Business Partners (HRBPs), Talent COEs, Finance, and business leaders with evidence-based recommendations.
- Enhances ROI from HRIS/analytics investments by closing the “last mile” from data to decisions.
- Supports compliance, fairness, privacy, and ethical use of people data.

## Key Activities
- Define decision context and hypotheses aligned to business priorities.
- Review and interpret analytics outputs (dashboards, models, reports) and segment results.
- Conduct diagnostic deep dives (cohort/time-series analysis, root cause, drill-downs).
- Validate findings (statistical testing, sensitivity, causality checks where viable).
- Triangulate with qualitative inputs (interviews, survey comments, exit notes).
- Assess fairness/ethics and privacy implications of insights and proposed actions.
- Prioritize and frame insights with implications and recommended actions.
- Estimate business impact, costs, risks, and constraints; propose experiments where needed.
- Craft and socialize an insight narrative with visuals and executive summary.
- Obtain stakeholder feedback and sign-offs; refine and publish deliverables.
- Handoff to owners for action planning; define measures to track outcomes.
- Capture lessons learned and update knowledge repositories.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Workforce analytics outputs: dashboards, scorecards (e.g., turnover, time-to-fill), predictive model outputs (e.g., attrition risk), text analytics, pay analyses, skills and org design analytics.
- Data dictionaries/metric definitions and metadata (refresh cadence, coverage, caveats).
- Business context: strategy, workforce plans, budgets, headcount targets, hiring freezes, organizational changes.
- Qualitative inputs: manager interviews, employee survey comments, exit interview themes.
- Benchmarks: historical baselines, industry benchmarks, DEI representation targets.
- Policies/constraints: legal, compliance, labor relations, privacy (e.g., GDPR, CCPA), ethics guidelines.

Prerequisites:
- Data quality thresholds met (completeness, timeliness, consistency).
- Access approvals and privacy controls configured; de-identification where required.
- Agreed problem statement or decision to be supported; stakeholder alignment on scope.
- Standardized metric definitions and approved methodologies for key analyses.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Data integration, governance, and quality management (HRIS/ATS/LMS data).
- Generate/maintain workforce analytics (modeling, dashboards).
- HR strategy and planning to align insights to priorities.
- Change management and communications for downstream action adoption.

## Process Steps
1) Intake and scoping
- Confirm the decision/use case, timeframe, and success criteria.
- Identify stakeholders, decision owners, and required sign-offs.
- Review known constraints (budget, legal, union, regional limitations).

2) Assemble and validate inputs
- Pull latest analytics outputs, data dictionaries, and relevant documents.
- Confirm data quality checkpoints and understand model caveats.
- Gather qualitative context (interviews, survey highlights).

3) Rapid scan and hypothesis framing
- Perform a high-level scan of key metrics to flag anomalies and trends.
- Draft initial hypotheses (e.g., “Turnover spike linked to comp compression in job family X”).
- Prioritize hypotheses based on materiality and feasibility to test.

4) Deep-dive analytics and segmentation
- Drill down by business unit, job family, location, tenure, level, manager, diversity segments.
- Apply appropriate analyses:
  - Trend/time-series and seasonality decomposition.
  - Cohort and survival analysis (e.g., post-hire attrition by tenure bands).
  - Funnel analysis (recruiting pipeline conversion).
  - Pay equity and compa-ratio distribution; promotion velocity.
  - Skill gap and internal mobility patterns; learning impact analysis.
  - Org structure/design indicators (span of control, layers, ONA if available).

5) Validate findings
- Statistical testing (e.g., t-tests, chi-square) for differences between segments.
- Sensitivity analysis (e.g., threshold changes, alternate segmentations).
- Where causal inference is necessary and feasible, apply appropriate methods (e.g., propensity score matching, difference-in-differences) or propose controlled pilots.

6) Fairness, privacy, and ethics review
- Check for potential bias in models and interpretations.
- Ensure privacy thresholds are respected (e.g., minimum cell sizes).
- Document ethical considerations and mitigation steps.

7) Triangulate with qualitative evidence
- Compare quantitative patterns with manager/employee feedback, exit interview themes, and pulse comments to confirm or challenge findings.

8) Synthesize insights and implications
- Distill to a small set of prioritized insights with:
  - What: concise finding with magnitude and direction.
  - So what: business implications and affected segments.
  - Now what: recommended actions, owners, and timeline.

9) Estimate impact and feasibility
- Quantify value at stake (e.g., cost of turnover avoided, time-to-fill reduction).
- Assess cost, effort, dependencies, risks, and change complexity.
- Recommend experiments/pilots where uncertainty is high; define success metrics.

10) Craft narrative and visualization
- Produce an executive summary and 1–3 page insight brief per theme.
- Create annotated visuals (before/after, trend lines, segmentation charts).
- Include methodology appendix and data caveats.

11) Socialize and refine
- Conduct review sessions with HRBPs, COEs, Legal/Privacy, and business leaders.
- Capture feedback, resolve challenges, and incorporate refinements.

12) Approvals and publication
- Obtain required sign-offs (Data Governance, HR leadership, Legal as applicable).
- Publish to the analytics portal and notify stakeholders with a concise digest.

13) Handoff and action enablement
- Align with owners on action plans, pilots, and timelines.
- Define monitoring plan, metrics, and reporting cadence to track outcomes.

14) Retrospective and knowledge management
- After action cycles, evaluate outcomes versus estimates.
- Document lessons learned and update playbooks/templates.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Insight briefs and executive summaries (prioritized findings, implications, recommendations).
- Annotated dashboards and drill-down views tailored to target audiences.
- Root cause analysis artifacts (driver trees, fishbone diagrams) and segmentation packs.
- Impact models and business cases (assumptions, value at stake, sensitivity).
- Experiment/pilot charters with success metrics and guardrails.
- Fairness, privacy, and ethics assessment notes.
- Stakeholder sign-offs and action handoff records.
- Knowledge base entries and reusable templates.

Success criteria:
- Insights are accurate, explainable, and decision-ready.
- Recommendations are adopted by owners within agreed timeframes.
- Measurable improvements observed in target outcomes post-implementation.
- Positive stakeholder feedback on clarity, relevance, and utility.
- Compliance with privacy, fairness, and governance standards.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- People Analytics Lead: Owns the process, prioritization, quality control, and stakeholder management.
- People Data Scientist/Analyst: Performs analyses, validation, and visualization; drafts insights and impact estimates.
- HR Business Partner (HRBP): Provides business context; validates implications; co-owns action planning with business leaders.
- COE Leads (Talent Acquisition, Learning, Rewards, DEI): Provide domain expertise; co-design interventions; ensure feasibility.
- Business Leaders/Line Managers: Validate operational relevance; sponsor actions/pilots; provide resources.
- Data Governance/Privacy Officer and Legal: Review privacy, ethics, compliance; approve sensitive analyses.
- HRIS/IT/Data Engineering: Ensure data availability, quality, access control; support tooling.
- Change Management/Communications: Package messages; support adoption of recommended actions.
- Finance/Workforce Planning: Validate financial impact and alignment to plans/budgets.
- Project/Program Manager: Tracks actions, dependencies, and outcomes.

## Best Practices
- Start with the decision: tie insights to specific choices, not generic reporting.
- Standardize metric definitions and maintain a data catalog with business context.
- Use iterative analysis: quick scans, then deeper validation where warranted.
- Segment smartly: by controllable levers (manager, process step) and meaningful cohorts.
- Combine quantitative and qualitative data to avoid false narratives.
- Emphasize interpretability; avoid black-box insights that leaders can’t act on.
- Visualize simply; highlight magnitudes, deltas, and uncertainty.
- Quantify impact and costs; propose pilots when causality is uncertain.
- Embed fairness/privacy checks and minimum reporting thresholds.
- Maintain reproducibility (code repositories, notebooks, versioned datasets).
- Establish a feedback loop: track which recommendations are adopted and effective.
- Create reusable templates for insight briefs and business cases.

## Common Challenges
- Data quality and coverage gaps
  - Solution: Data quality SLAs, automated checks, clear caveats, and prioritization to close gaps.
- Conflicting metric definitions across teams
  - Solution: Central metric governance, approved definitions, and a living data catalog.
- Spurious correlations or overinterpretation
  - Solution: Hypothesis-driven approach, validation tests, and triangulation.
- Privacy and small populations
  - Solution: Suppression thresholds, aggregation, de-identification, and Legal review.
- Stakeholder skepticism or low adoption
  - Solution: Early engagement, co-creation with HRBPs/leaders, clear “so what,” and quick wins.
- Limited analytical capacity
  - Solution: Prioritization framework, templated analyses, self-service guides, and training.
- Tool fragmentation and access issues
  - Solution: Standard tool stack, governed access, and a single portal for insight artifacts.
- Ethical concerns and bias in models
  - Solution: Bias testing, fairness metrics, alternative analyses, and ethics review body.

## Performance Metrics
- Time to insight (from intake to published brief).
- Percentage of insights with validated root causes.
- Recommendation adoption rate and time to adoption.
- Estimated vs. realized impact variance (forecast accuracy).
- Stakeholder satisfaction (e.g., post-brief survey/NPS).
- Compliance metrics (privacy threshold adherence; number of escalations).
- Rework rate due to data or definition issues.
- Coverage of priority areas (e.g., proportion of top workforce risks analyzed).
- Share of insights accompanied by pilots/experiments and their success rate.
- Knowledge artifact completeness and reuse rate.

## Technology and Tools
- Core systems: HRIS (e.g., Workday, SAP SuccessFactors), ATS (e.g., Greenhouse), LMS (e.g., Cornerstone), Performance/Engagement platforms (e.g., Qualtrics).
- Data and analytics: Data warehouse/lake (e.g., Snowflake, BigQuery), ETL/ELT (e.g., dbt, Fivetran), notebooks (Jupyter, RStudio), Python/R (pandas, scikit-learn), SQL.
- BI and visualization: Tableau, Power BI, Looker; presentation tools for storytelling.
- People analytics platforms: Visier, Crunchr, One Model; pay equity tools.
- Text/NLP and ONA: NLP libraries and platforms; ONA tools (e.g., Polinode) where applicable.
- Data governance and privacy: Collibra/Alation (catalog), OneTrust (privacy), access management.
- Collaboration and knowledge management: Confluence/SharePoint, Git for version control, ticketing (Jira/ServiceNow).
- Experimentation and A/B testing: Platforms or lightweight frameworks for pilots.

## Overview
Understand IT customer communities is the process of identifying, engaging, and learning from distinct groups of IT customers (e.g., business units, roles, locations, user segments) to surface their needs, pain points, expectations, and desired outcomes. It enables IT to move beyond ad hoc requests to a structured, collaborative understanding of who its customers are, how they use IT services, and what value they expect. The process underpins service strategy, product roadmaps, portfolio prioritization, change management, and customer communications.

Purpose:
- Build a shared, current view of IT customer segments and their unique contexts (personas, use cases, constraints).
- Establish and maintain two-way communication channels and communities (formal and informal).
- Continuously collect and synthesize voice-of-customer (VoC) and usage data to inform IT decisions.
- Improve trust, adoption, satisfaction, and business outcomes through transparent engagement.

Role in the organization:
- Feeds upstream service/portfolio planning, architecture decisions, and budgeting with customer evidence.
- Informs downstream processes (requirements, design, change, training, support) with targeted insights per community.
- Acts as the backbone for the broader “Develop and manage IT customer relationships” capability.

## Key Activities
- Stakeholder and community mapping: identify customer groups by business capability, role, geography, application/service usage, and accessibility needs.
- Persona and journey development: create personas, empathy maps, and key user journeys/workflows per community.
- Channel setup and governance: establish collaboration spaces (forums, Teams/Slack channels, advisory boards), moderation norms, and privacy/compliance rules.
- Engagement planning and execution: schedule interviews, surveys, focus groups, ride-alongs, and community events; recruit champions.
- Data gathering and listening: integrate operational data (tickets, incidents, changes, telemetry, adoption metrics) with qualitative feedback.
- Insight synthesis and validation: thematic coding, sentiment/driver analysis, and playback sessions to confirm understanding.
- Backlog creation and linkage: translate insights into opportunities, requirements epics, and service improvements linked to communities.
- Communication and closed-loop feedback: publish findings, decisions, roadmaps, and outcomes; acknowledge and close the loop on submissions.
- Continuous monitoring: measure engagement, satisfaction, adoption, and issue trends per community; refresh profiles regularly.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Organizational structure, business capability maps, and contact rosters.
- IT service catalog, CMDB, and list of key applications/services per business unit.
- Historical ITSM data (incidents, requests, problems), change/release calendars.
- Usage and experience telemetry (e.g., login patterns, performance, crash reports).
- Existing customer research, surveys, and escalation logs.
- Strategic objectives and upcoming initiatives that affect customers.
- Policies: privacy (GDPR/CCPA), records retention, acceptable use, accessibility standards.

Prerequisites:
- Executive sponsorship (CIO/IT leadership) and clear objectives/scope.
- Identified Business Relationship Managers (BRMs)/community owners.
- Approved communications plan and channels; branding templates.
- Data governance and consent approach for collecting/processing feedback.
- Tooling access (survey, community platform, analytics) and trained moderators.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 8.1 Develop and manage IT customer relationships (overall governance).
- Service portfolio management and enterprise architecture (to align insights to roadmaps).
- ITSM (incident/problem/change) for operational data and outreach.
- Compliance, privacy, and security for engagement and data handling.
- Knowledge management and training for content creation and dissemination.

## Process Steps
1) Define scope and objectives
- Clarify target domains (e.g., end-user computing, ERP, data platforms) and expected outcomes (e.g., reduce ticket volumes, improve adoption).
- Agree on success metrics, cadence, and initial communities to profile.

2) Assemble the team and assign roles
- Nominate BRMs, community managers, analysts, UX researchers, and champions.
- Establish RACI for engagement, analysis, and communications.

3) Gather baseline data
- Pull org charts, service catalog mappings, top ticket types, outage history, telemetry, previous surveys, and change calendars.
- Identify existing groups (user councils, steering committees, Yammer/Teams/Slack channels).

4) Segment and map communities
- Segment by business capability, role persona, geography/time zone, accessibility/language, and critical application usage.
- Produce a community map: community name, purpose, size, owner, key services, pain points, channels, champions.

5) Develop initial profiles
- Create personas and empathy maps; outline top jobs-to-be-done, workflows, constraints, and success measures per community.
- Draft key journeys (e.g., onboarding, month-end close, field visit) with touchpoints to IT services.

6) Establish engagement channels and governance
- Set up or adopt channels (e.g., Discourse/Teams forums, advisory boards, office hours).
- Define charters, participation norms, moderation rules, escalation paths, and privacy/consent statements.
- Ensure accessibility and localization as needed.

7) Plan engagement calendar
- Define quarterly advisory boards, monthly community calls, periodic surveys, and targeted studies (interviews, ride-alongs).
- Set SLAs for acknowledging feedback (e.g., within 2 business days) and closing the loop (e.g., within 30 days).

8) Execute discovery and listening
- Conduct mixed-method research: interviews, group sessions, surveys, polls, social listening, shadowing.
- Capture structured notes in a research repository; tag by community, theme, service, and severity.

9) Integrate operational/usage data
- Correlate VoC with ITSM data, telemetry (performance/crash), adoption metrics, knowledge search trends, and training consumption.

10) Analyze and synthesize insights
- Perform thematic coding and sentiment/driver analysis to identify top needs, pain points, and opportunity areas.
- Quantify impact (affected users, business process criticality, cost/time impact).

11) Validate with communities
- Playback findings in community sessions; confirm accuracy, prioritize using collaborative methods (e.g., dot voting, impact/effort).
- Adjust profiles/personas and priorities based on feedback.

12) Create and link deliverables
- Produce updated community profiles, personas, journey maps, and an opportunities/requirements backlog.
- Link items to service and product roadmaps; create problem records where appropriate.

13) Communicate and close the loop
- Publish summaries, decisions, and roadmaps by community; acknowledge contributions and explain trade-offs.
- Provide self-service content (FAQs, knowledge articles, training) targeted to communities.

14) Monitor, measure, and improve
- Track KPIs by community; review quarterly.
- Refresh community map and profiles; rotate champions; adapt channels based on engagement data.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Community map and stakeholder registry with owners and champions.
- Personas, empathy maps, and key journey maps per community.
- Engagement plan/calendar and channel directory with governance artifacts.
- Thematic insight reports and validated priority lists per community.
- Opportunities/requirements backlog linked to services/products and business outcomes.
- Communications artifacts: summaries, roadmaps, FAQs, knowledge articles.

Deliverables:
- Community Charter(s)
- Research Repository/Insight Database
- Quarterly Community Health Report
- Baseline and trend CSAT/NPS per community
- Closed-loop feedback log (acknowledged, planned, delivered)

Success criteria:
- Comprehensive coverage of critical communities (e.g., >90% of business-critical roles mapped).
- Sustained engagement (response/attendance rates) and positive sentiment trends.
- Measurable improvements linked to community insights (e.g., reduced P1 incidents, increased adoption).
- High closed-loop rate and reduced time-to-acknowledgment for feedback.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor (CIO/IT LT): Set vision, remove blockers, approve scope and policy.
- Business Relationship Manager (BRM): Own community relationships, prioritize needs, coordinate engagement.
- Community Manager: Set up channels, moderate discussions, manage calendar, ensure closed-loop communications.
- Service/Product Owners: Translate insights into backlog and roadmaps; report progress to communities.
- UX Researcher/Designer: Plan and conduct research, create personas/journeys, synthesize insights.
- Data/Insights Analyst: Integrate ITSM/telemetry data, perform analysis, build dashboards.
- Communications Specialist: Craft messages, ensure clarity, accessibility, and localization.
- Privacy/Compliance Officer: Oversee consent, data handling, and policy adherence.
- Enterprise Architect: Align insights to target architectures and standards.
- ITSM Lead/Problem Manager: Link issues to problem records; track resolution and trend reduction.
- Community Champions (from business): Advocate, recruit members, validate findings, drive adoption.

## Best Practices
- Start with critical value streams and expand iteratively; avoid boiling the ocean.
- Use mixed methods (qualitative and quantitative) to triangulate insights.
- Maintain a single source of truth for community profiles and insights; tag everything.
- Practice closed-loop communication: acknowledge, act, and report back on every feedback thread.
- Ensure inclusivity and accessibility (WCAG standards) across channels and materials.
- Localize content and schedule sessions for global time zones; provide recordings and translations.
- Protect privacy: minimize PII, get explicit consent, and apply retention policies.
- Empower community champions with recognition, early access, and clear roles.
- Publish and update service/product roadmaps transparently with community input.
- Avoid survey fatigue: small, targeted pulses; re-use instruments for trend analysis.
- Measure what matters: tie insights to outcomes (productivity, risk reduction, revenue enablement).

## Common Challenges
- Low engagement or survey fatigue
  - Solution: diversify channels, shorten surveys, offer value (early previews, recognition), and show impact of feedback.
- Unrepresentative input (loudest voices dominate)
  - Solution: stratified sampling, targeted outreach, and weighted prioritization across segments.
- Fragmented tooling and data silos
  - Solution: integrate ITSM, telemetry, and research repositories; standardize tags and taxonomies.
- Trust deficit with IT
  - Solution: transparent communications, consistent follow-through, quick wins, and visible leadership participation.
- Conflicting priorities across communities
  - Solution: shared prioritization framework (value, risk, effort), governance forums, and publish trade-off rationales.
- Privacy/compliance risks
  - Solution: consent management, data minimization, anonymization, and periodic audits.
- Champion burnout/turnover
  - Solution: rotate roles, lighten load with enablement kits, and formal recognition programs.

## Performance Metrics
Engagement and coverage:
- % of critical communities identified and profiled
- Active community members and participation rate per channel
- Survey response rate and event attendance

Listening and responsiveness:
- Time to acknowledge new feedback
- Closed-loop rate (% of feedback with a documented response/outcome)
- Number of validated insights per quarter

Experience and outcome:
- Community-level CSAT/NPS/eNPS trends
- Adoption/usage rates for targeted services (by community)
- Ticket volume and mean time to resolve for top issues (by community)
- Reduction in repeat incidents/problems linked to community-prioritized items

Effectiveness and alignment:
- % of roadmap items linked to community insights
- Time-to-insight (from data collection to validated finding)
- Diversity/representation index across communities (roles/geos/languages)
- Content effectiveness: knowledge/article helpfulness and deflection rates

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM and CMDB: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, Remedy for ticket/op data and service mapping.
- Community and collaboration platforms: Microsoft Teams, Slack, Discourse, Viva Engage/Yammer.
- Survey and VoC: Qualtrics, Medallia, Microsoft Forms, SurveyMonkey (with pulse survey capability).
- Research repository and knowledge: Dovetail, Aurelius, Notion, Confluence; SharePoint/Wiki for artifacts.
- Analytics and BI: Power BI, Tableau, Looker; data lake/warehouse for integration.
- Experience/telemetry: Dynatrace, New Relic, Aternity, Splunk, Azure Monitor, Google Analytics (for portals).
- Product feedback/roadmapping: Jira, Azure DevOps, ProdPad, Aha!, UserVoice.
- Communications: Email marketing/marketing automation (e.g., Mailchimp), intranet, newsletters, townhalls, webinars.
- Translation/localization and accessibility: Language services, captioning tools, accessibility checkers, WCAG linters.
- Consent and data governance: OneTrust, BigID, or internal consent registries and retention tooling.

Process Details:
# [8.1.2.1] Understand Business Requirements for IT Capabilities

## Overview
This process defines how the organization systematically elicits, analyzes, validates, and prioritizes business requirements that drive IT capabilities—both in the current environment and for future transformation. Its purpose is to:
- Ensure IT initiatives directly support business strategies, OKRs, and regulatory obligations.
- Translate business needs into clear, testable, and prioritized requirements for solution design, portfolio selection, and roadmap planning.
- Surface gaps in current capabilities and inform sequencing of change.

Role in the organization:
- Anchors IT strategy, architecture, and delivery to measurable business value.
- Serves as the upstream input to demand/portfolio management, enterprise architecture, solution design, and funding decisions.
- Enables transparent, traceable decision-making across business and IT stakeholders.

## Key Activities
- Stakeholder identification and engagement planning.
- Scope definition and alignment to business outcomes.
- Elicitation of functional and non-functional requirements (NFRs).
- Current-state (as-is) and future-state (to-be) process/capability mapping.
- Requirements analysis, modeling, and consolidation.
- Prioritization and dependency mapping.
- Validation and sign-off with business sponsors and IT owners.
- Creation and maintenance of traceability between requirements, objectives, and test cases.
- Handover to architecture, portfolio, and delivery teams.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Business strategy, OKRs, roadmaps.
  - Existing IT service catalog, CMDB/application inventory, architecture standards.
  - As-is process maps, SLAs/OLAs, incident/problem/change data, user feedback.
  - Regulatory/compliance requirements; risk and audit findings.
  - Budget constraints, headcount plans, vendor/contract constraints.
  - Prior business cases, demand pipeline/backlog, technology roadmaps.

- Prerequisites:
  - Executive/business sponsor and IT owner identified.
  - Defined scope, objectives, and success criteria (initial).
  - Stakeholder map and engagement plan; access to SMEs.
  - Agreed methodology/templates and repository (version control).
  - Data privacy/ethics approvals for research (as needed).

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Develop and manage IT customer relationships (stakeholder access, context).
  - IT strategy/enterprise architecture (standards, principles, target states).
  - IT demand/portfolio management (intake, prioritization, funding).
  - IT service management (service definitions, performance data).
  - Risk/compliance management (regulatory inputs and approvals).

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and charter
   - Confirm sponsor, business objectives, scope, timeline, and constraints.
   - Deliverables: Charter, RACI, engagement plan.

2. Stakeholder mapping and onboarding
   - Identify roles across business units, IT, compliance, security, data, finance, and customers/users; map influence/interest.
   - Deliverables: Stakeholder register, communication plan.

3. Context and baseline analysis
   - Review strategy, OKRs, KPIs; analyze current services, processes, incidents, change requests, and usage data.
   - Deliverables: Context summary, problem/opportunity statement, initial hypotheses.

4. Elicitation planning
   - Select techniques: interviews, workshops, journey mapping, process mining, document analysis, surveys, shadowing.
   - Deliverables: Elicitation plan, research instruments, consent/ethics approvals.

5. Elicit requirements and insights
   - Run sessions to capture:
     - Functional needs (what outcomes, use cases, user stories).
     - NFRs (performance, security, availability, data quality, usability, interoperability).
     - Constraints (regulatory, budget, timelines).
     - Pain points, waste, risks, and success metrics.
   - Deliverables: Elicitation notes, initial backlog, personas/journeys, as-is maps.

6. Model and analyze
   - Consolidate inputs; create models: process maps, capability maps/heatmaps, context/data flow diagrams, information models, service blueprints.
   - Validate feasibility with architecture/security/data teams.
   - Deliverables: Analysis models, gap assessment, dependency map.

7. Define future-state outcomes and requirements
   - Articulate to-be capabilities, policies, and service levels aligned to business outcomes.
   - Draft clear, testable requirements (BRD, epics/features, user stories with acceptance criteria).
   - Deliverables: Future-state models, NFR catalog, BRD/backlog.

8. Prioritize and sequence
   - Apply frameworks (MoSCoW, WSJF, value vs. effort, risk reduction) with stakeholders.
   - Identify MVP and release increments; map dependencies.
   - Deliverables: Prioritized backlog, high-level roadmap, value hypothesis.

9. Validate and sign off
   - Conduct review workshops; resolve conflicts and ambiguities.
   - Secure approval from sponsor, IT owner, security/compliance.
   - Deliverables: Signed BRD/backlog, decision log, updated risk/assumptions.

10. Traceability and readiness
    - Link requirements to OKRs, benefits, risks, test cases, and architectural principles.
    - Define Definition of Ready for downstream teams.
    - Deliverables: Traceability matrix, DoR checklist.

11. Handover and governance
    - Present outcomes to portfolio, architecture, and delivery leads.
    - Establish change control for requirement updates; schedule periodic reviews.
    - Deliverables: Handover pack, governance cadence.

12. Measure and improve
    - Capture KPIs and stakeholder feedback; refine process and artifacts.
    - Deliverables: KPI dashboard, retrospectives, continuous improvement actions.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Business Requirements Document (BRD) or equivalent.
- Prioritized requirements backlog (epics, features, user stories) with acceptance criteria.
- Non-functional requirements catalog and service level targets.
- As-is and to-be process/capability and journey maps; capability heatmaps.
- Context and data flow diagrams; information models/glossary.
- Gap analysis and dependency map; high-level roadmap/MVP definition.
- Traceability matrix (requirements to OKRs, risks, tests).
- Decision log, risks/assumptions/issues/constraints (RAID) updates.
- Handover pack for architecture/portfolio/delivery.

Success criteria:
- Requirements are clear, testable, feasible, prioritized, and traceable to business objectives.
- Stakeholder sign-off achieved; minimal post-sign-off volatility.
- Downstream teams confirm Definition of Ready is met.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Business Sponsor/Product Sponsor: Owns business outcomes; approves scope and sign-off; arbitrates priorities.
- Business Relationship Manager: Orchestrates stakeholder engagement; aligns needs to IT services; manages expectations.
- Business Analyst/Product Owner: Plans and leads elicitation; documents and manages backlog; ensures quality and traceability.
- Enterprise/Domain Architect: Ensures alignment with target architecture and principles; assesses feasibility and integration.
- Data Architect/Owner: Defines data requirements, quality, lineage, governance needs.
- Security/Compliance Officer: Identifies regulatory/security controls; validates NFRs and compliance obligations.
- IT Service Owner/Process Owner: Provides current service/process insights; defines service-level needs and constraints.
- UX/CX Researcher or Designer: Leads journey mapping, usability, accessibility requirements.
- QA/Test Lead: Ensures requirements are testable; defines acceptance criteria and traceability to tests.
- Portfolio/PMO: Integrates requirements into portfolio and roadmap; supports prioritization/funding.
- Finance Partner: Validates financial constraints and benefits assumptions.

## Best Practices
- Align to standards: BABOK for requirements, ITIL 4 for services, TOGAF for architecture, COBIT for governance.
- Start with outcomes: tie every requirement to OKRs/benefits; define value hypotheses and leading indicators.
- Capture NFRs early: performance, availability, security, privacy, interoperability, observability, supportability.
- Use multiple elicitation methods to reduce bias; include frontline users and customers.
- Visual over verbose: models and examples accelerate alignment; keep documentation lean but sufficient.
- Maintain a shared glossary to eliminate ambiguity; standardize templates.
- Separate “what” from “how”; avoid premature solutioning; document constraints explicitly.
- Prioritize iteratively; validate with prototypes or examples where possible.
- Enforce traceability and change control; version requirements.
- Embed accessibility, data ethics, and privacy by design.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Ambiguous or conflicting requirements: Use structured templates, examples, and decision logs; facilitate resolution workshops with clear decision rights.
- Hidden stakeholders or low engagement: Map stakeholders broadly; leverage BRMs and sponsors; offer varied engagement formats; track participation.
- Scope creep: Define scope boundaries and DoR; implement change control with impact analysis.
- Solution bias: Reframe to outcomes; use “problem statements” and “jobs-to-be-done”; time-box solutioning.
- Missing NFRs: Use NFR checklists and quality scenarios; involve security/ops early; validate via prototypes or performance modeling.
- Data availability/quality issues: Engage data owners early; define data quality rules; plan for cleansing/governance.
- Regulatory surprises: Early compliance review; maintain a regulatory requirement register; schedule gates.
- Distributed teams/time constraints: Use asynchronous tools; concise artifacts; record sessions; apply working agreements.

## Performance Metrics
- Lead time: kickoff to signed-off requirements.
- Requirements volatility: changes after sign-off (%) and causes.
- Coverage and quality: % requirements with acceptance criteria, tests, and traceability to OKRs.
- Stakeholder satisfaction: survey/NPS post-process.
- Defect leakage attributable to requirements (UAT/production).
- Rework rate/time due to unclear requirements.
- Prioritization effectiveness: value delivered per release vs. plan; WSJF adherence.
- NFR validation rate: % NFRs verified via tests/proofs.
- Engagement metrics: stakeholder attendance/response rates.
- Cycle time for decisions and conflict resolution.

## Technology and Tools
- Requirements/backlog management: Azure DevOps, Jira/Confluence, Rally, Jama, Polarion, DOORS Next.
- Collaboration and workshops: Miro/Mural, Microsoft Teams, Zoom, Slack, Confluence/SharePoint.
- Process and architecture modeling: Visio, Lucidchart, Bizagi, ARIS, Sparx EA, Bizzdesign, LeanIX.
- Service/asset data: ServiceNow/CMDB, ITSM suites for incidents/problems/SLAs.
- Data and analytics: Power BI/Tableau/Looker; process mining (Celonis, Process Intelligence).
- Survey/user research: Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey, UserTesting.
- Test management and traceability: Zephyr, Xray, qTest, TestRail.
- Document control and e-signature: SharePoint, Google Workspace, DocuSign.

Process Details:
## Overview
Understand IT landscape is the structured process of discovering, documenting, and validating the organization’s end-to-end technology environment—hardware, software, networks, cloud, data flows, and their relationships to business capabilities and services. Its purpose is to establish an accurate, current-state (as-is) view that enables impact analysis, risk management, transformation planning, cost optimization, compliance, and continuity of IT services. Within Develop and manage IT customer relationships, this process ensures IT understands the operating context and constraints affecting customers’ transformation needs, so that solutions are realistic, secure, and aligned to business priorities.

Key outcomes include a baseline inventory of IT assets and services, a mapped dependency model from business capabilities to applications and infrastructure, identification of risks and technical debt, and a governed repository (e.g., CMDB/EA tool) as a single source of truth.

## Key Activities
- Define scope and taxonomy
  - Agree the domains to include (endpoints, data centers, cloud, SaaS, applications, data, integrations, networks, security tooling).
  - Adopt standard definitions and modeling conventions (e.g., services, applications, CIs, environments).
- Discover and collect data
  - Automated discovery and ingestion (on-prem, cloud, SaaS).
  - Manual collection via SME interviews and surveys for gaps, business context, and non-discoverable attributes (owners, SLAs, RTO/RPO).
- Reconcile and normalize
  - De-duplicate, normalize names, enrich with tagging, and reconcile against authoritative sources (HR, finance, procurement).
- Map relationships and dependencies
  - Link business capabilities/processes to services, applications, data stores, infrastructure, and vendors; document interfaces and data flows.
- Assess health, risk, and lifecycle
  - Identify end-of-support/end-of-life, vulnerabilities, capacity/performance issues, compliance gaps, and technical debt.
- Document and visualize
  - Create and version logical and physical diagrams, service maps, data flow diagrams, and topology views.
- Validate and obtain sign-off
  - Review with application and service owners; resolve discrepancies; establish baseline.
- Publish and govern
  - Update CMDB/EA repository; define ownership and update cadence; integrate with change, CI/CD, and procurement to keep data fresh.
- Report insights
  - Provide dashboards and briefs that inform transformation options, cost models, risk mitigations, and prioritization.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs
  - Business context: strategy, critical business capabilities/processes, compliance obligations.
  - Existing repositories: CMDB, ITAM/SAM data, application portfolio catalog, service catalog.
  - Infrastructure inventories: AD/Entra ID, SCCM/Intune, virtualization platforms, storage/NAS, network inventories, DNS/IPAM.
  - Cloud accounts and org structure: AWS/Azure/GCP orgs/subscriptions/projects; tags/labels; IaC repositories.
  - Security and monitoring: vulnerability scanners, EDR, SIEM, APM, log aggregation, endpoint inventories.
  - Integration registries: API gateways, ESB/iPaaS, service meshes, data pipelines.
  - Contracts/licensing: vendor lists, license entitlements, maintenance/support dates.
  - Organizational data: owners, support groups, vendors, locations, cost centers.
- Prerequisites
  - Executive sponsorship and scope confirmation.
  - Tooling access and credentials approved, with info security review of discovery methods.
  - Data governance and privacy guidelines for scanning and data handling.
  - Time windows and change freezes for active scans where required.
  - Named data stewards/owners for key domains (apps, infra, cloud, data).
- Dependencies on other processes
  - IT Asset Management (ITAM) and Software Asset Management (SAM).
  - Service Configuration Management (CMDB) and Change Enablement.
  - Enterprise Architecture and Application Portfolio Management.
  - Security (asset discovery, vulnerability management), Data Governance.
  - Vendor/Procurement and Finance (cost and contract data).
  - Service Catalog/Service Portfolio Management.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and plan
   - Appoint an IT Landscape Lead and cross-functional working group.
   - Define objectives (e.g., 95% asset coverage, 90% dependency mapping for Tier 1 services).
   - Set scope, taxonomy, and modeling standard (e.g., ITIL CSDM, TOGAF layers).
   - Establish governance: steering cadence, decision rights, data quality thresholds.

2. Prepare tools and integrations
   - Validate CMDB/EA/ITAM tooling and data model.
   - Configure connectors to HR, procurement, finance, cloud providers, directory services.
   - Set up automated discovery (on-prem agents/appliances, cloud APIs, SaaS discovery, CASB as needed).
   - Define tag/label standards and naming conventions.

3. Baseline documentation sweep
   - Collect existing diagrams, inventories, runbooks, architecture decision records, DR plans.
   - Perform gap analysis versus desired data model (owners, lifecycle, RTO/RPO, data classification, compliance).

4. Execute automated discovery
   - Run network and credentialed scans for servers, endpoints, network devices, databases, middleware.
   - Ingest cloud inventories (compute, storage, network, managed services, security groups).
   - Enumerate container/k8s workloads and registries; collect SBOMs if available.
   - Discover SaaS usage via SSO logs and CASB; reconcile sanctioned vs. unsanctioned apps.

5. Manual enrichment and validation
   - Interview application owners for business fit, criticality, SLAs, data classifications, integration points, and pain points.
   - Survey for non-discoverable attributes (business capability mapping, RTO/RPO, vendor dependencies).
   - Identify shadow IT and temporary/experiment environments.

6. Reconcile and normalize
   - De-duplicate and merge records across sources.
   - Normalize software and hardware names/versions; align to product catalog and lifecycle data.
   - Enrich with financials (run-rate cost, committed spend), contract dates, and EoL/EoS.

7. Map dependencies and flows
   - Build service maps: user-to-service-to-application-to-data-to-infrastructure, including external vendors.
   - Document data flows and integrations (batch, APIs, messaging), sensitivity, and jurisdictions.
   - Capture environment segmentation (prod/non-prod) and DR topology.

8. Assess health, risk, and readiness
   - Identify vulnerabilities, unsupported tech, capacity constraints, single points of failure.
   - Rate technical debt and modernization inhibitors (e.g., tight coupling, proprietary lock-in).
   - Flag compliance gaps (e.g., encryption, residency, access control).

9. Document and visualize
   - Produce as-is architecture artifacts: capability-to-app mappings, application rationalization views, network/topology diagrams, DFDs, service dependency matrices.
   - Version-control artifacts; store in shared repository with metadata.

10. Review and sign-off
    - Conduct owner and security reviews; resolve discrepancies.
    - Obtain approval from domain leads (apps, infra, cloud, security, data) for baseline.

11. Publish and integrate
    - Update CMDB/EA/ITAM repositories as the single source of truth.
    - Integrate with change, CI/CD, and procurement to auto-update records on changes (e.g., IaC pipelines auto-register CIs).

12. Operate and continuously improve
    - Define refresh cadence (e.g., cloud daily, on-prem weekly, manual attributes quarterly).
    - Monitor data quality KPIs; run exception reports (orphaned assets, untaged cloud, stale records).
    - Run periodic recon with vulnerability and EDR platforms to detect drift.
    - Feed insights into transformation roadmaps and budgeting; track realized improvements.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Baseline as-is IT landscape model and repository (CMDB/EA/APM updated).
- Asset inventories and portfolios
  - Hardware, software, cloud resources, SaaS catalog, data stores.
  - Ownership, criticality, environment, lifecycle, location, compliance, costs.
- Dependency and flow artifacts
  - Service maps, integration inventories, data flow diagrams, network/topology diagrams.
- Risk and health assessments
  - EoL/EoS list, vulnerability and misconfiguration hotspots, capacity constraints, single points of failure.
- Rationalization candidates and modernization inhibitors
  - Duplicative apps/services, shadow IT, licensing optimization opportunities, tech debt register.
- Reports and dashboards
  - Coverage and accuracy KPIs, cost baselines by service/capability, compliance posture.
- Success criteria
  - Agreed coverage thresholds met (e.g., >95% of production assets discovered).
  - Accuracy validated by owners (>90%).
  - All Tier 1 services mapped end-to-end with RTO/RPO captured.
  - CMDB/EA repository adopted as authoritative source; integrated with change and CI/CD.
  - Actionable insights produced (e.g., prioritized rationalization list, risk remediation plan).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- IT Landscape Lead / Enterprise Architect
  - Owns process, scope, modeling standards, and governance; coordinates across teams.
- CMDB/Configuration Manager
  - Designs data model, integrations, and discovery schedules; manages data quality and audits.
- IT Asset Manager (Hardware/Software/SaaS)
  - Ensures inventory completeness, license alignment, and lifecycle data; reconciles with finance/procurement.
- Application Owners / Service Owners
  - Provide business context, integrations, SLAs, and validate mappings; maintain accuracy over time.
- Infrastructure Leads (Compute/Storage/Network/Database)
  - Provide platform inventories, topology, and constraints; validate dependencies and performance.
- Cloud Platform Team (AWS/Azure/GCP)
  - Configure cloud inventory connectors, enforce tagging policies, provide cost and posture data.
- Security (Vulnerability/EDR/Identity)
  - Supply asset and risk data; approve scanning methods; validate data classification and controls.
- Data Governance / Privacy
  - Ensure proper handling of sensitive data and cross-border data flow documentation.
- Procurement/Finance
  - Provide vendor, contract, and cost data; reconcile spend with inventory.
- Project/Change Managers
  - Align updates with change windows; ensure post-change CMDB updates.
- Tool Administrators (EA, APM, Monitoring, Discovery)
  - Maintain platforms used for modeling, discovery, visualization, and reporting.

## Best Practices
- Establish a single source of truth using a well-defined data model (e.g., ITIL CSDM) and integrate rather than duplicate data.
- Combine automated discovery with owner validation; automate wherever possible, but require human stewardship for context.
- Enforce tagging/naming policies and IaC-driven registration so new assets are automatically classified and mapped.
- Map from business capability to technology; prioritize Tier 1 services and critical data flows first.
- Version-control architecture artifacts; treat landscape documentation as living documentation with change hooks.
- Standardize environments and patterns (reference architectures) to simplify mapping and reduce drift.
- Include SaaS and shadow IT via SSO logs and CASB; maintain a sanctioned SaaS catalog.
- Capture lifecycle and risk attributes (EoL/EoS, CVEs, RTO/RPO, data classification) as first-class fields.
- Govern data quality with KPIs, ownership, and regular audits; publish exception reports to accountable owners.
- Build privacy and security into discovery (credential management, least-privilege, scan windows).
- Start iteratively (by domain or business area) and expand; avoid big-bang efforts that go stale before completion.

## Common Challenges
- Incomplete or stale data across silos
  - Mitigation: automate discovery; integrate with change/CI/CD; enforce update policies.
- Shadow IT and unmanaged SaaS
  - Mitigation: monitor SSO/CASB; implement intake for new SaaS; communicate sanctioned options.
- Poor tagging and naming hygiene
  - Mitigation: enforce policies via guardrails and policy-as-code; block non-compliant deployments.
- Rapidly changing cloud and container environments
  - Mitigation: near-real-time cloud and k8s inventory; auto-registration from IaC; drift detection.
- Lack of ownership and accountability
  - Mitigation: assign owners at CI/service level; include in performance objectives; use RACI in governance.
- Tool sprawl and disconnected repositories
  - Mitigation: integrate with a central model; rationalize tools; define authoritative sources per attribute.
- Privacy and security concerns with scanning
  - Mitigation: security-reviewed methods, credential vaulting, scoped scans, and maintenance windows.
- Multi-vendor and hybrid complexity
  - Mitigation: standardize interfaces/patterns; maintain vendor metadata and support dates; adopt reference architectures.

## Performance Metrics
- Coverage
  - % of production assets discovered and modeled.
  - % of Tier 1 services with end-to-end dependency maps and RTO/RPO recorded.
- Accuracy and freshness
  - % of records validated by owners in last 90 days.
  - Average time to update records after a change (MTTU).
  - Stale record rate (% older than threshold).
- Completeness
  - % of assets with owner, environment, lifecycle, criticality, and tags populated.
  - Dependency coverage (% of integrations documented per service).
- Risk and compliance
  - #/rate of EoL/EoS technologies in production.
  - % of assets missing required controls (encryption, backups, monitoring).
  - Audit findings related to asset/configuration accuracy.
- Cost and optimization
  - % of spend mapped to services/capabilities.
  - Cloud tag compliance rate; unidentified spend as % of total.
  - Rationalization savings identified/realized.
- Operational value
  - Reduction in incidents/change failures due to unknown dependencies.
  - Time to perform impact analysis for a proposed change or incident.

## Technology and Tools
- CMDB and Service Mapping
  - ServiceNow (Discovery, Service Mapping, CSDM), BMC Helix/ADD, Micro Focus UCMDB.
- IT Asset Management and SAM
  - Flexera One, Snow, ServiceNow SAM, Microsoft MECM/Intune for endpoints.
- Cloud and container inventory
  - AWS Config/Organizations, Azure Resource Graph/Policy, GCP Asset Inventory; Kubernetes APIs, Rancher; image registries (Artifactory/Harbor).
- Discovery, vulnerability, and endpoint
  - Tanium, Qualys, Rapid7, CrowdStrike asset graph, EDR platforms for endpoint inventories.
- Enterprise Architecture and APM (portfolio)
  - LeanIX, MEGA HOPEX, Ardoq, Sparx EA, Archi (ArchiMate).
- Monitoring and APM (telemetry-informed mapping)
  - Dynatrace, AppDynamics, New Relic, Datadog (service maps, dependency tracing).
- Network and IPAM
  - NetBox, SolarWinds, Infoblox, Cisco DNA Center.
- Identity and SaaS discovery
  - Okta/Azure AD sign-in logs, CASB/SSPM (Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, Netskope, BetterCloud).
- Data governance and classification
  - BigID, Varonis, OneTrust, cloud-native DLP/classification.
- Cost and FinOps
  - CloudHealth, Cloudability, AWS Cost Explorer, Azure Cost Management.
- DevOps/IaC integration
  - Terraform, CloudFormation, Ansible; CI/CD platforms to auto-register/update CIs; SBOM generation (CycloneDX, Syft/Grype, Snyk/Black Duck).
- Visualization and documentation
  - Diagrams.net, Visio, PlantUML, Graph-based views; Wikis for process docs.

Selection and integration guidance:
- Choose a central model (CMDB/EA) and integrate other tools via APIs; avoid duplicating golden attributes.
- Implement role-based access and audit trails; vault credentials for discovery.
- Use event-driven updates from CI/CD and cloud change events to keep data current.
- Prefer tools that support open standards (ArchiMate, SBOM formats, CMDB APIs) to reduce lock-in.
