# [8.1.4.7] Develop Business Cases

## Overview
This process produces a decision-ready business case for IT transformation initiatives. It articulates the current situation, problem/opportunity, proposed solution options, value proposition, financial analysis, risks, and measurable outcomes for IT customers and governance bodies. The business case enables informed prioritization and funding decisions within the IT portfolio, aligns initiatives to enterprise strategy and architecture, and establishes accountability for benefits realization.

Within the broader “Provide IT transformation guidance” process, business cases translate customer requirements and transformation opportunities into an executable, economically justified plan. The output becomes the foundation for portfolio approvals, project initiation, procurement, and subsequent benefits tracking.

## Key Activities
- Define problem/opportunity and scope: Clarify drivers (e.g., risk, compliance, cost, customer experience, growth), stakeholders, and boundaries.
- Develop solution options: Include status quo (do-nothing), incremental improvement, and transformative options; assess fit with enterprise architecture and strategy.
- Build the value proposition: Link outcomes to business strategy and customer KPIs; quantify benefits and identify benefit owners.
- Estimate costs and timeline: Total cost of ownership across CapEx/OpEx, one-time vs. recurring, lifecycle (3–7 years), implementation roadmap and milestones.
- Perform financial analysis: Model cash flows, ROI, NPV, IRR, payback, TCO, and compare options; include sensitivity and scenario analysis.
- Assess risks and compliance: Identify risks, controls, security/privacy impacts, regulatory requirements, and business continuity implications.
- Define operating model impacts: Org/process changes, change management, training, support model, service levels, and sourcing implications.
- Create benefits realization plan: Metrics, baselines, targets, timing, and accountability.
- Develop governance and delivery approach: Stage-gates, resourcing, vendor strategy, procurement plan, and dependencies.
- Socialize and obtain approvals: Review with stakeholders, refine, and present to governance bodies for decision.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Documented customer requirements and desired outcomes (from prior analysis).
  - Current-state performance data and baselines (cost, risk, service levels, KPIs).
  - Enterprise strategy, IT strategy, and architecture principles/standards.
  - Technology roadmaps and reference architectures.
  - Budget constraints, funding model, and portfolio prioritization criteria.
  - Compliance, security, privacy, and regulatory requirements.
  - Market intelligence and vendor options (if applicable).
- Prerequisites:
  - Identified executive sponsor and business owner.
  - Agreement on problem statement and success criteria at a high level.
  - Access to financial modeling standards and cost rates (labor, cloud, licenses).
  - Availability of SMEs in architecture, security, finance, operations, legal/procurement.
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - 8.1.4.3+ Collect and analyze customer requirements.
  - 8.1.4.5 Identify opportunities and prioritize outcomes.
  - Enterprise Architecture review process.
  - Portfolio/PPM stage-gate framework (concept to funding).
  - Risk management and GRC processes.
  - Procurement/vendor management processes.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and plan
   - Confirm sponsor, stakeholders, scope, and timeline aligned to portfolio cadence.
   - Create a business case plan and RACI; book EA, Security, Finance, and PMO checkpoints.
   - Deliverable: Business case plan, stakeholder map.

2. Define current state and problem/opportunity
   - Document current capabilities, pain points, constraints, KPIs, and risks.
   - Establish the “do-nothing” baseline including risk/cost exposure.
   - Deliverable: Current-state summary, baseline metrics.

3. Define outcomes and success measures
   - Translate business needs into measurable outcomes (e.g., reduce processing time by 30%, improve availability to 99.95%).
   - Align to strategy/OKRs and regulatory obligations.
   - Deliverable: Outcomes/KPI framework with targets and timing.

4. Develop solution options and high-level architecture
   - Generate at least three options incl. do-nothing; consider buy/build/partner, cloud vs on-prem, and reuse of existing platforms.
   - Validate alignment with EA standards, data, integration, and security patterns.
   - Deliverable: Options analysis with pros/cons, constraints, and fit-to-strategy score.

5. Market scan and sourcing approach (if applicable)
   - Identify vendor landscape, reference pricing, contract models, and licensing metrics.
   - Confirm sourcing strategy (sole source, RFP/RFQ, cooperative agreements).
   - Deliverable: Market scan summary, sourcing recommendation.

6. Cost estimation and schedule
   - Build TCO: CapEx, OpEx, implementation services, change management, training, migration, decommissioning, support, compliance, sustainability/energy costs.
   - Phase the schedule and milestone plan; include dependencies and resource needs.
   - Deliverable: Cost model (3–7 year horizon), high-level roadmap.

7. Benefit identification and quantification
   - Identify financial benefits (cost avoidance, cost reduction, revenue uplift) and non-financial benefits (risk reduction, CX, compliance).
   - Assign benefit owners and realization timing; define measurement methods and data sources.
   - Deliverable: Benefits register with quantification and attribution.

8. Financial analysis and scenarios
   - Compute ROI, NPV, IRR, payback; compare options on a consistent basis.
   - Perform sensitivity (e.g., ±20% costs/benefits), scenario analysis (optimistic/base/pessimistic), and switching cost considerations.
   - Deliverable: Financial model with scenarios and assumptions log.

9. Risk, security, and compliance assessment
   - Identify key risks, mitigations, and residual risk; include cybersecurity, privacy, resiliency, vendor risk, and regulatory impacts.
   - Complete preliminary DPIA/PIA/SRA if applicable.
   - Deliverable: Risk register, security/privacy assessment summary.

10. Operating model, change, and service impacts
    - Define org/process changes, training, communications, support model (ITSM), SLAs/OLAs, and service catalog updates.
    - Deliverable: Operating model impact summary, high-level change plan.

11. Recommendation and implementation approach
    - Select preferred option; articulate rationale tied to strategy, value, and risk.
    - Outline delivery approach (agile/incremental vs. waterfall), stage-gates, governance, and procurement path.
    - Deliverable: Recommended option and implementation plan.

12. Draft business case package
    - Compile executive summary, problem/opportunity, options, financials, risks, roadmap, benefits realization plan, and appendices.
    - Ensure traceability from requirements to outcomes to metrics.
    - Deliverable: Business case document and executive presentation.

13. Review, iterate, and obtain approvals
    - Conduct reviews with Finance, EA, Security, Legal/Compliance, Procurement, and PMO.
    - Address comments; secure sign-offs; present to portfolio/governance board.
    - Deliverable: Approved business case, decision record.

14. Handover and tracking setup
    - Register the initiative in PPM; establish baseline KPIs and benefits tracking.
    - Transition artifacts to delivery team; define next-stage entry criteria.
    - Deliverable: PPM entry, benefits realization plan in tracking tool, handover pack.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Business case document and executive presentation
- Financial model (cash flows, NPV/IRR/ROI, scenarios) and assumptions log
- Options analysis with recommended option
- Benefits register and benefits realization plan
- Risk register and security/privacy assessment summary
- High-level solution architecture and implementation roadmap
- Sourcing/procurement approach and preliminary vendor analysis (if applicable)
- Governance approvals and decision log; PPM record
- Success criteria:
  - Approved by required governance bodies within target cycle time
  - Clear, measurable outcomes with assigned owners
  - Sound financials with validated assumptions and sensitivity analysis
  - Alignment to strategy, EA standards, and compliance requirements
  - Defined delivery and benefits realization approach

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Owns vision and funding pathway; resolves escalations.
- Business Owner/Process Owner: Defines business outcomes; owns benefits realization.
- IT Business Partner/Account Manager: Orchestrates process; ensures business alignment.
- Enterprise Architect: Ensures solution alignment, feasibility, and standards compliance.
- Security/Privacy Officer: Assesses security, privacy, and compliance impacts.
- Finance Partner/Controller: Provides costing standards; validates financial models.
- Portfolio/PMO Lead: Ensures stage-gate compliance; integrates into portfolio planning.
- Solution/Technical Lead: Provides technical options, estimates, and delivery approach.
- Procurement/Vendor Management: Advises on sourcing strategy and vendor risk.
- Legal/Compliance: Reviews contractual and regulatory considerations.
- Change Management/HR/Training: Defines organizational change and enablement needs.
- Service Management Lead: Defines support model, SLAs, and service catalog impacts.
- Data/Analytics Lead: Confirms data impacts and measurement methods for benefits.

## Best Practices
- Use standardized templates and modeling assumptions to enable comparability.
- Include a mandatory “do-nothing” baseline and at least one credible alternative.
- Involve Finance, EA, Security, and Business Owner from the outset; co-author key sections.
- Quantify both financial and non-financial benefits; assign benefit owners and baselines.
- Model total lifecycle costs (implementation, run, upgrades, decommissioning).
- Perform sensitivity and scenario analysis; avoid single-point estimates.
- Reference benchmarks (industry, vendor, internal) and document sources.
- Align to strategy and capability maps; show how the initiative advances target state.
- Address operating model and change impacts up front; budget for adoption.
- Integrate FinOps for cloud initiatives (rightsizing, commit discounts, egress).
- Capture assumptions and constraints transparently; maintain a decision log.
- Embed security/privacy by design; consult early to prevent late-stage rework.
- Plan decommissioning/technical debt retirement to realize full value.
- Keep the executive summary crisp; tailor content to governance criteria.

## Common Challenges
- Over-optimistic benefits or underestimated costs
  - Mitigation: Use independent reviews, benchmarks, and conservative ranges; perform sensitivity analysis.
- Vague or non-measurable outcomes
  - Mitigation: Define SMART KPIs; secure agreement on baselines and targets.
- Misalignment with strategy or architecture
  - Mitigation: Early EA engagement; use capability and roadmap mapping.
- Hidden compliance/security impacts
  - Mitigation: Early privacy/security assessments; include remediation costs.
- Stakeholder conflict or unclear ownership
  - Mitigation: RACI, facilitated workshops, and executive sponsorship to align priorities.
- Data gaps for modeling
  - Mitigation: Use proxies/benchmarks; state assumptions; plan for data collection.
- Procurement delays and vendor lock-in risk
  - Mitigation: Early sourcing strategy; explore modular contracts and exit clauses.
- Underestimating change management and adoption effort
  - Mitigation: Include change budget, training plan, and adoption metrics.

## Performance Metrics
- Cycle time to approved business case (submission to decision)
- Approval rate at first governance review
- Forecast accuracy: variance of cost/benefit at Stage N vs. actuals at N+1 or post-implementation
- Benefits realization rate at 6/12/24 months vs. plan
- Percentage of business cases with:
  - Assigned benefit owners and baselined KPIs
  - Completed security/privacy assessment
  - Sensitivity/scenario analysis included
  - Alignment to EA standards documented
- Stakeholder satisfaction score (sponsor, Finance, EA)
- Rework rate (number of review iterations or deferrals)

Target thresholds should align to organizational maturity (e.g., cycle time ≤ 6 weeks; forecast variance ≤ ±15% at business case stage).

## Technology and Tools
- Portfolio and project management: Planview, Clarity PPM, Jira Align, ServiceNow PPM
- Financial modeling and TBM/FinOps: Excel/Google Sheets with models; Apptio, Cloudability/CloudHealth, Azure Cost Management
- Enterprise architecture and roadmapping: LeanIX, Sparx EA, Ardoq, BiZZdesign
- Requirements and work management: Jira, Azure DevOps, Rally; Confluence/SharePoint for documentation
- Risk and compliance: ServiceNow GRC, Archer, OneTrust (PIA/DPIA), security risk tools
- Procurement and vendor management: SAP Ariba, Coupa; vendor intelligence (Gartner/Forrester, G2)
- Collaboration and visualization: Miro/Mural (option mapping, value stream), PowerPoint/Google Slides (exec deck)
- Data sources: CMDB, APM/observability platforms, ITSM reports, finance systems for baseline costs
- E-signature and workflow: DocuSign/Adobe Sign; governance workflows integrated with PPM

Process Details:
## Overview
Develop transformation roadmap is the structured process of turning an approved IT transformation vision and business case into a time-phased, feasible, and funded execution blueprint. It sequences initiatives and dependencies from current state to target operating model and architecture, balancing value delivery, risk, capacity, and constraints.

Purpose:
- Translate strategic intent and value proposition into actionable, staged releases/waves of change across applications, data, infrastructure, security, processes, and organization.
- Provide a single source of truth for what will be delivered, when, by whom, and at what cost, with clear dependencies and benefits milestones.
- Enable governance, funding, and resource allocation decisions and ongoing portfolio adjustments.

Role in the organization:
- Connects upstream guidance (customer requirements, opportunity prioritization, transformation business case) with downstream execution (programs, projects, product increments).
- Aligns IT investment and capacity to business portfolios, value streams, and OKRs.
- Supports risk management, compliance, and change management across enterprise functions.

## Key Activities
- Define scope and guiding principles for the transformation roadmap.
- Baseline current state capabilities, assets, and constraints.
- Define target state (architecture, operating model, capabilities, service model).
- Identify, decompose, and prioritize transformation initiatives and epics.
- Map dependencies (technical, organizational, vendor, regulatory) and critical paths.
- Sequence initiatives into timeboxed waves/releases with value milestones.
- Develop migration plans (applications, data, integrations, infrastructure).
- Build resource, vendor, and financial plans (funding and benefits profiles).
- Conduct scenario planning and risk-adjusted prioritization.
- Create roadmap artifacts (heatmaps, Gantt/roadmaps, dependency matrices).
- Validate with stakeholders; iterate and obtain approvals.
- Establish governance, change control, and review cadences.
- Publish and communicate the roadmap and transition to delivery governance.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved transformation vision, business case, value proposition, and target outcomes/OKRs.
- Current-state assessments: enterprise and solution architectures, application and service portfolios, CMDB, infrastructure topology, data landscape, security posture, process maps, skill inventory.
- Target operating model (high-level) and architectural principles/guardrails.
- Regulatory/compliance requirements and risk appetite.
- Funding envelope, cost constraints, and benefit expectations.
- Vendor landscape, existing contracts, and sourcing strategy.
- Capacity forecasts and resource constraints (internal teams and partners).

Prerequisites:
- Executive sponsorship and decision-making framework defined.
- Initial backlog of opportunities/initiatives with high-level sizing.
- Stakeholder map and engagement plan.
- Agreed prioritization criteria (e.g., strategic alignment, WSJF, risk, compliance).

Dependencies on other processes:
- Upstream: Collect and analyze customer requirements; Identify opportunities and prioritize outcomes; Develop and support business case; Target architecture definition; IT portfolio analysis.
- Downstream: Program and project initiation; Procurement and vendor management; Delivery and release management; Organizational change management; Benefits realization tracking; Architecture governance.

## Process Steps
1) Establish roadmap scope and principles
- Confirm transformation objectives, value metrics, and time horizons (e.g., 3–5 year strategic, 12–18 month rolling plan, 90-day increments).
- Set guardrails: architecture principles, security-by-design, data privacy, cloud strategy, sourcing boundaries, operational SLOs.

2) Baseline current state
- Consolidate inventories: applications, integrations, infrastructure, data domains, services, contracts, teams.
- Assess capability maturity and pain points; quantify technical debt and risk hot spots.
- Validate cost-to-serve baseline (run and change), demand pipeline, and capacity.

3) Define target state slices
- Translate target operating model into target capabilities, value streams, product/service model, and platform strategy.
- Define north-star architecture patterns (e.g., domain-driven design, API-first, eventing, zero trust).
- Specify non-functional requirements and compliance needs.

4) Identify and structure initiatives
- Decompose the transformation into epics/features/workstreams across domains (applications, data, infrastructure/platform, security, process, org/change).
- Draft acceptance criteria and leading value indicators for each initiative.

5) Prioritize and sequence
- Score initiatives using agreed criteria (strategic fit, benefit, effort/cost, risk, urgency, regulatory).
- Map dependencies and constraints; identify critical paths and no-regret moves.
- Create waves/releases (e.g., Wave 0 foundation, Wave 1 pilot, Wave 2 scale) with 3–6 month horizons, each with clear exit criteria.

6) Develop migration strategies
- Application rationalization: retire, rehost, replatform, refactor, replace; plan coexistence and cutovers.
- Data migration: domain-by-domain approach, data quality remediation, lineage, encryption, residency.
- Integration strategy: API layers, message buses, sequencing of integration rewires.
- Infrastructure/platform: cloud landing zones, network segmentation, identity, observability.

7) Build resource, vendor, and financial plans
- Estimate capacity by role; identify skill gaps; plan hiring/reskilling/partnering.
- Align sourcing model and vendor selection waves; negotiate contract terms aligned to roadmap.
- Create a time-phased budget (CapEx/OpEx); link benefits to milestones; compute NPV/IRR where applicable.

8) Risk and scenario analysis
- Run scenarios (e.g., budget ±15%, regulatory change, vendor delay); model impact on scope and timing.
- Define risk mitigations and contingency buffers; document risk-adjusted plan.

9) Governance and change control design
- Define decision rights, escalation paths, stage gates, and architecture compliance checks.
- Set review cadences: quarterly business reviews, monthly portfolio sync, weekly dependency forums.
- Establish change control: criteria for roadmap changes, intake workflow, and impact assessment.

10) Produce roadmap artifacts
- Integrated master roadmap and domain roadmaps.
- Dependency matrix and heatmaps; critical path visualization.
- Milestone plan and release calendar; migration wave plans and cutover windows.
- Communication and training plan; stakeholder-specific views.

11) Validate and secure approvals
- Socialize drafts with business sponsors, product leaders, architects, finance, risk, and operations.
- Incorporate feedback, finalize, and obtain formal approval and funding gates.

12) Publish and handover to delivery
- Publish to portfolio and planning tools; align with product/program backlogs.
- Kick off initial waves; confirm entry criteria for Wave 0/1.
- Transition to ongoing roadmap management with defined metrics and reporting.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Approved, version-controlled transformation roadmap with time-phased initiatives and benefits.
- Sequenced migration plan across applications, data, integrations, and infrastructure.
- Resource, vendor, and financial plan aligned to releases.
- Governance model, change control, and review cadence.
- Risk register with mitigations and contingency plans.

Deliverables produced:
- Integrated master roadmap and domain-specific roadmaps.
- Initiative backlog with epics/features, dependencies, and acceptance/value criteria.
- Architecture target-state summary and reference patterns.
- Application portfolio rationalization decisions.
- Data migration and integration plans.
- Release calendar and cutover playbooks (for near-term waves).
- Benefits realization plan and OKRs.
- Stakeholder communications and training plan.
- Decision log, assumptions, and constraints register.

Success criteria:
- Roadmap is approved by key stakeholders and funded.
- Clear linkage of initiatives to business objectives and measurable KPIs.
- Feasible sequencing with resource and vendor commitments secured.
- Risks and dependencies documented with viable mitigations.
- Near-term waves are execution-ready with defined entry/exit criteria.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor/Business Owner: Set objectives, approve scope/funding, resolve cross-business conflicts.
- CIO/CTO: Own IT strategy alignment, approve roadmap guardrails and major technology decisions.
- Enterprise Architect: Define target state and principles; ensure architectural coherence; chair architecture reviews.
- Solution/Domain Architects: Elaborate domain roadmaps; define migration designs and non-functional requirements.
- Portfolio/Program Manager: Integrate plans; manage dependencies, stage gates, and reporting; run scenario planning.
- Product Owners/Value Stream Leads: Define outcomes and prioritize features; validate benefits and user impact.
- Finance/IT Controlling: Build funding model, track CapEx/OpEx and benefits; support investment gating.
- Security, Risk, and Compliance Leads (CISO, DPO): Embed security/privacy-by-design; ensure regulatory alignment.
- Data/Analytics Leader: Own data strategy, migration, quality, and governance alignment.
- Platform/Infrastructure Lead: Plan platform evolution, capacity, and operational readiness.
- Change Management/HR/L&D: Plan org design, change impact, communications, and training.
- Vendor Management/Procurement: Align sourcing and contracts to roadmap waves; manage SLAs and incentives.
- PMO/Agile CoE: Establish standards, governance cadence, metrics, and continuous improvement.

## Best Practices
- Start with outcomes: tie initiatives to measurable business value and OKRs; avoid tech-for-tech’s-sake.
- Use capability and value stream mapping to prioritize where change yields the most value.
- Plan in waves with short feedback loops; keep a 12–18 month rolling plan updated quarterly.
- Balance foundational enablers (identity, observability, security) with visible wins to sustain sponsorship.
- Apply risk-adjusted sequencing; tackle critical dependencies and “no-regret” moves early.
- Include non-functional and compliance requirements from the outset (performance, resilience, privacy).
- Co-create with business stakeholders and users; validate assumptions via pilots.
- Maintain a single source of truth in portfolio tooling; version-control roadmap artifacts.
- Integrate change management, communications, and training into each wave.
- Use scenario planning to handle budget/priority changes; define clear change control.
- Align incentives and contracts with outcomes, not just outputs; leverage value-based milestones.
- Track and actively reduce technical debt; include remediation items in each wave.

## Common Challenges
- Shifting priorities and scope creep: Mitigate with strong portfolio governance, change control, and OKR alignment.
- Underestimating integration/data complexity: Conduct early data discovery, lineage mapping, and integration impact analysis.
- Resource and skill gaps: Use skills assessment, targeted hiring/reskilling, and partner capacity planning.
- Vendor lock-in or delivery risk: Stage sourcing, dual-track vendor options for critical domains, outcome-based contracts.
- Legacy constraints and coexistence: Design interim states and strangler patterns; plan for extended dual-run where needed.
- Insufficient business buy-in: Engage sponsors early, show quick wins, and maintain transparent benefit tracking.
- Security and compliance surprises: Involve security/privacy from step one; run compliance impact assessments by wave.
- Unrealistic timelines: Use evidence-based estimating, buffer critical paths, and run scenario sensitivity analysis.
- Overlapping initiatives and conflicts: Maintain a dependency matrix; run cross-domain planning ceremonies.

## Performance Metrics
- Alignment and value
  - Percentage of initiatives mapped to strategic objectives/OKRs.
  - Planned vs realized benefits (value delivered) by wave.
- Timeliness and predictability
  - Milestone adherence (% on-time) for roadmap waves.
  - Lead time from business case approval to roadmap approval.
  - Roadmap churn rate (% scope change per quarter).
- Financial
  - Budget variance (CapEx/OpEx) by wave.
  - NPV/IRR tracking vs business case.
- Risk and quality
  - Number of unresolved critical dependencies; risk exposure trend.
  - Architecture compliance rate at gates; security/privacy findings per wave.
  - Technical debt burn-down trend.
- Capacity and throughput
  - Capacity utilization by key roles; staffing health (vacancy/turnover in critical skills).
  - Throughput of initiative approvals and change requests.
- Stakeholder satisfaction
  - Sponsor and user satisfaction scores for roadmap transparency and outcomes.

## Technology and Tools
- Enterprise architecture and portfolio
  - LeanIX, Ardoq, BiZZdesign for capability maps, application portfolio, dependencies.
  - ServiceNow Strategic Portfolio Management, Planview, Jira Align, Microsoft Project for portfolio and roadmap management.
- Product and delivery planning
  - Jira, Azure DevOps, Aha!, ProductPlan for backlogs, releases, and visualization.
- Financial planning and TBM
  - Apptio, ServiceNow Financial Modeling, Anaplan for cost modeling and benefits tracking.
- CMDB and discovery
  - ServiceNow CMDB, Device42 for current-state asset and dependency data.
- Integration and data mapping
  - Mulesoft/Anypoint, Boomi, Kafka for integration strategy; data catalog/lineage tools like Collibra, Alation.
- Collaboration and visualization
  - Confluence, SharePoint for documentation; Miro, Lucidchart for maps and diagrams; Power BI/Tableau for metrics dashboards.
- Governance and risk
  - GRC tools (ServiceNow GRC, OneTrust) for risk, compliance, and policy controls.
- Change enablement
  - Learning platforms (LMS), communications tools, and survey platforms for adoption metrics.

These tools should be integrated where possible to create a single source of truth for the roadmap, with automated data flows for inventories, financials, metrics, and delivery status.

Process Details:
## Overview
Define Service Level Agreement is the process of designing, negotiating, approving, and maintaining formal commitments for the performance of IT services. It converts customer needs and business priorities into measurable service targets, establishes how performance will be measured and reported, aligns internal and supplier commitments to support those targets, and communicates results to management.

This process enables:
- Clear expectations between IT and customers (internal or external)
- Alignment of service targets with business outcomes and risk appetite
- Feasible targets backed by operations, suppliers, and budgets
- Consistent measurement, reporting, and continuous improvement
- Governance for changes, renewals, and dispute resolution

It is a core component of IT service management and ties closely to the service catalog, operational level agreements (OLAs), underpinning contracts (UCs), and performance evaluation/reporting.

## Key Activities
- Elicit and validate service level requirements (SLRs) from customers and stakeholders
- Define service scope, service tiers, and associated targets (SLOs/SLIs)
- Establish measurement methodology, data sources, and reporting cadence
- Draft SLA terms including responsibilities, escalation paths, exclusions, and remedies
- Validate feasibility with operations, capacity, security, and suppliers
- Align and/or create required OLAs and UCs to support SLA targets
- Perform risk, cost, and legal/compliance review; negotiate and finalize
- Obtain approvals and signatures; publish and communicate SLA
- Configure monitoring, dashboards, alerting, and automated reporting
- Periodically review performance, report to management, and drive improvements
- Manage SLA changes, renewals, and terminations as services evolve

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Business objectives, critical processes, and risk tolerance
  - Service descriptions and catalog entries (scope, dependencies, service hours)
  - Historical performance data and incident/problem trends
  - Customer SLRs and priority use cases
  - Regulatory, security, and compliance requirements
  - Vendor contracts and standard provider SLAs
  - Operational capabilities and capacity constraints
  - Cost-to-serve data and budget constraints
  - Enterprise architecture and DR/BCP requirements
- Prerequisites:
  - Defined service ownership and governance model
  - Baseline monitoring and observability for key services
  - An approved service catalog entry or draft description
  - Access to legal, risk, and vendor management support
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Develop and manage IT service levels (parent process)
  - Service catalog management
  - Availability, capacity, and continuity management
  - Incident, problem, and change management
  - Information security and compliance
  - Vendor/supplier management and contract management
  - IT financial management/chargeback-showback
  - Performance measurement and reporting

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and scope
   - Identify service(s) requiring an SLA, stakeholders, and drivers (new service, renewal, regulatory requirement).
   - Define scope: customers, environments, service tiers, geographies, and timeframe.

2. Gather requirements
   - Conduct workshops with business relationship managers, service owners, and customers to capture SLRs.
   - Prioritize needs (e.g., availability, response times, throughput, RPO/RTO, security, support hours).
   - Document assumptions, dependencies, and constraints.

3. Define measurement framework
   - Specify Service Level Indicators (SLIs) and Service Level Objectives (SLOs) per service.
   - Define formulas, data sources, sampling intervals, and calculation windows (e.g., 99.9% monthly uptime).
   - Establish incident priority definitions and mapping to response and resolution targets.
   - Define maintenance windows, planned outage handling, and exclusion criteria.

4. Draft SLA
   - Include: service description, scope, roles/responsibilities, support hours, service windows, targets, reporting cadence, escalation matrix, customer responsibilities, security/privacy obligations, data location/residency, compliance requirements, change control, review schedule, remedies/credits with caps, dispute resolution, force majeure, term/renewal/termination.
   - Align language to be specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, and time-bound.

5. Feasibility and alignment check
   - Validate with operations, SRE, capacity, availability, and security teams.
   - Confirm monitoring coverage and data quality; identify gaps and remediation.
   - Map required OLAs (internal teams) and UCs (suppliers) to support targets.

6. Costing and risk assessment
   - Model cost to achieve/maintain targets by tier (e.g., 99.9% vs 99.99%).
   - Assess risks (technical, operational, compliance); update risk register.
   - Propose mitigations (redundancy, scaling, process changes) and associated costs.

7. Legal and compliance review
   - Obtain legal input on terms, liabilities, confidentiality, data protection, and regulatory clauses.
   - Validate alignment with enterprise policies, certifications (e.g., ISO 27001), and industry regulations.

8. Negotiate and iterate
   - Review draft with customer; negotiate targets, responsibilities, and remedies.
   - Use data and trade-offs (cost vs performance) to reach agreement.
   - Iterate document until consensus on feasibility and value.

9. Finalize support structure
   - Finalize and, if needed, create/update OLAs and UCs to underpin the SLA.
   - Ensure vendor SLAs in multi-supplier environments are harmonized (avoid conflicts, clarify handoffs).

10. Approvals and signature
   - Capture approvals from service owner, operations, finance, legal, risk, and customer representative.
   - Execute signatures via approved contract process; store in contract repository and link to service catalog.

11. Implement monitoring and reporting
   - Configure monitoring tools, SLIs, dashboards, alerts, and automated SLA calculations.
   - Establish reporting templates and schedules for customers and management.
   - Test measurement end-to-end and validate data integrity.

12. Communicate and enable
   - Publish SLA summary in the service catalog and knowledge base.
   - Brief service desk and operations; update runbooks and escalation guides.
   - Communicate to stakeholders: start date, review cadence, where to access reports.

13. Operate and report
   - Track performance continuously; generate periodic reports.
   - Conduct management and customer reviews; highlight trends, risks, and improvement actions.

14. Continuous improvement and change control
   - Log breaches and root causes; agree corrective actions and due dates.
   - Manage SLA changes via change management; update OLAs/UCs accordingly.
   - Periodically reassess targets vs business needs; adjust tiers as needed.

15. Renewal or termination
   - Review SLA prior to expiry; renegotiate or terminate based on service lifecycle and business strategy.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Signed SLA document and version history
- Updated service catalog entry with SLA summary
- Mapped and updated OLAs and UCs
- Monitoring configurations, dashboards, and reporting pack
- Communication and enablement materials (runbooks, escalation matrices)
- Management reports on SLA performance and breaches
- Risk assessment and mitigation plan
- Continuous service improvement (CSI) backlog and action tracker

Success criteria:
- SLA signed by all parties and published
- Measurement and reporting operational with validated data
- SLA compliance rate meets or exceeds targets
- No unresolved disputes on measurement or scope
- Underpinning OLAs/UCs aligned and active
- Positive customer satisfaction and reduced escalations

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Service Level Manager: Owns SLA process, facilitates workshops, drafts and maintains SLAs, coordinates reviews, tracks performance, reports to management.
- Service Owner/Product Owner: Defines service scope, approves targets, ensures operational feasibility, sponsors improvements.
- Business Relationship Manager/Customer Representative: Captures business needs, negotiates terms, confirms acceptability.
- Operations Lead/SRE/Support Manager: Validates feasibility, configures monitoring, meets targets, executes escalations.
- Capacity/Availability/Continuity Managers: Provide modeling, constraints, and recommendations for targets and risk mitigations.
- Information Security Officer/Privacy Officer: Ensures security and regulatory clauses and controls are addressed.
- Vendor Manager/Procurement: Aligns supplier contracts and SLAs, negotiates UCs, manages multi-supplier dependencies.
- Legal Counsel/Risk/Compliance: Reviews legal terms, liabilities, and compliance requirements.
- Finance/ITFM: Validates cost implications, service credits, and budget alignment.
- Quality Assurance/PMO: Ensures process adherence and documentation quality.

## Best Practices
- Tie targets to business outcomes; avoid vanity metrics.
- Use the SLI/SLO framework and define precise calculation methods and time windows.
- Set targets that are measurable, controllable by the provider, and economically feasible.
- Define incident priorities and map to response/resolution SLAs; standardize across services.
- Specify exclusions, planned maintenance windows, and data integrity rules.
- Employ service tiers (e.g., Bronze/Silver/Gold) to match varying needs and budgets.
- Align SLAs with OLAs/UCs; avoid promises not supported by internal/supplier capabilities.
- Automate monitoring and reporting; minimize manual calculations.
- Include security, privacy, and compliance obligations explicitly.
- Adopt error budgets and review burn rates to balance reliability and change velocity.
- Establish clear escalation paths and governance for changes and disputes.
- Schedule regular reviews (e.g., quarterly) and link findings to a CSI backlog.
- In multi-supplier models (SIAM), define handoffs, clock starts/stops, and responsibility matrices.

## Common Challenges
- Ambiguous definitions leading to disputes
  - Solution: Standardize metric definitions, include examples, and specify inclusions/exclusions.
- Unrealistic targets vs budget or capability
  - Solution: Provide costed options per tier; validate feasibility before negotiation.
- Poor monitoring coverage and data quality
  - Solution: Implement observability improvements and data governance; pilot measurements before go-live.
- Multi-supplier accountability gaps
  - Solution: Align OLAs/UCs; define end-to-end ownership, handoffs, and shared SLAs where needed.
- Scope creep and changing requirements
  - Solution: Govern changes via formal change control and scheduled reviews.
- Incentive misalignment (e.g., gaming metrics)
  - Solution: Use balanced metrics, cross-validate data, and include qualitative reviews.
- Legal and compliance complexity
  - Solution: Early legal/Compliance involvement; maintain clause libraries and standards.
- Disparate regional or regulatory needs
  - Solution: Use regional annexes and data residency clauses; maintain a global baseline with local variants.

## Performance Metrics
- Coverage and timeliness
  - % of in-scope services with signed SLAs
  - Time from initiation to signed SLA (cycle time)
  - % of SLIs measured automatically vs manually
- Compliance and quality
  - SLA compliance rate by service and target
  - Number and severity of SLA breaches; mean time to restore compliance
  - Data integrity score (e.g., % of periods with validated, complete data)
  - % of OLAs/UCs aligned to SLA targets
- Value and outcomes
  - Customer satisfaction (CSAT/NPS) for covered services
  - Service credit frequency and value paid vs caps
  - Reduction in major incidents or escalations post-SLA
- Governance and improvement
  - Review cadence adherence (% completed on time)
  - Number of SLA-related disputes and time to resolution
  - CSI actions delivered on time; breach root-cause closure rate

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM and SLM platforms: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, BMC Helix/Remedy, Cherwell/Freshservice for SLA definitions, workflows, OLAs/UCs, and reporting.
- Monitoring and observability: Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic, AppDynamics, Splunk, Prometheus/Grafana, Zabbix, SolarWinds; cloud-native tools like AWS CloudWatch, Azure Monitor, GCP Cloud Monitoring; synthetic and RUM tools for availability and performance.
- Network and endpoint monitoring: ThousandEyes, Kentik, Netscout for end-to-end KPIs.
- Contract lifecycle management and e-signature: Icertis, Conga, Ironclad, DocuSign, Adobe Acrobat Sign.
- BI and reporting: Power BI, Tableau, Looker for management dashboards and customer reports.
- CMDB and service mapping: ServiceNow CMDB/Discovery, Device42 for dependency mapping to support end-to-end SLAs.
- Collaboration and knowledge: Confluence, SharePoint, Teams/Slack for documentation, reviews, and communication.
- Capacity and availability planning: Turbonomic, VMware Aria, native cloud advisors for feasibility analysis.
- SIAM coordination: Multi-supplier orchestration tools and RACI matrices to manage handoffs and shared SLAs.
- Automation: Scripting/RPA to collect metrics, calculate SLAs, and distribute reports.

Process Details:
# [8.1.5.6] Negotiate and establish service level agreements

## Overview
This process defines how the organization negotiates, documents, approves, and operationalizes Service Level Agreements (SLAs) with internal or external customers. SLAs set measurable expectations for IT services (e.g., availability, response/resolution times, performance, data protection) and clarify responsibilities, priorities, reporting, and escalation paths.

Purpose:
- Align IT service commitments with business outcomes and risk appetite.
- Establish clear, measurable service targets and how they are measured.
- Prevent ambiguity and disputes through standardized definitions and processes.
- Enable effective governance, reporting, and continual improvement.

Role in the organization:
- Core component of IT Service Level Management (ITIL/ISO 20000).
- Bridges customer needs (service level requirements) with IT’s operational capabilities and supplier commitments (OLAs and underpinning contracts).
- Supports portfolio, capacity/availability/security/continuity planning, incident/major incident management, and vendor management.

Scope:
- Applies to new services, changes to existing services, renewals, and customer-specific variations.
- Covers corporate-, customer-, and service-level agreement layers where relevant.

## Key Activities
- Validate service level requirements (SLRs) and business context.
- Baseline current service performance and feasibility.
- Draft SLA terms, targets, measurement methods, and exclusions.
- Align internal OLAs and supplier Underpinning Contracts (UCs) to support targets.
- Cross-functional review with operations, security, compliance, legal, finance, and vendor management.
- Customer negotiation (terms, targets, incentives, reporting).
- Pilot/validate metrics collection and reporting (shadow measurement).
- Approvals, signature, and controlled publication.
- Tool configuration for monitoring and SLA calculation/reporting.
- Communication, onboarding, and periodic review governance setup.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Service description and catalog entry (scope, features, service tiers/offerings).
- Customer business requirements/SLRs, RFP/SOW if applicable.
- Historical performance/baseline data (availability, response/resolution, throughput, latency, error rate).
- Dependency map/CMDB for the service (apps, infra, vendors).
- Risk/criticality classification (e.g., tiering, RTO/RPO needs).
- Regulatory and contractual requirements (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, PCI, SOC 2, data residency).
- Cost model and pricing assumptions for service tiers and credits.
- Standard SLA templates, clause library, and legal/compliance policies.
- Existing OLAs and supplier contracts; vendor capabilities and commitments.

Prerequisites:
- Service is defined in the service catalog with measurable components.
- Monitoring/observability can capture required SLI metrics.
- Named roles (Service Owner, Service Level Manager, Account/Customer Manager) assigned.
- Negotiation mandate and approval authorities established.
- Draft reporting cadence and dashboards conceptually designed.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Develop and maintain IT service catalog (8.1.5.x).
- Define/maintain service targets and measurement (8.1.5.x).
- Supplier and contract management (for UCs).
- Risk, compliance, and security management.
- Incident/major incident, request, problem, change, and release management.
- Capacity, availability, continuity, and DR planning.
- Financial management and pricing.
- Configuration management/CMDB and monitoring operations.

## Process Steps
1) Intake and scope confirmation
- Receive SLA request or trigger (new service, renewal, or change).
- Confirm customer, service(s), geography/time zones, business criticality, and timeline.
- Identify agreement layer(s): corporate/customer/service-level.
- Output: Scoped SLA request; stakeholder list; target timeline.

2) Gather and validate requirements
- Review SLRs, regulatory constraints, and risk appetite.
- Clarify priorities: availability vs. performance vs. recovery vs. support hours.
- Confirm incident severity definitions and business hours.
- Output: Requirements log; clarified definitions.

3) Baseline and feasibility assessment
- Analyze historical performance and current capabilities.
- Validate monitoring coverage and data quality.
- Identify constraints and cost to achieve proposed targets.
- Output: Feasibility analysis with options (tiers/targets/costs/risks).

4) Draft SLA
- Use approved template; include:
  - Scope and definitions (services, in/out of scope, business hours, time zones).
  - Service targets and SLOs/SLIs (availability %, response/resolution times by severity, performance KPIs, RTO/RPO, provisioning lead times).
  - Measurement method (data source, sampling, rounding, exclusions, maintenance windows, force majeure).
  - Roles/responsibilities (customer and provider).
  - Prioritization rules, escalation matrix, and comms.
  - Reporting cadence and review governance (QBR/EBR).
  - Service credit schedule or other remedies; cap and calculation examples.
  - Security/privacy, DR testing commitments, change windows.
  - Onboarding, exit/termination and transition obligations.
- Output: Draft SLA v1.

5) Align internal OLAs and supplier UCs
- Ensure OLAs and UCs support targets with tighter or equal commitments.
- Identify gaps and negotiate updates with internal teams/vendors.
- Output: Confirmed/aligned OLA/UC commitments; gap remediation plan.

6) Cross-functional review
- Review with operations, SRE, security/privacy, continuity, legal, compliance, finance/pricing, vendor management.
- Resolve conflicts (e.g., target vs. cost, regulatory implications).
- Output: Redlined draft; risk register updates; go/no-go for customer negotiation.

7) Customer negotiation
- Present proposal with rationale, trade-offs, and tier options.
- Negotiate targets, measurement, exclusions, incentives/credits, and reporting.
- Use structured concession log; avoid custom one-offs unless justified.
- Output: Agreed terms (subject to approval); updated draft.

8) Pilot and validate measurement
- Shadow-run collection and calculation for at least one reporting cycle where possible.
- Validate metric accuracy, time boundaries, pause conditions, and dashboards.
- Output: Validation report; adjustments to definitions or tooling.

9) Approvals and signature
- Obtain internal approvals according to delegation of authority.
- Obtain customer signatures via approved e-signature process.
- Output: Executed SLA; version number; effective and review dates.

10) Publish and operationalize
- Register SLA in the SLA/contract repository and CMDB linkage.
- Configure SLA rules in ITSM and monitoring platforms; update escalation matrices.
- Communicate to service desk, operations, major incident team, and customer.
- Update runbooks; conduct enablement/training.
- Output: Activated SLA; operational readiness confirmed.

11) Govern and improve
- Track performance; deliver reports per cadence.
- Trigger Service Improvement Plans (SIPs) when chronic risks or breaches occur.
- Periodically review SLA relevance; manage amendments via change control.
- Output: Reports, QBR/EBR minutes, SIPs, controlled amendments/renewals.

Decision gates:
- G1: Feasibility approved for negotiation.
- G2: Cross-functional approval to offer to customer.
- G3: Final legal/finance approval to sign.
- G4: Operational readiness sign-off.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Executed SLA document(s) with unique ID and effective dates.
- Aligned OLAs and supplier UCs that underpin the SLA.
- SLA configuration in ITSM/observability tools and reporting dashboards.
- Communication pack (summary of targets, escalation, how-to for staff and customer).
- Baseline and validation report for metrics.
- Governance schedule (QBR/EBR calendar), escalation matrix, and SIP templates.
- Repository updates (contract library, CMDB/service catalog references).
Success criteria:
- SLA meets SMART criteria; is feasible, measurable, and cost-justified.
- Measurement and reporting operate without material disputes.
- 100% of SLA-covered services have aligned OLAs/UCs.
- Customer acknowledges clarity; minimal interpretation disputes in first two cycles.
- On-time negotiation and activation versus agreed timeline.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Service Level Manager (Process Owner)
  - Orchestrates end-to-end process; ensures template and policy adherence; maintains SLA repository.
- Service Owner
  - Defines service scope/targets; accountable for operational feasibility and delivery against SLA.
- Account/Customer Success Manager
  - Leads customer communications and negotiations; manages relationship and reviews.
- Operations Manager/SRE Lead
  - Validates achievability; ensures monitoring, on-call, and incident practices support targets.
- Monitoring/Reporting Analyst or Tooling Administrator
  - Implements SLA rules, dashboards, and reports; validates data integrity.
- Security/Privacy Officer
  - Ensures security, privacy, and data residency clauses meet policy/regulation.
- Business Continuity/DR Lead
  - Aligns RTO/RPO and DR test cadence with SLA commitments.
- Capacity/Availability Manager
  - Confirms capacity plans and availability architecture support targets.
- Legal Counsel
  - Reviews terms, liabilities, IP, remedies, and compliance; advises on negotiation boundaries.
- Finance/Pricing
  - Validates cost, credits, and pricing model; approves financial exposure.
- Vendor/Supplier Manager
  - Aligns suppliers’ commitments; negotiates UCs; ensures SIAM cohesion.
- Change/Release Manager
  - Ensures SLA changes follow formal change control and that maintenance windows are coordinated.
- Customer Roles (Business Owner, Vendor Management, Legal)
  - Provide requirements, approve terms, and participate in reviews.

## Best Practices
- Standardize first: Use tiered SLA catalogs (e.g., Bronze/Silver/Gold) with pre-approved targets and costs to reduce custom one-offs.
- Make targets SMART and unambiguous: Define time zones, business hours vs 24x7, clock start/stop/pause rules, rounding, and exclusions.
- Separate SLOs and SLAs: Use internal SLOs that are as strict or stricter than external SLAs; employ error budgets for agility without breaching commitments.
- Align end-to-end: Ensure OLAs/UCs meet or exceed the external SLA; avoid “watermelon SLAs” (green outside, red inside).
- Use data-driven baselining: Set targets from real performance data and transparent cost/benefit analysis.
- Prefer outcome-oriented metrics: E.g., user transaction success rate, service availability experienced by end users, not just system uptime.
- Calibrate incentives: Structure credits with caps and thresholds; avoid punitive clauses that drive unsafe behaviors.
- Include strong definitions: Severity matrix, maintenance windows, planned vs unplanned downtime, change freezes, and force majeure.
- Govern with cadence: Establish QBR/EBR with standard agenda (performance, incidents, SIPs, risks, demand forecast).
- Pilot metrics: Shadow run and reconcile data with the customer before go-live to prevent early disputes.
- Design for resilience: Tie availability targets to architecture patterns (HA, multi-zone), DR tests, and capacity reserves.
- Document escalation: Named contacts, 24x7 paths for major incidents, and exec escalation.
- Manage scope creep: Log and quantify any requested customizations; revisit cost and risk.
- Review annually or at material change: Trigger renegotiation on major architecture, demand, or regulatory shifts.
- Maintain a clause library: Pre-approved legal and compliance language for common scenarios (data protection, subcontractors, audit rights).

## Common Challenges
- Overpromising/underestimating effort
  - Mitigation: Data-based baselines, cross-functional feasibility reviews, and tiered offerings.
- Ambiguous definitions and measurement disputes
  - Mitigation: Precise SLA language, examples of calculations, and validated data sources.
- Misaligned suppliers
  - Mitigation: Update UCs/OLAs first; enforce SIAM processes and multi-supplier runbooks.
- Insufficient monitoring coverage
  - Mitigation: Instrument SLIs early; require monitoring readiness as a gate to signature.
- Excessive customization
  - Mitigation: Govern exceptions with approval thresholds; prefer standardized tiers.
- Regulatory non-compliance risks
  - Mitigation: Early security/privacy/legal involvement; data residency and audit clauses.
- Time zone and holiday complications
  - Mitigation: Explicit business calendars per region; shared holiday lists.
- Credit liability and financial exposure
  - Mitigation: Caps, cure periods, SIPs, and balanced incentive structures.
- Changes in business demand
  - Mitigation: Include demand forecasting review in QBRs; elastic capacity plans; renegotiation triggers.
- Major incident carve-outs misunderstood
  - Mitigation: Clearly define exclusions vs. included events; ensure comms during major incidents.

## Performance Metrics
Process effectiveness KPIs:
- SLA negotiation cycle time (intake to signature).
- First-time-right rate (no material disputes in first reporting cycle).
- Percentage of services with current, signed SLAs.
- SLA standardization rate (% using standard tiers/templates).
- Coverage alignment: % SLAs with supporting OLAs/UCs in place.
- Metric automation rate (% of SLA metrics auto-collected/calculated).
- Dispute rate (number of measurement disputes per quarter).
- Number of renegotiations/amendments outside planned review.
- Customer satisfaction with SLA clarity (survey).
- Financial exposure: total credits paid vs. total contract value; variance to forecast.

Service performance KPIs (as defined per SLA):
- Availability attainment (% vs target), excluding defined maintenance.
- Response and resolution target compliance by severity.
- End-user performance SLI compliance (e.g., p95 latency, success rate).
- DR posture compliance (RTO/RPO achieved; DR test success).
- SIP closure effectiveness (time to remediate chronic breaches).

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM platforms with SLA management:
  - ServiceNow, BMC Helix/Remedy, Jira Service Management, Cherwell/Freshservice.
- Observability and monitoring:
  - Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, AppDynamics, Prometheus/Grafana, Splunk/Elastic, synthetic monitoring tools.
- SLO/error budget and reliability tooling:
  - Nobl9, Blameless, FireHydrant; SLO plugins for observability stacks.
- Contract lifecycle management and e-signature:
  - Icertis, Agiloft, DocuSign CLM, Ironclad; DocuSign/Adobe Sign for execution.
- Collaboration and document management:
  - Confluence/SharePoint/Google Workspace; version control for templates.
- CMDB and service mapping:
  - ServiceNow CMDB, BMC Atrium; dependency mapping tools.
- BI/reporting:
  - Power BI, Tableau, Looker for SLA dashboards and QBR packs.
- Risk/compliance management:
  - Archer, OneTrust; policy libraries for regulatory clauses.

Actionable configuration considerations:
- Implement SLA calculation rules with clear calendars (business hours vs 24x7), pause conditions (awaiting customer), and time zones.
- Tag incidents/requests to services and severities consistently for accurate SLA reporting.
- Maintain an SLA registry mapped to services and customers with version history and renewal dates.
- Automate distribution of SLA reports and QBR decks; include drill-downs to incident and change data.

# [8.1.6.4] Communicate IT Capabilities

## Overview
Communicate IT Capabilities is the structured, ongoing process of conveying the goals, objectives, services, and value of the IT function to stakeholders across the organization. It ensures employees, managers, and executives understand what IT can deliver, how to engage IT, and how IT contributes to business outcomes and strategic priorities. This process strengthens IT-customer relationships, improves adoption of IT services, reduces shadow IT, aligns demand with IT’s roadmap, and builds trust through transparent, two-way communication.

This process sits within Manage IT Customer Relationships and works in close coordination with Business Relationship Management (BRM), Service/Portfolio Management, Enterprise Architecture, ITSM, Organizational Change Management (OCM), and Internal Communications.

## Key Activities
- Develop capability narratives and value propositions
  - Translate IT capabilities into business outcomes, benefits, and use cases.
  - Align narratives to enterprise strategy, OKRs, and departmental goals.
- Stakeholder segmentation and persona definition
  - Identify audience groups (executives, business unit leaders, end-users, operations, compliance, technical partners).
  - Tailor messages, depth, and channels per persona.
- Communication planning and channel strategy
  - Define cadence (e.g., quarterly roadmaps, monthly newsletters, roadshows).
  - Select channels (intranet, ITSM portal, email, town halls, webinars, collaboration tools).
- Content creation and curation
  - Create presentations, one-pagers, service catalog entries, FAQs, videos, demos, case studies, infographics, success stories.
  - Maintain a single source of truth for IT capabilities and roadmaps.
- Enablement and spokesperson readiness
  - Train BRMs, service owners, and champions on key messages and Q&A.
- Delivery and engagement
  - Execute campaigns, briefings, workshops, and office hours.
  - Coordinate with internal communications for enterprise-wide messaging.
- Feedback and measurement
  - Capture feedback via surveys, polls, Q&A, and analytics.
  - Track engagement, comprehension, and impact on service adoption/demand quality.
- Continuous improvement and content lifecycle management
  - Review and refresh content regularly.
  - Iterate messaging based on data and stakeholder input.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs
  - Enterprise and business unit strategies, OKRs, and transformation agendas
  - IT strategy, operating model, and capability map
  - IT service catalog and service-level commitments (SLAs/OLAs)
  - Portfolio and roadmap (programs, releases, timelines, dependencies)
  - Use cases and case studies, value realization metrics
  - Brand and internal communications guidelines
  - Prior communications performance analytics and customer feedback
  - Regulatory, security, and compliance requirements
- Prerequisites
  - Executive sponsorship (CIO and business leadership)
  - Governance for communication approvals and content standards
  - Defined audience segments and stakeholder map
  - Content repository and publishing workflows
  - Identified liaisons/champions in each department
  - Accessibility and localization standards (as applicable)
- Dependencies on other processes
  - [8.1.6] Manage IT customer relationships (overall coordination)
  - BRM: customer insights, demand signals, stakeholder access
  - Service Portfolio/ITSM: accurate service definitions and catalog entries
  - Enterprise Architecture: capability and roadmap coherence
  - Portfolio/PMO: program timelines, milestones, dependencies
  - OCM/Training: change impacts and enablement materials
  - Information Security/Legal: content compliance and approvals
  - Data/Analytics: metrics and reporting for effectiveness

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and scope
   - Confirm objectives for the communication period (e.g., educate on new capabilities, drive adoption, reduce shadow IT).
   - Define target audiences and key messages tied to business outcomes.
2. Gather and validate inputs
   - Collect updated strategy, roadmaps, service changes, and value metrics from service owners, EA, PMO, and BRMs.
   - Identify change impacts and training needs with OCM.
3. Craft capability narratives and value propositions
   - Express capabilities in business terms: problem statement, outcome, benefits, proof points.
   - Map each capability to business processes, KPIs, and compliance considerations.
4. Build the communication plan and channel mix
   - Determine cadence, channels, and sequencing.
   - Create an editorial calendar with owners and deadlines.
   - Define success metrics per activity (e.g., open rates, attendance, adoption).
5. Develop content and assets
   - Produce core collateral: executive brief, deck, one-pagers, updated catalog entries, demo scripts, FAQs.
   - Create persona-specific variants (executive summary vs. end-user how-to).
   - Ensure accessibility (captions, alt text) and localization where needed.
6. Review and approvals
   - Content review by service owners, EA, InfoSec, Legal, Internal Comms.
   - Final sign-off by IT Communications Manager and relevant executives.
7. Enable spokespeople and champions
   - Conduct briefing sessions with BRMs, service owners, and departmental champions.
   - Provide talking points, Q&A, and feedback capture templates.
8. Execute communications
   - Publish intranet/ITSM portal updates and announcements.
   - Run town halls, roadshows, webinars, and team briefings.
   - Disseminate newsletters, posts in collaboration tools, and targeted emails.
9. Engage and listen
   - Facilitate Q&A, office hours, and “Ask IT” sessions.
   - Collect comments, questions, and support themes to refine content and services.
10. Measure and report
    - Track engagement (views, opens, attendance), comprehension (polls/quizzes), and behavioral impact (adoption, reduced shadow IT).
    - Produce a performance dashboard and insight summary for IT leadership and BRMs.
11. Iterate and sustain
    - Update content repositories, FAQs, and service catalog entries.
    - Adjust messages and channels based on data.
    - Schedule the next cycle and embed lessons learned.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Outputs
  - Approved communication plan and editorial calendar
  - Capability narratives and value propositions
  - Updated IT service catalog entries and intranet/portal pages
  - Content assets: presentations, one-pagers, videos, demos, FAQs, case studies
  - Recorded sessions and Q&A transcripts
  - Stakeholder engagement and performance dashboards
- Deliverables
  - Executive briefings and department-targeted sessions
  - Training/enablement packages for spokespeople and champions
  - Repository of current, version-controlled assets (single source of truth)
- Success criteria
  - Stakeholders can articulate IT’s role and how to engage services
  - Increased adoption of promoted capabilities and improved demand quality
  - Reduced instances of shadow IT and misrouted requests
  - Positive movement in IT-customer satisfaction/relationship metrics
  - Content freshness and coverage targets met (e.g., 100% of tier-1 services have updated collateral)

## Roles and Responsibilities
- CIO / IT Leadership
  - Sponsor the process; align messages to enterprise strategy; deliver executive briefings.
- IT Communications Manager (Process Owner)
  - Owns communication strategy, plan, approvals, and analytics; governs content standards.
- Business Relationship Managers (BRMs)
  - Provide customer insights; tailor and deliver messages to business units; capture feedback.
- Service Owners / Product Managers
  - Supply accurate service details, benefits, roadmaps; review and approve service content; support demos.
- Enterprise Architects
  - Ensure capability alignment to architecture and strategy; validate value propositions.
- PMO / Portfolio Managers
  - Provide program timelines, release content, and dependencies for scheduling communications.
- OCM / Training Lead
  - Integrate change impacts; create end-user enablement and training materials.
- Information Security / Compliance / Legal
  - Review content for security, privacy, and regulatory compliance.
- Internal Communications / HR Comms
  - Advise on channels and enterprise comms standards; amplify messages.
- Departmental Champions / Liaisons
  - Act as local advocates; relay departmental needs; facilitate two-way communication.
- Data and Analytics Lead
  - Define metrics, build dashboards, and analyze communication effectiveness.

## Best Practices
- Speak the language of the business: outcomes, value, and risk reduction; avoid technical jargon.
- Maintain a single source of truth: centralized, version-controlled repository linked to the ITSM portal.
- Use storytelling and proof points: case studies, metrics, and demos to make capabilities tangible.
- Segment and personalize: tailor content by persona, business unit, and region.
- Establish a predictable cadence: e.g., quarterly capability roadmaps, monthly newsletters, semiannual roadshows.
- Make it two-way: office hours, Q&A forums, polls, and feedback loops in every major communication.
- Align with change management: bundle comms with training and support for launches and changes.
- Ensure accessibility and inclusivity: captions, readable formats, plain language, localization.
- Govern content lifecycle: owners, review frequency, expiry dates, and archival policies.
- Measure what matters: link communications to adoption, demand quality, and business KPIs—not just vanity metrics.
- Coordinate across IT: BRMs, service owners, EA, and InfoSec co-create messages to ensure accuracy and trust.
- Leverage champions: build a cross-functional network to amplify messages and capture local needs.

## Common Challenges
- Technical jargon and complexity
  - Solution: Plain-language guidelines, editorial review, and persona-based summaries.
- Information overload and channel fatigue
  - Solution: Curate and prioritize; use targeted messaging and a clear cadence; consolidate into digestible assets.
- Outdated or inconsistent content
  - Solution: Content ownership and review schedules; automated reminders; version control and expiry dates.
- Low engagement from business stakeholders
  - Solution: Tie messages to their KPIs; include quick wins and relevant use cases; leverage executive sponsorship and champions.
- Misalignment with project timelines
  - Solution: Integrate with PMO calendars; use a rolling 90-day window; contingency messaging for delays.
- Trust deficits or prior negative experiences
  - Solution: Transparency about constraints; publish SLAs and performance; share successes and lessons learned.
- Regional or regulatory differences
  - Solution: Localize content; involve compliance early; adapt messages to local processes.
- Shadow IT persists despite comms
  - Solution: Emphasize value, speed, and safety of sanctioned services; highlight risks and provide easy engagement paths.

## Performance Metrics
- Awareness and comprehension
  - Percentage of target stakeholders who can articulate IT capabilities (survey)
  - Comprehension quiz/poll scores after sessions
- Engagement
  - Attendance rates, email open/click-through, intranet page views, video watch time
  - Participation in Q&A, office hours, and community forums
- Coverage and quality
  - Percentage of key services with up-to-date collateral
  - Content freshness (average age vs. review cycle)
- Business impact
  - Adoption rates of promoted services and features
  - Demand quality (percentage of well-formed requests; reduction in rework)
  - Reduction in shadow IT incidents or noncompliant tool usage
- Relationship health
  - IT CSAT/NPS by stakeholder segment
  - BRM-reported relationship score or alignment index
- Operational efficiency
  - Time to publish from content request to release
  - Number of communication defects (inaccuracies, retractions)

## Technology and Tools
- Intranet/CMS: SharePoint, Confluence, or similar for content hub and single source of truth.
- ITSM Portal and Service Catalog: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management for service definitions and engagement pathways.
- Collaboration and messaging: Microsoft Teams, Slack, Yammer/Viva Engage for targeted posts and discussions.
- Email/Marketing automation: Outlook distribution groups, Mailchimp, HubSpot for newsletters and campaigns.
- Events and webinars: Zoom, Microsoft Teams Live, Webex for town halls and demos.
- Survey and feedback: Microsoft Forms, Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey; in-session polls.
- Analytics and dashboards: Power BI, Tableau for engagement and impact reporting.
- Digital Asset Management: Central repository for videos, images, and approved templates.
- Roadmapping/Portfolio: Aha!, Jira Align, Planview for roadmap visuals integrated into messaging.
- Enterprise Architecture repository: LeanIX, Alfabet for capability mapping references.
- Knowledge base: Confluence, SharePoint knowledge pages, or ITSM knowledge modules.
- Accessibility and localization: Captioning and translation tools; style checkers for plain language.
- Chatbots and virtual agents: ITSM virtual agents to guide users to capabilities and FAQs.

This end-to-end process, when executed with discipline and continuous feedback, ensures the organization understands and leverages IT’s capabilities, enabling better business outcomes, improved satisfaction, and maximized value from technology investments.
