Process Details:
## Overview
Manage IT requirements is the disciplined process of translating business objectives and customer needs into clear, testable, and prioritized IT requirements for hardware, software, data, and services. It ensures that IT solutions are feasible, secure, compliant, scalable, and delivered on time and within budget. Within the IT customer relationship context, this process provides a consistent, transparent way to capture the voice of the customer, align expectations, and manage scope across multiple touchpoints.

This process:
- Bridges business goals to actionable technical specifications and delivery backlogs.
- Balances functional needs with non-functional requirements (security, performance, availability, compliance, scalability, usability, observability).
- Underpins solution design, procurement/vendor selection, testing and validation, change management, and service transition.
- Supports roadmap planning, release scheduling, and lifecycle management.

## Key Activities
- Initiate and scope requirements effort aligned to business objectives and constraints.
- Stakeholder identification, engagement, and communication planning.
- Elicit requirements using structured techniques (interviews, workshops, Gemba, prototyping).
- Analyze, model, and refine requirements (process, data, interface, user interaction, integration).
- Define and quantify non-functional requirements (NFRs) and service levels (SLOs/SLAs/OLAs).
- Assess technical feasibility, risks, options, and total cost of ownership (TCO).
- Prioritize requirements and maintain a managed backlog.
- Specify requirements with clear acceptance criteria and traceability.
- Validate and secure stakeholder sign-off; baseline requirements.
- Govern changes via a controlled change process.
- Prepare procurement-ready packages (RFP/RFQ) when needed.
- Support design, build, test, and deployment with ongoing requirements management.
- Measure performance of the requirements process and drive continuous improvement.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs to begin this process:
  - Business objectives, value drivers, and success metrics (OKRs/KPIs)
  - High-level business requirements or demand requests
  - Current-state architecture, application and infrastructure inventory (CMDB)
  - Standards and reference architectures; technology guardrails
  - Regulatory, legal, data privacy, and security policies (e.g., SOX, HIPAA, GDPR)
  - Existing SLAs/OLAs, service catalogs, and product roadmaps
  - Capacity and performance baselines, utilization trends
  - Budget constraints, timelines, release calendars, change blackout windows
  - Known risks, issues, and dependencies from related initiatives

- Prerequisites that must be met:
  - Defined governance and RACI for requirements decisions and approvals
  - Access to a requirements repository/ALM tool and version control
  - Approved templates and checklists (BRD/SRS/user stories/NFR checklist)
  - Identified product owner or business sponsor and IT owner
  - Stakeholder map and communication plan
  - Data classification and handling policy
  - Alignment with enterprise architecture principles and IT strategy

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - IT customer relationship management and demand intake (8.1.x)
  - Enterprise/solution architecture governance
  - Portfolio and project management (intake, prioritization, funding)
  - Risk, compliance, and security management
  - Vendor management and procurement
  - IT service management (change, configuration, release)
  - Quality assurance and testing
  - Budgeting and financial management

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and Scope
   - Confirm business objectives, scope boundaries, constraints, and success criteria.
   - Define assumptions, dependencies, risks, and target timelines.
   - Establish governance cadence (workshops, reviews, sign-offs) and RACI.

2. Stakeholder Identification and Engagement
   - Map stakeholders across business, IT, security, compliance, operations, support, and vendors.
   - Plan communication touchpoints aligned with customer relationship mgmt.

3. Elicit Requirements
   - Use interviews, workshops, journey mapping, process walkthroughs, shadowing, surveys, and document analysis.
   - Capture functional requirements (use cases, user stories) and context (personas, scenarios).
   - Identify interfaces, integrations, data sources/targets, and reporting needs.
   - Surface constraints (legal, regulatory, technical debt, platform limitations).

4. Define Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs)
   - Quantify performance (e.g., p95 latency, throughput), availability (SLO/SLI), scalability, capacity, recovery (RTO/RPO), security, privacy, accessibility (WCAG), usability, observability, data quality.
   - Define environmental and operational requirements (monitoring, logging, alerting).

5. Analyze and Model
   - Create models: BPMN process flows, context diagrams, data models (ER), sequence diagrams, state diagrams, UI wireframes.
   - Validate consistency, completeness, and remove ambiguities.
   - Conduct impact analysis on current systems and services.

6. Assess Feasibility and Options
   - Evaluate solution options (build vs buy vs reuse; cloud vs on-prem vs hybrid).
   - Estimate TCO, time-to-value, and risk profile for each option.
   - Consult architects, security, and operations for guardrail alignment.

7. Prioritize and Plan
   - Prioritize using MoSCoW, WSJF, or value vs effort.
   - Create and groom a backlog with dependencies and release alignment.
   - Identify MVP scope and phased delivery plan.

8. Specify Requirements and Acceptance Criteria
   - Produce BRD/SRS and/or user stories with INVEST quality and clear acceptance criteria.
   - Define data migration, cutover, and decommissioning requirements where applicable.
   - Establish traceability from business objectives to requirements to tests.

9. Validate and Baseline
   - Review with stakeholders; resolve conflicts and gaps.
   - Obtain formal approval and baseline the requirements set and version.

10. Prepare for Procurement (if applicable)
   - Create RFP/RFQ requirements package, evaluation criteria, and compliance matrices.
   - Include security, compliance, and integration requirements in vendor scope.

11. Govern Changes
   - Implement a change control process with impact analysis, approvals, and re-baselining.
   - Communicate changes to delivery, testing, and operations teams.

12. Support Delivery and Testing
   - Clarify requirements during design/build; update traceability.
   - Ensure test cases align with acceptance criteria and NFR validation.
   - Participate in design reviews, threat modeling, and performance test planning.

13. Readiness and Transition
   - Validate operational requirements (monitoring, runbooks, support models).
   - Confirm documentation completeness and training needs.
   - Verify NFRs via performance, security, DR tests; confirm SLAs.

14. Post-Implementation Review and Continuous Improvement
   - Collect feedback vs success criteria; analyze defects linked to requirements.
   - Update requirements repository, patterns, and checklists with lessons learned.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Expected outputs:
  - Approved and baselined requirements (functional and NFRs)
  - Prioritized backlog with acceptance criteria
  - Traceability matrix (objectives → requirements → design → tests → deployment)
  - Requirements models (process maps, data models, interface specs, wireframes)
  - Feasibility and options analysis with recommendations
  - RFP/RFQ package and vendor evaluation criteria (if applicable)
  - Change log and version history

- Deliverables produced:
  - Business Requirements Document (BRD)
  - Software/Systems Requirements Specification (SRS) compliant with ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148
  - User stories and epics with acceptance criteria
  - NFR catalog and SLO/SLI definitions
  - Data migration and cutover requirements
  - Security/privacy requirements and threat model
  - Test requirement coverage and acceptance sign-offs
  - Operational readiness requirements (runbooks, monitoring, support)

- Success criteria:
  - Stakeholder-approved, unambiguous, testable requirements aligned to objectives
  - Full traceability through testing and deployment
  - NFRs validated and SLAs met in production-like testing
  - Minimal late-stage requirement changes and rework
  - Delivery on time/budget for the agreed scope with customer satisfaction targets met

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Business Sponsor/Product Owner: Defines business objectives and priorities; approves requirements and scope.
- IT Business Relationship Manager: Coordinates customer interactions, aligns expectations, escalates issues.
- Business Analyst/Requirements Engineer: Leads elicitation, analysis, specification, and traceability.
- Enterprise Architect: Ensures alignment to enterprise strategy, standards, and roadmaps.
- Solution Architect: Translates requirements into solution architecture; assesses feasibility and options.
- Security/Privacy Officer: Defines and validates security, privacy, and compliance requirements.
- Data Architect/Steward: Specifies data models, quality, lineage, and governance requirements.
- Infrastructure/Platform/Network Leads: Define capacity, performance, availability, and operational requirements.
- QA/Test Lead: Maps requirements to test cases; validates acceptance criteria and NFRs.
- Project/Delivery Manager or Scrum Master: Plans and tracks delivery, dependencies, and change control.
- Vendor/Procurement Manager: Manages RFPs, vendor responses, and contract alignment to requirements.
- Change/Release Manager: Aligns requirement changes to change calendar and release plans.
- Operations/Service Owner: Confirms supportability, monitoring, runbooks, and SLAs.

## Best Practices
- Align early and often: Tie requirements to measurable business outcomes and OKRs.
- Make requirements testable: Use clear acceptance criteria and quantify NFRs.
- Use standard frameworks: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 for requirements; BPMN/UML for modeling.
- Prioritize ruthlessly: Apply MoSCoW/WSJF and define an MVP; avoid “gold plating.”
- Shift-left security and quality: Integrate threat modeling, privacy, and test planning during analysis.
- Maintain a single source of truth: Centralized repository with versioning and traceability.
- Reuse where possible: Standards, patterns, APIs, and reference architectures to reduce time and risk.
- Prototype and validate: Wireframes, clickable prototypes, or POCs to derisk ambiguity.
- Specify operational requirements: Monitoring (metrics, logs, traces), alerting, support model, SLOs, DR.
- Plan for data: Data quality, migration, archival/retention, classification, and encryption.
- Govern change: Lightweight but effective change control with impact and cost/time analysis.
- Engage the right roles: Bring architects, security, operations, and compliance to workshops.
- Document assumptions and constraints explicitly: Revisit at key checkpoints.
- Accessibility and inclusivity: Bake WCAG and usability into requirements.
- Cloud economics: Include cost guardrails, autoscaling policies, and FinOps requirements.

## Common Challenges
- Ambiguous or conflicting requirements
  - Solution: Structured elicitation, modeling, and facilitated prioritization; clear acceptance criteria.
- Scope creep and uncontrolled changes
  - Solution: Baseline requirements; formal change control; MVP and phased delivery.
- Under-specified NFRs leading to performance or reliability issues
  - Solution: Quantify NFRs early; performance modeling and non-functional testing plans.
- Stakeholder misalignment or low engagement
  - Solution: Defined governance cadence, stakeholder mapping, and transparent communication.
- Integration and legacy constraints
  - Solution: Early impact analysis, POCs, incremental integration, strangler patterns.
- Security and compliance gaps discovered late
  - Solution: Shift-left threat modeling, privacy impact assessments, and control mapping.
- Vendor lock-in or solution bias
  - Solution: Options analysis with objective criteria; interoperability and exit requirements.
- Data quality and migration complexity
  - Solution: Data profiling, cleansing, migration rehearsal plans, and rollback criteria.
- Unrealistic timelines vs capacity
  - Solution: Value-based prioritization, phased releases, clear dependency management, and resourcing plans.

## Performance Metrics
- Requirements quality:
  - % requirements with clear acceptance criteria
  - Requirements defect density (defects traced to requirements per release)
  - Rework effort due to requirements changes
- Timeliness and flow:
  - Cycle time from intake to baseline
  - Lead time from baseline to delivery-ready design
  - On-time sign-offs vs plan
- Stability and change:
  - Requirements volatility (% change post-baseline)
  - Change approval turnaround time and impact (cost/schedule)
- Coverage and validation:
  - % requirements traced to test cases and deployed features
  - % NFRs validated in pre-production tests
  - Compliance coverage for applicable controls
- Outcomes and satisfaction:
  - Stakeholder satisfaction (CSAT) with requirements process
  - Achievement of defined business KPIs post-implementation
  - Incident rate in first 30/90 days attributable to missed requirements

## Technology and Tools
- Requirements and backlog management: Jira (with Xray/Zephyr), Azure DevOps, Jama Connect, IBM DOORS Next, Rally
- Documentation and collaboration: Confluence, SharePoint, Google Workspace, Miro/Mural
- Modeling: BPMN tools (Signavio, Bizagi), UML/ER (Sparx EA, Lucidchart, draw.io), wireframing (Figma, Balsamiq)
- Architecture and portfolios: LeanIX, Ardoq, Sparx EA; EA repositories and standards catalogs
- Testing and traceability: TestRail, Zephyr, Xray; traceability plugins; requirements-test linkage
- ITSM/CMDB: ServiceNow, BMC Helix for service catalogs, SLAs, CI relationships
- Security and compliance: Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, Secure Controls Framework mapping tools, data discovery/classification
- Performance and capacity: APM (Dynatrace, New Relic, AppDynamics), capacity planning tools, cloud calculators
- Procurement and vendor evaluation: RFP management tools, scorecards, contract repositories
- Version control and automation: Git platforms, CI/CD pipelines to tie requirements to builds and deployments

Process Details:
## Overview
Assess SLA compliance is the recurring process that calculates, validates, and reports how well IT services met the service targets committed in Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for a specific review period (e.g., monthly, quarterly). It consolidates data from multiple operational sources (e.g., incidents, monitoring, change records) and applies defined measurement rules, exclusions, and weightings to compute an overall attainment percentage per target and per SLA.

Purpose:
- Provide an objective, auditable view of SLA performance against customer commitments.
- Identify breaches, near misses, trends, and systemic issues to drive service improvement.
- Trigger contractual outcomes (e.g., service credits) and inform customer communications and governance.

Role in the organization:
- Integral to IT Service Level Management and customer relationship management.
- Bridges operational performance (Incident/Change/Monitoring) with contractual obligations.
- Supports governance, risk, and compliance through evidence-based reporting and audit trails.

## Key Activities
- Define in-scope SLAs and review periods; lock measurement windows.
- Retrieve SLA targets, thresholds, weights, calendars, and exclusion rules.
- Collect, normalize, and quality-check source data (availability, incidents, response/resolution, performance).
- Apply exclusions (e.g., approved maintenance, force majeure) according to contract.
- Calculate attainment at the service target level; aggregate to SLA-level results.
- Validate results with Service Owners and resolve data anomalies.
- Classify breaches and root causes; quantify service credits (if applicable).
- Produce reports/dashboards and secure internal and customer sign-offs.
- Record actions (SIPs/RCAs) and feed insights to continuous improvement.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Executed SLAs and associated artifacts:
  - Service targets and definitions (e.g., availability %, response/resolution times).
  - Measurement methods, formulas, and thresholds (pass/fail, tiered credits).
  - Target weightings and materiality rules.
  - Business calendars, time zones, and service hours (e.g., 24x7 vs business hours).
  - Exclusion criteria (planned maintenance, customer-caused, force majeure).
- Operational data sources for the review period:
  - Incident and request records (including priority, open/close timestamps).
  - Monitoring and availability data (events, uptime, latency, synthetic tests).
  - Change records (planned windows, CAB approvals) for exclusion validation.
  - Configuration/service mapping (CMDB) to tie events/incidents to services.
  - Vendor/Underpinning Contracts (UC) and internal OLAs for dependency analysis.
- Service catalog/service definitions and customer-to-service mappings.
- Prior period results, disputes, and agreed adjustments (if any).

Prerequisites:
- Agreed and baselined SLA definitions in a controlled repository.
- Accurate CMDB/service maps linking components to customer-facing services.
- Monitoring/ITSM tools configured to capture required data and timestamps.
- Defined review cadence, reporting templates, and approval workflow.
- Data governance standards (naming, time zone handling, data retention).

Dependencies on other processes:
- Manage Service Level Agreements (definition/changes).
- Incident, Problem, Change, and Event/Monitoring Management.
- Configuration Management (CMDB) and Service Mapping.
- Vendor Management (UCs/OLAs, third-party data).
- Availability and Capacity Management.
- Service Reporting and Customer Communication Management.
- Financial Management (service credits) and GRC/audit.

## Process Steps
1) Initiate review cycle
- Triggered by calendar (e.g., monthly on the 1st business day).
- Service Level Manager (SLM) confirms in-scope customers/services and period.

2) Lock the measurement period
- Freeze window to prevent late data alterations; snapshot key datasets.
- Publish a “data freeze” notice and cutoff time for operational backfills.

3) Retrieve SLA definitions
- Pull latest, approved SLA versions, targets, weights, formulas, calendars, and exclusion rules from the contract repository.
- Verify no mid-period amendments; if changes exist, segment calculations by effective dates.

4) Confirm measurement rules
- Validate operational definitions (e.g., “availability” = minutes up / total service minutes excluding approved maintenance).
- Reconfirm time zone/business hours and holiday calendars.
- Document assumptions in a period-specific measurement plan.

5) Extract source data
- ITSM: incidents/requests with fields needed for SLA clocks and pauses.
- Monitoring/APM: uptime, response times, synthetic checks, SLO burn rates.
- Change: planned maintenance windows, approvals, blackout windows.
- CMDB/service maps: affected services/CIs for each event/incident.
- Vendor data: third-party availability/performance feeds or attestations.

6) Data quality checks
- Completeness: all days/hours covered; no missing feeds.
- Consistency: timestamp formats, time zones, daylight savings handling.
- Accuracy: duplicate incidents, misclassified priorities, backdated closures.
- Outliers: anomalous values flagged for review.
- Log and remediate issues; escalate systemic defects to Tool Admin/Data Steward.

7) Normalize and apply exclusions
- Align data to service time windows (24x7 vs business hours).
- Apply approved exclusions:
  - Planned maintenance per CAB-approved changes.
  - Force majeure per contract definitions.
  - Customer-caused or third-party-caused (if contractually allowed).
- Document each exclusion with evidence (change ID, customer email, vendor notice).
- Maintain an exclusion register for audit.

8) Calculate target-level attainment
- Availability example:
  - Service minutes = total minutes in period minus approved maintenance minutes.
  - Downtime minutes = sum of incident/monitoring outage minutes mapped to service.
  - Availability % = (Service minutes − Downtime minutes) / Service minutes × 100.
- Incident response/resolution:
  - Determine SLA clock start/stop events; apply pauses if defined.
  - Compute % of tickets meeting target times by priority.
- Performance/latency:
  - Use percentile-based measures if defined (e.g., 95th percentile <= target).
- Security/backup/capacity (if included):
  - Calculate compliance rates (e.g., % servers patched within policy).
- Record for each target: numerator/denominator, result, pass/fail, evidence links.

9) Aggregate to SLA-level results
- Apply target weights and materiality rules to compute overall SLA attainment.
- If tiered or “all-or-nothing” logic exists, apply as specified.
- Example weighted formula:
  - SLA score = Σ(target attainment × target weight). Keep a calculation sheet.

10) Validate results
- Conduct internal review with Service Owners and Process Owners.
- Investigate anomalies; reconcile discrepancies across monitoring and ITSM.
- Independent QA/check by Reporting Analyst or Internal Audit if required.

11) Identify breaches and at-risk trends
- Flag breached targets and calculate degree of shortfall.
- Analyze root cause categories (people/process/technology/vendor).
- Identify chronic issues, seasonal patterns, and leading indicators.

12) Determine contractual outcomes
- Calculate service credits or earn-backs per SLA terms.
- Prepare credit memo inputs for Finance; include calculations and evidence.

13) Produce and approve reports
- Generate customer-facing reports/dashboards:
  - Executive summary, target-by-target results, breaches, trends, SIPs/RCAs.
  - Clear visuals and supporting evidence links.
- Follow approval workflow: Service Owner → SLM → Account/Customer Manager.

14) Customer communication and sign-off
- Distribute to customers per agreed cadence and channel.
- Host review meeting; capture disputes or clarifications.
- Resolve disputes or document as exceptions; obtain formal sign-off.

15) Record improvements and close period
- Log required actions (SIPs, problem tickets, automation requests).
- Archive datasets, calculations, and approvals; update the audit repository.
- Retrospective on process timeliness, errors, and improvement ideas.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- SLA Compliance Report (per customer/service, per period).
- Target-level calculation sheets with evidence and audit trail.
- Exclusion register with justification and approvals.
- Breach log with root cause classification and impact quantification.
- Service Improvement Plans (SIPs) and assigned actions.
- Service credit calculations and Finance handoff (if applicable).
- Executive dashboards (trend lines, heatmaps, attainment by service).
- Signed customer acceptance/acknowledgment.
Success criteria:
- Reports delivered by agreed due date with <1% data error rate.
- 100% of calculations traceable and reproducible with evidence.
- All breaches have documented RCA and action plans.
- Customer sign-off obtained within agreed window; minimal disputes.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Service Level Manager (Process Owner)
  - Owns the assessment process, timelines, and quality; resolves disputes.
  - Ensures SLA definitions are current and interprets measurement rules.
- Service Owner
  - Reviews and validates service data and results; leads RCAs and SIPs.
- Reporting/Data Analyst
  - Builds datasets, performs calculations, conducts data quality checks, builds dashboards.
- Tool Administrator (ITSM/Monitoring)
  - Ensures data availability, configuration, integrations, and timestamp fidelity.
- Incident/Change/Problem Managers
  - Maintain process data quality; supply context for exclusions and root causes.
- CMDB/Service Mapping Owner
  - Ensures accurate service-to-CI mapping to attribute outages correctly.
- Vendor Manager
  - Gathers third-party performance evidence; manages UC alignment and credits.
- Account/Customer Manager
  - Communicates results to customers; coordinates sign-offs and relationship aspects.
- Finance Analyst
  - Applies service credit policies and posts financial entries when required.
- Internal Audit/Compliance (as applicable)
  - Performs independent spot checks for adherence to policy and contracts.

## Best Practices
- Maintain a single, version-controlled repository for SLA/OLA/UC definitions.
- Use precise operational definitions and examples for each target; eliminate ambiguity.
- Automate data ingestion and calculations; minimize manual adjustments.
- Enforce a data freeze and documented change-control for post-freeze corrections.
- Align to customer business calendars and time zones; explicitly handle DST and holidays.
- Apply exclusions conservatively and transparently with evidence and approvals.
- Weight targets based on customer value; avoid overemphasis on easily-met metrics.
- Use percentile-based performance measures for latency to reflect user experience.
- Perform independent QA of calculations each cycle; rotate reviewers periodically.
- Provide near-real-time attainment dashboards so teams can act before period end.
- Tag root causes consistently; feed findings into Problem Management and SIPs.
- Simulate SLA outcomes when proposing target changes to avoid unintended consequences.
- Keep an auditable trail: raw data snapshots, transformations, calculation logic, approvals.
- Periodically recalibrate mappings (services, CIs, incidents) to reduce misattribution.
- Train stakeholders on SLA logic, exclusions, and evidence requirements.

## Common Challenges
- Ambiguous SLA language leading to disputes
  - Solution: Maintain operational definitions with worked examples; update contracts/templates.
- Data quality issues (incorrect priorities, backdated tickets, missing monitoring)
  - Solution: Data quality rules, validation dashboards, and process controls; hold owners accountable.
- Time zone and calendar discrepancies
  - Solution: Standardize to UTC internally; convert to customer TZ only for presentation; manage holiday tables.
- Incorrect service attribution due to poor CMDB/service mapping
  - Solution: Regular CMDB audits; use automated service mapping and event correlation.
- Overuse or inconsistent application of exclusions
  - Solution: Clear policy, approval workflow, and exclusion register with evidence; periodic audit sampling.
- Vendor dependency gaps (late or inconsistent third-party data)
  - Solution: Contractual reporting SLAs; integrate vendor portals/APIs; define provisional calculations.
- Manual, spreadsheet-heavy processes that don’t scale
  - Solution: Implement an SLA engine, ETL pipelines, and BI dashboards with role-based access.
- Mid-period SLA changes
  - Solution: Effective-dated versions; segment calculations by date ranges; rigorous change control.
- Disputes over service credits
  - Solution: Pre-agreed formulas, roundings, and examples; early sharing of preliminary results; independent verification.

## Performance Metrics
- Timeliness: % of reports delivered on or before due date.
- Accuracy: Data error/rework rate; number of customer disputes per period.
- Automation: % of targets auto-calculated vs manual.
- Completeness: % of SLAs reported with full evidence and sign-off.
- SLA attainment: Overall attainment %; # of breached targets; breach severity index.
- Predictive control: # of “at-risk” alerts issued mid-period and avoided breaches.
- Root cause closure: % of breaches with RCA completed within X days; % with SIP actions closed on time.
- Exclusion governance: # and % of excluded minutes/events with approvals; audit exceptions.
- Cycle efficiency: End-to-end assessment cycle time; analyst hours per SLA.
- Financial impact: Value of service credits as % of contract value; trend over time.

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM platforms: ServiceNow, BMC Helix/Remedy, Jira Service Management (SLA clocks, incident/request data).
- Monitoring/APM/Observability: Dynatrace, AppDynamics, New Relic, Datadog, Prometheus, Grafana, Elastic, Splunk, SolarWinds (availability/performance metrics).
- Event and Availability Management: Opsgenie, PagerDuty, Moogsoft, ServiceNow Event Mgmt.
- CMDB and Service Mapping: ServiceNow Discovery/Service Mapping, Dynatrace service topology.
- Data integration and storage: ETL/ELT tools (Informatica, Talend, Azure Data Factory, dbt), data lake/warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Azure Synapse).
- SLA calculation/analytics: Native ITSM SLA engines, custom SQL/Python, or dedicated SLA calculators.
- BI and reporting: Power BI, Tableau, Looker; scheduled distribution and role-based access.
- Workflow and approvals: ITSM workflows, low-code platforms (Power Automate), digital signature tools.
- Calendar/time management: Enterprise calendar services with holiday management; UTC normalization utilities.
- Data quality and governance: Data catalog/lineage (Collibra, Alation), validation scripts, audit logging.
- Document management and evidence archive: SharePoint/Confluence or GRC systems with retention policies.
- Vendor integration: Vendor portals/APIs for UC data; EDI or SFTP pipelines.

The “Define and communicate digital transformation strategy” process establishes the organization’s north star for integrating digital technologies into business operations, products, and services. It articulates the vision, value objectives, operating model impacts, technology direction, and the change approach required to realize measurable business outcomes. It also ensures the strategy is clearly tailored and communicated to all stakeholder segments, enabling aligned decision-making, coordinated execution, adoption, and continuous improvement.

Role in the organization:
- Guides investment decisions and prioritization across the IT and business portfolio.
- Provides guardrails for architecture, data, security, and delivery practices.
- Aligns product, operations, and customer experience teams on a shared roadmap and outcomes (OKRs).
- Drives culture and capability shifts toward product-centric, data-driven, and customer-centric ways of working.
- Establishes a cadence for review and refinement as market, technology, and organizational needs evolve.

## Key Activities
- Define digital vision, value thesis, and success outcomes.

Process Details:
## Overview
Develop IT Strategic Alignment is the structured process of ensuring the IT function, its portfolio, operating model, and people are deliberately aligned to the organization’s business vision, goals, and value streams. It translates enterprise strategy into actionable IT outcomes, roadmaps, and funding priorities; defines how IT will create and protect value; and sets up the governance mechanisms to keep alignment current as business needs evolve.

This process sits within Define Business Technology and Governance Strategy and connects enterprise strategy to enterprise architecture, portfolio management, and execution. It establishes the “line of sight” from business objectives to IT capabilities, platforms, products, services, and teams. The result is a shared, measurable plan and cadence that coordinates priorities across business divisions and IT.

Business value delivered:
- Improves return on IT investment through value-based prioritization
- Reduces waste and duplication by guiding technology choices and rationalization
- Accelerates time-to-value by aligning funding, capacity, and roadmaps to strategic outcomes
- Increases transparency and trust with business stakeholders via co-created objectives and governance
- Strengthens risk management and compliance through explicit decision rights and guardrails

Frameworks often referenced: COBIT (governance and performance), TOGAF/ArchiMate (architecture alignment), ITIL/IT4IT (service/value streams), SAFe/Lean Portfolio Management (portfolio alignment), Balanced Scorecard/OKRs (outcome focus), TBM (technology business management).

## Key Activities
- Understand business strategy and context: synthesize enterprise goals, value streams, market/regulatory drivers, and risk appetite.
- Stakeholder engagement and alignment: identify stakeholders, define engagement plan, co-create alignment objectives and principles.
- Current-state assessment: analyze IT capabilities, architecture, application landscape, services, spend, skills, risk, and performance baselines.
- Define strategic themes and guiding principles: distill how IT will support strategic outcomes and set decision guardrails.
- Target-state definition: outline target capabilities, platforms, data and integration needs, operating model, and sourcing approach.
- Portfolio alignment and prioritization: map business objectives to IT outcomes and initiatives; prioritize using value, risk, and dependency criteria.
- Roadmapping and funding: build multi-horizon roadmaps; align budgets/funding to products/value streams; set investment guardrails.
- Objectives and measures: define enterprise-to-team OKRs/KPIs and benefits realization plans.
- Governance setup: establish decision rights, forums, cadence, and compliance checkpoints (e.g., Architecture Review Board, Portfolio Review Board).
- Communication and change enablement: socialize the plan, cascade objectives, train stakeholders, and manage change.
- Ongoing monitoring and course-correction: run quarterly reviews, adjust portfolio and roadmaps, track outcomes, and continuously improve.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Enterprise strategy, business unit strategies, and strategic objectives
- Value streams and business capability maps (or inputs to create them)
- Risk appetite, regulatory/compliance requirements, security and data policies
- Current IT landscape: architecture principles, application/infrastructure inventory, CMDB, integration catalogs
- IT operating model and sourcing model (internal, managed services, cloud)
- Financials: current spend by tower/value stream (TBM taxonomy if available), budget constraints, funding cycles
- Demand backlog and in-flight project/product portfolio
- Performance baselines: service levels, customer satisfaction, delivery lead times, incident/problem rates
- Workforce and skills inventory; vendor contracts and SLAs
- Market/technology trends and benchmarks

Prerequisites:
- Executive sponsorship (CIO/CTO and business executives)
- Agreed scope and cadence (e.g., annual strategy, quarterly alignment)
- Access to data sources (portfolio, finance, architecture, risk)
- Defined minimal governance framework (decision rights, escalation path)

Dependencies on other processes:
- 8.2 Develop and manage IT business strategy (upstream strategic direction)
- 8.2.1 Define business technology and governance strategy (principles, decision rights)
- Enterprise/solution architecture definition and standards
- IT portfolio and investment management
- Demand management and intake
- Financial planning and budgeting
- Risk, security, and compliance management
- Organizational change management and communications
- Workforce planning and vendor management

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and Charter
- Appoint process owner and sponsor.
- Define objectives, scope, success criteria, timeline, and governance cadence.
- Confirm data sources and toolset; assign a core working group.

2) Stakeholder Identification and Engagement Planning
- Map stakeholders across business units, finance, risk, security, data, operations, and IT delivery.
- Analyze interests, influence, and alignment needs; define engagement approach and communications plan.
- Schedule alignment workshops and executive checkpoints.

3) Business Context Synthesis
- Consolidate enterprise goals, strategic themes, value streams, regulatory drivers, and competitive insights.
- Translate into explicit business outcomes (e.g., revenue growth in segment X, NPS improvement, cost-to-serve reduction).
- Document constraints and strategic assumptions.

4) Current-State IT Assessment
- Capability assessment: rate IT capabilities against needed maturity.
- Architecture and application portfolio: identify redundancies, obsolescence, technical debt, integration bottlenecks.
- Operating model: evaluate team topology, product vs. project setup, DevSecOps maturity.
- Financials: analyze spend by tower/value stream; unit economics; run vs. change split.
- Risk and compliance posture: key risks, audit findings.
- Performance: baseline delivery lead time, reliability, SLAs, satisfaction.

5) Define Strategic Themes and Guiding Principles
- Co-create 4–7 strategic IT themes linked to business outcomes (e.g., “Digital self-service at scale,” “Data-driven decisions”).
- Establish guiding principles (e.g., “cloud-first where compliant,” “product-aligned funding,” “platform over point solutions”).
- Validate with executives.

6) Target-State and Operating Model Definition
- Target architecture: capability heatmap, reference architectures, data/integration patterns, platform choices.
- Operating model: product/value stream alignment, platform teams, decision rights, sourcing mix.
- Guardrails: security, privacy, data governance, FinOps/Cloud cost guardrails.

7) Alignment Mapping and Initiative Framing
- Build a traceability matrix mapping business objectives → IT outcomes → capabilities/platforms → initiatives.
- Draft initiative one-pagers: problem/opportunity, outcomes and measures, scope, dependencies, options, high-level cost/benefit, risks.
- Identify quick wins vs. strategic bets; cluster initiatives into epics/portfolios.

8) Prioritization and Portfolio Shaping
- Define scoring criteria: strategic fit, value (benefits), risk, urgency, regulatory, customer impact, dependency, capacity fit.
- Run portfolio prioritization (e.g., WSJF, MoSCoW, benefit/risk scoring).
- Balance portfolio across horizons (H1/H2/H3) and maintain run/change balance and risk/regulatory commitments.

9) Objectives, Metrics, and Benefits Realization
- Define enterprise-to-team OKRs aligned to themes; specify leading and lagging indicators.
- Create benefits realization plans with owners, baselines, measurement methods, and realization windows.

10) Roadmapping and Funding Alignment
- Build multi-horizon roadmaps (12–36 months) by capability/platform/product; show dependencies and milestones.
- Align funding to products/value streams; define investment envelopes and guardrails.
- Confirm capacity plans (internal/partner) and sourcing strategies.

11) Governance and Controls Setup
- Establish or calibrate governance forums (Portfolio Review Board, Architecture Review Board, Risk/Security Council).
- Codify decision rights (who decides, who inputs, who is informed) and escalation paths.
- Define compliance checkpoints (architecture conformance, data/security, financial) and cadence (monthly/quarterly).

12) Socialization and Sign-off
- Communicate strategy-on-a-page, alignment map, roadmaps, and funding plans to stakeholders.
- Secure executive approval and document sign-off.
- Publish artifacts in a central repository; brief delivery and operations teams.

13) Cascade and Implement
- Cascade OKRs and priorities to portfolios, product teams, and shared services.
- Update portfolio tool/backlog; initiate change requests or charters where needed.
- Align vendor roadmaps and contracts; adjust SLAs and KPIs.

14) Monitor, Review, and Course-Correct
- Conduct quarterly business reviews (QBRs) and portfolio reviews.
- Track progress to OKRs and benefits; adjust priorities based on new demand, performance, risk.
- Run retrospectives and incorporate lessons learned.

15) Continuous Improvement
- Refresh alignment at least annually; update artifacts as business strategy evolves.
- Improve data quality (portfolio, CMDB, financials) and automation of metrics.
- Mature the operating model (e.g., expand product funding, platform consolidation, DevSecOps practices).

## Outputs and Deliverables
- IT Strategy on a Page linking business outcomes to IT themes
- Guiding principles and decision guardrails
- Business capability heatmap and value stream alignment
- Target-state architecture overview and reference architectures
- Alignment matrix (objectives → outcomes → capabilities/platforms → initiatives)
- Initiative one-pagers and prioritized portfolio backlog
- Multi-horizon roadmaps (capability, platform, product)
- Funding model and investment envelopes; budget allocation by value stream/product
- OKRs/KPIs and benefits realization plans
- Governance model: decision rights, forum charters, calendar, compliance checkpoints
- Communications and change enablement plan
- Signed approvals and versioned documentation in a central repository

Success criteria:
- Executives and key stakeholders endorse the alignment and funding plan
- ≥80% of IT spend and active initiatives traceable to strategic objectives
- Measurable progress on defined OKRs within review periods
- Improved stakeholder satisfaction and fewer misaligned or duplicate initiatives
- Architecture conformance and risk/compliance adherence improve over baseline

## Roles and Responsibilities
- CIO/CTO (Sponsor): Owns overall alignment outcomes; approves themes, funding, and governance.
- Head of Strategy/Enterprise PMO: Coordinates planning cadence; ensures cross-enterprise alignment; integrates with enterprise planning.
- Enterprise Architect (Owner/Lead): Facilitates capability and architecture alignment; maintains principles and target state.
- Portfolio Manager/LPM: Runs prioritization and portfolio balancing; maintains portfolio backlog and roadmaps.
- Business Relationship Manager/Product Portfolio Leads: Gather business needs; co-create outcomes and OKRs; validate value hypotheses.
- Finance Business Partner/TBM Analyst: Provides cost baselines, investment options, and funding scenarios; supports benefits tracking.
- CISO/Data Officer/Risk Officer: Ensures security, privacy, data governance, and risk considerations in principles and checkpoints.
- HR/Workforce Planning: Aligns skills, roles, and org design to the operating model; plans sourcing and capacity.
- Architecture Review Board/Portfolio Review Board (Governance Bodies): Make/ratify decisions; ensure compliance with guardrails.
- Change Management/Communications: Develops and executes the comms and training plan; supports adoption.
- Product Owners/Delivery Leaders: Translate aligned priorities into backlogs and release plans; report progress and outcomes.

## Best Practices
- Co-create with business leaders; use value streams and capability-based planning as a common language.
- Use OKRs to focus on outcomes over outputs; align from enterprise to team levels.
- Adopt a product/value stream operating model; shift from project to product funding where feasible.
- Maintain transparent, living roadmaps; publish alignment artifacts for broad visibility.
- Apply lightweight, principle-based governance; focus on enabling decisions and speed, not bureaucracy.
- Balance horizons (optimize H1 execution, invest in H2 growth, seed H3 innovation).
- Use data-driven portfolio decisions: TBM cost transparency, benefits realization, risk-adjusted value scoring.
- Standardize on reference architectures and platform-first approaches to reduce duplication and technical debt.
- Establish a regular cadence (e.g., quarterly portfolio reviews) and tie to budgeting windows.
- Integrate security, privacy, and compliance by design via early checkpoints and guardrails.
- Continuously improve through retrospectives and metric-driven adjustments.

## Common Challenges
- Siloed priorities and weak business engagement: Solve with formal BRM roles, joint workshops, shared OKRs, and governance forums.
- Shifting strategies and interruptions: Address via quarterly re-planning, capacity buffers, and clear change control.
- Legacy/technical debt blocking progress: Create a funded modernization roadmap; quantify debt costs; couple with business outcomes.
- Shadow IT and tool sprawl: Provide clear platform offerings, chargeback/showback transparency, and federated governance.
- Lack of measurable outcomes: Build capability to define and track OKRs/benefits; train leaders on outcome-based planning.
- Data quality gaps (portfolio, CMDB, finance): Establish ownership, data standards, and automated integrations; perform periodic data hygiene.
- Misaligned funding cycles: Move toward rolling-wave funding and product-aligned budgets; align planning with finance cadence.
- Skills and capacity constraints: Use workforce planning, upskilling, and strategic sourcing; sequence initiatives realistically.
- Decision latency: Clarify decision rights, empower forums, and set SLA for approvals.

## Performance Metrics
Alignment and value:
- Percent of IT spend and initiatives mapped to strategic objectives
- Portfolio alignment score (weighted by value and risk)
- Benefits realization rate vs. plan; value delivered per quarter

Stakeholder and delivery:
- Stakeholder alignment/satisfaction index (e.g., BRM NPS)
- Lead time from demand to approved priority; decision cycle time in governance forums
- Roadmap adherence and replan variance

Architecture and risk:
- Architecture conformance rate at gates and in production
- Reduction in redundant applications/platforms; technical debt trend
- Compliance findings remediated on plan; risk exposure reduction

Operating model:
- Percent of funding allocated to products/value streams
- Team/flow metrics (throughput, WIP, predictability)
- Cost-to-serve or unit cost improvements for key services

- Enterprise Architecture and APM: LeanIX, BiZZdesign, Orbus iServer, MEGA Hopex; Archi/ArchiMate modeling
- Portfolio/PPM and LPM: Planview, Clarity, ServiceNow SPM, Jira Align, Azure DevOps, Aha!
- OKR/Performance: WorkBoard, Gtmhub, Perdoo, Microsoft Viva Goals

- Collaboration and Visualization: Confluence/SharePoint, Miro/Mural, Power BI/Tableau for dashboards

# [8.2.1.6] Maintain IT Strategic Alignment

## Overview
Maintain IT Strategic Alignment is the ongoing process of ensuring the IT function remains tightly coupled to the organization’s business objectives, priorities, and outcomes. It translates business strategy into IT objectives, guardrails, and decision-making criteria; ensures the IT portfolio, architecture, funding, and operating model reflect those priorities; and continuously monitors and adjusts execution to deliver intended business value.

This process is critical to:
- Maximize value from IT investments by focusing on what matters most to the business.
- Reduce waste and duplication through architectural and portfolio coherence.
- Accelerate time-to-value via clear decision rights, standards, and prioritization.
- Enable agility by regularly re-aligning to evolving strategies, market changes, and risk posture.

It sits under Define Business Technology and Governance Strategy and is tightly integrated with Enterprise Architecture, IT Portfolio Management, Demand Management, Program/Project Management (PMO), Information Security, Data Governance, and Financial Management.

## Key Activities
- Maintain an IT alignment framework: principles, decision rights, criteria, and governance cadence.
- Cascade strategic objectives into IT OKRs/KPIs and product/domain roadmaps.
- Align the IT portfolio: intake, prioritization, funding, and rebalancing by strategic themes.
- Enforce architectural alignment via standards, reference architectures, and design reviews.
- Synchronize demand and capacity across divisions and product/platform teams.
- Manage alignment governance: Architecture Review Board (ARB), Investment/Portfolio Board, Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs).
- Monitor and report alignment: dashboards, benefits realization, compliance to standards.
- Communicate and engage stakeholders; manage change and adoption.
- Identify and remediate misalignment (exceptions, shadow IT, duplications).
- Continually improve alignment mechanisms based on performance insights.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved enterprise/business strategy, strategic goals, OKRs/KPIs, and risk appetite.
- Current IT strategy and target-state architecture principles/standards.
- Business capability map and value streams.
- Current IT portfolio (programs, projects, products), budgets, and run/grow/transform mix.
- Demand pipeline (requests, epics), business cases, and prioritization criteria.
- Compliance and security requirements; regulatory obligations.
- Resource and capacity data (teams, skills, vendor capacity).

Prerequisites:
- Defined governance bodies and charters (ARB, Portfolio/Investment Board, PMO/EPMO).
- Traceability model and repositories (e.g., linking objectives → capabilities → initiatives → epics → features).
- Agreed alignment criteria and scorecards (e.g., strategic fit, value, risk, TCO, architecture fit).
- Tooling to support portfolio, architecture, and OKR management.
- Stakeholder roles assigned (BRMs, architects, product owners, finance partners).

Dependencies on other processes:
- Define and maintain IT strategy and architecture.
- IT Portfolio Management and Demand Management.
- Program/Project/Agile Delivery Management.
- Information Security and Risk Management.
- Financial Planning and TBM/FinOps for cost transparency.
- Vendor/Sourcing Management.
- Organizational Change Management and Communications.

## Process Steps
1. Establish alignment context
   - Confirm latest enterprise strategy, OKRs, and risk/compliance updates.
   - Review IT strategic themes, architecture principles, and technology guardrails.
   - Update alignment criteria and weighting (e.g., strategic fit, capability impact, risk-adjusted value).

2. Maintain governance and decision rights
   - Operate ARB and Portfolio/Investment Board with clear charters, quorum, and SLAs.
   - Maintain RACI for alignment decisions (e.g., who approves exceptions, prioritization, funding).
   - Set cadence: monthly ARB, bi-weekly demand triage, quarterly portfolio reviews/QBRs, annual strategy refresh.

3. Cascade strategy into actionable objectives
   - Translate business OKRs into IT OKRs at enterprise, domain, and product/team levels.
   - Map strategic themes to business capabilities and value streams; identify target outcomes.
   - Publish alignment guide: principles, prioritization criteria, scorecards, and examples.

4. Align roadmaps and portfolio
   - Conduct alignment workshops with divisions/BRMs and product/platform teams.
   - Review and update roadmaps (12–18 months) with explicit links to objectives and capabilities.
   - Apply intake and prioritization workflows; score new/ongoing demand against alignment criteria.
   - Rebalance the portfolio by theme (transform/grow/run) and by capability gaps.
   - Approve, defer, pivot, or stop items that do not meet alignment thresholds.

5. Enforce architectural alignment
   - Maintain standards and reference architectures (domain, data, security, integration).
   - Run solution intent/design reviews at key stages; manage exceptions with time-bound remediation plans.
   - Monitor adherence (e.g., EA compliance %) and reduce duplication (apps, data stores, tooling).

6. Align funding and capacity
   - Allocate budgets to strategic themes and product/platform lines (product-centric funding).
   - Ensure capacity planning reflects prioritized demand; adjust sourcing (internal/external) as needed.
   - Apply TBM/FinOps practices to manage cost and value, especially for cloud spend.

7. Execute, monitor, and report alignment
   - Maintain traceability from objectives → initiatives → outcomes → benefits.
   - Build alignment dashboards (portfolio alignment index, benefits realization, EA compliance, exception aging).
   - Run QBRs with divisions to review progress, value, risks, and course corrections.
   - Capture decisions, rationales, and changes in the system of record.

8. Manage change and communications
   - Publish alignment decisions, roadmaps, and standards to stakeholders.
   - Provide training and guidance to product teams on alignment practices, OKRs, and architecture guardrails.
   - Engage continuously through BRMs and communities of practice.

9. Identify and remediate misalignment
   - Detect shadow IT, redundant solutions, budget drift, or architecture non-compliance.
   - Initiate corrective actions: consolidation, re-architecture, scope adjustment, or project cessation.
   - Track exceptions and remediation to closure with clear owners and deadlines.

10. Review and improve the alignment process
   - Conduct retrospectives each quarter to assess governance effectiveness and cycle times.
   - Refine criteria, scorecards, and cadences based on outcomes and stakeholder feedback.
   - Update playbooks, templates, and enablement materials.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- IT alignment framework/policy, decision rights/RACI, and governance cadences.
- Strategic alignment guide: principles, criteria, scorecards, and thresholds.
- Mapped traceability: objectives → capabilities/value streams → initiatives/epics.
- Updated product/domain roadmaps and dependency maps.
- Prioritized and funded portfolio by strategic theme, with stop/pivot decisions documented.
- Architecture standards and reference architectures; exception/waiver register.
- Alignment dashboards and QBR packs (progress, benefits, risks, decisions).
- Benefits realization reports and variance analyses.
- Communications and training artifacts (enablement decks, FAQs).
- Corrective action plans for misalignment and their closure evidence.

Success criteria:
- High percentage of investments traceable to strategic objectives with realized benefits.
- Portfolio and architecture coherence (reduced duplication, increased standard adherence).
- Positive stakeholder alignment and satisfaction scores.
- Timely decision-making and minimal exception aging.
- Demonstrable contribution to business outcomes (revenue growth, efficiency, risk reduction).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- CIO/Head of IT Strategy: Owns alignment framework, ensures enterprise fit, resolves escalations.
- Enterprise Architect (EA) Lead: Maintains principles/standards, runs ARB, ensures architecture coherence.
- Domain/Solution Architects: Review solutions, ensure standards compliance, manage exceptions.
- Portfolio/PMO Lead: Runs intake, prioritization, portfolio balancing, and reporting; manages stage gates.
- Business Relationship Managers (BRMs): Interface with business units, translate needs, ensure traceability and adoption.
- Product Owners/Platform Owners: Maintain roadmaps/OKRs, align backlogs, report on outcomes.
- Finance/TBM/FinOps Partners: Align funding to themes, provide cost transparency, monitor value for money.
- Information Security and Risk Leads: Ensure alignment with security policies and risk appetite; assess risk impacts.
- Data Governance Lead: Ensure data strategies and standards support business objectives.
- Change Management/Communications: Drive awareness, training, and stakeholder engagement.
- Business Unit Leaders/Strategy Office: Provide strategic direction, participate in prioritization and QBRs, co-own outcomes.

## Best Practices
- Use business capability and value stream maps as the common language to align IT work to outcomes.
- Maintain end-to-end traceability from business objectives to deployed features and benefits.
- Adopt OKRs and a balanced scorecard to balance outcomes across value, risk, cost, and compliance.
- Operate Lean Portfolio Management with transparent criteria and WIP limits; stop low-value work early.
- Fund persistent, product/platform teams aligned to strategic themes, not just projects.
- Apply reference architectures and technology guardrails with a pragmatic exception process.
- Institutionalize QBRs with data-driven reviews of outcomes and benefits realization.
- Embed TBM and FinOps for cost transparency and continual optimization, especially in cloud environments.
- Standardize templates and scorecards; automate wherever possible to reduce governance friction.
- Tie incentives and performance goals to alignment and business outcomes, not output volume.
- Leverage frameworks: COBIT (governance), TOGAF (architecture), SAFe/Lean Portfolio (execution), BRM Institute (business relationship), ITIL (service management).

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Shifting business priorities: Use quarterly rebalancing and dynamic funding; keep short feedback loops via QBRs.
- Shadow IT and tool sprawl: Strengthen intake and ARB; provide fast pathways and approved patterns; showcase value of alignment.
- Siloed decision-making: Establish cross-functional boards and BRM network; use shared capability maps and OKRs.
- Unclear ownership: Define product/platform ownership and RACI; publish contact points in the catalog/CMDB.
- Misaligned incentives: Align performance management and funding with outcomes and strategic themes.
- Measurement gaps: Implement traceability and benefits tracking; standardize value hypotheses and success metrics upfront.
- Legacy constraints: Create modernization roadmaps; sequence debt remediation tied to business value.
- Capacity bottlenecks: Improve portfolio WIP management; adjust sourcing; prioritize by value/risk.
- Over-governance slowing delivery: Right-size controls by risk; automate checks; pre-approved patterns.
- M&A and organizational changes: Rapidly reconcile capability maps and portfolios; set interim standards and carve-out plans.

## Performance Metrics
Leading indicators:
- Portfolio alignment index (% of investment aligned to strategic themes/objectives).
- Roadmap traceability coverage (% initiatives with objective/capability mapping).
- Architecture compliance rate (% solutions meeting standards; number and aging of exceptions).
- Governance throughput and cycle time (intake-to-decision days; ARB SLA adherence).
- Strategic theme funding accuracy (variance vs plan).
- Stakeholder alignment score (surveyed BU/BRM satisfaction).

Lagging indicators (outcomes):
- Benefits realization (% planned benefits realized; value delivered vs business case).
- Reduction in redundancy (count/cost of duplicate apps/tools retired).
- Time-to-value (idea-to-first-value lead time).
- Risk posture improvement (reduction in high-risk exceptions; audit findings closed).
- Run/grow/transform balance optimized (mix aligned to strategy).
- Adoption and usage metrics for delivered capabilities.

Health metrics:
- Number of stop/pivot decisions and savings realized.
- Exception backlog and average time to remediate.
- OKR attainment at domain/product levels.

## Technology and Tools
- Enterprise Architecture: BiZZdesign, LeanIX, Orbus iServer/ABACUS, Sparx EA (capability maps, standards, reference architectures).
- Portfolio/PPM and Demand: Planview, Clarity, ServiceNow APM/PPM, Jira Align, Azure DevOps Boards/Portfolio, Rally.
- OKR and Performance: WorkBoard, Perdoo, Gtmhub, Ally.io, or OKRs in existing collaboration suites.
- Roadmapping and Product Management: Aha!, Productboard, Jira Product Discovery.
- Financial/TBM/FinOps: Apptio, CloudHealth/Cloudability, native CSP cost tools.
- Collaboration and Knowledge: Confluence/SharePoint, Miro/Mural for mapping, Teams/Slack for communications.
- CMDB/Service Catalog: ServiceNow, BMC Helix for service and product catalogs and ownership clarity.
- BI/Dashboards: Power BI, Tableau, or embedded PPM/EA reporting for alignment dashboards.
- Compliance/Risk: Archer, ServiceNow GRC, OneTrust for policy alignment and risk tracking.

These tools should enable traceability, automation of governance workflows, transparent reporting, and collaboration across IT and business stakeholders.

# [8.2.2.2] Determine IT Portfolio Investment Balance

## Overview
This process determines the uninvested (available-to-allocate) amount within the approved IT portfolio funding envelope for the current planning horizon (e.g., fiscal year, multi-year capital plan). It consolidates approved budget, actuals, commitments, and forecasted needs across run, change, and transform activities to produce an accurate, timely view of funds that remain uncommitted and can be deployed or reserved.

Purpose:
- Provide a single, authoritative view of uninvested funds by segment (e.g., CAPEX/OPEX, business unit, strategic theme, run/grow/transform).
- Enable portfolio governance decisions such as funding new initiatives, increasing/ decreasing reserves, rebalancing, or returning funds.
- Ensure compliance with financial policies and audit requirements through traceability and reconciliation with Finance systems.

Role in the organization:
- A key control within IT portfolio management and IT finance that supports strategy execution, risk management, and financial stewardship.
- Input to related processes such as portfolio prioritization, funding approvals, intake, and re-planning.

## Key Activities
- Establish approved portfolio baselines and segmentation (e.g., CAPEX/OPEX, cost centers).
- Gather actuals and commitments (POs, contracts, invoices) and in-flight project forecasts.
- Classify spend into standard commitment categories (run-rate fixed, hard committed, soft committed, earmarks/reserves).
- Calculate uninvested balance by segment and consolidate to portfolio level.
- Perform reconciliation and variance analysis with Finance and cost center owners.
- Run scenario modeling (e.g., various reserve levels, currency impacts, slippage).
- Present findings to the portfolio governance body and record decisions.
- Publish and communicate updated available-to-allocate balances and update systems of record.
- Monitor and trigger recalculation on schedule or when threshold events occur.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved IT portfolio budget/baseline by segment (annual and, if applicable, multi-year).
- Actuals year-to-date from ERP/Finance (by account, project, cost center).
- Open commitments from procurement/contracts (POs, SOWs, vendor agreements).
- In-flight project baselines and Estimate-to-Complete (ETC)/forecast from PPM.
- Run-the-business fixed obligations (licensing, maintenance, payroll allocations).
- Earmarks/reserves (e.g., innovation, contingency, regulatory holdbacks).
- Pipeline items with probability and rough-order-of-magnitude (ROM) costs.
- Financial reference data (chart of accounts, CAPEX/OPEX mapping, FX rates, capitalization rules).

Prerequisites:
- Approved IT portfolio funding envelope and segmentation definitions.
- Governance policy defining commitment categories and calculation rules.
- Data integrations or established procedures to collect finance/PPM/procurement data.
- Calendar and cadence aligned with Finance close (e.g., monthly) and portfolio reviews.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [8.2.2.1] Define IT portfolio strategy and segmentation.
- Portfolio intake and prioritization (for pipeline and earmarks).
- Funding approval and budgeting (for baselines).
- Project/program management (for ETC/forecasts).
- Procurement and vendor management (for commitments).
- Financial close and reporting (for actuals, reconciliations).

## Process Steps
1. Initiate cycle and set scope
   - Confirm as-of date (e.g., post monthly close) and planning horizon.
   - Confirm segments to report (CAPEX/OPEX, BU, strategic themes, run/grow/transform).

2. Retrieve baselines
   - Pull approved portfolio budget by segment from ERP/EPM.
   - Validate against prior cycle and note changes/approved re-baselines.

3. Collect financials
   - Actuals YTD: Pull from ERP by project/cost center and account.
   - Commitments: Pull open POs, contracted amounts, and accrued liabilities.
   - Fixed run-rate: Confirm recurring obligations (licenses, support, payroll allocations).

4. Collect portfolio forecasts
   - For in-flight initiatives: Gather updated ETC and forecast by month from PPM.
   - For pipeline: Obtain probability-weighted ROM and expected start timing.
   - For reserves: Verify policy and remaining balance for contingency/innovation/regulatory.

5. Classify spend
   - Categorize each item as:
     - Fixed run-rate (non-discretionary)
     - Hard committed (contracts/POs)
     - Soft committed (approved initiatives pending contract; governance-approved earmarks)
     - Forecast to complete for in-flight
     - Pipeline (probability-weighted if policy requires)
   - Map each item to CAPEX/OPEX, segment, and time bucket.

6. Calculate uninvested balances
   - For each segment and at portfolio total, compute:
     - Total approved funds
     - Less: Actuals YTD
     - Less: Hard commitments (remaining)
     - Less: Forecast to complete (in-flight)
     - Less: Policy reserves and approved earmarks
     - Optionally: Less probability-weighted pipeline (if held back proactively)
     - Equals: Uninvested balance (available-to-allocate)
   - Provide both cash and accrual views if required.
   - Distinguish current-year vs multi-year carryover implications.

7. Adjust for timing and risk
   - Apply FX updates, cost escalators, and known rate changes.
   - Adjust for capitalization policy impacts (e.g., shift OPEX/CAPEX).
   - Include risk-adjusted buffers based on portfolio risk profile.

8. Reconcile and validate
   - Reconcile with Finance for actuals, commitments, and reserve accounting.
   - Validate against cost center owner and PM inputs; resolve variances.
   - Check for double-counting (e.g., avoid counting both ETC and full PO if ETC includes committed spend).

9. Analyze and model scenarios
   - Create scenarios (e.g., 0%/50%/100% pipeline reserve; lower/higher contingency).
   - Assess sensitivity to slippage, vendor delays, or deferrals.
   - Identify surplus/deficit by segment and recommend actions.

10. Governance review and decision
    - Present findings, risks, and recommendations to Portfolio Review Board (PRB)/CIO/IT Finance.
    - Obtain decisions on reallocations, holdbacks, and funding of new items.
    - Record approvals and update funding authorizations.

11. Publish and update systems
    - Distribute summary and detailed reports/dashboards to stakeholders.
    - Update PPM, ERP/EPM, and intake portals with available-to-allocate amounts.
    - Store working papers and decisions for audit.

12. Monitor and trigger re-run
    - Establish thresholds (e.g., >5% variance, >$X change) that trigger an off-cycle update.
    - Align with monthly close and quarterly strategic reviews.

Control points:
- Segregation of duties between calculation (PMO/Portfolio) and approval (PRB/Finance).
- Documented reconciliation and sign-offs.
- Audit trail of data pulls, assumptions, and decisions.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Uninvested balance report by segment and consolidated total as-of date.
- Reconciliation pack: mapping from ERP/PPM/procurement to portfolio view.
- Scenario analysis and recommendations (e.g., reallocations, reserve adjustments).
- Governance decisions log and updated funding authorizations.
- Updated dashboards/scorecards and data refresh in systems of record.
- Audit-ready documentation (assumptions, sources, calculations).

Success criteria:
- Accuracy within agreed tolerance (e.g., ±1% portfolio-level; ±3% segment-level).
- Availability by agreed SLA post-close (e.g., within 5 business days).
- Reconciled and signed off by IT Finance and PRB.
- Actionable insights leading to timely funding decisions.
- No material audit findings; clear traceability of numbers.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- CIO / Head of IT
  - Accountable for final allocation decisions and threshold policies.
- IT Portfolio Manager / PMO Lead
  - Responsible for end-to-end process execution, calculation, and reporting; presents to governance.
- IT Finance Business Partner
  - Responsible for financial data integrity, reconciliation, and policy adherence; co-approves results.
- Project/Program Managers
  - Provide ETC/forecasts; explain variances; validate commitments and timing.
- Procurement / Vendor Management
  - Provide contract/PO data; confirm delivery schedules and financial obligations.
- Cost Center Owners / Service Owners
  - Validate run-rate costs and segment-level forecasts; identify risks/opportunities.
- Enterprise Architect / Strategy Lead
  - Consulted to align segment view with strategic themes and roadmaps.
- Data/BI Analyst
  - Supports data integration, dashboards, and scenario modeling.
- Internal Audit / Compliance
  - Informed; may review process controls and evidence.

RACI summary (narrative):
- Accountable: CIO/Head of IT. Responsible: Portfolio Manager and IT Finance. Consulted: PMs, Procurement, Cost Center Owners, Architecture. Informed: PRB members, Audit, Business stakeholders.

## Best Practices
- Use a single source of truth for each data domain (ERP for actuals, PPM for ETC, Procurement for commitments).
- Standardize commitment categories and avoid double-counting between ETC and commitments.
- Maintain separate views for CAPEX vs OPEX and for run vs change vs transform.
- Align cadence with Finance close and implement rolling forecasts (monthly).
- Apply probability weighting for pipeline cautiously; reflect policy and risk appetite.
- Maintain minimum and maximum reserve guardrails; revisit quarterly.
- Automate data extraction and reconciliation to reduce cycle time and errors.
- Include timing considerations (cash vs accrual, revenue recognition, capitalization).
- Manage FX and inflation assumptions centrally and document changes.
- Keep an auditable trail of assumptions, approvals, and versioned reports.
- Visualize balances and trends with drill-down to segment and initiative.
- Implement thresholds for off-cycle recalculation and governance escalation.

## Common Challenges
- Data latency and inconsistency across systems
  - Solution: Automate integrations; define data cut-off times; implement data quality checks.
- Double-counting or misclassification (e.g., ETC includes committed costs)
  - Solution: Clear classification rules; reconciliation templates; training for PMs/analysts.
- Shadow IT and untracked spend
  - Solution: Strengthen intake and cost center governance; periodic spend discovery with Finance.
- Forecast inaccuracy and project slippage
  - Solution: Rolling forecasts; forecast accuracy KPIs; variance root-cause reviews; contingency buffers.
- CAPEX/OPEX misallocation or policy changes
  - Solution: Finance partnership; policy guides; pre-implementation reviews for capitalization.
- Currency and rate volatility for global portfolios
  - Solution: Standard FX rates per period; sensitivity analysis; hedging strategies where applicable.
- Multi-year funding and carryover complexity
  - Solution: Separate current-year vs multi-year views; track committed carryover explicitly.
- Tool fragmentation and manual reporting
  - Solution: Consolidated BI layer; standardized data model; RPA for routine reconciliations.

## Performance Metrics
- Available-to-allocate balance by segment and trend over time.
- Forecast accuracy (ETC vs actuals) at initiative and portfolio levels.
- Variance to approved budget (absolute and percentage).
- Cycle time from financial close to published balance.
- Percentage of funds uninvested beyond policy threshold (e.g., >10% at Q3).
- Carryover rate to next fiscal period; aging of uninvested funds.
- Reconciliation completeness and number of audit exceptions.
- Number and impact of off-cycle recalculations triggered by thresholds.
- Ratio of discretionary to non-discretionary spend.
- Alignment of uninvested funds with strategic themes (e.g., % available in “transform”).

## Technology and Tools
- ERP/Finance: SAP S/4HANA, Oracle ERP Cloud, Microsoft Dynamics (actuals, GL, AP).
- EPM/Planning: Anaplan, Workday Adaptive, Oracle EPM (budgets, forecasts).
- PPM/Portfolio: Planview, Clarity, Jira Align, Microsoft Project Online (baselines, ETC).
- Procurement/Contracts: SAP Ariba, Coupa, Ivalua, DocuSign CLM (POs, contracts).
- BI/Analytics: Power BI, Tableau, Qlik (dashboards, variance, scenarios).
- Data Integration: ETL/ELT tools and data warehouse/lakehouse for consolidated model.
- Time/Resource: Tempo, Planview Capacity, Smartsheet Resource (optional capacity view).
- Collaboration and Documentation: SharePoint/Confluence for artifacts and audit trail.
- RPA/Automation: UiPath, Power Automate to streamline data pulls and reconciliations.
