Process Details:
## Overview
Develop and maintain service/solution architectures defines how IT services and solutions are structured, integrated, secured, deployed, and evolved across the organization’s technology landscape. The process ensures that every service or solution has a well-documented, fit-for-purpose architecture that aligns with enterprise principles, business strategy, non-functional requirements (NFRs), and regulatory obligations. It also establishes mechanisms to continuously update, optimize, or retire architectures in response to performance data, new demands, risk findings, and technology changes.

This process sits within the broader IT service/solution lifecycle and architecture governance. It provides:
- A reusable, consistent approach to designing and evolving architectures
- Reference architectures, standards, and patterns that accelerate delivery and reduce risk
- Guardrails to maintain interoperability, security, reliability, and cost-effectiveness over networks, clouds, and hybrid environments
- Feedback loops so operational learnings inform ongoing architectural improvements

## Key Activities
- Establish and maintain reference architectures, standards, and patterns for services/solutions
- Baseline current-state architectures (as-is) and dependencies across applications, data, integrations, and networks
- Define target and transition architectures aligned to business capabilities, roadmaps, and NFRs
- Conduct architectural evaluations and risk assessments (e.g., ATAM, threat modeling)
- Run architecture governance (reviews, approvals, waivers, exception management)
- Document and manage Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
- Provide architecture guidance during implementation (design support, code/infra reviews)
- Monitor conformance, performance, cost, and security posture; drive improvements
- Manage technical debt, deprecation, and end-of-life (EOL) plans
- Maintain the architecture repository and ensure knowledge is discoverable and current

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Business strategy, product/service roadmaps, and capability models
- IT strategy, enterprise architecture principles and guardrails
- Service catalog and service portfolio priorities
- Current-state architecture artifacts (CMDB, network diagrams, app/integration inventories)
- NFRs and quality attribute scenarios (security, reliability, performance, scalability, operability, cost)
- Regulatory, compliance, privacy, and security requirements
- Technology standards and preferred vendor/platform lists
- Operational data: incident/problem trends, performance telemetry, capacity/utilization, cost/FinOps data
- Risk register, audit findings, and vulnerability reports
- Vendor roadmaps and end-of-support timelines

Prerequisites:
- Defined architecture governance model (roles, forums, review criteria, waiver policy)
- Architecture repository and modeling standards (e.g., ArchiMate/C4, naming/versioning)
- Tooling for documentation, version control, and policy/conformance checks
- Skilled architecture roles (solution, domain, security, data, network, cloud)

Dependencies on other processes:
- Enterprise architecture management and technology standards (8.5.3.x)
- Demand/portfolio management and solution delivery lifecycle
- Information security governance, risk, and compliance
- IT service management (change/release/configuration), capacity/availability/continuity
- Vendor/supplier management and procurement
- Data management and integration governance
- DevOps/SRE practices for delivery and operations feedback

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and scope
- Trigger: new service/solution, significant change, performance/security/cost issue, technology refresh.
- Define scope, objectives, stakeholders, critical constraints, and success criteria.
- Select applicable reference architectures and standards.

2) Baseline current state
- Inventory involved services, applications, data stores, APIs, integrations, network topologies, identities, and environments.
- Map dependencies and data flows; identify shared services and external providers.
- Capture current NFR performance, cost, risks, and technical debt.

3) Elicit and refine requirements
- Translate business needs into functional scope and NFRs (with measurable targets/SLOs).
- Create quality attribute scenarios (e.g., “handle 3x traffic in seasonal peaks with p95 < 200 ms”).
- Record regulatory and data classification needs; define RTO/RPO/disaster recovery requirements.

4) Define architecture principles and guardrails in context
- Apply enterprise principles (e.g., security-by-design, API-first, least privilege, zero trust, cloud-native).
- Confirm technology constraints (approved platforms, data residency, network segmentation).

5) Design target architecture
- Produce multiple views: logical (capabilities/domains), application/service, data and integrations, security, deployment/infrastructure/network, operations/observability.
- Select architectural styles (e.g., microservices vs. modular monolith, event-driven, SOA) based on trade-offs.
- Specify interfaces and contracts (API specs, schemas), data models, identity/authorization patterns, and networking (topology, segmentation, ingress/egress, latency, bandwidth, edge/CDN needs).
- Define operability: telemetry, SLOs/SLIs, alerting, runbooks, chaos/resiliency patterns, backup/restore.
- Evaluate cost model and scalability; include FinOps guardrails.

6) Evaluate and validate
- Conduct threat modeling and security design review.
- Perform risk assessment and compliance review.
- Run architectural trade-off analysis (e.g., ATAM, cost-performance-resilience trade-offs).
- Where uncertainty is high, plan PoCs/spikes to validate feasibility and performance.

7) Define transition architecture and roadmap
- Break target into incremental releases with dependency mapping.
- Plan data migration, interoperability, and backward compatibility.
- Define deprecation/EOL strategy for legacy components.
- Estimate effort, costs, and risks; align with portfolio and release plan.

8) Governance and approval
- Present to Architecture Review Board (ARB) or equivalent.
- Address feedback; record decisions in ADRs; obtain approvals or time-bound waivers.
- Register standards/pattern updates triggered by the design.

9) Document and publish
- Store models/diagrams, ADRs, standards, and roadmaps in the architecture repository.
- Tag assets with metadata (version, owners, lifecycle state); link to CMDB and service catalog.
- Communicate the architecture to delivery and operations teams; run enablement sessions.

10) Support implementation
- Provide architecture office hours, design clinics, and code/infra reviews.
- Implement policy-as-code and automated conformance checks in CI/CD (e.g., OPA, Terraform policies).
- Update architecture with implementation learnings; keep ADRs current.

11) Monitor and maintain
- Track SLOs, performance, reliability, security posture, cost; compare against NFRs.
- Assess ongoing conformance; manage exceptions, risks, and tech debt.
- Periodically review architecture health; trigger optimization or modernization initiatives.

12) Retire or evolve
- When architectures underperform or become inefficient: re-architect, refactor, replace, or retire.
- Execute deprecation plan; communicate timelines and migration paths.
- Capture post-implementation reviews; feed improvements into reference architectures and standards.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Architecture artifacts: current-state and target-state models/diagrams; multiple views (business, application, data, integration, security, infrastructure/network, deployment, operations)
- Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) with rationale and implications
- Reference architectures, standards, and reusable patterns updated or created
- NFR specifications, SLOs/SLIs, capacity models, threat models, DR patterns
- Interface definitions and data contracts (API specs, schemas, events)
- Transition architectures, roadmaps, and deprecation/EOL plans
- Governance outputs: ARB approvals, waivers/exceptions (time-bound), conformance reports
- Risk and compliance assessments; remediation plans
- Architecture repository updates with traceability to services in the catalog and CMDB

Success criteria:
- Alignment with enterprise principles and regulatory requirements
- Measurable attainment of NFRs and SLOs in production
- Reduced integration issues, incidents, and change failure rates
- Improved time-to-market through reuse of patterns and standards
- Cost efficiency targets met (e.g., run-rate, unit economics)
- High conformance rate and limited, time-bound exceptions
- Positive stakeholder satisfaction (product, engineering, operations, security)

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Enterprise Architect: Defines enterprise principles/standards; ensures alignment across domains; chairs ARB.
- Solution Architect: Leads architecture for a specific service/solution; produces artifacts; drives trade-offs and ADRs.
- Domain Architects:
  - Application/Software: Service decomposition, application patterns, resiliency.
  - Data: Data models, integration patterns, lineage, governance, privacy.
  - Integration: APIs, eventing, messaging, EDI/B2B, service meshes.
  - Security: Threat modeling, identity/authorization, encryption, compliance.
  - Infrastructure/Cloud/Network: Deployment topologies, connectivity, performance, DR.
- Service Owner/Product Owner: Provides business context, prioritizes NFRs, accepts architecture deliverables.
- Engineering Lead/Tech Lead: Implements architecture; ensures development alignment; contributes to ADRs.
- SRE/Operations Lead: Defines SLOs, observability, reliability and capacity practices; runs chaos/resiliency tests.
- Change/Release Manager: Aligns releases with transition architecture; ensures change governance.
- Risk/Compliance Officer, Privacy Officer: Validates regulatory alignment; manages audits.
- Vendor/Partner Manager: Aligns third-party capabilities and contracts to architecture.
- ARB/Design Authority: Reviews/approves designs; manages waivers and exceptions.
- Portfolio/Program Manager: Sequencing and funding of transition roadmap.

## Best Practices
- Use layered architecture principles and domain-driven design to minimize coupling and maximize cohesion.
- Adopt standard frameworks and languages (TOGAF/IT4IT, ArchiMate, C4) for consistent modeling.
- Create and curate reference architectures and pattern catalogs; favor proven, reusable solutions.
- Capture decisions via ADRs; store all artifacts in version control with traceability.
- Define NFRs early with measurable SLOs; validate via performance, resiliency, and security testing.
- Security- and privacy-by-design (threat modeling, zero trust networking, least privilege, encryption by default).
- API-first and contract-first integration; use versioning and backward compatibility strategies.
- Treat architecture as code where feasible (IaC, policy-as-code, templates, golden paths).
- Implement automated conformance checks in CI/CD and pre-deploy gates.
- Incorporate FinOps practices; design for cost transparency and right-sizing.
- Plan for failure: bulkheads, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers; test via chaos engineering.
- Establish clear deprecation/EOL policies; communicate timelines and migration paths.
- Regularly review architecture health; use metrics to trigger improvement work.
- Socialize architectures early and often; run design clinics and enablement to reduce friction.

## Common Challenges
- Stakeholder misalignment and unclear NFRs
  - Solution: Facilitate early workshops; define quality attribute scenarios; formalize SLOs.
- Fragmented documentation and knowledge silos
  - Solution: Centralized repository, standards for modeling/metadata, mandatory ADRs.
- Shadow IT and deviation from standards
  - Solution: Offer golden paths, self-service templates, and supportive governance; automate guardrails.
- Legacy constraints and complex dependencies
  - Solution: Transition architectures, strangler patterns, incremental modernization, feature toggles.
- Vendor lock-in and platform sprawl
  - Solution: Abstraction via APIs, portability patterns, platform evaluation with exit strategies.
- Performance and reliability gaps discovered late
  - Solution: Early performance modeling, load testing, chaos engineering, capacity planning.
- Insufficient security-by-design
  - Solution: Mandatory threat modeling, secure defaults, security gates in pipelines, continuous scanning.
- Documentation rot
  - Solution: Versioned artifacts tied to releases; “living documentation” practices; ownership with SLAs for updates.

## Performance Metrics
- Architecture conformance rate (% of solutions meeting standards without exceptions)
- Exception/waiver count and aging (time to remediate)
- Time-to-approve architecture (request to ARB decision cycle time)
- Reuse rate of reference architectures/patterns
- NFR attainment in production (SLO compliance, latency p95/p99, error budgets)
- Reliability metrics (availability, change failure rate, MTTR)
- Security and compliance (number of critical findings, time-to-remediate, audit pass rate)
- Efficiency and cost (compute/storage utilization, unit cost per transaction, cost vs. budget)

- Tech debt trend and burn-down for architecture items
- Documentation freshness (% artifacts updated within policy timeframe)
- Stakeholder satisfaction (survey scores for product/engineering/operations)

- Enterprise architecture and modeling: LeanIX, Orbus iServer, Avolution ABACUS, MEGA HOPEX, Sparx EA, Archi; languages: ArchiMate, UML, BPMN, C4 model; diagramming: draw.io/diagrams.net, Lucidchart.

Process Details:
## Overview
Confirm change/release compliance is the control checkpoint that ensures every change or release entering production meets the organization’s change, release, security, and regulatory requirements. It verifies that the change has been properly authorized, tested, documented, risk-assessed, and packaged according to policy before deployment, and that any exceptions are formally approved and recorded.

This process protects service stability, security, and audit readiness by:
- Preventing unauthorized or inadequately validated changes from reaching live environments.
- Ensuring separation of duties and approvals are enforced.
- Verifying that release artifacts, configurations, and documentation align with standards.
- Providing an auditable trail for regulators and internal control frameworks (e.g., ITIL Change Enablement, ISO 20000/27001, SOC 2, SOX ITGC, NIST 800-53 CM/SA controls).

It sits between change planning/build/test and deployment execution and is a key gate in the overall change and release management lifecycle.

## Key Activities
- Validate change classification and risk level (standard, normal, emergency).
- Confirm prerequisite approvals (technical, business, security, CAB).
- Verify testing and validation evidence (unit, integration, UAT, performance, security).
- Review implementation, backout/rollback, and contingency plans.
- Validate release packaging (versioning, artifact integrity, SBOM, licenses).
- Confirm environment readiness and change window compliance.
- Check segregation of duties and access controls for implementers.
- Validate CMDB and service mapping accuracy and planned updates.
- Confirm monitoring, alerting, and post-deployment verification plans.
- Assess regulatory/privacy impacts and confirm mitigating controls (e.g., DPIA outcomes).
- Review communication plans and stakeholder notifications.
- Document outcomes, decisions, and evidence; approve or block deployment.
- Manage exceptions and waivers with defined risk acceptance.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved change/release record in the ITSM tool with risk classification and change model.
- Documented approvals to date (requester, service owner, product owner, technical leads).
- Test and validation evidence (test plans, results, defects addressed, sign-offs).
- Security assessments (SAST/DAST/SCA results, vulnerability disposition, penetration test results if applicable).
- Release artifacts and metadata (build numbers, signatures, hashes, SBOM, licenses).
- Implementation plan, backout/rollback plan, contingency plan, deployment checklist.
- Impact analysis and dependency list (services, CIs, integrations, suppliers).
- Change calendar entry with scheduled window/blackout check and communications plan.
- Monitoring/observability plan (KPIs, dashboards, alerts) and runbooks.
- Data/privacy assessment when personal or sensitive data is in scope.
- Evidence of SoD controls (separate approver vs implementer), access reviews, and change freeze exceptions if applicable.

Prerequisites:
- Change was assessed, built, and tested per defined lifecycle.
- Relevant control policies and standards are current and accessible.
- Required approvers are designated and available (or delegates defined).
- CI/CD pipeline integrated with policy gates where applicable.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Change initiation, assessment, and authorization.
- Release planning and build/package management.
- Service validation and testing.
- Information security risk assessment and vulnerability management.
- Configuration and asset management (CMDB).
- Service level and availability management (change windows).
- Communication and stakeholder management.
- Supplier and third-party change management (if vendor-delivered components).

## Process Steps
1. Intake and completeness check
   - Retrieve the change/release record and verify required fields and artifacts are attached.
   - Confirm change type (standard/normal/emergency) and risk score; ensure correct model/template used.
2. Policy and control mapping
   - Identify applicable policies/controls (e.g., ISO 27001 A.12 change control, SOX ITGC, SOC 2 Change Management, NIST CM-3/CM-4/SA-10).
   - Load the corresponding compliance checklist for the change type and risk level.
3. Automated controls execution (where possible)
   - Run pipeline gates and policy-as-code checks (e.g., OPA/Conftest) for:
     - Approval presence and SoD checks.
     - Test coverage thresholds and results ingestion.
     - Security scan thresholds (SAST/DAST/SCA), vulnerability policy adherence.
     - Artifact integrity (signature verification, checksum), SBOM presence, license policy.
     - Infrastructure as Code linting/compliance (CIS benchmarks where applicable).
4. Manual review for non-automatable controls
   - Validate impact analysis, dependency mapping, and service risk assessment.
   - Review implementation and rollback plans for clarity, timing, and feasibility; confirm rollback is tested or rehearsed.
   - Confirm monitoring/alerting and runbooks are ready; verify canary/blue-green strategy if used.
   - Validate environment readiness and that the change fits a permitted window (no blackout, maintenance concurrency checks).
   - Ensure communications plan covers all stakeholders and SLAs; verify customer notices if required.
5. Security and privacy confirmation
   - Confirm remediation or acceptance of high/critical vulnerabilities.
   - Verify secrets management approach and access provisioning are compliant.
   - If personal data is impacted, confirm DPIA outcomes and data protection controls (encryption, minimization).
6. Approvals and CAB/governance check
   - Verify required approvals are captured (service owner, product owner, security, QA, business, operations).
   - Route to CAB or delegated authority for high-risk/normal changes; ensure emergency CAB for urgent cases with post-review scheduled.
7. Exceptions and risk acceptance
   - If any control cannot be met, initiate an exception request with compensating controls and defined expiry.
   - Obtain formal risk acceptance from the accountable risk owner.
8. Final go/no-go decision
   - Aggregate automated and manual findings into a compliance decision.
   - If go: record approval, conditions (if any), and readiness for deployment.
   - If no-go: document deficiencies, required remediations, and resubmission path.
9. Recordkeeping and audit trail
   - Attach evidence, checklists, approvals, and decision rationale to the change record.
   - Tag release artifacts with compliance status; update CMDB tasks for post-deployment updates.
10. Pre-deployment handoff
    - Communicate decision to release/deployment teams; confirm on-call coverage and monitoring.
    - Ensure change calendar is locked and notifications are sent.
11. Post-deployment compliance verification
    - Validate that post-implementation checks passed (smoke tests, health checks).
    - Confirm CMDB updates are completed and monitoring is in place.
    - Log any deviations; initiate PIR if incidents or non-compliance occur.
12. Continuous improvement
    - Analyze metrics and audit findings; refine checklists and automation coverage.
    - Update standard change catalog and risk models based on outcomes.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Compliance decision (approved, approved with conditions, or rejected).
- Completed compliance checklist and audit evidence package.
- Documented exceptions/waivers with risk acceptance and expiry dates.
- Updated change/release record with all approvals and artifacts attached.
- Tagged/attested release artifact(s) indicating compliance status.
- CMDB update tasks and validation notes.
- Communications sent to stakeholders and deployment schedule confirmed.

Success criteria:
- 100% of production changes have a recorded compliance decision and evidence.
- No unauthorized or policy-violating changes deployed.
- No material audit findings related to change management.
- Low rate of change-related incidents/regressions post-deployment.
- Timely cycle time through compliance without bottlenecks for low-risk changes.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Change Manager / Change Enablement Lead: Owns the process, ensures policy adherence, facilitates CAB, makes final compliance decision for normal/high-risk changes.
- Release Manager: Coordinates release packaging, scheduling, and readiness; ensures artifacts and documentation are complete.
- Service Owner / Business Owner: Confirms business impact, approves risk, validates functional readiness and communications.
- Product Owner / Delivery Lead: Ensures scope, acceptance criteria, and UAT sign-off; accountable for delivery quality.
- Security Officer / AppSec: Reviews security scans, threats, and mitigations; approves security-related controls and exceptions.
- QA/Testing Lead: Validates test coverage/results and sign-off.
- Operations Lead / SRE: Reviews implementation and rollback plans, environment readiness, monitoring and runbooks.
- CAB (Change Advisory Board): Provides governance and approval for significant changes.
- Configuration Manager: Ensures CI relationships, CMDB accuracy, and post-deployment updates.
- Risk and Compliance Officer / Internal Audit: Advises on regulatory requirements; reviews exceptions; audits evidence.
- Deployment Engineer / DevOps: Executes deployment following approved plan and gates; ensures SoD with approvers.

## Best Practices
- Use risk-based change models: pre-approved standard changes for low risk; normal/emergency with appropriate scrutiny.
- Shift-left compliance: embed checks in CI/CD (tests, security, artifact signing, SBOM generation).
- Policy as code: automate enforcement of approvals, scan thresholds, and SoD in pipelines and ITSM workflows.
- Immutable, signed artifacts and provenance: use attestations (e.g., SLSA) and verify at deploy time.
- Strong rollback readiness: require tested backout plans; prefer progressive delivery (canary, blue/green).
- Maintain a living compliance checklist per change type; keep it concise and automatable.
- Enforce SoD: implementers cannot be final approvers; restrict prod access and use break-glass controls with logging.
- Keep CMDB and service maps accurate; integrate with discovery and deployment tooling to auto-update relationships.
- Time changes wisely: respect blackout windows; avoid high-risk deployments during peak periods; communicate broadly.
- Document once, reuse often: auto-link pipeline results and scans into the change record to avoid manual uploads.
- Manage exceptions rigorously: time-bound, risk accepted by accountable owner, compensating controls, tracked to closure.
- Conduct regular PIRs and audits; feed findings back into policy and automation.

## Common Challenges
- Speed vs control: Teams view compliance as a bottleneck.
  - Solution: Risk-based models, pre-approved standards, heavy automation of checks.
- Incomplete or inconsistent evidence:
  - Solution: Integrate pipelines with ITSM; auto-ingest artifacts and results; use templates.
- Tool fragmentation:
  - Solution: Integrate ITSM, CI/CD, security scanners, and CMDB; adopt APIs and webhooks.
- Emergency changes bypassing controls:
  - Solution: Define emergency model with minimal safe checks and mandatory post-implementation review.
- Poor CMDB/service mapping causing impact blind spots:
  - Solution: Improve discovery, enforce update tasks, verify during compliance checks.
- Weak SoD and privileged access sprawl:
  - Solution: Enforce RBAC, approvals, and just-in-time access; audit regularly.
- Third-party/vendor changes outside governance:
  - Solution: Extend requirements to suppliers, require change notifications and evidence from vendors.
- Cloud-native complexity (ephemeral infra, microservices):
  - Solution: Use GitOps, declarative IaC, environment policies, and runtime policy enforcement.

## Performance Metrics
- Compliance pass rate on first submission (%).
- Cycle time from submission to compliance decision (median/95th percentile).
- Percentage of changes with complete, audit-ready evidence (%).
- Automated controls coverage (% of checks automated).
- Exception rate (% changes with waivers) and exception closure on time (%).
- SoD violations detected (count) and time to remediate.
- Change-related incidents within 7/30 days post-deployment (rate).
- Audit findings related to change management (count, severity).
- Standard vs normal/emergency change mix (% standard; aim to increase).
- Post-implementation verification completion within SLA (%).

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM/ITIL platforms: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, BMC Helix/Cherwell for change records, approvals, calendars, CAB.
- CI/CD and release orchestration: GitHub/GitLab/Azure DevOps, Jenkins, Argo CD/Flux (GitOps), Spinnaker.
- Policy-as-code and gating: Open Policy Agent (OPA), Conftest, Sentinel; build quality gates (e.g., SonarQube).
- Security scanning: SAST/DAST (e.g., Checkmarx, Veracode), SCA/OSS license (e.g., Snyk, Mend), container/IaC scanners (e.g., Trivy, Checkov).
- Artifact and provenance: Artifactory/Nexus, container registries; code signing (Sigstore/cosign), SBOM tools (CycloneDX/SPDX, Syft/Grype).
- Configuration and infra: Terraform, Ansible, Puppet, Chef; cloud policy guardrails (Azure Policy, AWS Config).
- Observability: Prometheus/Grafana, Datadog, New Relic, Splunk; synthetic testing.
- GRC and risk management: ServiceNow GRC, Archer, OneTrust (for privacy/DPIA).
- Access control and secrets: HashiCorp Vault, cloud KMS, PAM/JIT access systems.
- CMDB and service mapping: ServiceNow Discovery, Dynatrace/AppDynamics service maps; automated dependency mapping.
- Collaboration and e-signatures: Confluence/SharePoint for knowledge; DocuSign/Adobe Sign where formal signatures are required.

[8.6.3.3] Assess IT change/release risk
Level: 4

Process Details:
## Overview
Assess IT change/release risk is the structured evaluation of potential adverse impacts and likelihoods associated with deploying an IT change or release. It provides an objective risk rating, required mitigations, and a recommendation to proceed, delay, or reject. This process is a gating step within Manage Change Deployment Control and supports reliable, secure, and compliant deployments by aligning change decisions with business risk tolerance.

Purpose:
- Prevent service outages, security incidents, compliance breaches, and degraded user experience caused by changes/releases.
- Ensure appropriate controls, testing, and rollback strategies are in place before deployment.
- Provide transparent, auditable risk decisions to stakeholders (e.g., CAB, service owners).

Role in the organization:
- Balances speed and stability by tailoring rigor to risk (e.g., standard vs. normal vs. emergency changes).
- Feeds CAB and go/no-go decisions with evidence-based risk information.
- Integrates with ITSM, DevOps, Security, QA, and GRC to create a single risk view for each change/release.

## Key Activities
- Triage and classification of the change/release (type, scope, criticality, timing).
- Data collection (technical details, test evidence, dependencies, service criticality, change history).
- Risk identification across domains: availability, performance, confidentiality, integrity, compliance, financial, operational, third-party, data, usability.
- Impact and likelihood analysis using standardized criteria and historical data.
- Risk scoring and rating (e.g., Low/Medium/High/Critical) and documentation in a risk register.
- Risk treatment planning (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) and control selection.
- Residual risk evaluation and approval routing (e.g., CAB for high risk).
- Communication of risk and required actions to all stakeholders.
- Exceptions handling (emergency changes) and post-implementation review input.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved/qualified Change or Release record with description, business justification, scope, environments.
- Deployment plan, backout/rollback plan, and, if applicable, roll-forward plan.
- Test evidence: unit/integration, UAT, performance, security (SAST/DAST), regression results.
- Architecture and design artifacts; updated CMDB CIs and service dependency map.
- Service criticality (e.g., tiering), SLAs/SLIs/SLOs, error budget status.
- Operational readiness: monitoring/alerting plans, runbooks, on-call coverage, capacity analysis.
- Compliance requirements and data classification (e.g., PII, PCI, HIPAA, SOX scope).
- Change calendar and blackout/freeze windows.
- Historical data: similar past changes, incident/KEDB records, change failure rate.

Prerequisites:
- Change categorized (Standard/Normal/Emergency) and scoped.
- CI relationships current in CMDB; release contents baselined.
- Test environments representative and stable; required sign-offs for test completion.
- Security scans completed for in-scope components.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Change enablement/intake, release planning, testing and QA, vulnerability management, configuration and asset management (CMDB), incident/problem management (for historical context), GRC/risk management, security assessment and threat modeling, capacity and performance management, service continuity/disaster recovery.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate assessment
   - Trigger: new/updated change or release enters “Assessment” state.
   - Assign risk assessor (Change Manager or delegated Risk Analyst).
   - Confirm change type and scope; identify stakeholders (service owner, tech lead, security, QA, release manager).

2. Collect and validate inputs
   - Pull change details from ITSM tool; link affected CIs/services from CMDB.
   - Verify availability of deployment, test, and rollback plans.
   - Gather test and security evidence.
   - Check change calendar for conflicts; review error budget and SLOs.

3. Contextualize and decompose
   - Identify impact domains: availability, performance, confidentiality, integrity, compliance, financial, operational/process, vendor/third-party, data migration.
   - Determine blast radius, reversibility, novelty, complexity, and timing sensitivity.
   - Map dependencies and upstream/downstream services.

4. Identify risks and failure modes
   - Use checklists and threat modeling to enumerate plausible adverse scenarios.
   - Include human, process, and tooling risks (e.g., manual steps, missing runbooks).

5. Analyze impact and likelihood
   - Rate potential impact (e.g., 1–5) per domain using standard criteria tied to SLAs, data classification, revenue, regulatory exposure.
   - Rate likelihood using complexity, novelty, test coverage, change failure history, environment parity, vendor risk.
   - Consider compounding risks for concurrent changes.

6. Compute risk score and rating
   - Apply weighted formula tailored to organization (example: Risk Score = max(Impactdomain × Weightdomain) × Likelihood).
   - Translate to rating bands (e.g., 1–4 Low, 5–8 Medium, 9–12 High, >12 Critical).
   - Document rationale; attach evidence links.

7. Define risk treatments and controls
   - For each material risk, select controls and integrate into the plan:
     - Deployment strategies: canary/blue-green, feature flags, dark launches.
     - Testing: additional regression/performance/security tests.
     - Operational: enhanced monitoring, SLO burn alerts, capacity reservations, runbook updates.
     - Governance: segregation of duties, peer reviews, approvals.
     - Backout enhancements: tested rollback, data snapshot/backup, checkpointing, downtime notice.
     - Compliance: data masking, encryption, logging, access review.
   - Update deployment and backout plans accordingly.

8. Evaluate residual risk and readiness
   - Reassess likelihood/impact after controls.
   - Determine residual risk rating and compare to risk appetite/thresholds.
   - Validate readiness checklist:
     - Rollback tested and time-bounded
     - On-call and support coverage confirmed
     - Observability dashboards and alerts configured
     - Communications drafted (business, users, service desk)
     - Maintenance window approved; change collisions resolved

9. Decision and approvals
   - Low risk: auto-approve per policy or Change Manager approval.
   - Medium risk: Change Manager plus Service Owner approval.
   - High/Critical: CAB review; may require Security/Compliance sign-off and executive notification.
   - Emergency: expedited minimal assessment; document deferred activities; schedule PIR.

10. Communicate and record
    - Publish risk assessment summary in the change/release record.
    - Notify stakeholders of rating, required controls, and go/no-go recommendation.
    - Update risk register/GRC with notable risks and accepted residual risk approvals.

11. Pre-deployment checkpoint
    - Confirm all required controls implemented.
    - Re-validate no new conflicts; recheck monitoring and rollback readiness.
    - Final go/no-go sign-off based on unchanged risk posture.

12. Post-implementation review input
    - After deployment, capture outcomes vs. predicted risk (incidents, SLO impact, rollbacks).
    - Feed learnings into risk models, weights, and checklists.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Risk assessment report (attached to change/release): scope, scenarios, impact/likelihood, scoring, residual risk, required controls, decision.
- Updated deployment and backout plans reflecting treatments.
- Approval records and, if applicable, risk acceptance with owner and timebox.
- Risk register entries for significant or accepted risks.
- Stakeholder communications (CAB packet, end-user/service desk notices).
- Post-deployment outcomes and lessons learned.

Success criteria:
- Every in-scope change has a documented risk rating and decision before deployment.
- Required controls implemented; residual risk within appetite.
- Reduced change-related incidents, rollbacks, and SLO breaches relative to baseline.
- Audit-ready traceability of evidence and approvals.
- Predictive accuracy improves over time (ratings correlate with outcomes).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Change Manager: Owns the assessment process, ensures inputs completeness, facilitates approvals/CAB, enforces policy, tracks metrics.
- Risk Analyst/Change Risk Assessor: Performs analysis, computes scores, recommends treatments and decisions, documents results.
- Service Owner: Provides business impact, risk appetite context; approves residual risk; ensures operational readiness.
- Technical Lead/Implementer: Supplies technical details, testing evidence; updates deployment and rollback plans; implements controls.
- Release Manager: Coordinates multi-change releases; ensures integrated risk assessment across components.
- Information Security Officer: Reviews security, privacy, and compliance risks; mandates security controls; approves where required.
- QA/Test Lead: Validates test adequacy; recommends additional testing based on risk.
- SRE/Operations Lead: Confirms monitoring, capacity, on-call readiness; advises on deployment strategies and rollback feasibility.
- Enterprise/Domain Architect: Reviews architectural risk and dependency impacts.
- Compliance/GRC Officer or DPO (as applicable): Reviews regulatory risks; records risk acceptance; ensures documentation for audits.
- CAB Members: Review high-risk changes; endorse go/no-go decisions.
- Change Requestor: Initiates change, provides context and evidence, addresses gaps.

## Best Practices
- Use a standardized, transparent risk scoring model with documented criteria and weights; periodically recalibrate with real outcomes.
- Automate risk data collection and preliminary scoring from ITSM, CMDB, CI/CD, test, and security tools; require human review for high-impact areas.
- Tailor rigor to risk: pre-approved standard changes with minimal assessment; deeper analysis for normal; concise but documented for emergency.
- Emphasize reversibility: prioritize changes with tested rollback/feature flags; avoid big-bang releases where possible.
- Employ progressive delivery (canary/blue-green), feature toggles, and staged rollouts to reduce blast radius.
- Integrate SLOs/error budgets: block or add controls if error budgets are depleted.
- Maintain and use dependency maps; avoid concurrent risky changes on shared components.
- Enforce segregation of duties and peer reviews for high-risk changes.
- Include non-technical risks: communications, support readiness, training, and vendor dependencies.
- Keep a knowledge base of known risky patterns and successful mitigations; reuse checklists.
- Track and learn: run PIRs for high-risk and emergency changes; adjust models and controls based on findings.
- Embed compliance-by-design: default logging, access control, encryption, data protection controls in change templates.

## Common Challenges
- Incomplete or low-quality inputs
  - Solution: Gate changes with mandatory fields and evidence; use templates and checklists; tool-based validation.
- Underestimation bias and time pressure
  - Solution: Calibrated scoring based on history; require independent reviewer for medium/high risk; enforce SLAs that protect assessment time.
- Poor CMDB accuracy and hidden dependencies
  - Solution: Continuous discovery, service mapping; require dependency validation in assessment; monitor drift.
- Tool fragmentation
  - Solution: Integrate ITSM with CI/CD, testing, security, and monitoring; centralize assessment artifacts.
- Emergency changes bypassing controls
  - Solution: Minimal viable assessment with post-change PIR; limit and monitor emergency usage; define strict criteria.
- Inadequate rollback plans
  - Solution: Mandate tested rollback steps for non-trivial changes; simulate rollbacks in lower environments; require time-boxed rollback plans.
- Insufficient observability
  - Solution: Pre-deployment monitoring runbooks and SLO alerts; synthetic tests; logging and trace coverage thresholds.
- Conflicting change schedules
  - Solution: Change calendar collision checks; CAB coordination; freeze windows for peak periods.

## Performance Metrics
- Coverage: Percentage of changes with completed risk assessments before deployment.
- Timeliness: Average assessment lead time; percentage completed within SLA.
- Quality: Percentage of high-risk changes with additional controls implemented; audit findings related to change risk.
- Outcome correlation: Change failure rate and incident rate by risk rating; rollback rate; MTTR for change-related incidents.
- Predictive accuracy: Ratio of unexpected incidents from Low/Medium-rated changes; calibration drift over time.
- Stability impact: SLO burn attributable to changes; number of SLO breaches post-change.
- Governance: Number of emergency changes; percentage with PIR completed; risk acceptances by level and expiry.
- Process health: CAB rework/deferral rate due to inadequate assessment; duplicate effort or handoff delays.

Targets should be tailored to organizational maturity and risk appetite; trend analysis is as important as point targets.

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM and Change Enablement: ServiceNow, BMC Helix, Jira Service Management (with change risk calculators/workflows).
- CMDB and Discovery/Service Mapping: ServiceNow CMDB, Device42, Dynatrace Service Map.
- CI/CD and Release Orchestration: Jenkins, GitLab CI/CD, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, Spinnaker, Argo CD/Rollouts.
- Testing/QA: Selenium, JMeter, k6, Postman, Cypress; unit/integration frameworks.
- Security: SAST/DAST (SonarQube, Checkmarx, Snyk, OWASP ZAP), dependency scanning, container/IaC scanning, vulnerability management (Qualys, Tenable).
- Observability: Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, Prometheus/Grafana, Splunk, Elastic, OpenTelemetry.
- Feature Flags and Progressive Delivery: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, CloudBees Feature Management.
- GRC/Risk Register: Archer, ServiceNow GRC, OneTrust.
- Collaboration and Approvals: Slack/Teams with ChatOps bots, Confluence/Wikis for runbooks, e-signature for risk acceptance.
- Scheduling/Change Calendar: Integrated ITSM calendars; calendar collision detection.
- Threat Modeling: Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, OWASP Threat Dragon.

Process Details:
## Overview
Consolidate IT change is the process of bundling multiple approved IT changes into coordinated deployments to optimize downtime, resource usage, and business impact. It ensures that infrastructure, application, middleware, database, network, security, and configuration changes that affect the same services or environments are evaluated and scheduled together where appropriate, reducing change collisions, minimizing the number of maintenance windows, and improving overall release quality.

This process sits within Manage change deployment control and connects Change Enablement (ITIL) with Release Management and Deployment practices. It uses a governed approach to select, group, schedule, and execute change bundles, aligning with business calendars and technical dependencies while maintaining risk controls and auditability.

Primary objectives:
- Reduce total downtime by consolidating compatible changes into fewer windows.
- Improve resource efficiency by coordinating teams and automation tooling.
- Decrease change collisions and environment drift through dependency-aware planning.
- Maintain or improve change success rates and post-deployment stability.

Scope includes normal and standard changes; emergency changes are generally excluded from consolidation (except for post-facto documentation and CMDB updates).

## Key Activities
- Intake and triage of change candidates for consolidation from the change queue.
- Dependency/impact analysis across services, components, and environments.
- Change bundling strategy definition (by service, environment, risk, or release train).
- Schedule alignment with maintenance windows, blackout periods, and business events.
- Capacity and resource planning for cross-team execution.
- Risk assessment of the consolidated bundle and gatekeeping decisions.
- Consolidated release planning and runbook creation (sequence, back-out, validations).
- Communication planning and stakeholder alignment (internal and external).
- CAB/approval cycle for the consolidated deployment.
- Execution orchestration, monitoring, and incident linkage.
- Post-deployment validation, reporting, closure, and lessons learned.
- Continuous improvement of consolidation heuristics and policies.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved change records with clear scope, risk/impact ratings, planned duration, and test evidence.
- CMDB/service maps and dependency data (applications, infra, data stores, integrations).
- Change calendar with maintenance windows, blackout dates, and freeze periods.
- Business calendars (peak periods, product launches, regulatory deadlines).
- Test results, sign-offs, and deployment artifacts/packages.
- Resource calendars (on-call rosters, vendor availability).
- Policies/standards (change categories, segregation of duties, SOX/GxP requirements).
- SLAs/OLAs and third-party maintenance schedules.

Prerequisites:
- Defined consolidation eligibility criteria (e.g., exclude emergency, cap bundle risk).
- Standard maintenance windows catalog per service/region.
- Tooling integration between ITSM (change), CMDB, CI/CD, and release orchestration.
- Trained roles (Change Manager, Release Manager, Change Coordinators) and documented RACI.
- Communication channels and templates for stakeholder notifications.
- Back-out/rollback strategies defined and tested for included changes.
- Environment readiness criteria (pre-prod signoff, data migration rehearsals where applicable).

Dependencies on other processes:
- Change request creation, assessment, and authorization.
- Release management, environment management, and deployment orchestration.
- Configuration management (CMDB accuracy), test/QA, and security review.
- Incident, problem, and knowledge management for post-change handling.
- Capacity, availability, and vendor management.
- Risk and compliance management (audit trails, approvals).

## Process Steps
1. Define consolidation window and scope
   - Establish the consolidation cycle (e.g., weekly, biweekly, monthly release train).
   - Confirm applicable services/environments and blackout constraints.
   - Publish intake deadlines for inclusion.

2. Intake eligible changes
   - Pull change candidates from ITSM meeting inclusion gates: status (approved), type (standard/normal), environment, risk band, required window length.
   - Exclude emergency/out-of-cycle changes from the bundle; plan separate handling.

3. Perform dependency and conflict analysis
   - Use CMDB/service maps to identify technical and sequencing dependencies.
   - Detect conflicts (e.g., two schema changes affecting same table, overlapping network maintenance).
   - Check for cross-service impacts and shared components (e.g., message bus, identity provider).

4. Cluster and prioritize bundles
   - Group changes by:
     - Service/application or platform
     - Environment (prod vs. region X)
     - Deployment method/tooling compatibility
     - Risk level and duration
   - Apply heuristics:
     - Avoid mixing unrelated high-risk changes in a single bundle.
     - Prefer bundling changes touching the same outage domain to minimize downtime.
   - Define bundle candidates with preliminary scope and sequencing.

5. Select deployment window
   - Align with maintenance window policy, business calendar, and vendor availability.
   - Validate runtime duration fits within the window with contingency buffer (e.g., 30%).
   - Consider global time zones and consumer impact.

6. Capacity and readiness planning
   - Confirm availability of implementers, approvers, test leads, and on-call support.
   - Verify artifacts are deployment-ready (builds, scripts, IaC plans).
   - Ensure back-out plans exist for each change and are compatible in a bundle context.

7. Assess cumulative risk and decide bundle composition
   - Aggregate risk using a scoring model (e.g., weighted by service criticality, change type, blast radius).
   - Run “what-if” scenarios to split bundles if cumulative risk exceeds threshold.
   - Finalize inclusion/exclusion and document rationale.

8. Create consolidated release plan and runbook
   - Define step-by-step sequence, dependencies, checkpoints, and hold points.
   - Establish verification steps (technical health, business smoke tests, NFRs).
   - Define combined back-out strategy (component-level vs. full bundle rollback).
   - Prepare communications (internal, customer-facing if required) and status reporting plan.

9. Obtain approvals
   - Submit bundle plan to CAB/Change Authority with risk summary, schedule, and mitigation.
   - Secure security, compliance, and business owner sign-offs as required.
   - Record approvals and conditions in ITSM.

10. Pre-deployment readiness review (T-24 to T-2 hours)
    - Freeze change scope; lock artifacts.
    - Validate environment readiness (capacity, dependencies, licenses, certificates).
    - Confirm monitoring dashboards, alert thresholds, and war room logistics.
    - Rehearse critical steps and back-out if complex.

11. Execute consolidated deployment
    - Initiate bridge/ChatOps channel and follow the runbook sequence.
    - Use orchestration tools for automated steps; track timestamps and outcomes.
    - Enforce hold points for validation gates before proceeding to next sequence.

12. Validate and stabilize
    - Execute technical and business validation scripts/tests.
    - Monitor telemetry and error budgets; observe for a defined soak period.
    - Decide go/no-go for bundle completion; if thresholds breached, execute back-out plan.

13. Communicate and transition to operations
    - Send completion status, residual risks, and support instructions to Service Desk.
    - Update user-facing communications if applicable.

14. Close changes and update records
    - Update each change record with actuals, outcomes, and evidence (logs, reports).
    - Update CMDB/as-built documentation and knowledge articles (KEDB if new known errors).
    - Link incidents/problems to the relevant changes.

15. Review and improve
    - Conduct a consolidated Post-Implementation Review (PIR) within 3–5 business days.
    - Analyze metrics (success rate, downtime saved, deviations) and capture lessons learned.
    - Adjust consolidation criteria, windows, and automation based on findings.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Approved consolidated deployment schedule and change bundles.
- Integrated release plan and executable runbook with sequencing and back-out.
- Communication artifacts (stakeholder notices, customer advisories).
- Updated enterprise change calendar and CMDB entries.
- Post-implementation review report with findings and action items.

Deliverables produced:
- Bundle definition document (scope, composition, risk assessment).
- Consolidated test/validation plan and results.
- Operational handover package (support model, monitoring updates, knowledge base).
- Audit trail: approvals, execution logs, evidence of controls.

Success criteria:
- Bundle executed within window with no unplanned high-severity incidents (e.g., no P1/P2).
- Cumulative downtime reduced versus executing changes individually.
- Change success rate at or above target; minimal or zero rollbacks.
- Stakeholders informed per plan; no violation of freeze/blackout policies.
- Complete and compliant documentation for audit.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Change Manager: Owns consolidation policy, chairs CAB, ensures governance, approves bundles per authority.
- Release Manager: Designs bundle, creates runbook, coordinates cross-team execution, manages readiness and go-live.
- Change Coordinators/Owners (per change): Provide details, ensure test/back-out readiness, execute assigned steps, update records.
- Service/Application Owners: Validate business impact, approve windows, provide post-deploy validation, accept outcomes.
- Technical SMEs (App, Infra, Network, DB, Security): Perform impact analysis, implement changes, support validation and rollback.
- QA/Test Lead: Confirms test coverage, signs off pre-prod results, coordinates production validation.
- CAB/Change Authority: Reviews aggregated risk, approves or rejects bundle, sets conditions.
- Service Desk/Support Lead: Prepares communications, updates KEDB, manages initial incident triage.
- Incident Manager (on-call): Leads incident response during/after deployment if needed.
- Compliance/Risk Officer (as required): Verifies adherence to regulatory or internal controls.

## Best Practices
- Use a well-maintained CMDB with service maps to drive dependency-aware bundling.
- Standardize maintenance windows and adopt release trains to set expectations and improve predictability.
- Cap cumulative risk per bundle; split high-risk changes into dedicated windows.
- Prefer progressive delivery patterns (canary, blue-green, feature flags) to reduce blast radius.
- Automate as much as possible: deployment, validation checks, and back-out processes.
- Maintain a single enterprise change calendar integrating business events and vendor schedules.
- Enforce strict readiness criteria and scope freeze before go-live.
- Rehearse complex or risky changes in production-like environments with data subsets as appropriate.
- Establish clear communication templates and timelines for all stakeholders.
- Track and continuously refine consolidation heuristics based on PIR insights.
- Segregate duties and maintain audit trails, especially for regulated environments.
- Include non-functional validations (performance, security, observability) in validation gates.

## Common Challenges
- Hidden dependencies causing collisions or unexpected impact
  - Mitigation: Improve service mapping; require dependency declaration; run change collision checks.
- Over-bundling leading to “big bang” risk
  - Mitigation: Enforce risk caps; split bundles; stage changes; use progressive rollout.
- Resource contention and vendor constraints
  - Mitigation: Early capacity planning; vendor scheduling agreements; flexible windows.
- Poor CMDB data quality
  - Mitigation: Data quality KPIs; discovery tools; mandate CMDB updates as part of change closure.
- Inadequate back-out planning for combined changes
  - Mitigation: Design compatible rollback strategies; test back-outs; use transactional/feature-flag patterns.
- Communication gaps across teams/time zones
  - Mitigation: Standard comms plans; ChatOps channels; clear RACI; timezone-aware scheduling.
- Excessive CAB cycle time delaying releases
  - Mitigation: Pre-CAB reviews; risk-based approvals; standard change automation; standing CAB for release trains.
- Environment drift between test and prod
  - Mitigation: IaC and configuration drift detection; promote artifacts; enforce change parity across environments.

## Performance Metrics
- Consolidated change success rate (%) and rollback rate (%).
- Percentage of changes deployed via consolidation vs. standalone.
- Average number of changes per bundle and per maintenance window.
- Schedule adherence (start/finish vs. plan) and deployment duration variance.
- Unplanned downtime minutes attributable to consolidated changes.
- Incident rate within 7 days post-deployment (P1/P2/P3) and MTTR.
- Reduction in total maintenance windows per period compared to baseline.
- Resource utilization efficiency (e.g., engineer hours per change reduced).
- CAB lead time and approval cycle time for bundles.
- Change collision occurrences detected pre-deploy vs. escaped to production.
- Stakeholder satisfaction (survey) post major consolidated releases.
- CMDB update compliance rate tied to change closures.

Target thresholds should be set based on organizational maturity and baselined over time.

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM platform: ServiceNow, BMC Helix, Jira Service Management (change records, calendar, approvals).
- CMDB and service mapping: ServiceNow CMDB/Discovery, Device42, Apptio Cloudability (for mapping cloud resources).
- Release orchestration/CI-CD: Jenkins, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions, Octopus Deploy, Spinnaker, Argo CD.
- Infrastructure as Code and config management: Terraform, Ansible, Puppet, Chef.
- Deployment strategies and feature management: Kubernetes, Helm, LaunchDarkly, Unleash, AWS AppConfig.
- Monitoring/observability: Prometheus/Grafana, Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, Splunk.
- AIOps and change risk prediction (optional): ServiceNow Predictive Intelligence, Moogsoft, BigPanda.
- Test automation: Selenium/Cypress, JMeter/k6, Postman/Newman.
- Runbook automation and ChatOps: Rundeck, Ansible AWX, PagerDuty/Aircall bridges, Slack/MS Teams.
- Project/portfolio and resource planning: Jira/Advanced Roadmaps, Microsoft Project, Smartsheet.
- Reporting/BI: Power BI, Tableau, ITSM native analytics.

# [8.6.3.5] Create and Communicate Deployment Schedule

## Overview
This process defines, baselines, and communicates the detailed schedule for deploying IT changes, releases, and service updates. It ensures deployments occur at the right time, in the right sequence, with the right resources and approvals, and with minimal business disruption. It sits within Manage Change Deployment Control and bridges planning/approval activities with execution, providing a single source of truth for when and how deployments occur and who is impacted.

Primary objectives:
- Consolidate inputs (release scope, risk, dependencies, resource availability) into a realistic schedule.
- Prevent conflicts across environments, systems, and teams by aligning with the enterprise change calendar and maintenance/blackout windows.
- Secure approvals (e.g., CAB) and stakeholder buy-in.
- Communicate timely, accurate information to all affected parties (internal and external).
- Enable auditability and regulatory compliance for change timing and communications.

Scope:
- Applies to normal, standard, and emergency changes, across infrastructure, applications, data, and security updates.
- Covers production and non-production environments where schedule coordination is required.
- Includes pre-deployment notifications, go/no-go checkpoints, deployment windows, verification periods, and rollback windows.

## Key Activities
- Consolidate deployment requirements: change scope, sequencing, maintenance windows, blackout periods, service impact, and regulatory constraints.
- Draft and evaluate schedule options (e.g., phased, big-bang, blue/green, canary, rolling).
- Align resources: engineers, approvers, release managers, operations, service desk, vendors.
- Conflict detection and resolution using the enterprise change calendar and CMDB-based dependencies.
- Risk-based timing decisions, including business critical periods and customer impact windows.
- Secure approvals (Release Manager, Change Manager, CAB).
- Create and execute a communication plan with tiered audiences and timelines.
- Baseline, publish, and maintain the deployment schedule as a controlled artifact.
- Monitor schedule adherence and issue real-time updates during the deployment window.
- Capture evidence and metrics for audit and continual improvement.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Approved change records (scope, risk rating, impact, backout plan).
  - Release plan and deployment strategy (e.g., blue/green, canary).
  - Dependency map/CMDB data (services, CIs, upstream/downstream).
  - Environment maintenance windows and business blackout calendars.
  - Resource availability (engineering, QA, operations, service desk, vendor).
  - Regulatory/compliance constraints (e.g., SOX, PCI change windows).
  - Test sign-offs and readiness criteria.
  - Communication requirements (customers, internal operations, regulators).
- Prerequisites:
  - Change risk assessment completed.
  - Technical runbook and backout plan in place.
  - Monitoring/alerting prepared for post-deploy verification.
  - Feature flag strategy (if applicable).
  - Contact trees and escalation paths updated.
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Change assessment and approval (CAB) [8.6.3.x].
  - Release planning and readiness [8.6.2.x].
  - Configuration management (CMDB) [8.x].
  - Incident management (standby during deploy) [7.x].
  - Communication/Stakeholder management [8.0/Business Relationship].

## Process Steps
1. Initiate scheduling
   - Trigger: Approved change(s) or release ready for deployment scheduling.
   - Assign a Schedule Owner (typically the Change or Release Manager).

2. Gather inputs and constraints
   - Collect change tickets, risk ratings, impact analysis, runbooks, and verification plans.
   - Pull calendars: enterprise change calendar, maintenance windows, blackout/freeze periods, holidays, vendor windows.
   - Confirm resource availability (including after-hours coverage if applicable) across time zones.

3. Map dependencies and potential conflicts
   - Use CMDB/service maps to identify upstream/downstream systems and shared infrastructure.
   - Check for overlapping deployments, capacity-impacting activities, DR tests, or major events.

4. Define scheduling options
   - Propose one or more deployment windows with:
     - Start/end time, buffer, and rollback window.
     - Phasing by region, customer segment, or service tier (e.g., canary first).
     - Verification and smoke testing duration.
     - Freeze and contingency windows.
   - Consider customer traffic patterns and SLO/SLA commitments.

5. Risk review and mitigation embedding
   - Align with risk level: higher-risk changes get longer verification and rollback windows, additional approvals, or phased rollout.
   - Incorporate mitigations: feature flags, toggle checks, parallel-run, blue/green, automatic rollback triggers.

6. Resource alignment and readiness checks
   - Confirm on-call coverage (engineering, SRE, DBA, network, service desk, incident manager).
   - Confirm vendor participation if required.
   - Validate monitoring dashboards, alert thresholds, and logging are prepared.

7. Draft schedule and internal review
   - Document draft schedule in the ITSM tool (single source of truth).
   - Internal review with Release Manager, Technical Lead, Service Owner, Security/Compliance (if applicable).

8. Conflict resolution and calendar authorization
   - Run automated conflict detection against the enterprise change calendar.
   - Resolve conflicts via rescheduling, sequencing changes, splitting deployments, or consolidating releases.
   - Escalate conflicts to CAB if needed.

9. Approval and baseline
   - Obtain required approvals (Change Manager, Service Owner, CAB).
   - Baseline schedule version and lock changes behind change control.

10. Communication planning
   - Build a communication plan by audience:
     - Internal: service desk, NOC/SOC, operations, support, executive stakeholders.
     - External: customer admins, end users, regulators (if required).
   - Define channel, content, and timing (e.g., T-5 days, T-24 hours, T-1 hour, live updates, completion notice).
   - Prepare artifacts: maintenance notices, release notes, FAQs, status page updates, calendar invites.

11. Publish schedule
   - Update ITSM change calendar and project/release calendars.
   - Send initial notifications; attach to change records and knowledge base page.
   - Create calendar events in Outlook/Google with brief and runbook links.

12. Pre-deployment confirmations
   - Send reminders (e.g., T-24h, T-1h).
   - Confirm go/no-go meeting participants and decision criteria.
   - Validate backout plan viability and data backups.

13. Execute communication during deployment window
   - Start-of-window notice (“maintenance started”).
   - Periodic progress updates per plan.
   - Real-time issue escalation communications if variance exceeds thresholds.
   - If schedule changes, issue updated ETA and reason; update calendars and ITSM ticket.

14. Close-out communications and artifacts
   - Completion notice with results and any known issues.
   - Post-deployment verification status and incident summary (if any).
   - Update change records with actual start/end times, variances, and evidence.

15. Post-implementation review (PIR) inputs
   - Capture schedule adherence, conflicts encountered, communications effectiveness.
   - Log lessons learned to improve future scheduling and comms.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Baseline deployment schedule (version-controlled, time-zone normalized).
- Communication plan and executed communications (notices, status page posts, calendar invites).
- Updated ITSM change and release records (final approved schedule, evidence, approvals).
- Conflict analysis and resolution record.
- Stakeholder sign-offs for schedule and go/no-go.
- Audit evidence: timestamps, recipients, content, approvals, and any schedule changes.
- Success criteria:
  - No violations of blackout/freeze or regulatory windows.
  - All required approvals obtained before the window.
  - Communications delivered to all required audiences within defined lead times.
  - Schedule adherence within defined variance (e.g., ±15 minutes).
  - No unplanned service impact beyond communicated window.
  - Effective rollback window preserved (if unused, still available).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Change Manager (Process Owner)
  - Owns scheduling process, ensures compliance, runs conflict checks, secures approvals, baselines schedule.
- Release Manager (Schedule Creator/Coordinator)
  - Drafts schedule and communication plan, coordinates resources, runs go/no-go, and manages schedule changes.
- Deployment/Technical Lead
  - Provides runbook timing, dependencies, and feasibility; confirms verification and rollback windows.
- Service Owner/Product Owner
  - Validates business impact and timing; ensures stakeholder alignment; approves schedule.
- CAB (Change Advisory Board)
  - Reviews conflicts and risk; approves schedule for higher-risk or cross-domain changes.
- Operations/SRE/Infrastructure Teams
  - Provide resource availability; execute deployment tasks; staff on-call; report progress.
- QA/Test Lead
  - Confirms testing sign-offs and defines post-deploy verification activities.
- Security/Compliance
  - Ensures adherence to regulatory constraints; approves if special windows required.
- Service Desk/NOC/SOC
  - Prepares customer-facing and internal scripts; monitors and communicates during window; handles inquiries.
- Communications/Marketing or Customer Success (if customer impacting)
  - Crafts and distributes customer notices, release notes, and status page updates.
- Vendor/Third-Party Representatives
  - Aligns external dependencies and windows; provides support and confirmation during deployment.
- Incident Manager (On Standby)
  - Coordinates incident response if deployment causes service degradation; may trigger rollback.

## Best Practices
- Maintain a single source of truth: ITSM change calendar integrated with team calendars.
- Use time-zone-aware scheduling; publish in UTC and local time for impacted regions.
- Apply risk-based scheduling: higher risk gets earlier windows in the week, longer verification, and phased rollout.
- Respect business-critical periods and enforce freeze/blackout windows with exceptions via formal waiver.
- Include buffer and rollback windows; never schedule right up against another high-risk change.
- Prefer low-traffic windows informed by real telemetry, not assumptions.
- Standardize maintenance windows per service; reduce ad-hoc timing.
- Use feature flags/gradual rollout to decouple code deployment from feature release.
- Automate conflict detection and notifications; integrate CMDB/service maps.
- Dry runs for complex changes; rehearse timing and handoffs.
- Tiered communication with templates; require read receipts/ack for critical internal audiences.
- Real-time status updates via agreed channels (e.g., status page, Slack/Teams bridge).
- Baseline and version-control the schedule; track all deviations and reasons.
- Establish clear go/no-go criteria and escalation paths.
- Ensure accessibility and localization in customer notices where applicable.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Conflicting changes on shared infrastructure
  - Solution: Automated conflict checks, CAB arbitration, standardized maintenance windows, and dependency mapping via CMDB.
- Resource constraints or time zone misalignment
  - Solution: Global on-call rosters, follow-the-sun coverage, rotate windows, and early resource booking.
- Last-minute scope changes
  - Solution: Enforce schedule change control with impact assessment; reschedule or split change; require leadership approval for late changes.
- Inaccurate or outdated calendars
  - Solution: Integrate ITSM with calendars; mandate updates as part of change closure; audit calendar accuracy.
- Vendor window limitations
  - Solution: Pre-negotiate windows; maintain vendor calendar; align SLAs; include vendor in scheduling reviews.
- Communication gaps leading to surprise outages
  - Solution: Tiered comms plan, lead-time SLAs, customer status pages, and internal comms scripts for service desk.
- Overruns and missed rollback windows
  - Solution: Timeboxing, strict go/no-go checkpoints, automated rollback criteria, clearly defined cutoffs.
- Regulatory non-compliance
  - Solution: Embed regulatory checks in approval workflow; retain evidence; involve compliance early.
- High volume during peak seasons
  - Solution: Seasonal freeze periods, batching changes, increased CAB frequency, and risk-based gating.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs)
- Schedule lead time: % of deployments scheduled ≥ X days before execution by risk tier.
- Conflict rate: # of conflicts detected pre-approval vs. post-approval; % resolved without reschedule.
- Schedule adherence: avg. start/end variance; % deployments within ±15 minutes of plan.
- Communication timeliness: % notices sent within SLA (T-5 days, T-24h, etc.); acknowledgment rate for critical internal audiences.
- Change success rate: % deployments without incident or rollback attributable to scheduling.
- Reschedule frequency: # and % of deployments rescheduled within T-48h of window.
- Freeze/blackout compliance: # of violations; exception rate with waivers.
- Customer impact metrics: # of unplanned impacts outside communicated windows; status page update latency.
- CAB cycle time: time from draft schedule to approval for high-risk changes.
- Audit completeness: % of changes with complete schedule and comms evidence.

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM and Change/Release Management
  - ServiceNow, BMC Helix/Remedy, Jira Service Management, Cherwell.
- Change calendar and conflict detection
  - ITSM calendar modules; integrations with Outlook/Google Calendar; automated conflict rules.
- CMDB and dependency mapping
  - ServiceNow CMDB/Service Mapping, Dynatrace, New Relic, Datadog Service Catalog.
- CI/CD and deployment orchestration
  - Jenkins, GitLab CI/CD, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, Spinnaker, Argo CD, Harness.
- Feature flags and progressive delivery
  - LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Split.io.
- Monitoring, logging, and APM
  - Datadog, Splunk, New Relic, Prometheus/Grafana, Elastic.
- Communication and notification
  - Email/SMS gateways, Microsoft Teams/Slack, PagerDuty/Opsgenie, Atlassian Statuspage, in-app messaging tools.
- Runbook automation and scheduling
  - Ansible, Rundeck, SaltStack; calendar scheduling tools; time-zone libraries.
- Governance and evidence
  - Document repositories (Confluence, SharePoint), e-signature/approval capture, audit trail tools.

This process ensures deployments are executed predictably, safely, and transparently by turning disparate planning inputs into a well-controlled and well-communicated schedule, reducing operational risk and improving stakeholder confidence.
