# [8.7.2.3] Create and Maintain IT Support Model

## Overview
This process defines, implements, and maintains the IT support model that governs how users receive assistance for IT services and solutions. It translates the IT service support strategy into a practical operating framework covering support tiers (or swarming), channels, processes, roles, tools, SLAs/OLAs/UCs, and governance. It ensures support is reliable, scalable, user-centric, and aligned to business outcomes, while integrating with broader ITSM practices (incident, request, problem, change, knowledge, configuration).

Primary objectives:
- Provide a clear, consistent structure for how users engage IT support
- Optimize speed to restore service, first contact resolution, and user satisfaction
- Efficiently allocate resources and capacity across channels and tiers/teams
- Ensure compliance, security, and auditability of support operations
- Enable continuous improvement through metrics, feedback, and iterative design

Scope includes enterprise IT and, where applicable, shared service support across business units and regions (e.g., follow-the-sun).

## Key Activities
- Assess current-state support model and demand (volumes, channels, skills, pain points)
- Design target operating model (TOM) for support: tiers or swarming, channels, hours, coverage
- Define processes and procedures for incident, request, access, problem, major incident
- Establish SLAs/OLAs/UCs and escalation matrices
- Design organizational roles, staffing model, and workforce management approach
- Define knowledge management and shift-left strategy (KCS, self-service, automation)
- Configure enabling tools and integrations (ITSM, contact center, monitoring, CMDB)
- Develop SOPs, playbooks, runbooks, and training
- Pilot, iterate, and roll out
- Govern, review, and continuously improve the support model
- Maintain documentation, versioning, and change control for the model

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- IT service portfolio and service catalog with support offerings
- Business strategy, risk posture, compliance requirements (e.g., ISO 20000/27001, SOC, HIPAA)
- Historical support data (volumes, channels, MTTR, FCR, CSAT, major incidents)
- User personas, locations, languages, and time zones
- Existing ITSM processes, tools, integrations, and data models (categories, CMDB)
- Vendor contracts and underpinning contracts (UCs), OLAs between internal teams
- Budget constraints, hiring plans, and service coverage expectations
- Technology architecture and monitoring/observability strategy

Prerequisites:
- Defined service support strategy and vision (parent process)
- Executive sponsorship and governance structure for ITSM
- Access to data sources and SMEs (service owners, app owners, operations)
- Agreement on decision rights and change control for the support model

Dependencies on other processes:
- Incident, Major Incident, Request Fulfillment, Access Management, Problem, Change Enablement
- Knowledge Management, Configuration Management (CMDB), Asset Management
- Vendor Management and Contract Management
- Workforce Management, Training/Enablement, Communications/OCM
- Security Operations and IAM
- Monitoring/AIOps and NOC processes
- Service Portfolio/Service Catalog Management

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and plan
- Appoint Support Model Owner and core team (process, service desk, tool admin, service owners)
- Confirm scope, objectives, constraints, timeline, and governance
- Establish success criteria and baseline metrics

2) Assess current state
- Analyze demand: volumes by category/channel/time, severity mix, backlog, seasonality
- Map current processes, escalation paths, and tool configurations
- Evaluate user experience: CSAT/NPS feedback, VOC, pain points
- Assess knowledge assets, deflection rates, and self-service adoption
- Review staffing, skills, WFM practices, and on-call arrangements
- Identify compliance gaps, audit findings, and risk

3) Define target support principles and scope
- Choose support paradigm: tiered model vs. swarming vs. hybrid
- Define support scope per service: incidents, requests, access, “how-to,” break-fix, VIP support
- Establish coverage model: business hours, extended, 24x7, follow-the-sun
- Set channel strategy: portal/self-service, chatbot/virtual agent, chat, phone/IVR, email, social
- Define accessibility, language, and inclusion requirements

4) Design processes and flows
- Incident management: intake, triage, categorization, prioritization, diagnostics, resolution
- Request fulfillment: standard request catalog, approvals, fulfillment paths, SLAs
- Access management: standard access packages, segregation of duties, controls
- Problem management: detection, analysis, known errors, permanent fixes
- Major incident management: severity model, roles (MIM), comms cadence, war rooms
- Escalation policies: functional and hierarchical, swarming triggers, vendor engagement
- Integrations with change enablement (RFC creation), CMDB updates, and monitoring alerts
- Define deflection paths to knowledge and automation

5) Define service levels and performance framework
- Set SLAs (response, restore/fulfill, comms), aligned to business criticality
- Define OLAs between internal resolver teams and UCs with vendors
- Establish KPI framework, reporting cadence, and dashboards
- Define quality assurance, sampling, and coaching approach

6) Design organization, roles, and WFM
- Determine team structure, roles, and skill matrix; define RACI
- Plan staffing levels using demand forecasts and occupancy targets
- Define on-call schedules, handoffs, and follow-the-sun procedures
- Establish training, certification, and career pathing

7) Knowledge and shift-left strategy
- Adopt Knowledge-Centered Service (KCS) practices
- Define article lifecycle, templates, and ownership
- Identify automation candidates and create self-service content (virtual agent flows, runbooks)
- Build taxonomy for categories, services, and knowledge alignment

8) Tooling and data design
- Configure ITSM platform: forms, fields, categories, workflows, SLAs, assignment rules
- Set up omnichannel contact center, IVR, chat, virtual agent, and routing logic
- Integrate monitoring/AIOps, CMDB, endpoint management, remote support tools
- Create reporting and analytics pipelines; ensure data quality and governance

9) Documentation and enablement
- Produce the Support Model document, SOPs, playbooks, and escalation matrices
- Create major incident runbooks and comms templates
- Develop training materials and conduct enablement for agents and stakeholders
- Communicate changes to users (service portal updates, announcements)

10) Pilot and iterate
- Select pilot scope (e.g., a service or region)
- Validate processes, SLAs, tooling, and knowledge; collect feedback
- Address defects, adjust staffing, fine-tune routing and categorization

11) Rollout and stabilization
- Execute phased rollout plan; monitor KPIs and VoC closely
- Provide hypercare and additional coaching
- Confirm decommissioning of legacy workflows/channels

12) Operate, govern, and improve
- Run weekly operational reviews and monthly service reviews
- Track KPIs, SLAs, quality, and continuous improvement backlog
- Trigger updates based on change events (new services, M&A, tool changes, volume spikes)
- Conduct periodic audits and annual model refresh

## Outputs and Deliverables
- IT Support Model document (version-controlled) including scope, principles, processes, org, channels, coverage, SLAs/OLAs/UCs, and governance
- Process maps, SOPs, runbooks, playbooks, and escalation matrices
- Major incident handbook and communication templates
- Service catalog updates and request catalog design
- Knowledge articles, KCS roles and procedures, and content roadmap
- ITSM tool configurations, routing rules, categories, and dashboards
- Staffing model, WFM schedules, on-call rosters
- Training curricula and completion records
- Vendor OLAs/UCs and integration procedures
- Communications plan and user-facing guidance
Success criteria:
- Agreed SLAs consistently met or exceeded
- Improved FCR, MTTR, CSAT/NPS, and deflection rate
- Reduced transfer, escalation, and reopen rates
- High agent quality scores and reduced attrition
- Compliance with audits and security policies
- Stakeholder satisfaction and model adoption

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Support Model Owner: Accountable for the model design, governance, and continuous improvement
- Service Desk Manager: Owns day-to-day operations, staffing, and performance
- ITSM Process Owners (Incident/Request/Problem/Change/Knowledge): Define standards, ensure adherence, and drive improvements in their domains
- Major Incident Manager: Leads major incidents, communications, and post-incident reviews
- Knowledge Manager: Implements KCS, oversees content lifecycle and quality
- ITSM Platform Administrator: Configures workflows, SLAs, routing, integrations, and reporting
- Service Owners / Application Owners: Define support needs, provide L2/L3 expertise, maintain runbooks and OLAs
- NOC/Monitoring Lead: Integrates alerts, SRE/SOC interfaces, and event correlation
- Security/IAM Lead: Ensures secure access processes and compliance
- Vendor Manager: Manages UCs/OLAs with third parties and vendor escalations
- Workforce Management Lead: Forecasts demand, plans staffing, and monitors adherence
- Training/Enablement Lead: Develops and manages training and certifications
- Communications/OCM: Plans and executes user/agent communications
- Data/Reporting Analyst: Builds dashboards, analyzes trends, and supports decision-making
- Quality Assurance Lead: Defines QA framework, conducts evaluations, and coaching

## Best Practices
- Align with ITIL 4 practices and ISO/IEC 20000 principles; integrate with COBIT governance
- Design for user experience: simple channels, clear entry points, and accessible self-service
- Adopt shift-left and KCS to empower self-service and agent knowledge reuse
- Consider swarming for complex domains to reduce handoffs; use tiers for scale where appropriate
- Standardize taxonomy for categories, services, and configuration items; tie to CMDB
- Automate high-volume tasks (password resets, software installs) and use virtual agents
- Implement robust major incident practice with clear severity, comms, and postmortems
- Use data-driven WFM and forecast seasonality; apply follow-the-sun for global coverage
- Maintain strong OLAs and UCs; test vendor escalations and joint exercises
- Establish continuous improvement cadence with metric reviews and user feedback loops
- Govern changes to the support model via change control and versioning
- Ensure security-by-design in support flows and remote assistance tools
- Regularly test disaster recovery/business continuity for the support function
- Keep the number of channels manageable; ensure true omnichannel context and history

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Unclear scope and decision rights: Establish RACI, governance board, and change control for the model
- Tool sprawl and poor integrations: Consolidate onto a primary ITSM platform; use iPaaS and standard APIs
- Bad data and misclassification: Standardize taxonomy; add mandatory fields; QA and coaching; machine learning-assisted categorization
- High transfer/escalation rates: Improve triage scripts, knowledge, and swarming; tune routing rules
- Knowledge gaps and low deflection: Implement KCS; incentivize contributions; curate top tasks for self-service
- Unrealistic SLAs: Base on historical data and capability; align expectations with business criticality
- Agent turnover and skill gaps: Career paths, training programs, coaching, and recognition
- Global/language/time zone issues: Follow-the-sun playbooks, multilingual support, regional knowledge adaptations
- Vendor delays: Strong UCs, regular vendor reviews, and escalation paths; maintain parallel workarounds
- Major incident chaos: Pre-defined MIM role, runbooks, communication cadence, and drills

## Performance Metrics
Operational effectiveness:
- SLA attainment (response/restore/fulfill)
- First Contact Resolution (FCR) rate
- Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA), Mean Time to Resolve/Restore (MTTR)
- Deflection rate (self-service/virtual agent containment)
- Transfer and escalation rates; reopen rate
- Backlog volume and aging; work-in-progress limits
- Major incident time to detect/declare/communicate/resolve

User and quality outcomes:
- CSAT and NPS (overall and by channel)
- Quality evaluation scores; error rates
- Average handle time (AHT), queue time, abandonment rate
- Channel mix and containment (IVR/chatbot)

Productivity and cost:
- Contacts per user per month; tickets per device/service
- Cost per contact/ticket; agent utilization and occupancy
- Forecast accuracy vs. actual volume; schedule adherence
- Knowledge usage, creation, and link rates; KCS health indicators

People and compliance:
- Agent eNPS/engagement; attrition rates
- Training/certification completion
- Audit findings, policy adherence, and security incident counts linked to support

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM platforms: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, BMC Helix, Cherwell/Freshservice
- Omnichannel/contact center: Genesys, Amazon Connect, Five9, NICE; chat and web messaging
- Virtual agents/chatbots: ServiceNow VA, Microsoft Power Virtual Agents, Ada
- Knowledge management: KCS-enabled KBs (ServiceNow KB, Confluence), search/relevance tools
- Monitoring/AIOps and observability: Dynatrace, Datadog, Splunk, New Relic, Elastic
- CMDB and discovery/service mapping: ServiceNow Discovery/Service Mapping, Device42
- Endpoint management/remote support: Microsoft Intune/SCCM, Jamf, BeyondTrust, TeamViewer
- Identity and access management: Azure AD/Entra, Okta, SailPoint; approvals and access workflows
- Automation/RPA: UiPath, Power Automate, Ansible; runbook automation (xMatters, Rundeck)
- On-call and incident response: PagerDuty, Opsgenie, VictorOps; collaboration (Teams, Slack) for ChatOps
- Workforce management and QA: Calabrio, Verint, NICE; call recording and quality tools
- Analytics and reporting: Power BI, Tableau; ITSM native dashboards
- Survey and feedback: Qualtrics, Medallia, ITSM-integrated CSAT
- Documentation and version control: SharePoint/Confluence, Git for configuration as code

Process Details:
# [8.7.4.3] Determine Ongoing IT Infrastructure Capabilities

## Overview
This process assesses the current capabilities of the organization’s IT infrastructure and identifies gaps and needs to meet current and projected business demand. It provides a systematic, data-driven view of how well infrastructure resources (on-premises, cloud, and hybrid) support performance, availability, security, compliance, cost efficiency, and scalability targets. The output informs planning, prioritization, budgeting, and execution of enhancements within the broader infrastructure resource planning process.

Purpose:
- Establish an accurate, current-state baseline of infrastructure assets, configurations, utilization, and performance.
- Identify risks, bottlenecks, technical debt, and capacity shortfalls against growth and resilience objectives.
- Recommend actionable improvements and a roadmap to enhance capabilities.

Role in the organization:
- Feeds annual and quarterly infrastructure planning, service-level management, business continuity, and financial planning.
- Enables proactive investment decisions (e.g., refresh cycles, cloud optimization, automation) and reduces unplanned outages or reactive spend.
- Aligns infrastructure with enterprise architecture standards and business strategy.

Cadence:
- Conduct a comprehensive review quarterly, with monthly health checks for critical services.

Scope examples:
- Data center compute/storage/network, virtualization platforms, containers/Kubernetes, public cloud IaaS/PaaS, databases, backup/DR, network security, end-user computing, observability tooling, and supporting automation.

## Key Activities
- Define assessment scope, objectives, and evaluation criteria.
- Inventory and validate infrastructure components and service dependencies.
- Baseline current performance, capacity, availability, and cost.
- Evaluate capability dimensions (capacity, resilience, security, lifecycle, operability, cost, sustainability).
- Forecast demand and stress-test scenarios (e.g., growth, new products, M&A).
- Perform gap and risk analysis; quantify impacts.
- Prioritize remediation/enhancements and develop an actionable roadmap.
- Socialize findings; obtain governance approval.
- Update CMDB/asset records and track improvements.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Business strategy, growth forecasts, and demand pipeline (projects, product roadmaps).
- Current SLAs/SLOs/OLAs and criticality tiers for services.
- CMDB/IT asset inventory, including lifecycle and warranty/support status.
- Monitoring/observability data (metrics, logs, traces), capacity/utilization reports.
- Incident, problem, and change records; availability reports.
- Security vulnerability/patch posture, compliance assessments.
- Financial/FinOps data (cost, unit economics, license utilization).
- Vendor contracts, support levels, and EoL/EoS notices.
- DR/BCP requirements and test results.

Prerequisites:
- Governance sponsorship and clear decision rights.
- Defined evaluation framework (capability model, scoring rubric).
- Access to required systems and data with agreed data quality standards.
- Service maps or dependency mappings for critical services.

Dependencies on other processes:
- IT Asset/Configuration Management (CMDB accuracy and discovery).
- Capacity and Availability Management.
- Demand/Portfolio Management (pipeline and growth inputs).
- Incident/Problem/Change Management (operational data).
- Information Security Management (controls and risk posture).
- IT Financial Management/FinOps (cost and optimization).
- Vendor/Supplier Management (supportability and contracts).
- Enterprise Architecture (standards and target architectures).
- Business Continuity/DR Management.

## Process Steps
1. Plan and Scope
   - Clarify objectives, success criteria, and decision timelines.
   - Select scope: services, platforms, regions, and time horizon.
   - Establish evaluation criteria across capability dimensions.
   - Confirm stakeholders, roles, and assessment cadence.

2. Data Collection and Validation
   - Extract inventory and configuration data from CMDB and discovery tools; reconcile discrepancies.
   - Gather utilization and performance metrics (CPU, memory, storage IOPS/latency, network throughput/latency, database wait times, queue depths).
   - Collect availability and reliability data (uptime, incident rates, MTTR, change success rate).
   - Pull security and compliance data (vulnerabilities, patch levels, control coverage, IAM hygiene).
   - Assemble cost and license data (on-prem TCO, cloud spend by tag, unit costs, license true-up status).
   - Confirm DR posture (RTO/RPO, test outcomes, backup coverage).
   - Document dependencies and service maps for critical services.

3. Establish Baselines
   - Create performance and capacity baselines per platform and critical service.
   - Compute headroom, saturation points, and trends (e.g., 95th percentile utilization).
   - Normalize cost to unit economics (per vCPU-hour, per GB-month, per transaction).

4. Demand and Scenario Forecasting
   - Translate business growth and project pipeline into resource demand using historical ratios or capacity models.
   - Model scenarios (expected, aggressive growth, seasonal peaks, outage/DR) and assess impact on headroom and SLAs.
   - Include non-functional requirements changes (e.g., tighter latency SLOs, increased data retention).

5. Capability Evaluation
   - Assess maturity across dimensions:
     - Capacity/Performance: utilization, throughput, latency, scaling mechanisms.
     - Resilience/Availability: redundancy, failover, RTO/RPO, maintenance windows.
     - Security: patch cadence, vulnerability backlog, network segmentation, ZTNA/IAM controls.
     - Compliance: regulatory alignment (e.g., data residency), audit readiness.
     - Lifecycle/Technical Debt: EoL/EoS hardware/software, unsupported firmware.
     - Operability/Automation: IaC adoption, configuration drift, CI/CD integration, runbook maturity.
     - Observability: metrics/logs/traces coverage, SLO error budgets.
     - Cost Efficiency/FinOps: right-sizing, reservations/commitments, waste (idle, orphaned, overprovisioned).
     - Vendor Supportability: contract SLAs, multi-vendor risk.
     - Skills/Resourcing: coverage for 24x7 operations, specialist skills.
     - Sustainability: power usage, cooling, carbon footprint, e-waste practices.
     - Architecture Alignment: standards compliance, cloud/container strategy fit.
   - Score each area using a defined rubric (e.g., 1–5) and produce a heatmap.

6. Gap, Risk, and Constraint Analysis
   - Identify gaps between current state and targets (SLOs, growth needs, standards).
   - Quantify business impact (risk to revenue, customer experience, compliance penalties).
   - Record risks with likelihood/impact; map constraints (budget, lead times, skills).

7. Prioritization and Options Analysis
   - Develop solution options for each gap (e.g., right-size, scale-out, platform refresh, cloud migration, automation).
   - Evaluate options on value, risk reduction, cost, time-to-benefit, and dependency complexity.
   - Prioritize using a scoring model; align with portfolio priorities.

8. Roadmap and Investment Plan
   - Build a time-phased roadmap (near-term 0–3 months, mid-term 3–12 months, long-term 12–24 months).
   - Define initiatives, owners, milestones, budget estimates, and success metrics.
   - Identify quick wins (e.g., cloud waste reclamation, patch backlog reduction).

9. Review and Governance
   - Present findings and recommendations to Architecture Review Board, IT leadership, and service owners.
   - Secure approvals and funding decisions; document Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).

10. Execution Handover and Documentation Updates
    - Create or update:
      - Capability Assessment Report and heatmap.
      - Gap/Risk register entries.
      - Backlog items in work management tools.
      - CMDB and asset records (state, ownership, lifecycle).
      - Standard operating procedures and runbooks if process changes result.

11. Communication and Continuous Monitoring
    - Communicate outcomes to affected teams and business stakeholders.
    - Establish ongoing monitoring with alerts tied to headroom thresholds and SLO error budgets.
    - Set review checkpoints to track progress against roadmap and KPI trends.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Infrastructure Capability Assessment Report (executive summary and detailed appendix).
- Capability heatmap and maturity scores by domain.
- Baseline performance/capacity dashboards and unit economics.
- Demand forecasts and scenario analysis results.
- Gap and Needs Register with prioritized recommendations.
- Risk register updates with mitigation plans.
- Remediation and investment roadmap with cost/benefit.
- Architecture Decision Records for key choices.
- Updated CMDB/asset lifecycle statuses and service maps.
- Backlog items/epics for remediation in the delivery tool.

Success criteria:
- Accurate, validated baseline with >95% inventory coverage for in-scope assets.
- Agreed, funded roadmap addressing top risks/gaps within defined timelines.
- Improved leading indicators (e.g., capacity headroom, patch compliance, cloud waste) within 1–2 quarters.
- Stakeholder satisfaction and alignment with business growth plans.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Infrastructure Manager: Owns the process, scope, and final recommendations; ensures cross-domain coordination.
- Capacity/Performance Engineer: Builds baselines, models demand, and produces forecasts.
- Enterprise/Infrastructure Architect: Defines evaluation criteria, ensures architectural alignment, authors ADRs.
- Service Owners: Provide SLOs, operational constraints, and validate impact on services.
- ITAM/CMDB Manager: Ensures asset and configuration data quality; runs discovery and reconciliation.
- Cloud/Platform Engineers (Compute/Storage/Network/DB/Kubernetes): Supply platform metrics, constraints, and options.
- Security Architect/Engineer: Provides vulnerability, patch, and control coverage posture; assesses risk.
- FinOps/IT Finance Analyst: Provides cost data, unit economics, and optimization opportunities.
- Vendor/Supplier Manager: Provides contract/EoL insights and vendor performance data.
- BRM/Product Owners: Supply business demand signals and validate prioritization.
- PMO/Portfolio Manager: Integrates roadmap into portfolio; tracks delivery outcomes.

## Best Practices
- Maintain a single source of truth (CMDB) with automated discovery and strong data governance.
- Standardize tagging and metadata (owner, environment, cost center, application, criticality) across on-prem and cloud.
- Use SLOs and error budgets to connect infrastructure health to business outcomes.
- Adopt IaC and configuration management to reduce drift and speed remediation.
- Right-size and optimize continuously; embed FinOps practices (commitments, schedules, decommissioning).
- Implement service mapping and dependency mapping for all Tier-1 and Tier-2 services.
- Apply a consistent capability rubric and produce visual heatmaps to ease decision-making.
- Incorporate DR/BCP requirements and regularly test RTO/RPO assumptions.
- Automate reports and dashboards; integrate monitoring and work management tools.
- Include sustainability metrics (power, carbon, e-waste) in scoring and investment cases.
- Time-box assessments and use iteratively improving cycles rather than one-time big-bang reviews.

## Common Challenges
- Incomplete or inaccurate inventory and dependency data
  - Mitigation: Automate discovery; enforce CMDB governance; implement mandatory tagging; periodic audits.
- Shadow IT and unmanaged cloud resources
  - Mitigation: Cloud account governance, tag policies, budget guardrails, and network discovery.
- Data quality and tooling sprawl
  - Mitigation: Define system-of-record per data domain; consolidate tools; establish data stewardship.
- Forecast uncertainty
  - Mitigation: Scenario-based planning; sensitivity analysis; rolling forecasts; align with product roadmaps.
- Skills gaps for new platforms (cloud, containers)
  - Mitigation: Training plans, hiring, managed services, or consulting augmentation.
- Budget constraints and long lead times (hardware, network)
  - Mitigation: Prioritize high ROI quick wins; reserve capacity; negotiate with vendors; consider cloud or managed options.
- Security and compliance misalignment with rapid changes
  - Mitigation: Embed security early; continuous compliance monitoring; automated policy checks.
- Organizational silos slowing decisions
  - Mitigation: Cross-functional review boards; shared KPIs; joint planning workshops.

## Performance Metrics
Leading indicators:
- Inventory coverage: percentage of in-scope assets discovered and reconciled.
- Capacity headroom per critical resource and service (CPU/mem/IOPS/network).
- Forecast accuracy (variance between predicted and actual utilization).
- Patch/vulnerability backlog age; time-to-remediate critical vulnerabilities.
- Percentage of assets within support lifecycle (not EoL/EoS).
- Cloud waste percentage (idle/orphaned/overprovisioned resources).
- Observability coverage (percentage of critical services with SLOs and error budgets).

Lagging indicators:
- SLA/SLO attainment rate and error budget burn.
- Incident rate and mean time to restore (MTTR) for capacity-related incidents.
- Change success rate for infrastructure changes tied to remediation efforts.
- Cost per unit of capacity (compute/storage/network) and trend over time.
- Risk exposure reduction (count and severity of high risks mitigated).
- Roadmap execution adherence (milestones completed on time and within budget).
- Stakeholder satisfaction (survey scores from service owners and business stakeholders).

Targets should be set per environment and service tier and reviewed quarterly.

## Technology and Tools
- CMDB and Discovery: ServiceNow, BMC Helix, device and cloud discovery tools (e.g., agent-based and network scanning).
- Observability/Monitoring: Prometheus/Grafana, Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic; cloud-native (CloudWatch, Azure Monitor, GCP Cloud Operations).
- Network and Infra Monitoring: NetFlow/sFlow tools, SNMP-based NMS, APM/NPM tools.
- Capacity and Optimization: Turbonomic, VMware vRealize/Aria, Apptio/Cloudability, native cloud cost explorers.
- ITAM/License: Flexera, Snow; vendor license dashboards.
- Security and Compliance: Vulnerability scanners, SIEM, CSPM/CNAPP tools, patch management.
- Automation and Configuration: Terraform, Ansible, Puppet/Chef; CI/CD systems; image and golden template management.
- DR/Backup: Enterprise backup tools, replication/orchestration platforms; runbook automation.
- Portfolio/Work Management and Documentation: Jira/Azure DevOps, Confluence/SharePoint, Power BI/Tableau for reporting.
- Architecture Repositories: LeanIX, MEGA/HOPEX, or EA wikis for standards and ADRs.

Implementation tips:
- Integrate data flows to minimize manual effort (APIs, data lakes).
- Standardize dashboards with drill-downs by service, environment, and region.
- Enforce tag policies and CMDB updates as part of change workflows.
- Use playbooks for common findings (e.g., right-size patterns, EoL refresh, patch acceleration).

This process, executed consistently, provides the evidence and alignment needed to keep infrastructure capabilities ahead of business demand while controlling risk and cost.

Process Details:
## Overview
Maintain service support knowledge repository is the process of creating, curating, governing, and continuously improving the knowledge used to deliver IT support. It ensures that accurate, findable, secure, and reusable knowledge is available to service desk agents, engineers, and end users (self-service) at the moment of need. The process aligns with ITIL Knowledge Management and Knowledge-Centered Service (KCS) practices, reduces mean time to resolve, improves first contact resolution, deflects tickets to self-service, accelerates onboarding, and preserves organizational know‑how for competitive advantage.

Scope includes:
- Defining knowledge standards, taxonomy, workflows, and lifecycle.
- Capturing knowledge from incidents, problems, changes, releases, and vendor sources.
- Reviewing, approving, publishing, and retiring knowledge assets.
- Enabling access through ITSM tools, portals, chat, and search.
- Measuring usage and quality; driving continuous improvement and knowledge transfer.

## Key Activities
- Establish governance: policies, roles, responsibilities, workflows, compliance controls.
- Design information architecture: taxonomy, categories, metadata, tags, search synonyms, templates.
- Configure and integrate tools: knowledge base, ITSM/ticketing, search, analytics, chatbots, SSO/IAM.
- Capture and author knowledge: shift‑left authoring at case resolution; seed and migrate legacy content.
- Review and publish: quality checks, approvals, versioning, controlled rollout to audiences.
- Enable access and usage: embed knowledge in agent workspace, self-service portal, virtual agents.
- Maintain and improve: scheduled reviews, feedback processing, deduplication, archival, retirement.
- Knowledge transfer: coaching, communities of practice, training, post‑incident reviews, release briefings.
- Monitor and report: KPIs, dashboards, health checks, audits, backlog management for gaps.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Incident, request, problem, and major incident records with resolution notes and workarounds.
  - Known error database items and problem root cause analyses.
  - Change and release notes, service introductions, configuration details (CMDB).
  - Vendor/product documentation, FAQs, security advisories.
  - User feedback (ratings, comments), search analytics, ticket-to-article linkage data.
  - Existing legacy knowledge repositories to migrate.

- Prerequisites:
  - Approved knowledge management policy and governance model.
  - Defined taxonomy, metadata schema, article templates, and style guide.
  - Role definitions (e.g., Knowledge Manager, Authors, Reviewers) and training.
  - Configured knowledge platform integrated with ITSM, search, and SSO.
  - Data classification and access model (public/internal/restricted) with retention rules.
  - Defined SLAs/OLAs for article creation, review, and updates.
  - Security, privacy, and compliance guidelines (e.g., ISO 27001, GDPR/PII handling).

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Incident, Request, Problem, Change and Release Management (sources and triggers).
  - Service Catalog and CMDB (context and linkage).
  - Major Incident and Post‑Incident Review (high-value learnings).
  - Training and Communications (enablement and adoption).
  - Continual Improvement/CSI (backlog and prioritization).
  - Information Security and Data Governance (controls and audits).

## Process Steps
1. Plan and govern
   - Define objectives and success criteria aligned to support goals (e.g., FCR improvement, deflection).
   - Approve policy, roles, and RACI; establish governance board and meeting cadence.
   - Set SLAs for create/review/publish; define compliance checkpoints and audit schedule.

2. Design information architecture
   - Create taxonomy aligned to services, products, platforms, and user personas.
   - Define metadata (service, CI, audience, sensitivity, lifecycle state, owner, tags).
   - Build templates (troubleshooting, how‑to, FAQ, known error, runbook) with required fields.
   - Configure search synonyms, stop words, relevancy tuning rules, and facets.

3. Configure tools and integrations
   - Select and configure knowledge platform; enable versioning, workflows, approvals.
   - Integrate with ITSM (auto-suggest articles in agent workspace and portal).
   - Connect analytics, feedback collection, and chatbot/virtual agent; enable SSO/IAM and access controls.
   - Set up migration utilities for legacy content and backup/DR procedures.

4. Seed and migrate content
   - Inventory legacy sources; de-duplicate and map to new taxonomy.
   - Migrate prioritized articles; assign owners; set initial review dates and sensitivity labels.
   - Publish a curated “starter set” for top contact drivers.

5. Establish capture and authoring flow (KCS-aligned)
   - Embed “capture in the workflow”: agents convert resolutions into articles as part of ticket closure.
   - Create intake channels from PIRs, root cause analyses, release notes, and vendor advisories.
   - Route drafts to appropriate queues based on service/technology and sensitivity.

6. Review, approve, and publish
   - Conduct peer review for accuracy, completeness, clarity, and compliance with template and style.
   - Security/compliance check for PII, secrets, and license content; apply classification and access.
   - Approve and publish to defined audiences (agents vs. end users); notify stakeholders.

7. Promote access and adoption
   - Enable contextual surfacing: auto-suggest in tickets, service portal search, chatbot answers.
   - Communicate new/updated articles via release notes, newsletters, and in-tool notifications.
   - Run enablement sessions and microlearning for agents on writing and using knowledge.

8. Maintain and lifecycle management
   - Apply review cadence by criticality (e.g., monthly for top drivers, quarterly for standard).
   - Monitor signals: low helpfulness, high bounce, aging, low reuse; trigger updates or retirement.
   - Merge duplicates, fix broken links, update screenshots/videos; maintain translation/localization.
   - Archive or retire obsolete content with redirects; retain versions per policy.

9. Feedback and continuous improvement
   - Process comments/ratings; close the loop with submitters.
   - Analyze search terms, zero-result queries, and contact drivers to identify knowledge gaps.
   - Prioritize a knowledge backlog; assign to owners; track to completion.
   - Conduct periodic quality audits and calibrations; coach authors; recognize top contributors.

10. Measure, report, and adjust
   - Publish dashboards (usage, quality, impact); review in governance forums.
   - Correlate knowledge metrics with support outcomes (FCR, MTTR, deflection, CSAT).
   - Iterate IA, templates, search tuning, and workflows based on insights.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Published, version-controlled knowledge articles (how‑to, troubleshooting, known errors, FAQs, runbooks).
- Taxonomy, templates, style guide, and governance documentation.
- Knowledge base health reports, dashboards, and audit logs.
- Knowledge backlog and gap analysis.
- Training materials and communications for authors and consumers.
- Archived/retired content repository with retention evidence.

- Success criteria:
  - Measurable improvements in FCR, MTTR, self-service success/deflection.
  - High article quality and freshness (on-time reviews, high helpfulness scores).
  - Broad adoption (high agent link/reuse rate, portal engagement).
  - Compliance with security/privacy policies; audit findings resolved on time.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Knowledge Manager: Owns policy, governance, IA, metrics, and continuous improvement; chairs governance board.
- Knowledge Domain Owners/Content Owners (by service/technology): Approve content; ensure accuracy; manage lifecycle.
- Knowledge Authors/Agents: Capture and author articles during case work; apply templates and tagging.
- Reviewers/Approvers (SMEs, Security/Compliance): Validate technical correctness and policy compliance.
- KCS Coach/Trainer: Coaches authors, runs calibrations, maintains writing standards.
- Service Desk Manager: Drives adoption, link rate, and coaching within the team.
- Problem Manager: Ensures known errors and workarounds are documented and maintained.
- Release/Change Manager: Triggers knowledge updates for releases/changes; validates rollout communications.
- ITSM/KM Platform Admin: Configures workflows, permissions, search, analytics; maintains integrations.
- Information Security/Data Protection Officer: Oversees classification, access controls, PII/secret scanning.
- Data Analyst/BI: Builds dashboards; conducts trend and impact analyses.
- Communications/Training: Plans and delivers enablement and awareness.

## Best Practices
- Adopt KCS principles (capture, structure, reuse, improve) and embed authoring in the workflow.
- Use standardized templates and a clear style guide; write for the intended audience level.
- Maintain a robust taxonomy and metadata; use consistent tagging and search synonyms.
- Prefer “single source of truth” and link to authoritative vendor docs rather than duplicating.
- Implement strong governance with clear SLAs for review/update; automate reminders and escalations.
- Optimize search: relevancy tuning, synonyms, facets; monitor zero‑result queries.
- Integrate knowledge everywhere: agent workspace, portal, chatbot, email responses.
- Apply security by design: classification, least‑privilege access, secret scanning, and audits.
- Leverage rich media (screenshots, short videos) and step-by-step guides for usability.
- Localize/translate prioritized content; maintain translation workflows tied to source updates.
- Recognize and reward contributions; gamify participation to increase engagement.
- Conduct regular quality calibrations and peer reviews; run content “hygiene days.”
- Use analytics to drive decisions; tie knowledge work to business outcomes (CSAT, cost to serve).

## Common Challenges
- Stale or duplicate content: Mitigate with ownership, review cadences, deduplication tools, and retirement workflows.
- Low adoption by agents: Provide KCS training, embed capture in ticket closure, track link rate, and coach.
- Poor findability: Improve taxonomy, tags, synonyms, and search tuning; apply better titles and summaries.
- Security/privacy risks: Enforce classification, scanning for PII/secrets, and restricted access; train authors.
- Tool fragmentation: Consolidate repositories; integrate with ITSM and search; migrate legacy content.
- Inconsistent quality: Use templates, style guides, peer review, and coach authors; measure quality scores.
- Limited time to document: Promote “good enough” drafts with iterative improvement; allocate knowledge time in capacity plans.
- Change-driven content drift: Tie knowledge tasks to change/release workflows; require updates as exit criteria.

## Performance Metrics
- Utilization and quality:
  - Article reuse/link rate per ticket and per agent.
  - Helpfulness score and comment sentiment.
  - Search success rate; zero-result and zero-click search rates.
  - Unique views, bounce rate, time on page for top articles.
  - Percentage of articles reviewed on time; content freshness index; orphaned articles rate.

- Impact on support outcomes:
  - First Contact Resolution (FCR) rate.
  - Mean Time to Resolve (MTTR) and backlog aging for top categories.
  - Self-service success and deflection rate (portal/virtual agent).
  - Reduction in repeat contacts and duplicate incidents.
  - CSAT/NPS for support interactions referencing knowledge.

- Efficiency and throughput:
  - Time to publish from draft; cycle time by workflow stage.
  - Contribution rate (articles per agent/SME per period).
  - Coverage of top contact drivers (knowledge availability vs. demand).
  - Localization turnaround time and coverage.

- Compliance and risk:
  - Access control violations, PII/secret detection incidents, and time to remediate.
  - Audit findings count and closure rate.

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM and Knowledge Platforms: ServiceNow Knowledge, Jira Service Management + Confluence, BMC Helix, Cherwell, Freshservice.
- Search and Analytics: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, built‑in search tuning, BI tools (Power BI, Tableau), session analytics.
- AI/Automation: Article suggestion and summarization, ticket-to-article linking, intent detection for chatbots, duplicate detection.
- Collaboration/Authoring: Confluence, SharePoint, markdown editors, screen capture and video tools (Snagit, Loom).
- Virtual Agents/Portals: MS Power Virtual Agents, ServiceNow Virtual Agent, custom chat; responsive self-service portals.
- Integration and Governance: SSO/IAM (Azure AD, Okta), DLP/secret scanners, classification/labeling, backup/DR, translation/localization services.
- Compliance and Security: PII redaction tools, audit logging, role-based access control, encryption at rest/in transit.

Process Details:
## Overview
Coordinate with external support providers is the process of planning, governing, and operating the end-to-end coordination model between the organization’s IT support function and third parties (e.g., SaaS vendors, MSPs, cloud providers, OEMs, telcos, systems integrators). Its purpose is to ensure seamless, secure, and efficient support delivery across organizational and supplier boundaries, aligned to defined service levels and business needs.

This process:
- Translates the service support plan into a multi-provider operating model with clear responsibilities, SLAs/OLAs/underpinning contracts (UCs), escalation paths, and integrated workflows.
- Establishes governance, communication, and performance management for day-to-day operations and major incidents.
- Ensures risk, compliance, access, and data handling obligations are met while optimizing cost, speed, and customer experience.

It sits within Define service support planning and works closely with Supplier Management, Service Level Management, Incident/Problem/Change Management, Knowledge Management, Access Management, Security & Compliance, and Procurement.

## Key Activities
- Define multi-provider coordination strategy and governance (SIAM-aligned if multi-supplier).
- Align and negotiate back-to-back SLAs/OLAs/UCs that support business SLAs.
- Map and integrate operational processes (incident, request, problem, change, maintenance notifications).
- Implement and maintain technical “e-bonding” between ITSM tools where appropriate.
- Establish escalation matrices, communication channels, and major incident roles.
- Onboard and offboard providers (access, training, knowledge, contacts, runbooks).
- Manage vendor performance, service reviews, and continuous improvement plans.
- Ensure compliance, security, and data protection requirements (DPAs, audits, access reviews).
- Coordinate change and release planning across providers; align freeze calendars.
- Maintain a provider portfolio, entitlements, and support contracts including renewals/exit plans.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Service support plan, service catalog entries, and target SLAs.
  - List of services/components requiring external support and their support tiers (L1/L2/L3).
  - Provider information: existing contracts, capabilities, coverage, and support entitlements.
  - Compliance and security requirements (e.g., ISO 27001, SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, PCI), DPAs, data classifications.
  - Tool landscape and integration capabilities (ITSM, CMDB, monitoring, comms).
  - Budget constraints and cost model (per-incident, retainer, outcome-based).
  - CMDB/asset inventory and architecture standards.

- Prerequisites:
  - Supplier due diligence completed or in progress (risk assessment, references, certifications).
  - Legal/procurement templates and guidelines available (MSA, SOW, SLA, DPA).
  - Internal roles and RACI for service ownership and supplier management established.
  - Defined support policies (hours, languages, time zones, security, escalation).
  - Leadership endorsement of the coordination model and governance cadence.

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Supplier Management and Procurement (selection, contracting, renewals).
  - Service Level Management (SLA/OLA/UC alignment).
  - Incident, Request, Problem, Change Enablement, and Release Management (operational execution).
  - Knowledge Management (runbooks, KB sharing).
  - Access Management and IAM (least-privilege, JIT access).
  - Configuration Management (CMDB data quality).
  - Risk & Compliance (third-party risk, audits, regulatory adherence).
  - Financial Management (cost tracking, service credits).

## Process Steps
1) Plan the coordination model
   - Review service support plan, identify services/components involving external providers.
   - Select coordination approach (single-provider, multi-provider, SIAM-style integration).
   - Define governance structure (steering, operational, and technical working groups).
   - Deliverables: Coordination Strategy, RACI, Governance Charter.

2) Analyze and align obligations
   - Inventory existing contracts and entitlements; identify gaps vs. business SLAs.
   - Define back-to-back SLAs and underpinning contracts to support end-to-end targets.
   - Draft/update DPA, data transfer mechanisms, security and audit clauses.
   - Deliverables: SLA/OLA/UC matrix, Contract gap analysis, DPA updates.

3) Design process integrations
   - Map cross-provider workflows for incident/request/problem/change/maintenance notifications.
   - Define triage and escalation criteria (severity matrix, L1/L2/L3 ownership).
   - Establish major incident roles, war room rules, and communications protocol.
   - Deliverables: Process Integration Maps, Escalation Matrix, Major Incident Playbook.

4) Implement tool and data integration
   - Choose integration method (API e-bonding, middleware, email-to-case, portal).
   - Define field mappings, ticket state synchronization, attachments, and PII masking.
   - Configure monitoring/alerting integration and event correlation where needed.
   - UAT with test cases; validate SLA clocks across systems and error handling.
   - Deliverables: Integration Design, Configured Connectors, UAT Results, Data Handling SOP.

5) Establish access and security controls
   - Provision SSO/JIT access with least privilege; enable PAM for elevated actions.
   - Define joiner/mover/leaver process and access review cadence (e.g., quarterly).
   - Implement logging/monitoring of vendor activity; define break-glass procedures.
   - Deliverables: Access Roster, Role Profiles, Access Review Schedule, Audit Logging Plan.

6) Prepare knowledge, training, and runbooks
   - Create shared KB articles, diagnostic trees, and runbooks aligned to providers’ scope.
   - Define knowledge lifecycle (authoring, review, approval, versioning).
   - Train internal L1/L2 and vendor teams on handoffs, tools, SLAs, and security.
   - Deliverables: Runbook Library, KB Pack, Training Completion Records.

7) Onboard providers operationally
   - Kickoff meeting, exchange 24/7 contact lists, escalation paths, and maintenance windows.
   - Pilot period with limited scope; measure handoff quality and SLA adherence.
   - Confirm readiness checkpoints before full go-live.
   - Deliverables: Contact Sheet, Handover Checklist, Pilot Report, Go-live Readiness Sign-off.

8) Execute day-to-day operations
   - Route tickets per triage matrix; monitor SLAs; manage changes and freezes with providers.
   - Conduct daily/weekly operational syncs and queue health checks.
   - Ensure providers submit RCAs for P1/P2 incidents with corrective actions.
   - Deliverables: Operational Logs, RCA Documents, Updated Action Registers.

9) Manage performance and continuous improvement
   - Monthly/quarterly service reviews covering SLAs, incidents, problems, changes, customer feedback, and risks.
   - Trigger Service Improvement Plans (SIPs) and corrective actions; apply service credits/earnbacks per contract.
   - Maintain a multi-provider risk register; implement automation/knowledge updates.
   - Deliverables: Service Review Packs, SIPs, Performance Dashboards, Risk Register updates.

10) Ensure compliance and audit readiness
    - Collect evidence for audits (SLA reports, access reviews, SOC reports, security tests).
    - Test BCP/DR with providers; align RTO/RPO and failover procedures.
    - Deliverables: Audit Evidence Repository, BCP/DR Test Reports.

11) Renewal, exit, and offboarding
    - Evaluate performance vs. value; decide on renewal or transition.
    - Execute exit plan: knowledge capture, data return/destruction, access revocation, tool disconnects.
    - Financial reconciliation and lessons learned.
    - Deliverables: Renewal/Exit Decision, Offboarding Checklist, Final Reconciliation, Lessons Learned.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Governance artifacts: Coordination Strategy, RACI, Governance Charter, Contact/Escalation Lists.
- Contracts and agreements: Updated SLAs/OLAs/UCs, DPA, Security Requirements, Maintenance Window MOUs.
- Operational documentation: Process maps, Major Incident Playbook, Runbooks/KB, Change/Freeze Calendars.
- Technical integrations: E-bonded ticketing connectors, field mappings, UAT results, monitoring hooks.
- Security/compliance: Access rosters, PAM configurations, access review evidence, audit logs, SOC/ISO attestations on file.
- Performance management: Dashboards, Service Review packs, SIPs, RCAs, Risk Register.
- Offboarding/transition: Exit plans, data returns/destruction certificates, access revocation records.

Success criteria:
- Back-to-back SLAs enable meeting business SLAs ≥ target (e.g., ≥ 95%).
- Reduced MTTR and seamless handoffs between parties; low reopen rate.
- Compliance obligations met; no critical audit findings; timely access reviews.
- Positive customer CSAT and stakeholder feedback on joint incident handling.
- Integration uptime ≥ 99.9%; minimal manual rework.
- Cost within budget; transparent service credits/earnbacks applied when due.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Service Owner: Accountable for service outcomes; ensures SLAs/OLAs alignment; chairs service reviews.
- Supplier/Vendor Manager: Manages contracts, performance, credits/SIPs, renewals/exit; owns RACI and contact lists.
- Service Integration Lead (SIAM role, if multi-provider): Orchestrates end-to-end processes across providers; single throat to choke during multi-supplier incidents.
- Support Managers (Internal L1/L2/L3): Operate day-to-day queues, triage/escalations, knowledge upkeep.
- Incident Manager / Major Incident Manager: Coordinates major incidents, war rooms, communications, and RCAs.
- Problem Manager: Drives root cause, trend analysis, and long-term fixes across provider boundaries.
- Change Manager/CAB: Governs provider changes, risk assessment, scheduling, and freeze windows.
- Security/Compliance Lead: Oversees DPAs, access controls, audits, vulnerability/patch requirements.
- Integration Engineer/ITSM Administrator: Designs and maintains ticketing e-bonding, monitoring integrations, reporting.
- Procurement/Legal: Negotiates contracts, DPAs, terms; ensures commercial and legal compliance.
- Finance/AP: Tracks spend, invoices, service credits.
- External Provider Roles: Account Manager, Support Lead, Escalation Manager, SMEs, NOC.

## Best Practices
- Adopt a SIAM-inspired model for multi-supplier environments with a defined service integrator role.
- Establish end-to-end SLAs supported by back-to-back UCs; avoid gaps and conflicts.
- Use standard contract language for response/resolution targets, RCAs, SIPs, credits/earnback, and data protection.
- Implement robust e-bonding for tickets with field parity, attachment handling, and error monitoring.
- Maintain clear escalation matrices, 24/7 contacts, and war room protocols; run joint simulations.
- Enforce least privilege, JIT access, PAM, and quarterly access reviews; enable activity logging with tamper-proof audit trails.
- Share and co-maintain runbooks/KB; require vendors to author and update knowledge as part of obligations.
- Align maintenance windows and change freezes; ensure providers attend CAB as needed.
- Schedule regular service reviews with data-driven insights; trigger SIPs for sustained misses.
- Plan for resilience: backup vendor options where feasible; maintain vendor exit strategies to avoid lock-in.
- Ensure global coverage strategy (follow-the-sun where needed) with standardized shift handovers.

## Common Challenges
- Misaligned SLAs leading to end-to-end breaches
  - Solution: Create SLA/OLA/UC matrix; negotiate back-to-back targets; model E2E scenarios before signing.
- Ambiguous scope and handoffs
  - Solution: Detailed RACI, triage matrices, and runbooks; pilot and refine.
- Tool integration failures or data quality issues
  - Solution: Use robust APIs, retry/queue mechanisms, monitoring; CMDB quality gates; periodic reconciliation.
- Communication gaps during major incidents
  - Solution: Predefined comms plan, single incident commander, regular updates cadence, post-mortems with actions.
- Security and data protection risks
  - Solution: DPAs, PII masking, data residency controls, SOC2/ISO attestations, access logging, periodic audits.
- Time-zone/language barriers
  - Solution: Follow-the-sun model, multilingual coverage, standardized handover templates.
- Vendor turnover or inconsistent staffing
  - Solution: Require minimum staffing levels, certification requirements, and knowledge transition obligations.
- Access delays and privilege creep
  - Solution: JIT automation, onboarding SLAs for access, role-based profiles, quarterly access reviews.
- Cost overruns
  - Solution: Transparent rate cards, demand forecasting, cost-per-ticket reporting, service credit governance.

## Performance Metrics
- SLA attainment (per provider and E2E): % incidents/requests meeting response and resolution targets.
- MTTA/MTTR (by severity and provider): Median/95th percentiles; trend over time.
- Handoff cycle time: Time from internal escalation to provider acceptance; target < X minutes.
- Reopen rate and escalation rate: % tickets reopened or escalated; indicates quality issues.
- First Contact Resolution rate (for provider-owned categories).
- Backlog aging: Tickets older than thresholds by priority; aging trend.
- Major incident metrics: Time to engage provider, time to restore, RCA delivery within X business days.
- Change success rate (provider changes): % without incident/rollback; change-induced incident count.
- Integration health: Connector uptime, sync error rate, message latency.
- Knowledge quality: Article usage, helpfulness score, time to update after incident.
- Compliance metrics: Access review completion on time, audit findings count/severity, DPA adherence tests.
- Cost metrics: Cost per ticket/request, variance vs. budget, service credits earned/applied.
- Relationship health: Quarterly vendor scorecard, stakeholder satisfaction/NPS.

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM platforms: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, BMC Helix/Remedy, Freshservice (ticketing, SLAs, KB).
- Integration/middleware: ServiceNow Spokes, Mulesoft, Boomi, Workato, webhooks, REST APIs, message queues.
- Monitoring/observability: Datadog, New Relic, Splunk, Elastic, Prometheus/Grafana; alert routing via PagerDuty/Opsgenie.
- CMDB/Asset: ServiceNow CMDB, Device42; discovery tools for accuracy.
- Identity and access: Okta, Azure AD, SailPoint; PAM tools like CyberArk/BeyondTrust; JIT access.
- Security/compliance and risk: Archer, OneTrust, Vanta/Drata; SIEM (Splunk, Sentinel); vulnerability management (Tenable, Qualys).
- Knowledge and documentation: Confluence, ServiceNow KB, SharePoint; runbook repositories with version control (Git).
- Communications: Microsoft Teams/Slack for channels and incident bridges; Zoom/telephony for war rooms; Statuspage for user comms.
- Contract and procurement: Coupa, Ariba, Ivalua; e-signature (DocuSign, Adobe Sign).
- Reporting/BI: Power BI, Tableau; ITSM-native analytics for dashboards.

Process Details:
# [8.7.5.9] Triage IT Service Delivery Incidents

## Overview
Triage IT service delivery incidents is the rapid assessment and prioritization process used to sort incident records so that the organization responds in the right order and with the right resources. It ensures that service disruptions, degradations, and performance issues are quickly understood, classified, prioritized, and routed to the most appropriate resolver group, with timely stakeholder communication and escalation when warranted.

This process sits at the front of Incident Management. It bridges detection/intake and technical resolution by:
- Validating and enriching incident records.
- Determining impact, urgency, and business risk to set priority.
- Declaring and coordinating major incidents when criteria are met.
- Routing to the correct assignment group and initiating communication.
- Linking to knowledge, problems, changes, and known errors to accelerate recovery.

Effective triage reduces downtime, improves customer experience, protects regulatory and contractual obligations, and optimizes utilization of IT support capacity.

## Key Activities
- Intake and de-duplication of incidents and alerts from all channels.
- Initial classification: incident vs. request vs. event vs. security incident.
- Impact and urgency assessment using a standard priority matrix.
- Business criticality check (service tier, affected users, revenue/risk).
- Context enrichment (CI/CMDB associations, change calendar, known errors).
- Major incident evaluation and invocation when thresholds are met.
- Assignment/routing to the appropriate resolver group or swarm team.
- Stakeholder notification and customer updates per communication plan.
- Initial workarounds/runbook triggers where applicable.
- Continuous re-triage and reprioritization as new information emerges.
- Documentation, linkage (problem, change, knowledge), and handoff.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Incident/alert record with time, source, description, and reporter/contact.
  - Service catalog entries and CI/CMDB relationships for impacted components.
  - SLA/OLA definitions, priority matrix, business criticality/tiering.
  - Major incident criteria and escalation paths.
  - Change calendar/maintenance windows and release notes.
  - Known Error Database (KEDB) and knowledge articles/runbooks.
  - On-call schedules and resolver group roster/contact details.
  - Monitoring and observability signals (logs, metrics, traces, synthetics).
  - Customer impact data (user counts, geographies, revenue, compliance impact).

- Prerequisites:
  - ITSM tool configured with incident categorization, priority calculator, routing rules, and SLA timers.
  - Defined incident types and severity/priority model with examples.
  - Integrated monitoring/event correlation and de-duplication tooling.
  - Up-to-date CMDB/service maps and service criticality tiers.
  - Approved major incident procedure and communication templates.
  - Trained triage analysts and on-call structure with OLAs for acceptance.
  - Knowledge base and runbook library maintained and searchable.

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Event Monitoring/Detection (to create incidents/alerts).
  - Incident Logging and Categorization standards.
  - Major Incident Management (when declared).
  - Problem Management (linking to problems/known errors).
  - Change Enablement (assessing change collisions and planned work).
  - Service Level Management (SLAs/OLAs and reporting).
  - Knowledge Management (articles/runbooks).
  - Configuration Management (CMDB accuracy).

## Process Steps
1. Receive and acknowledge
   - Intake from portal, phone, chat, email, monitoring, or API.
   - Confirm receipt to reporter or source system; start SLA/OLA timers.

2. Validate and de-duplicate
   - Confirm minimum required data (service, symptoms, impact, contact).
   - Merge duplicates via correlation rules; create parent-child relationships.

3. Classify the record
   - Determine whether it is an incident, service request, change, security incident, or information inquiry.
   - Route non-incident types to their appropriate workflows immediately.

4. Enrich with context
   - Link service/CI via CMDB and service maps.
   - Pull related open incidents/events; check KEDB/knowledge for known issues or workarounds.
   - Check change calendar for planned maintenance or recent changes.
   - Add environment, version, region, and affected customer segment if known.

5. Assess impact and urgency
   - Quantify users/customers affected, business process disruption, regulatory risk, and financial exposure.
   - Determine urgency (time sensitivity, data loss, safety/security).
   - Apply the priority matrix to set P1–P5 (or per organizational scheme).

6. Evaluate major incident criteria
   - Compare conditions against predefined MI thresholds (e.g., service Tier 0 or Tier 1 outage, multi-region impact, high revenue loss).
   - If met, immediately declare major incident, page on-call teams, and transfer to Major Incident Management while retaining triage role for intake of related incidents.

7. Initial containment/workaround (if applicable)
   - If a validated workaround/runbook exists, initiate or instruct reporters (e.g., failover, cache flush, rollback) in coordination with resolvers and change controls if needed.
   - Document actions taken and results.

8. Assign and route
   - Use routing rules to assign to the most appropriate resolver group (application, platform, network, database, vendor).
   - For ambiguous ownership, initiate a swarm/bridge with cross-functional SMEs.
   - Notify the assignee and secure acceptance per OLA.

9. Communicate
   - Provide the first customer update within defined timeframes (e.g., P1 within 15 minutes) with status, scope, and next update time.
   - Notify internal stakeholders (service owner, product owner, business reps) per comms matrix.
   - If customer-facing, update status page as per policy.

10. Link records
   - Link to related problems, known errors, changes, and parent/child incidents.
   - Tag with incident category/subcategory for reporting and trend analysis.

11. Monitor and re-triage
   - Track for new information; adjust impact/priority; re-assign if necessary.
   - Ensure update cadence is maintained; trigger escalation if OLAs at risk.

12. Handoff and document
   - Confirm receipt by resolver team and that the ticket status reflects “In Progress.”
   - Ensure triage notes include impact assessment, supporting evidence, steps taken, communications sent, and next actions.

13. Close triage stage
   - Mark triage complete when properly prioritized, routed, and acknowledged, or when resolved during triage.
   - Capture categorization accuracy flags and misroutes for continual improvement.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Outputs:
  - Enriched, prioritized incident record with accurate classification and CI/service linkage.
  - Assignment to the appropriate resolver group with acceptance.
  - Initial customer/stakeholder communications and status updates.
  - Declared major incident when thresholds met, with handoff to MI process.
  - Initiated workaround actions when applicable.

- Deliverables:
  - Triage notes and impact/urgency rationale.
  - Communication artifacts (emails, chat transcripts, status page entries).
  - Parent-child incident relationships and links to problems/changes/knowledge.
  - Triage performance data and misroute/false-MI tags for improvement.

- Success criteria:
  - Right-first-time routing and priority assignment.
  - SLA/OLA compliance for time-to-triage and time-to-first-update.
  - Timely and correct major incident declarations.
  - Reduction in duplicate/noise incidents impacting resolver capacity.
  - Positive customer satisfaction on initial handling.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Service Desk Analyst / Triage Analyst
  - Perform initial validation, enrichment, classification, prioritization, and routing.
  - Initiate first communications and apply known workarounds.
  - Maintain update cadence and escalate per OLAs.

- Incident Coordinator / Triage Lead
  - Oversee triage flow, resolve ambiguities, ensure MI criteria evaluation.
  - Facilitate swarming, verify assignment, and ensure communication quality.
  - Drive re-triage and orchestrate escalations.

- Major Incident Manager (when applicable)
  - Lead major incident process once declared, run bridges/war rooms, coordinate comms.
  - Maintain MI timeline and stakeholder updates.

- Resolver Group SMEs (L2/L3 Support, SRE, Network, DB, App Support)
  - Accept assignment, confirm scope, advise triage on classification and priority adjustments.
  - Execute or validate workarounds/runbooks.

- Service Owner / Product Owner
  - Provide business impact input, confirm service criticality, approve customer communications as needed.

- Problem Manager
  - Link incidents to problems/known errors; advise on recurring issues.

- Change Manager
  - Validate conflicts with change calendar; coordinate emergency changes if required for remediation.

- NOC/Monitoring Team
  - Manage alert correlation, suppression, and enrichment; support de-duplication.

- Vendor/Third-Party Support
  - Engage per support contracts; acknowledge and participate in triage/resolution.

## Best Practices
- Use a standardized, example-driven impact/urgency-to-priority matrix; avoid role-based bias (e.g., “VIP auto-P1”) unless policy-backed.
- Automate enrichment (CI, ownership, change context) and routing with rules and AIOps to reduce manual effort.
- Implement alert de-duplication and correlation to prevent noise storms; route events to incidents only when action is required.
- Maintain accurate service maps/CMDB and service tiering; review quarterly.
- Define, publish, and rehearse major incident criteria and activation procedures.
- Adopt swarming for ambiguous or cross-domain incidents; avoid ping-pong reassignments.
- Time-box triage actions; set clear internal targets (e.g., P1 triage in 5 minutes, P2 in 15 minutes).
- Keep communication clear, consistent, and time-bound; use templates with who/what/impact/next update.
- Shift-left with runbooks and knowledge; enable service desk to trigger safe, reversible actions.
- Review misroutes, false MIs, and reprioritizations in weekly ops reviews; feed improvements into rules and training.
- Separate severity (technical) from priority (business impact/urgency) but map consistently.
- Integrate security incident criteria and handoff to ISMS/SOC when appropriate.

## Common Challenges
- Incomplete or low-quality incident data
  - Solution: Enforce required fields, guided forms, dynamic intake prompts, and reporter coaching; automate data enrichment.

- Alert floods and noisy monitoring
  - Solution: Implement correlation, suppression, and thresholding; tune monitors; use SLO-based alerting.

- Misclassification and misrouting
  - Solution: Provide decision trees, examples, and continuous feedback; use ML-based routing with human-in-the-loop review.

- Inconsistent priority decisions across shifts/teams
  - Solution: Calibrate with scenario catalogs and simulations; publish reference cases and runbooks; conduct regular audits.

- Delayed escalations and stakeholder communication
  - Solution: Automate paging based on priority; enforce update cadence via the ITSM tool; use comms templates and status pages.

- Poor CMDB/service mapping accuracy
  - Solution: Establish ownership and KPIs for CMDB health; automate discovery; align with change and release processes.

- Conflicts with planned changes or maintenance windows
  - Solution: Integrate change calendar; require triage to check and document change context; ensure rollback readiness.

- Overuse or underuse of major incident process
  - Solution: Clear MI thresholds, decision aids, and post-MI reviews; track false positives/negatives and refine criteria.

## Performance Metrics
- Time to triage (MTTA for triage): average time from creation to prioritized and assigned.
- Time to first meaningful customer update by priority.
- Right-first-time routing rate: percentage not reassigned after initial assignment.
- Priority accuracy: percentage of incidents not reprioritized after first hour.
- Reassignment rate and average number of hops per incident.
- Major incident detection accuracy: true MI rate, false MI rate, time to declaration.
- Deduplication/correlation effectiveness: ratio of alerts to actionable incidents.
- Percentage of incidents with complete required fields at triage completion.
- SLA/OLA compliance for triage and acceptance by resolver groups.
- Age of untriaged incidents by priority; backlog beyond target thresholds.
- Customer satisfaction with initial handling (CSAT) for incidents.
- Automation coverage: percentage of incidents auto-enriched/auto-routed.
- Update cadence compliance per priority.

Target examples (adjust to organizational goals):
- P1 triage within 5 minutes; first update within 15 minutes; 95% compliance.
- Right-first-time routing > 85%.
- Reassignment rate < 10%.
- False MI rate < 5% of declared MIs.

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM platforms: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, BMC Helix/Remedy, Ivanti/Cherwell, Freshservice.
- Monitoring and observability: Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic, AppDynamics, Splunk, Elastic, Prometheus/Grafana.
- AIOps and event correlation: Moogsoft, BigPanda, PagerDuty Event Intelligence, ServiceNow ITOM, Opsgenie integrations.
- On-call and paging: PagerDuty, Atlassian Opsgenie, xMatters, VictorOps/Splunk On-Call.
- CMDB and service mapping: ServiceNow Discovery/Service Mapping, Device42, NetBox.
- Knowledge and runbook automation: Confluence, ServiceNow KB, Rundeck, Ansible Automation Platform, StackStorm.
- Communication and ChatOps: Slack, Microsoft Teams, Zoom; status pages (Atlassian Statuspage, Status.io).
- Telephony/omnichannel intake: Contact center platforms integrated with ITSM (e.g., Genesys, Five9).
- Change calendar and release tools: ServiceNow Change, Jira, GitOps/CI/CD tools integrated for deployment context.
- Analytics and reporting: ITSM native reporting, Power BI/Tableau, Elastic/Kibana.
