Process Details:
## Overview
Develop maintenance strategies is the process of defining the optimal set of maintenance policies, tactics, and frequencies for each asset or asset class to achieve business objectives at the lowest lifecycle cost and risk. It translates maintenance policies into actionable strategies—what to maintain, how, when, and by whom—based on asset criticality, failure modes, operating context, risk appetite, and regulatory requirements.

Its role in the organization:
- Aligns maintenance effort with business outcomes (safety, availability, quality, cost, compliance).
- Standardizes how assets are maintained across sites and asset classes.
- Balances preventive, predictive, and run-to-failure approaches to minimize total cost of ownership.
- Provides the foundation for maintenance planning, scheduling, execution, spares management, and budgeting.
- Ensures auditability and compliance with internal policies and external regulations.

Standards and frameworks commonly referenced:
- ISO 55000 Asset Management
- IEC 60812 FMEA/FMECA
- SAE JA1011/JA1012 RCM
- ISO 14224 Equipment reliability data
- SMRP Best Practices; OSHA/ISO 45001 (safety); industry-specific (e.g., FDA 21 CFR, NERC, API RP).

## Key Activities
- Define scope and objectives for the strategy (asset classes, targets, constraints).
- Collect and analyze asset and failure data (work history, condition data, OEM guidance).
- Perform asset criticality analysis and risk assessment.
- Conduct FMEA/RCM to identify failure modes and consequences.
- Select maintenance policies per failure mode: preventive (time/usage-based), condition-based/predictive, run-to-failure (RTF), redesign/engineering change.
- Define maintenance tasks and frequencies; build standard job plans.
- Optimize intervals and mix using reliability modeling and cost-risk trade-offs.
- Define condition monitoring program (sensors, rounds, routes, thresholds).
- Determine spares/BOM strategy and MRO stocking parameters.
- Estimate resource and budget implications.
- Validate strategy with operations, safety, quality, and finance; manage approvals.
- Document strategies; encode in CMMS/EAM/APM.
- Pilot, refine, and roll out; set review cadence and continuous improvement loop.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Asset register and hierarchy; asset criticality criteria and scoring model.
- Work order history: failures, MTBF/MTTR, downtime, costs, causes.
- OEM manuals, warranties, recommended maintenance.
- Regulatory and compliance requirements; safety and environmental constraints.
- Operating context: duty cycles, production requirements, environmental conditions.
- Condition monitoring data (vibration, oil, thermography), process historian data.
- BOMs/parts lists; spares inventory levels and lead times.
- Risk register, incident/near-miss records; prior RCAs.
- Financial data: cost of downtime, labor rates, maintenance budget.
- Current maintenance plans and task library, procedures, SOPs.

Prerequisites:
- Defined maintenance policy framework and governance (risk appetite, approval matrix).
- Functional CMMS/EAM/APM with accurate asset master data.
- Cross-functional team available (maintenance, reliability, operations, safety, QA, supply chain).
- Minimum data quality standards or plan for data gap mitigation.
- Document control and change management process.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Upstream: Create/update asset register; Assess asset criticality; Analyze asset performance; Define maintenance policies and standards; Establish risk and compliance requirements.
- Downstream: Create maintenance plans and job plans; Schedule maintenance; Execute maintenance; Manage MRO/spares; Train personnel; Monitor and improve maintenance performance.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and scope
   - Trigger: new assets, performance issues, policy updates, regulatory changes, or lifecycle reviews.
   - Define scope (asset classes/sites), objectives (availability, risk, cost), constraints (budget, resources), success metrics, and timeline.
   - Appoint strategy owner; form cross-functional team.

2. Gather and validate data
   - Extract asset master data, work history, costs, performance metrics, OEM recommendations.
   - Compile regulatory requirements and safety/environmental constraints.
   - Assess data quality; perform cleansing or define assumptions and confidence levels.

3. Perform asset criticality analysis
   - Use a standardized model (safety, environmental, production, quality, maintainability, detectability).
   - Rank assets; select analysis depth (e.g., full RCM for high-criticality, streamlined for medium, templated for low).

4. Conduct FMEA/RCM
   - For each critical asset/class, identify functions, functional failures, failure modes, effects, and consequences.
   - Determine detectability and current controls; quantify risk priority (RPN or risk matrix).
   - Reference industry failure mode libraries where available.

5. Select maintenance policies per failure mode
   - Choose PM (time/usage), CBM/PdM, RTF, or redesign based on consequence, failure pattern, and economic analysis.
   - Document rationale and triggers; define condition indicators and thresholds if CBM/PdM.

6. Define tasks, frequencies, and job plans
   - For each selected policy, define standard tasks: scope, frequency/trigger, estimated duration, required skills, tools, parts, safety precautions (LOTO, permits), quality checks, acceptance criteria.
   - Create standard job plans and checklists; link to asset classes and locations.

7. Optimize intervals and mix
   - Apply reliability modeling (Weibull, Crow-AMSAA) and cost-risk analysis (PM optimization) to set intervals.
   - Balance over-maintenance vs risk of failure; simulate impact on availability, cost, and risk.

8. Condition monitoring and predictive program definition
   - Select technologies (vibration, ultrasound, oil, thermography, motor current analysis).
   - Define routes, sampling frequencies, alarm thresholds, data flows to APM/CMMS, and automated work triggers.
   - Specify sensor requirements for assets lacking instrumentation.

9. Spares and BOM strategy
   - Validate BOMs; identify critical spares; set min/max and reorder points based on criticality, lead time, and failure rates.
   - Define kitting requirements for standard jobs; align with procurement strategies and vendor agreements.

10. Resource and budget planning
    - Aggregate labor hours, craft mix, tools, external services, and materials per period.
    - Estimate OPEX/CAPEX implications (e.g., sensors, redesigns); build business case.

11. Risk, safety, and compliance review
    - Conduct formal risk assessment (HAZOP/What-if as applicable).
    - Verify regulatory compliance and quality requirements; include permits and documentation needs.
    - Update risk register with residual risks and controls.

12. Stakeholder validation and approval
    - Review with operations, safety/quality, finance, and site leadership.
    - Resolve conflicts; finalize strategy; obtain approvals per governance matrix.

13. Document and implement in systems
    - Publish maintenance strategy documents with version control.
    - Configure CMMS/EAM: task lists, job plans, maintenance plans, routes, CBM triggers, task-to-asset/class assignments, planned costs.
    - Update asset masters, BOMs, and spares parameters; integrate with APM/condition monitoring systems.

14. Pilot and refine
    - Select pilot assets; execute for a defined period.
    - Monitor KPIs (PM compliance, failures, downtime, cost); capture feedback; adjust tasks/frequencies.

15. Full rollout and training
    - Train planners, schedulers, technicians, and operators on new tasks and CBM methods.
    - Roll out across in-scope assets; ensure change management communications.

16. Monitor, audit, and improve
    - Establish review cadence (e.g., quarterly for critical assets; annual for others) and triggers (major failure, duty change).
    - Conduct strategy effectiveness reviews; perform RCAs for significant events; update strategy and systems as needed.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Maintenance strategy dossier per asset class/asset:
  - Objectives and targets; criticality score; FMEA/RCM worksheets; selected policies with rationale.
  - Task library and standard job plans; schedules/intervals; CBM/PdM specifications and thresholds.
  - Spares/BOM strategy; resource and budget estimates; risk and compliance controls.
  - Implementation mapping in CMMS/EAM/APM; training materials.
- Configuration changes in CMMS/EAM/APM and updated asset/BOM master data.
- Approval records and version-controlled documents.
- Pilot and rollout reports; lessons learned and improvement log.

Success criteria:
- Strategies approved and implemented in systems.
- Reduction in unplanned downtime and critical failures for in-scope assets.
- Improved PM compliance and planning metrics without cost overruns.
- Demonstrable compliance with regulatory and safety requirements.
- Positive ROI within targeted timeframe (e.g., 12–24 months).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Asset Manager/Owner: Defines business objectives, approves strategies, prioritizes scope.
- Reliability Engineer (Process Owner): Leads FMEA/RCM, interval optimization, defines CBM/PdM, authors strategy.
- Maintenance Engineer: Develops job plans, tools, and procedures; ensures maintainability and safety.
- Maintenance Planner/Scheduler: Configures CMMS plans, routes, and job plans; readiness for scheduling.
- Operations/Production Representative: Provides operating context, production constraints; validates practicality and windows.
- Safety/HSSE: Reviews tasks for safe execution; ensures permits/LOTO and regulatory adherence.
- Quality/Compliance: Ensures adherence to quality/GxP or industry-specific requirements; audit readiness.
- Supply Chain/MRO: Validates BOMs; sets stocking parameters; aligns vendor contracts.
- Finance/Controller: Reviews cost-benefit, budgets, and ROI.
- IT/OT/Systems Analyst: Ensures CMMS/APM configuration, integrations, data flows.
- Data Analyst: Prepares reliability data, models failure distributions, maintains dashboards.
- External OEM/Vendors (as needed): Provide technical recommendations, specialized services.

Governance tip: Use a RACI for each major step and a stage-gate approval (Define, Analyze, Decide, Deploy) with documented sign-offs.

## Best Practices
- Start with criticality: apply full RCM to critical assets; use templated strategies for low-risk assets.
- Data-driven decisions: use actual failure and cost data; quantify risk and value.
- Standardize: leverage corporate task libraries, templates, and naming conventions.
- Balance maintenance mix: avoid over-reliance on PM; deploy CBM/PdM where failure patterns support it.
- Close the loop: embed feedback from execution and RCAs to continuously refine strategies.
- Pilot then scale: test strategies on representative assets; refine before roll-out.
- Integrate systems: ensure CMMS, APM, condition monitoring, and inventory systems are synchronized.
- Manage change: train stakeholders; communicate why changes are made and expected benefits.
- Document rigorously: maintain version-controlled strategy records, assumptions, and rationales for auditability.
- Safety first: build safety steps into every job plan; validate permits and isolations.
- Review cycles: set periodic reviews and event-based triggers (duty changes, repeated failures).
- Align with OEM but validate: calibrate OEM recommendations against actual duty and failure data.

## Common Challenges
- Poor or incomplete data: Mitigate with data cleansing, standard coding, and leveraging industry data; document assumptions.
- Cultural resistance: Address via stakeholder engagement, clear benefits, and training; start with quick wins.
- Over-maintenance and calendar bias: Use reliability modeling and PM optimization; shift to usage/condition triggers.
- System integration gaps: Plan integrations and data governance; use middleware and standardized interfaces.
- Resource constraints: Prioritize by criticality; phase implementation; use contractors/OEMs strategically.
- Compliance complexity: Involve quality early; use traceable approval workflows and audit trails.
- Inaccurate BOMs/spares: Conduct targeted BOM verification and critical spare reviews; implement kitting.
- Strategy drift: Prevent with scheduled reviews and KPI monitoring; enforce change control.

## Performance Metrics
- Coverage and quality
  - Percent of critical assets with approved strategies.
  - Percent of assets with up-to-date strategies (within review cycle).
  - Strategy quality audit score (completeness, rationale, alignment to standards).
- Reliability and risk outcomes
  - Unplanned downtime and critical failure frequency.
  - MTBF and MTTR for in-scope assets.
  - Risk exposure reduction (e.g., number of high-risk failure modes mitigated).
- Maintenance mix and efficiency
  - Planned vs unplanned work ratio; PM/PdM/CM breakdown.
  - PM compliance and schedule adherence.
  - Predictive alert precision and lead time; percentage of PdM alerts converted to planned work.
- Cost and inventory
  - Maintenance cost as % of RAV and cost per unit output.
  - Overtime rate; contractor spend vs plan.
  - MRO stockouts for critical spares; inventory turns.
- Process health
  - Time to develop and approve strategies; pilot cycle time.
  - Number of RCAs leading to strategy updates.
  - Training completion and competency for new tasks.

Set targets per asset class and review monthly/quarterly.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Infor EAM, Oracle EAM—strategy configuration, job plans, routes, maintenance plans.
- APM/Analytics: GE APM, Aveva APM, Aspen Mtell, Seeq, TrendMiner—PdM models, analytics, dashboards.

# [10.3.1.2] Analyze Assets and Predict Maintenance Requirements

## Overview
This process evaluates the current health of assets and projects their future maintenance needs to minimize unplanned downtime, optimize cost, ensure safety/compliance, and support production targets. It uses asset condition, performance, and failure data to recommend the right maintenance strategy (run-to-failure, time-based, condition-based, predictive) and to forecast work, parts, and budget. It is a core element of maintenance planning and a key input to scheduling, budgeting, and inventory planning.

Scope includes all productive assets and critical utilities/facilities. It covers periodic analysis cycles and event-driven analyses (e.g., after failures or step changes in operating context).

## Key Activities
- Establish analysis cadence and triggers (periodic, risk-based, event-driven).
- Collect and validate asset data (master data, history, condition, operating context).
- Assess current condition and asset health indices.
- Analyze failure history and reliability (FMEA/RCM, Weibull, MTBF/MTTR).
- Build/update predictive and condition-based models and thresholds.
- Determine maintenance requirements (tasks, triggers, intervals, resource needs).
- Forecast workload, parts, and budget; assess risk and business impact.
- Review, approve, and update CMMS/EAM maintenance plans and master data.
- Monitor model and strategy performance; execute continuous improvement.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Asset registry and hierarchy, criticality ratings, locations, BOMs/spares.
  - Maintenance history: work orders, failure codes, causes, corrective actions, downtime, costs.
  - Condition data: inspections, vibration, thermography, ultrasound, oil analysis, OEM diagnostics.
  - Operational data: load, duty cycle, starts/stops, process conditions, ambient environment.
  - OEM manuals, warranty terms, recommended maintenance, bulletins.
  - Regulatory/compliance requirements (e.g., pressure vessels, lifting equipment).
  - Production plans, utilization targets, SLAs; risk tolerance and safety policies.
  - Previous maintenance strategies, job plans, routes, CBM rules, predictive models.
- Prerequisites:
  - Accurate, current asset master data and criticality analysis.
  - Configured CMMS/EAM and access to historians/APM/IoT data (IT/OT connectivity).
  - Defined failure coding taxonomy (e.g., ISO 14224) and closed-loop work order completion discipline.
  - Data governance and quality standards; trained personnel; safety permits for inspections.
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - [10.3.1] Plan asset maintenance (strategy and resource planning).
  - Asset registration/master data management.
  - Perform inspections and condition monitoring routes.
  - Failure reporting, analysis, and defect elimination (RCFA).
  - Inventory management for spares and MRP.
  - Management of change (MOC) for strategy/model updates.
  - Budgeting and capital planning for instrumentation upgrades.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate analysis
   - Trigger by calendar (e.g., quarterly), criticality-based frequency, after failures, post-overhaul/commissioning, OEM bulletin, regulatory change, or unusual trends.
2. Define scope and objectives
   - Select assets by criticality, performance issues, or lifecycle stage. Clarify goals (reduce failures, extend intervals, comply with regulation).
3. Gather data
   - Extract from CMMS/EAM (WO history, costs), historians/APM (sensor and condition data), OEM docs, inspection reports, production logs. Capture operational context and duty changes.
4. Validate and cleanse data
   - Check master data consistency; reconcile duplicates; standardize failure codes; remove sensor drift/outliers; fill missing values or flag low-confidence assets.
5. Baseline current condition
   - Compute asset health index (normalized composite of condition, performance, age, and criticality); compare to control limits; document anomalies.
6. Reliability and risk analysis
   - Trend MTBF/MTTR; perform Weibull/survival analysis for failure modes; develop/refresh FMEA/RCM for critical assets; estimate risk using consequence x likelihood; map P-F intervals where applicable.
7. Build/update models and rules
   - Condition-based: set thresholds/alarms using SPC or OEM limits; define escalation criteria.
   - Predictive: train/refresh models (e.g., anomaly detection, RUL estimators) with feature sets from vibration, process, and usage data; validate with backtesting; ensure explainability.
   - Physics-based or hybrid models for critical failure modes where data is sparse.
8. Determine maintenance requirements
   - Choose strategy per failure mode (run-to-failure, TBM, CBM, PdM) aligned to risk and economics.
   - Define tasks, frequencies/triggers, and lead times aligned to P-F intervals; specify required skills, tools, permits, and estimated durations.
   - Identify inspection routes, sensor needs, and sampling plans (e.g., oil analysis intervals).
9. Forecast workload, spares, and budget
   - Convert predicted tasks into monthly/quarterly work volumes; estimate labor hours and craft mix.
   - Forecast spare parts demand (min/max levels, reorder points) based on predicted replacements and lead times; update BOMs where gaps exist.
   - Quantify expected risk reduction and avoided downtime; prepare budget/CapEx requests (e.g., sensors).
10. Review and approval
    - Conduct cross-functional review (Operations, Maintenance, Reliability, HSE, Finance). Evaluate safety/compliance, production impact, and ROI; finalize decisions and document MOC.
11. Update systems and documentation
    - Create/update PM/PdM tasks, job plans, and CBM rules in CMMS/EAM; configure alerts in APM/historian; version-control strategies, models, and thresholds; update training and SOPs.
12. Communicate and enable
    - Brief planners/schedulers and technicians; update dashboards; align shutdown/turnaround windows with predicted needs.
13. Monitor and refine
    - Track outcomes (predictions vs. actual events, work deferrals, alarm performance). Investigate misses/false alarms; retrain models; update strategies after RCFA outcomes.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Updated maintenance strategies per asset/class (RCM decisions, task lists, intervals).
- Predictive/CBM rules and thresholds; configured alerts and dashboards.
- Maintenance workload forecast and resource plan (labor hours by craft, periodized).
- Spare parts demand forecast; updated min/max, reorder points, and BOMs.
- Budget and business case documentation (cost/benefit, risk reduction).
- Asset health indices, RUL estimates, and risk register updates.
- Work orders/PMs generated or rescheduled; inspection routes and sampling plans.
- Changes documented via MOC; updated SOPs and training materials.
- Success criteria:
  - Reduced unplanned downtime and emergency work.
  - Improved schedule adherence and maintenance cost optimization.
  - Compliance with regulatory and OEM requirements.
  - Forecast accuracy within target thresholds.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Reliability Engineer: Lead analysis, RCM/FMEA, modeling strategy, threshold setting, and continuous improvement.
- Maintenance Planner: Translate requirements into job plans, estimate labor, create PMs/WOs, coordinate with scheduling.
- Condition Monitoring Technician/Specialist: Execute inspections and routes; collect/interpret vibration, oil, thermal, ultrasound data.
- Data/Analytics Engineer or APM Analyst: Build/maintain data pipelines, develop predictive models, validate and monitor model performance.
- Maintenance Supervisor: Provide execution feedback, ensure data capture quality in WOs, and support adoption.
- Operations/Asset Owner: Provide operating context, constraints, and priorities; approve downtime windows; validate practicality.
- Inventory/Procurement Analyst: Align spares forecasts and lead times; adjust stocking policies; manage supplier engagement.
- HSE/Compliance Officer: Verify safety, environmental, and statutory compliance implications.
- IT/OT Engineer: Ensure connectivity, cybersecurity, historian/APM reliability, and system integrations.
- Finance/Business Partner: Validate cost/benefit analyses and support budget approvals.
- OEM/Vendor SME: Provide technical insights, bulletins, and recommended practices.

## Best Practices
- Prioritize by criticality; apply most rigorous analysis to high-risk assets.
- Use standardized taxonomies (e.g., ISO 14224) for failure coding and asset classes.
- Apply RCM per SAE JA1011/JA1012; maintain living FMEA records.
- Combine leading indicators (condition data) with lagging indicators (failures, costs).
- Calibrate thresholds with SPC and align actions to the P-F curve to ensure adequate planning lead time.
- Validate predictive models with backtesting and pilot deployments; ensure explainable outputs for field adoption.
- Ensure data quality at the source: mandatory WO fields, sensor calibration, and automated data checks.
- Close the loop: feed RCFA findings and execution feedback into strategy updates.
- Govern changes via MOC with version control and traceability.
- Integrate CMMS/EAM, APM, and historians; avoid manual re-entry; use APIs and event-driven triggers.
- Secure OT networks and protect data privacy; follow least-privilege access.
- Train cross-functional teams; share visual health dashboards to build trust in analytics.
- Plan instrumentation upgrades strategically (value-at-risk driven).

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Poor data quality and inconsistent failure codes
  - Solution: Enforce mandatory fields, standardized codes, automated validation, and technician training.
- Sparse failure data on critical assets
  - Solution: Use physics-of-failure, OEM guidance, Bayesian updating, and similarity-based learning from sister assets.
- Sensor drift/noise causing false alarms
  - Solution: Routine calibration, redundant sensing, signal filtering, and dynamic thresholds with hysteresis.
- Model drift with changing duty cycles
  - Solution: Monitor model performance, retrain on sliding windows, include context variables, and use MLOps practices.
- Organizational resistance and low adoption
  - Solution: Involve end users early, demonstrate ROI with pilots, provide training, and ensure clear actionable alerts.
- Integration gaps across systems
  - Solution: Implement middleware/APIs (e.g., MQTT/Kafka), master data governance, and a unified asset ID strategy.
- Budget constraints for instrumentation
  - Solution: Prioritize high-criticality assets, quantify risk reduction, and leverage portable condition monitoring tools.
- Regulatory changes
  - Solution: Maintain compliance watch, map regulations to asset classes, and predefine update playbooks.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs)
- Prediction accuracy:
  - Failure prediction precision/recall within the P-F interval; MAPE for workload/spares forecasts.
- Reliability and availability:
  - MTBF/MTTR trends; asset availability; OEE impact; percent emergency work.
- Maintenance mix and effectiveness:
  - Ratio of PdM/CBM vs. PM vs. corrective work; PM/PdM compliance rate; avoided failures/downtime.
- Cost performance:
  - Maintenance cost per replacement asset value (RAV); cost per unit output; parts stockouts and rush orders.
- Process and data quality:
  - WO data completeness; time from alert to action; alarm false-positive/negative rates; model drift indicators.
- Inventory and planning:
  - Forecast bias, service level for critical spares, lead-time adherence.
- Safety/compliance:
  - Compliance audit findings; incidents attributable to asset failure.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Oracle eAM, Infor EAM for PMs/WOs, master data, and cost capture.
- APM/Analytics: GE APM, AVEVA Predictive Analytics, Aspen Mtell, Uptake; Python/R, Jupyter, scikit-learn, TensorFlow.
- Data acquisition and historians: OSIsoft PI, Aveva Historian, Ignition; IoT platforms (AWS IoT, Azure IoT, PTC ThingWorx); message buses (MQTT, Kafka).
- Condition monitoring: Vibration analyzers/online systems, ultrasound detectors, thermal cameras, oil analysis kits/labs, motor current signature analysis.
- Reliability tools: ReliaSoft Weibull++, BlockSim; RCM/FMEA software (APIS IQ, Isograph).
- BI and dashboards: Power BI, Tableau, Grafana for health indices, alerts, and KPI tracking.
- Mobile tools: Technician mobile apps for inspections, data capture, and guided diagnostics.
- Governance and MLOps: Version control (Git), model registry, CI/CD for analytics, data catalogs, and cybersecurity tools.

## Overview
Specify maintenance policies is the process of defining, approving, and communicating the rules, standards, and decision logic that govern how assets are maintained across the organization. It establishes the maintenance strategies (e.g., preventive, predictive, run-to-failure), prioritization principles, safety and compliance expectations, documentation standards, and approval workflows that guide planning and execution.

Its purpose is to:
- Align maintenance practices with business objectives (safety, reliability, cost, compliance, sustainability).
- Standardize maintenance decisions across sites and asset classes to reduce variability and risk.
- Enable planners and technicians with clear, actionable guidance embedded in CMMS/EAM and work instructions.

Role in the organization:
- Provides the foundation for maintenance plans, PM templates, schedules, and STO (shutdown/turnaround/outage) planning.
- Interfaces with Asset Management, Operations, HSE, Quality, Procurement, and Finance to ensure cohesive lifecycle asset care.
- Supports auditability and continuous improvement, enabling risk-based decision-making and measurable performance outcomes.

## Key Activities
- Define policy scope and hierarchy (corporate, site, asset-class, system-level, work-instruction).
- Select maintenance strategies per asset class/criticality (RCM, CBM/PdM, time-based PM, RBM, run-to-failure by design).
- Establish prioritization and risk criteria (safety, environment, production impact, quality, compliance).
- Set standards for task intervals, triggers, inspection routes, condition-monitoring thresholds, and acceptance criteria.
- Define safety, environmental, and regulatory requirements (LOTO, permits-to-work, isolation standards, regulatory checks).
- Specify documentation, data, and record-keeping standards (asset taxonomy, BOMs, PM templates, inspection forms).
- Define roles, competencies, approval workflows, and change control (governance model).
- Integrate policies into CMMS/EAM and supporting tools; create templates and master data.
- Communicate, train, and roll out policies; manage exceptions and localizations.
- Monitor compliance and effectiveness; review and update on a defined cadence.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Asset register with hierarchy, taxonomy, and criticality ratings.
  - OEM recommendations, warranties, and technical manuals.
  - Historical failure data, MTBF/MTTR, root cause analyses (RCAs), and bad actor lists.
  - Regulatory and industry standards (e.g., ISO 55000, ISO 14224, ISO 31000, OSHA, NERC, FDA cGMP, API/ASME, IEC 61511 as applicable).
  - Business objectives and risk appetite; production plans; safety/environmental policies.
  - Current maintenance plans, PM library, spare parts/BOMs, and inventory policies.
- Prerequisites:
  - Governance structure defined (policy owner, approver, change control).
  - CMMS/EAM master data foundation and document control in place.
  - Cross-functional core team (Maintenance, Reliability, Operations, HSE, Quality, Procurement).
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Asset criticality assessment and risk management.
  - Maintenance strategy development (RCM/FMECA/RBM).
  - Resource and budget planning; MRO inventory management.
  - Compliance management, training management, and document control.
  - CMMS/EAM configuration and data governance.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and define scope
   - Confirm policy objectives, in-scope sites and asset classes, and policy hierarchy.
   - Identify regulatory regimes and business constraints (availability targets, budget caps).

2. Assemble cross-functional team and governance
   - Assign policy owner, author(s), reviewers, approvers; define RACI and change-control thresholds.
   - Schedule workshops and set cadence for reviews.

3. Gather and analyze inputs
   - Compile OEM guidance, historical performance, RCAs, PM compliance, emergency work rates, and warranty terms.
   - Validate asset register and criticality matrix; identify data gaps.

4. Define policy framework and decision logic
   - Establish standard maintenance strategies by criticality and asset class (e.g., High-critical rotating: PdM + RBM; Low-critical utilities: run-to-failure).
   - Specify triggers: time-based intervals, run hours, condition thresholds, event-based (start-up/shutdown), and regulatory frequencies.
   - Create a standardized prioritization matrix (e.g., Safety/Environment/Regulatory/Production/Quality scores leading to Priority 1–5).

5. Set safety, compliance, and quality requirements
   - Codify LOTO, permits-to-work, isolation verification, confined space, and hot work requirements within maintenance context.
   - Define mandatory regulatory inspections, certifications, and documentation retention periods.

6. Standardize data and documentation
   - Define asset taxonomy and naming standards; reference ISO 14224 or internal standards.
   - Mandate BOM completeness, lubrication standards, inspection forms, and acceptance criteria.
   - Specify documentation formats, version control, and storage locations in DMS/CMMS.

7. Specify roles, competencies, and approvals
   - Define who can author PMs, approve changes, execute tasks, and perform sign-offs (e.g., PE-required approvals for safety-critical changes).
   - Define competency and training requirements for specialized tasks (e.g., vibration analysis level, thermography certification).

8. Integrate into CMMS/EAM and tools
   - Build/refresh master data: functional locations, equipment records, PM templates, job plans, routes, measurement points, and condition rules.
   - Configure workflows, priorities, SLAs, and notification/escalation rules in CMMS.
   - Link MRO policies: min/max levels, critical spares classification, kitting standards.

9. Pilot and validate
   - Pilot on selected asset classes/sites; assess feasibility, workload impact, and risk coverage.
   - Capture feedback, adjust intervals/triggers, and finalize approval.

10. Approve, communicate, and train
    - Execute formal approval; publish in DMS with versioning and effective dates.
    - Run role-based training and toolbox talks; update onboarding materials.

11. Monitor compliance and performance
    - Track PM/PdM compliance, emergency work %, schedule adherence, backlog health, and audit findings.
    - Conduct periodic audits and management reviews; capture deviations and corrective actions.

12. Review and improve
    - Set review cycles (e.g., annually or after significant failures/regulatory changes).
    - Incorporate learnings from RCAs, condition-monitoring insights, and technology updates.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Policy documents:

  - Critical spares policy and stocking rules; STO maintenance standards.
- Master data and system configuration:
  - Updated asset taxonomy, BOMs, measurement points, job plans, and CMMS workflows.
- Governance and training:
  - RACI, authority matrix, change-control process, training materials and records.
- Success criteria:
  - Policies approved, published, and embedded in CMMS; >95% PM/PdM compliance within 3 months; emergency work <10–15% of total labor; audit compliance with zero major findings; measurable improvement in availability and reduction in repeat failures on critical assets.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Asset Management/Engineering Lead (Process Owner): Owns policy framework, ensures alignment with asset strategy and business goals, approves changes.
- Reliability Engineer: Leads RCM/FMECA, defines strategies and intervals, sets condition-monitoring thresholds, reviews performance.
- Maintenance Planner/Scheduler: Translates policy into PMs and job plans, ensures CMMS configuration, monitors compliance and backlog.
- Maintenance Supervisor/Technicians: Execute per policy, provide feedback, record high-quality data and measurements.
- Operations Representative: Aligns maintenance windows and priorities with production plans; approves access and permits.
- HSE/Regulatory Compliance: Ensures safety and environmental requirements are explicit and auditable; conducts/oversees audits.
- Quality/Validation (where applicable): Ensures GMP/quality impacts are controlled; approves changes in validated environments.
- Procurement/MRO: Implements critical spares policies, vendor SLAs, and warranty management per policy.
- IT/CMMS Administrator: Configures system workflows, data fields, integrations, and access controls; maintains DMS.
- Finance/Controlling: Aligns budget controls, RAV-based cost tracking, and CAPEX/OPEX treatment with policy.
- OEM/Vendors/Service Providers: Provide technical recommendations, comply with policy requirements and documentation.

## Best Practices
- Base policies on risk and reliability methods (RCM, RBM, FMECA) rather than solely on time-based PMs.
- Use asset criticality to drive strategy depth and frequency; reserve detailed PdM for high-impact assets.
- Integrate safety (LOTO, permits), regulatory checks, and quality controls directly into PM templates and workflows.
- Standardize data (taxonomy, naming, measurement points) to enable analytics; align to ISO 14224 where practical.
- Leverage condition monitoring and predictive analytics (vibration, ultrasound, oil analysis, thermography, IIoT) with clear thresholds and response actions.
- Set clear prioritization rules and SLAs; avoid “everything is Priority 1.”
- Pilot changes, quantify effects, and scale; maintain strict document control with versioning and effective dates.
- Embed policy rules in CMMS to reduce ambiguity (auto-prioritization, mandatory fields, approval gates).
- Align with OEM recommendations and warranties, but adapt to operating context and historical performance.
- Review policies at defined intervals and after major incidents; tie improvements to RCA outcomes and KPIs.

## Common Challenges
- Over-complex policies reduce adoption: Keep principles simple, provide decision trees, and build job plan libraries.
- Data quality gaps (asset register, BOMs) undermine execution: Run data cleansing projects and enforce master data standards.
- Misalignment with operations: Establish joint prioritization and maintenance window agreements; include Operations in approvals.
- Over- or under-maintenance: Use evidence-based intervals; monitor PM effectiveness (find/no-find rates) and adjust.
- Limited skills for PdM technologies: Define competency requirements; provide training or use specialized vendors initially.
- CMMS not configured to support policy: Engage IT/CMMS early; configure workflows, fields, and automation before rollout.
- Resistance to change: Communicate the “why,” show quick wins with pilots, and secure executive sponsorship.
- Regulatory compliance gaps: Map requirements to specific PMs, maintain traceability, and conduct internal audits.

Level: 4

Process Details:
## Overview
Integrate preventive maintenance into operations schedule is the process of planning and embedding time-based, usage-based, and condition-based preventive maintenance (PM) work into the production schedule for assets that are also used for manufacturing or service delivery. Its purpose is to sustain asset reliability and regulatory compliance while minimizing impact to throughput, customer service levels, and cost. It coordinates maintenance and production planning across multiple time horizons (long-, mid-, and short-term), aligns resource availability, and sets governance for schedule creation, approval, communication, and change control.

This process is critical to:
- Preserve equipment health and prevent unplanned downtime via timely PM.
- Optimize overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) by placing PM in low-demand or opportunistic windows.
- Ensure regulatory, safety, and quality compliance (e.g., calibration, statutory inspections).
- Balance conflicting objectives across Maintenance, Operations, Quality, HSE, and Supply Chain.

## Key Activities
- Extract and prioritize due PM work (time/usage/condition-based) from the CMMS/EAM within the planning horizon.
- Estimate resource requirements and durations (multi-craft, permits, parts, vendors).
- Model capacity and constraints across production and maintenance calendars (shifts, changeovers, cleaning, labor skills).
- Identify and reserve candidate maintenance windows (opportunistic and planned).
- Scenario planning and what-if analysis to assess throughput, cost, and risk impacts.
- Cross-functional scheduling, approval, and freeze control for the integrated plan.
- Pre-execution readiness (kitting, permits, lockout/tagout plans, access coordination).
- Execution-day handover, isolation, and progress communication.
- Post-execution verification, schedule adherence measurement, and continuous improvement.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Preventive maintenance master plans, task lists, and frequencies (time and meter-based) from CMMS/EAM.
  - Asset criticality, risk ranking, and maximum deferral policies.
  - Production master schedule/forecast (S&OP/IBP outputs), planned orders, and demand prioritization.
  - Resource calendars: maintenance crafts, operators, supervision, vendor availability.
  - Asset/line calendars: operating shifts, planned downtimes, changeovers, sanitation/CIP, regulatory blackout windows.
  - Parts availability and lead times, PM BOMs, tooling and test equipment availability.
  - Duration standards, historical actuals, and productivity factors.
  - Safety/quality constraints: permits required, JHAs, validation/QA signoff steps, calibration tolerances.
  - Site constraints: utilities outages, SIMOPS, access restrictions.
  - Live condition/predictive triggers (sensors, counters) and usage accrual rates.

- Prerequisites:
  - Maintained asset hierarchy with accurate master data (locations, work centers, capacities).
  - Approved PM strategies and deferral/combination rules (RCM/FMEA-based).
  - Defined governance for schedule cadence, approval thresholds, and freeze periods.
  - Agreed service levels: asset availability targets, maximum deferral intervals.
  - Standard job plans with estimated durations and skill profiles.
  - Defined downtime coding standards and integration to MES/APS.

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - [10.3.1] Plan asset maintenance (strategies, task definition, and resource planning).
  - Work order management and prioritization.
  - Materials management for MRO/spares.
  - Production planning and scheduling (APS/MES).
  - HSE permit-to-work and LOTO.
  - Quality/Calibration management.
  - Vendor management for contracted maintenance.
  - Change management/Management of Change (MoC).

## Process Steps
1. Define planning horizons and cadence
   - Long-term (3–18 months): align major PMs/inspections with S&OP cycles; rough-cut capacity and outages.
   - Mid-term (4–12 weeks): build a rolling integrated plan; reserve maintenance windows; align parts and vendors.
   - Short-term (1–4 weeks): create a frozen integrated schedule; finalize jobs, permits, kits, and crafts.
   - Near real-time (0–7 days): S&OE adjustments for exceptions under defined change-control rules.

2. Compile PM demand for the horizon
   - Pull due/forecast-due PMs by time/usage, including condition-based triggers.
   - Apply grouping rules to bundle PM tasks on the same asset to reduce starts/stops.
   - Apply maximum deferral and regulatory windows to set latest permissible dates.

3. Estimate job requirements
   - Confirm standard durations vs. latest actuals; adjust for access, cleaning, cooldown/warmup, QA checks.
   - Identify skill requirements, headcount, shifts, special tools, and vendor involvement.
   - Validate parts availability; create reservations or trigger procurement for shortages.
   - Pre-check special constraints (confined space, hot work, calibration drift limits).

4. Map production constraints and candidate windows
   - Import production plan, changeovers, sanitation, and planned downtimes from APS/MES.
   - Identify low-demand blocks, switchovers, or windows where PM can be opportunistic.
   - Define blackout periods (promotions, quarter-end, regulatory campaigns).

5. Capacity modeling and what-if scenarios
   - Model equipment, labor, and vendor capacity across alternatives:
     - Scenario A: PM during planned changeovers/cleaning (SMED-enabled “pit stops”).
     - Scenario B: Off-shift/weekend PM with overtime.
     - Scenario C: Consolidated outage across multiple adjacent assets/utilities.
     - Scenario D: Staggered micro-windows with micro-stoppages.
   - Evaluate throughput impact, OEE, cost, and risk per scenario.
   - Use digital simulation where available to validate queue times and WIP impact.

6. Cross-functional scheduling and approval
   - Conduct weekly integrated planning meeting (Maintenance, Production, Quality, HSE, Materials, Finance).
   - Review scenarios, risks (KPI impacts, deferrals), and confirm preferred windows.
   - Approve schedule per authority thresholds; assign schedule codes (firm, tentative).
   - Establish freeze periods (e.g., 72-hour lock) and escalation path for changes.

7. Publish and integrate the schedule
   - Push approved downtimes to APS/MES as planned events with codes and durations.
   - Schedule work orders in CMMS against the selected windows and resources.
   - Generate and distribute the integrated Gantt/line calendar to stakeholders.
   - Notify impacted areas (utilities, logistics, EHS, QA, security) and external vendors.

8. Pre-execution readiness (T−7 to T−1 days)
   - Kitting and staging of parts/tools at point-of-use; verify critical spares.
   - Prepare permits (LOTO, hot work, confined space), JHAs, and isolation plans.
   - Pre-job brief scheduling; SIMOPS review; ensure calibration standards ready if needed.
   - Confirm vendor arrival and site access; verify scaffolding/access, lifts, and isolations.
   - MES/SCADA tags and interlocks prepared; create downtime events placeholders.

9. Execution-day control
   - Operations handover and asset isolation per LOTO plan; verify zero-energy state.
   - Maintenance executes job plan; provide start/stop updates via mobile CMMS.
   - QA/HSE hold points executed; capture variances and additional findings.
   - If variance threatens window, trigger escalation and predefined decision tree (extend, partial, defer).

10. Completion, restart, and verification
   - Remove locks, conduct functional checks, and restart per SOP.
   - QA release/calibration verification as applicable.
   - Record actual durations, parts consumed, causes of variance, and downtime codes.
   - Update usage counters and next PM due in CMMS.

11. Post-execution review and continuous improvement
   - Measure schedule adherence, window utilization, and production impact.
   - Analyze deferrals, rework, and emergent work; update job plans and durations.
   - Update PM strategies if repeated non-value tasks or excessive frequency observed.
   - Feed insights to reliability engineers for RCM review and to planners for standards updates.

12. Exception handling
   - Production surge or urgent order: evaluate risk-based deferral within policy; require approval by predefined authority.
   - Unplanned breakdown near PM due: convert to corrective plus opportunistic PM bundle if safe and practical.
   - Parts/vendor no-show: swap to alternate window or substitute task bundle; update schedule and notify stakeholders.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Integrated production-maintenance schedule with reserved downtime windows.
- Scheduled PM work orders with assigned resources and durations.
- Downtime events created in APS/MES and isolation/permit packages.
- Kitted parts lists and staging confirmations.
- Communications: outage notices, vendor POs/confirmations, pre-job briefs.
- Updated master data: actuals, next due dates, counters, and standard durations.

Success criteria:
- PM completion rate within window and by due date thresholds (e.g., >95% on-time).
- Minimal unplanned impact: plan vs. actual downtime variance within tolerance (e.g., ±10%).
- No safety or quality incidents; permits executed correctly.
- Throughput and OEE targets met/maintained across the period.
- Limited and controlled deferrals within policy; zero regulatory overdue tasks.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Maintenance Planner: compiles PM demand, estimates durations, kitting requests, schedules WOs.
- Maintenance Scheduler: builds integrated maintenance calendar, resolves resource conflicts, publishes schedule.
- Production Planner/Scheduler: provides production plan, allocates windows, approves downtime insertion.
- Operations Manager/Line Supervisor: authorizes handover, ensures operators available for isolation/restart, enforces freeze.
- Reliability Engineer: optimizes PM strategies, conducts deferral risk assessments, reviews failure data.
- Maintenance Supervisor/Lead: executes work, manages crafts and vendors, reports progress and actuals.
- Storeroom/MRO Buyer: ensures parts availability, manages reservations and expedited orders.
- HSE/Permit Coordinator: prepares and audits permits, LOTO plans, and JHAs; oversees SIMOPS.
- Quality/Validation: manages calibration/validation holds and releases; verifies GMP compliance.
- IT/OT/MES Administrator: ensures system integrations, downtime event interfaces, and data integrity.
- Finance/Cost Controller: tracks cost and assesses impact of downtime vs. production.
- External Vendor/Contractor: executes specialized PM tasks per schedule and site rules.
- Executive Sponsor/Plant Leader: resolves priority conflicts and approves high-impact changes.

## Best Practices
- Use a rolling horizon with firm-frozen and flexible periods; enforce change control with clear authority limits.
- Synchronize PM with natural production pauses: changeovers, sanitation/CIP, cleanouts, batch ends.
- Apply SMED and “pit stop” methods to shorten PM tasks and reduce downtime.
- Bundle tasks by asset/system to reduce the number of stops; plan parallel work with clear critical path and SIMOPS controls.
- Keep accurate standard times; update after each cycle and apply learning curves.
- Opportunistic maintenance: trigger PM when unplanned short stops occur if prerequisites are met.
- Pre-kitting and point-of-use staging to minimize search and wait time.
- Maintain critical spares for PM; classify by risk and replenishment lead time.
- Use what-if simulations to quantify throughput, OEE, and service impacts before approval.
- Define strict deferral rules with risk scoring tied to asset criticality and failure modes.
- Reserve “maintenance buffers” in the weekly schedule to absorb small overruns without impacting production.
- Integrate condition monitoring to shift from purely time-based to predictive windows where feasible.
- Standardize downtime codes and ensure they flow through MES/CMMS for consistent analytics.
- Conduct pre-job briefs and post-job reviews to reinforce safety and continuous improvement.

## Common Challenges
- Conflicting priorities between throughput goals and PM compliance
  - Solution: governance with freeze periods, executive tie-breakers, and quantified risk/benefit scenarios.

- Inaccurate duration estimates leading to overrun
  - Solution: use historical actuals, add contingency buffers, and adopt SMED and parallel tasking.

- Parts or vendor unavailability
  - Solution: early kitting checks, vendor SLAs aligned to schedule, critical spares stocking strategies.

- Poor data quality or system integration gaps
  - Solution: master data stewardship, standardized calendars, and API-based integration between CMMS, APS, and MES.

- Unplanned breakdowns disrupting schedule
  - Solution: opportunistic bundling of PM during repair, dynamic rescheduling rules, and protected maintenance buffers.

- Regulatory/calibration windows with limited flexibility
  - Solution: long-horizon visibility, pre-approval of alternate windows, and escalation for non-moveable compliance tasks.

- SIMOPS and access constraints causing delays
  - Solution: consolidated outage planning, permit coordination, and clear area control ownership.

## Performance Metrics
- PM on-time completion rate (% by due date and within window).
- Schedule adherence (maintenance): planned vs. actual start/finish within tolerance.
- Plan vs. actual downtime variance (minutes or %).
- Maintenance window utilization (% productive time within reserved window).
- OEE impact of PM (delta OEE vs. baseline over period).
- Deferral rate and average days deferred by criticality class.
- Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and Mean Time To Repair (MTTR) on assets with integrated PM.
- Percentage of PM executed opportunistically vs. planned.
- Parts availability at T−1 (kitting completeness rate).
- Safety and quality leading indicators: permit compliance rate, pre-job brief completion, number of SIMOPS conflicts.
- Cost per PM event/hour and cost of lost production per PM event.
- Percentage of PM with updated standard times after execution (learning adoption rate).

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Infor EAM, Oracle eAM for PM plans, WOs, parts, and history.
- APS/Production Scheduling: SAP PP/DS, Siemens Opcenter APS, Aspen Plant Scheduler, PlanetTogether, Oracle ASCP/Production Scheduling.
- MES/SCADA/Historians: to manage downtime events, track counters/usage, and provide real-time status.
- Condition Monitoring/IIoT Platforms: vibration, temperature, oil analysis; predictive analytics to inform window timing.
- Digital twin/Simulation tools: to model throughput and test scheduling scenarios.
- Mobile maintenance apps: field execution, time capture, and permit workflows.
- Permit-to-work/LOTO systems: integrated safety controls.
- Collaboration tools and dashboards: integrated Gantt views, KPIs, and alerts.
- Integration middleware/APIs: synchronize calendars, work orders, and downtime events across CMMS, APS, MES; enforce common master data (assets, work centers, calendars).
- Analytics/BI: KPI tracking, variance analysis, and continuous improvement insights.

Process Details:
## Overview
Conduct Resource Planning is the process of analyzing maintenance workload and aligning the right mix of labor, skills, materials, tools, contractors, and access windows to meet maintenance commitments. It transforms the prioritized maintenance demand (from preventive, predictive, corrective, and improvement work) into a feasible resource plan across multiple horizons (annual, 13-week rolling, weekly), ensuring work can be scheduled and executed safely, on time, and within budget.

This process is central to asset reliability and cost control:
- It prevents schedule breaks by confirming resource availability before work is scheduled.
- It balances internal labor capacity with contractor use and overtime, reducing bottlenecks and overtime spikes.
- It drives material readiness and kitting, reducing delays and wrench-time losses.
- It supports compliance with regulatory, safety, and environmental requirements by ensuring qualified resources and necessary permits are accounted for.

## Key Activities
- Forecast maintenance workload by time horizon (annual, 13-week rolling, weekly) from PM programs, condition-based triggers, backlog, and outages/turnarounds.
- Assess current and projected resource capacity (internal labor, skill sets, shifts, tools, equipment, materials, contractors, budget).
- Identify resource gaps and constraints (skills, materials lead times, access windows, permits, special tools).
- Develop a resource plan:
  - Labor capacity plan and leveling (by craft/skill and shift).
  - Contractor augmentation plan and sourcing.
  - Materials and critical spares plan, including kitting and staging.
  - Tools, equipment, and facilities plan (specialized test equipment, scaffolding, cranes, work bays).
  - Permits and access plan (LOTO, confined space, hot work, site access).
  - Cost/budget alignment and approvals.
- Coordinate with Operations for asset access windows, production downtimes, and risk trade-offs.
- Generate requisitions and reservations (materials, tools, contractors); initiate procurement actions.
- Communicate and publish resource plans, constraints, and readiness status to stakeholders.
- Monitor plan adherence; update forecasts with actuals; manage changes and emergent work.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Prioritized maintenance demand: approved work orders, PM schedules, PdM alerts, regulatory tasks, outage scopes.
  - Job plans with estimated hours, crew size, skills, duration, BOMs, special tools, permits, risk ratings.
  - Asset criticality and risk prioritization criteria.
  - Labor rosters, shift patterns, leave calendars, skill matrices, certifications.
  - Inventory data: stock levels, reorder points, supplier lead times, critical spares list.
  - Contractor framework agreements, vendor master data, rate cards, safety qualifications.
  - Historical performance: estimate accuracy, schedule adherence, productivity (wrench time), material stockouts.
  - Budget constraints and cost center allocations.
  - Site constraints: access rules, safety policies, permit-to-work process, environmental constraints, seasonal/weather factors.

- Prerequisites:
  - Current maintenance strategy and policies defined (PM/PdM frequencies, RCM outputs).
  - CMMS/EAM master data accuracy (asset hierarchy, BOMs, job plans, locations).
  - Governance cadence in place (weekly planning meeting, 13-week lookahead, outage readiness reviews).
  - Agreed planning time fences (frozen and flexible windows).

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Maintenance strategy definition and task identification.
  - Work identification, screening, and prioritization.
  - Work order planning (ensuring scope, estimates, BOMs are defined).
  - Storeroom/inventory management and procurement.
  - Operations coordination for production schedules and access.
  - HSE management for permits and competency requirements.
  - Budgeting and financial control.

## Process Steps
1. Establish planning horizons and cadence
   - Define long-term (12–18 months), medium-term (13-week rolling), and short-term (weekly) horizons.
   - Confirm frozen window policies (e.g., freeze next week’s schedule by Wednesday) and change-control rules.

2. Compile and forecast workload
   - Extract prioritized work orders from CMMS: PMs due, PdM-based work, corrective backlog by priority, regulatory tasks.
   - Include known outage/turnaround scopes and capital tie-ins.
   - Convert workload into time-phased labor hours by craft/skill and materials demand by period.
   - Adjust for seasonal patterns and production campaigns; apply historical completion rates and estimate accuracy factors.

3. Assess resource capacity
   - Labor: calculate available hours by craft/skill/shift factoring holidays, training, leave, meetings, and non-wrench time.
   - Tools/equipment: availability of special tools, test equipment, lifting devices, vehicles, work bays.
   - Materials: check stock on hand, reserved stock, open POs, supplier lead times, critical spare health.
   - Contractors: capacity from framework vendors, mobilization times, and qualified personnel availability.
   - Access/permits: planned downtime windows, permit processing times, and site access limitations.
   - Budget: available spend for labor (regular/overtime), materials, contractors per period.

4. Identify gaps and constraints
   - Compare demand vs. capacity by period and craft; flag shortages/excesses.
   - Identify jobs with long-lead materials; mark as “materials critical path.”
   - Highlight skills credential gaps, permit bottlenecks, and equipment/tool conflicts.
   - Quantify budget variances.

5. Develop the resource plan
   - Labor leveling:
     - Re-sequence non-critical work to level load; adjust shift allocations; plan cross-skilling or training where feasible.
     - Define overtime plans with thresholds and approvals.
   - Contractor supplementation:
     - Determine scope packages for contractors; issue work packages and initiate sourcing per rate cards/frameworks.
   - Materials plan:
     - Generate reservations and purchase requisitions; set required-by dates aligned to schedule.
     - Initiate kitting and staging; assign kitting due dates.
   - Tools and equipment plan:
     - Reserve shared tools and lifting equipment; schedule inspections/calibrations before use.
   - Access and permits:
     - Book outage windows with Operations; pre-apply for permits with estimated start/end; plan isolations and LOTO.
   - Cost plan:
     - Roll up expected costs; reconcile with budget; propose trade-offs or deferrals for overruns.
   - Risk and contingency:
     - Identify high-risk jobs; add contingency buffers, alternate vendors, or spare tooling as needed.

6. Validate feasibility and secure approvals
   - Review plan in cross-functional meeting (Maintenance, Operations, HSE, Stores, Procurement, Finance).
   - Resolve conflicts and approve the plan for the planning horizon.

7. Communicate and publish
   - Distribute resource plans by craft/week, materials readiness reports, kitting status, contractor allocations, and access windows.
   - Update CMMS work orders with readiness statuses (e.g., materials complete, permits pre-approved, tools reserved).

8. Trigger execution enablers
   - Create and route purchase requisitions and service entry requests.
   - Issue pick lists to Stores; begin kitting and staging.
   - Confirm contractor work orders and site inductions.
   - Prepare shift rosters and labor assignments.

9. Monitor and control
   - Track plan adherence: schedule breaks due to resource shortfalls, stockouts, or access delays.
   - Manage changes: apply change-control for emergent work and scope changes within/after frozen window.
   - Update forecasts with actuals; adjust capacity plans and procurement as needed.

10. Close the loop and improve
    - Capture actual labor hours, material consumption, contractor costs, and causes of delays.
    - Measure estimate accuracy and resource plan accuracy; update job plans, BOMs, and lead times.
    - Refine safety stock, reorder points, and vendor lead times based on performance.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Resource plan by horizon:
  - 12–18 month headcount and capacity plan by craft/skill.
  - 13-week rolling resource plan (labor, contractors, materials, tools).
  - Weekly ready-to-schedule resource pack aligned to frozen schedule.
- Labor plans: shift rosters, overtime plans, training/cross-skilling plans.
- Contractor plans: scope packages, requisitions/POs, onboarding schedules.
- Materials plans: reservations, purchase requisitions, kitting lists, staging locations, required-by dates.
- Tools/equipment reservations and calibration schedules.
- Access and permit plans: outage bookings, pre-approved permits, LOTO plans.
- Budget alignment report and cost forecasts.
- Risk register and mitigation actions for constrained resources.
- Success criteria:
  - Work is scheduled only when resources are confirmed and ready.
  - Minimal schedule breaks due to resource shortages.
  - Cost within budget and overtime within approved thresholds.
  - Compliance tasks resourced and completed on time.
  - Safety and quality requirements satisfied (qualified personnel, correct tools, permits in place).

- Maintenance Supervisor/Foreman: validates labor availability, approves overtime, confirms crew assignments, provides actuals.

## Best Practices
- Use rolling horizons: annual capacity, 13-week lookahead, and weekly frozen schedule with clear gates.
- Plan only ready work: apply a work readiness checklist (scope, estimates, BOM, materials available, permits identified, access confirmed).
- Standardize job plans and BOMs to improve estimate accuracy and repeatability.
- Implement kitting and staging before scheduling; use material availability codes to gate scheduling.
- Maintain skills matrices and certification tracking; plan cross-training to reduce skill bottlenecks.
- Level-load labor to target steady utilization; use planned overtime and contractors to handle peaks.
- Maintain contractor framework agreements and pre-qualifications for rapid mobilization.

- Integrate CMMS with ERP procurement and inventory; automate requisitions and reservations from job plans.
- Apply risk-based prioritization (asset criticality, safety/regulatory impact) when resolving capacity conflicts.
- Hold weekly planning meetings with visual management (constraint boards, kitting status, access windows).
- Enforce change-control, especially within the frozen window; protect schedule stability.
- Use scenario planning for outages/major events; simulate crew/tools/material constraints.
- Capture actuals and feedback to improve estimates, BOMs, and stocking policies.

## Common Challenges
- Inaccurate job estimates and BOMs leading to under/over-provisioning.
  - Solution: standardize job plans, calibrate with actuals, use parametric estimating and historical productivity factors.
- Material stockouts and long lead times causing schedule breaks.
  - Solution: early identification of long-lead items, safety stock for critical spares, expediting rules, vendor performance management.
- Labor/skill shortages and certification gaps.
  - Solution: cross-training programs, contractor augmentation, proactive certification tracking, flexible shift arrangements.
- Conflicts with production schedules and limited access windows.
  - Solution: formal access negotiation with Operations, lock-in outage windows, align PM cycles with production campaigns.
- High volume of emergent work disrupting plans.
  - Solution: protected capacity buffers, triage process, root cause analysis to reduce repeat failures, improve PdM coverage.
- Poor data quality in CMMS (asset BOMs, skills, calendars).
  - Solution: data governance, ownership, periodic audits, and cleanup campaigns.
- Budget constraints and cost overruns.
  - Solution: prioritize by risk, defer low-criticality work, use TCO evaluations, strengthen cost forecasting and variance review.
- Tool and equipment conflicts (e.g., crane availability).
  - Solution: centralized tool reservation system, preventive maintenance on tools, alternate tool sourcing plans.
- Permit and HSE delays.
  - Solution: pre-application, permit bundling where permissible, clear lead-time SLAs, digital permit-to-work.

## Performance Metrics
- Schedule adherence due to resources: percentage of schedule kept without resource-caused breaks.
- Resource plan accuracy: forecasted vs. actual labor hours by craft; MAPE for materials demand.
- Labor utilization and wrench time: percent of paid hours spent on tools; target by craft/crew.
- Overtime rate and variance: overtime hours as a percent of total, vs. plan.
- Contractor dependency: contractor hours/cost as a percent of total; variance to plan.
- Materials readiness: percent of jobs fully kitted before scheduling; material-related delay rate.
- Stockout rate for maintenance demand; expediting frequency and cost.
- PM/PdM completion on time: percent completed within window due to resource availability.
- Backlog health: weeks of backlog by craft; aging distribution of priority work.
- Permit readiness: percent of jobs with permits pre-approved before schedule freeze.
- Cost performance: planned vs. actual maintenance cost by category (labor/materials/contractors/tools).
- Lead time adherence: procurement lead time vs. promised; internal cycle time to kit and stage.
- Safety and compliance: incidents related to resource issues; audit findings due to staffing/competency gaps.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: IBM Maximo, SAP PM, Infor EAM, Oracle eAM for work orders, job plans, skills, BOMs, kitting, reservations.
- ERP procurement and inventory: SAP MM, Oracle SCM to manage POs, supplier lead times, contracts, and inventory.
- Capacity planning and scheduling: built-in CMMS modules, Primavera P6/MS Project for outages, or APS tools.
- Predictive maintenance and condition monitoring: IIoT sensors, vibration analysis, oil analysis; integrates to generate PdM work.
- Inventory optimization: MRO parts optimization tools for safety stock and reorder point setting.
- Mobile workforce management: mobile CMMS apps for time capture, materials issuance, and work completion feedback.
- Digital permit-to-work and LOTO systems; HSE compliance platforms.
- BI/analytics dashboards: Power BI/Tableau for KPIs, resource plan accuracy, and variance analysis.
- Collaboration tools: shared calendars, Teams/Slack for cross-functional planning and change-control communication.
- GIS/route optimization (for field assets): Esri, route planning to optimize crew travel and tooling.
