Process Details:
## Overview
Create work plans is the process of defining how maintenance work will be performed safely, efficiently, and to the desired quality. It converts maintenance needs and strategies into actionable, repeatable job plans that specify scope, steps, resources, safety controls, and acceptance criteria. Work plans are the foundation for scheduling, materials kitting, cost estimation, and execution control, ensuring consistency and reliability across preventative, corrective, and emergent maintenance.

Purpose:
- Standardize maintenance execution to reduce variation, risk, and rework.
- Ensure right parts, tools, skills, and permits are available before work starts.
- Shorten downtime and improve wrench time by removing barriers in advance.
- Capture institutional knowledge as reusable job plans for future work.

Role in the organization:
- Bridges strategy and execution within asset management, supporting reliability, safety, and cost objectives.
- Enables cross-functional coordination (Operations, Maintenance, HSE, Stores, Engineering).
- Provides the primary input to scheduling and to materials/stores kitting.
- Supports compliance with regulatory, OEM, and internal standards.

## Key Activities
- Scope and classify work: preventive, corrective, predictive, shutdown/turnaround, regulatory.
- Conduct field verification (job walk-down) to validate scope and site conditions.
- Decompose work into tasks and sequence (method of statement/standard maintenance procedure).
- Estimate labor by craft, skill, headcount, and duration; identify crew constraints.
- Identify and reserve materials, spares, and consumables; define kitting needs.
- Identify tools, test equipment, lifting/rigging, and rentals; verify calibration needs.
- Plan safety controls and permits (JHA, LOTO, confined space, hot work).
- Define quality checks, inspection/hold points, and acceptance criteria.
- Compile documentation: drawings, P&IDs, OEM manuals, photos, isolation diagrams.
- Develop contingency plans for common risks; define stop-work and escalation criteria.
- Cost and risk assessment; identify shutdown/production impacts and prerequisites.
- Package the plan in the CMMS/EAM; create/update standard job plans for repeat work.
- Review and approve with stakeholders; hand off to scheduling and materials for kitting.
- Capture feedback post-execution to improve the job plan library.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved work request/work order and priority/criticality ranking.
- Asset master data: hierarchy, location, specifications, warranties, criticality.
- Maintenance strategies and triggers (PM routines, condition-based alerts, OEM requirements).
- Historical work order data and failure modes (FMEA/RCM outputs).
- OEM manuals, SOPs/SMPs, drawings, P&IDs, photos, digital twins.
- Bill of materials (BOM), parts catalogs, inventory availability, lead times.
- Site conditions: access constraints, isolation points, utilities, environmental conditions.
- Regulatory and safety requirements relevant to the job (e.g., OSHA, NFPA, API, GMP).

Prerequisites:
- Configured CMMS/EAM with asset registry, work types, and job plan templates.
- Permit-to-work and LOTO programs in place.
- Defined maintenance planning standards (task breakdown, estimating, coding).
- Trained planners and designated SMEs for technical review.
- Stores/inventory processes for kitting and reservations.
- Vendor and contractor frameworks (MSAs, HSE requirements) if external resources are needed.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 10.3.1 Plan asset maintenance (inputs from maintenance requirements, strategies, and prioritization).
- 10.3.2 Schedule maintenance work (downstream consumer of work plans).
- 10.3.3 Execute maintenance work (uses the plan; provides feedback).
- 10.3.1.x Manage asset master data and BOM (data quality dependency).
- 10.x Change management/MOC (if work changes design or operating conditions).

## Process Steps
1. Intake and validation
   - Receive approved work request or PM trigger in CMMS.
   - Validate asset, location, priority, and scope completeness.
   - Classify work type (PM/CM/EM, regulatory, shutdown) and assign planner.

2. Preliminary risk and impact assessment
   - Review asset criticality, production impact, and safety/environmental risk.
   - Determine need for special controls (e.g., hot work, confined space) and potential shutdown windows.

3. Field verification (job walk-down)
   - Visit the job site with operations and a craft SME.
   - Confirm failure symptoms, access constraints, isolation points, and lifting paths.
   - Take photos/measurements; verify part numbers; note special conditions (e.g., corrosion, insulation, scaffolding needs).

4. Define scope and method
   - Draft clear scope statement with in/out-of-scope elements.
   - Select or create a method of statement/standard maintenance procedure (SMP).
   - Break work into discrete tasks and logical sequence; identify dependencies and wait times.

5. Estimate resources
   - Labor: estimate hours by craft/skill level, headcount, and shifts; identify specialized certifications required.
   - Tools/equipment: list hand tools, calibrated instruments, rigging, lifts; plan rentals and delivery.
   - Materials/spares: generate pick list with part numbers, quantities, substitutes; include consumables and gaskets/seals.
   - Services: specify contractor support (e.g., scaffolding, NDT, machining).

6. Safety planning
   - Conduct a Job Hazard Analysis (JHA) and define controls (PPE, barriers, LOTO steps, purging/venting, gas tests).
   - List required permits (hot work, confined space, energized work, line break) and responsible approvers.
   - Define stop-work criteria and emergency procedures.

7. Quality and compliance planning
   - Define inspection/hold points, torque values, calibration checks, tolerances, and test methods.
   - Reference applicable standards (OEM specs, regulatory codes).
   - Determine documentation needed for compliance (as-found/as-left data, photos, sign-offs).

8. Logistics and constraints
   - Identify site access, isolation timing, production coordination, and windows of opportunity.
   - Plan scaffolding, cranes, or temporary facilities.
   - Confirm waste handling and environmental compliance (spill plans, waste manifests).

9. Materials and kitting coordination
   - Check inventory availability; create reservations; initiate procurement for shortages.
   - Define kitting list; coordinate pick/pack and staging location; set needed-by date aligned with schedule lead time.
   - Verify critical spares and long-lead items; set go/no-go criteria based on material readiness.

10. Costing and approvals
    - Compile planned labor, materials, rentals, and services for cost estimate.
    - Assign cost centers/WBS elements; capture budget impact.
    - Route for review and approval per governance (Maintenance, Operations, HSE, Engineering as required).

11. Package the work plan
    - Assemble a complete job plan in CMMS, including:
      - Scope and task list with step-by-step instructions.
      - Safety controls and permit requirements.
      - Materials/tools lists, drawings, and photos.
      - Resource estimates, skill requirements, and duration.
      - Quality checks and acceptance criteria.
      - Constraints, prerequisites, and contingency plans.
    - Attach documents and link to asset, BOM, and related master data.

12. Handover to scheduling and stores
    - Mark plan “Ready for Scheduling” when materials/permits preconditions are met or clearly flagged.
    - Share plan with scheduler for slotting; confirm kitting schedule with stores.
    - Communicate special requirements to supervisors/contractors.

13. Standardization and library management
    - For repeatable jobs, create or update a standard job plan template with version control.
    - Tag with metadata (asset class, failure mode, interval) to enable reuse.

14. Post-execution feedback loop
    - After job completion, review variance (planned vs. actual).
    - Update estimates, steps, materials, and controls based on learnings.
    - Capture photos and as-left measurements; close the loop in the job plan library.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Approved work plan/job package for each work order.
- Standard job plan templates for recurring tasks.
- Complete materials list and kitting request with reservations.
- Safety JHA, permit list, and isolation plan.
- Quality/inspection checklist and acceptance criteria.
- Cost estimate and resource plan by craft.
- Supporting documents: drawings, OEM manuals excerpts, photos.
- Updated asset/BOM/master data where gaps were discovered.

Success criteria:
- Plan meets the organization’s planning quality standard (e.g., complete, accurate, safe).
- Materials and tools are available at job start; permits ready or clearly scheduled.
- Minimal scope change during execution; low rework rate.
- Planned vs. actual labor/cost/duration variance within tolerances.
- No recordable safety or environmental incidents attributable to planning gaps.
- Reusability: plan added to library and used in future similar jobs.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Maintenance Planner: Owns end-to-end plan development, estimates, documentation, and CMMS data entry; coordinates kitting and approvals.
- Reliability Engineer: Provides failure mode insights, criticality input, standards; reviews and improves standard job plans.
- Maintenance Supervisor/Lead: Provides craft input, validates feasibility, and ensures plan is practical for crews.
- Operations/Asset Owner: Confirms scope, access windows, isolation/production constraints; approves operational risks.
- HSE/Permit Authority: Reviews JHA, defines permits and safety controls; approves high-risk activities.
- Stores/Materials Management: Validates part numbers, availability; executes reservations and kitting; flags lead-time risks.
- Engineering (if applicable): Reviews technical content, drawings, and changes; supports MOC where design is affected.
- Scheduler: Consumes the plan to build schedules; confirms resource and material readiness gates.
- Procurement/Vendor Management: Sources long-lead items and external services; ensures vendor qualifications and HSE compliance.

## Best Practices
- Standardize: Build and maintain a library of standard job plans for common PMs and repetitive corrective work; version-controlled and searchable.
- Plan quality checklist: Use a formal checklist (scope clarity, steps, materials, safety, QA, docs, costs) before marking “Ready.”
- Job walk-downs: Require site verification for non-trivial jobs to reduce surprises and improve estimates.
- Kitting: Pre-kit all materials for planned work; store kits in a dedicated area with job/order ID.
- Estimating discipline: Use historical data and estimating norms; calibrate estimates regularly based on variance analysis.
- Visual instructions: Include annotated photos, diagrams, and torque charts; use QR codes to access digital docs.
- Safety integration: Embed JHA and LOTO steps directly in the task list; pre-identify permits and responsible approvers.
- Parts data quality: Maintain accurate BOMs; correct part numbers during planning; feed gaps back to master data governance.
- Skill-based planning: Specify skills/certifications; avoid generic “mechanic” where specialist skills are needed.
- Gatekeeping: Define readiness gates (scope freeze, materials ≥95% available, permits planned) before scheduling.
- Feedback loop: Conduct brief post-job reviews; update the plan; track plan reuse and improvement over time.
- Risk-based prioritization: Align planning depth to job criticality and complexity; don’t over-plan low-risk tasks.
- Digital enablement: Use CMMS/EAM, mobile devices, and digital signatures to streamline and track plan completeness.

## Common Challenges
- Poor asset/BOM data leading to wrong parts or missing materials.
  - Solution: Continuous BOM cleansing; enforce part verification during walk-downs; master data governance.
- Inaccurate estimates causing schedule slips and overtime.
  - Solution: Use historicals and norms; review variance monthly; train planners in estimating.
- Scope creep during execution.
  - Solution: Scope freeze policy; change control with impact assessment; separate follow-up work orders.
- Material stockouts or long lead times discovered late.
  - Solution: Early availability checks; critical spares strategy; lead-time flags; alternate/substitute parts approval workflow.
- Insufficient safety planning and late permits.
  - Solution: Embed permits in planning; pre-approval where possible; permit readiness gates.
- Coordination gaps with operations (isolation, access).
  - Solution: Joint walk-downs; weekly production-maintenance alignment; lock isolation plans early.
- Over-reliance on tribal knowledge not captured in plans.
  - Solution: Document SMEs’ steps; include photos/video; make updates mandatory post-execution.
- Planner role drift into expediting.
  - Solution: Protect planner time; clear RACI; measure planning throughput and quality, not firefighting.

## Performance Metrics
- Planning accuracy: Planned vs. actual labor hours (target ±10–20%) and costs.
- Plan completeness score: Percentage of plans meeting checklist criteria before scheduling.
- Material readiness: Percentage of jobs fully kitted before start; stockout rate for planned jobs.
- Schedule adherence enablement: Percentage of scheduled work started on time due to plan readiness.
- Wrench time improvement: Uplift in productive time attributed to planning quality.
- Rework rate: Percentage of jobs requiring rework due to planning deficiencies.
- Cycle time: Average days from work request approval to plan “Ready for Scheduling.”
- Library reuse: Percentage of jobs using standard job plans; time saved via reuse.
- Safety performance: Number of permit delays or incidents linked to planning gaps.
- Data quality improvements: Number of BOM updates and master data corrections originating from planning.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Infor EAM, Oracle eAM, IFS – for work orders, job plans, materials, and approvals.
- Scheduling tools: Primavera P6, Microsoft Project – downstream consumers for sequencing and resource leveling.
- Reliability/APM: Asset Performance Management, FMEA/RCM tools for failure modes and strategies.
- Document management: SharePoint, OpenText – controlled storage of SOPs, drawings, photos, and revisions.
- Mobile workforce apps: For accessing job plans, capturing photos, and feedback in the field.
- EHS/Permit-to-work systems: Integrated permit workflows, LOTO management, JHA templates and e-signatures.
- Inventory and kitting: ERP/MM modules, barcode/RFID for kit tracking and reservations.
- Estimating libraries: Craft norms, OEM time standards, historical productivity databases.
- Visualization: Digital twins, 3D models, AR-enabled work instructions for complex jobs.
- Analytics/BI: Dashboards for plan quality, variance, and continuous improvement tracking.
- Collaboration: Tools for cross-functional reviews and approvals with audit trails.

- Materials: Parts list with numbers, quantities, substitutes, and consumables.

- Conduct pre-job readiness check using a standardized checklist; verify all resources on hand, permits approved or queued, and access/downtime confirmed.
- Resolve gaps or escalate risks; approve for execution.
- Communicate final job package to execution team; update status to “Ready to Execute” in CMMS.

11) Monitor and adjust
- Track any late changes in scope/schedule; re-validate resources, update allocations, and communicate impacts.
- If deferral occurs, de-stage kits appropriately and preserve materials condition.

12) Post-execution follow-up (resource closure)
- Process returns to inventory; update consumption and costs; close POs if applicable.
- Capture actuals for labor, materials, rentals; reconcile variances; update BOM and job plan learnings.
- Trigger replenishment for consumed stock; record defects/nonconformances with vendors or tools.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Resource allocation plan for labor, materials, tools, and services.
- Complete, staged kits with documentation and QA/ITP checkpoints.
- Approved POs/contracts and reservations; confirmed rental and logistics bookings.
- Verified competencies and certifications; contractor onboarding records.
- Approved or queued permits-to-work; LOTO lists; JSA/method statements.
- Pre-job readiness checklist and approval sign-off.
- CMMS/EAM updates: status set to Ready, reservations committed, costs tracked.

Success criteria:
- 100% of required resources available at job start.
- No start delays due to resource gaps.
- All assigned personnel fully compliant with training/certifications.
- Materials/tooling correct and fit-for-purpose; calibration current.
- Permits and access in place; safety prerequisites satisfied.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Maintenance Planner: Defines resource requirements, creates job packages, initiates procurement/kitting.
- Scheduler: Reserves labor and critical shared resources; aligns resource readiness with schedule windows.
- Maintenance Supervisor/Lead: Confirms crew assignment, validates competencies, approves readiness.
- Storeroom/Inventory Coordinator: Picks, kits, stages, issues/returns, manages stock levels and cycle counts.
- Procurement/Buyer: Sources materials/services, issues POs, expedites, manages supplier communications.
- Contracts Manager/Vendor Manager: Oversees service contracts, vendor compliance, and performance.
- EHS/Permit Coordinator: Manages permits, LOTO processes, safety prerequisites, contractor HSE onboarding.
- Operations Coordinator: Confirms equipment availability, isolation/downtime windows, and site access.
- Tool Crib/Calibration Technician: Ensures tool availability, inspection, and calibration compliance.
- Quality/Inspector: Defines/executes QA checkpoints, verifies critical characteristics.
- Reliability/Asset Engineer: Advises on alternates, critical spares strategy, and technical standards.

## Best Practices
- Maintain high-quality job plans with accurate BOMs, standard task lists, and estimated hours.
- Integrate CMMS with LMS/HR to automatically validate certifications before assignment.
- Use kitting and staging with barcoded labels; standardize kit checklists for repeat jobs.
- Implement critical spares strategy and min/max policies; review based on asset criticality and lead times.
- Establish framework agreements and rate cards for common services and rentals.
- Use vendor scorecards and SLAs; conduct periodic business reviews for key suppliers.
- Keep calibration schedules synchronized with tool reservations; block assignment if calibration due.
- Run weekly readiness reviews for next-week work; gate schedule commit on resource readiness.
- Apply 5S to storerooms and staging areas; perform cycle counts and root cause stockout analysis.
- Build a cross-skilling and succession plan to mitigate skill shortages; maintain a skills matrix.
- Document lessons learned; continuously update BOMs and job plans post-execution.

## Common Challenges
- Long lead times or obsolete parts: Mitigate with critical spares, alternate part qualifications, repair/refurb options, and early procurement triggers.
- Skill/certification gaps: Maintain real-time competency matrix; schedule training; use prequalified contractors.
- Inventory inaccuracies: Improve cycle counting, barcoding/RFID, and transaction discipline.
- Last-minute scope changes: Use change control; re-run readiness checks; maintain contingency stock and flexible contractor capacity.
- Tool/calibration unavailability: Link tool crib to CMMS reservations; forecast demand; maintain spares or rental agreements.
- Permit and access delays: Pre-plan permit submissions; standardize isolation lists; align with operations outage calendars.
- Vendor performance issues: Apply SLAs, penalties/earn-backs; diversify suppliers; track on-time delivery and quality.
- Budget constraints: Prioritize by criticality and risk; bundle buys; leverage contracts and negotiated terms.

## Performance Metrics
- Work start on-time rate due to resource readiness (%).
- Kit completeness rate (%) and rework due to missing/incorrect items.
- Schedule compliance (%), specifically resource-caused delays.
- Stockout rate (%) for maintenance-critical items; inventory accuracy (%).
- Procurement cycle time (PR to PO) and supplier on-time delivery (%).
- Contractor onboarding lead time and certification compliance rate (%).
- Tool availability (%) and calibration compliance (%).
- Wrench time (%) and labor utilization (%), correlated to resource readiness.
- Emergency purchase rate (%) and premium freight incidents.
- Cost variance per work order (planned vs actual) attributable to resource issues.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: IBM Maximo, SAP PM, Oracle eAM, Infor EAM for work orders, reservations, kitting, and status.
- ERP/Procurement: SAP MM/Ariba, Oracle Procurement Cloud, Coupa for POs, contracts, and supplier management.
- WMS/Inventory: RF/barcode or RFID-enabled systems; vending machines for consumables.
- LMS/HRIS: SuccessFactors, Workday, Cornerstone to manage competencies and certifications; integrate with CMMS.
- EHS/Permit-to-Work: ePTW systems for permits, LOTO, and risk assessments.
- Scheduling: Primavera P6, MS Project, or CMMS-native schedulers.
- Calibration/Tooling: Calibration management software; tool crib systems.
- Contractor Management: Avetta, ISNetworld for prequalification and compliance.
- Document Management: SharePoint, Aconex, or CMMS DMS modules for drawings, manuals, and method statements.
- Analytics/Dashboards: BI tools (Power BI, Tableau) for KPIs and exception alerts.

Process Details:
## Overview
Manage maintenance work safety is the structured process of preventing harm to people, assets, and the environment during maintenance activities. It ensures compliance with applicable laws and standards (e.g., OSHA, NFPA, ISO 45001, local regulations) and embeds safety controls into the planning, scheduling, execution, and close-out of maintenance work. This process is integral to asset reliability and uptime: safe work is a prerequisite for effective maintenance, regulatory compliance, and organizational reputation.

Objectives:
- Eliminate or reduce risks associated with maintenance tasks, including non-routine and high-hazard work.
- Ensure regulatory compliance and readiness for inspections/audits.
- Standardize safety practices across in-house teams and contractors.
- Enable safe, efficient scheduling by integrating safety planning with work management and asset operations.

Scope:
- Applies to all maintenance activities (preventive, predictive, corrective, breakdown, shutdown/turnaround).
- Covers routine and non-routine/hazardous tasks, including confined space, hot work, electrical, elevated work, line breaking, heavy lifts, and SIMOPS (simultaneous operations).
- Encompasses employees, contractors, and visitors at maintenance sites.

## Key Activities
- Risk assessment and job safety analysis (JSA/JHA) for maintenance tasks.
- Permit-to-Work (PTW) administration and control for hazardous/non-routine work.
- Energy isolation and Lockout/Tagout (LOTO), including zero-energy verification.
- Contractor safety management: qualification, onboarding, supervision, and performance monitoring.
- Safety training, competency verification, and toolbox talks/pre-job briefs.
- Site controls: barricading, signage, access control, fire watch, attendants.
- Gas testing, atmospheric monitoring, and environmental controls (e.g., spill prevention).
- Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) specification, issuance, and compliance checks.
- Management of Change (MoC) for scope, conditions, or method changes.
- Incident/near-miss reporting and investigation; corrective and preventive actions (CAPA).
- Safety audits, inspections, and behavioral safety observations.
- Emergency preparedness and drills specific to maintenance tasks.
- Documentation and recordkeeping for compliance and continuous improvement.
- Re-energization, restoration, and pre-startup safety review (PSSR) for critical assets.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved maintenance work order with scope, asset details, and schedule.
- Asset information: P&IDs, single-line diagrams, isolation points, arc-flash labels, OEM manuals.
- Hazardous materials information: Safety Data Sheets (SDS), inventories, waste handling protocols.
- Regulatory and company safety standards and procedures.
- Contractor qualifications, insurance, and safety performance metrics (where applicable).
- Risk register and historical incident/near-miss data for similar tasks.
- Environmental constraints (permits, emissions limits, noise/time restrictions).

Prerequisites:
- Defined safety management system aligned with ISO 45001 (policies, roles, procedures).
- Trained and competent workforce; current certifications for specific tasks (e.g., electrical qualified person, confined space attendant, forklift).
- Calibrated safety equipment available (gas detectors, LOTO devices, fall protection).
- Operational readiness: emergency response plan, first-aid, eyewash/showers, spill kits.
- Active PTW and LOTO programs with designated Authorizers/Issuing Authorities.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Maintenance planning and scheduling [10.3.2]: scoping, resource planning, coordination of SIMOPS.
- Contractor management and procurement: prequalification, onboarding, contracts with safety clauses.
- Asset operations: isolation support, system depressurization, and restoration coordination.
- Compliance and audit management: regulatory inspections, internal audits.
- Incident management and CAPA: investigations, lessons learned.
- Change management: MoC for deviations during execution.

## Process Steps
1. Trigger and Screening
   - Receive an approved work order.
   - Screen task for risk category (routine vs. non-routine; PTW requirement; high-risk flags such as confined space, hot work, energized work, working at heights, line breaking, heavy lift).
   - Identify SIMOPS and potential conflicts in the schedule or area.

2. Pre-Job Risk Assessment
   - Conduct a Job Hazard Analysis (JHA/JSA) with the executing crew and contractor (if applicable).
   - Identify hazards (mechanical, electrical, chemical, thermal, radiation, ergonomic) and environmental impacts.
   - Apply the hierarchy of controls (eliminate, substitute, engineer, admin, PPE) to define controls.
   - Determine monitoring needs (gas testing, noise, heat stress).

3. Permit-to-Work Planning
   - Select required permits: General Work, Hot Work, Confined Space Entry, Electrical/Energized Work, Working at Heights, Excavation, Line Breaking, Lifting Operations, Radiation, etc.
   - Prepare permit pack including JHA, drawings, isolation lists, rescue plans, and emergency contacts.
   - Assign roles: Permit Requester, Issuer/Authorizer, Area Owner, Fire Watch, Attendant, Spotter, Lift Director.

4. Isolation and LOTO Planning
   - Develop a written isolation plan referencing P&IDs/schematics and energy sources (electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical, thermal, gravitational).
   - Identify lock points and required devices; prepare group lockout with lockbox if multiple teams.
   - Plan verification steps (test-try) and zero-energy confirmation.
   - Schedule with Operations for system depressurization, purging/inerting, and drains/blinds as needed.

5. Competency and Readiness Checks
   - Verify training and certifications of all personnel (including contractors).
   - Inspect PPE and safety equipment readiness (calibration dates, inspection tags).
   - Confirm availability of rescue equipment and responders for high-risk work (e.g., confined space retrieval).

6. Permit Issuance and Pre-Job Brief
   - Conduct a toolbox talk: scope, hazards, controls, roles, communication, stop-work authority, emergency procedures.
   - Issue permits with time-bound validity; ensure signatures by all required parties.
   - Establish site controls: barricades, signage, exclusion zones, fire-resistant blankets, ventilation, lighting.

7. Execution with Ongoing Controls
   - Implement LOTO; perform zero-energy verification and document it.
   - Conduct initial gas testing; record results; set frequency for re-testing; maintain continuous atmospheric monitoring if required.
   - Monitor compliance: PPE usage, safe behaviors, adherence to JHA and permits.
   - Manage SIMOPS through regular coordination with nearby activities.
   - Document changes; if conditions change, pause work and initiate MoC or re-permitting.

8. Inspections, Audits, and Observations
   - Perform spot checks and formal permit audits.
   - Record safety observations (positive and at-risk) and correct unsafe conditions immediately.
   - Capture near-misses; encourage reporting and stop-work where needed.

9. Incident Response (if triggered)
   - Execute emergency procedures; notify EHS and site leadership.
   - Secure the area; preserve evidence; provide medical aid.
   - Begin incident reporting and initiate root cause analysis after stabilization.

10. Work Completion and Close-Out
   - Housekeeping: remove waste, tools, temporary supports, and restore area.
   - Close permits; cancel and remove locks following group lockout protocol; verify equipment integrity.
   - Conduct post-job review: what went well, issues, near-misses, and lessons learned.
   - For critical equipment or high-risk tasks, perform Pre-Startup Safety Review (PSSR) prior to re-energization.

11. Documentation and Continuous Improvement
   - Update CMMS/EAM with permit numbers, JHAs, inspection results, incidents, and actions.
   - Track corrective actions to closure; update risk registers and procedures.
   - Analyze KPIs; communicate findings to crews and management; adjust training and standards as needed.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Approved and closed permits, JHAs/JSAs, LOTO records, gas test logs.
- Training and briefing attendance records; contractor orientation records.
- Audit and inspection checklists with findings; behavioral observation logs.
- Incident/near-miss reports with root cause and CAPA.
- PSSR reports for critical work; MoC records for scope changes.
- Updated CMMS/EAM work order history with safety artifacts.
Success criteria:
- Zero serious injuries/fatalities; regulatory compliance maintained.
- 100% of applicable high-risk jobs executed under correct permits and controls.
- All incidents and near-misses investigated with actions closed on time.
- Positive audit outcomes; continuous improvement actions implemented.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- EHS/Safety Manager
  - Owns safety standards and PTW/LOTO programs; ensures regulatory alignment.
  - Oversees audits, incident investigations, and KPI reporting.
- Maintenance Manager/Supervisor
  - Ensures safety is integrated into planning and execution; enforces stop-work authority.
  - Verifies competency, staffing, and supervision for safe execution.
- Maintenance Planner/Scheduler
  - Flags safety requirements during planning; sequences work to avoid SIMOPS conflicts.
  - Ensures safety documentation is attached to work orders.
- Permit Issuer/Authorizer
  - Reviews JHA and controls; issues and controls permits; verifies field conditions.
- Isolation Authority/Authorized Person
  - Designs and verifies LOTO plans; confirms zero-energy state; controls lockbox.
- Operations/Area Owner
  - Approves work in area; coordinates depressurization/venting; manages SIMOPS.
- Skilled Trades/Craft Workers
  - Execute work per JHA and permits; attend toolbox talks; report hazards; exercise stop-work.
- Contractor Supervisor
  - Ensures contractor team compliance; conducts briefings; interfaces with Permit Issuer and Site Supervisor.
- Confined Space Attendant/Fire Watch/Spotter
  - Performs continuous monitoring duties per permit requirements.
- Emergency Response Team/First Aiders
  - Respond to incidents; support drills and preparedness.
- Environmental Coordinator
  - Ensures environmental controls, waste management, and reporting.

## Best Practices
- Use a risk-based PTW system with digital workflows, mandatory attachments, and geofenced/area-based controls.
- Apply the hierarchy of controls; avoid defaulting to PPE as the primary control.
- Standardize JHA templates and require team-based development at the job site.
- Implement robust LOTO with group lock boxes, device standardization, and two-person verification.
- Integrate SIMOPS reviews into daily/shift planning; hold permit coordination meetings.
- Require pre-task toolbox talks and post-task reviews for learning capture.
- Conduct frequent field leadership safety engagements and behavioral observations.
- Enforce contractor safety prequalification and performance monitoring (TRIR, citations, audit scores).
- Maintain calibrated, intrinsically safe gas detectors and defined re-test frequencies.
- Use MoC for any deviations in method, equipment, or conditions; suspend and reauthorize permits as needed.
- Perform PSSR for critical assets after invasive maintenance or safety system impairment.
- Leverage visual management: barricade standards, color-coded permits, arc-flash labels, isolation tags.
- Run periodic emergency drills tailored to maintenance scenarios (confined space rescue, arc flash, spill).

## Common Challenges
- Schedule pressure leading to shortcuts
  - Mitigation: embed safety gates in schedules; empower stop-work; management reinforces safety over speed.
- Incomplete hazard identification
  - Mitigation: require field verification, peer review of JHAs, and use of checklists for high-risk tasks.
- Contractor non-compliance or cultural mismatch
  - Mitigation: rigorous prequalification, onboarding, supervision, and performance clauses with incentives/penalties.
- Documentation gaps and permit errors
  - Mitigation: digital PTW with validation rules; permit audits; training for Issuers and Requesters.
- SIMOPS conflicts
  - Mitigation: daily coordination meetings, area maps, and visual controls; SIMOPS risk assessments.
- LOTO failures or bypasses
  - Mitigation: standardized devices, lockbox use, verification tests, periodic LOTO audits, disciplinary policy for violations.
- Changing conditions mid-job
  - Mitigation: enforce MoC; require re-briefs when conditions change; time-bound permits.
- Fatigue and shift handover issues
  - Mitigation: fatigue management policy; structured handover checklists; limit overtime on high-risk tasks.

## Performance Metrics
- Total Recordable Incident Rate (TRIR) and Lost Time Incident Rate (LTIR) for maintenance activities.
- High-risk job coverage: percent of high-risk tasks completed with correct permits and JHAs (target 100%).
- LOTO compliance rate and number of LOTO audit nonconformances.
- Permit quality score (audit-based) and permit rejection/rework rate.
- Near-miss reporting rate per 10,000 work hours; ratio of leading to lagging indicators.
- Time to close CAPA from audits/incidents; percentage closed by due date.
- Training and certification compliance rate for assigned roles.
- PTW cycle time (request to issuance) for planning effectiveness.
- SIMOPS conflicts identified vs. unresolved; number of stop-work interventions initiated.
- PSSR compliance for critical work; deviations found at PSSR.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Infor EAM, Oracle eAM for integrating safety artifacts with work orders.
- EHS platforms: Sphera, Enablon, Intelex, VelocityEHS for audits, incidents, actions, and compliance management.
- Electronic Permit-to-Work (ePTW) and Isolation Management: ISSoW, Yokogawa RAP, eVision, EcoOnline; digital lockbox tracking.
- LOTO hardware: standardized locks, hasps, devices, tags; group lock boxes and shadow boards.
- Gas detection: multi-gas personal monitors, fixed detectors, bump/calibration stations; remote sensing for confined spaces.
- Confined space and work-at-height gear: retrieval systems, tripods, SRLs, harnesses, anchor points.
- Electrical safety: insulated tools, voltage testers for test-try, arc-rated PPE; NFPA 70E-compliant labeling software.
- Lifting and rigging: load monitoring, lift planning software, certified slings/shackles with inspection tracking.
- Mobile apps: JHA creation, inspections, observations, and training verification with QR/NFC badge scanning.
- Contractor management systems: ISNetworld, Avetta, Veriforce for prequalification and document control.
- Training/LMS: Skillsoft, SAP SuccessFactors, Cornerstone for role-based safety training assignments.
- Visualization and analytics: BI dashboards (Power BI/Tableau) with real-time KPIs; digital twins/P&IDs for isolation planning.
- Communications: radios with intrinsically safe certification, digital signage, and andon/permit boards.

Process Details:
## Overview
Perform preventative asset maintenance encompasses all planned, proactive tasks designed to keep assets in reliable working condition and prevent unplanned failures. It spans time-based, usage-based, and condition-based activities such as inspections, lubrication, adjustments, cleaning, calibration, and parts replacement per manufacturer recommendations, engineering standards, and regulatory codes.

Purpose:
- Reduce unplanned downtime, safety incidents, and lifecycle cost by addressing wear and degradation before failure.
- Comply with regulatory, warranty, and contractual obligations.
- Maintain asset performance within specified tolerances and extend useful life.

Role in the organization:
- Supports operational continuity and product/service quality by ensuring asset availability and capability.
- Provides a feedback loop to asset strategy and risk management (e.g., optimizing maintenance intervals and tasks).
- Feeds data to reliability engineering and capital planning through accurate work history and condition trends.

## Key Activities
- Maintenance strategy execution: Carrying out time/usage/condition-based PM tasks aligned with asset criticality and OEM guidance.
- Work identification and triggering: Generating PM work orders from schedules, meters, or condition thresholds.
- Job planning and preparation: Defining scope, steps, tools, permits, parts, quality checks, and acceptance criteria.
- Scheduling and coordination: Aligning PM windows with operations, safety, and resource availability; bundling tasks to minimize downtime.
- Parts staging (kitting) and tool readiness: Ensuring required materials and calibrated instruments are available at point of use.
- Safety and permit-to-work: Performing pre-job risk assessment, lockout/tagout (LOTO), and obtaining required permits.
- Execution: Performing inspections, lubrication, cleaning, adjustments, replacements, calibrations, and functional tests.
- Quality assurance and verification: Post-maintenance testing, performance verification, and documentation of results.
- Work order closeout: Recording labor, parts, measurements, failure/condition codes, photos, and recommendations.
- Follow-up and escalation: Creating corrective work requests for defects found; deferring or rescheduling PMs with documented risk.
- Continuous improvement: Reviewing PM effectiveness and updating intervals, job plans, and BOMs based on data.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Asset master data: Asset register, hierarchy, criticality, location, technical data, warranties.
- PM program: Task lists, frequencies, triggers (time/meter/condition), job plans, acceptance criteria.
- OEM manuals, engineering standards, regulatory requirements.
- Work history, failure modes, and reliability data to inform intervals and tasks.
- Meter readings and condition monitoring data (vibration, thermography, oil analysis, etc.).
- Spare parts lists/BOMs, inventory levels, approved vendors.
- Resource availability: Qualified technicians, certifications, tools, calibrated instruments.
- Safety documentation: JSA/TRA templates, LOTO procedures, MSDS, permits.

Prerequisites:
- CMMS/EAM configured with PM library, asset master, and scheduling rules.
- Governance for risk-based maintenance and deferral approvals.
- Established permit-to-work and LOTO programs.
- Calibrated tools and test equipment within due dates.
- Access arrangements: site access, scaffolding, cranes, confined space prep if needed.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Maintenance planning and scheduling (to define scope, plan materials, and schedule windows).
- MRO inventory and procurement (to source and stage parts).
- Asset strategy and reliability (to define PM content and optimization).
- Operations coordination/production planning (to release assets and provide process isolation).
- HSE management (permits, hazard controls).
- Vendor management (OEM service support and warranties).

## Process Steps
1) Initiate PM trigger
- CMMS automatically generates PM work order based on calendar, meter, or condition threshold.
- Validate trigger against asset status (e.g., in-service, seasonal operation) and production calendar.

2) Review and plan work order
- Planner verifies scope against job plan; adjusts tasks for asset configuration and recent history.
- Confirm required permits, tools, test equipment, and parts; create pick list and kitting request.
- Estimate labor hours and required skill sets; add QA checks and acceptance criteria.
- If task requires shutdown or special access, coordinate with operations to identify a window.

3) Schedule and coordinate
- Scheduler places WO in the weekly schedule, grouping with related PMs on the same asset/area.
- Operations issues isolation plans and approves downtime; HSE confirms permit requirements.
- Notify stakeholders and affected areas; communicate expected duration and impacts.

4) Stage materials and tools
- Storeroom kits parts and consumables; reserve and calibrate test instruments.
- Arrange specialty tools, access equipment, scaffolding, and lifting resources as needed.
- Verify spares availability; if stockout risk, escalate to procurement for expedite or substitution.

5) Pre-job safety and permit-to-work
- Conduct pre-job briefing and Job Safety Analysis (JSA); review MSDS, energy sources, and hazards.
- Obtain and display permits (LOTO, hot work, confined space, electrical, excavation).
- Implement LOTO per procedure; verify zero energy state and test for hazards.

6) Execute preventative maintenance tasks
- Perform tasks per standardized job plan and OEM specs (e.g., inspect, lubricate, tighten, clean, replace wear parts, calibrate).
- Record as-found conditions, measurements, and anomalies; capture photos/videos where useful.
- Use specified torque values, tolerances, and calibration procedures; replace consumables with correct/spec’ed items.
- Maintain housekeeping and contamination control; segregate waste and returned parts.

7) Inspect, test, and verify
- Conduct functional checks, calibration verification, and performance tests against acceptance criteria.
- If defects are found that cannot be corrected within scope, create follow-up corrective work with priority and risk noted.
- For safety or compliance-critical equipment, obtain QA/QC or third-party signoff as required.

8) Restore and handover
- Remove LOTO per procedure, restore utilities/process, and perform operational checks with Operations.
- Update machine settings and control parameters as needed; verify alarms and interlocks.

9) Documentation and closeout
- Enter detailed work order closeout in CMMS: tasks completed, labor hours, parts used, condition readings, failure codes, and pass/fail results.
- Attach certificates (calibration), test results, and photos; note improvement opportunities.
- Complete permit closures and file regulatory records.
- Return unused parts to stock; update BOM accuracy if discrepancies found.

10) Review and continuous improvement
- Supervisor reviews data quality and compliance; Reliability Engineer analyzes trends and PM effectiveness.
- Adjust PM frequency or content based on findings; initiate RCM review or FMEA updates if warranted.
- Track deferrals and their risk; ensure follow-ups are prioritized.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Completed PM work orders with full documentation.
- Inspection and test records; calibration certificates; permit records.
- Updated asset history, condition data, and meter readings in CMMS.
- Parts consumption transactions; updated BOM and inventory records.
- Follow-up corrective work requests for identified defects.
- Compliance evidence for audits and regulatory bodies.

Success criteria:
- PM tasks completed within scheduled window and to technical standards.
- No safety or environmental incidents; permits executed correctly.
- Asset performance verified within specified tolerances after PM.
- Documentation complete and accurate; no overdue compliance-related PMs.
- Reduction in unplanned failures and stable/improving reliability metrics.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Maintenance Planner: Validates scope, prepares job plans, identifies parts/tools, and estimates labor.
- Scheduler: Sequences and assigns work, coordinates with operations, manages weekly schedule adherence.
- Maintenance Technicians: Execute PM tasks safely and to spec; capture data and close out WOs.
- Maintenance Supervisor/Lead: Oversees execution, ensures quality and safety, approves closeouts.
- Operations Coordinator/Area Owner: Approves downtime, isolates/restores equipment, participates in functional tests.
- Reliability Engineer: Analyzes data, optimizes PM content/frequency, leads RCM/FMEA, sets condition thresholds.
- Storeroom/MRO Specialist: Kits and issues parts, manages inventory accuracy, handles returns and repairs.
- HSE Specialist: Oversees permits, JSAs, compliance, and incident prevention.
- QA/Calibration Technician: Performs/verifies calibrations and quality checks on critical instruments.
- CMMS/EAM Administrator: Maintains master data, PM library, and reporting dashboards.
- Vendors/OEMs: Provide specialized services, updates, and technical support; honor warranties.

## Best Practices
- Risk-based maintenance: Tailor PM intervals and scope using asset criticality, FMEA, and reliability data.
- Standardized job plans: Use detailed steps, torque values, photos, and checklists to ensure consistency and quality.
- Kitting and staging: Pre-stage all materials and tools to reduce delays and increase wrench time.
- Route-based inspections: Group similar inspection tasks to reduce travel and improve data consistency.
- Condition-based and predictive techniques: Integrate vibration, ultrasound, thermography, oil analysis to fine-tune PMs and detect early faults.
- Data discipline: Enforce complete, structured WO closeout including failure and condition codes.
- Mobile execution: Use mobile CMMS for real-time data capture, photos, barcodes/RFID scans.
- Permit and safety rigor: Use digital permit-to-work, LOTO checklists, and pre-job JSAs.
- Continuous optimization: Periodically review PM effectiveness; eliminate non-value tasks and adjust intervals (PMO/RCM).
- Spares strategy: Maintain critical spares with min/max levels and obsolescence management; align with PM demand.
- Bundling and window planning: Align PMs across systems during planned outages to minimize disruptions.
- Calibration program: Maintain a calibration schedule for tools and instruments, traceable to standards.
- Cleanliness and lubrication excellence: Apply “clean-to-inspect” and precision lubrication practices.
- Knowledge capture: Embed lessons learned into job plans and asset records.

## Common Challenges
- Over-maintenance or under-maintenance
  - Solution: Apply RCM and reliability data to right-size PM scope and frequency; pilot changes and monitor outcomes.
- Schedule conflicts with production
  - Solution: Long-horizon coordination, blackout calendars, and bundling; use opportunity windows.
- Parts stockouts and wrong parts
  - Solution: Critical spares analysis, vendor-managed inventory, BOM accuracy audits, and kitting verification.
- Poor data quality in WO closeouts
  - Solution: Mandatory fields, mobile forms with guided inputs, technician training, supervisor data reviews.
- Access and safety constraints (confined spaces, energized systems)
  - Solution: Early permit planning, specialized training, engineered access solutions, lockout verification devices.
- Skill gaps for specialized PM tasks
  - Solution: Skills matrix, targeted training, certifications, and selective outsourcing with knowledge transfer.
- Tool and instrument calibration lapses
  - Solution: Tool calibration management with alerts; block issuance of out-of-calibration instruments.
- Defect discovery beyond PM scope
  - Solution: Clear process for creating and prioritizing corrective WOs; risk-based deferral governance.
- Remote or distributed assets
  - Solution: Route optimization, remote condition monitoring, mobile connectivity, and local spares caches.
- Change resistance to PM optimization
  - Solution: Stakeholder engagement, evidence-based proposals, and governance with post-implementation reviews.

## Performance Metrics
- PM compliance rate: Completed PMs on or before due date (%).
- Schedule adherence: PMs completed as scheduled vs. moved or deferred (%).
- Planned vs. unplanned maintenance ratio: Hours or cost.
- Wrench time: Percentage of technician time spent on tools vs. delays.
- Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) for PM-covered assets.
- PM effectiveness: Percentage of failures preceded by missed/ineffective PM tasks; defects found per PM.
- First-time quality/first-time fix rate: PMs requiring no rework within a defined period.
- Rework rate: PMs reopened due to issues within X days.
- Cost metrics: PM cost per asset, PM cost as % of asset replacement value, cost avoidance vs breakdowns.
- Backlog health: PM backlog size and age, number of PM deferrals and associated risk.
- Compliance metrics: Past-due safety/compliance-critical PMs (count, hours).
- Inventory support: PMs delayed due to parts stockouts (%), kit completeness rate.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM systems: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Oracle eAM, Infor EAM, AssetWorks for PM plans, scheduling, work orders, and history.
- Mobile maintenance apps: For real-time WO execution, data capture, barcoding/RFID scanning, photo documentation.
- Condition monitoring and PdM: Vibration analyzers, ultrasound detectors, IR cameras, oil analysis kits, motor circuit analyzers; IoT sensors and gateways.
- Calibration management: Software to track instrument/tool calibration schedules and certificates.
- Scheduling and optimization: Gantt-based planners, constraint-based schedulers, route optimization tools for field assets.
- MRO inventory management: Storeroom systems, barcode/RFID, vendor-managed inventory, kitting workflows.
- Safety systems: Digital permit-to-work, LOTO management, gas detection, confined space monitoring.
- Knowledge and documentation: Digital procedures, OEM manuals, drawings, 3D models/digital twins, AR remote assistance for complex tasks.
- Analytics and dashboards: BI tools and reliability analytics to monitor KPIs, trigger thresholds, and optimize PM intervals.
- Communication and collaboration: Work coordination tools integrated with CMMS for notifications and approvals.

Level: 4

Process Details:
## Overview
Perform corrective asset maintenance and repairs is the process of restoring an asset to its intended function after a failure, fault, or degradation is detected. It is reactive work triggered by incidents, alarms, inspections, or operator reports. The purpose is to minimize safety risk and downtime, meet regulatory codes, protect product quality, and preserve asset life at the lowest total cost. This process closes the loop between detection of a fault and returning the asset to safe, verified operation, while capturing data to prevent recurrence and improve reliability.

Corrective maintenance includes emergency (run-to-failure, immediate response), urgent (near-term), and deferred corrective work (planned into a future window). It complements preventive and predictive maintenance by addressing unplanned issues and feeding insights back into maintenance strategies.

## Key Activities
- Fault detection and reporting (operator, monitoring system, inspection)
- Safety risk assessment and immediate containment (make-safe, lockout-tagout)
- Work request logging and triage (priority, criticality, impact)
- Planning and assignment (scope, skills, parts, permits)
- Scheduling and coordination with operations
- Parts, tools, and access preparation (kitting, permits, isolations)
- Execution of diagnosis and repair
- Testing, verification, and regulatory compliance checks
- Return-to-service and handover
- Documentation, closeout, and cost capture
- Root cause analysis (as applicable) and follow-up actions
- Warranty and vendor management (claims, service calls)
- Lessons learned and updates to maintenance strategies

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Work request details: asset ID, location, symptoms, time observed, impact
  - Asset data: hierarchy, criticality, manuals, drawings, job plans, BOM
  - Historical data: failure history, previous repairs, open deviations
  - Operating data: alarms, trends, condition monitoring readings
  - Safety/environmental requirements: MSDS, JSA templates, permit needs
  - Warranty/contract info: coverage, SLAs, OEM contacts
  - Spare parts availability and lead times
- Prerequisites:
  - Asset master in CMMS/EAM with current hierarchy and attributes
  - Trained and authorized personnel (skills, certifications)
  - Safety programs and procedures (LOTO, hot work, confined space, electrical)
  - Access to tools, calibrated test equipment, and PPE
  - Defined prioritization matrix and escalation paths
  - Communication channels between maintenance, operations, HSE, QA
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - [10.3.1] Plan asset maintenance (planning standards, job plans)
  - [10.3.2] Schedule asset maintenance (resource leveling, windows)
  - Work order management and approvals
  - Inventory and procurement for spares and services
  - EHS permit-to-work and risk management
  - Quality/validation for regulated assets (e.g., GMP, FDA, NERC)
  - IT/OT support for diagnostics, patches, access
  - Change control/configuration management when design changes occur

## Process Steps
1. Detect and report fault
   - Sources: operator observation, alarms (SCADA/IIoT), inspection findings, product quality deviations, BMS/BAS alerts.
   - Operator applies immediate containment if safe: stop equipment, isolate leaks, initiate emergency procedures as required.
   - Create work request in CMMS/EAM with details and attachments (photos, readings, alarm IDs).

2. Triage and prioritize
   - Screen for safety, environmental, and production impact.
   - Assign priority using asset criticality and a risk matrix.
   - Categorize as emergency (immediate), urgent (24–72 hours), or deferred.
   - Check warranty/contract status; decide OEM vs internal repair.
   - Acknowledge requester and communicate expected response time.

3. Make safe and control risk
   - Perform preliminary risk assessment (JSA).
   - Apply energy isolation (LOTO), depressurize, drain, purge as required.
   - Assess permits needed (hot work, confined space, electrical, work at height).
   - Set barricades and signage; notify affected stakeholders.

4. Assign and plan
   - Supervisor assigns qualified technician(s); reliability engineer engaged for complex failures.
   - Planner scopes the job: diagnostics steps, repair method, labor hours, skills, special tools, lifting/rigging, PPE.
   - Review manuals and prior work orders; prepare digital work instructions.
   - Identify parts and consumables; check stock and kit materials. If not available, initiate procurement and decide on expedite or workaround.
   - Prepare permits and isolation plan; pre-stage access (keys, clearances).

5. Schedule and coordinate
   - Align with operations on downtime window; bundle with other tasks if beneficial.
   - Book resources (personnel, vendor, equipment).
   - Communicate schedule and change impacts; update CMMS dates.

6. Execute diagnosis and repair
   - Conduct toolbox talk; verify permits and LOTO.
   - Perform diagnostics (visual, vibration, thermal, electrical tests, loop checks).
   - Identify root cause hypotheses; validate with measurements.
   - Repair/replace components, adjust, or patch software as per procedure.
   - Observe torque, torque-angle, clearance, cleanliness, and contamination control standards.
   - If major scope change arises, pause for re-approval/change control and re-planning.

7. Test and verify
   - Perform functional tests, calibration, leak tests, pressure/hydro tests, or SAT as applicable.
   - Validate against specifications and regulatory codes; QA/QC witness if required.
   - Trial run under load where safe; monitor performance and confirm stability.

8. Return to service
   - Clear work area; remove LOTO using two-person verification as required.
   - Restore protective devices and instrumentation; update control system states.
   - Handover to operations with operational checks; obtain acceptance.

9. Document and close
   - Complete work order fields: failure code, cause code, remedy code, time stamps, labor, parts used, as-found/as-left readings, photos.
   - Update asset records: BOM, drawings, firmware versions, as-built configuration.
   - Record permits closed and calibration certificates.
   - Book costs to cost centers/WBS; capture warranty claim details if applicable.
   - Close the work order in CMMS after review by supervisor/planner.

10. Post-repair review and follow-up
    - If high impact or repetitive, initiate RCA (5-Whys, RCFA) and define corrective/preventive actions.
    - Create follow-up work orders (e.g., alignment check in 1 week, oil analysis).
    - Update PM/PdM strategy, job plans, and spares min/max as needed.
    - Share lessons learned in knowledge base; brief team and operations.

Decision notes:
- Emergency path: Steps 1–3 may be compressed; minimal planning; immediate execution by on-call crew. Post-event, conduct formal documentation and RCA.
- Deferred corrective: More detailed planning and kitting to increase first-time fix rate and reduce MTTR during the scheduled window.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Restored asset functionality meeting specified performance and regulatory standards
- Completed and closed work order with full history and cost capture
- Updated asset records (as-built, BOM, firmware/software versions)
- Test and calibration results; QA/QC sign-offs; permit records
- RCA report and corrective/preventive action items (when applicable)
- Warranty claim submissions and vendor service reports
- Communications to stakeholders (operations acceptance, downtime report)

Success criteria:
- Asset passes verification tests and meets performance specs
- Safety and environmental controls maintained; zero recordable incidents
- MTTR within target; downtime minimized within agreed SLA
- First-time fix achieved without rework within 30 days
- Complete, accurate documentation captured in CMMS/EAM
- No recurrence of the same failure mode within defined monitoring window

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Requester/Operator: Detect/report fault; initial containment; provide context and access; participate in handover.
- Maintenance Planner: Scope and plan job; prepare work instructions; kit parts; estimate labor and duration.
- Maintenance Supervisor: Triage, prioritize, approve work; assign resources; ensure safety compliance; review/close work orders.
- Technicians (Mechanical/Electrical/Instrumentation/Controls): Perform diagnostics, repairs, testing; document as-found/as-left; adhere to procedures.
- Reliability Engineer: Lead/assist RCA; analyze failure data; update strategies and standards.
- Stores/Inventory: Manage spares availability; issue and receive parts; update stock; support warranty returns.
- Procurement/Vendor Management: Source parts/services; manage expedite; handle OEM coordination and contracts.
- HSE: Oversee risk assessments, permits, and compliance; audit safety practices.
- Quality/Validation: Witness tests; ensure compliance with quality systems; approve return-to-service for regulated assets.
- Operations Coordinator/Production: Approve downtime; support isolation and restart; accept handover.
- IT/OT Support: Facilitate diagnostics, firmware/patching, access control; ensure cybersecurity.
- Finance/Cost Control: Track costs, chargebacks, warranty recovery.
- OEM/Vendor Field Service: Provide specialized repair and certification when required.

## Best Practices
- Use a CMMS/EAM with standardized failure, cause, and remedy codes to improve data quality and analytics.
- Apply a clear priority and escalation matrix tied to asset criticality and risk.
- Enforce safety rigor: LOTO, permits, JSAs, and toolbox talks for every job; verify isolations.
- Increase first-time fix rate via thorough planning, kitting, and pre-job briefings.
- Maintain accurate asset master data, BOMs, and as-built documentation; update after changes.
- Leverage condition monitoring and diagnostics to shorten fault isolation time.
- Capture as-found/as-left measurements and photos; attach to work orders.
- Use mobile devices for real-time data entry, checklists, and digital work instructions.
- Standardize job plans and checklists for recurring repairs; continuously improve them.
- Manage critical spares with risk-based min/max, obsolescence tracking, and vendor SLAs.
- Conduct RCAs for high-impact or repeat failures; implement corrective/preventive actions.
- Track warranty status and claims aggressively to reduce repair costs.
- Coordinate with operations to bundle corrective work into planned outages when possible.
- Protect OT/ICS systems with change control and cybersecurity practices during software-related repairs.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Incomplete problem descriptions
  - Use structured request forms with required fields and photo uploads; train operators on effective reporting.
- Parts unavailability or long lead times
  - Maintain risk-based spares; use kitting; establish vendor consignment and expedite agreements; consider 3D-printed interim parts where appropriate and approved.
- Access constraints and permits
  - Early permit planning; alternative access equipment; schedule off-hours; pre-stage permits.
- Safety incidents and near misses
  - Strengthen JSA quality; peer checks on LOTO; near-miss reporting and learning system.
- Insufficient skills for complex diagnostics
  - Cross-train staff; maintain skills matrix; leverage OEM support and AR-enabled remote assist.
- Recurring failures
  - Formal RCAs; update PM/PdM; address design weaknesses; adjust operating procedures.
- Poor data quality in CMMS
  - Mandate closure data fields; supervisor review; periodic data quality audits; code lists training.
- Coordination with operations causing delays
  - Define SLAs and communication protocols; daily/weekly maintenance-operations huddles; shared schedule boards.
- Vendor delays and warranty hurdles
  - Use clear contracts with response SLAs; pre-approved vendor lists; proactive warranty tracking and documentation.

## Performance Metrics
- MTTR (Mean Time to Repair)
- Corrective maintenance downtime hours (planned vs unplanned)
- Percentage of emergency work vs total corrective work
- First-time fix rate
- Response time (time to acknowledge and time to dispatch)
- Schedule compliance for urgent/deferred corrective work
- Rework/recurrence rate within 30/90 days
- Work order closure quality (required fields completeness)
- Labor wrench time percentage for corrective jobs

- Critical spares stockout rate
- Warranty recovery rate and cycle time
- Safety metrics: TRIR, near-miss rate, permit violations
- QA pass rate on post-repair verification
- OEE impact attributable to corrective events
- Backlog age and prioritization distribution

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Infor EAM, Oracle eAM, ServiceNow FSM
- Mobile maintenance apps and digital work instruction platforms
- Condition monitoring and APM: vibration, ultrasound, thermography, oil analysis, motor current, APM suites
- Control/monitoring: SCADA, DCS, BMS/BAS, IIoT platforms with alerting
- Diagnostic and test equipment: multimeters, oscilloscopes, calibrators, pressure/vacuum gauges, analyzers
- Safety systems: LOTO kits, gas detectors, permit-to-work software
- Inventory and procurement systems integrated with CMMS
- Scheduling and resource tools: Primavera P6, MS Project, or CMMS-native
- QA/Validation and calibration management systems
- RCA tools and knowledge bases: TapRooT, Apollo, 5-Whys templates, wikis
- Remote assist: AR/VR tools for OEM support and on-the-job guidance
- Reporting/BI: Power BI, Tableau for KPIs and dashboards
- Specialized tools: alignment lasers, torque tools, lifting/rigging, NDT (UT, PT, RT), drones/robotics for hard-to-access areas
- Cybersecurity tools for OT patching and configuration control

Identify unplanned maintenance requirements is the process of detecting, validating, and documenting asset issues that require immediate or near-term corrective action outside of planned or routine schedules. It ensures emerging or current defects, failures, and anomalies are caught early, triaged for safety and business impact, and translated into clear, prioritized maintenance work requests.

Purpose:
- Protect people, environment, and assets by rapidly recognizing unsafe or degraded conditions.
- Minimize unplanned downtime and product/service quality impacts.
- Comply with regulatory and code requirements by identifying and flagging nonconformities.
- Feed accurate data into maintenance management to enable swift response and continuous improvement.

Role in the organization:
- Serves as the front end of reactive maintenance within the asset lifecycle.

Process boundaries:
- Starts when a potential or actual asset issue is detected by people or systems.
- Ends when a validated, prioritized unplanned maintenance request is created in the CMMS/EAM and accepted for planning/scheduling or escalated as an emergency work order.

## Key Activities
- Detect potential failures or abnormal conditions through alarms, inspections, operator observations, or analytics.
- Verify and triage the signal to rule out false positives and confirm the issue.

- Notify and escalate to stakeholders per the escalation matrix.
- Capture baseline data for subsequent diagnostics and RCA.
- Handover to maintenance planning/scheduling or emergency execution.

## Process Steps
1) Detect a potential issue
- Triggers: alarms (SCADA/DCS/BMS), vibration/temperature/oil analysis out-of-limits, inspection findings, operator observations (noise, smell, leaks, abnormal readings), customer complaints, energy anomalies, cyber/OT alerts impacting assets, OEM bulletins.
- Record initial time detected.

2) Ensure immediate safety and stabilize
- If imminent hazard: stop equipment if safe to do so, initiate LOTO/isolation, activate emergency response if required, secure area and communicate.
- Document any immediate containment performed.

3) Triage and validate
- Confirm the signal: cross-check with secondary indicators, verify sensor health, review recent work/changes, consult trend data in historian.
- Distinguish real failure vs. nuisance/false alarm; clear alarms if not valid and log findings.

4) Gather initial evidence
- Capture photos/videos, meter readings, parameters, smells/sounds observations, error codes, serial number/asset ID, environmental conditions, and any recent changes.
- Check maintenance history and known failure modes.

5) Assess risk and impact
- Apply risk matrix considering:
  - Safety/environmental/regulatory risk.
  - Production/service impact and downtime risk.
  - Quality/compliance risk.
  - Asset criticality and redundancy availability.
- Decide if emergency status is warranted.

6) Classify the requirement
- Category: Breakdown (asset unavailable), Emergency (immediate action required), Urgent corrective (near-term risk), Corrective/deferred (can be planned later).
- Select failure codes per taxonomy (e.g., failure mode, cause, effect).

7) Assign priority and response target
- Use standard priority matrix (e.g., P1 emergency, P2 high, P3 medium, P4 low) aligned to SLAs and criticality.
- Determine required response window (e.g., P1 within 1 hour).

8) Create the unplanned maintenance request in CMMS/EAM
- Include: asset ID and location, symptoms/observations, readings/attachments, time detected and downtime start (if applicable), safety status/LOTO, classification and priority, suspected cause, reporter details, linked incidents/quality deviations, recommended temporary controls/workaround.

9) Notify and escalate
- Auto-notify maintenance supervisor/planner, operations owner, EHS/Quality if applicable.
- For emergencies, initiate emergency work order path and dispatch per on-call rota.

10) Check constraints and resources preliminarily
- Identify critical spares availability and lead times; note if stockout risk exists.
- Flag need for specialized tools, permits, or vendor support.

11) Handover for action
- For emergency: dispatch technician/team and begin execution under emergency protocol.
- For non-emergency: hand off to planning/scheduling with all documentation and data.

12) Log and close identification stage
- Ensure data quality checks pass (mandatory fields, correct codes).
- Mark identification complete; track KPIs (detection-to-request time, accuracy, etc.).

Decision notes:
- If evidence is inconclusive, schedule a rapid diagnostic check; do not downgrade safety controls.
- If repeated similar events occur, flag for reliability engineering review and alarm rationalization.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Validated unplanned maintenance request or emergency work order in CMMS/EAM.
- Assigned priority, classification, and response target.
- Documented safety status and any containment actions.
- Stakeholder notifications and escalations executed.

Deliverables:
- Complete CMMS record with attachments (photos, logs, parameter snapshots).
- Initial failure codes and suspected cause.
- Downtime record initiation if asset is unavailable.
- Triggers to related processes (EHS incident, quality deviation, MOC) when applicable.

Success criteria:
- Issues are detected early and accurately validated.
- Correct priority and classification assigned on first pass.
- Complete, high-quality work request created within target time.
- Safety risks controlled promptly; no uncontrolled escalation.
- Appropriate stakeholders notified without delay.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Asset Operator/Production Technician: Detect and report issues; perform safe immediate containment; provide observations and data; initiate CMMS request if authorized.
- Control Room/SCADA Analyst: Monitor alarms; filter false positives; notify field teams; capture trend data/screenshots.
- Maintenance Technician (on-call): Support validation; advise on immediate actions; execute emergency containment; document technical details.
- Maintenance Supervisor/Team Lead: Oversee triage; confirm classification/priority; authorize emergency response; ensure communications and shift coverage.
- Maintenance Planner: Validate request completeness; ensure proper coding; accept into planning/scheduling; coordinate permits and resources.
- Reliability Engineer: Review repeat events; refine thresholds; update FMEA/failure codes; recommend predictive/condition-based triggers; lead RCA initiation criteria.
- EHS Officer: Advise on safety controls; determine incident reportability; ensure LOTO and hazard controls are followed.
- Quality Representative: Assess product/service impact; open quality deviations if needed.
- Stores/Inventory Specialist: Confirm spares availability and reservations; flag shortages.
- IT/OT Support: Validate sensor/communications integrity; restore monitoring; support alarm system health.
- Vendor/OEM: Provide remote diagnostics or site support for specialized assets.

## Best Practices
- Standardize defect reporting with clear definitions, examples, and mandatory data fields; use guided mobile forms with photos and barcoded asset IDs.
- Maintain and periodically review a priority and risk matrix aligned to asset criticality and SLAs.
- Implement alarm management practices (rationalization, shelving policies, suppression logic, performance reviews) to reduce nuisance alarms.
- Integrate CMMS with SCADA/BMS/APM to auto-create draft work requests with context (time series data, alarm IDs).
- Use a common failure coding standard (e.g., ISO 14224 or corporate taxonomy) for consistent analytics and RCA.
- Require immediate safety assessment and LOTO decision tree in the identification workflow.
- Capture baseline condition snapshots at detection to support troubleshooting and prevent data loss.
- Establish an escalation matrix with clear time-bound triggers (e.g., if not acknowledged in 10 minutes, escalate to supervisor; 30 minutes to manager).
- Conduct shift handover reviews of open unplanned issues with an issues log.
- Train operators and maintainers on abnormal condition recognition (sounds, smells, heat, vibration) and reporting discipline.
- Maintain critical spares lists and min/max levels; link to asset criticality and failure history.
- Regularly audit data quality in unplanned requests and feed back to teams.
- Include contractors in the reporting process with access to mobile request tools and safety protocols.

## Common Challenges
- High false alarm rate leading to alarm fatigue.
  - Solution: Alarm rationalization, improved sensor health monitoring, analytics to filter noise.
- Underreporting or delayed reporting by operators.
  - Solution: Simplify reporting via mobile, reinforce just culture, recognition for timely reporting, training.
- Poor data quality in requests (missing asset ID, vague symptoms).
  - Solution: Mandatory fields, barcode/QR scanning, guided forms, supervisor validation gate.
- Misprioritization causing resource misallocation.
  - Solution: Standard priority matrix, quick risk assessment checklists, supervisory review.
- Safety controls not applied promptly.
  - Solution: Embed LOTO prompts, require safety status before request submission, EHS involvement.
- Access constraints (confined space, elevated work).
  - Solution: Early permit planning, alternate inspection methods (drones, thermal imaging).
- Spares unavailability prolonging downtime.
  - Solution: Critical spares strategy, early store check, vendor consignment agreements.
- Recurrent failures not escalated to reliability.
  - Solution: Automatic pattern detection in CMMS, thresholds for repeat events triggering RCA.
- Communication gaps across shifts or functions.
  - Solution: Standard notifications, shift handover log, incident rooms for major events.

## Performance Metrics
- Mean Time to Detect (MTTD): from issue onset/alarm to detection.
- Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA): detection to human acknowledgment.
- Detection-to-Request Time: detection to CMMS request creation.
- First-Pass Classification Accuracy: % of requests not reclassified later.
- First-Pass Data Completeness: % of requests meeting mandatory data/attachments.
- Emergency Response Compliance: % of emergencies met within SLA response times.
- False Positive Rate: % of alarms/work requests closed as no-fault-found.
- Safety Containment Time: detection to LOTO/containment applied when required.
- Unplanned-to-Planned Ratio: volume and hours; trend over time.
- Repeat Failure Rate: % of unplanned events recurring within defined window.
- Downtime Attributed to Late Identification: hours lost due to delayed detection/reporting.
- Alarm Flood Events: count and duration exceeding defined thresholds.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Infor EAM, Oracle EAM, UpKeep, Fiix.
- Mobile maintenance/inspection apps with barcode/QR/NFC asset identification, offline capture, photo/video.
- SCADA/DCS/BMS and data historians (e.g., OSIsoft PI, Aveva) for real-time monitoring and trends.
- Condition monitoring and APM/IIoT platforms: vibration, ultrasound, thermography, oil analysis, electrical signature analysis; anomaly detection analytics.
- Alerting and on-call management: pagers/phones, SMS/email alerts, tools like PagerDuty or Opsgenie.
- Collaboration/communications: radios, Microsoft Teams/Slack integrated with alerts, digital shift logs.
- Safety systems: electronic LOTO management, permit-to-work systems.
- Quality and EHS systems: incident and deviation management (e.g., Enablon, Intelex), integration with CMMS.
- Inventory systems integrated with CMMS for spares visibility.
- Diagnostics tools: handheld thermal cameras, vibration analyzers, multimeters, portable data loggers.
- Visualization dashboards for KPIs and alarm performance.

This documentation can be used to train personnel, configure supporting systems, and drive continuous improvement in unplanned maintenance responsiveness and safety.
