Process Details:
# [10.3.3.5] Perform Unplanned Maintenance and Repairs

## Overview
Perform Unplanned Maintenance and Repairs covers all corrective work required to restore asset functionality when failures, breakdowns, or emergent defects occur outside of scheduled preventive or routine maintenance. The process ensures a rapid, safe, and controlled response that minimizes downtime, protects people and the environment, and preserves asset integrity and compliance.

Purpose:
- Restore asset functionality and safety as quickly and safely as possible.
- Capture failure data to improve reliability and reduce recurrence.
- Protect production, service levels, and regulatory compliance.

Role in the organization:
- Provides the incident response capability for asset failures.
- Interfaces closely with Operations, HSE, Quality, and Reliability to manage risk, contain impacts, and drive continuous improvement.
- Feeds critical insights back into asset strategies, PM programs, and spares management.

## Key Activities
- Event detection and notification (alarms, operator reports, condition monitoring alerts).
- Triage and prioritization (classify Emergency/Urgent/Deferrable).
- Make-safe actions and hazard control (isolation, lockout/tagout).
- Work intake and work order creation in CMMS/EAM.
- Permitting (hot work, confined space, electrical, excavation) and risk assessment (JSA).
- Diagnostic testing and troubleshooting.
- Repair, replace, or temporary workaround implementation.
- Quality checks, functional testing, and return-to-service.
- Documentation of failure mode, parts/labor used, time to repair, and downtime.
- Post-incident review/root cause analysis (as needed) and follow-up corrective actions.
- Communication and escalation management.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Incident notification/alert with asset ID, symptoms, and location.
- Asset master data (registry, criticality, BOM, drawings, schematics, OEM manuals).
- Maintenance history and failure codes.
- Spare parts availability and tool lists.
- Operating permits and site access permissions.
- Safety procedures (LOTO, PPE requirements, MSDS/SDS).

Prerequisites:
- Trained, authorized personnel with current certifications.
- Established on-call roster and escalation matrix.
- CMMS/EAM configured for rapid work order creation and prioritization.
- Permit-to-work system in place.
- Emergency response and incident command protocols accessible.
- Calibrated test equipment and validated procedures.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [10.3.1] Plan maintenance (ensures asset data, critical spares, and procedures exist).
- HSE management (risk assessments, permits, incident reporting).
- Procurement and inventory management (expedite parts, vendor services).
- Contractor management (prequalified vendors, mobilization).
- Change control/MOC (if design/setting changes are made).
- Quality management (release to production, revalidation if required).
- Operations management (shutdown/startup coordination).

## Process Steps
1) Detect and Notify
- Source: SCADA/DCS/BMS alarms, operator observation, IoT alert, inspection finding, customer complaint.
- Action: Log the event; if life-safety or environmental risk, trigger emergency response.

2) Initial Response and Make Safe
- Operations or first responder technician performs immediate actions to stabilize:
  - Stop equipment as needed, isolate energy sources, execute LOTO.
  - Evacuate/cordon area if necessary.
  - Activate spill/fire response as applicable.
- Document initial conditions (photos, alarm history).

3) Triage and Classification
- Maintenance supervisor or duty engineer classifies priority using a standard matrix:
  - Emergency: Immediate risk to life/environment or critical production stop.
  - Urgent: Significant impact within hours.
  - Deferrable: Limited impact; can be scheduled within days.
- Determine need for incident command structure and cross-functional coordination.

4) Create and Prioritize Work Order
- Create a CMMS/EAM work order capturing:
  - Asset, symptoms, alarms, time of failure, operational context.
  - Priority, required skills/trades, predicted parts/tools.
  - Safety risks and required permits.
- Link any related incident/quality deviations.

5) Permits and Risk Assessment
- Conduct JSA/THA and secure necessary permits (hot work, confined space, electrical).
- Confirm LOTO and zero-energy state. Test for dead. Gas test if confined space.
- Verify PPE and special controls (arc flash boundaries, fall protection).

6) Mobilize Resources
- Assign qualified technicians; notify on-call if after-hours.
- Reserve tools, test equipment, and spare parts; kit materials when possible.
- Engage OEM/contractor if specialized expertise or warranty applies.

7) Diagnose and Troubleshoot
- Use standardized fault isolation procedures and OEM manuals.
- Gather data: error codes, vibration/thermography, electrical measurements, process parameters, recent changes.
- Identify failure mode and root cause hypothesis; update work order notes.

8) Execute Repair or Temporary Workaround
- Choose path: repair, replace component, or implement temporary bypass with approved risk controls.
- Follow standard work instructions and torque/clearance specifications.
- Adhere to quality checks (e.g., cleanliness, lubrication, alignment, tolerances).
- If parts shortage: evaluate substitution, cannibalization from non-critical asset (with approval), expedite procurement.

9) Test and Verify
- Remove LOTO per procedure; perform no-load and load tests as applicable.
- Validate interlocks, sensors, control logic, and protective systems.
- Confirm product/process quality (QC checks) and regulatory parameters.

10) Return to Service and Handover
- Obtain Operations acceptance; complete return-to-service checklist.
- Update performance parameters/settings; monitor closely for burn-in period.
- Communicate status to stakeholders (operations, planning, management).

11) Document and Close
- Capture:
  - Failure code, cause code, action taken.
  - Time stamps (response time, diagnosis time, repair time), MTTR.
  - Parts used (lot/batch if traceable), labor hours, costs.
  - Test results and as-found/as-left data.
- Attach photos, instrument readings, and permit records.
- Close work order when all fields complete and approvals obtained.

12) Post-Event Review and Follow-Up
- Criteria for deeper analysis: safety incident, regulatory breach, high downtime/cost, repeat failures.
- Perform RCA (5-Whys, fishbone, fault tree) and define CAPAs:
  - Update PM tasks, spares strategy, training, design changes (via MOC).
  - Raise planned corrective work orders for any deferred work.
- Update knowledge base/runbooks and communicate lessons learned.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Restored asset functionality and safe operating state.
- Accurate CMMS/EAM work order record with complete failure data.
- Updated asset history and reliability dataset.

Deliverables:
- Work order with diagnostics, actions, test results, labor/parts/costs.
- Permits, JSA, LOTO records, and compliance documentation.
- Incident report (if applicable), RCA report, and CAPA tasks.
- Updated drawings/schematics or setpoints if changed (with MOC).

Success criteria:
- Asset returned to service within targeted MTTR and without rework.
- No safety or environmental incidents during repair.
- Complete, accurate documentation captured within defined SLA.
- Minimal production/operations impact and confirmed quality compliance.
- Reduction in recurrence for similar failures over time.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Maintenance Technician: Execute diagnostics and repairs; follow safety and quality procedures; document findings and work performed.
- Maintenance Supervisor/Lead: Triage, prioritize, assign resources, ensure permits and safety compliance, coordinate with Operations, approve closure.
- Operations/Production: Initiate notifications, make-safe actions, provide process context, approve return-to-service, adjust operating conditions.
- HSE Specialist: Advise on hazards, permits, and controls; investigate incidents; verify compliance.
- Planner/Scheduler: Support unplanned work by checking spares, preparing kits, coordinating contractors; convert follow-up work into planned backlog.
- Reliability Engineer: Analyze failure data, lead RCA, recommend changes to PMs/design; maintain failure codes and bad actor lists.
- Warehouse/Stores: Provide and issue spares/tools; manage critical spares and emergency procurement.
- Procurement/Vendor Management: Expedite parts/services; manage warranties and OEM support.
- Quality/QA: Assess product/process impact; approve validation and release where required.
- IT/OT Support: Support control systems, alarms, and diagnostics; maintain CMMS and mobile tools availability.
- Contractors/OEMs: Provide specialized repair services; adhere to site safety and documentation requirements.

## Best Practices
- Use a clear priority matrix and escalation protocol; practice with drills.
- Standardize triage and diagnosis via runbooks and fault trees for critical assets.
- Enforce strict LOTO and permit-to-work; perform point-of-work risk assessments.
- Keep accurate asset BOMs and maintain critical spare parts with min/max levels.
- Enable technicians with mobile CMMS, digital work instructions, and offline access.
- Capture complete failure coding and as-found data to power reliability analytics.
- Apply first-time fix practices: pre-diagnosis, parts kitting, and correct tooling.
- Conduct targeted RCAs on high-impact or repeat failures; implement CAPAs via MOC.
- Maintain an on-call roster and service-level targets for response and MTTR.
- Integrate condition monitoring to reduce unplanned events and improve triage.
- Hold brief post-job reviews; update knowledge base and train across shifts.
- Coordinate closely with Operations for safe shutdown/startup and run-in monitoring.

## Common Challenges
- Incomplete asset data or missing drawings/BOMs
  - Solution: Data cleansing projects; enforce data completeness on new assets; scan and centralize documentation.
- Spare parts unavailability or wrong parts
  - Solution: Criticality-based spares strategy; vendor stocking agreements; parts kitting; cross-reference alternates.
- Access and safety constraints (confined spaces, energized systems)
  - Solution: Permit rigor, specialized training, and pre-staged rescue plans; schedule windows with Operations.
- Poor communication and delays in escalation
  - Solution: Clear call tree, incident command roles, and stakeholder updates via centralized channels.
- Repeat failures due to underlying causes not addressed
  - Solution: Trigger thresholds for RCA; implement CAPAs and update PMs/designs.
- Quality or regulatory compliance gaps in emergency repairs
  - Solution: Use approved temporary repairs with defined expiry; QA review before full release; follow MOC.
- Scope creep during urgent repairs
  - Solution: Define minimum viable repair to restore safe function; defer improvements to planned work orders.

## Performance Metrics
- Mean Time to Respond (MTTRsp): Notification to technician on tools.
- Mean Time to Repair (MTTR): Technician start to return-to-service.
- Emergency Work Ratio: Emergency hours or WOs as a % of total maintenance.
- First-Time Fix Rate: Jobs resolved without repeat visits within X days.
- Rework Rate: Percentage of repairs requiring additional corrective action.
- Unplanned Downtime: Hours of production loss attributed to breakdowns.
- Cost of Unplanned Maintenance: Labor, parts, contractor, overtime costs.
- Parts Stockout Incidents: Count and duration impacting repairs.
- Documentation Completeness: % WOs with failure/cause/action codes, attachments.
- Safety Metrics: TRIR during maintenance, LOTO/permit compliance rate.
- Warranty Recovery: Value of costs recovered from OEMs.
- Post-Repair Quality Escapes: Defects traced to maintenance within X days.

Targets should be set by asset criticality and industry benchmarks.

## Technology and Tools
- CMMS/EAM: SAP PM, IBM Maximo, Infor EAM, Oracle EAM for work orders, history, failure codes, and costs.
- Mobile Maintenance Apps: Offline-capable, photo/video capture, digital signatures.
- SCADA/DCS/BMS/IIoT Platforms: Alarms, trends, condition monitoring inputs.
- Permit-to-Work and LOTO Systems: Digital permitting, isolation points, tags.
- Diagnostic Tools: Vibration analyzers, thermal cameras, ultrasound, electrical test instruments (insulation testers, multimeters), pressure/vacuum gauges, alignment tools.
- Knowledge Base/Runbooks: Standard fault isolation guides, OEM manuals, digital drawings.
- Inventory and Procurement: Integrated MRP, critical spares planning, vendor portals.
- Collaboration/Incident Management: Radios, incident command tools, chat/war rooms, e-logs and shift handover systems.
- Reliability Analytics: RCA tools, FMEA, Weibull/MTBF analytics, dashboarding/BI.
- AR/Remote Assist: Expert guidance for complex repairs; live annotations.
- Safety Equipment: Gas detectors, fall protection, arc-rated PPE, confined space kits.

This process, when executed with discipline and supported by the right data, tooling, and cross-functional coordination, minimizes disruption, safeguards people and assets, and continuously reduces the volume and impact of unplanned events.

# [10.4.1.2] Perform cost vs. benefit analysis for replacement

## Overview
This process evaluates whether to retain, repair/refurbish, replace, redeploy, or retire an asset at or approaching end-of-life. It balances total lifecycle economics with risk, service levels, compliance, safety, sustainability, and strategic alignment.

Its purpose is to:
- Optimize total cost of ownership (TCO) and reduce operational risk.
- Ensure asset decisions support organizational strategy, capacity, and standardization.
- Provide a defensible, auditable basis for capital allocation and end-of-life actions.
- Enable timely decisions that minimize downtime and disruption.

Role in the organization:
- A component of 10.4 Manage asset end-of-life and a key input to 10.4.1 Develop exit strategy.
- Feeds downstream processes (procurement, decommissioning/disposal, project execution).
- Interfaces with reliability/maintenance, finance, operations, EHS, procurement, IT/OT security, sustainability, and risk management.

Applicable asset classes include production equipment, facilities and utilities, fleet, IT/OT hardware and software, tools/instruments, and non-productive assets.

## Key Activities
- Trigger and scope definition: Identify candidate assets and clarify business objectives and constraints.
- Data gathering and validation: Technical condition, performance, cost, risk, compliance, and market data.
- Alternatives development: Retain, repair/overhaul, replace (like-for-like or upgrade), redeploy, lease/rent, as-a-service, consolidate, or retire without replacement.
- Financial modeling: TCO, NPV/IRR/payback, tax and depreciation impacts, residual/salvage value, disposal cost.
- Risk and scenario analysis: Reliability, safety, compliance, cyber risk, supply chain, lead times; sensitivity and scenario testing.
- Non-financial evaluation: Service levels, quality, ESG impacts (energy, emissions, circularity), strategic fit.
- Stakeholder alignment and recommendation: Cross-functional review and decision support.
- Approvals and handoff: Governance sign-offs, budget requests, procurement triggers, and documentation.
- Post-decision follow-up: Update asset strategy and risk register; define benefits realization measures.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Asset master data and criticality classification from EAM/CMMS.
  - Maintenance history (MTBF, MTTR, cost trends), condition assessments, failure modes (RCA).
  - Utilization, throughput, OEE, downtime logs and cost of downtime assumptions.
  - Vendor notices (end-of-life/support), warranty status, parts availability.
  - Repair/refurbishment quotes and lead times; replacement options, specs, quotes, and lead times.
  - Energy and consumables usage and rates; expected efficiency gains.
  - Disposal/decommissioning costs and residual value/trade-in.
  - Compliance and safety requirements; known gaps and remediation costs.
  - Financial parameters: discount rate/WACC, hurdle rates, depreciation/tax rules, capitalization policy.
  - Demand and production plans; capacity or reliability requirements; SLAs/OTIF targets.
  - ESG data: carbon factors, water usage, circularity options; regulatory e-waste/hazardous disposal rules.

- Prerequisites:
  - Asset is flagged by trigger (e.g., high failure rate, obsolescence notice, safety noncompliance, excess capacity).
  - Current asset register and cost data are up to date and validated.
  - Defined decision criteria and thresholds (e.g., repair cost exceeds X% of replacement cost; minimum IRR).
  - Assigned analysis owner; cross-functional team identified.
  - Access to vendor, market, and disposal service information.

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - 10.4.1 Develop exit strategy (provides strategic context and initial criteria).
  - Asset performance management and reliability engineering (inputs on condition and risk).
  - Capital planning and budgeting (funding availability and prioritization).
  - Procurement and supplier management (market intelligence, quotes, contracting).
  - Decommissioning and disposal management (execution considerations and costs).
  - Change management and commissioning (for replacement/upgrade transitions).

## Process Steps
1. Trigger and intake
   - Receive trigger (alerts, KPIs, audit findings, vendor EoL, capacity changes).
   - Log request in EAM/PMO system; assign owner; define timeline based on risk and operational impact.

2. Define scope and decision criteria
   - Clarify objectives (cost reduction, reliability, capacity, compliance, ESG).
   - Confirm constraints (budget, footprint, utility limits, IT/OT standards, cybersecurity baselines).
   - Agree decision thresholds and metrics (NPV, IRR, payback, MCDA weighting).

3. Gather and validate data
   - Extract asset and maintenance history; validate data quality.
   - Obtain repair/refurb quotes and feasibility; confirm lead times and resource availability.
   - Obtain replacement options (like-for-like, upgraded technology, lease/as-a-service), with total costs, performance, and lead times.
   - Estimate downtime cost per hour/day, including ripple effects (lost production, expedited freight, service penalties).
   - Collect energy/consumables data; estimate savings from alternatives.
   - Determine disposal/decommissioning/sanitization costs and residual value.
   - Confirm tax and accounting impacts (remaining book value, write-offs, depreciation schedules, incentives/grants).
   - Check compliance/safety gaps and remediation costs for each option.
   - Gather ESG impacts (embodied carbon of new asset vs operational savings; circular options).

4. Develop alternatives set
   - Define feasible options: run-to-failure with mitigations, repair/overhaul/refurbish, parts cannibalization, replace/upgrade, lease/rent, as-a-service, consolidate/redeploy, retire without replacement.
   - Document assumptions, dependencies, and changeover requirements for each.

5. Quantify costs and benefits (lifecycle)
   - For each alternative, build a 5–15 year lifecycle model (aligned to asset class life):
     - Capex or upfront costs (purchase, installation, commissioning, training, IT integration).
     - Opex (maintenance, energy, consumables, licenses, support, cybersecurity).
     - Downtime costs (planned/unplanned), quality/scrap, rework.
     - Compliance and safety costs/avoidance.
     - Insurance premium impacts, spares inventory implications.
     - Disposal/decommissioning and residual value at end of horizon.
   - Apply discount rate; compute NPV, IRR, payback; include tax effects.

6. Assess risks and uncertainties
   - Identify key risks (reliability, safety, compliance, supply chain, obsolescence, cyber, vendor viability).
   - Perform sensitivity analysis (tornado chart) on top drivers (downtime cost, failure rate, energy price, lead time).
   - Run scenarios (e.g., demand high/low, inflation high, parts shortage persists).
   - Where material, use probabilistic modeling (e.g., Monte Carlo) for failure and downtime variability.

7. Evaluate non-financial criteria
   - Use a weighted multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) across: safety/compliance, service levels, flexibility/capacity, technology standardization, ESG, cybersecurity, user experience, strategic alignment.
   - Document trade-offs and any must-meet criteria.

8. Consolidate recommendation
   - Compare baseline (retain) vs alternatives; present ranked options with rationale.
   - Include implementation approach, timeline, changeover/transition plan, and operational impact.
   - Provide funding request (capex/opex), procurement strategy, and risk mitigations.

9. Review and approvals
   - Cross-functional review with Operations, Maintenance, Finance, EHS, IT/OT Security, Sustainability, Procurement, Risk/Legal as applicable.
   - Update analysis per feedback; secure approvals per governance thresholds and delegation of authority.

10. Handoff and execution readiness
   - Create decision package: analysis report, model files, assumptions log, MCDA worksheet, decision record, and approval trail.
   - Trigger downstream processes: procurement sourcing, project initiation, decommissioning planning, data/system updates, communications.

11. Post-decision follow-up
   - Update asset strategy and risk register.
   - Define benefits realization KPIs and baseline; schedule post-implementation review (e.g., 6–12 months).
   - Archive documentation for audit and lessons learned.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Outputs:
  - Cost-benefit analysis report with financial models (TCO, NPV/IRR/payback).
  - MCDA scoring and non-financial evaluation.
  - Recommended option with justification, risks, mitigations, and implementation plan.
  - Funding request and procurement intake package.
  - Updated asset records and risk register entries.

- Deliverables:
  - Decision package (slides + detailed annex + model workbook).
  - Assumptions and data sources register; sensitivity/scenario analyses outputs.
  - Disposal plan outline (if required), including data sanitization for IT assets.
  - Approval documentation and audit trail.

- Success criteria:
  - Decision made within agreed cycle time with complete, accurate, and auditable analysis.
  - Approved option meets or exceeds financial thresholds and risk tolerance.
  - Post-implementation benefits meet forecast within agreed variance.
  - Compliance, safety, and cybersecurity requirements met.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Asset/Facilities Manager: Process owner; defines scope, coordinates analysis, and presents recommendation.
- Reliability/Engineering: Provides condition assessments, failure modeling, and repair/refurb feasibility.
- Maintenance Lead: Provides maintenance history, parts/supplier insights, and practical constraints.
- Operations Manager: Quantifies downtime impacts; validates service/capacity needs and changeover plans.
- Finance/Cost Analyst: Builds/validates financial models; applies tax and accounting rules; ensures hurdle rates.
- Procurement/Sourcing: Obtains quotes; assesses supplier risk; advises on contract terms and warranties.
- EHS/Compliance: Identifies regulatory and safety requirements; evaluates disposal/hazardous handling.
- IT/OT and Cybersecurity: Ensures replacement complies with standards; scopes data migration/sanitization.
- Sustainability/ESG: Assesses energy/emissions impacts and circularity; advises on reporting and credits.
- Risk Management/Legal: Reviews risk profile, insurance implications, and contractual protections.
- Project Manager/PMO: Prepares execution and transition plans upon approval.
- External Vendors/Service Providers: Provide technical proposals, repair/refurb options, and support roadmaps.

## Best Practices
- Use standardized templates and a central model library to ensure consistency and comparability.
- Include the full cost of downtime and quality impacts; align assumptions with Operations and Finance.
- Consider the widest feasible set of alternatives, including lease/as-a-service and redeployment/consolidation.
- Incorporate total cost of risk: safety, compliance, cyber, vendor viability, and supply chain resilience.
- Apply sensitivity and scenario analysis; highlight the few variables that drive most of the decision.
- Avoid sunk-cost fallacy; evaluate forward-looking economics only.
- Align to technology and platform standards to reduce long-term complexity and support costs.
- Include ESG and circular economy factors: energy efficiency, embodied carbon, reuse/refurbish options.
- Validate data quality; reconcile EAM/CMMS data with finance and operational logs.
- Use asset criticality to prioritize and set rigorous criteria for high-impact assets.
- Engage cross-functional reviewers early to surface constraints and speed approvals.
- Document assumptions and decisions for auditability and future learning; conduct post-implementation reviews.
- Negotiate total value (warranty, spares, training, buy-back, performance guarantees), not just purchase price.

## Common Challenges
- Incomplete or poor-quality data
  - Mitigation: Data validation steps; triangulate with multiple sources; use conservative assumptions; flag data gaps.
- Underestimating downtime and changeover costs
  - Mitigation: Time-and-motion review; involve Operations; simulate cutover; include learning curve/training.
- Bias toward repair or replacement due to stakeholder preferences
  - Mitigation: Standard criteria, MCDA, and cross-functional governance; present fact-based comparisons.
- Lead time and supply chain uncertainty
  - Mitigation: Scenario analysis; pre-qualification of alternatives; consider rental/temporary capacity; early procurement.
- Hidden compliance or cybersecurity requirements
  - Mitigation: EHS and IT/OT reviews; include certification/testing costs; plan data sanitization and decommissioning controls.
- Disposal constraints and costs (e-waste, hazardous materials)
  - Mitigation: Engage certified recyclers early; factor disposal logistics; explore take-back programs.
- Funding constraints and timing vs budget cycles
  - Mitigation: Stage-gate approvals; bridge with rental/repair; prepare robust business case for out-of-cycle funding.
- Tax/accounting surprises (write-offs, lease implications)
  - Mitigation: Early Finance involvement; model alternative accounting treatments; check incentives/grants.

## Performance Metrics
- Decision cycle time from trigger to approval.
- Percentage of analyses using standardized templates and including sensitivity/scenario analysis.
- Forecast accuracy: variance of realized costs/benefits vs business case at 6–12 months.
- Reduction in unplanned downtime and maintenance cost post-decision.
- ROI metrics: average NPV/IRR/payback of approved replacements vs thresholds.
- Energy consumption and emissions reduction achieved vs baseline.
- Compliance and safety outcomes: number of issues mitigated; zero audit findings related to end-of-life decisions.
- Percentage of high-criticality assets with current cost-benefit analyses.
- Share of assets leveraging circular options (refurbish/reuse/recycle) where viable.

## Technology and Tools
- EAM/CMMS: SAP PM/EAM, IBM Maximo, Infor EAM, Oracle eAM, UpKeep, Fiix.
- Asset performance management and condition monitoring: GE APM, AVEVA, AspenTech, PTC; IoT sensors; digital twins.
- ERP/Finance: SAP S/4HANA, Oracle ERP Cloud, NetSuite; fixed asset modules; tax engines.
- Financial modeling and risk: Excel/Google Sheets with standardized templates; @RISK, Crystal Ball for Monte Carlo; cost estimation tools.
- BI/Analytics: Power BI, Tableau, Qlik for dashboards and scenario visualization.
- Procurement and contract management: SAP Ariba, Coupa, Ivalua; CLM systems for warranties/SLAs/terms.
- PLM and vendor portals: for BOMs, support roadmaps, obsolescence notices.
- ESG/carbon accounting: Persefoni, Sphera, Watershed for emissions and circularity analysis.
- Document management and workflow: SharePoint, Confluence, ServiceNow for approvals and audit trails.
- Decommissioning/disposal: Certified e-waste and hazardous disposal vendor systems; data sanitization tools for IT assets.

This process yields transparent, risk-aware, and financially sound asset end-of-life decisions, enabling organizations to maximize value, protect operations, and meet compliance and sustainability commitments.

Process Details:
# [10.4.11.5] Recognize need to disposition hazardous materials/waste

## Overview
This process detects when hazardous materials or wastes require disposition and establishes the appropriate, compliant approach for dispositioning them. It bridges routine operations and the downstream packaging, transport, and disposal processes by:
- Identifying triggers that create hazardous waste or convert stored materials into waste (e.g., expiration, obsolescence, process change, equipment decommissioning).
- Determining whether materials meet regulatory definitions of hazardous waste and classifying the waste stream.
- Selecting the disposition pathway (e.g., reuse, return, treatment, recycling, disposal) in alignment with legal, environmental, health, safety, and corporate standards.

The process supports regulatory compliance, risk reduction, environmental stewardship, and cost control by ensuring timely recognition and proper routing of hazardous materials and wastes before accumulation limits are exceeded or risks materialize.

## Key Activities
- Monitor and detect disposition triggers: inventory status, expirations, process or asset changes, spill cleanups, and nonconforming product.
- Perform preliminary risk and regulatory screening using Safety Data Sheets (SDS), regulatory definitions, and historical waste profiles.
- Make hazardous waste determinations and classifications (e.g., characteristic, listed, universal, special, biohazard, radioactive, e-waste).
- Characterize quantity, location, accumulation start date, and generator implications.
- Evaluate disposition hierarchy and recommend approach: minimize, reuse, return to vendor, permitted on-site treatment, recycling, off-site treatment/disposal.
- Initiate documentation (waste determination, waste profile, approval requests) and coordinate with internal/external stakeholders.
- Log and track recognition events, approvals, and schedule for pickup/next steps.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Material information: SDS, technical data sheets, product labels, prior waste profiles, UN/ADR/IMDG classifications (if known).
  - Operational signals: inventory reports, expiration alerts, production change notices, maintenance/decommissioning plans, lab closeout notices.
  - Inspection and audit findings: satellite accumulation area (SAA) inspections, 5S/Gemba walk observations, spill/incident reports, nonconforming product reports.
  - Regulatory requirements: applicable local/national regulations (e.g., RCRA/TSCA in US, ADR/CLP/REACH in EU), permits, consent orders, internal EHS policies.
- Prerequisites:
  - Designated EHS/Waste Coordinators and trained personnel.
  - Approved waste management plan and waste identification procedures.
  - Access to SDS management, EHS compliance systems, and waste tracking tools.
  - Contracts/Master Service Agreements with qualified waste service providers (TSD facilities, haulers).
  - Site-specific emergency response and hazard communication programs.
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - [10.4.11.1] Maintain waste inventory and storage areas.
  - [10.4.11.2] Identify hazardous materials and maintain SDS.
  - [10.4.11.3] Develop and maintain waste management plans.
  - [10.4.11.4] Monitor regulatory changes and permits.
  - Downstream: [10.4.11.6] Package/label, [10.4.11.7] Transport, [10.4.11.8] Dispose/confirm destruction.
  - Upstream: [10.2] Decommission assets, [10.1] Procure materials, [10.3] Operate assets.

## Process Steps
1. Detect trigger and initiate case
   - Triggers include: impending/actual expiration, obsolete stock, process/lab change or shutdown, asset decommissioning, spill cleanup residues, rejected batches, container damage, prohibited substance phase-outs, banned chem notices, product recalls, returned samples, excess inventory, damaged/defective batteries or electronics.
   - Originator logs a recognition event in the EHS/waste system with location, material ID, quantity estimate, condition, and photos.
2. Immediate risk control and segregation
   - If hazards are acute (reactive, flammable, toxic gas, mercury release, lithium battery thermal risk), isolate the area per site emergency procedures and notify EHS.
   - Do not mix materials. Keep incompatible materials separated. Place in secondary containment if safe to do so.
3. Gather information and documents
   - Retrieve SDS, prior waste profile, batch records, and any analytical data.
   - Record container type/size, labels, manufacturer lot, and last use date. Note unknowns or defaced labels.
4. Perform hazardous waste determination (regulatory screening)
   - Determine if the material is a waste under applicable regulations (no intended use, cannot be returned to service).
   - Classify by category:
     - Hazardous chemical waste: listed or characteristic (ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, toxicity).
     - Universal waste: batteries, lamps, pesticides, mercury devices, aerosol cans (as applicable).
     - Special wastes: PCBs, asbestos, refrigerants, e-waste/WEEE, oil/antifreeze, paint.
     - Biological or infectious waste (if applicable).
     - Radioactive or mixed waste (involve Radiation Safety Officer).
   - If unknown: follow “unknowns” protocol (secure, analyze via approved lab, conservatively manage until classified).
5. Characterize and document
   - Estimate quantity and set Accumulation Start Date (ASD) if waste is generated.
   - Assign waste codes and DOT/ADR class/UN for transport planning (informational at this stage).
   - Complete Hazardous Waste Determination form and draft or update Waste Profile.
   - Identify generator status implications (VSQG/SQG/LQG or jurisdictional equivalent); alert EHS if thresholds may be exceeded.
6. Evaluate disposition options (waste management hierarchy)
   - Source reduction/minimization (e.g., transfer unopened, in-date material for internal reuse; adjust orders).
   - Vendor return/take-back programs (chemicals, cylinders, electronics).
   - On-site permitted treatment (e.g., neutralization) if authorized in permits. If not authorized, proceed to off-site.
   - Recycling/recovery (e.g., solvent recovery, metals, batteries).
   - Off-site treatment and disposal (e.g., fuel blending, incineration, stabilization and landfill) through qualified TSD.
   - For time-sensitive/reactive chemicals (e.g., peroxide formers, picric acid crystals, pyrophorics), engage specialists; do not attempt to open or handle beyond securing.
7. Approvals and coordination
   - Route the proposed disposition for approvals (EHS, operations owner, finance if cost thresholds, legal/compliance for special waste).
   - If new waste stream or new TSD, complete vendor qualification and insurance checks.
   - Notify wastewater or air permit owners if any on-site treatment or discharge is proposed.
8. Plan next steps and handoff
   - Create pickup request/work order with preliminary classification, quantities, and packing notes.
   - Update waste inventory and SAA/Central Accumulation Area schedules to ensure time limits are met.
   - Communicate requirements to area owners (labeling, segregation, container condition) pending pickup.
9. Track and close recognition event
   - Monitor status until downstream packaging/transport is scheduled.
   - Close the recognition record with final chosen disposition path, approvals, and any learnings (e.g., minimization opportunities).

Note: Actual packaging, marking, labeling, shipping paper preparation, and transport occur in downstream processes and require competent, trained personnel.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Recognized waste/material record logged in EHS/waste system.
- Completed Hazardous Waste Determination and draft/approved Waste Profile(s).
- Classification summary: waste codes, hazard classes, UN numbers (if known), special handling notes.
- Chosen disposition approach with approvals.
- Accumulation and storage plan (location, ASD, segregation requirements).
- Pickup/work order request with estimated quantities and timelines.
- Notifications/alerts for generator status, permit implications, or regulatory reporting needs.
- Success criteria:
  - Recognition occurs before accumulation or expiration limits are breached.
  - 100% of recognized items receive documented waste determination.
  - Zero regulatory violations or unsafe conditions arising from unrecognized hazardous wastes.
  - Increased diversion to reuse/recycling where feasible and compliant.
  - Timely handoff to packaging/transport (within defined SLA).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Site EHS Manager/Coordinator
  - Owns the process, ensures regulatory alignment, approves determinations and disposition paths, manages vendor qualification, and oversees training.
- Waste Stream Owner/Originator (Operations/Lab/Maintenance)
  - Identifies triggers, initiates recognition events, provides material/batch context, ensures safe interim storage and labeling.
- Area Supervisor/Operations Manager
  - Ensures resources and access for segregation and inspections; approves operational impacts.
- Waste Coordinator/Technician
  - Conducts site walkdowns, validates quantities, updates inventory, coordinates pickups.
- Regulatory/Compliance Specialist
  - Interprets regulatory requirements, monitors generator status, manages reporting obligations.
- Radiation/Biosafety Officer (as applicable)
  - Leads classification and disposition decisions for radioactive or biological wastes.
- Procurement/Supply Chain
  - Engages vendor take-back/return programs; prevents recurrence via purchasing controls.
- Finance/Cost Control
  - Reviews and approves high-cost disposal choices, tracks cost per waste stream.
- Qualified Waste Service Provider (TSD) and Hauler
  - Provides profiling guidance, acceptance criteria, and downstream treatment/disposal services.
- Quality/QA
  - Coordinates on nonconforming product disposition and documentation linkage.
- IT/Systems Support
  - Maintains EHS/waste tracking systems, alerts, and integrations.

## Best Practices
- Apply the waste management hierarchy: avoid, reduce, reuse, recycle before disposal.
- Maintain a current waste stream library with approved profiles to expedite determinations.
- Use proactive triggers: automated expiration alerts, change management linkage, decommissioning checklists, and periodic area inspections.
- Standardize labels and visual controls to clearly distinguish “material” vs “waste,” and mark Accumulation Start Dates.
- Segregate incompatibles rigorously; never mix unknowns or different waste streams.
- Establish an “unknowns” protocol including rapid lab analysis and conservative handling.
- Integrate SDS management with waste determination workflows.
- Train front-line staff to recognize common special wastes (batteries, lamps, aerosols, refrigerants, PCBs, e-waste).
- Track generator status in near-real time; set automated alerts for threshold crossings.
- Pre-qualify multiple TSD facilities to avoid delays and leverage best treatment options.
- Conduct after-action reviews for large or unusual recognition events to drive minimization and purchasing changes.
- Document and practice escalation procedures for time-sensitive/reactive chemicals.

## Common Challenges
- Ambiguous classification or incomplete information
  - Solution: Require SDS attachment; maintain historical profiles; use lab analysis for unknowns.
- “Orphan” or legacy containers found during cleanouts
  - Solution: Unknowns protocol, conservative hazard assumptions, specialist support.
- Mixing of wastes due to poor segregation or space constraints
  - Solution: SAA design improvements, color-coded containers, routine audits, capacity planning.
- Delays in approvals leading to accumulation time risks
  - Solution: SLA-based approvals, escalation paths, pre-approved profiles for common streams.
- Regulatory changes affecting classifications
  - Solution: Regulatory watch, periodic profile reviews, refresher training.
- Vendor capacity or acceptance limitations
  - Solution: Multi-vendor strategy, early engagement, alternate treatment paths.
- Lithium battery and e-waste recognition and handling
  - Solution: Specific training, dedicated containers, quick removal from production areas, vendor take-back.
- Cost escalation
  - Solution: Stream-level cost tracking, source reduction initiatives, contract renegotiation.

## Performance Metrics
- Time to Recognition: elapsed time from trigger to recorded recognition event.
- Time to Determination: recognition to completed waste determination/profile.
- Compliance Rate: percentage of recognized items with complete documentation and timely ASD labeling.
- Accumulation Compliance: number of days in SAA/CAA vs. regulatory limits; zero overdue events.
- Generator Status Accuracy: variance between calculated and reported generator status by month.
- Diversion Rate: percentage of tonnage diverted to reuse/recycling versus disposal.
- Cost per Unit Managed: cost per kg/litre by waste stream; trend over time.
- Incident Rate: number of non-compliances or near misses related to unrecognized hazardous waste.
- Rework Rate: percentage of profiles rejected by TSD on first submission.
- Training Coverage: percentage of relevant staff current on recognition training.

## Technology and Tools
- EHS and Waste Management Systems: Enablon, Sphera, Intelex, VelocityEHS, Encamp (for profiling, tracking, reporting).
- SDS Management Tools: 3E/Verisk, Chemwatch, SDSonline.
- Inventory and Asset Systems: ERP (SAP, Oracle), CMMS (Maximo), LIMS for labs; integrated expiration and change alerts.
- Mobile Inspection/Reporting Apps: for SAA audits, photo capture, barcoding/RFID tagging.
- Regulatory Intelligence: Enhesa, RegScan for updates on waste classifications and thresholds.
- Analytics/Dashboards: BI tools for KPIs, generator status alerts, and cost analytics.
- Communication/Workflow: Ticketing and approval tools (ServiceNow, Jira) integrated with EHS systems.

This process should be tailored to local regulatory regimes and site conditions. Only trained and authorized personnel should make hazardous waste determinations and select disposition pathways, and specialist support should be engaged for highly reactive or non-routine materials.

# [11.1.1.1] Determine Risk Tolerance for Organization

## Overview
This process defines the organization’s risk tolerance—the acceptable levels of variation in outcomes relative to objectives—across all material risk categories (strategic, financial, operational, compliance, and reputational). It translates strategy and risk capacity into clear, quantified limits and qualitative boundaries that guide decision-making, capital allocation, control design, and issue escalation.

Purpose:
- Align risk-taking with strategic objectives and stakeholder expectations.
- Convert enterprise risk appetite and capacity into actionable, measurable tolerances.
- Enable consistent risk-based decisions and monitoring across the enterprise.

Role in the organization:
- Foundational element of the enterprise risk framework and policies [11.1.1].
- Feeds risk limits, key risk indicators (KRIs), stress-testing, business planning, and performance management.
- Enables effective governance by the Board and risk committees under [11.1] Manage enterprise risk.

## Key Activities
- Define scope, time horizon, and risk taxonomy coverage for tolerance-setting.
- Assess risk capacity (maximum risk the organization can absorb without threatening viability).
- Elicit and align risk appetite with the Board and executive leadership.
- Quantify risk-return trade-offs using scenarios, stress tests, and statistical measures.
- Set enterprise-level risk tolerance statements and thresholds (quantitative and qualitative).
- Cascade tolerances to business units, functions, and products as specific limits and KRIs.
- Establish breach thresholds, exception handling, and escalation protocols.
- Approve, communicate, implement, and embed tolerances into policies and processes.
- Monitor adherence and trigger periodic and event-driven reviews.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Strategic plan, financial targets, and risk-return objectives (e.g., growth, ROE, margin).
- Risk capacity analysis inputs: capital and liquidity plans, debt covenants, regulatory minima, rating agency thresholds, insurance coverage, business continuity and resilience capabilities.
- Historical loss/incidents and near-miss data; KRI/KPI trends.
- Risk assessments and registers across enterprise risk categories.
- External context: macroeconomic outlook, industry benchmarks, regulatory expectations (e.g., COSO ERM, ISO 31000; for regulated sectors, Basel/Solvency II/NAIC as applicable).
- Scenario and stress-testing library; model documentation and assumptions.
- Current policies, standards, and existing risk limits.

Prerequisites:
- Enterprise risk framework and policy established [11.1.1].
- Risk taxonomy and definitions agreed (appetite vs tolerance vs capacity).
- Governance bodies in place (Board/Risk Committee, Executive Risk Committee).
- Data governance and reporting capabilities to monitor KRIs.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [11.1] Manage enterprise risk (governance, oversight).
- [11.1.1] Establish the ERM framework and policies (policy base, taxonomy, roles).
- Risk identification and assessment processes (to understand material risks).
- Capital/liquidity planning and treasury management.
- Compliance management and internal control frameworks.
- Business continuity and resiliency planning (to set operational tolerances).

## Process Steps
1) Plan and scope
- Define objectives, scope (risk categories, entities, geographies), and time horizons (e.g., 1-year tactical, 3–5-year strategic).
- Agree principles: prioritization, materiality thresholds, confidence levels, monitoring cadence.

2) Assess risk capacity
- Quantify the maximum risk the organization can bear without breaching survival constraints:
  - Financial: minimum capital/liquidity buffers, debt covenants, rating requirements, insurance recoveries.
  - Operational: maximum tolerable downtime (MTPD), safety constraints, critical third-party dependencies.
  - Regulatory/compliance: non-negotiable requirements and penalties.
- Document capacity ranges and constraints by risk category.

3) Articulate risk appetite (top-down)
- Facilitate Board and Executive sessions to articulate desired risk posture and trade-offs (growth vs volatility, innovation vs control).
- Draft qualitative appetite statements by category (e.g., “Low appetite for safety incidents; moderate appetite for market risk aligned to strategy”).

4) Analyze risk-return and scenarios (bottom-up)
- Model Earnings-at-Risk, Cash-Flow-at-Risk, Value-at-Risk, Tail-VaR, Economic Capital, loss distributions as relevant.
- Run base, stressed, and reverse stress scenarios; assess correlations and concentrations.
- Evaluate impact on strategic and financial targets under multiple states of the world.

5) Define risk tolerance thresholds
- Convert appetite and capacity into measurable tolerance thresholds per risk category:
  - Financial: max annual EaR (e.g., ≤ 8% of EBITDA at 95% CL), liquidity coverage floor, FX sensitivity.
  - Operational: max critical system downtime per quarter, max defect rates, safety incident zero tolerance thresholds.
  - Compliance: zero tolerance for willful violations; quantified tolerance for inadvertent errors with corrective action standards.
  - Cyber/technology: max probable loss per incident; RTO/RPO for tier-1 services.
  - Third party: max concentration by supplier/region; max disruption days tolerated.
  - Reputational/Customer: max NPS decline; max media severity index incidents.
- Specify thresholds as ranges with RAG (red/amber/green) bands and explicit breach/escalation triggers.

6) Validate consistency and aggregate impact
- Aggregate tolerances across categories; test coherence against capacity and strategic targets.
- Challenge and refine assumptions with Finance, Treasury, BU leaders, Compliance, and Internal Audit.

7) Cascade and translate to limits and KRIs
- Map enterprise tolerances to business unit/product/functional limits and KRIs.
- Define measurement methods, data sources, and calculation frequency.
- Establish exception management: who can approve, time-bounded exceptions, compensating controls.

8) Governance review and approval
- Present the Risk Tolerance Framework, including analysis, thresholds, and cascade, to Executive Risk Committee and Board/Risk Committee.
- Incorporate feedback; record formal approval and effective date; version controls.

9) Communicate and embed
- Update policies, standards, and procedure documents with new tolerances and limits.
- Train leaders and staff; integrate into planning, pricing, new product approval, vendor management, project gating, and incentive plans.
- Configure GRC systems, dashboards, alerts, and workflows.

10) Monitor and manage breaches
- Track KRIs vs thresholds; generate alerts for amber and red conditions.
- Execute breach protocols: root-cause analysis, corrective actions, escalation to committees/Board as defined.
- Manage approved exceptions with expiry and periodic review.

11) Review and continuous improvement
- Periodic review (at least annually) and event-driven review after major incidents, acquisitions, regulatory changes, or strategic shifts.
- Refresh scenarios, data, and models; incorporate audit/compliance findings and lessons learned.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Risk Tolerance Framework document and Risk Appetite Statement (RAS).
- Quantitative tolerance thresholds per risk category with RAG bands.
- Cascade matrix mapping enterprise tolerances to BU/functional limits and KRIs.
- KRI catalog with definitions, data sources, owners, and reporting cadence.
- Breach and exception management procedures and approval matrices.
- Board/Committee minutes and approvals; training and communication materials.
- Configured dashboards/alerts in GRC/BI tools; monitoring reports.

Success criteria:
- Board-approved risk tolerances aligned to strategy and within capacity.
- 100% cascade coverage to material BUs/functions and critical processes.
- Real-time or timely monitoring with clear breaches and swift remediation.
- Reduced frequency/severity of tolerance breaches over time.
- Positive internal audit/compliance reviews; regulator and rating agency comfort where relevant.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Board of Directors / Risk Committee: Approves appetite and tolerances; oversees adherence; challenges management.
- CEO and Executive Team: Own risk-taking posture; ensure alignment with strategy; resolve trade-offs.
- Chief Risk Officer (CRO) / ERM Function: Leads process; develops framework; runs analyses; proposes thresholds; monitors and reports; manages breaches and exceptions governance.
- CFO / Treasury / FP&A: Quantifies capacity; runs financial risk analyses; ensures alignment with capital/liquidity plans.
- Business Unit Leaders: Translate tolerances into operational limits; own adherence and corrective actions.
- Compliance / Legal: Advise on regulatory constraints; define zero-tolerance areas; validate compliance impacts.
- CISO/CTO/COO: Define technology/operational tolerances (RTO/RPO, uptime, safety); ensure monitoring capability.
- Procurement/Third-Party Risk Management: Apply tolerances to vendor selection, concentration, and resilience.
- Internal Audit: Provides independent assurance on design and effectiveness; tests adherence and reporting integrity.
- Data/Analytics: Ensure data quality, modeling, and dashboarding capability.
- HR/Compensation: Align incentives and training with tolerance objectives.

## Best Practices
- Anchor tolerances to capacity and strategy; avoid setting them solely from historical averages.
- Combine top-down (Board) and bottom-up (analytics) approaches; run iterative challenge sessions.
- Use clear, few, decision-useful metrics per category; define calculation methods and data lineage.
- Include forward-looking measures and stress scenarios; conduct reverse stress testing.
- Employ RAG thresholds with explicit actions, owners, and timelines.
- Cascade logically; avoid double-counting and ensure aggregation reflects correlations.
- Distinguish appetite (broad posture), tolerance (acceptable variation), and limits (operational constraints).
- Codify zero-tolerance areas (e.g., willful compliance breaches, severe safety incidents).
- Embed tolerances into planning, pricing, new initiatives, and vendor contracts; align incentives.
- Maintain version control, change management, and comprehensive documentation.
- Pilot tolerances in select units before enterprise rollout; refine based on feedback.
- Automate monitoring and alerts; conduct regular model validation and data quality checks.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Conflicting stakeholder views on risk: Use facilitated workshops, scenario narratives, and decision simulations to reveal trade-offs and reach consensus.
- Data quality and model limitations: Implement data governance, back-testing, and sensitivity analyses; document assumptions and limitations.
- Overly complex metrics: Prioritize a small set of high-signal indicators; provide user training and job aids.
- Misalignment across units: Use a standard cascade methodology; reconcile with BU strategies and budgets; enforce through governance.
- Regulatory or rating agency constraints: Map tolerances to hard constraints; include compliance sign-off; maintain evidence for exams.
- Difficulty translating into operations: Integrate thresholds into workflows, system controls, SLAs, and project gates; monitor exceptions.
- Cultural resistance: Communicate the “why,” tie to incentives, highlight successes, and engage change champions.
- Breach fatigue and alert overload: Calibrate RAG bands; tier KRIs by criticality; implement alert deduplication and thresholds.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs/KRIs)
- Governance and adoption:
  - Time to approve tolerances from initiation to Board sign-off.
  - Coverage: % of material risk categories and BUs with defined and cascaded tolerances.
  - Training completion rate for targeted roles.

- Adherence and control:
  - Number and severity of tolerance breaches per quarter; median time-to-remediate.
  - Exception count, duration outstanding, and recurrence rate.
  - % KRIs with on-time reporting and validated data quality.

- Risk-return outcomes:
  - Earnings/Cash-Flow-at-Risk vs tolerance bands; volatility of key financial metrics.
  - Capital and liquidity buffer utilization vs targets.
  - Loss events above severity thresholds and trend over time.

- Assurance and effectiveness:
  - Internal audit findings related to tolerance design/monitoring; remediation timeliness.
  - Regulator/rating agency feedback (if applicable).
  - Stakeholder satisfaction (Board/executive survey on clarity and usefulness).

## Technology and Tools
- GRC Platforms: RSA Archer, ServiceNow GRC, MetricStream, OneTrust GRC to manage policies, KRIs, workflows, breaches, and evidence.
- Risk Analytics and Scenario Tools: SAS, Python/R, @RISK/Crystal Ball, Monte Carlo engines for VaR/EaR/CFaR, stress tests, and reverse stress testing.
- BI/Dashboarding: Power BI, Tableau, Qlik for tolerance dashboards, RAG visualizations, and drill-downs.
- Finance/Treasury Systems: SAP, Oracle, Kyriba for capital/liquidity data feeding capacity analysis.
- BCM/Operational Resilience: Fusion, Everbridge, ServiceNow Ops for RTO/RPO, MTPD alignment and monitoring.
- Cybersecurity/IT Monitoring: SIEM (Splunk, QRadar), APM (Dynatrace, AppDynamics), uptime monitors to track technology tolerances.
- Data Management: Data lakes/warehouses, MDM, data quality tools (Collibra, Informatica) for lineage and accuracy.
- Collaboration and Document Control: SharePoint/Confluence, e-signature tools for versioning and approvals.

This process ensures the organization explicitly defines, approves, and operationalizes the risk it is willing and able to take, creating a consistent basis for decision-making, monitoring, and accountability across the enterprise.

Process Details:
# [11.1.2.1] Identify Enterprise-Level Risks

## Overview
Identify Enterprise-Level Risks is the systematic process of discovering, surfacing, and documenting risks that could thwart the organization’s strategic objectives, impair capital and earnings, or damage reputation. It sits within the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) cycle and informs subsequent risk assessment, prioritization, response planning, and monitoring. This process ensures senior leadership and the board have a current, organization-wide view of material risks and emerging threats across strategic, financial, operational, compliance, cyber/technology, third-party, and ESG dimensions.

Objectives:
- Build a reliable, repeatable pipeline of enterprise risks aligned to objectives and risk appetite.
- Create a common language and taxonomy for enterprise risks.
- Enable efficient downstream assessment, treatment, and reporting.

Cadence:
- Formal enterprise risk identification cycle: semi-annual or annual.
- Event-driven (ad hoc) identification: upon major strategic changes, incidents, regulatory shifts, significant external events, or board requests.

Frameworks:
- Align with COSO ERM and ISO 31000 principles (context, identification, analysis, evaluation, treatment, monitoring).

## Key Activities
- Establish context and scope (objectives, appetite, boundaries, materiality thresholds).
- Maintain and apply an enterprise risk taxonomy and risk universe.
- Collect input from internal/external sources (workshops, interviews, data analysis, horizon scanning).
- Draft clear risk statements using cause–event–impact format.
- Tag and classify risks (category, business unit, process, objective, geography, time horizon).
- De-duplicate, rationalize, and consolidate enterprise-level risks.
- Perform initial screening to identify potentially material risks and emerging risks.
- Validate with risk owners and governance bodies; obtain sign-off.
- Record in the enterprise risk register and communicate to stakeholders.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Organizational context: mission, strategy, objectives, risk appetite/tolerances.
- Prior risk registers, KRI trends, loss/incident and near-miss data, audit/compliance findings.
- External intelligence: regulatory changes, macroeconomic and geopolitical outlooks, industry threat reports, competitor analysis, ESG trends.
- Business plans, change portfolios (M&A, major programs, new products/markets), third-party profiles.

Prerequisites:
- Approved ERM policy, governance, and roles.
- Defined risk taxonomy and materiality criteria.
- Templates for risk identification and risk statements.
- Access to data sources (GRC, incident systems, SIEM, vendor risk, finance, ops).

Dependencies on other processes:
- Define ERM policy and risk appetite (11.1 Manage Enterprise Risk).
- Coordinate ERM activities (11.1.2) and governance (risk committees, board).
- Incident/issue management; internal audit and compliance monitoring.
- Strategic planning and capital planning; third-party risk management; cyber risk management.

## Process Steps
1. Plan the cycle
   - Confirm scope, objectives, and timeline.
   - Align with board/committee calendars and strategic planning milestones.
   - Publish plan, roles, deliverables, and materiality thresholds.

2. Establish context and risk criteria
   - Review strategic objectives and risk appetite/tolerances.
   - Confirm risk categories, definitions, and tagging schema.
   - Set thresholds for “enterprise-level” versus “local” risks; define emerging risk criteria.

3. Gather inputs and evidence
   - Pull prior risk registers, KRI dashboards, incident/loss data, audit/compliance findings.
   - Compile external scans (PESTLE), regulator priorities, industry studies, macro/geo outlooks.
   - Inventory major change initiatives, dependencies, and third-party exposures.

4. Engage stakeholders
   - Identify risk owners, business risk champions, and subject matter experts.
   - Schedule cross-functional workshops and interviews (strategy, finance, IT/cyber, ops, HR, legal, ESG, supply chain, sales, product).
   - Provide pre-read materials and risk statement templates.

5. Apply identification techniques
   - Facilitated workshops and structured interviews.
   - Scenario planning and stress/hypothesis testing tied to strategic objectives.
   - Process/value-chain walkthroughs and bow-tie cause analysis for critical risks.
   - Text mining of incident tickets/claims; horizon scanning; control self-assessments.
   - Third-party risk reviews; change/project portfolio scans.

6. Draft risk statements
   - Use cause–event–impact format (Because of [cause], [risk event] may occur, leading to [impact] on [objectives]).
   - Include triggers, sources, affected objectives/processes, time horizon, and preliminary indicators.
   - Avoid control language; focus on uncertainty and impact.

7. Classify and tag
   - Assign categories (strategic, financial, operational, compliance, cyber/tech, ESG, third-party).
   - Tag by business unit, geography, processes, products, and stakeholders.
   - Map to objectives and risk appetite elements.

8. Rationalize and consolidate
   - De-duplicate similar risks across units; consolidate to enterprise-level themes.
   - Distinguish risks from issues/incidents and from root causes.
   - Maintain traceability from consolidated risks to source inputs.

9. Initial screening and prioritization (non-binding)
   - Perform quick inherent risk screening (likelihood/impact/time horizon) to flag potential materiality.
   - Identify “emerging risks” with low current likelihood but high potential impact.
   - Note known key risk indicators (KRIs) if available.

10. Validate and assign ownership
   - Review with risk owners and functional leads; refine statements and tags.
   - Present proposed enterprise risk list to the ERM committee for endorsement.
   - Assign executive sponsors and primary risk owners for each enterprise risk.

11. Record and communicate
   - Enter risks into the enterprise risk register with metadata and version control.
   - Produce summary outputs (heatmap/landscape, top risks list, emerging risks brief).
   - Distribute to stakeholders and feed downstream assessment and treatment processes.

12. Close and improve
   - Capture lessons learned and feedback from participants.
   - Update taxonomy, templates, and playbooks.
   - Schedule ad hoc triggers for interim identification if conditions change.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Enterprise risk register entries with:
  - Risk statements (cause–event–impact), triggers, sources, time horizon.
  - Tags/classifications; linkage to objectives and processes.
  - Ownership assignments and governance status.
- Consolidated enterprise risk landscape (top risks, emerging risks, themes).
- Supporting artifacts: workshop notes, interview summaries, data extracts, rationalization logs.
- Communication pack for executives/board (overview, trends, notable changes).
Success criteria:
- Risks are clearly articulated, de-duplicated, and linked to objectives and appetite.
- Appropriate ownership confirmed; governance endorsement obtained on schedule.
- Stakeholders agree risks reflect internal/external realities; minimal rework in assessment phase.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Board/Audit or Risk Committee: Oversight, challenge, approval of enterprise risk list.
- Executive Leadership (CEO/CFO/CIO/CISO/CHRO/BU Heads): Provide strategic inputs; own enterprise risks; sponsor actions.
- Chief Risk Officer (CRO)/ERM Lead: Own the process; set standards; facilitate identification; ensure quality and governance.
- ERM Team: Plan, coordinate, analyze inputs; run workshops; maintain registers; produce reporting.
- Business Unit Risk Champions/Process Owners: Contribute domain insights; identify unit-level risks; validate and escalate enterprise-level items.
- Compliance/Legal: Input on regulatory/compliance risks; horizon scanning; alignment with obligations.
- Internal Audit: Advisory challenge; share assurance insights; maintain independence from ownership.
- Finance/Treasury: Input on financial/liquidity/market risks; scenario assumptions.
- IT/Cyber/Privacy: Input on cyber/technology/data risks and threat landscape.
- Third-Party Risk Manager/Procurement: Input on vendor and supply-chain exposures.
- Strategy/PMO: Input on strategic initiatives and change-induced risks.
- ESG/Sustainability: Input on environmental, social, and governance risks and stakeholder expectations.

## Best Practices
- Anchor to objectives and risk appetite; identify risks that matter to value creation and preservation.
- Use a consistent taxonomy and standardized risk statement template.
- Combine multiple techniques (workshops, data analytics, horizon scanning) to reduce bias and blind spots.
- Separate cause, risk event, impact, and existing controls; avoid embedding controls in risk statements.
- Promote cross-functional participation and challenge to prevent siloed views.
- Maintain traceability from consolidated risks back to sources; version control the register.
- Include time horizon (short/medium/long-term) and emerging risk designation.
- Define materiality thresholds up front and apply them consistently.
- Integrate with strategic planning, capital allocation, and change governance calendars.
- Leverage technology to automate data collection, de-duplication, tagging, and reporting.
- Protect confidentiality and ensure ethical handling of sensitive risk information.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Incomplete stakeholder participation: Secure executive sponsorship; schedule early; use asynchronous input channels.
- Ambiguous risk statements: Train on cause–event–impact; provide exemplars and coaching; implement quality checks.
- Confusing issues/incidents with risks: Include a triage step and criteria; maintain separate logs with cross-references.
- Duplicates and fragmentation: Central rationalization; enforce taxonomy; use tooling to identify similar entries.
- Bias (recency, availability, optimism): Use external data, structured scenarios, and independent challenge from ERM/Internal Audit.
- Overemphasis on heatmaps: Focus on clear narratives, linkage to objectives, and KRIs; treat heatmaps as secondary visuals.
- Stale registers: Set refresh cadence; event-driven triggers; monitor external signals and KRIs for new entries.
- Misalignment with appetite: Map each risk to appetite statements; escalate where exposures exceed tolerances.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs/KRIs)
- Coverage:
  - % of strategic objectives mapped to at least one enterprise risk.
  - % business units/functions participating in the cycle.
- Quality:
  - % of risk statements passing quality checks (cause–event–impact, tagging completeness).
  - De-duplication rate and consolidation ratio (local to enterprise).
- Timeliness:
  - Cycle time from kickoff to governance approval.
  - On-time completion rate versus plan.
- Relevance:
  - % of enterprise risks linked to KRIs and to specific objectives/processes.
  - Variance between identified risks and subsequent incidents/losses (hit rate).
- Engagement:
  - Stakeholder satisfaction scores; number of challenge items resolved.
- Dynamics:
  - Number of new/emerging risks added per cycle; time to record after trigger event.

## Technology and Tools
- GRC/IRM platforms: ServiceNow IRM, MetricStream, RSA Archer, LogicGate, Riskonnect, OneTrust.
- Collaboration and documentation: Microsoft Teams, SharePoint, Confluence, Miro/Mural (workshops), survey tools (Qualtrics/Forms).
- Data sources and analytics:
  - Incident/loss systems; audit and compliance findings repositories.
  - SIEM/SOAR and threat intel feeds (for cyber risks).
  - Vendor risk/TPRM platforms; supply chain risk tools.
  - Financial and macroeconomic data providers; news/ESG analytics; horizon scanning services.
  - NLP/text mining for ticket/incident analysis; de-duplication and clustering tools.
- Visualization and reporting: Power BI/Tableau; ERM dashboards and heatmaps.
- Templates and repositories: Standard risk statement forms, taxonomy dictionaries, rationalization logs, version-controlled risk registers.
