- Risk/compliance review processes.

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and align
- Confirm scope, goals, constraints, and sponsorship expectations.
- Gather inputs: impacts, stakeholders, readiness, training timelines, risk.
- Identify comms lead, approvers, and channel owners; define SLAs.

2) Define objectives and success metrics
- Translate change goals into SMART comms objectives (e.g., 90% of impacted staff can correctly state what/why/when/how by X date).
- Select leading and lagging KPIs; define baselines and targets.

3) Segment audiences and map stakeholders
- Create audience personas (role, location, change impact level, language, shift patterns).
- Map influence/sender preferences (e.g., executive sponsor, line managers).
- Prioritize by impact and risk; identify groups needing tailored messaging.

4) Develop message framework
- Craft core narrative: purpose, urgency, benefits, risks, WIIFM, call-to-action.
- Create a message matrix mapping key messages to audience segments and channels.
- Prepare FAQs, escalation talking points, and myth-busting content.
- Define tone and style per brand and cultural norms.

5) Select channels and cadence
- Choose channels per audience reach and engagement (email, intranet, town halls, Teams/Slack, digital signage, leadership cascades, HRIS notifications).
- Define cadence by phase (pre-launch awareness, readiness, launch, reinforcement).
- Establish sender hierarchy (executive kickoff, manager cascades, SME deep-dives).

6) Build the editorial and campaign calendar
- Plot messages, send dates, senders, dependencies, and blackout windows.
- Include translation timelines, compliance review windows, and A/B tests.
- Coordinate with training and system release milestones.

7) Plan governance and approvals
- Document approval workflow and SLAs (e.g., Comms lead > Legal > Sponsor).
- Set version control, naming conventions, and content repository.
- Define crisis/issue comms triggers and decision-makers.

8) Address risk, compliance, and accessibility
- Review for privacy, labor relations, and regulatory considerations.
- Ensure inclusive design: alt text, captions, reading level, accessible formats.
- Classify communications by sensitivity (public/internal-confidential).

9) Resource and budget planning
- Estimate copywriting, design, translation, tools, and event costs.
- Assign roles for drafting, design, localization, delivery, analytics.

10) Develop assets and enablement materials
- Draft and design templates: emails, articles, slides, posters, videos.
- Build manager toolkits: briefing guide, printable talking points, Q&A, timelines.
- Prepare quick reference guides and support scripts for help desk.

11) Measurement and feedback design
- Instrument channels for analytics; define survey pulses and timing.
- Set up feedback channels (forms, Q&A inbox, office hours, comment threads).
- Establish dashboards and reporting cadence.

12) Pilot, test, and iterate
- Run A/B tests on headlines, calls-to-action, and timing with a pilot group.
- Validate comprehension and sentiment; adjust content and channels.

13) Launch and manage
- Execute per calendar; ensure timely executive and manager cascades.
- Monitor delivery, engagement, and feedback in near real time.
- Adjust messaging and cadence based on performance and readiness.

14) Closeout and learn
- Compare KPIs to targets; synthesize insights and lessons learned.
- Archive assets and decisions; update playbooks and templates.
- Transition to BAU comms for reinforcement if needed.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Communications strategy brief with objectives, scope, and metrics.
- Audience segmentation and stakeholder map/personas.
- Message framework and narrative; FAQ and talking points.
- Channel strategy and sender plan; editorial/campaign calendar.
- Creative assets and templates; manager/champion toolkits.
- Governance and approval workflow; approval log.
- Risk/compliance checklist and outcomes.
- Localization and accessibility plan.
- Measurement plan, dashboards, and reporting cadence.
- Distribution lists and channel configurations.
- Lessons learned and archived repository.

Success criteria:
- Timely, consistent communications aligned with change milestones.
- Targeted reach and comprehension thresholds met or exceeded.
- Positive sentiment trend and reduced resistance signals.
- Demonstrated contribution to adoption KPIs (e.g., behavior completion rates).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive sponsor: Sets vision; announces change; reinforces importance; approves key messages.
- Change leader/owner: Ensures alignment to business outcomes; provides content inputs; resolves conflicts.
- Change manager: Integrates comms with training, readiness, and adoption; tracks risks.
- Communications lead: Owns plan development, messaging, channel strategy, calendar, and analytics.
- Corporate/Brand communications: Ensures tone, brand, and corporate standards; supports high-visibility events.
- Legal/Compliance/Privacy: Reviews for regulatory and policy adherence; advises on risk mitigation.
- HR/Employee relations: Advises on workforce implications and labor considerations.
- IT/Channel owners: Enable delivery via platforms; provide analytics; ensure technical reliability.
- Localization/Accessibility specialist: Manages translation, cultural adaptation, and accessibility.
- People managers: Cascade messages; contextualize for team; solicit feedback; confirm understanding.
- Change champions/ambassadors: Advocate and model behaviors; provide grassroots feedback.
- Training lead: Aligns comms with learning content and schedules.
- Analytics/Insights: Sets up measurement and analyzes engagement and sentiment.
- PMO/Project manager: Tracks milestones, dependencies, and resource allocation.
- Service desk/Support: Prepares to handle inquiries; feeds issues back to comms team.

## Best Practices
- Align to change frameworks (e.g., ADKAR) to sequence messages: awareness before desire, knowledge, and reinforcement.
- Segment and personalize: Tailor messages to roles, impacts, language, and time zones.
- Clarify WIIFM for each audience; emphasize benefits and actions required.
- Use a message map to maintain consistency across channels and senders.
- Leverage trusted senders: executives for direction; managers for “what it means for me.”
- Layered, multi-channel approach with appropriate frequency and repetition.
- Keep it simple: clear calls-to-action, plain language, and scannable formats.
- Enable managers with kits and talking points; provide rehearsal time.
- Establish two-way feedback and act visibly on input to build trust.
- Pilot and A/B test to optimize timing, subject lines, and framing.
- Design for inclusivity and accessibility from the start (WCAG, captions).
- Coordinate with training and release plans to avoid message collisions.
- Maintain a single source of truth (intranet hub) and link all comms to it.
- Formalize governance: approval SLAs, version control, and change log.
- Plan for risk scenarios and crisis communications with pre-approved templates.

## Common Challenges
- Message overload and channel fatigue: Consolidate updates, set blackout windows, and prioritize critical messages.
- Inconsistent or conflicting messages: Use a central message map and single source of truth; enforce approvals.
- Low manager cascade compliance: Track cascade completion; provide easy-to-use kits; secure sponsor reinforcement.
- Insufficient targeting: Improve segmentation using role/location data; test and refine based on analytics.
- Delayed approvals: Define SLAs and escalation paths; pre-brief approvers; use parallel reviews where possible.
- Resistance and negative sentiment: Address concerns openly; showcase quick wins; leverage champions.
- Language and cultural barriers: Localize content; use regional examples; engage local leaders.
- Accessibility gaps: Conduct accessibility reviews; provide alternative formats and captions.
- Measurement blind spots: Instrument channels up front; combine quantitative analytics with qualitative feedback.
- Tech limitations: Work with channel owners to enable features; devise fallbacks; schedule maintenance windows.

## Performance Metrics
Leading indicators:
- Plan readiness: % assets approved before milestone; adherence to calendar.
- Reach and delivery: Delivery rate, open rate, unique reach, attendance at events.
- Engagement: Click-throughs, time on page, video completion, reactions/comments.
- Manager cascade completion: % managers who conducted briefings on time.
- Awareness and understanding: Pulse survey correct recall rates; comprehension quizzes.
- Sentiment: Net sentiment on internal social channels and survey verbatims.

Lagging indicators:
- Behavior/action completion: % completing required steps by deadline.
- Support impact: Volume and type of help desk tickets; repeat inquiries.
- Adoption and proficiency: Usage analytics of new tools/processes; error rates.
- Resistance indicators: Number of escalations, opt-out rates, negative feedback trends.

Targets and thresholds should be defined per audience and change impact, with baselines from prior initiatives where available.

## Technology and Tools
- Intranet/CMS: SharePoint, Confluence, or similar for hub pages and archives.
- Email and campaign tools: Microsoft 365/Exchange, Outlook Campaigns, Marketo, Mailchimp (for internal newsletters).
- Collaboration platforms: Microsoft Teams, Slack, Viva Engage/Yammer for social amplification and Q&A.
- Event and webinar tools: Teams Live, Zoom Webinars, Webex for town halls and training.
- Survey and pulse tools: Qualtrics, Glint, Microsoft Forms for awareness and sentiment checks.
- Analytics: Power BI, Tableau; built-in channel analytics (O365, Viva Insights, Google Analytics for intranet).
- Design and content: Adobe Creative Cloud, Canva; video tools (Camtasia, Loom).
- Translation/localization: Smartling, Phrase, Lokalise; glossaries and TMS integrations.
- Accessibility tools: WAVE, Axe, captions/subtitles generators.
- Work management: Jira, Asana, Monday.com for calendar, approvals, and tasks.
- Knowledge base and support: ServiceNow, Zendesk for FAQs and support scripts.
- Digital signage and on-prem channels: ScreenCloud or similar for frontline communications.

Process Details:
# [13.4.2.8] Establish/Clarify New Roles

## Overview
This process defines, validates, and communicates new or changed roles resulting from an organizational change initiative. It ensures people understand their responsibilities, decision rights, reporting lines, and success measures so the new operating model can function as intended. This stream typically follows change impact analysis and precedes training, staffing, and go-live.

Purpose:
- Translate the target operating model and redesigned processes into clear, actionable roles.
- Prevent ambiguity, duplication, or gaps in accountability that undermine adoption.
- Align roles to job architecture, compensation, compliance, and workforce plans.

Role in the organization:
- Acts as the bridge between process/capability design and people deployment.
- Coordinates closely with HR, line leaders, compliance, and change management to drive adoption and minimize disruption.

## Key Activities
- Role identification and consolidation (based on process/capability design and impact assessment).
- Role definition: accountabilities, responsibilities, decision rights, competencies, KPIs.
- Mapping to job architecture and grading; compensation alignment.
- RACI development across affected processes.
- Organizational structure and reporting line updates.
- Decision rights and governance alignment (e.g., RAPID, DMN).
- Compliance, labor relations, and regulatory review (e.g., SoD, union, local labor law).
- Access/permissions profile design (IAM/SoD).
- Staffing and transition planning (redeploy, recruit, upskill).
- Stakeholder review, sign-offs, and change communications.
- Integration with training plans, performance management, and knowledge transfer.
- Version control and continuous improvement after go-live.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Target Operating Model (TOM), process maps, and capability model.
- Change impact assessment and stakeholder analysis.
- Strategic objectives, success measures, and value case.
- Current org charts, job architecture, job descriptions, and competency frameworks.
- HR policies, compensation bands, geographic labor constraints, union agreements.
- Compliance requirements (e.g., segregation of duties, data privacy).
- Tool/system landscape and access control standards.
- Budget envelope and headcount guidelines.

Prerequisites:
- Executive sponsorship and change governance in place.
- Agreement on scope and design principles for roles (e.g., spans and layers, decision rights).
- Baseline of current roles and skills inventory.
- Resourcing for org design, HRBP, compensation, legal/compliance, and change management.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [13.4.2.1] Define change objectives and scope.
- [13.4.2.2] Assess change impacts.
- [13.4.2.4] Design future processes and capabilities.
- [13.4.2.6] Develop communication plan.
- [13.4.2.7] Develop training plan.
- Workforce planning, recruiting, and talent management processes.
- IT access provisioning and identity governance processes.

## Process Steps
1) Confirm design guardrails and criteria
- Align on role design principles (e.g., avoid overlap, minimize exceptions, align spans/layers).
- Define success criteria for role clarity and adoption.
- Approvers: Change Sponsor, Org Design Lead, HRBP.

2) Identify roles required by the future state
- Derive roles from process steps, handoffs, controls, and decision points.
- Consolidate or split roles where appropriate; challenge title inflation.
- Draft a role catalog with unique identifiers.

3) Define role accountabilities and decision rights
- For each role, document:
  - Purpose statement and major outcomes.
  - Core accountabilities and key responsibilities.
  - Decision rights using a standard (e.g., RAPID) and approvals needed.
  - Interfaces and handoffs to other roles/teams.
  - KPIs owned or influenced by the role.
- Create/update RACI matrices for key processes.

4) Specify competencies and qualifications
- Map required competencies, certifications, and experience levels.
- Distinguish “must-have” vs. “nice-to-have.”
- Identify reskilling/upskilling needs for incumbents.

5) Align with job architecture and compensation
- Map roles to job families/levels and pay bands.
- Validate market benchmarks; maintain internal equity.
- Flag roles requiring market pricing or special allowances.

6) Validate compliance and risk controls
- Run segregation-of-duties checks for roles with system access.
- Review data privacy, licensing, and jurisdictional labor law constraints.
- Engage legal/works councils/unions where required.

7) Update organizational structure and reporting lines
- Propose reporting relationships, spans, and layers.
- Update org charts and governance bodies (committees, forums) impacted.
- Ensure clarity for dotted-line and matrix relationships.

8) Define access profiles and system entitlements
- Translate role responsibilities into application access bundles.
- Prepare role-based access control (RBAC) configurations and SoD exceptions if any.
- Coordinate with IAM and IT security for provisioning plans.

9) Conduct stakeholder reviews and iterate
- Socialize with line managers, process owners, HR, and compliance.
- Pilot key roles in select teams or run tabletop simulations of workflows/handoffs.
- Incorporate feedback; finalize artifacts.

10) Plan staffing and transition
- Build a staffing plan: redeployment, backfills, hiring, contractors, timing.
- Create a transition plan: effective dates, knowledge transfer, shadowing.
- Define change impacts for individuals, including reward/incentive implications.
- Align with training curricula and onboarding content.

11) Approvals and documentation control
- Obtain formal sign-offs (Sponsor, HR, Legal/Compliance, Finance if budget impacts).
- Baseline and version-control role artifacts in a central repository.

12) Communicate and prepare for rollout
- Prepare tailored communications: FAQs, org announcements, manager toolkits.
- Deliver manager enablement sessions to reinforce messages and handle Q&A.
- Update job postings, internal mobility portals, and HRIS records.

13) Execute transition and support
- Provision system access, update distribution lists, re-route workflows.
- Implement staffing moves; initiate training and coaching; run hypercare.
- Track adoption, resolve role conflicts, and adjust as needed.

14) Measure and continuously improve
- Monitor KPIs, pulse surveys, and issue logs.
- Conduct a post-implementation review; refine roles and RACIs if performance gaps persist.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Role catalog with unique role IDs.
- Role profiles/role charters: purpose, accountabilities, decision rights, KPIs, competencies.
- Updated job descriptions mapped to job architecture and compensation bands.
- RACI matrices for affected processes.
- Decision rights and governance matrix (e.g., RAPID assignments).
- Updated org charts and spans/layers analysis.
- Access profiles/RBAC definitions and SoD assessment results.
- Staffing and transition plans; hiring requisitions where needed.
- Training needs analysis and role-based learning paths.
- Communication assets: FAQs, manager guides, employee briefs.
- Approved change log and version-controlled documentation in repository.
Success criteria:
- Employees report high role clarity and confidence.
- Minimal role conflicts/escalations and clean audit outcomes (SoD, compliance).
- Handoffs and decision-making occur at the right levels with expected speed/quality.
- Process performance improves to target without sustained disruption.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Approves role design principles and final role set; removes roadblocks.
- Org Design Lead: Owns role architecture, spans/layers, and overall coherence.
- HR Business Partner (HRBP): Ensures alignment with HR policies, talent implications, and change impacts.
- Compensation/Total Rewards: Maps roles to grades/bands; conducts market pricing; ensures internal equity.
- Legal/Compliance/Privacy: Reviews regulatory, labor law, SoD, and privacy implications; approves where required.
- Line Managers: Validate practicality of roles; own staffing, coaching, and performance alignment.
- Process Owners: Ensure roles align with process outcomes and controls; co-own RACIs.
- Change Management Lead: Integrates communications, engagement, and adoption tactics.
- Learning and Development: Defines role-based learning paths and enables knowledge transfer.
- IT Security/IAM: Designs and implements access profiles; conducts SoD checks.
- PMO/Program Manager: Schedules, tracks, and governs approvals, risks, and dependencies.
- Talent Acquisition/Workforce Planning: Executes hiring/redeployment plans.
- Works Council/Union Representatives (where applicable): Consults or negotiates per local requirements.

## Best Practices
- Start with the work, not titles: derive roles from processes, outcomes, and decisions.
- Co-design with stakeholders: involve managers, process owners, and doers to ensure practicality.
- Use simple, standard frameworks: RACI for accountability; RAPID or similar for decision rights.
- Minimize exceptions: standardize roles across similar teams to ease staffing and training.
- Pilot and iterate: test roles in limited scope and refine before broad rollout.
- Align to job architecture: maintain equity, mobility, and clear career paths.
- Embed compliance early: run SoD and legal checks during design, not after.
- Enable managers: provide coaching guides, talking points, and escalation paths.
- Integrate with performance management: tie role accountabilities to KPIs and incentives.
- Plan for knowledge transfer: structured handovers, shadowing, and documentation.
- Govern and version-control: maintain a single source of truth; track changes to roles.
- Consider DEI: design inclusive roles, avoid unintended adverse impact, and ensure accessible communications.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Ambiguity or overlap between roles
  - Solution: Tighten accountabilities; clarify decision rights; update RACI; run scenario walkthroughs.
- Resistance to change or title inflation
  - Solution: Communicate the “why”; link to value; set naming standards; use market-aligned titles.
- Misalignment with compensation/grade
  - Solution: Early comp partner engagement; apply job architecture rules; benchmark roles.
- Overloaded roles or unrealistic spans
  - Solution: Workload analysis; adjust spans/layers; redistribute tasks; phase responsibilities.
- Unclear decision rights leading to slow decisions
  - Solution: Use a decision-rights framework; publish governance; train managers on escalation paths.
- Compliance/SoD violations discovered late
  - Solution: Embed IAM/SoD reviews in design; predefine access bundles; plan compensating controls.
- Geographic/legal constraints
  - Solution: Localize role design; consult legal/works councils early; plan phased implementation.
- Insufficient staffing capacity or skills gaps
  - Solution: Redeployment plans, targeted hiring, upskilling, and interim coverage strategies.
- Inadequate manager enablement
  - Solution: Manager toolkits, rehearsal sessions, and ongoing office hours during hypercare.
- Poor documentation and version control
  - Solution: Central repository, naming/version standards, and change control workflow.

## Performance Metrics
Leading indicators:
- Role clarity index (pulse survey within 2–4 weeks of comms).
- Percentage of roles with approved profiles, RACIs, and decision-rights documented.
- Training completion and assessment scores for role-based learning.
- Access provisioning accuracy and cycle time at go-live.
- Percentage of employees staffed into new roles by target date.

Lagging indicators:
- Number of escalations due to unclear accountability.
- Handoff error rate or rework due to role confusion.
- Time-to-fill critical roles and internal mobility rate.
- Early-tenure turnover in newly created roles (first 6–12 months).
- Audit/compliance findings related to SoD, privacy, or labor law.
- Process performance improvement (e.g., cycle time, quality, NPS) attributable to new roles.

Targets and thresholds:
- ≥90% role clarity index; ≤5% access errors at go-live; ≥95% staffing completion by effective date; zero high-severity compliance findings.

## Technology and Tools
- HRIS/HCM: Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle HCM for job profiles, org charts, and staffing.
- Org design and modeling: OrgVue, Nakisa, Visier for spans/layers and scenario modeling.
- Process/RACI mapping: Microsoft Visio, Lucidchart, ARIS, Signavio for process flows and RACIs.
- Document and knowledge management: SharePoint, Confluence, Google Drive with version control.
- IAM/GRC: Okta, SailPoint, Azure AD, ServiceNow Access; SoD tools (e.g., SAP GRC).
- Project/Change management: Jira, ServiceNow, Smartsheet, MS Project; change calendars.
- Communication and enablement: MS Teams, Slack, Zoom; email campaign tools; intranet.
- Learning: LMS/LXP (Cornerstone, Docebo), digital adoption platforms (WalkMe, Whatfix).
- Survey/Feedback: Qualtrics, Glint, Culture Amp for role clarity pulses and sentiment.
- Analytics/Reporting: Power BI, Tableau for KPI tracking and dashboards.
- E-signature/Approvals: DocuSign, Adobe Sign for formal sign-offs when needed.

Process Details:
## Overview
Reengineering business processes and systems is the structured redesign of how work is performed and supported by technology to achieve step-change improvements in outcomes (cost, speed, quality, experience, compliance). Within Manage change > Implement change, this process takes approved change objectives and transforms them into redesigned operating processes, enabling systems, and supporting structures that deliver the desired results. It aligns people, process, data, and technology, starting from the target outcomes and working backward to create fit-for-purpose processes that are standardized, controlled, and measurable.

Primary goals:
- Eliminate waste, reduce variance, and simplify workflows while ensuring compliance and control.
- Rationalize and modernize the application and data landscape to support the new processes.
- Increase automation and straight-through processing where valuable.
- Establish process governance, metrics, and continuous-improvement mechanisms.
- Ensure adoption through targeted change management (communications, training, support).

This process builds on the selected process improvement methodology (for example, Lean, Six Sigma, BPM, Design Thinking), applying it consistently with enterprise architecture and change governance.

## Key Activities
- Define scope, objectives, and design principles for reengineering.
- Baseline current-state processes, systems, data, and performance (process mining, mapping).
- Analyze root causes of pain points and constraints (bottlenecks, risks, compliance gaps).
- Design target operating processes (To-Be), roles, controls, and decision models.
- Reengineer enabling systems and data (rationalize, configure, integrate, automate).
- Validate designs via simulation, prototypes, and pilots; refine based on feedback.
- Plan and execute implementation (backlog, releases, migration, training, cutover).
- Transition to steady-state operations with control plans and performance dashboards.
- Track benefits realization and feed continuous improvement.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Approved change objectives, business case, and success criteria.
  - Selected process improvement methodology and design standards (BPMN/DMN, UX, data).
  - Current-state artifacts: process maps/SOPs, KPIs, SLAs, risk/control registers, system inventory, integration maps, data dictionaries, customer feedback.
  - Regulatory and policy requirements (SOX, GDPR, HIPAA, GxP, ISO).
  - Architecture principles and guardrails; technology roadmaps.
  - Resource plan and budget; change and communications strategy.

- Prerequisites:
  - Executive sponsorship and governance structure (steering committee, design authority).
  - Identified process owner(s) and cross-functional team members.
  - Access to data sources needed for baseline and analysis.
  - Defined scope boundaries and constraints (timeline, compliance, markets, products).

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Select a process improvement methodology [13.4.x ref].
  - Define change strategy and roadmap; stakeholder engagement.
  - Risk management, compliance assessment, and information security reviews.
  - Portfolio governance for funding and prioritization.
  - Data governance, enterprise architecture, and IT change/release management.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and scope
   - Confirm objectives, target outcomes, and success metrics.
   - Define scope, assumptions, constraints, and exclusions.
   - Establish governance (roles, decision rights, stage gates).
   - Build a cross-functional team (business, IT, data, risk/compliance, CX, operations).
   - Create a high-level delivery roadmap and communication plan.

2. Baseline current state (As-Is)
   - Inventory processes, variants, and systems; identify stakeholders and customers.
   - Map processes using BPMN; capture roles, inputs/outputs, controls, and handoffs.
   - Use process mining and data analysis to quantify cycle times, wait times, rework, and defects; baseline KPIs.
   - Document pain points, failure modes, and customer experience issues (journey maps).
   - Identify regulatory obligations and existing control design/effectiveness.
   - Catalog integrations, data lineage, and data quality issues.

3. Analyze and diagnose
   - Perform value stream and waste analysis (Lean 8 wastes); bottleneck analysis.
   - Root cause analysis (5 Whys, fishbone) for top issues.
   - Variance analysis across geographies, products, or channels.
   - Risk and control gap assessment; map to compliance requirements.
   - Technology assessment: application fit, customization debt, integration complexity, NFRs (performance, availability, security).
   - Opportunities assessment: automation (workflow, RPA), self-service, straight-through processing, data standardization.

4. Define target outcomes and design principles
   - Set measurable targets (e.g., cycle time -40%, first pass yield +20%, cost/txn -25%).
   - Establish principles: customer-centric, standardize-then-automate, minimal customization, privacy/security by design, segregation of duties, exception handling, reusable APIs, data at the source, design for operations.
   - Confirm non-functional requirements and compliance criteria.

5. Design Target Operating Model (To-Be)
   - Process design:
     - Create To-Be process maps (BPMN) with swimlanes, events, decisions (DMN), and exception paths.
     - Define standard work, work-in-process limits, and service levels.
     - Specify controls and audit trail requirements; map to risk control matrix.
   - Organization and roles:
     - Define roles/responsibilities (RACI), required skills, and staffing model.
     - Propose org or role changes (e.g., centralized intake, control owner).
   - Data and information:
     - Define data model changes, master data ownership, data quality rules, and retention.
     - Specify critical data elements and lineage updates.
   - Performance and governance:
     - Define KPIs, dashboards, review cadence, and continuous improvement loop.

6. Reengineer systems and architecture
   - Option analysis: reuse vs configure vs replace; fit-gap against To-Be.
   - Application rationalization; determine build/buy decisions.
   - Solution architecture: target landscape, integration patterns (APIs/iPaaS), eventing.
   - Automation design: workflow/BPM, RPA, decision services, OCR/ML where appropriate.
   - UX design: forms, validations, accessibility, error handling.
   - Security and compliance: IAM, least privilege, SoD, encryption, logging, DPIA/TRA.
   - Non-functional design: capacity, resiliency, observability, supportability.
   - Implementation backlog: epics/stories, acceptance criteria, traceability to requirements.

7. Validate designs
   - Walkthroughs with SMEs; design authority review and approval.
   - Simulation of To-Be flows (where available) to forecast performance.
   - Prototypes/pilots in a controlled environment; capture feedback.
   - Update business case and benefits profile based on validated assumptions.

8. Implementation planning
   - Release plan: waves/increments; dependencies and cutover strategy (big bang vs phased).
   - Data migration: scope, mapping, cleansing, reconciliation, dual-run plans.
   - Test strategy: unit, SIT, UAT, performance, security, compliance/validation (e.g., GxP).
   - Change impacts: stakeholder impact assessment, training needs analysis, comms plan.
   - Operational readiness: support model, knowledge base, runbooks, SLAs, service catalog updates.
   - Risk management: RAID log with mitigations; contingency plans.

9. Build and configure
   - Agile delivery cadence with demos and stakeholder reviews.
   - Configure systems, develop integrations, automate workflows/bots, and build decision services.
   - Develop training materials, SOPs, work instructions, and job aids in parallel.
   - Prepare data migration scripts and execute test loads.
   - Maintain requirements traceability; manage change requests via governance.

10. Test and accept
   - Execute SIT; remediate defects; regression cycles.
   - UAT with business owners using real-life scenarios; sign-offs against acceptance criteria.
   - Performance and security testing; resolve findings.
   - Compliance validation (controls testing, documentation, e-signatures where required).

11. Deploy and cutover
   - Go-live readiness review; go/no-go decision by governance.
   - Execute cutover plan (backups, data migration, feature toggles, rollback plan).
   - Communications blast; deliver training; enable support channels.
   - Hypercare with enhanced monitoring and rapid defect resolution.

12. Transition to operations
   - Formal handover to operations/support; finalize runbooks, SOPs, and KPIs.
   - Activate process control plan; start performance reporting.
   - Close project documentation; archive artifacts and update repositories.

13. Benefits realization and continuous improvement
   - Track KPIs vs baseline; validate savings and experience outcomes.
   - Conduct post-implementation review and lessons learned.
   - Maintain a continuous improvement backlog; schedule incremental enhancements.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Process deliverables:
  - To-Be process maps (BPMN), decision models (DMN), and exception handling.
  - Standard operating procedures, work instructions, and control descriptions.
  - RACI and role definitions; skills/training matrix.
  - Process control plan, KPIs, and dashboard specifications.

- System and data deliverables:
  - Target solution architecture, integration specs, API contracts.
  - Configured applications, workflow automations, bots, and decision services.
  - Data model updates, master data governance artifacts, migration scripts and reconciliation reports.
  - Security and privacy artifacts (IAM roles, DPIA, threat model, logging/audit design).

- Change and enablement deliverables:
  - Implementation roadmap and release plan.
  - Test plans, cases, and traceability matrix; UAT sign-offs.
  - Training materials, comms assets, knowledge base articles, runbooks.
  - Go-live checklist, cutover plan, rollback plan, and hypercare plan.

- Success criteria:
  - Achievement of targeted KPIs within agreed stabilization period.
  - Compliance and control effectiveness validated with no material audit findings.
  - User adoption and proficiency metrics met (e.g., >90% training completion, system usage).
  - Benefits realization aligned to business case (e.g., ROI, payback period).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Owns vision and funding; clears escalations; approves key decisions.
- Process Owner: Accountable for process performance, scope, and To-Be design approval.
- Change/Transformation Lead: Orchestrates reengineering, governance, and stakeholder alignment.
- Business Architect: Aligns design with business capabilities and operating model.
- Process Analyst/Industrial Engineer: Maps/analyzes As-Is and designs To-Be; defines KPIs.
- Product Owner (IT): Owns backlog and value delivery across releases.
- Solution/Enterprise Architect: Defines target architecture and integration patterns.
- Data Architect/Steward: Owns data model, quality rules, and governance.
- Automation Lead (BPM/RPA): Designs and delivers workflow/robotic automation.
- UX Designer: Designs user journeys, forms, and accessibility standards.
- Compliance/Risk Officer: Ensures regulatory adherence and control design effectiveness.
- Information Security: Performs threat modeling, IAM design, and security testing.
- QA/Test Manager: Defines and executes test strategy; ensures traceability.
- Project/Program Manager: Plans, tracks, manages RAID, and reporting.
- Training and Communications Lead: Delivers enablement and adoption activities.
- Operations/Support Lead: Prepares runbooks, SLAs, and support transition.
- Finance/Benefits Analyst: Tracks benefits realization and validates savings.

## Best Practices
- Start with outcomes: design backward from measurable business and customer results.
- Standardize before automating; remove waste and simplify first.
- Use data-driven insights: leverage process mining and analytics to quantify gaps.
- Model with standards (BPMN/DMN) for clarity and maintainability.
- Minimize customization: prefer configuration and standard capabilities to reduce technical debt.
- Design for controls and compliance from the outset (SoD, audit trails, retention).
- Embed security and privacy by design; conduct DPIAs and threat modeling early.
- Build in observability: logs, metrics, traces mapped to KPIs and error budgets.
- Deliver iteratively: pilot high-value slices, learn fast, and scale.
- Incorporate human-centered design; focus on usability and employee experience.
- Maintain a single source of truth for process and system artifacts with version control.
- Align with enterprise architecture and data governance; avoid creating new silos.
- Plan robust testing and migration; rehearse cutover and rollback.
- Establish a change network (champions) to drive adoption and feedback loops.

## Common Challenges
- Scope creep and conflicting priorities
  - Mitigation: Clear scope statement, stage gates, change control board, prioritized backlog.
- Fragmented ownership and lack of buy-in
  - Mitigation: Active sponsor, defined process owner, stakeholder engagement plan, change champions.
- Poor data quality and limited visibility
  - Mitigation: Data profiling/cleansing plan, master data governance, process mining.
- Over-customization and technical debt
  - Mitigation: Architecture guardrails, design authority reviews, configuration-first approach.
- Integration complexity and legacy constraints
  - Mitigation: API-first strategy, incremental strangler patterns, integration inventory and testing.
- Underestimating compliance and security
  - Mitigation: Early risk/control mapping, security/privacy assessments, compliance validation testing.
- Inadequate testing and rushed cutovers
  - Mitigation: Comprehensive test strategy, rehearsals, feature flags, rollback plans.
- Adoption gaps and training shortfalls
  - Mitigation: Role-based training, just-in-time enablement, embedded help, hypercare.
- Process variance and localization needs
  - Mitigation: Global design with governed local extensions; manage variants explicitly.
- Benefits not realized
  - Mitigation: Tie KPIs to benefits, regular tracking, accountability with corrective actions.

## Performance Metrics
- Efficiency and quality:
  - Cycle time and lead time reduction; touch time vs wait time.
  - First pass yield; defect/rework rate; right-first-time percentage.
  - Cost per transaction/case; productivity (units/hour, FTE hours saved).
  - Automation/straight-through processing rate; exception rate.

- Experience and service:
  - Customer satisfaction (CSAT/NPS); employee satisfaction (eNPS).
  - SLA attainment; queue length and backlog aging; abandonment rate (if applicable).

- Compliance and risk:
  - Control effectiveness; number of audit findings; policy/SoD violations.
  - Data quality scores for critical elements; incident rate (security/privacy).

- Delivery and stability:
  - On-time milestone and release adherence; change failure rate; mean time to restore.
  - Defect density and escaped defects; test coverage; performance vs NFRs.
  - Adoption metrics: training completion, active users, task completion time.

- Benefits realization:
  - Realized vs planned savings/revenue uplift; ROI; payback period.
  - Time to value; percentage of benefits verified by Finance.

## Technology and Tools
- Process and analysis:
  - Process mining: Celonis, UiPath Process Mining, Software AG.
  - Modeling and documentation: Signavio, Camunda Modeler, Visio, Bizagi (BPMN/DMN).
  - Simulation: AnyLogic, Simul8; scenario modeling tools.
  - Requirements and collaboration: Confluence, Miro, Jama, Lucid.

- Workflow and automation:
  - BPM/workflow: Camunda, Appian, Pega, ServiceNow Flow.
  - RPA/Intelligent automation: UiPath, Automation Anywhere, Blue Prism.
  - Decision services: DMN engines, business rules management systems.
  - Document capture: OCR/ICR and IDP platforms.

- Systems and integration:
  - ERP/CRM and core systems: SAP, Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics, Salesforce.
  - Integration/iPaaS and APIs: MuleSoft, Boomi, Azure Integration Services, Apigee.
  - Data: ETL/ELT (Informatica, dbt), data quality/profiling, MDM platforms.
  - Identity and security: IAM, PAM, SIEM; data protection/DLP.

- Delivery and quality:
  - Agile/DevOps: Jira/Azure DevOps, Git, CI/CD pipelines, artifact repositories.
  - Testing: Selenium/Cypress, Postman, JMeter, security testing suites.
  - Monitoring/observability: Grafana/Prometheus, Splunk, Dynatrace, AppDynamics.

- Reporting and governance:
  - BI/analytics: Power BI, Tableau, Qlik.
  - ITSM and change: ServiceNow, BMC; CMDB.
  - Document management: SharePoint, document control systems (with versioning and approvals).

Process Details:
# [13.4.3.4] Monitor Change

## Overview
Monitor Change is the structured, ongoing assessment of a change initiative’s execution and outcomes. It ensures the change is progressing at the right pace, delivering intended impacts, and generating desired levels of adoption and engagement. It provides real-time insight into stakeholder reactions, sentiment, and performance, enabling early risk detection, timely course corrections, and informed decision-making.

Role in the organization:
- Governs the “check and adjust” aspect of change implementation.
- Aligns sponsors, project teams, and business units on progress and impact.
- Protects business continuity by identifying disruptions quickly.
- Accelerates benefit realization by removing adoption barriers and reinforcing successful behaviors.
- Provides data for steering committees and management to make evidence-based decisions.

## Key Activities
- Define the monitoring plan: indicators, baselines, targets, thresholds, cadence, and reporting.
- Instrument data sources: surveys, system usage analytics, service desk tickets, process KPIs, training data, and sentiment channels.
- Collect and validate data: automate feeds where possible; perform quality checks and bias detection.
- Analyze adoption, performance, and sentiment: trend analysis, segmentation, variance and root cause analysis.
- Report and communicate insights: dashboards and narratives tailored to stakeholders.
- Trigger interventions: corrective actions, reinforcement, communication updates, training adjustments.
- Manage issues, risks, and decisions: maintain RAID items and escalate per governance model.
- Capture lessons learned and update the monitoring plan based on findings.
- Transition to business-as-usual (BAU) monitoring once stabilization targets are met.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved change plan with scope, milestones, and benefits.
- Defined success metrics and targets (leading and lagging indicators).
- Baseline measures for impacted processes, systems, and behaviors.
- Stakeholder map, change impact assessment, and communications/training plans.
- Data access agreements and permissions; integration points for analytics.
- Governance structure (steering committee, decision rights, escalation paths).

Prerequisites:
- Executive sponsorship and visible support.
- Change agents/change network in place across impacted areas.
- Data privacy/compliance guidelines agreed (e.g., anonymity thresholds).
- Tools and dashboards provisioned; data quality checks configured.
- Training calendar and content mapped to monitoring milestones.
- Incident/problem management processes operational for impact tracking.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Plan Change (metric definitions, baselines, monitoring strategy).
- Execute/Implement Change (activities whose progress is monitored).
- Manage Stakeholder Engagement and Communications (input to and actions from insights).
- Training/Enablement (adjustments based on monitoring outcomes).
- Benefits Realization/Value Tracking (downstream use of monitoring data).
- Risk and Issue Management (shared with PMO/ITSM).

## Process Steps
1. Establish monitoring approach
   - Confirm objectives, success criteria, indicators, and targets.
   - Define cadence (e.g., weekly dashboards, monthly sentiment deep dives).
   - Set RAG thresholds and alert conditions; define escalation protocols.

2. Instrument and integrate data sources
   - Enable telemetry (system usage, feature adoption, process cycle times).
   - Configure survey pulses and feedback channels (anonymous where appropriate).
   - Integrate service desk/ticketing data for disruption signals.
   - Connect training/LMS data for completion and proficiency tracking.
   - Validate data lineage, quality, and refresh frequencies.

3. Baseline and segment
   - Capture pre-change baselines for all KPIs.
   - Segment by stakeholder group, location, role, function, and release wave.
   - Document assumptions and known confounders.

4. Collect and validate data (continuous)
   - Automate data ingestion; schedule manual inputs where needed.
   - Perform completeness, accuracy, and timeliness checks.
   - Monitor response rates and mitigate survey fatigue.

5. Analyze performance and adoption
   - Compare actuals vs. targets and baselines; visualize trends.
   - Conduct variance analysis and root cause analysis (5 Whys, fishbone).
   - Triangulate quantitative metrics with qualitative feedback.
   - Identify hotspots and bright spots.

6. Report and communicate
   - Produce tailored dashboards and executive summaries.
   - Highlight RAG status, risks, and decisions needed.
   - Share insights with change agents and owners; provide “so what/now what.”

7. Trigger interventions and adjustments
   - Execute corrective actions: targeted training, coaching, process tweaks, communication updates, job aids.
   - Reinforce successful behaviors: recognition, reuse of effective tactics.
   - Log actions, owners, due dates; track effect on KPIs.

8. Governance and escalation
   - Review status in change control and steering forums.
   - Escalate threshold breaches per predefined paths.
   - Align on scope/time/cost implications if course corrections are material.

9. Compliance, ethics, and data protection
   - Ensure adherence to privacy policies; enforce minimum cohort sizes.
   - Anonymize/aggregate sensitive data; maintain audit logs.

10. Iterate and stabilize
   - Reassess thresholds and indicators as the change matures.
   - Define stabilization criteria and handoff plan to BAU.
   - Capture lessons learned and update organizational playbooks.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Change Monitoring Plan (indicators, baselines, thresholds, cadence, roles).
- Dashboards and scorecards (executive, operational, team views).
- Weekly/monthly monitoring reports and executive summaries.
- Risk/Issue/Decision logs with action plans.
- Intervention backlog with owners and due dates.
- Lessons learned and knowledge artifacts.
- BAU monitoring handoff package.

Success criteria:
- Adoption and proficiency meet or exceed targets within planned timelines.
- Minimal business disruption (e.g., incidents within tolerance).
- Stakeholder sentiment at/above threshold and improving.
- Compliance with new processes/policies consistently achieved.
- Realized benefits tracking to plan; stabilization criteria met.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Champion change; remove barriers; approve major interventions.
- Change Lead/OCM Manager: Own monitoring process; synthesize insights; drive interventions.
- Change Analyst/OCM Analyst: Data collection, validation, analysis, dashboarding.
- Change Agents/Champions: Local feedback, pulse checks, on-the-ground interventions.
- Project/Program Manager: Integrate with project governance; manage RAIDs and schedule impact.
- Product Owner/Process Owner: Act on insights; prioritize backlog to improve adoption/usability.
- Data/BI Analyst: Build pipelines, ensure data quality, advanced analytics.
- Communications Lead: Tailor and deliver targeted messages based on insights.
- Training/Learning Lead: Adjust training content and cadence; track completion and effectiveness.
- HR/People Partner: Align incentives, performance measures, and reinforce behaviors.
- Service Desk/IT Ops: Provide incident/problem data; coordinate user support.
- PMO/Steering Committee: Review status, make decisions, and allocate resources.

## Best Practices
- Define both leading (readiness, sentiment, training completion) and lagging (productivity, error rates) indicators.
- Triangulate data: combine telemetry, surveys, and qualitative feedback for a balanced view.
- Predefine thresholds and action playbooks to accelerate response.
- Segment insights to target interventions where they matter most.
- Maintain psychological safety and anonymity to improve feedback quality.
- Visualize trends and deltas vs. baseline, not just point-in-time values.
- Establish a predictable cadence and keep reports concise and decision-oriented.
- Close the loop: communicate actions taken in response to feedback.
- Pilot and A/B test communications or training variants before broad rollout.
- Embed change KPIs into line management scorecards to drive accountability.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Low survey response or bias: Short pulses, rotate questions, ensure anonymity, use incentives, complement with passive data.
- Data fragmentation and poor quality: Centralize in a BI layer, define data standards, automate ETL, assign data ownership.
- Conflicting signals (e.g., high usage but low sentiment): Conduct targeted interviews; analyze task success and error rates; review UX frictions.
- Resistance or disengaged leadership: Provide leader-specific dashboards; coach sponsors; showcase peer success stories.
- Alert fatigue and slow interventions: Use clear RAG rules, prioritize top 3 issues, maintain an intervention backlog with SLAs.
- Privacy concerns: Aggregate small cohorts; follow data minimization; obtain consent; follow legal/privacy guidance.
- Scope creep in metrics: Stick to a critical few; revisit only at stage gates.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs)
Adoption and behavior:
- Active user/adopter rate, frequency of use, feature adoption rates.
- Time to proficiency; training completion and assessment scores.
- Compliance rates to new processes/policies.

Operational impact:
- Process cycle time, throughput, error/defect/rework rates.
- Service desk incidents, severity mix, time-to-resolve related to the change.
- Stabilization time post go-live; productivity delta vs. baseline.

Stakeholder experience:
- Sentiment score (e.g., CSAT/eNPS-like), confidence/readiness index.
- Feedback volume and resolution rate; change advocacy/ambassador NPS.

Benefit realization:
- Benefit attainment vs. plan (cost savings, revenue uplift, risk reduction).
- Utilization of new capabilities; reduction in legacy workaround usage.

Governance effectiveness:
- On-time delivery of monitoring reports; action closure rate and SLA adherence.
- Number of escalations resolved within agreed timelines.

Set RAG thresholds and trigger conditions for each KPI and review regularly.

## Technology and Tools
Data and analytics:
- BI/Visualization: Power BI, Tableau, Qlik.
- Data integration: Azure Data Factory, Fivetran, Informatica; data lake/warehouse.
- Statistical tools: Python/R, Excel with Power Query.

Feedback and sentiment:
- Survey/pulse platforms: Qualtrics, Medallia, Culture Amp, Microsoft Forms.
- Collaboration analytics: Microsoft 365/Viva Insights, Slack analytics, Workplace.
- Qualitative analysis: NVivo, thematic coding tools.

Digital adoption and telemetry:
- Digital adoption platforms: WalkMe, Pendo, Whatfix.
- Product analytics: Mixpanel, Amplitude.
- A/B testing/feature flags: LaunchDarkly, Optimizely.

Enablement and support:
- Learning management: Workday Learning, Cornerstone, SAP SuccessFactors.
- Knowledge base and guides: Confluence, SharePoint, Seismic.
- ITSM/ticketing: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, Zendesk.

Project and governance:
- Project/portfolio tools: Jira, Azure DevOps, MS Project, Smartsheet.
- RAID and decision logs: Confluence, Planner, Notion.

Security and compliance:
- Data masking/anonymization utilities; role-based access controls.

Implementation tips:
- Start with a minimal viable dashboard covering critical indicators; iterate.
- Automate data refreshes and alerting; document data definitions and owners.
- Ensure single sign-on and appropriate access controls for sensitive dashboards.

Process Details:
## Overview
Capture and reuse lessons learned from change process is the systematic practice of documenting, validating, and disseminating insights from completed (or in-flight) change initiatives so they can be reused to improve future changes. It closes the loop in the change lifecycle by turning experiences—successes, failures, risks, and mitigation strategies—into institutional knowledge, best practices, and reusable assets (case studies, playbooks, checklists). This process:
- Prevents recurrence of issues and reduces risk in future changes
- Accelerates delivery by providing proven patterns and guidance
- Improves change outcome quality and stakeholder satisfaction
- Builds organizational memory across functions and time
- Supports continuous improvement, compliance, and auditability

It operates as part of 13.4 Manage change, under 13.4.4 Sustain improvement, and integrates tightly with change monitoring, performance analysis, and best practice identification.

## Key Activities
- Plan and govern lessons learned management (scope, taxonomy, roles, cadence)
- Capture lessons via structured methods (After-Action Reviews, retrospectives, interviews, surveys, metrics analysis)
- Analyze and synthesize insights (root cause, contributing factors, impacts, recommendations)
- Validate and standardize (peer review with experienced personnel and SMEs)
- Classify and store (tagging, metadata, searchability, access controls)
- Create reusable artifacts (case studies, best practice guides, checklists, templates, guardrails)
- Disseminate and embed (training, communications, communities of practice, methodology updates)
- Integrate into delivery workflows (stage-gate criteria, change templates, risk registers)
- Measure usage and impact (KPIs, feedback loops) and continuously improve the knowledge base

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs
- Change records and documentation (charters, plans, stakeholder analyses, comms, rollout plans)
- Outcome data and KPIs (performance metrics pre/post change, adoption/utilization, benefit realization)
- Risk/issue logs, incident/problem records, defect logs, rollout/rollback details
- Stakeholder feedback (surveys, interviews, support tickets, complaints, praise)
- Project retrospectives/AAR notes, sprint retrospectives, post-implementation reviews
- Regulatory/compliance constraints relevant to the change

Prerequisites
- Change initiative has reached a defined milestone (e.g., go-live + stabilization period) or a significant event occurred (major issue, rollback, exceptional success)
- Governance structure and taxonomy for lessons learned are defined
- Knowledge repository and submission workflow are available
- Experienced personnel are identified and engaged for capture and validation
- Data access is granted; confidentiality and retention requirements clarified

Dependencies on other processes
- 13.4.3 Monitor and control change (provides performance data and issue logs)
- 13.4.4.1 Monitor the performance of re-engineered processes (feed of KPIs)
- 13.4.4.x Identify best practices (cross-feed; curated into standards)
- Knowledge management processes (content lifecycle, taxonomy, search)
- Risk management and audit/compliance (controls, evidence requirements)
- Training/enablement and communications functions

## Process Steps
1) Define scope and objectives
- Identify which changes will undergo lessons capture (all above a threshold, all with incidents, pilots, regulatory changes).
- Set objectives: reduce recurrence of top 5 issues by X%, publish lessons within Y days, produce case studies for strategic programs.

2) Establish governance and standards
- Define roles (owner, reviewers, approver), SLAs (e.g., publish within 15 business days of closeout), quality criteria.
- Define taxonomy and metadata (change type, domain, process area, tooling, risk category, lifecycle stage, impact, severity).
- Create standardized templates for lesson entries, case studies, and best practice guides.

3) Prepare the capture plan for each change
- Schedule capture events: AAR/PIR (post-implementation review), retrospectives, midpoint check-ins.
- Identify participants: include experienced personnel (SMEs, senior practitioners), change champions, users, sponsors, and delivery team members for a 360° view.
- Collect artifacts: metrics, logs, communications, decisions, exceptions.

4) Execute capture sessions
- Conduct structured sessions (AAR: what was supposed to happen, what happened, why, and how to improve).
- Use facilitation techniques to ensure psychological safety and candor; avoid blame.
- Supplement with targeted interviews and short surveys to include broader stakeholders.

5) Analyze and synthesize insights
- Perform root cause analysis (5 Whys, fishbone) on significant issues and success drivers.
- Quantify impacts (cost/time saved or lost, adoption rates, incident volumes, customer satisfaction shifts).
- Identify patterns across multiple changes (emerging best practices or systemic issues).

6) Draft lesson entries and reusable content
- For each lesson, capture:
  - Context: change scope, constraints, environment
  - Trigger: what event or decision led to the outcome
  - Actions taken
  - Outcome: qualitative and quantitative results
  - Root cause/contributing factors
  - Recommendation: what to do differently or repeat
  - Applicability conditions and limitations
  - Metadata/tags and related artifacts (links to change records, tickets)
- Create higher-order artifacts when warranted: case studies, playbooks, checklists, templates, decision trees, risk controls.

7) Validate and review
- Peer review by experienced personnel and relevant SMEs for accuracy, completeness, and generalizability.
- Legal/compliance review if content contains sensitive data; anonymize as required.
- Approver signs off according to governance.

8) Publish and store
- Publish in the knowledge repository with clear titles, tags, and summaries.
- Set access controls and retention policies; version-control the content.
- Link lessons to relevant processes, standards, and methodology pages.

9) Disseminate and embed
- Communicate highlights via newsletters, town halls, and communities of practice.
- Integrate into:
  - Change request templates (pre-populated risks/controls)
  - Stage-gate checklists and readiness assessments
  - Training curricula and onboarding for change roles
  - Tooling (contextual guidance in Jira/Azure DevOps/ServiceNow)

10) Enable reuse and adoption
- Set triggers: require referencing relevant lessons in each new change charter and risk assessment.
- Provide search guides and tagging conventions; run micro-learning on how to find and apply lessons.
- Offer office hours or coaching by experienced personnel for complex reuse scenarios.

11) Measure and improve
- Track usage analytics (views, references in change artifacts, training completions).
- Collect user feedback and ratings on lessons and artifacts.
- Run periodic curation: deduplicate, retire outdated content, update with new evidence.
- Report KPIs and improvement outcomes to governance.

12) Audit and compliance
- Maintain evidence trail for audits (meeting notes, approvals, change links).
- Confirm adherence to SLAs and content standards; remediate gaps.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs
- Curated lessons learned entries with standardized metadata
- Case studies and best practice guides derived from real changes
- Reusable assets: checklists, templates, playbooks, guardrails, risk controls
- Updates to methodologies, standards, and stage-gate criteria

Deliverables
- Lessons learned repository content and index
- Post-implementation review reports and AAR summaries
- Communication artifacts (newsletters, CoP briefs, training modules)
- Metrics dashboards on capture and reuse performance

Success criteria
- 100% of eligible changes complete lessons capture within SLA
- Reduction in recurrence of top issues by X% within Y months
- Measurable reuse: Z% of new changes reference applicable lessons
- Positive user satisfaction with relevance and usability (e.g., >4/5)
- Demonstrable cycle time or cost improvements linked to reused lessons

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Champion culture of learning; ensure funding and policy support.
- Change Management Lead: Owns process governance, objectives, and reporting.
- Knowledge Manager/Lessons Learned Lead: Maintains taxonomy, templates, repository; facilitates capture; curates content.
- Experienced Personnel/SMEs: Validate accuracy; contribute nuanced insights; mentor others on reuse.
- Project/Change Manager: Plans and executes capture sessions; ensures artifacts and metrics are available; drafts content.
- Business Process Owner: Confirms applicability to processes; embeds best practices into SOPs.
- Data/Business Analyst: Quantifies impacts; builds dashboards; identifies patterns.
- Compliance/Legal: Reviews for regulatory, privacy, and contractual constraints; approves publication/anonymization.
- Communications/Training: Packages and disseminates content; integrates into training and onboarding.
- Tool Administrator: Configures repositories, workflows, permissions, and integrations.
- Community of Practice Lead: Socializes lessons; drives adoption across domains.
- Internal Audit/QA: Periodically audits adherence and content quality.

## Best Practices
- Standardize the capture template and keep it concise; require context, action, outcome, recommendation, applicability.
- Use a clear taxonomy and tagging scheme; allow both enterprise and domain-specific tags.
- Time-box capture activities close to events (e.g., within 2 weeks of go-live) to improve accuracy.
- Ensure psychological safety; separate performance evaluations from learning sessions.
- Include experienced personnel and diverse perspectives to avoid blind spots.
- Quantify impacts where possible; pair qualitative narratives with metrics.
- Anonymize sensitive details; implement tiered access for confidential lessons.
- Build reuse into workflows (stage gates require referencing lessons; templates link to top lessons).
- Curate continuously; assign content owners and review cadences (e.g., every 6–12 months).
- Promote findability: meaningful titles, summaries, and cross-links; invest in search optimization.
- Close the loop: publicize “wins” where a lesson prevented an issue or saved time/cost.
- Automate where possible (metadata pre-fill from change records; notifications; analytics).
- Align with continuous improvement frameworks (Kaizen, DMAIC) and existing PM/ITSM practices.

## Common Challenges
- Low participation and incomplete inputs
  - Solutions: Make capture mandatory at closeout; leadership sponsorship; simple submission forms; recognitions or incentives; schedule sessions in advance.
- Poor quality or overly generic lessons
  - Solutions: Clear templates with examples; facilitator coaching; SME review; emphasize actionable recommendations and applicability conditions.
- Limited reuse/adoption
  - Solutions: Embed in stage gates; require citation of lessons; integrate into training; proactive communications and CoP sessions.
- Duplicate or outdated content
  - Solutions: Curators and periodic reviews; version control; merge duplicates; archive stale content with sunset dates.
- Sensitive information and legal risks
  - Solutions: Anonymize; redact; apply access controls; compliance review.
- Tool fragmentation and poor findability
  - Solutions: Single source of truth; enterprise search; consistent taxonomy; integrations with delivery tools.
- Difficulty proving impact
  - Solutions: Link lessons to KPIs; track references in change artifacts; capture before/after metrics; case studies demonstrating outcomes.
- Cultural resistance and fear of blame
  - Solutions: Psychological safety, blameless postmortems, leadership modeling vulnerability, focus on systems not individuals.

## Performance Metrics
- Coverage and timeliness
  - % of eligible changes with completed lessons capture
  - Median time from change stabilization to publication
- Quality and relevance
  - Content quality score from SME review
  - % of lessons with quantified impact and clear applicability conditions
- Reuse and adoption
  - Reuse rate: % of new change charters or risk logs referencing lessons
  - Views, searches, unique users, and average time-on-page for lessons content
  - Training completion rates for lessons reuse modules
- Outcomes and impact
  - Reduction in recurrence of top N issues
  - Reduction in change-related incidents/rollbacks
  - Cycle time or cost savings attributed to reused lessons
  - Stakeholder satisfaction (e.g., survey scores) post-change
- Process health
  - Content freshness: % reviewed within last 12 months
  - Duplicate rate and archive rate
  - SLA adherence for review and approval

Target examples (adapt to context)
- ≥95% coverage, ≤15 business days to publish, ≥60% of new changes cite lessons, ≥25% reduction in repeated issues within 12 months, ≥4.2/5 user satisfaction.

## Technology and Tools
- Knowledge repository and search
  - Confluence, SharePoint, ServiceNow Knowledge, Notion, or equivalent
  - Enterprise search with relevance tuning and filters
- Change and delivery systems
  - ITSM (ServiceNow, Remedy) for change records; integrations for metadata and cross-links
  - Project/Agile tools (Jira, Azure DevOps, MS Project) for retrospectives and artifacts
- Workflow and forms
  - ServiceNow Flow Designer, Power Automate, Jira Workflows for submissions, reviews, and approvals
- Analytics and dashboards
  - Power BI, Tableau, or Looker for KPI tracking and impact analysis
- Collaboration and communication
  - Microsoft Teams, Slack, email campaigns, intranet portals for dissemination
- Survey and feedback
  - Microsoft Forms, Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey for stakeholder feedback and ratings
- Document management and compliance
  - Version control, access control, retention policies; DLP tools for sensitive content
- Training and enablement
  - Learning Management System (Cornerstone, Workday Learning) to embed lessons into curricula
- AI-assisted capabilities (optional)
  - Summarization of sessions, deduplication suggestions, tag recommendations, and suggested related content

Process Details:
## Overview
Develop governance model with roles and accountability is the process of defining how knowledge is owned, curated, protected, shared, and improved across the organization. It establishes the decision rights, policies, standards, roles, and operating mechanisms that ensure the organization’s collective knowledge is:

- Aligned to strategy and business outcomes
- Accurate, current, findable, secure, and compliant
- Owned and actively managed across its lifecycle
- Accessible to those who need it, with appropriate controls
- Sustainable through clear accountability and ongoing measurement

This process sits within the KM strategy domain and translates strategy into a practical operating model (who decides what, how decisions are made and enforced, and how performance is monitored). It provides the foundation for consistent KM execution across functions and regions, reducing risk, duplication, and waste while increasing reuse, speed-to-knowledge, and innovation.

## Key Activities
- Define governance objectives, scope, and principles aligned to the KM strategy
- Map stakeholders and establish a cross-functional governance coalition
- Assess current-state governance (roles, policies, processes, systems)
- Design the governance structure (e.g., KM Council/Board, Working Groups, Communities of Practice)
- Define roles, responsibilities, and decision rights (RACI) for the knowledge lifecycle
- Develop KM policies, standards, and procedures (creation, validation, metadata, access, retention)
- Define risk, compliance, security, and privacy controls tied to the knowledge lifecycle
- Establish performance management (KPIs, dashboards, reviews, audits)
- Create an implementation roadmap, change management, and communications plan
- Socialize, validate, and secure formal approval; plan for periodic review and continuous improvement

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Enterprise and business unit strategies, KM vision and objectives
  - Inventory of current knowledge repositories, content types, and owners
  - Existing policies: information security, privacy, records retention, data classification, IP
  - Regulatory and contractual requirements (e.g., data protection, industry standards)
  - Enterprise architecture, data governance frameworks, and IT service management practices
  - Risk assessments, audit findings, and incident reports related to information/knowledge
  - Cultural and change readiness insights; stakeholder maps; previous KM efforts

- Prerequisites:
  - Executive sponsorship and mandate for KM governance
  - Cross-functional core team (KM, IT, Security, Legal/Compliance, Records, HR/L&D, key business units)
  - Budget and capacity for design, socialization, and pilot rollout
  - Agreement on KM scope and priority domains (e.g., customer support knowledge, R&D, policies)

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - 13.5 Develop and manage enterprise-wide KM capability (overall KM operating model)
  - 13.5.1 Develop KM strategy (vision, goals, priority areas)
  - Data governance, records management, and information security governance
  - Legal/compliance and risk management processes
  - Change management and training enablement
  - Enterprise architecture and IT governance for platform decisions

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and frame
   - Confirm objectives, scope, timeline, and success criteria.
   - Appoint an Executive Sponsor and KM Governance Lead.
   - Output: Project charter and stakeholder engagement plan.

2. Assess current state
   - Identify existing governance structures, roles, content ownership, and policy gaps.
   - Map repositories, lifecycle practices, and risks.
   - Output: Current-state assessment and gap analysis.

3. Define governance principles and objectives
   - Examples: “Value-driven,” “Lightweight and scalable,” “Privacy-by-design,” “Federated with clear ownership,” “Automation-first.”
   - Output: Governance principles and prioritized objectives.

4. Design governance structure
   - Define bodies: KM Council/Board (cross-functional decision authority); Domain Working Groups; Taxonomy/Metadata Working Group; Content Quality panel; Communities of Practice.
   - Specify charters, meeting cadences, voting/approval methods, quorum rules.
   - Output: Governance structure and charters/terms of reference.

5. Define roles and accountabilities
   - Identify enterprise and domain roles (e.g., Knowledge Owners, Stewards, Curators, Community Leaders).
   - Create RACI for lifecycle stages: Create/Acquire, Validate, Classify/Tag, Publish, Discover/Use, Maintain, Archive/Dispose.
   - Output: Role catalog, RACI matrices, job descriptions or role definitions.

6. Establish decision rights and escalation paths
   - Specify who recommends, approves, consults, and is informed for key decisions (policies, standards, taxonomy changes, platform changes, exceptions).
   - Define conflict resolution and escalation routes.
   - Output: Decision rights matrix and escalation procedures.

7. Develop policy and standards suite
   - Core policies: Knowledge Management Policy, Acceptable Use, Content Quality, Metadata/Taxonomy, Access and Security, Retention and Disposition, Translation/Localization, Collaboration & Community.
   - Standards: Naming, tagging, versioning, review cycles, accessibility, interoperability.
   - Procedures/SOPs: Content submission and approval, review and refresh, exception handling, takedown/legal hold.
   - Output: Policy documents, standards, SOPs, templates.

8. Define risk and compliance controls
   - Map lifecycle controls to regulatory and contractual requirements (e.g., privacy, records, IP).
   - Integrate with security classification, DLP, IAM, legal hold, and retention schedules.
   - Output: Control framework, compliance mappings, and audit checklist.

9. Specify performance management and assurance
   - Select KPIs, thresholds, review cadences, and reporting formats.
   - Plan audits, control testing, and corrective action processes.
   - Output: Metrics catalog, dashboard design, assurance plan.

10. Design operating mechanisms
    - Meeting rhythms, decision logs, change control for policies/taxonomy, onboarding for new stewards, training and certification for roles.
    - Incentives and recognition for stewardship and reuse.
    - Output: Operating playbook and enablement materials.

11. Define technology enablement requirements
    - Workflow for approvals, metadata enforcement, retention automation, access controls, search analytics, dashboarding.
    - Integrations with CMS/knowledge platforms, GRC, records, and identity.
    - Output: Functional and non-functional requirements; backlog for IT.

12. Socialize and iterate
    - Conduct reviews with key business units, legal, security, and frontline users.
    - Pilot governance mechanisms in a priority domain; gather feedback and refine.
    - Output: Revised artifacts and pilot report.

13. Approve and adopt
    - Route policies and governance model for formal approval (KM Council, Legal, Executive Sponsor).
    - Publish in official policy repository; communicate effective dates and expectations.
    - Output: Approved governance package; communications plan executed.

14. Plan rollout and continuous improvement
    - Roll out role assignments, training, and onboarding; schedule periodic reviews.
    - Establish feedback loops and change request intake for governance updates.
    - Output: Implementation roadmap, training completion, CI backlog.

- Governance charter and structure (councils, working groups, CoPs) with terms of reference
- Role catalog with RACI matrices and role descriptions
- Decision rights matrix and escalation workflow
- KM policy suite, standards, SOPs, and templates
- Knowledge lifecycle model and ownership map
- Control framework and compliance mapping to regulations and enterprise policies
- Operating playbook (meeting cadences, decision logs, change control, onboarding)
- Technology enablement requirements and backlog
- Communications and change management plan; training materials
- Approval records and publication in policy repository

- Success criteria:
  - Formal approval by governing bodies and publication of policies
  - 100% coverage of priority domains with assigned Knowledge Owners and Stewards
  - Compliance readiness: controls mapped and testable; no critical audit gaps
  - Adoption indicators: policy acknowledgment rates, training completion, use of workflows
  - Early outcome signals: reduction in duplicate content, improved findability and reuse

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Authorizes governance, resolves escalations, secures funding, champions adoption.
- KM Governance Lead/Head of KM: Orchestrates design and rollout; chairs KM Council; owns KPIs.
- KM Council/Board (cross-functional leaders): Approves policies and standards; prioritizes investments; arbitrates cross-domain issues.
- Domain Knowledge Owners (per BU/function): Accountable for domain knowledge quality, risk, and compliance; approve content and lifecycle actions.
- Knowledge Stewards/Curators: Operate day-to-day processes (review/refresh, metadata, quality checks); monitor dashboards; drive corrections.
- Taxonomy/Metadata Manager: Manages vocabularies, tagging standards, and change control; ensures search/findability.
- Content Authors/SMEs: Create/maintain content; comply with standards; respond to steward feedback.
- Community of Practice Leaders: Facilitate peer knowledge sharing; surface best practices and governance feedback.
- Information Security Officer: Defines access controls, classification, and DLP requirements; reviews exceptions.
- Privacy Officer/Legal/Compliance: Ensures policies meet regulatory and contractual obligations; manages legal holds and takedowns.
- Records Manager/Archivist: Aligns retention/disposition with records schedules; oversees defensible deletion.
- IT Platform Owner/Enterprise Architect: Ensures platforms support governance workflows, metadata, and integrations; manages change.
- HR/L&D: Integrates roles into job profiles and performance objectives; delivers training and certification.
- Change Manager/Communications: Plans and executes stakeholder engagement, training, and adoption activities.
- Internal Audit/Risk: Tests controls; reports findings; verifies remediation.

## Best Practices
- Align to enterprise strategy and risk appetite; keep governance value-focused and outcome-driven.
- Use a federated model: central standards with domain ownership; avoid “one-size-fits-all.”
- Keep it lightweight: minimum viable policies with automation and guardrails embedded in tools.
- Define clear, unambiguous decision rights and escalation paths; publish a RACI.
- Integrate with existing governance (data, security, records) to avoid duplication.
- Treat taxonomy and metadata as first-class assets; manage with change control.
- Embed lifecycle into daily work: required fields, review reminders, automated retention.
- Incentivize stewardship and reuse; recognize communities and contributors.
- Pilot in high-impact domains; iterate before scaling.
- Measure leading and lagging indicators; review regularly and act on insights.
- Align to relevant standards where appropriate (e.g., ISO 30401 for KM, ISO 27001 for security, ISO 15489 for records).
- Ensure accessibility and inclusivity; support localization where needed.

## Common Challenges
- Role ambiguity and overlaps
  - Solution: Publish RACI and decision matrices; run role onboarding and clinics; update job descriptions.

- Overly heavy governance that hinders adoption
  - Solution: Start with MVP policies; automate checks; remove non-value steps; gather user feedback.

- Fragmented repositories and shadow systems
  - Solution: Catalog systems; define integration and consolidation roadmap; enforce platform standards for new content.

- Poor taxonomy and metadata quality
  - Solution: Establish taxonomy governance; mandate metadata; provide tagging aids and training; monitor search analytics.

- Resistance to change and low participation
  - Solution: Executive sponsorship, targeted communications, champions network, incentives, quick wins.

- Compliance gaps (privacy, retention, IP)
  - Solution: Map controls to regulations; embed legal hold and retention automation; conduct periodic audits.

- Global/regional inconsistencies
  - Solution: Global standards with local addenda; regional representatives on governance bodies; clear exception processes.

- Sustaining momentum
  - Solution: Regular council cadence, transparent dashboards, recognition programs, continuous improvement backlog.

- Governance coverage and readiness
  - % priority domains with assigned Owners/Stewards

  - Training completion rates for governance roles

  - Policy/standard approval cycle time
  - % content with required metadata and owner assigned
  - % content within review/refresh SLA

- Quality, access, and reuse outcomes
