Process Details:
# [13.9.2.1] Provide Sustainability Training

## Overview
Provide Sustainability Training is the structured process for planning, designing, delivering, and continuously improving sustainability education across the organization. It equips employees, leaders, suppliers, and key partners with the knowledge and skills to act in alignment with the company’s ESG strategy, regulatory obligations, and stakeholder expectations. The process ensures role-based enablement, measurable learning outcomes, and audit-ready records.

This process underpins the Manage Sustainability Capability by:
- Translating the sustainability strategy, targets, and risk controls into practical, role-relevant behaviors.
- Building organization-wide literacy on material ESG topics (e.g., climate, human rights, ethics, circularity, responsible sourcing).
- Supporting compliance with applicable standards and regulations (e.g., GRI, SASB/ISSB, CSRD, TCFD-influenced disclosures, modern slavery legislation, anti-corruption).
- Enabling continuous improvement, innovation, and culture change through learning communities and recognition.

## Key Activities
- Conduct training needs analysis (TNA) based on ESG materiality, risk, and role profiles.
- Define learning objectives and compliance requirements per audience segment.
- Design curriculum, learning paths, and modalities (e-learning, microlearning, workshops, toolbox talks, simulations).
- Develop or curate content; ensure accessibility, localization, and legal/compliance review.
- Plan resources, budget, schedule, and change management.
- Configure LMS/LXP, enrollment rules, and data integrations with HRIS and GRC.
- Deliver training and enablement through blended approaches and learning communities.
- Assess knowledge and certify where required; manage exceptions and escalations.
- Track completion, engagement, and outcomes; gather feedback (Kirkpatrick Levels 1–4).
- Report results for management, compliance, and external assurance; retain evidence.
- Continuously improve content and methods based on performance and regulatory change.
- Extend training to suppliers/partners as needed; incorporate into contracts.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Sustainability strategy, goals, policies, and codes of conduct.
  - ESG materiality assessment and risk register.
  - Regulatory and voluntary ESG reporting requirements (by region/industry).
  - Role taxonomy and org structure; audience segmentation (exec, managers, operations, procurement, finance, product, sales/marketing, facilities, IT, HR, EHS, supply chain).
  - Historical training data, audit findings, incidents, and corrective actions.
  - Available budget, resource plan, and training calendar.
  - Existing training platforms, content libraries, and vendor options.

- Prerequisites:
  - Governance established (sponsorship, RACI, decision rights).
  - Approved content standards (style, brand, accessibility, language).
  - Data privacy and security controls for learner data.
  - Legal/compliance review process for ESG claims and commitments.

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Sustainability strategy and policy management.
  - Risk and compliance management (GRC).
  - Enterprise Learning & Development (L&D) and HR (onboarding, performance).
  - IT for LMS/LXP, SSO, integrations.
  - Communications/Change Management.
  - Procurement/Vendor management (external content or delivery partners).
  - Internal Audit/Quality for assurance of training effectiveness and evidence.

## Process Steps
1. Establish governance and scope
   - Appoint Sustainability Training Lead and cross-functional working group (L&D, Legal, Compliance, EHS, HR, IT, Comms, Regional Leads).
   - Define scope (audiences, geographies, languages, topics, compliance obligations).
   - Approve RACI, budget, milestones, and success criteria.

2. Training needs analysis (TNA)
   - Map ESG risks and strategic priorities to roles and competencies.
   - Identify regulatory/assurance-driven training mandates.
   - Analyze gaps using surveys, interviews, performance and audit data.
   - Prioritize topics based on risk, impact, and readiness.

3. Define learning objectives and compliance criteria
   - For each audience/topic, write measurable objectives (e.g., “Calculate Scope 3 Category 1 emissions for assigned suppliers”).
   - Specify completion, recertification cadence, assessment standards, and evidence requirements.
   - Determine mandatory vs. elective status.

4. Design curriculum and learning paths
   - Create tiered pathways: foundational (all employees), role-based modules (e.g., procurement due diligence), leadership modules, and champion tracks.
   - Select modalities: e-learning, microlearning, instructor-led workshops, webinars, toolbox talks, simulations/VR, job aids, playbooks.
   - Build a training calendar aligned to business cycles (onboarding, performance reviews, budget season).

5. Build vs. buy and resourcing plan
   - Decide which content to develop internally vs. procure/curate externally.
   - Source SMEs; engage vendors if needed (RFP/RFQ).
   - Finalize resource plan (instructional designers, facilitators, translators).

6. Content development and localization
   - Develop storyboards, scripts, and assets; incorporate case studies and scenarios relevant to functions.
   - Ensure accuracy and legal review to avoid greenwashing.
   - Apply accessibility (e.g., WCAG) and inclusive design; provide transcripts and captions.
   - Localize for language and regional regulations; verify cultural fit.

7. Platform configuration and data readiness
   - Configure LMS/LXP courses, learning paths, due dates, and recurrence rules.
   - Integrate with HRIS for audience targeting; set up xAPI/SCORM tracking.
   - Set up dashboards and alerts; define data retention and privacy settings.

8. Pilot and quality assurance
   - Run pilots with representative users and regions.
   - Test usability, accessibility, assessment validity, and technical performance.
   - Address feedback; obtain final approvals (Sustainability, Legal/Compliance, L&D).

9. Communication and change enablement
   - Launch communications plan: leadership messages, FAQs, intranet pages, manager toolkits, incentives.
   - Engage Green Teams/Champions to promote and mentor.
   - Provide helpdesk and escalation path.

10. Delivery and facilitation
    - Roll out courses per plan; enable self-paced and scheduled sessions.
    - Provide offline or kiosk options for frontline workers.
    - Track real-time progress; send nudges and reminders.

11. Assessment, certification, and exception management
    - Administer knowledge checks, practical exercises, or simulations.
    - Issue certificates/badges; update skills matrices.
    - Manage non-compliance: escalation to managers, completion SLAs, corrective actions.

12. Measurement and reporting
    - Capture Level 1 (reaction), Level 2 (learning), Level 3 (behavior), and where feasible Level 4 (outcomes).
    - Report completion and impact to leadership, risk committees, and for audit/regulatory evidence.
    - Segment analytics by role, region, and function; identify hotspots.

13. Continuous improvement
    - Conduct after-action reviews; update content based on new regulations, audit findings, and strategy shifts.
    - Refresh cycle (e.g., annual for foundations; quarterly for regulatory updates).
    - Retire or replace outdated modules; maintain version control and archive evidence.

14. Supplier and partner enablement (as applicable)
    - Define supplier training requirements; embed in contracts and onboarding.
    - Provide access to training portal or shared content; track participation.
    - Include supplier metrics in sustainability reporting where relevant.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Training strategy and curriculum map by audience and topic.
- Learning objectives and compliance matrix.
- Developed/curated content (courses, toolkits, job aids, playbooks, simulations).
- LMS/LXP configurations, enrollment rules, and reporting dashboards.
- Communication materials and manager toolkits.
- Attendance/completion records, assessments, certificates/badges.
- Post-training evaluation reports and improvement plans.
- Audit-ready evidence pack (versioned content, approvals, attendance, assessment results).
- Supplier enablement package (requirements, access instructions, evidence collection).

- Success criteria:
  - Target audience coverage achieved (e.g., 95% completion within 60 days for mandatory modules).
  - Assessment pass rates and observed behavior change targets met.
  - Positive learner satisfaction (e.g., ≥4.3/5) and manager endorsement.
  - Reduction in relevant non-compliance incidents or audit findings.
  - Content maintained within defined currency window (e.g., updated within 90 days of regulatory change).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor (e.g., CSO/Chief Sustainability Officer)
  - Approves strategy, budget, and success criteria; champions the program.
- Sustainability Training Lead (Process Owner)
  - Owns TNA, curriculum, delivery plan, and continuous improvement; coordinates stakeholders.
- Sustainability SMEs (Climate, Human Rights, Circularity, EHS, etc.)
  - Provide expert content; validate accuracy and applicability.
- L&D/Instructional Design
  - Design learning experiences; develop content; ensure pedagogy and accessibility.
- Legal/Compliance
  - Review content for regulatory accuracy and legal risk; approve claims and commitments.
- HR Business Partners
  - Align with performance, onboarding, and competency frameworks; support adoption.
- IT/LMS Administrator
  - Configure platforms; manage integrations, data, and access; ensure uptime and support.
- Communications/Change Management
  - Develop and execute communication campaigns; stakeholder engagement.
- People Managers
  - Reinforce learning in daily work; ensure team completion; coach behavior change.
- Regional/Functional Leads
  - Localize content; coordinate delivery; monitor compliance in their areas.
- Internal Audit/Quality
  - Test controls; verify evidence; recommend improvements.
- Procurement/Vendor Manager
  - Source and manage external content providers and facilitators.
- Data Privacy/Security
  - Ensure compliance with data protection and retention policies.
- Supplier Relationship Managers (if applicable)
  - Communicate requirements; track supplier training adherence.

## Best Practices
- Align learning outcomes to ESG materiality, risk controls, and KPIs; avoid “one-size-fits-all.”
- Use role-based, scenario-driven learning with real examples and decision-making practice.
- Blend modalities and embed into workflows (microlearning, job aids, toolbox talks).
- Make accessibility and inclusivity non-negotiable; support multiple languages.
- Apply the Kirkpatrick model and focus on behavior change, not just completion.
- Establish Green Champions and communities of practice to sustain engagement.
- Gamify thoughtfully (badges, leaderboards) and recognize achievements.
- Update content frequently; maintain a single source of truth with version control.
- Integrate with onboarding and annual compliance cycles; automate recertifications.
- Include supplier enablement where supply chain risks are material.
- Guard against greenwashing; ensure claims are substantiated and balanced.
- Protect learner data; adhere to privacy-by-design and minimum retention.
- Pilot before enterprise rollout; iterate using feedback loops.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Low engagement or completion
  - Secure visible leadership sponsorship; set manager accountability; use reminders and incentives; keep modules short and relevant.
- Overly generic content
  - Co-create with SMEs; use role-based branching scenarios and local case studies.
- Rapidly changing regulations
  - Establish a regulatory watch; schedule quarterly content reviews; modularize for quick updates.
- Limited frontline access to digital learning
  - Provide kiosks, mobile/offline formats, QR codes on equipment; schedule supervised toolbox talks.
- Measuring impact beyond completion
  - Define behavior and outcome indicators upfront; embed on-the-job assignments and manager check-ins; track process KPIs linked to training.
- Global/local tension
  - Build a global core with localized addenda; engage regional leads; allow 20–30% localization.
- Greenwashing and legal risk
  - Mandatory legal/compliance review; use neutral, evidence-based language; cite sources.
- Resource constraints
  - Prioritize high-risk topics; leverage curated content; train-the-trainer to scale.
- Data quality and reporting gaps
  - Integrate LMS with HRIS; standardize data fields; perform routine data quality checks.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs)
- Coverage and compliance
  - Completion rate by audience and deadline.
  - Recertification on-time rate.
  - Overdue training count and aging.
- Learning effectiveness
  - Assessment pass rate; average score.
  - Knowledge retention (re-tests after 60–90 days).
  - Behavior change indicators (manager observations, adoption of new procedures).
- Business and risk outcomes
  - Reduction in relevant incidents, non-conformities, or audit findings.
  - Increase in improvement ideas submitted/implemented (e.g., energy, waste).
  - Supplier adherence to required training (percentage meeting contract terms).
- Experience and efficiency
  - Learner satisfaction (CSAT/NPS).
  - Time-to-deploy new/updated modules from identified need.
  - Cost per learner/hour; training hours per FTE.
  - Content freshness (days since last review); localization turnaround time.
- Accessibility and inclusivity
  - Accessibility compliance score; language coverage vs. target.

Targets should be tailored per organization and risk profile (e.g., ≥95% mandatory completion within 60 days; ≥85% pass rate; ≤2% overdue).

## Technology and Tools
- Learning platforms
  - LMS/LXP (e.g., SAP SuccessFactors, Workday Learning, Cornerstone, Degreed, EdCast).
  - Learning Record Store (xAPI) and analytics integration.
- Content creation and delivery
  - Authoring tools (Articulate 360/Rise, Adobe Captivate, Camtasia).
  - Virtual classrooms/webinars (MS Teams, Zoom) and engagement tools (Kahoot, Mentimeter).
  - AR/VR and simulation tools for EHS scenarios (as appropriate).
- Analytics and reporting
  - BI dashboards (Power BI, Tableau); survey tools (Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey).
  - GRC systems for mapping training to controls and audit evidence.
- Knowledge and document management
  - Intranet/SharePoint/Confluence for job aids and playbooks; version control repositories.
- Localization and accessibility
  - Translation management (Smartling, Lokalise); captioning/transcription services; accessibility checkers.
- Identity and integration
  - HRIS integration for audience targeting; SSO; API connectors.
- Credentialing
  - Digital badging/certification platforms (Credly, Accredible).

By executing this process with strong governance, role-based design, rigorous measurement, and continuous improvement, organizations can build the capabilities required to deliver on their sustainability commitments, reduce ESG risks, and demonstrate credible progress to stakeholders.

Process Details:
## Overview
Evaluate de-merger options is the structured assessment of whether to separate a business unit, subsidiary, or previously merged entity from the parent company, and which de-merger structure (e.g., spin-off, split-off, carve-out IPO, JV separation) best achieves strategic, financial, and operational objectives. The process assesses strategic fit, standalone viability, operational disentanglement complexity, financial value creation, tax/legal feasibility, stakeholder and market impacts, and timing.

Role in the organization:
- Informs portfolio optimization and long-term vision by determining if parts of the organization should operate independently to unlock value, sharpen focus, or reduce risk.
- Provides the Board and executive leadership a fact-based, comparable set of options and a clear go/no-go recommendation with a preferred path and execution outline.
- Bridges strategy and execution by aligning strategic rationale with high-level separation planning, cost/benefit modeling, and regulatory feasibility.

Primary outcomes:
- A de-merger evaluation report and recommendation (including option comparison, business case, and execution implications).
- Decision-ready artifacts for governance approvals (Board, regulatory consultations, labor engagement).

## Key Activities
- Define strategic rationale and evaluation criteria for separation.
- Identify and refine de-merger options and structures.
- Conduct strategic and market fit assessment (RemainingCo and SpinCo perspectives).
- Build carve-out financials and pro forma modeling; estimate separation and stranded costs.
- Perform valuation analyses and value creation comparisons across options.
- Assess tax, legal, and regulatory feasibility (including antitrust and industry-specific approvals).
- Map operational disentanglement: people, processes, tech, assets, contracts, IP, and compliance.
- Outline Day-1 readiness and Transition Service Agreements (TSAs) at a high level.
- Evaluate stakeholder and externality impacts (customers, suppliers, employees, creditors, investors).
- Risk assessment and mitigation planning.
- Option scoring and recommendation; prepare governance materials.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Corporate strategy and portfolio review, including prior synergy and performance analyses.
- Organizational and legal entity structures; intercompany relationships.
- Business unit-level P&L, cost allocation rules, balance sheets, cash flow, KPIs.
- Contract inventory (customers, suppliers, leases), change-of-control/assignment clauses.
- Shared services catalog (IT, finance, HR, facilities) and service consumption data.
- IT/application inventory, data maps, infrastructure dependencies, SaaS licensing.
- Workforce data (headcount, critical roles, unions, benefits, pensions).
- Tax attributes (NOLs, tax basis, jurisdictions), regulatory licenses and filings.
- Capital structure: debt covenants, rating agency considerations, liquidity headroom.

Prerequisites:
- Executive mandate to evaluate restructuring options and access to cross-functional data.
- Confidentiality and information handling protocols; advisor NDAs if applicable.
- A short list of candidate entities/units for potential de-merger.
- Defined decision timeline aligned with earnings cycles and regulatory calendars.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Upstream: Analyze deal options; define business concept and long-term vision; portfolio strategy.
- Parallel: Legal/regulatory due diligence; valuation and financial modeling; risk management.
- Downstream: Separation planning (SMO/PMO set-up), regulatory filings, stakeholder communications, execution of selected de-merger.

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and frame
- Appoint a De‑merger Evaluation Lead and establish a cross-functional working group with PMO support.
- Define strategic rationale hypotheses and evaluation criteria (value creation, feasibility, timing, risk).
- Approve scope, milestones, confidentiality rules, and advisor engagement.

2) Develop option set and structures
- Identify structural options: spin-off (pro rata), split-off (exchange), carve-out IPO, JV separation, asset divestiture to third party (if relevant as comparator), tracking stock elimination.
- Outline implications for ownership, control, cash proceeds, tax treatment, speed, and regulatory complexity.

3) Data collection and baselining
- Build a secure data room.
- Validate baseline performance for candidate unit and RemainingCo; true-up cost allocations.
- Inventory entanglements: people, processes, tech, facilities, IP, contracts, compliance obligations.

4) Strategic fit and market assessment
- Assess strategic coherence post-separation for both entities (focus, agility, investment needs).
- Analyze market dynamics, competitive responses, customer concentration, supplier power.
- Benchmark peers and precedent de-mergers in the sector.

5) Standalone and RemainingCo financials
- Construct carve-out financial statements (historical and projected) for SpinCo; pro forma RemainingCo.
- Estimate separation costs (one-time), stranded costs and mitigation plan, ongoing dis-synergies.
- Determine capital structure scenarios and liquidity needs for both entities.

6) Valuation and value creation analysis
- Value SpinCo and RemainingCo across options (DCF, trading comps, sum-of-the-parts, precedent transactions).
- Quantify value uplifts (multiple expansion, growth acceleration), cash proceeds (if any), and NPV vs. status quo.
- Sensitize for key risks (market conditions, execution slippage).

7) Tax, legal, and regulatory feasibility
- Tax: analyze tax-free vs. taxable treatment, jurisdictional issues, utilization of attributes, withholding and BEPS considerations.
- Legal: corporate law requirements, shareholder approvals, litigation exposure, IP/brand ownership.
- Regulatory: antitrust pre-assessment, sector regulators, foreign investment controls, labor/works council obligations.

8) Operational separation assessment
- High-level Target Operating Models for both entities.
- TSA scoping (scope, duration, pricing), service disentanglement paths, Day‑1 minimum viable state.
- IT: data segregation, application carve-out plan, identity access, licensing implications, cybersecurity.
- People: leadership and critical roles for SpinCo, retention plans, benefits/pension separation.
- Facilities and assets: real estate, equipment, logistics reconfiguration.

9) Stakeholder and externality analysis
- Employees and labor bodies, customers and key accounts, suppliers and partners, lenders and rating agencies, investors and indices, communities and ESG implications.
- Draft risk-based communication and engagement plan concepts (timing aligned with disclosure rules).

10) Risk assessment and mitigations
- Identify top risks: execution, regulatory, value leakage, customer churn, IT cutover, data/privacy.
- Define mitigations: phased separation, TSAs, contract novations, cost takeout programs, customer retention offers, clean rooms.

11) Option comparison and decision recommendation
- Build an option scorecard against criteria (value, feasibility, timing, risk, strategic fit).
- Select preferred option and two alternates; articulate why others are rejected.
- Prepare a decision memo and Board materials with clear go/no‑go and next-step execution roadmap.

12) Governance and next steps
- Present to Steering Committee and Board; incorporate feedback.
- If approved: trigger Separation Management Office (SMO), detailed workstreams, regulatory pre-filing consultations, and communications plan development.
- If not approved: document rationale, conditions for reconsideration, and alternative portfolio actions.

Gate checks:
- Gate 1: Framing and option set approved.
- Gate 2: Financials, feasibility, and risks reviewed.
- Gate 3: Final recommendation and execution readiness endorsed.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- De-merger evaluation report (executive summary, analyses, recommendation).
- Option scorecard and decision matrix.
- Carve-out financials and pro forma models (SpinCo and RemainingCo).
- Valuation analyses and sensitivity cases.
- Tax and regulatory feasibility memos; legal issue log.
- Operational separation assessment, high-level TOMs, TSA outline.
- Risk register with mitigations; Day‑1 readiness concept.
- Stakeholder impact assessment and communications considerations.
Success criteria:
- Clear, evidence-based recommendation with quantified value and risks.
- Demonstrated standalone viability and feasible separation path within constraints.
- Board decision achieved on time; no critical unknowns remaining.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor (CEO/Strategy Lead): Mandate, decision-making, stakeholder alignment.
- Corporate Strategy: Owns process, criteria, strategic fit assessment, recommendation synthesis.
- Corporate Development/M&A: Option design, valuation, market benchmarking, advisor coordination.
- Finance (CFO, FP&A, Controllership): Carve-out/pro forma financials, separation and stranded cost estimates, capital structure design.
- Tax: Tax structuring and feasibility assessment.
- Legal/Compliance: Corporate, securities, contractual, IP, labor, and regulatory analysis.
- Regulatory/GR: Engagement strategy with relevant authorities.
- Operations/Supply Chain: Operational disentanglement feasibility, TOM inputs.
- IT: Application/data separation, cybersecurity, licensing, Day‑1 capabilities.
- HR: Org design, leadership selection, retention, benefits and pension separation, labor engagement.
- Treasury/Investor Relations: Rating agency and investor impact analysis; communications inputs.
- Risk/Internal Audit: Risk identification, controls, and governance checks.
- Communications/PR: Messaging strategy and disclosure planning.
- Business Unit Leaders: Operational realities, customer impacts, feasibility inputs.
- External Advisors: Investment bank (structure and valuation), legal counsel, tax advisors, accounting and carve-out specialists, separation consultants.

## Best Practices
- Anchor evaluation on explicit strategic value logic and objective criteria agreed upfront.
- Develop robust carve-out financials early; validate cost allocations and identify stranded costs with mitigation plan.
- Engage tax and legal structuring at the outset to preserve optionality and avoid rework.
- Map entanglements comprehensively (people, process, tech, data, contracts) before committing to timelines.
- Use a formal option scorecard; avoid anchoring bias toward a preferred structure.
- Plan TSAs pragmatically (right-sized scope, clear SLAs, pricing) to protect business continuity and incentivize timely exit.
- Involve customers and suppliers through controlled, sequenced outreach once appropriate; prepare retention levers.
- Establish a Separation Management Office model during evaluation to ensure executable recommendations.
- Run scenario analyses for market volatility and regulatory outcomes; include contingency pathways.
- Protect confidentiality with clean teams and least-privilege access; mitigate leak risk.

## Common Challenges
- Deep operational entanglement and data interdependence: Mitigate via phased separation, robust TSA, and early IT/data segregation planning.
- Underestimated stranded costs: Conduct bottom-up analysis and implement cost takeout and shared services redesign.
- Regulatory and tax complexity across jurisdictions: Engage local counsel early; stage approvals; consider alternative structures.
- Contractual constraints (change-of-control, anti-assignment): Inventory and prioritize novations/amendments; negotiate early.
- Employee uncertainty and retention risk: Identify critical roles, deploy retention/communication plans, and provide clarity on leadership.
- Customer churn and supplier repricing: Proactive engagement, transitional assurances, and tailored commercial offers.
- Debt covenants and rating pressure: Model pro forma credit metrics; negotiate waivers; adjust capital structures.
- IT licensing and SaaS constraints: Review vendor terms; budget for duplicate licenses; plan identity and data migration carefully.

- Decision cycle time vs. plan.
- Accuracy of separation and stranded cost estimates vs. actuals in execution.
- NPV/value creation vs. status quo; market reaction (share price, TSR at 3/6/12 months post‑announcement).
- Standalone viability indicators (SpinCo EBITDA margin trajectory, liquidity headroom).
- Percentage of critical contracts assessed and novated by Day‑1 target in planning.
- TSA scope accuracy and duration adherence; TSA exit milestones met.
- Key talent retention rate through decision and Day‑1.
- Regulatory milestones achieved on time; number of material issues late-discovered.
- Stakeholder sentiment (employee pulse, key customer retention rate).
- Governance effectiveness (gate approvals on first pass; number of material rework cycles).

Process Details:
## Overview
Evaluate divesture options (also known as divestiture options) is the structured assessment of whether, how, and when to divest a department, business unit, or subsidiary. The process determines strategic fit, value creation potential, timing, structure, risks, and stakeholder impacts of divesting an internal entity previously flagged for potential separation. It compares viable divestiture structures (e.g., full sale, carve-out, spin-off, IPO carve-out, JV, closure) and recommends a course of action, including go/no-go and next steps.

Role in the organization:
- Supports portfolio optimization within the broader strategy-setting and restructuring agenda.
- Unlocks capital for redeployment, reduces complexity, and sharpens strategic focus.
- Mitigates risk by proactively managing underperforming, non-core, or high-risk assets.
- Informs governance and capital allocation decisions with fact-based analysis and scenarios.

Primary purpose:
- Produce a defendable, board-ready recommendation on whether to divest and which option maximizes risk-adjusted value while safeguarding customers, employees, and brand.

## Key Activities
- Define scope and decision criteria for the divestiture evaluation.
- Collect and validate business, financial, legal, tax, and operational data for the entity.
- Assess strategic rationale and alternatives (retain, transform, partner, divest).
- Analyze external environment and buyer universe; test market receptivity and timing.
- Evaluate divestiture structures (sale, carve-out, spin-off, IPO carve-out, JV, MBO, wind-down).
- Build valuation models and scenario analyses for each option, including proceeds and tax leakage.
- Conduct separation/entanglement assessment: stranded costs, TSAs, Day-1 readiness, timeline, cost-to-separate.
- Map regulatory, antitrust, and other approvals; identify showstoppers and mitigations.
- Assess stakeholder impacts (employees, unions/works councils, customers, suppliers, communities).
- Compile risk register and mitigation plan; evaluate reputational and ESG considerations.
- Formulate recommendation and implementation roadmap; seek governance approval.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Latest audited and management financials; segment reporting; forecasts and KPIs.
- Carve-out financials (or basis to construct them): revenue, EBITDA, cash flow.
- Business plans, operating model overview, org charts, role inventories, location footprint.
- Contract repository: key customers/suppliers, leases, IP licenses, debt covenants, change-of-control clauses, consents.
- Legal entity structure; ownership interests; intercompany agreements; guarantees.
- Tax attributes (NOLs, credits), transfer pricing, nexus and permanent establishment exposure.
- IT landscape: applications, infrastructure, integrations, data ownership; CMDB.
- HR and benefits: headcount, critical roles, retention risks, pensions, union agreements.
- Regulatory and compliance profile: permits, product approvals, data/privacy, export controls.
- Real estate and environmental reports; asset registers.
- Prior portfolio review outputs and preliminary divestiture candidate shortlist.

Prerequisites:
- Divestiture candidate has been identified in portfolio review or restructuring scan.
- Decision criteria and objectives clarified (value targets, timeline, risk appetite, ESG).
- Executive sponsor and cross-functional working team appointed; budget approved.
- Confidentiality and clean-team protocols established for sensitive data handling.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 1.1.5.3 Analyze deal options (parent): provides initial option set and high-level rationale.
- Enterprise risk management: risk appetite, materiality thresholds.
- Capital allocation and strategy processes: redeployment priorities and hurdle rates.
- Legal/compliance frameworks for M&A and information sharing.
- HR change management and communications protocols.

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and charter
- Appoint sponsor, steering committee, and workstreams (Finance/Valuation, Legal/Tax, Ops/IT, HR, Regulatory).
- Define scope (entities/regions/assets), decision gates, timeline, and success criteria.
- Approve data requests and confidentiality protocols; engage external advisors as needed.

2) Define decision criteria and baselines
- Confirm strategic rationale and alternatives to divest (fix/transform, partial sell-down, partnership).
- Set evaluation criteria: value creation (NPV, proceeds), risk, timing, execution complexity, stakeholder impact.
- Establish status quo baseline: standalone and consolidated performance, capital needs, risk profile.

3) Data collection and validation
- Compile financial, legal, operational, and HR data; reconcile intercompany positions.
- Construct carve-out financials if not available; identify gaps and assumptions.
- Validate data quality via internal audit/controllership; document limitations.

4) Market and timing assessment
- Analyze industry trends, consolidation, competitive dynamics, buyer universe, and appetite.
- Evaluate macro externalities: equity/debt market conditions, FX, commodity cycles, geopolitical/regulatory shifts.
- Conduct discreet market soundings (under NDA) where appropriate to test interest and valuation ranges.

5) Option identification and structuring
- Define viable divestiture structures given legal, tax, and regulatory constraints:
  - Full sale of shares or assets
  - Carve-out asset sale (with or without TSAs)
  - Spin-off to shareholders
  - Carve-out IPO (minority listing)
  - Joint venture or strategic partnership
  - Management buyout
  - Wind-down/closure
- Outline structure mechanics, perimeter, and sequencing for each option.

6) Separation and entanglement assessment
- Map functional entanglements: customers, supply chain, IT systems, data, facilities, shared services, IP.
- Estimate stranded costs and develop mitigation plan (restructure, outsource, shared services).
- Define TSA needs, scope, duration, and pricing methodology.
- Develop Day-1 readiness checklist and high-level separation plan, including cutover approach and costs.

7) Legal, regulatory, and tax analysis
- Identify required filings/approvals (antitrust/competition, foreign direct investment, CFIUS, sector regulators).
- Review change-of-control and consent requirements in key contracts and leases.
- Assess labor law/works council consultation requirements and timelines.
- Evaluate tax structuring to minimize leakage (step plans, asset vs share considerations, spin tax-free feasibility).

8) Valuation and financial modeling
- Build option-specific valuation models:
  - Entity value (DCF, trading comps, precedent transactions) and buyer-specific synergy potential.
  - Proceeds after taxes, fees, pension deficits, indemnities.
  - One-time separation costs and ongoing stranded costs.
  - Pro forma financials for RemainCo; impact on covenants, ratings, and investor narrative.
- Run scenarios (base/bull/bear) and sensitivity analyses (timing, buyer mix, macro variables).

9) Risk and stakeholder impact assessment
- Create risk register: regulatory, execution, operational continuity, reputational, cybersecurity/data, ESG.
- Map stakeholder impacts: employees (retention/benefits), customers (continuity/SLAs), suppliers, communities.
- Propose mitigations: retention and stay bonuses, customer assurance plans, supplier novations, communications.

10) Option comparison and recommendation
- Build an options matrix scoring against decision criteria with qualitative commentary.
- Identify preferred option(s), contingency options, and no-go conditions (threshold valuations, regulatory risks).
- Draft recommendation with rationale, value case, risk mitigations, and implementation roadmap.

11) Governance and decision
- Review with steering committee; iterate based on feedback.
- Prepare board package: executive summary, models, risk/mitigation, timetable, advisor input.
- Decision gate: approve preferred option, authorize next-phase execution (e.g., buyer outreach, regulatory pre-filing) or defer/cancel.

12) Handover to execution
- If approved, finalize execution plan: advisor mandates, data room preparation, clean team, TSA term sheet outline, stakeholder comms plan.
- Transition ownership to Divestiture Execution PMO with documented assumptions, risks, and dependencies.

Expected outputs:
- Divestiture Options Assessment Report and executive summary.
- Option comparison matrix with scoring and recommendation.
- Financial models and scenario analyses (entity valuation, proceeds, RemainCo pro forma).
- Separation blueprint: entanglement map, stranded cost plan, TSA scope/duration/pricing approach, Day-1 readiness checklist.
- Legal/regulatory/tax analysis memos; consent/approval map.
- Risk register with mitigations; stakeholder impact assessment.
- Proposed timeline and milestone plan; resource/budget estimate for execution.

Deliverables produced:
- Board/Investment Committee decision package and presentation.

- Go/no-go decision record and authorization to proceed.
- Handover dossier to execution PMO.

Success criteria:
- Clear, evidence-based recommendation aligned to strategy and value targets.
- Decision rendered by governance within planned timeline.
- Preferred option meets or exceeds hurdle rates and risk thresholds.
- Executable separation plan with identified mitigations and realistic timeline/budget.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor (e.g., CFO or Chief Strategy Officer): Owns business case; ensures alignment with strategy; chairs steering committee.
- Corporate Development Lead: Orchestrates process; integrates workstreams; leads market soundings and buyer universe analysis.
- Business Unit Leader: Provides operational insights and data; validates feasibility and continuity plans.
- Finance/Valuation Team: Builds carve-out financials, valuation models, pro forma impacts, and TSA pricing.
- Legal Counsel (internal and external): Structures deal options; reviews contracts and consents; assesses regulatory and antitrust pathways; drafts preliminary terms.
- Tax Advisor: Designs tax-efficient structures; quantifies tax leakage and step plans.
- HR Lead: Assesses people impacts; plans retention, consultations, and workforce transitions.
- IT/Separation Architect: Maps systems/data entanglements; defines separation approach and Day-1 readiness.
- Operations/Supply Chain Lead: Manages continuity risks; supplier novations; logistics and facilities.
- Compliance/Regulatory Affairs: Identifies and plans necessary approvals and notifications.
- Risk Management/Internal Audit: Challenges assumptions; validates controls; updates enterprise risk register.
- External Advisors (as needed): Investment bank (market, valuation, buyer outreach), consulting (separation planning), legal/tax firms, valuation specialists.
- PMO: Manages timeline, RAID (risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies), governance cadence, and documentation.

## Best Practices
- Start with a clear decision framework linking strategy, value, risk, and timing; avoid defaulting to a single structure.
- Build robust carve-out financials early; get limited-scope audit/review if needed to increase buyer confidence.
- Conduct early separation planning; quantify stranded costs and develop credible mitigation levers.
- Maintain optionality: progress two or more paths (e.g., sale vs spin) until one proves superior.
- Use clean teams and data minimization to manage antitrust and confidentiality risks during market soundings.
- Map and price TSAs realistically; avoid underestimating burden on RemainCo and set clear service exit plans.
- Engage stakeholders proactively (employees, unions/works councils, key customers/suppliers); sequence communications to protect value.
- Pre-assess regulatory hurdles; consider remedy packages or perimeter adjustments to reduce antitrust risks.
- Time the market: align with buyer budget cycles, financing windows, and sector sentiment.
- Embed ESG and reputational considerations; prepare a coherent narrative for investors and communities.

## Common Challenges
- Poor data quality or lack of carve-out financials: Solution: stand up a data workstream; use controllership support; obtain limited assurance; document assumptions.
- Underestimated separation complexity and costs: Solution: detailed entanglement mapping; involve IT/operations early; pilot Day-1 cutover scenarios; contingency budget.
- Valuation gaps with buyers: Solution: competitive process design, improved disclosure, adjusted perimeter, earn-outs or seller financing, maintain optionality (spin or IPO).
- Regulatory/antitrust obstacles: Solution: pre-filing consultations, remedy planning, alternative buyer sets, staggered or regional carve-outs.
- Stranded costs persisting at RemainCo: Solution: restructuring plan, shared services optimization, outsourcing, SG&A rebase targets tied to decision gate.
- Contractual consents and change-of-control roadblocks: Solution: early contract review, consent strategy, novation templates, incentive structures for counterparties.
- Employee attrition and morale risk: Solution: retention/stay plans, transparent communications, leadership availability, TSA continuity assurances.
- Customer churn during uncertainty: Solution: key account outreach, service guarantees, transitional pricing or SLAs, dedicated continuity teams.
- Tax leakage unexpectedly high: Solution: explore alternative structures (spin, asset vs share mix), jurisdictional planning, step plans to optimize basis.
- Information leakage and reputational risk: Solution: tight NDA processes, ring-fenced teams, clear comms protocols, “need-to-know” data controls.

## Performance Metrics
- Decision cycle time: days from initiation to governance decision.
- Value metrics:
  - Estimated net proceeds after tax and fees vs retain-and-improve NPV.
  - Pro forma EPS/ROIC impact on RemainCo.
  - Stranded cost mitigation rate (% mitigated within 12 months of close).
- Quality and readiness:
  - Completeness of carve-out financials (audit readiness score).
  - TSA scope accuracy (variance of actual vs planned duration/cost).
  - Separation cost accuracy (actual vs estimate at decision).
- Market and execution indicators:
  - Number and quality of interested buyers; indicative valuation range spread.
  - Regulatory risk rating and expected approval timeline adherence.
- Stakeholder outcomes:
  - Critical employee retention rate through close and 90 days post-close.
  - Key customer churn rate during process.
  - Issue closure rate from risk register before decision gate.

## Technology and Tools
- Project and portfolio management: MS Project, Smartsheet, Planner/Jira for milestones and RAID logs.
- Financial modeling and analytics: Excel with audit trails, Alteryx/Power BI/Tableau for scenario analysis and dashboards.
- Virtual data rooms: Datasite, Intralinks, Firmex for secure document sharing and clean-team controls.
- Contract analytics and CLM: Kira/Reveal, DocuSign CLM, Icertis for change-of-control and consent mapping.
- Legal entity and compliance: Diligent Entities, hCue for structure and governance tracking.
- IT discovery and CMDB: ServiceNow, Flexera, Azure/AWS inventories to map systems and integrations.
- HRIS and workforce analytics: Workday, SAP SuccessFactors for headcount, comp, retention analysis.
- TSA management and service catalog tools: ServiceNow, custom trackers for SLA definition and performance.
- Collaboration and documentation: SharePoint/Teams, Confluence for central repository and version control.
- Regulatory/antitrust research: Merger review databases, counsel toolkits, risk heatmaps.

Process Details:
## Overview
Identify and review customer touchpoints is the foundational process used to catalog, evaluate, and optimize every interaction a customer has with the organization across the entire lifecycle. Its purpose is to:
- Create a single, comprehensive inventory of touchpoints across channels (owned, paid, earned) and lifecycle stages (awareness to renewal/advocacy).
- Measure how each touchpoint contributes to customer experience, business outcomes, and operational efficiency.
- Pinpoint friction, gaps, overlaps, and “moments that matter” to guide investment and improvement.
- Establish ongoing governance and measurement so the touchpoint landscape remains current and actionable.

Role in the organization:
- Inputs the Customer Experience (CX) strategy with a concrete execution lens.
- Enables product, marketing, sales, and service teams to coordinate omni-channel experiences.
- Feeds prioritization for journey improvements, technology investments, and operational changes.
- Provides baseline metrics for assessing CX initiatives and tracking ROI.

## Key Activities
- Define scope and segmentation: customer segments/personas, lifecycle stages, regions, products.
- Inventory touchpoints: catalog all customer interactions across channels and ownership.
- Map journeys and service blueprints: visualize frontstage (customer-facing) and backstage (supporting processes, systems).
- Collect and synthesize data: quantitative (conversion, CSAT, AHT) and qualitative (surveys, interviews, call transcripts).
- Assess performance and experience: effectiveness, efficiency, effort, sentiment, accessibility, risk.
- Identify gaps, redundancies, and “moments that matter.”
- Prioritize touchpoints for improvement based on impact and feasibility.
- Define measurement plan and instrumentation: event taxonomy, tagging, sampling.
- Validate findings with stakeholders and assign owners.
- Produce an action roadmap and set up governance for continuous updates.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- CX strategy and objectives, brand promise and guidelines.
- Customer personas, segments, and lifecycle framework (e.g., Awareness, Consideration, Purchase, Onboarding, Use, Support, Renewal/Advocacy).
- Existing channel inventories, org charts, and process maps (if available).
- Access to data sources: web/app analytics, CRM, contact center data, survey platforms, social listening, transactional systems.

- Legal and privacy requirements, consents, and data sharing agreements.

Prerequisites:

## Process Steps
1) Define scope and objectives

  - Owned online: website, mobile app, portals, chat, email, in-app messaging, knowledge base.

4) Map journeys and service blueprints

- Executive summary and stakeholder workshop artifacts.

Success criteria:
- ≥95% coverage of touchpoints for in-scope journeys.
- ≥90% of touchpoints with defined owners and KPIs.
- Measurable improvements at prioritized touchpoints (e.g., +10% conversion, -15% AHT, +8 pts CSAT/NPS, +10% self-service containment).
- Reduction in failure demand (repeat contacts) and complaint rates.
- No critical compliance or accessibility gaps outstanding.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Approves scope, funding, and removes roadblocks.
- CX Program Lead: Owns process, coordinates cross-functional work, quality assurance of outputs.
- Journey Owner(s): Accountable for journey outcomes; prioritizes improvements.
- Channel/Touchpoint Owners (Marketing, Product, Sales, Service): Provide inputs, approve changes, and deliver improvements.
- UX/CX Researchers: Design and conduct qualitative research, usability testing.
- Data Analysts/Scientists: Define metrics, analyze data, build scorecards, derive insights.
- Web/App Analytics Specialist: Tagging plans, event taxonomy, dashboards.
- Data Engineering/IT: Data pipelines, integrations, data quality and access.
- Contact Center/Service Ops Manager: Operational metrics, call drivers, process inputs.
- Social Media/Community Manager: Social listening and engagement insights.
- Brand/Content Manager: Brand consistency review.
- Legal/Compliance and Privacy Officer: Compliance checks (GDPR/CCPA), consent and retention.
- Accessibility Specialist: WCAG conformance and inclusive design guidance.
- PMO/Project Manager: Plan, track, and report execution of improvements.
- Finance/Business Operations: Benefit and ROI modeling; cost to serve analysis.

## Best Practices
- Use an outside-in approach centered on customer goals and emotions.
- Combine quantitative and qualitative evidence; avoid relying on a single data source.
- Blueprint backstage processes to reveal root causes behind touchpoint issues.
- Standardize taxonomy, IDs, and definitions to ensure comparability and governance.
- Focus on “moments that matter” and high-volume/high-impact touchpoints first.
- Design for accessibility and inclusion from the outset.
- Implement privacy-by-design and transparent consent experiences.
- Keep the inventory evergreen with a defined refresh cadence and change control.
- Avoid vanity metrics; link touchpoint KPIs to business outcomes.
- Run test-and-learn experiments; instrument before you optimize.
- Close the loop with customers and employees; share what changed based on feedback.
- Leverage process mining and text analytics to uncover hidden or root-cause touchpoints.

## Common Challenges
- Siloed data and fragmented ownership
  - Solution: Establish RACI, use a CDP or data lakehouse, and implement data governance.
- Inconsistent definitions and naming conventions
  - Solution: Adopt a central taxonomy and enforce via templates and review gates.
- Attribution complexity across channels
  - Solution: Multi-touch attribution models, controlled experiments, and clear UTM standards.
- Survey fatigue and biased samples
  - Solution: Smart sampling, trigger-based surveys, rotate questions, combine with passive data.
- Legacy systems limiting instrumentation
  - Solution: Phased tagging plans, proxies where needed, modernization roadmap.
- Privacy/compliance risks
  - Solution: Privacy impact assessments, consent management platforms, least-privilege access.
- Overemphasis on one channel or metric
  - Solution: Balanced scorecards per touchpoint (experience, operational, financial, risk).
- Regional or segment differences masked in aggregates
  - Solution: Slice metrics by segment/region; create segment-specific journeys where needed.

## Performance Metrics
Coverage and governance:
- % of in-scope touchpoints identified and documented.
- % with assigned owner, defined KPIs, and current metadata.
- Time to complete inventory baseline; update cadence adherence.
- Data quality score (completeness, accuracy, timeliness).

Experience and effectiveness:
- CSAT/NPS/CES by touchpoint and stage.
- Conversion rate, goal completion, task success rate.
- Drop-off/abandonment and bounce rates.
- Sentiment from text/voice analytics.

Operational and financial:
- First contact resolution (FCR), average handle time (AHT), queue/wait times.
- Self-service containment rate; escalation rate.
- Cost to serve per touchpoint; repeat contact rate.
- Refund/return/defect rates.

Compliance and quality:
- Accessibility score (WCAG conformance) by touchpoint.
- Number/severity of compliance incidents; consent capture rate.
- Brand guideline adherence score.

Improvement velocity:
- Number of experiments/changes implemented per quarter.
- % of prioritized touchpoints with active improvement initiatives.
- Realized impact vs. forecasted (benefit tracking).

## Technology and Tools
- Journey mapping and collaboration: Miro, Lucid, Smaply, Figma.
- Voice of Customer (VoC) and surveys: Qualtrics, Medallia, SurveyMonkey, Delighted.
- Web/app analytics and tagging: Google Analytics, Adobe Analytics, Mixpanel, GTM/Launch.
- Product analytics and experimentation: Amplitude, Heap, Optimizely, LaunchDarkly.
- Heatmaps and session replay: Hotjar, FullStory.
- CRM and service: Salesforce, HubSpot, Zendesk, ServiceNow.
- Contact center and speech analytics: Genesys, Five9, NICE, CallMiner.
- Social listening: Sprinklr, Brandwatch, Talkwalker.
- CDP and integrations: Segment, mParticle; iPaaS like MuleSoft.
- Data platform and BI: Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks; Tableau, Power BI, Looker.
- Text analytics/NLP: Google Cloud NLP, AWS Comprehend.
- Accessibility and QA: Axe, WAVE, Lighthouse.
- Privacy and consent: OneTrust, TrustArc.
- Documentation and governance: Confluence, SharePoint, Collibra/Alation (data catalog).

Process Details:
# [1.2.8.2.2] Create Customer Journey Maps

## Overview
Creating customer journey maps is the structured process of visualizing how customers experience the organization across stages, channels, and touchpoints—from initial awareness to long-term loyalty. Journey maps synthesize qualitative and quantitative data into a single narrative that reveals customer goals, emotions, pain points, “moments of truth,” and operational drivers behind the experience.

Purpose:
- Build shared organizational understanding of the customer experience.
- Identify and prioritize opportunities to improve satisfaction, loyalty, conversion, and cost-to-serve.
- Align cross-functional teams on customer-centric improvements and measurements.
- Provide a foundation for designing the target (future-state) customer experience and service blueprints.

Role in the organization:
- Part of the CX strategy and design lifecycle under “Design customer experience.”
- Informs portfolio planning, product roadmaps, operational process improvements, channel strategy, content strategy, and measurement frameworks.
- Acts as a living artifact used by teams for decision-making, onboarding, and continuous improvement.

## Key Activities
- Define scope, persona(s), and journey scenario(s).
- Gather and analyze customer insight (qualitative and quantitative).
- Map the current-state journey (stages, touchpoints, channels, emotions, pain points, metrics).
- Validate with customers and frontline staff.
- Identify and prioritize opportunities and moments of truth.
- Design future-state journey and align with service blueprinting.
- Link opportunities to initiatives, backlog items, and KPIs.
- Socialize, govern, and maintain maps as living assets.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Customer personas and segments (goals, behaviors, needs).
- VOC data (NPS, CSAT, CES, surveys), support logs, call/chat transcripts, complaints.
- Digital analytics (web/app funnels, drop-offs, session replay), marketing analytics.
- Operational data (FCR, AHT, abandonment, backlog, SLA adherence).
- Existing process maps, service blueprints, SOPs, scripts, and policies.
- Channel inventory (web, app, IVR, retail, partner, email, social, field).
- Brand and CX design principles; accessibility and inclusion standards.
- Existing journey artifacts, if any (prior maps, research reports).

Prerequisites:
- Defined scope (persona, journey scenario, start/end states, channels, geographies).
- Executive sponsor and cross-functional participation secured.
- Access to customers (recruitment lists, panels) and frontline teams.
- Privacy and legal approvals for using customer data and conducting research.
- Tools access (collaboration boards, analytics, VOC platforms) and templates.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Develop customer experience strategy (1.2.8): vision, priorities, and design principles.
- Design customer experience (1.2.8.2): service blueprint alignment and operational feasibility.
- Persona development and segmentation (upstream CX research).
- Data governance and analytics (data quality, access, and compliance).
- Initiative intake/portfolio management (to fund and execute improvements).

## Process Steps
1) Define objectives and scope
- Clarify business outcomes (e.g., reduce onboarding abandonment by 20%, increase CSAT by 10 points).
- Select persona(s) and journey scenario(s) (e.g., “new customer onboarding”).
- Determine current-state vs. future-state mapping need and the time horizon.
- Agree on success criteria, deliverables, and timeline.
- Output: Scope brief and plan.

2) Assemble team and governance
- Identify roles (CX lead, researcher, analyst, service designer, channel owners, compliance).
- Establish cadence (workshops, reviews), decision rights, and RACI.
- Confirm budget, tooling, and participant incentives.
- Output: Roster, RACI, schedule, and tooling setup.

3) Collect and consolidate data
- Secondary research: VOC dashboards, analytics reports, complaint themes, prior studies.
- Primary research (as needed):
  - Customer interviews, contextual inquiry, diary studies, usability tests.
  - Frontline shadowing, call/chat analysis, store/branch observations.
- Extract structured metrics per stage (conversion, wait times, FCR, NPS drivers).
- Output: Research synthesis wall, evidence repository, consent records.

4) Synthesize insights
- Affinity mapping of quotes and observations to cluster needs, pain points, and emotions.
- Quantify issue magnitude and impact using data (e.g., dropout at step X = 35%).
- Identify “moments of truth” and emotional peaks/valleys.
- Output: Insight themes, prioritized pain points, evidence links.

5) Define journey stages and touchpoints
- Standardize stages (e.g., Awareness, Consideration, Purchase, Onboarding, Use, Support, Renewal/Advocacy) adapted to scenario.
- Inventory touchpoints and channels at each stage, including assisted and self-serve.
- Output: Stage framework and touchpoint inventory.

6) Create current-state journey map
For each stage, capture:
- Customer goal and context.
- Actions and tasks; decision points.
- Touchpoints and channels.
- Emotions/sentiment (e.g., 1–5 scale) and qualitative quotes.
- Pain points and root causes; risks and compliance constraints.
- Operational backstage processes/systems and ownership.
- Stage-level metrics (conversion, CSAT, time-on-task, FCR).
- Opportunities and assumptions.
- Output: Current-state journey map (visual + annotated), with evidence.

7) Validate and iterate
- Review with customers and frontline staff; conduct playback sessions.
- Test for accuracy, completeness, inclusivity, and accessibility considerations.
- Update map and document changes; finalize current-state version.
- Output: Validated current-state map and validation notes.

8) Identify and prioritize opportunities
- Ideation workshop to generate solution hypotheses.
- Use impact/effort matrix and link to business/experience KPIs.
- Bundle opportunities into themes; estimate benefits, costs, and risks.
- Output: Prioritized opportunity backlog with rationale.

9) Design future-state journey (optional but recommended)
- Define design principles and desired experiences per stage.
- Map future-state interactions, moments of truth, and emotional targets.
- Overlay service blueprint: frontstage vs. backstage people, processes, and systems.
- Outline content, policy, and capability changes required.
- Output: Future-state journey map and service blueprint overlays.

10) Define measurement and instrumentation
- Select KPIs per stage and global KPIs (e.g., NPS, churn, LTV).
- Design instrumentation plan (events, tagging, voice-of-customer triggers).
- Establish baselines and targets; define reporting cadences.
- Output: Measurement plan and dashboard requirements.

11) Handoff to execution
- Convert opportunities into initiatives/epics/features with acceptance criteria.
- Feed into portfolio intake, product roadmaps, and process improvement pipelines.
- Confirm owners, dependencies, and timelines.
- Output: Initiative charters, Jira/Azure DevOps backlog items.

12) Socialize and govern
- Publish maps in a central repository with version control.
- Run enablement sessions; create storytelling assets and playbooks.
- Define update cadence (e.g., quarterly) and owner for maintenance.
- Output: Communications plan, training materials, governance guide.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Current-state journey map(s) per persona/scenario (visual + annotated).
- Future-state journey map(s) and service blueprint overlays.
- Touchpoint/channel inventory.
- Research synthesis and evidence repository.
- Prioritized opportunity backlog with quantified impact.
- Measurement plan with baselines and targets.
- Storytelling deck and one-page summaries for executives.
- Governance and maintenance plan.

Success criteria:
- Maps validated by customers and frontline staff.
- Clear ownership and linkage to funded initiatives.
- Baseline metrics established; targets agreed.
- Cross-functional alignment (documented sign-offs).
- Demonstrable usage (views, references) and measurable improvements post-implementation.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Charter the effort, remove blockers, approve funding and prioritization.
- CX Lead / Service Design Lead: Own process and quality, facilitate workshops, ensure alignment to CX strategy.
- UX/CX Researcher: Plan and conduct research, synthesize insights, validate maps with customers.
- Data/Business Analyst: Aggregate and analyze quantitative data; define metrics and instrumentation.
- Service Designer: Map frontstage/backstage interactions; create service blueprint overlays.
- Product Owner(s): Translate opportunities into backlog items; align with product strategy.
- Channel/Operations Owners (Sales, Support, Retail, Digital): Provide operational insight; validate feasibility and ownership.
- Marketing/Content Strategist: Align messaging and content across touchpoints.
- IT/Architecture: Assess system impacts, feasibility, and integration needs.
- Legal/Compliance/Risk: Ensure regulatory and policy adherence; review changes.
- PMO/Portfolio Manager: Integrate initiatives into portfolio and track progress.
- Customer Panel/Advisory Group: Validate assumptions and proposed improvements.

## Best Practices
- Evidence-based mapping: Ground maps in mixed-method research, not assumptions.
- Right-sized scope: Map one persona and one scenario at a time to depth, not breadth.
- Co-creation: Involve customers, frontline staff, and cross-functional stakeholders in workshops.
- Standardized templates: Use consistent stage definitions, emotion scales, and data fields for comparability.
- Include emotions and “moments of truth”: Capture the human layer alongside process and tech.
- Omnichannel lens: Show channel transitions and handoffs; avoid web-only views.
- Backstage visibility: Include processes, systems, policies that shape the frontstage.
- Accessibility and inclusion: Consider diverse needs (language, disability, devices, cultural).
- Quantify pain points: Size issues with data to prioritize high-impact opportunities.
- Living artifact: Establish versioning, owners, and refresh cadence; link to dashboards and backlogs.
- Traceability: Link every stage/pain point to data sources and initiatives; maintain an evidence index.
- Privacy and ethics: Obtain consent, minimize PII exposure, and follow data-retention policies.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Scope creep: Timebox and define clear start/end states; maintain a parking lot for out-of-scope items.
- Limited customer access: Use multiple sources (VOC, frontline proxies) and secure panels early.
- Data silos/quality issues: Partner with data governance; document gaps; prioritize instrumentation improvements.
- Overly generic maps: Anchor to a specific persona and scenario with real evidence and quotes.
- Lack of adoption: Socialize early, tailor artifacts to audiences, and show quick wins linked to KPIs.
- Maps become static posters: Assign ownership and a refresh cadence; integrate into portfolio governance.
- Misalignment with feasibility: Use service blueprinting and include IT/operations early to surface constraints.
- Compliance concerns: Involve Legal/Compliance in scoping; anonymize and secure data.
- Too many personas: Prioritize by value and risk; create archetypes; map high-impact segments first.

## Performance Metrics
Process effectiveness:
- Cycle time to produce a validated journey map.
- Stakeholder satisfaction with the artifact and process (e.g., internal CSAT).
- Adoption/usage: Views, references in business cases, number of teams using the map.
- Update frequency and map “freshness” (time since last validation).
- Coverage: % of priority journeys/personas mapped.

Experience and business impact (by journey/stage):
- NPS/CSAT/CES at key stages and moments of truth.
- Conversion rates and funnel drop-offs by stage.
- Churn/retention, repeat purchase, upsell/cross-sell rates, LTV.
- Cost-to-serve (contact rate per customer, FCR, AHT).
- Complaint rates, rework/defect rates, SLA adherence.
- Digital adoption/self-service completion rates.
- Time-to-complete key tasks (e.g., onboarding time).

Measurement guidance:
- Set baselines pre-initiative and targets per stage.
- Instrument critical touchpoints (events, surveys).
- Create dashboards segmented by persona and channel.

## Technology and Tools
Collaboration and mapping:
- Visual collaboration: Miro, Mural, Lucid.
- Journey mapping platforms: TheyDo, Smaply, UXPressia, Milkymap.
- Documentation/repository: Confluence, SharePoint, Notion; version control practices.

Research and VOC:
- Survey/experience platforms: Qualtrics, Medallia, SurveyMonkey, InMoment.
- User research: UserTesting, UserZoom, dscout (diary), Lookback.
- Contact center analytics: Genesys, NICE, Five9; transcription via AWS Transcribe, Google Speech-to-Text.
- Social listening/text analytics: Sprinklr, Brandwatch, Clarabridge; NLP for sentiment and themes.

Analytics and instrumentation:
- Web/app analytics: GA4, Adobe Analytics, Mixpanel, Amplitude.
- Session replay/behavior: FullStory, Contentsquare, Hotjar.
- BI and dashboards: Tableau, Power BI, Looker.
- CDP/Integration: Segment, Tealium, mParticle; data lake/warehouse for joining datasets.

Execution and governance:
- Work/portfolio management: Jira, Azure DevOps, Trello, Asana.
- Service design/blueprinting: Figma, FigJam; blueprint templates in Miro/Mural.
- Privacy/compliance: Consent management (OneTrust), data masking and secure repositories.

Implementation tips:
- Create a standardized journey template in your chosen tool with required fields.
- Link evidence (e.g., quote IDs, dashboard URLs) directly in the map.
- Use shared taxonomies for stages, channels, and metrics to enable roll-up reporting.

- Measurement plan draft with baseline pull scheduled.
