# [1.2.8.2.3] Define Single View of the Customer for the Organization

## Overview
This process defines the standards, rules, and architecture needed to create a single, trusted, and actionable view of each customer across all channels and systems. It establishes the parameters for aggregating, reconciling, and governing customer data—demographics, identifiers, interactions, preferences, consents, and derived insights—so any team can reliably recognize and serve the same customer in a consistent way.

Purpose:
- Enable consistent customer recognition and personalized experiences across marketing, sales, service, commerce, and operations.
- Improve decision-making with accurate, complete customer profiles and interaction histories.
- Ensure compliant use of customer data aligned to consent, purpose limitation, and regional regulations.
- Reduce data duplication, inconsistency, and rework across systems.

Role in the organization:
- Foundational capability for customer experience design and activation (upstream of personalization, segmentation, next-best-action, loyalty).
- Core enabler of analytics, customer journey orchestration, and service operations.
- Key control point for data governance, privacy, and risk management.

## Key Activities
- Align business outcomes and customer experience use cases that the single view must support.
- Inventory and assess source systems, customer identifiers, and data quality.
- Define the enterprise customer identifiers and identity resolution strategy (deterministic/probabilistic).
- Design the customer 360 data model (core profile, relationships, interactions, consents, preferences, scores).
- Define data quality, matching, merging, and survivorship rules for the golden record.
- Establish consent, privacy, and retention rules; perform privacy impact assessments.
- Define integration patterns, APIs, and event schemas for ingesting and publishing profile data.
- Select/confirm enabling platforms and tools (MDM/CDP, data warehouse, streaming, catalog, consent).
- Prototype and validate with real use cases; measure match/completeness; refine.
- Establish data stewardship, governance workflows, and ongoing monitoring.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Customer experience strategy, journey maps, and prioritized use cases.
- Inventory of customer touchpoints and systems (CRM, service, commerce, POS, web/app, call center, loyalty, marketing tech).
- Current identifiers (account IDs, email, phone, device IDs, loyalty IDs, cookies), and data dictionaries from source systems.
- Data quality assessments, profiling reports, and known issues.
- Legal and compliance requirements (GDPR, CCPA, LGPD), consent frameworks, retention policies.
- Enterprise data architecture, security standards, and integration patterns in place.

Prerequisites:
- Executive sponsorship and funding for cross-functional data work.
- Data governance structure (council, policies, stewards) and privacy-by-design practices.
- Access to a scalable data platform (warehouse/lakehouse), integration pipelines, and identity resolution capability (in-house or vendor).
- Data sharing agreements and approvals with system owners.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [1.2.8.2] Design customer experience (to define desired interactions and data needs).
- Data strategy and architecture definition; integration architecture.
- Privacy, security, and legal compliance processes (DPIA/PIA).
- Master data governance and data quality management.

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and scope
- Confirm executive sponsor, product owner, and cross-functional working group.
- Define scope, target customer entities (individual, household, account), geographies, and channels.
- Agree on initial use-case-driven success criteria and timeline.

2) Elicit and prioritize use cases
- Gather top 5–10 use cases (e.g., cross-channel personalization, unified service history, churn prediction).
- For each, define required attributes, latency needs (real-time vs batch), and activation endpoints.

3) Source system discovery and assessment
- Catalog sources, data owners, and data contracts.
- Profile data for completeness, uniqueness, formats, and PII sensitivity.
- Map existing identifiers and identity touchpoints (authentication events, loyalty sign-ups, email capture).

4) Define enterprise identity strategy
- Select primary enterprise customer ID and crosswalk strategy.
- Specify identifier hierarchy and linking rules (email, phone, MAID, device IDs, cookies, CRM IDs, loyalty IDs).
- Determine deterministic rules (exact match, hashed email, phone E.164) and probabilistic signals (name/address similarity, IP/device co-occurrence), with confidence scoring.
- Define online-to-offline linkage and household/account relationships.
- Establish unmerge policy and audit trail for identity graph corrections.

5) Design the customer 360 data model
- Define core profile: identifiers, PII, preferences, consents, lifecycle status, relationships (household/account), segments, scores.
- Define interaction schema: standardized event taxonomy (view, add-to-cart, purchase, case created, email open), timestamps, channel, device.
- Define consent and preference sub-model: purposes, jurisdictions, timestamps, sources, proof.
- Define derived insights: RFM, CLV, churn propensity, NPS, next-best-action.
- Create data dictionary with definitions, formats, allowed values, ownership, and sensitivity classification.

6) Privacy, consent, and retention
- Map lawful bases, consent capture points, and purpose-based access rules.
- Define retention and minimization rules per data type and region; tokenization policies for PII.
- Conduct DPIA/PIA and define subject rights processes (access, deletion, portability) aligned to the single view.

7) Matching, merging, and survivorship rules
- Define match rules and thresholds; test for precision/recall trade-offs.
- Create survivorship rules: attribute precedence by source, recency, confidence; manage conflicts.
- Establish golden record creation/update process and auditability (lineage and “why” explanations).
- Document manual review workflows for exceptions and edge cases (e.g., minors, joint accounts).

8) Data quality and controls
- Define data quality dimensions and thresholds (completeness, validity, uniqueness, timeliness).
- Set validation and standardization rules (address standardization, phone normalization, email syntax).
- Implement monitoring, alerts, and data steward queues for remediation.

9) Architecture and tooling
- Choose build/buy/augment approach: MDM vs CDP vs lakehouse patterns (or hybrid).
- Define ingestion patterns (batch, CDC, streaming), real-time event collection, and API strategy for profile read/write.
- Define publish mechanisms (reverse ETL, event buses, APIs) to downstream systems.
- Establish security: encryption at rest/in transit, role-based access, purpose-based access control, key management.

10) Source-to-target mapping and contracts
- Create detailed mappings from each source to the 360 model, including transformations and consent context.
- Define data contracts (schemas, SLAs, versioning) with source system owners.

11) Prototype and validate
- Build a prototype with representative sources; run identity resolution at small scale.
- Measure match rate, duplicate reduction, profile completeness, consent coverage; refine rules.

12) Testing and sign-off
- Functional tests (merging, unmerge, API behaviors), performance tests (latency, throughput), and security tests.
- Business validation with channel owners using real scenarios; document results.
- Governance review and approvals (data, security, privacy).

13) Implementation plan and rollout
- Prioritize sources and consuming systems for phased rollout.
- Define cutover approach, synchronization with legacy identifiers, and dual-run period if needed.
- Train stewards, support teams, and consuming system owners.

14) Operate and improve
- Establish monitoring dashboards, operational SLAs, incident management, and change control.
- Conduct periodic rule tuning based on metrics; expand coverage to new channels and attributes.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Customer 360 data model and data dictionary.
- Enterprise identity strategy and policy (deterministic/probabilistic rules, thresholds, confidence scores).
- Golden record survivorship rules and unmerge policy.
- Consent and privacy model, DPIA/PIA documentation, retention schedule.
- Source inventory, source-to-target mappings, and data contracts.
- Integration architecture, API specs (profile read/lookup, merge/unmerge, consent update, event ingest).
- Data quality rules, validation scripts, and monitoring dashboards.
- Prototype results and test reports with baseline metrics.
- Operating model and RACI for stewardship and incident handling.
- Implementation roadmap and backlog.

Success criteria
- Achieve target match rate and duplicate reduction without unacceptable false merges.
- Meet latency SLAs for profile availability for prioritized use cases.
- Profile completeness and consent coverage meet thresholds required by use cases.
- Adoption by target consuming systems; measurable uplift in CX outcomes (e.g., personalization CTR, first-contact resolution).
- Zero material privacy/security incidents attributable to the single view.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Champion, funding, unblock cross-functional issues.
- Product Owner (Customer 360): Owns roadmap, backlog, acceptance criteria, stakeholder alignment.
- Enterprise/Data Architect: Defines architecture, data model, integration patterns.
- MDM/CDP Architect: Designs identity resolution, survivorship, and platform configuration.
- Data Engineers/Integration Engineers: Build pipelines, transformations, and APIs.
- Identity Resolution Analyst/Data Scientist: Designs and tunes match algorithms, evaluates precision/recall.
- Data Stewards (per domain/source): Monitor data quality, resolve exceptions, manage merges/unmerges.
- Privacy Officer/DPO and Legal: Define consent and lawful basis, conduct DPIA, approve policies.
- Security/InfoSec: Define and validate security controls, access models, encryption.
- System Owners (CRM, Marketing, Commerce, Service): Provide source data, align identifiers, adopt outputs.
- QA/Testing: Functional, performance, and security testing.
- Analytics/Insights: Define derived attributes/scores, validate business value.
- Change Manager/Training Lead: Communication, training, adoption support.

## Best Practices
- Use-case-driven scope: Start with high-value, clear use cases to bound data needs and latency.
- Privacy by design: Collect minimal data, maintain purpose-based access, and ensure explainability of matches.
- Establish an enterprise customer ID with crosswalks to channel IDs; avoid proliferating new IDs.
- Blend deterministic with probabilistic matching; use confidence scores and human-in-the-loop for edge cases.
- Versioned, extensible schemas and event taxonomies; data contracts with strict validation.
- Combine real-time and batch paths: Real-time identity stitching for interactions; batch for deep reconciliation.
- Transparent golden record lineage and “why” explanations to build trust and support compliance.
- Household/account relationships where relevant (B2C householding, B2B account-contact).
- Strong consent management: Purpose-specific, timestamped, traceable; enforce at access and activation.
- Continuous monitoring and rule tuning; A/B test the impact of identity tuning on business outcomes.
- Plan unmerge/remerge processes and tooling from the start.
- Avoid vendor lock-in via open schemas, APIs, and data portability; leverage a lakehouse as system of record.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Siloed systems and inconsistent IDs: Solve with cross-system identifier mapping, data contracts, and a governed enterprise ID.
- Poor data quality and duplicates: Implement standardization, validation, enrichment, and stewardship queues; set quality SLAs.
- Cookie deprecation and signal loss: Shift to first-party data, authenticated experiences, server-side tagging, and durable IDs.
- False merges or missed matches: Calibrate thresholds, use multi-signal matching and confidence scoring; monitor precision/recall.
- Latency constraints: Use streaming ingestion and low-latency profile stores for critical use cases; batch for the rest.
- Privacy/regulatory complexity: Enforce purpose-based access, automate consent checks, and maintain audit trails; run DPIAs.
- Organizational resistance: Demonstrate quick wins, align incentives, and formalize stewardship responsibilities.
- Unmerge complexity: Define strict policies, implement reversible merges with full lineage, and provide steward tooling.
- Vendor lock-in and scalability: Favor modular architecture, open standards, and cloud-native scale.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs)
Identity and quality:
- Match rate and duplicate reduction rate.
- Merge precision/recall; identity confidence score distribution.
- Profile completeness (%) for required attributes.
- Data quality scores (completeness, validity, uniqueness, timeliness).

Operational:
- Time-to-profile availability (ingest to activation) and real-time lookup latency.
- Error rates in pipelines; incident MTTR; unmerge/exception backlog.
- Coverage: % of active customers with enterprise ID and valid consent.

Compliance:
- Consent capture rate by purpose and region; suppression accuracy.
- Number of privacy/security incidents; time to fulfill subject rights requests.

Adoption and impact:
- Number of consuming systems and use cases live.
- Lift in personalization KPIs (CTR, conversion), service KPIs (FCR, AHT), and retention (churn reduction).
- Cost-to-serve and data operations efficiency improvements.

## Technology and Tools
- Master Data Management (MDM): Informatica MDM, Reltio, Semarchy.
- Customer Data Platform (CDP): Adobe Real-Time CDP, Salesforce Data Cloud, Twilio Segment, Tealium.
- Data platform: Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Azure Synapse; object storage (S3/GCS/ADLS).
- Streaming and messaging: Kafka, Confluent, Pub/Sub, Event Hubs; CDC tools (Debezium, StreamSets).
- ETL/ELT and transformation: Fivetran, Stitch, Informatica, dbt.
- Identity resolution and enrichment: Native MDM/CDP engines; LiveRamp, Neustar, Experian (where compliant).
- Consent and privacy: OneTrust, TrustArc; in-house consent APIs; CMP for web/app.
- Data catalog and governance: Collibra, Alation, Atlan; lineage tooling.
- API management and integration: Apigee, Kong, MuleSoft; GraphQL/REST for profile services.
- Tag management and server-side collection: Tealium iQ/Events, Google Tag Manager Server-Side.
- Security: Vault/HSM for key management, tokenization services, IAM/ABAC/RBAC enforcement.
- BI/Monitoring: Tableau, Power BI, Looker; observability (Datadog, Grafana, OpenTelemetry).

# [1.2.8.2.6] Align experience with brand values and business strategies

## Overview
This process ensures that every customer interaction reflects the brand’s values and advances the organization’s business strategy. It translates brand promise and strategic goals into concrete customer experience (CX) principles, standards, and measurable outcomes across channels and touchpoints. The objective is to deliver a relevant, differentiated, and credible value proposition through consistent product and service quality that customers can perceive and trust, while enabling the business to achieve growth, efficiency, and risk objectives.

Role in the organization:
- Bridges strategy and execution by converting brand and business strategy into actionable CX requirements.
- Guides design, operations, and communications to avoid dissonance between what the brand promises and what customers experience.
- Prioritizes investments in experiences that reinforce differentiation and deliver measurable business value.
- Establishes guardrails, governance, and metrics to maintain alignment over time.

## Key Activities
- Interpret brand values and business strategy into CX implications.
- Define brand-aligned experience principles and “non-negotiables.”
- Audit current experiences for brand and strategy alignment; identify gaps.
- Prioritize moments of truth and define required experience attributes per journey stage.
- Translate principles into service standards, content/UX guidelines, and operational requirements.
- Align policies, processes, incentives, and training to support the desired experience.
- Validate with customers and stakeholders; iterate as needed.
- Define KPIs and dashboards linking experience to brand and business outcomes.
- Create a roadmap and governance mechanism to sustain alignment.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Brand strategy: mission, values, positioning, promise, archetype, tone/voice, identity guidelines.
  - Business strategy: objectives/OKRs, market/segment targets, competitive strategy, growth and cost levers.
  - Customer insights: personas/JTBD, VoC (NPS/CSAT/CES), complaints/root-cause, brand perception studies.
  - CX artifacts: journey maps, service blueprints, channel inventories, prior CX standards.
  - Operational data: SLAs, performance reports, capacity and capability assessments.
  - Regulatory/compliance requirements and risk appetite.
- Prerequisites:
  - Executive sponsorship and a cross-functional working group (Brand, CX, Product, Ops, Legal, Data).
  - Access to current-state data and artifacts.
  - Defined scope (channels, journeys, regions) and success criteria.
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Upstream: Develop brand strategy, Develop business strategy, Develop customer experience strategy, Design customer journeys.
  - Downstream: Experience design and build, Content and communications, Service operations, Training and enablement, Quality assurance and monitoring.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and scope
   - Confirm objectives, scope, timelines, and governance.
   - Identify stakeholders and form a cross-functional squad.
   - Define decision rights and approval pathways (e.g., Brand Council, Risk/Legal).

2. Synthesize strategy into CX implications
   - Extract key brand attributes (e.g., trustworthy, effortless, expert, friendly) and business priorities (e.g., premium positioning, digital-first service).
   - Draft 4–6 CX principles that express how the brand should feel at each interaction (e.g., “Proactive clarity,” “Human when it matters”).
   - Articulate the experience value proposition and the “experience north star” statement.

3. Current-state alignment assessment
   - Conduct a “promise-to-proof” audit: for each brand promise, list existing proofs in the experience and gaps.
   - Review journey maps/service blueprints to assess alignment at moments of truth.
   - Analyze VoC and operational metrics for signs of brand dissonance (e.g., “friendly” brand with long queue times).
   - Document issues by channel, policy, process, and capability.

4. Define target experience attributes by journey stage
   - For each priority journey stage/moment of truth, specify desired attributes (speed, transparency, empathy, empowerment, personalization, accessibility).
   - Identify non-negotiables (e.g., response within 60 seconds on chat; all communications at 8th-grade reading level).
   - Establish trade-off rules aligned to strategy (e.g., prioritize accuracy over speed in regulated scenarios).

5. Translate into standards and requirements
   - Service standards and SLAs (e.g., first contact resolution, escalation paths).
   - UX/content guidelines (tone of voice exemplars, microcopy patterns, accessibility standards).
   - Operational requirements (staffing models, skill profiles, knowledge base content, tooling).
   - Policy/process changes to remove friction and ensure compliance with the brand promise.
   - Update design system tokens/components to encode brand experience cues.

6. Prioritize initiatives and build roadmap
   - Size impact vs. effort using strategic value and customer impact lenses.
   - Create a prioritized backlog of CX enhancements with dependencies, risks, and owners.
   - Develop business cases (benefits, costs, KPIs) for top initiatives.

7. Validate and iterate
   - Prototype critical moments; test with target segments for perceived brand fit and usability.
   - Run A/B or multivariate tests where possible (e.g., tone changes on key flows).
   - Refine principles, standards, and requirements based on evidence.

8. Enable organization
   - Develop playbooks, training modules, and coaching guides for frontline and back-office roles.
   - Align incentives and KPIs to reinforce desired behaviors.
   - Communicate changes with internal campaign and change management plan.

9. Measurement and governance setup
   - Define a measurement framework: tie experience KPIs to brand attributes and business goals.
   - Establish dashboards and review cadences (e.g., monthly Brand-CX Alignment Review).
   - Set up compliance checks and design reviews for new/changed experiences.

10. Implement and monitor
   - Hand off to delivery teams with clear acceptance criteria and “definition of done.”
   - Monitor performance, VoC, and brand perception; conduct periodic alignment audits.
   - Capture learnings and update standards and roadmaps continuously.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Outputs:
  - Experience value proposition and CX principles aligned to brand and strategy.
  - Promise-to-proof matrix and alignment gap assessment.
  - Target experience attributes per journey stage; non-negotiables and trade-off rules.
  - Service standards, UX/content guidelines, and updated design system components.
  - Policy/process change recommendations and enablement materials.
  - Prioritized initiative backlog and roadmap with business cases.
  - Measurement framework, KPI definitions, dashboards, and governance model.
- Success criteria:
  - Demonstrable reduction in brand-experience dissonance metrics (e.g., fewer “not as advertised” complaints).
  - Improvement in attribute-linked NPS/CSAT and brand perception scores.
  - Adherence to service standards and design guidelines in audits.
  - Positive business impact (conversion, retention, cross-sell, cost-to-serve) where targeted.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Executive Sponsor: Provides direction, removes roadblocks, approves major decisions/funding.
- CX Lead/Manager: Orchestrates the process, owns principles, standards, and measurement framework.
- Brand Manager/Director: Ensures fidelity to brand strategy; leads promise-to-proof translation.
- Strategy Lead: Aligns with corporate strategy and OKRs; validates prioritization logic.
- Product Managers: Convert requirements into backlog items; own delivery within product scope.
- Service/Operations Lead: Adapts processes, staffing, and SLAs to meet standards; owns operational readiness.
- UX/UI and Content Designers: Create guidelines, patterns, and prototypes that encode brand attributes.
- Data/Analytics: Builds dashboards, conducts tests, quantifies impact, and monitors KPIs.
- Research/VoC: Plans and executes customer validation and ongoing insight programs.
- Legal/Compliance/Risk: Reviews standards and changes for regulatory adherence.
- Training/L&D: Develops and delivers enablement content; tracks adoption.
- PMO/Transformation Office: Coordinates roadmap, dependencies, and reporting.
- Frontline Supervisors: Coach teams to behaviors; provide feedback loops from customers.

## Best Practices
- Limit CX principles to a memorable set (4–6) and tie each to specific operational behaviors and metrics.
- Make the brand promise tangible with proof points embedded at moments of truth.
- Use a customer-first lens (JTBD) to reconcile conflicts between brand aspiration and operational realities.
- Define non-negotiables and trade-off rules to guide real-time decisions.
- Build an omnichannel design system that encodes tone, accessibility, and interaction patterns.
- Align incentives and recognition programs to desired experience behaviors.
- Co-create with customers and frontline teams to ensure feasibility and authenticity.
- Establish a standing Brand-CX Council to review major experience changes.
- Instrument journeys with telemetry and VoC to detect misalignment early.
- Ensure inclusivity and accessibility to broaden credibility and trust.

## Common Challenges
- Vague or aspirational brand values
  - Solution: Translate into observable behaviors, standards, and examples; validate with customers.
- Siloed ownership across channels and functions
  - Solution: Cross-functional governance and shared KPIs; common design system and playbooks.
- Cost/complexity of delivering premium experiences
  - Solution: Prioritize high-impact moments; automate routine interactions; invest in training for critical touchpoints.
- Inconsistent tone and service levels across channels
  - Solution: Unified content and service standards; omnichannel QA and calibration.
- Legacy systems limiting experience delivery
  - Solution: Define experience layer requirements; use middleware and progressive modernization; sequence roadmap accordingly.
- Compliance constraints affecting transparency or speed
  - Solution: Early Legal/Risk involvement; pre-approved language libraries; scenario-based playbooks.
- Difficulty linking CX to brand/business outcomes
  - Solution: Attribute-based NPS/CSAT, econometric models, and controlled experiments to quantify impact.
- Global vs. local brand execution conflicts
  - Solution: Create guardrails with localisation leeway; test locally while preserving core principles.

## Performance Metrics
- Experience quality:
  - NPS/CSAT/CES at journey stage level, tagged by brand attributes.
  - First Contact Resolution (FCR), time-to-resolution, queue times against standards.
  - Complaint rates related to expectation mismatch.
- Brand impact:
  - Attribute association, trust, differentiation, consideration, brand equity indices.
  - “Brand fit” scores from concept/usability tests.
- Operational and behavioral outcomes:
  - Conversion rate, repeat purchase rate, churn/retention, ARPU/LTV, cross-sell/upsell.
  - Cost-to-serve, handle time, digital containment, error/defect rates.
- Adoption and governance:
  - Design review pass rate, standards compliance audit score.
  - Training completion and post-training behavioral adherence.
  - Cadence adherence for Brand-CX reviews; backlog throughput and lead time.
- Financial:
  - ROI of CX initiatives; impact on revenue/profit targets tied to strategy.

## Technology and Tools
- VoC and survey platforms: Qualtrics, Medallia, InMoment for NPS/CSAT/CES and text analytics.
- Journey analytics and orchestration: Adobe Journey Analytics, Thunderhead, Glassbox, Mixpanel.
- Brand and asset management: Frontify, Bynder to govern brand guidelines and assets.
- Design and prototyping: Figma, FigJam/Miro, Sketch; design tokens to encode brand cues.
- CMS/Content Ops: Adobe Experience Manager, Contentful; tone and language libraries.
- CRM/CDP: Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics, Segment, mParticle to enable personalization aligned with brand.
- Contact center/CCaaS: Genesys, NICE, Five9; QA tools for tone and standards adherence.
- Knowledge management: Guru, Confluence, Zendesk Guide for consistent guidance and messaging.
- Analytics and BI: Tableau, Power BI, Looker; experimentation tools like Optimizely, Adobe Target.
- Monitoring/APM/RUM: New Relic, Datadog, Dynatrace, Catchpoint to track digital experience SLAs.
- Project/Portfolio and governance: Jira/Azure DevOps, Aha!, ServiceNow for workflows, approvals, and roadmaps.
- Research and testing: UserTesting, Validately, dscout for perception and usability validation.

# [1.2.8.2.7] Develop Content Strategy

## Overview
Develop Content Strategy is the structured planning, development, and governance of content across channels and formats to deliver the right content to the right customer at the right time. Within the customer experience (CX) design context, this process translates customer insights, journey maps, and brand strategy into a cohesive content roadmap and operating model that improves customer satisfaction, speeds decision-making, and drives business outcomes (e.g., acquisition, activation, retention, advocacy).

Purpose:
- Align content with customer needs and business objectives across the end-to-end journey.
- Define what content to create, where it lives, how it’s managed, and how success is measured.
- Establish governance, standards, and workflows to ensure consistent quality, compliance, and efficiency.
- Enable omnichannel delivery and personalization at scale using a defined content model and metadata.

Role in the organization:
- Serves as the connective tissue between CX design, brand, product marketing, digital, support, and sales enablement.
- Guides content operations and investments; defines how content supports strategic initiatives and differentiates the experience.
- Provides guardrails for compliant, accessible, and on-brand communication in all markets and channels.

## Key Activities
- Audience and journey insight synthesis: Translate personas, JTBD (jobs to be done), and journey pains into content needs.
- Content inventory and audit: Catalog, assess quality, performance, findability, and currency of existing assets.
- Competitive and landscape analysis: Benchmark content topics, formats, SEO footprint, and channel plays.
- Content mission, principles, and voice: Define the purpose, tone, and experience principles for content.
- Messaging architecture: Create value propositions, proof points, and message maps by persona and stage.
- Content pillars and topic clusters: Establish themes and topic clusters for topical authority and SEO.
- Channel and format strategy: Decide where and how content appears (web, app, email, social, in-product, support, sales).
- SEO/Discovery strategy: Keyword universe, on-page guidelines, schema, internal linking, and search intent mapping.
- Personalization framework: Rules, segments, decisioning logic, and guardrails for tailored content.
- Information architecture, taxonomy, and metadata: Define content model, tags, schema, and content relationships.
- Editorial calendar and roadmap: Time-phased plan of campaigns, always-on content, and experimentation.
- Governance model and RACI: Roles, responsibilities, review/approval workflows, SLAs, and change control.
- Accessibility and compliance standards: WCAG, privacy, IP, brand, and industry-specific regulatory requirements.
- Localization/translation plan: Markets, languages, transcreation guidelines, and turnaround SLAs.
- Content design system and templates: Reusable content patterns, briefs, templates, and component library.
- Measurement framework and dashboards: KPIs, event taxonomy, UTM standards, and reporting cadence.
- Operating model and resourcing: Budget, capacity planning, sourcing mix (in-house/agency), and training.
- Lifecycle management: Refresh, repurpose, and sunset policies to control content debt.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- CX artifacts: Personas, JTBD, journey maps, service blueprints, moments that matter.
- Brand and product strategy: Brand platform, tone/voice, visual identity, product roadmap, value propositions.
- Performance data: Web/app analytics, search data (GSC), social listening, CRM/CDP segments, support tickets, sales insights.
- Market/competitive research: Competitor content audits, share-of-voice, category trends.
- Policies and standards: Privacy (GDPR/CCPA), legal/compliance, accessibility (WCAG 2.2+), security, data governance.
- Technology landscape: CMS/DAM capabilities, MAP/CRM/CDP, experimentation/personalization tooling constraints.
- Content inventory: Existing assets and metadata.

Prerequisites:
- Executive sponsor and cross-functional content council identified.
- Agreement on business objectives and north-star KPIs for content.
- Access to analytics and customer research.
- Defined brand voice and core messaging (or a plan to create them).
- Initial tooling selected or available (CMS, DAM, workflow).

## Process Steps
Phase 1: Initiation and Alignment
1) Confirm objectives and scope
- Actions: Align on business goals, target segments, journey stages, markets, and channels in scope. Define success criteria.

## Best Practices
- Start with customer jobs and journey “moments that matter” to prioritize content.
- Use pillar–cluster models to build topical authority and internal linking structures.
- Adopt a modular content model (components/atoms) to enable reuse and omnichannel delivery (COPE).
- Establish a single taxonomy and metadata standard across CMS, DAM, and MAP; enforce tags at creation.
- Build accessibility and compliance into templates and workflows (shift-left compliance).
- Define clear CTAs and measurement for every asset; avoid “content without a job.”
- Balance efficiency and creativity with templates, but allow space for innovation and testing.
- Use test-and-learn: A/B/N tests, search experiments, and controlled releases; document learnings.
- Manage content debt: set review cadences and sunset policies; prioritize updates over net-new when appropriate.
- Create a content council for cross-functional alignment and decision-making.
- Localize with intent: transcreate high-impact assets; provide market-level flexibility within global guardrails.
- Maintain a robust editorial brief template capturing audience, intent, messaging, SEO, accessibility, CTAs, and measurement.

## Common Challenges
- Siloed content and duplication
  - Solution: Central inventory, DAM adoption, taxonomy governance, and a content council.
- Inconsistent voice and quality
  - Solution: Style guides, templates, training, managing editor role, and QA checklists.
- Bottlenecked approvals
  - Solution: Streamlined RACI, SLA-based workflows, parallel reviews, and pre-approved microcopy libraries.
- Poor discoverability and low organic performance
  - Solution: Topic clusters, schema markup, internal linking, and technical SEO hygiene.
- Measurement gaps and unclear ROI
  - Solution: Standardized tagging, clear KPIs per asset, dashboards, and assisted-conversion attribution.
- Tech fragmentation
  - Solution: Integrate CMS/DAM/MAP/CDP; define content IDs and shared taxonomies; reduce redundant tools.
- Global–local misalignment
  - Solution: Global guardrails + local playbooks; governance with regional representation.
- Accessibility and compliance risks
  - Solution: Bake into templates, automated checks, reviewer training, and audit schedules.

Process Details:
## Overview
Carry out post-launch analytics to test acceptability in the market is the structured process of measuring and interpreting how a newly launched product or service is received by target customers. It quantifies early market response, validates assumptions, identifies improvement opportunities, and informs go/no-go and scale/adjust decisions. This process focuses on both marketing performance (awareness, reach, acquisition efficiency) and product/service performance (usage, satisfaction, retention, quality), integrating multiple data sources to create a holistic view.

Role in the organization:
- Confirms product-market fit signals and commercial viability following launch
- Drives rapid iteration of marketing, pricing, packaging, and product features
- Creates a feedback loop into product lifecycle management, roadmap prioritization, and future launches
- Enables governance: evidence-based decisions for scaling investment, channel mix, and inventory
- Demonstrates compliance with organizational standards for data quality, privacy, and performance reporting

Scope:
- Timeframe: typically from launch (T+1 day) through the first 90–180 days, with ongoing monitoring thereafter
- Applies to digital products, physical goods, and services across B2C/B2B contexts
- Feeds into [2.1.2.5] Conduct post launch review and [2.1] Govern and manage product/service development program

## Key Activities
- Define objectives, hypotheses, and success metrics (primary and guardrail KPIs)
- Ensure instrumentation and data readiness (tracking, tagging, taxonomies)
- Collect and integrate data across channels and systems
- Execute baseline and cohort analyses to isolate launch impact
- Conduct funnel, retention, and engagement analytics; monitor quality and support signals
- Run attribution/marketing mix analyses and channel performance diagnostics
- Capture direct customer feedback (surveys, reviews, interviews) and perform sentiment analysis
- Perform competitive and market benchmarking
- Synthesize insights; recommend actions for marketing, product, pricing, and operations
- Communicate findings via dashboards and reports; track decisions and impacts
- Establish continuous monitoring and iteration (experiments, A/B tests, geo-lifts)

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Launch plan with target segments, channels, markets, and timing
- Defined hypotheses and KPIs (e.g., PMF indicators, ROAS targets, retention)
- Instrumentation: event tracking schema, UTM convention, tag manager setup, pixel placements, SDKs
- Data sources: web/app analytics, ad platforms, CRM/CDP, POS/e-commerce, support/ticketing, reviews, survey tools, product telemetry, finance/returns, retailer syndicated data (e.g., NielsenIQ/Circana)
- Master data: product SKUs, pricing, packaging, channel mapping, customer/segment taxonomy
- Baseline data: pre-launch benchmarks or synthetic controls
- Compliance approvals: privacy, consent management, data use agreements

Prerequisites:
- Data pipelines and warehouse connectivity in place; initial QA passed
- Campaigns and channels configured according to taxonomy (UTM, audience IDs)
- Support operations and VOC capture ready (NPS/CSAT, in-app prompts)
- Attribution/MMM approach defined; experimentation framework established
- Access and roles provisioned; dashboard shells templated

Dependencies on other processes:
- [2.1.2.4] Launch execution and change control (ensures accurate deployment)
- Product master data management and pricing updates
- Customer data governance and consent management
- Issue/defect management and escalation
- Financial reporting and revenue recognition policies

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and align
- Kickoff with Product, Marketing, Data, Sales/CS, Finance to confirm objectives, hypotheses, KPIs, time horizons, and decision gates (e.g., scale, pause, iterate).
- Document counter-metrics/guardrails (e.g., CAC, churn, defect rate).

2) Instrumentation and data readiness check
- Audit tracking (events, parameters, IDs), UTM governance, SDK versions, pixels, retail POS feeds.
- Validate data freshness, completeness, and accuracy with automated checks; fix gaps quickly.

3) Establish baselines and cohorts
- Define pre-launch baselines or synthetic controls; identify seasonality and major confounders.
- Define cohorts: acquisition channel, campaign, segment/persona, geography, device, SKU/plan, first-touch date/week.

4) Collect and integrate data
- Ingest data into warehouse/CDP; schedule ELT/ETL jobs; reconcile IDs across systems.
- Tag production data snapshots for reproducibility; capture marketing spend and promo calendars.

5) Data quality assurance
- Run checks: null rates, duplicates, outliers, schema drift, time skews, attribution coverage.
- Reconcile revenue orders vs. payments vs. cancellations/returns.

6) Early read (T+3 to T+7 days)
- Awareness and acquisition: reach, impressions, CTR, CVR, CAC, ROAS proxies.
- Product signals: activation rate, time-to-value, onboarding completion, early retention (D1/D7), support contact rate, crash/defect rate.
- Identify anomalies, capacity constraints, or stockouts.

7) Funnel and adoption analysis
- Map awareness → consideration → conversion → activation → engagement → retention; identify drop-offs.
- Feature adoption curves, usage frequency, stickiness (DAU/MAU), session durations.

8) Retention and lifetime value analysis
- Cohort retention (D1/D7/D30/D90); churn drivers via behavioral features and feedback.
- Early LTV and payback models; sensitivity to discounting and returns.

9) Marketing performance and attribution
- Channel/campaign contribution via MTA where feasible; triangulate with MMM/geo-lift for incrementality.
- Optimize channel mix; identify saturation and diminishing returns.

10) Customer feedback and sentiment
- Deploy PMF survey (e.g., “How disappointed if no longer available?”), NPS/CSAT/CES, in-product micro-surveys.
- Analyze reviews and social listening for themes and sentiment; quantify top issues.

11) Quality, reliability, and operations
- Track defect/incident rates, response/resolution times, warranty claims, return reasons, app crashes.
- Retail-specific: distribution ACV, velocity (units/store/week), voids, out-of-stocks, share vs. category.

12) Competitive and market context
- Benchmark price, features, ratings, share of voice; overlay competitor promotions or macro events.

13) Synthesize insights and recommend actions
- Summarize what’s working/not; root cause analysis for gaps.
- Propose concrete actions: creative iterations, landing page fixes, pricing tests, feature tweaks, onboarding changes, channel reallocations, supply adjustments.

14) Decision meeting and action tracking
- Present to governance forum; record decisions, owners, target impacts, and timelines.
- Update backlog for product/marketing; prioritize based on impact vs. effort.

15) Continuous monitoring and iteration (T+14 to T+90+ days)
- Establish weekly dashboards and alerts; run experiments (A/B, geo-lift).
- Re-forecast based on observed performance; document lessons learned for the broader post-launch review.

Gateways:
- Gate A (T+7): Continue, pivot, or pause certain channels/segments
- Gate B (T+30): Scale investment, adjust pricing/packaging, roadmap commits
- Gate C (T+90): Proceed to broader rollout or lifecycle adjustments

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Dashboards: launch KPI dashboard, channel performance, funnel/retention, quality/support, VOC and sentiment
- Reports: T+7, T+30, T+90 post-launch analytics reports with insights and recommendations
- Models and analyses: attribution/MMM summaries, early LTV/payback, elasticity, cohort analyses
- Action plan and decision log: prioritized actions, owners, timelines, expected impact
- Data assets: curated datasets, code/notebooks, data dictionary updates
- Lessons learned and risks/issues register

Success criteria:
- Timely delivery of early read (≤7 days) and periodic reports
- Data quality meets thresholds (completeness, accuracy, freshness)
- Clear, actionable recommendations adopted by stakeholders
- Positive movement in leading indicators (e.g., activation, early retention) and guardrails respected
- Demonstrable business impact: improved ROAS, reduced CAC, higher velocity, higher CSAT/NPS

## Best Practices
- Define primary KPIs and guardrails up front; pre-register hypotheses to limit p-hacking
- Audit instrumentation before and after launch; maintain a tracking taxonomy and UTM governance
- Use cohorts and segment deeply (channel, creative, geo, device, persona, SKU/plan)
- Triangulate attribution: combine MTA with MMM/geo experiments for incrementality
- Establish synthetic controls or baselines; adjust for seasonality and external events
- Measure PMF directly (Sean Ellis question) in addition to behavioral metrics
- Build reproducible analytics: versioned code, parameterized reports, documented data lineage
- Automate data quality checks and alerting; monitor data freshness SLAs
- Include counterfactual thinking and sensitivity analyses; report uncertainty ranges
- Close the loop: tie insights to actions, track adoption and realized impact
- Respect privacy and ethics: consent management, data minimization, aggregation where needed

## Common Challenges
- Data fragmentation and delays across platforms and retailers
  - Mitigation: centralized warehouse/CDP, standardized IDs, SLA monitoring, late-arriving data handling
- Mis-tagged campaigns or broken tracking
  - Mitigation: tag governance, pre-flight QA, ongoing audits, server-side tracking where appropriate
- Attribution disputes and overreliance on last-click
  - Mitigation: MMM/geo-lift tests, unified measurement framework, decision rules
- Small sample sizes or biased early adopters
  - Mitigation: extend windows, combine cohorts, Bayesian estimation, careful interpretation
- External confounders (competitor promos, seasonality, PR)
  - Mitigation: controls, event calendars, synthetic control methods, robust baselining
- Retail out-of-stocks and distribution gaps masking demand
  - Mitigation: inventory/ops monitoring, demand-adjusted metrics, coordinated replenishment
- Returns/defects depressing true acceptance
  - Mitigation: include returns/claims in KPIs; root-cause analysis; quality fixes
- Privacy and tracking limitations (ITP, ATT, regulations)
  - Mitigation: first-party data, server-side events, consent optimization, aggregated measurement

Process Details:
## Overview
Review Market Performance is the structured, recurring process used to evaluate how a newly launched or updated product/service is performing in the market, diagnose drivers of performance, and identify opportunities to increase market position. It consolidates quantitative and qualitative signals (e.g., sales, usage, digital engagement, customer feedback) into actionable insights and decisions. This process closes the loop between launch and continuous improvement, informing product roadmaps, pricing and promotion strategies, channel optimization, and customer experience enhancements.

Role in the organization:
- Validates whether the post-launch performance meets commercial, customer, and operational objectives.
- Surfaces issues early (e.g., adoption barriers, quality defects, messaging misalignment) to minimize revenue leakage and churn.
- Prioritizes improvements and experiments that have the highest impact on growth and profitability.
- Enables governance by providing standardized readouts and decisions to the product/service lifecycle management program.

Typical cadence: daily/weekly operational monitoring for leading indicators; monthly/quarterly deep-dive reviews for strategic direction.

## Key Activities
- Define measurement plan and targets (North Star metric, KPIs, guardrails) and analytic hypotheses.
- Ingest, validate, and harmonize market, customer, and operational data.
- Monitor performance dashboards and automated alerts for anomalies or threshold breaches.
- Analyze performance by segment, channel, geography, cohort, and time period, including funnels and paths.
- Triangulate quantitative metrics with qualitative insights (surveys, reviews, support tickets, sales feedback).
- Conduct root cause analysis of variances vs. plan, benchmarks, and control groups.
- Identify growth opportunities and risks; develop recommendations and experiments.
- Prioritize actions (impact, confidence, effort) and assign owners, timelines, and success measures.
- Report findings and decisions; update backlogs, roadmaps, and forecasts.
- Track action outcomes and continuously refine the measurement plan.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Commercial data: orders/sales, revenue, margin, returns/refunds, inventory/stock-outs.
- Digital data: web/app traffic, acquisition channels, conversion funnels, engagement/usage, retention/churn.
- Customer feedback: NPS/CSAT/CES, reviews/ratings, social listening, support tickets/call logs, sales/CSM notes.
- Marketing data: spend, impressions, CTR, CAC, campaign attribution, promo calendars.
- Pricing and competitive data: price lists, discounts, competitor pricing/features/assortment, share-of-voice.
- Operational/quality: defect rates, SLA adherence, delivery times, incident logs.
- Benchmark/plan: business case targets, forecasts, control group baselines, historical comparables.
- Master/reference data: product/service master, channel/region hierarchies, customer segments/personas.
- Legal/compliance constraints: consent flags, data usage permissions.

Prerequisites:
- Post-launch measurement plan with defined KPIs, metric definitions, and target thresholds.
- Instrumentation and tagging implemented and validated across touchpoints.
- Data pipelines and dashboards set up with ownership, refresh cadence, and data quality checks.
- Role clarity and governance (meeting cadence, decision rights, escalation paths).
- Privacy and data governance in place; consent management and PII handling compliant.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 2.1.2.5 Conduct post-launch review (parent discipline).
- Data management and governance (master data, data quality, access control).
- Customer feedback management and market research collection.
- Sales operations, pricing and promotion management, and channel management.
- Issue/defect management and quality assurance.
- Product change management and release/experiment management.

## Process Steps
1) Set objectives and hypotheses
- Confirm North Star metric, primary KPIs (e.g., adoption, conversion, revenue, retention), and guardrails (e.g., CSAT, defect rate, CAC).
- Document hypotheses (e.g., “Feature X will lift conversion by 5% for Segment A”) and expected leading indicators.

2) Prepare measurement and data environment
- Validate instrumentation (events, IDs, parameters), tracking plan coverage, and consent.
- Ensure data ingestion schedules, schema, and joins across sources (CRM, analytics, ERP, ad platforms).
- Run data quality checks: completeness, timeliness, duplication, outliers; resolve issues or flag caveats.

3) Establish baseline and segmentation
- Define baseline (plan, pre-launch, control group, or competitor benchmark).
- Confirm segmentation keys: customer persona, cohort, channel, region, product variant/SKU, price tier.

4) Monitor leading indicators and set alerts
- Configure automated alerts for KPI and guardrail thresholds (e.g., conversion drop > X%, spike in refunds, negative sentiment surge).
- Daily/weekly scan of dashboards for anomalies and trends.

5) Analyze performance
- Descriptive: KPI trends vs. plan and baseline; funnel conversion; cohort retention; path/behavior flow.
- Diagnostic: variance decomposition (mix, price, volume); channel and campaign attribution; promo impact; A/B test results; regression or uplift analysis; seasonality and calendar effects.
- Qualitative triangulation: top verbatims, themes, sentiment drivers; support ticket categories/root causes; sales feedback from the field.

6) Identify drivers, issues, and opportunities
- Synthesize drivers of over/underperformance by segment and channel.
- Map issues to root causes (e.g., UX friction, message-market mismatch, distribution gaps, price sensitivity, quality defects).
- Generate opportunity hypotheses (new channels, pricing tests, onboarding improvements, feature enhancements, content updates).

7) Recommend actions and prioritize
- For each recommendation, define: expected impact, confidence level, effort/cost, owner, timeline, success metric.
- Use a prioritization framework (RICE/ICE) to rank; create an action backlog and experiment plan.

8) Decide and assign
- Present findings in a standardized readout; capture decisions, trade-offs, and approvals.
- Assign owners for actions/experiments; log in work management system with due dates and dependencies.

9) Implement and track
- Execute experiments or changes with proper tagging and guardrails.
- Monitor post-change impact vs. counterfactual (control/holdout) and guardrails; iterate as needed.

10) Communicate and institutionalize learning
- Share outcomes, playbooks, and updated benchmarks; update forecasts and the product roadmap.
- Archive insights in a searchable repository; update the measurement plan and dashboard definitions.

11) Governance and continuous improvement
- Run monthly/quarterly deep dives; audit metric definitions; retire vanity metrics.
- Review process KPIs (e.g., time-to-insight) and address bottlenecks.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Performance dashboards and automated alerting rules.
- Standard readout pack (executive summary, KPI trends, drivers, risks, decisions).
- Insight and decision log with traceability to actions and outcomes.
- Prioritized action and experiment backlog with owners and business cases.
- Root cause analyses and issue tracker with remediation plans.
- Updated forecasts, benchmarks, and metric definitions.
- Customer insight summaries (themes, sentiment, personas impacted).
- Updated product roadmap inputs and change requests (pricing, packaging, UX, channels).

Success criteria:
- KPIs tracked reliably and on time; alerts detect issues before material impact.
- Material improvements in target KPIs versus baseline after actions.
- High adoption rate of recommendations; closed-loop tracking shows ROI.
- Data quality within defined thresholds; stakeholder satisfaction with insights.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product Manager (Accountable): Owns objectives/hypotheses, prioritizes actions, secures decisions, updates roadmap.
- Product Marketing Manager (Responsible): Interprets market/customer signals, messaging tests, competitive intel, channels recommendations.
- Data/Business Analyst (Responsible): Builds dashboards, runs analyses, produces insights and readouts.
- Data Engineer/Analytics Engineer (Responsible): Maintains data pipelines, models, and data quality monitoring.
- Web/App/Product Analytics Specialist (Responsible): Ensures instrumentation, cohorts, funnels, experimentation design and analysis.
- Market Research/Customer Insights Lead (Responsible): Surveys, panels, qualitative synthesis, sentiment analysis.
- Sales Operations/Commercial Lead (Consulted): Shares pipeline/field feedback, channel performance, promo effectiveness.
- Customer Support/Success Lead (Consulted): Provides tickets themes, churn drivers, satisfaction trends.
- Finance Business Partner (Consulted): Validates revenue/margin impacts, supports forecasting and ROI.
- Supply Chain/Operations Lead (Consulted): Inventory, fulfillment, SLA, quality/returns implications.
- Legal/Privacy (Consulted): Ensures compliant data usage and claims; reviews competitive messaging.
- Executive Sponsor/Steering Committee (Informed/Approver): Reviews readouts, approves major pivots and investments.

Note: Tailor RACI by organization scale; in smaller teams, roles may be combined.

## Best Practices
- Define a clear metrics hierarchy: North Star metric, strategic KPIs, and operational guardrails with unambiguous definitions.
- Instrument before you launch; validate tagging in a staging environment and re-validate post-launch.
- Triangulate quant and qual: let customer verbatims contextualize numbers; avoid acting on numbers alone.
- Segment deeply: by cohort, persona, acquisition channel, geography, and product variant to uncover non-obvious drivers.
- Use control groups and pre/post baselines; correct for seasonality, promotions, and exogenous shocks.
- Automate routine monitoring and alerts to focus analyst time on diagnosis and recommendations.
- Maintain a single source of truth (centralized semantic layer, governed dashboards, metric dictionary).
- Treat recommendations as hypotheses; use experimentation to validate; publish playbooks of what works.
- Monitor guardrails (CSAT, defect rates, costs) to avoid improving one KPI at the expense of others.
- Include competitive and category context; track share-of-voice and relative pricing/feature parity.
- Ensure privacy and compliance; collect and use data with clear consent and data minimization.
- Establish a predictable cadence and concise readouts; document decisions and outcomes.
- Close the loop: link every insight to an action and measure the impact of that action.

## Common Challenges
- Data silos and inconsistent metric definitions
  - Solution: Implement a semantic layer/metrics catalog; enforce governance and shared definitions.
- Incomplete or inaccurate instrumentation
  - Solution: Maintain a tracking plan, perform QA, add automated event validation, and instrument feature flags.
- Attribution complexity across channels
  - Solution: Use multi-touch attribution and/or marketing mix modeling; triangulate with controlled experiments.
- Small sample sizes in early post-launch
  - Solution: Focus on leading indicators and directional insights; aggregate cohorts; use Bayesian or hierarchical models.
- Confounding factors (promotions, outages, seasonality)
  - Solution: Use control groups, synthetic controls, or difference-in-differences; annotate dashboards with events.
- Bias in surveys and reviews
  - Solution: Apply sampling controls, weight responses, and use mixed-method research; analyze open-text themes.
- Operational constraints masking demand (stock-outs, limited distribution)
  - Solution: Normalize KPIs for availability; segment by in-stock exposure; coordinate with supply chain.
- Action paralysis or low adoption of insights
  - Solution: Prioritize with clear impact/effort, assign owners, set deadlines, track adoption and ROI, and escalate blockers.
- Privacy and compliance risks
  - Solution: Enforce consent, anonymization, and access controls; involve Legal/Privacy early.

## Performance Metrics
Effectiveness KPIs:
- Commercial: revenue vs. plan, gross margin, average order value, unit economics, LTV/CAC, repeat purchase rate.
- Acquisition and conversion: traffic by channel, CTR, CVR by funnel stage, CAC, ROAS.
- Engagement and retention (for services/digital): DAU/MAU, time-in-product, feature adoption, cohort retention/churn.
- Customer experience: NPS, CSAT, CES, complaint/ticket rate, returns/refunds rate, app/store ratings, sentiment index.
- Operational/quality: defect/incident rate, SLA adherence, on-time delivery, stock-out rate.
- Market position: share-of-voice, category rank, competitive win rate, price index vs. competitors.

Process KPIs:
- Time to insight (launch to first actionable insight), dashboard refresh latency.
- Data quality score (% completeness, accuracy, timeliness).
- Readout cadence adherence (% on-time), stakeholder satisfaction with insights.
- Insight-to-action rate, average cycle time from insight to implemented action.
- Experiment velocity (# tests per period) and win rate (% tests with positive, significant impact).
- Percentage of actions with measured ROI; forecast accuracy over time.

## Technology and Tools
- Data platform: data warehouse/lake (e.g., Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift), lakehouse (e.g., Databricks).
- Ingestion and transformation: ELT/ETL (e.g., Fivetran, Stitch), transformation/metrics layer (e.g., dbt, LookML, MetricFlow).
- BI and visualization: Tableau, Power BI, Looker, Mode; alerting via email/Slack.
- Web/app/product analytics: GA4, Adobe Analytics, Mixpanel, Amplitude, Heap; session replay/heatmaps (e.g., Hotjar, FullStory).
- Experimentation and feature flagging: Optimizely, LaunchDarkly, VWO, Statsig.
- Customer feedback and research: Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey, Medallia; social listening (Brandwatch, Sprinklr); review syndication (Bazaarvoice); app store consoles.
- CRM/CDP and marketing: Salesforce, HubSpot; CDP (Segment, mParticle); ad platforms and MTA/MMM tools.
- Competitive intelligence: price trackers, share-of-voice tools, app/category ranking tools.
- Collaboration and documentation: Confluence/Notion, Jira/Azure DevOps, Aha!/Productboard, Slack/Teams.
- Data quality and observability: Great Expectations, Monte Carlo, Bigeye.
- Privacy/compliance: consent management platforms (OneTrust, TrustArc); data access controls.

Process Details:
## Overview
Review effectiveness of supply chain and distribution network is a post-launch evaluation process that assesses how well the end-to-end supply chain supports a new or updated product/service after it reaches the market. It determines whether procurement, manufacturing, warehousing, transportation, last-mile delivery, and reverse logistics are meeting demand, service levels, quality expectations, cost targets, sustainability requirements, and compliance obligations across all stakeholders (customers, partners, suppliers, vendors, internal departments).

Purpose:
- Verify the supply chain and distribution network can reliably meet market demand for the launched product/service.
- Identify bottlenecks, risks, and inefficiencies by node and hand-off (supplier, inbound, plant, DC, carrier, last-mile).
- Quantify performance against targets; implement corrective and preventive actions (CAPA).
- Capture lessons learned to stabilize current operations and inform future launches, product lifecycle decisions, and network design.

Role in the organization:
- Provides objective, data-driven feedback to the product/service development program during post-launch.
- Feeds S&OP/IBP, demand/supply planning, procurement, quality, and customer service with insights and actions.
- Enables governance decisions (e.g., capacity investments, supplier changes, routing guides, inventory policy adjustments).
- Supports compliance, cost-to-serve management, and customer satisfaction/retention goals.

## Key Activities
- Define scope and targets: service levels, cost, quality, sustainability, compliance thresholds for the launched SKU(s)/service(s).
- Collect and validate performance data across the network (ERP, WMS, TMS, OMS, supplier portals, 3PLs, carriers).
- Map and analyze end-to-end flow, capacities, and constraints (from input to shop floor to delivery).
- Segment analysis by channel, region, customer tier, and product portfolio to find localized issues.
- Conduct root-cause analysis for variances (e.g., OTIF misses, backorders, damage, returns).
- Partner and stakeholder reviews (suppliers, 3PLs, carriers, sales, customer service).
- Develop and execute corrective/preventive action plans with owners, timelines, and KPIs.
- Update master data, SOPs, routing guides, safety stock and reorder policies, packaging specs.
- Report outcomes to governance and integrate into S&OP/IBP cycles; monitor sustained performance.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Demand plan, sales forecast, and actual orders by channel/region/customer.
- Product master data: SKUs, BOM, pack dimensions/weights, handling/storage requirements, regulatory constraints.
- Supply plans: production schedules, capacity plans, supplier lead times, MOQ, yield assumptions.
- Operational data: inventory positions, ATP/CTP status, WIP, cycle counts, backorders, expedites.
- Logistics data: carrier assignments, routing guide, transit times, delivery appointments, tracking events.
- Quality and returns data: defect codes, damage rates, RMA volumes, root-cause notes.
- Cost data: freight, warehousing, handling, packaging, duties, cost-to-serve.
- Service commitments: SLAs, OTIF/Fill Rate targets, customer-specific requirements, penalties.
- Sustainability/compliance requirements: emissions targets, packaging regulations, documentation accuracy.

Prerequisites:
- Agreed KPI definitions and data governance (common calendar, time zones, units, service definitions).
- System access and data integration with partners (EDI/API, file shares) and internal systems (ERP/WMS/TMS/OMS/BI).
- Post-launch review cadence defined (e.g., weekly for first 4–6 weeks, monthly thereafter; formal 30/60/90-day gates).
- Established escalation thresholds and decision rights (who can approve capacity/cost changes).
- NDAs and data-sharing agreements with external partners; privacy and security controls.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 2.1.2.5 Conduct post launch review (parent process).
- S&OP/IBP for demand-supply balancing.
- Supplier and partner management (onboarding, performance management).
- Quality management and CAPA.
- Change control and master data governance.
- Risk management and business continuity.
- Financial planning and cost management.

## Process Steps
1) Plan the review
- Confirm scope: SKUs/services, geographies, channels, customer segments, time horizon.
- Reaffirm targets: OTIF, fill rate, order cycle time, inventory health, cost-to-serve, return rate, emissions, compliance.
- Establish cadence: daily monitoring for critical KPIs during hypercare, weekly working sessions, 30/60/90-day gate reviews.

2) Build the data set
- Extract data from ERP, WMS, TMS, OMS, supplier/carrier portals for the review period.
- Reconcile data: align order IDs, shipment IDs, timestamps, and locations. Validate master data (dimensions, pack configs).
- Assess data quality: duplicate orders, missing events, latency; issue data quality tickets where needed.

3) Map the end-to-end flow
- Document current state process map and network path: suppliers → inbound transport → plant/CM → DC → carrier → customer → reverse.
- Identify capacities and constraints: supplier lead time variability, production capacity, dock capacity, carrier capacity, cut-off times, cold chain.

4) Analyze performance
- Calculate KPIs at each node and hand-off (see Performance Metrics).
- Segment results by region/channel/customer/service level; highlight variances vs. target and budget.
- Use control charts to distinguish normal variation from special causes; quantify cost/impact of misses.

5) Deep-dive by exception
- Prioritize top exceptions by customer impact and cost: OTIF misses, backorders, split shipments, damages, claims, high DOS, aged inventory.
- Conduct root-cause analysis using 5 Whys/Fishbone across categories: demand signal, supply constraints, data, process, people, technology.
- Validate with stakeholders (e.g., carrier POD analysis, warehouse pick accuracy check, supplier ASN timeliness).

6) Partner and stakeholder reviews
- Run targeted sessions: suppliers (OTIF, lead time, ASN), 3PLs (dock-to-stock, pick accuracy), carriers (on-time, claims), customer service (complaints, NPS).
- Review adherence to SLAs and routing guides; identify needed contract or guide adjustments.

7) Develop action plan
- Define corrective and preventive actions with SMART owners/dates: e.g., add safety stock, adjust reorder points, change carrier, re-slot SKU, revise pack.
- Quantify expected benefit, cost, and risk. Obtain approvals per governance thresholds.
- Establish control plan: monitoring metrics, thresholds, and triggers for escalation.

8) Pilot and implement
- Pilot changes in a contained scope (select DC, region, or customer) for 2–4 weeks.
- Measure effect vs. baseline; adjust and scale successful interventions.
- Update SOPs, work instructions, routing guides; train impacted teams and partners.

9) Update master data and systems
- Amend product master (dimensions, weights), transportation attributes (NMFC, hazard), inventory policies (safety stock, reorder points), carrier lanes.
- Ensure synchronization across ERP/WMS/TMS/OMS and partner systems; verify through test transactions.

10) Report and govern
- Produce a post-launch supply chain performance report and dashboard with trend graphs, exceptions, actions, and residual risks.
- Present at governance forums and S&OP/IBP; decide on capacity investments, supplier diversification, or network redesign if warranted.

11) Continuous monitoring and lessons learned
- Maintain weekly dashboards during stabilization; taper to monthly.
- Document lessons learned for future launches; feed into playbooks and network design models.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Post-launch supply chain performance report (executive summary + detailed analytics).
- KPI dashboards and scorecards by node/partner/channel.
- Root-cause analysis documentation and heat maps.
- Corrective/Preventive Action Plan with owners, timelines, and expected benefits.
- Updated SOPs, routing guides, packaging specs, inventory policies, and master data.
- Partner performance reviews and QBR materials; contract/RFP recommendations if needed.
- Risk register updates and contingency plans.
- Decision log and governance meeting minutes.

Success criteria:
- Service levels stabilize at or above targets (e.g., OTIF ≥ 95%, fill rate ≥ 98%).
- Cost-to-serve within budget; reduced expedites and penalties.
- Inventory health meets policy (turns, DOS, minimal stockouts/overstocks).
- Quality/damage/return rates within thresholds.
- Sustained KPI improvements for 2–3 consecutive cycles; actions closed on time.
- Positive customer feedback/NPS trend; compliance and documentation accuracy > 99%.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Supply Chain Performance Manager: Owns the review, orchestrates data, analysis, and action plans; reports to governance.
- Logistics/Distribution Manager: Reviews carrier performance, routing guides, transit times; implements transport actions.
- Warehouse/DC Manager: Assesses receiving, putaway, slotting, picking, pack/ship, dock-to-stock; leads DC improvements.
- Manufacturing/Operations Manager: Evaluates schedule adherence, throughput, yields; drives capacity and process fixes.
- Procurement/Supplier Manager: Manages supplier OTIF, lead-time variability, ASNs; leads supplier corrective actions.
- Demand Planning Lead: Validates forecast accuracy and bias; improves forecasting and signal sharing.
- Customer Service/Sales Ops: Provides customer feedback, complaints, order issues; aligns service priorities.
- Quality Manager: Analyzes defects, damages, returns; leads CAPA and packaging improvements.
- Transportation/Carrier Manager: Manages carrier SLAs, claims, tender acceptance, network capacity.
- IT/Data Analyst: Data integration, validation, KPI calculation, dashboards; process mining and root-cause analytics.
- Finance/Cost Analyst: Cost-to-serve analysis, budget variance, ROI for actions.
- Compliance/Regulatory: Ensures documentation, labeling, and regulatory adherence (e.g., hazmat, cold chain).
- Sustainability Lead: Calculates emissions, packaging waste; identifies greener alternatives.
- 3PLs/Carriers/Suppliers: Provide data, attend reviews, execute agreed actions.

## Best Practices
- Adopt a closed-loop PDCA cycle with clear gates (T+30/60/90 days).
- Use standardized KPI definitions and a single source of truth (data model, calendar, units).
- Segment analysis by channel/customer/tier and ABC/XYZ to target actions where impact is highest.
- Build visibility via EDI/API with partners (ASN, ship notice, proof of delivery, inventory).
- Employ control charts and exception-based monitoring; focus on statistically significant variances.
- Apply Theory of Constraints to address system bottlenecks; avoid local optimizations that hurt end-to-end flow.
- Perform multi-echelon inventory optimization for safety stock and reorder policies.
- Maintain robust master data governance; validate dimensions/weights and packaging early.
- Run joint business reviews with partners using shared scorecards; align incentives and SLAs.
- Use digital twins/network modeling for scenario testing (promotion spikes, lane closures, capacity shifts).
- Incorporate reverse logistics and quality feedback into forward flow improvements.
- Bake in compliance and sustainability targets (documentation accuracy, CO2e per shipment) as first-class KPIs.

## Common Challenges
- Data quality and latency across disparate systems and partners.
  - Solutions: MDM, automated validation rules, harmonized identifiers, control totals, SLAs for data timeliness.
- Forecast volatility or bias driving whiplash in supply.
  - Solutions: Demand sensing, CPFR with key customers, promo planning integration, bias monitoring and re-forecast cadence.
- Capacity constraints at suppliers, plants, DCs, or carriers.
  - Solutions: Flex capacity agreements, dual sourcing, cross-docking, alternate lanes, shift changes, overtime with clear cost caps.
- Last-mile variability and missed delivery appointments.
  - Solutions: Appointment scheduling systems, dynamic routing, carrier mix optimization, delivery time windows aligned with customer SLAs.
- High damage/return rates.
  - Solutions: Packaging redesign, handling SOPs, shock/tilt indicators, targeted training, root-cause CAPA.
- Siloed decision-making and slow escalations.
  - Solutions: Daily tiered huddles, clear escalation matrix, integrated control tower visibility.
- Compliance/documentation errors.
