# [2.2.3.1.1] Define Basic Functional Requirements

## Overview
Define Basic Functional Requirements is the process of determining what the product/service must do to satisfy customer and market needs, expressed as clear, testable, value-driven functions. In the marketing environment, this focuses on features and capabilities that enable positioning, demand generation, lead capture/fulfillment, customer engagement, and measurable outcomes (e.g., acquisition, conversion, retention).

This process translates business and marketing objectives, user insights, and regulatory constraints into functional requirements that guide design, development, and go-to-market planning. It ensures the organization builds the right capabilities, aligned to the product strategy, target segments, channels, and brand promise, while remaining feasible within technical, operational, and cost constraints.

Role in the organization:
- Anchors product/service scope and feature set to market needs and commercial goals.
- Enables cross-functional alignment among Product, Marketing, Sales, Compliance, Engineering, and Operations.
- Creates a baseline for downstream design, prototyping, development, and testing.
- Reduces delivery risk by clarifying acceptance criteria and traceability to objectives and marketing KPIs.

## Key Activities
- Clarify scope and objectives for the basic functional layer (must-do capabilities, MVP/MMF).
- Elicit and synthesize needs from market research, personas, journeys, JTBD (jobs-to-be-done), and stakeholder inputs.
- Translate needs into functional requirements, user stories/use cases, and acceptance criteria.
- Map requirements to marketing processes (e.g., campaign execution, lead capture, attribution, offers, pricing/promotion).
- Prioritize requirements using value/impact and feasibility frameworks (e.g., MoSCoW, RICE).
- Validate feasibility with architecture, data, security, and compliance (advertising and privacy).
- Model process flows and data flows to inform integration with MarTech/CRM/CDP and the fulfillment chain.
- Define instrumentation and analytics needs to measure marketing outcomes.
- Review and obtain cross-functional approval; baseline and maintain traceability.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Product vision, positioning, value proposition, and target segments.
- Marketing objectives and KPIs (e.g., acquisition targets, conversion rates, CAC, ROAS).
- Market research, competitive analysis, and VOC/UX insights (personas, JTBD, journey maps).
- Existing product/service capabilities and backlog; gap analysis.
- Regulatory/compliance requirements (privacy, consent, advertising standards, claims substantiation, accessibility).
- Technical constraints and platform guidelines (architecture, integration patterns, data models).
- Budget, timeline, and capacity constraints.

Prerequisites:
- Executive or product-level mandate to proceed (e.g., initiative charter/brief).
- Stakeholder availability (Product, Marketing, Engineering, Compliance, Sales/CS, Data/Analytics).
- Access to relevant systems and data sources (analytics, CRM, CDP, prior studies).
- Defined definition-of-ready quality criteria for requirements.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Upstream: Generate and define new product/service ideas; Define product/service development requirements [2.2.3]; Define product/service requirements [2.2.3.1].
- Downstream: Detailed requirements and specification; Experience/technical design; Prototyping and validation; Backlog management and development; Test planning.

## Process Steps
1) Kickoff and scope alignment
- Actions: Confirm objectives, success measures, target segments, scope boundaries (MVP/MMF), and marketing channels.
- Roles: Product Manager (lead), Marketing Lead, Business Analyst, Architect, Compliance.
- Artifacts: Scope statement, high-level objectives/KPIs, assumptions/constraints.

2) Stakeholder and user context synthesis
- Actions: Review personas, JTBD, journeys; analyze market/competitive insights; identify key use cases and pain points; determine claims to be supported.
- Roles: UX/Research, Marketing, Product, Data Analyst.
- Artifacts: Context packet (personas, journeys), problem statements, opportunity hypotheses.

3) Elicit functional needs
- Actions: Run workshops/interviews; capture capabilities needed to support marketing processes:
  - Demand generation (campaign setup, segmentation, offers, personalization).
  - Discovery and conversion (search/SEO metadata, landing pages, product information, pricing/promo rules).
  - Lead and order capture (forms, validation, consent, attribution, checkout).
  - Engagement and retention (notifications, onboarding, loyalty).
  - Measurement (events, UTM governance, attribution, dashboards).
- Roles: BA (facilitator), Marketing Ops, Product, Sales/CS, Compliance, Data/Analytics, Engineering reps.
- Artifacts: Elicitation notes, capability list, preliminary constraints/risks.

4) Draft functional requirements and user stories
- Actions: Translate needs into atomic, testable functional requirements and stories with acceptance criteria (e.g., Given-When-Then). Specify:
  - Triggers, actors, preconditions, and success outcomes.
  - Edge cases and failure handling.
  - Data inputs/outputs (including PII handling and consent).
  - Instrumentation events for KPIs.
- Roles: BA (author), QA (testability), Data Analyst (instrumentation), Security/Privacy (data handling).
- Artifacts: Functional Requirements Document (FRD) or backlog of epics/stories; acceptance criteria; data/event dictionary.

5) Process and data flow modeling
- Actions: Map end-to-end flows linking marketing systems (CMS, CDP, CRM, MAP, analytics) and core product/services; depict integrations, handoffs, and SLAs.
- Roles: Architect, BA, Marketing Ops, Engineering.
- Artifacts: BPMN/L3 process maps, integration/data flow diagrams.

6) Feasibility and compliance assessment
- Actions: Review requirements for technical feasibility, performance and scalability basics, integration complexity, security/privacy, and advertising/claims compliance; refine as needed.
- Roles: Architect, Security/Privacy, Compliance/Legal, Engineering Lead.
- Artifacts: Feasibility notes, risk log, compliance checklist updates.

7) Prioritization and scoping
- Actions: Score requirements by value/impact (e.g., revenue, CAC, conversion) and effort/risk; select MVP/MMF; identify dependencies; set release slices.
- Roles: Product Manager (decision), Marketing Lead, Engineering Lead, Finance (if needed).
- Artifacts: Prioritized backlog (MoSCoW/RICE), release plan, dependency map.

8) Validation with stakeholders and rapid experiments
- Actions: Validate core assumptions via prototypes, wireframes, content mockups, or A/B tests; adjust requirements to reflect learnings.
- Roles: UX/Product Design, Product, Marketing, Engineering, Data.
- Artifacts: Prototype results, updated stories/criteria.

9) Final review, sign-off, and baselining
- Actions: Conduct formal review; ensure completeness, consistency, and traceability; obtain approvals; baseline version; define change control.
- Roles: Product (approve), Marketing (approve), Engineering, Compliance, QA.
- Artifacts: Signed-off FRD/backlog; traceability matrix; change log.

10) Handover to downstream teams
- Actions: Walk through requirements with Design, Engineering, QA, and Ops; confirm Definition of Ready; schedule refinement and test case derivation.
- Roles: BA, Product, QA Lead, Engineering Lead.
- Artifacts: Handover deck, backlog in work management tool, initial test scenarios.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Functional Requirements Document or structured backlog of epics/stories.
- Acceptance criteria for each functional requirement.
- Process and data flow diagrams.
- Event/instrumentation specification aligned to marketing KPIs.
- Prioritized backlog with MVP/MMF scope and release plan.
- Traceability matrix linking requirements to objectives, personas, and compliance items.
- Risk/assumption/decision logs.
- Formal approvals and baseline record.

Success criteria:
- 100% of baseline requirements are clear, testable, and prioritized with acceptance criteria.
- Traceability established from requirements to objectives/KPIs and back to test cases.
- Stakeholder sign-off achieved within agreed timelines with no critical open risks.
- Minimal scope churn post-baseline; low defect leakage attributable to requirement gaps.
- Instrumentation requirements enable reporting of target KPIs at launch.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product Manager: Owns scope, prioritization, and approvals; ensures alignment to strategy and commercial goals.
- Business Analyst: Facilitates elicitation; authors requirements, acceptance criteria, and traceability; maintains artifacts.
- Marketing Lead/Marketing Operations: Provides channel/process needs; defines campaign, segmentation, offer, and attribution requirements; validates marketing measurement needs.
- UX/Research: Provides personas, journeys, and usability insights; assists in validation/prototyping.
- Solution/Enterprise Architect: Assesses feasibility; defines integration patterns and data flows.
- Engineering Lead/SME: Estimates effort; identifies technical constraints; ensures Definition of Ready.
- Data/Analytics: Defines events, tagging, UTM governance, attribution logic, and KPI calculations.
- Compliance/Legal: Reviews advertising claims, consent/privacy, accessibility, and regulatory requirements.
- Security/Privacy: Ensures secure data handling, consent capture, and PII minimization.
- QA/Test Lead: Ensures requirements are testable; seeds test cases from acceptance criteria.
- Sales/Customer Success: Validates lead lifecycle, handoff, and feedback loops; contributes customer insights.
- Operations/Supply Chain (as applicable): Validates feasibility for fulfillment, pricing/promo execution, SLAs.
- Finance (as needed): Confirms commercial thresholds (pricing, margin, promotion guardrails).

## Best Practices
- Focus on the “what” and “why,” not the “how.” Avoid prematurely locking into solutions.
- Write atomic, testable requirements with clear acceptance criteria and edge cases.
- Use consistent templates and nomenclature; standardize story and criteria formats.
- Maintain end-to-end traceability to objectives, personas, journeys, and tests.
- Prioritize ruthlessly using value and feasibility; define a clear MVP/MMF.
- Include analytics and instrumentation requirements upfront; define event semantics and data governance.
- Embed privacy-by-design, consent management, and accessibility requirements from the start.
- Model business and data flows to expose integration needs early (CRM, CDP, MAP, CMS, PIM).
- Validate assumptions quickly via prototypes or experiments; iterate before baselining.
- Control scope with a lightweight change control process post-baseline.
- Plan for localization, brand consistency, and content operations where applicable.
- Involve QA early to ensure testability and reduce rework.

## Common Challenges
- Ambiguity or overlap in requirements
  - Solution: Use examples and Gherkin-style criteria; facilitate clarification workshops; maintain a glossary.
- Conflicting stakeholder priorities
  - Solution: Apply agreed prioritization framework; tie decisions to KPIs and strategy; escalate via governance.
- Scope creep after baseline
  - Solution: Enforce change control; assess impact on value, cost, and timeline; maintain transparent trade-off logs.
- Underestimating integration complexity (CRM/CDP/MAP/CMS)
  - Solution: Early architecture reviews; map data contracts; pilot critical integrations.
- Compliance and privacy surprises
  - Solution: Engage Compliance and Privacy at elicitation; maintain a regulatory checklist; validate claims substantiation sources.
- Missing instrumentation for marketing KPIs
  - Solution: Define event taxonomy and tracking requirements as first-class items; align with analytics early.
- Overengineering vs. MVP needs
  - Solution: Align on MMF; defer nice-to-haves; timebox discovery and experiments.
- Accessibility and localization gaps
  - Solution: Include WCAG and localization acceptance criteria; involve accessibility SMEs.

## Performance Metrics
- Lead time to baseline requirements (start to sign-off).
- Percentage of requirements with complete acceptance criteria.
- Requirements volatility rate post-baseline (changes per sprint/release).
- Defect leakage attributable to requirement gaps (in QA/UAT/production).
- Stakeholder satisfaction score at sign-off and post-release.
- Traceability completeness (requirements linked to objectives and test cases).
- Coverage of key personas/journeys (requirements mapped to journey stages).
- Cycle time from requirement handover to test case readiness.
- Percentage of requirements with defined instrumentation for KPIs.
- On-time delivery of MVP/MMF scope into downstream phases.

## Technology and Tools
- Requirements and backlog management: Jira, Azure DevOps, Rally; Confluence/Notion for documentation.
- Process and architecture modeling: BPMN tools (Lucidchart, Visio, Draw.io), ArchiMate tools.
- Prototyping and design: Figma, Sketch, Adobe XD.
- Collaboration and workshops: Miro, Mural, Teams, Zoom.
- Data and analytics: GA4, Adobe Analytics, Amplitude/Mixpanel; Looker/Tableau/Power BI.
- Marketing technology integration: CMS (e.g., Contentful, Adobe AEM), CDP (Segment, mParticle), CRM (Salesforce, HubSpot), MAP (Marketo, Eloqua, Braze), Tag Manager (GTM, Tealium).
- Consent and compliance: OneTrust, TrustArc; accessibility checkers (axe, WAVE).
- Test management: Zephyr, Xray, TestRail; BDD tools (Cucumber) for acceptance criteria.
- Traceability and requirements quality: Jama Connect, Polarion, ReqSuite; linters/templates.
- Documentation and version control: Git for versioning specifications; knowledge repositories.

Process Details:
## Overview
Derive interoperability requirements for products and services is the process of determining how a product or service will reliably connect, exchange, interpret, and use data with other systems across multi-vendor, multi-network, and multi-service environments. It translates business and product goals into precise, testable requirements for interfaces, protocols, data models, security, performance, and compliance so that solutions can integrate within an ecosystem without custom rework.

Purpose:
- Ensure products/services can interoperate with external partners, platforms, and legacy systems using accepted standards and well-defined interfaces.
- Reduce integration cost, time-to-onboard partners, and risk of vendor lock-in.
- Establish non-functional expectations (reliability, security, latency, scalability) specific to cross-system operations.
- Provide a clear basis for design, procurement, testing, certification, and partner onboarding.

Role in the organization:
- A level-5 process within product/service requirements definition, feeding architecture, design, vendor selection, and verification.
- Bridges product management, enterprise/integration architecture, security, data governance, network engineering, QA, and supplier management.
- Ensures requirements are aligned with enterprise architecture, regulatory obligations, and the standards strategy.

## Key Activities
- Elicit interoperability needs from business use cases, user journeys, and partner scenarios.
- Map the ecosystem: identify systems, vendors, networks, and services to interoperate with.
- Assess applicable standards, profiles, and regulatory requirements.
- Define interface requirements: APIs, events, messaging, files/EDI, and control interfaces.
- Define data model and semantics, including canonical models and mappings.
- Define security and trust requirements (identity, authentication, authorization, encryption, key/cert management).
- Define performance, capacity, and availability requirements across integrations.
- Define compatibility and versioning strategy (backward/forward compatibility, deprecation).
- Define integration patterns, error handling, observability, and operational requirements.
- Validate feasibility with suppliers, partners, and internal teams; prototype if needed.
- Prioritize, baseline, and trace requirements to business goals and test cases.
- Plan conformance and interoperability testing and certifications.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Product/service vision and high-level requirements.
- Business process flows, use cases, and partner onboarding scenarios.
- Inventory of existing systems, interfaces, and data entities.
- Enterprise architecture standards, integration guidelines, and technology roadmap.
- Security policies, data classification, privacy and regulatory constraints.
- Network topology, connectivity constraints, and environment types (on-prem, cloud, edge).
- SLAs/SLOs, performance targets, availability and disaster recovery objectives.
- Vendor and partner capability statements and interface specifications (if available).
- Known industry standards and profiles relevant to the domain.

Prerequisites:
- Cross-functional team identified (product, architecture, data, security, QA, operations, vendor management).
- Stakeholder map and access to internal and external SMEs.
- Agreed definition of done for requirements and acceptance criteria format.
- Access to requirements and documentation repositories.
- Initial test environment or sandbox plan for feasibility checks.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Upstream: Define product/service requirements; Analyze target markets; Establish standards strategy.
- Parallel: Data governance and MDM; Security and privacy requirement definition.
- Downstream: Solution architecture and interface design; Vendor selection and contracting; Test planning and development; Partner onboarding and certification.

## Process Steps
1) Plan and scope
- Confirm objectives, in-scope/out-of-scope systems, partners, networks, and services.
- Define interoperability levels to cover: technical (connectivity), syntactic (data format), semantic (meaning), organizational (process), and policy (compliance).
- Establish timeline, RACI, and communication plan.

2) Elicit interoperability use cases
- Capture end-to-end flows requiring cross-system interactions, including error and exception paths.
- Document data exchanges, directionality, frequency, volumes, timing constraints, and triggers (request/response or event-driven).
- Identify onboarding, configuration, provisioning, and deprovisioning needs for partners.

3) Ecosystem and capability mapping
- Build an integration context diagram: producers, consumers, brokers, networks, control planes.
- Catalog existing interfaces and constraints (legacy protocols, batch windows, throttling).
- Identify candidate integration patterns: REST/gRPC, messaging (AMQP/MQTT), event streaming, file/EDI, OPC UA/industrial, etc.

4) Standards and compliance assessment
- Identify applicable industry standards and profiles (e.g., OpenAPI/JSON/XML, OAuth 2.0/OIDC, SAML, ISO 20022 for payments, HL7 FHIR for healthcare, GS1/EDI for supply chain, OPC UA/MQTT for industrial, ISO/IEC security standards).
- Determine network standards (TLS 1.2+/mTLS, IPv6, DNS, NTP for time sync).
- Record regulatory and certification requirements (e.g., GDPR/CCPA, HIPAA, PCI DSS, telecom/3GPP profiles, sector-specific certifications).

5) Define data and semantics
- Establish a canonical data model for shared entities and events where feasible.
- Specify schemas (JSON Schema, XML Schema, Avro/Protobuf) and namespace/version conventions.
- Define semantic mappings to/from partner/vendor models, including transformation rules and lossless constraints.
- Define identifiers, master data ownership, data lineage, and synchronization approach (e.g., CDC, golden record).
- Define data quality and validation rules.

6) Define interfaces and protocols
- Select protocols and patterns per use case with rationale.
- Specify API requirements: endpoints, methods, idempotency rules, pagination, error codes, rate limits, retry/backoff policies, timeouts.
- Specify event/messaging requirements: topics/queues, event contracts, ordering, at-least/exactly-once semantics, replay/retention.
- Specify file/EDI transfer requirements: formats, naming, encryption, delivery guarantees, acknowledgments.
- Define Interface Control Documents (ICDs) and/or API specifications (OpenAPI/AsyncAPI).

7) Define security and trust
- Identity and access: OAuth 2.0/OIDC, SAML for B2B, client credentials/JWT profiles, fine-grained authorization (ABAC/RBAC).
- Transport and data protection: TLS 1.2+ with modern cipher suites, mTLS where appropriate, encryption at rest, key rotation.
- Trust anchors: PKI, certificate management, CA policies, secrets management.
- Privacy: data minimization, pseudonymization, consent propagation, data residency.
- Security operations: threat modeling for interfaces, logging requirements, security headers, API gateway/WAF policies.

8) Define performance and reliability
- Define latency budgets (p50/p95/p99), throughput, concurrency, payload size limits.
- Availability targets and failover expectations across boundaries (active-active/active-passive).
- Resilience: retry policies, circuit breakers, bulkheads, timeouts, dead-letter queues.
- QoS, prioritization, and backpressure handling for shared infrastructure.

9) Define compatibility, versioning, and lifecycle
- Versioning strategy (semantic versioning, URI versioning for APIs, schema evolution rules).
- Backward/forward compatibility requirements and deprecation timelines.
- Multi-version support policy and sunsetting criteria.
- Vendor and network compatibility matrix (supported versions, options, cipher suites, profiles).

10) Define observability and operations
- Logging, correlation IDs, audit trails, metrics, traces, and span attributes to propagate across systems (OpenTelemetry).
- Health checks, synthetic monitors, contract tests in CI.
- Supportability: runbooks, onboarding checklists, configuration management.

11) Testability and conformance
- Define acceptance criteria and conformance profiles per interface/protocol.
- Plan for interoperability testing: contract testing (e.g., Pact), schema validation, negative testing, fuzzing, soak tests.
- Identify external certification programs and test tooling.

12) Validate and prioritize
- Review requirements with stakeholders, partners, and vendors; run POCs or simulations if needed.
- Prioritize using MoSCoW or similar; flag dependencies and technical debt.
- Update risk register and mitigation plans.

13) Baseline, trace, and approve
- Baseline the Interoperability Requirements Specification (IRS) with sign-offs.
- Ensure traceability from business requirements to interoperability requirements to test cases.
- Store in the requirements repository and communicate to design, procurement, and QA.

14) Manage change
- Establish change control for interfaces and schemas.
- Communicate changes to partners via release notes and deprecation policy.
- Keep compatibility and standards conformance matrices up to date.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Interoperability Requirements Specification (IRS) covering interfaces, data, security, performance, and compliance.
- Interface Control Documents (ICDs), API specifications (OpenAPI), event contracts (AsyncAPI), and schema artifacts.
- Canonical data model and mapping specifications.
- Standards and conformance matrix listing adopted standards and required profiles.
- Compatibility matrix across vendors, versions, networks, and options.
- Interoperability test plan and acceptance criteria; certification requirements where applicable.
- Risk register and mitigation actions specific to interoperability.
- Onboarding checklist and integration guidelines for partners.
- Baseline and traceability records in the requirements tool.

Success criteria:
- Stakeholder and vendor sign-off on the IRS and ICDs.
- 100% traceability from business use cases to interoperability requirements and test cases.
- Feasibility demonstrated via POC or sandbox where risk is high.
- Conformance tests defined for all interfaces; no critical gaps.
- Alignment with enterprise standards and regulatory requirements confirmed.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product Manager: Owns business goals and prioritization; approves scope and acceptance criteria.
- Enterprise/Systems Architect: Leads the overall interoperability architecture and alignment with standards.
- Integration Architect: Selects integration patterns; defines interface and messaging requirements.
- Data Architect/Steward: Owns canonical models, schemas, mappings, identifiers, and data quality rules.
- Security Architect/Officer: Defines identity, encryption, authorization, and compliance requirements.
- Network Architect/Engineer: Defines connectivity, routing, QoS, and network security constraints.
- QA/Test Lead: Defines conformance and contract tests; plans interoperability testing.
- Vendor/Supplier Manager: Coordinates with vendors; gathers partner capabilities and constraints.
- Compliance/Privacy Officer: Ensures regulatory and privacy requirements are embedded.
- Dev Leads/Solution Engineers: Provide feasibility feedback; prototype and validate requirements.
- Service/Operations Lead: Defines observability and support requirements; prepares runbooks.

## Best Practices
- Start with end-to-end use cases and data flows; design for the ecosystem, not a single point integration.
- Prefer open, widely adopted standards and well-documented profiles; avoid proprietary lock-in.
- Use contract-first design for APIs/events and enforce with CI pipeline validations.
- Establish a canonical data model for shared entities; manage mappings systematically.
- Design for backward compatibility; publish a clear versioning and deprecation policy.
- Implement zero trust principles and least privilege for cross-organization integrations.
- Build for resilience: timeouts, retries with backoff, idempotency keys, circuit breakers.
- Standardize error models and correlation IDs across all interfaces.
- Define latency budgets and performance SLAs early; test under realistic loads and network conditions.
- Invest in observability and contract testing; simulate partner systems with mocks/virtual services.
- Maintain a living compatibility and standards conformance matrix.
- Engage suppliers and partners early; co-create interoperability profiles and test cases.
- Document onboarding guides and checklists to reduce partner integration time.

## Common Challenges
- Ambiguous semantics and mismatched data models
  - Mitigation: Define canonical models, explicit field semantics, and mapping rules; include examples and edge cases.
- Legacy systems with proprietary or batch-only interfaces
  - Mitigation: Use adapters/gateways; schedule windows; staged modernization; file-to-API bridges.
- Version sprawl and breaking changes
  - Mitigation: Semantic versioning, strict deprecation policy, API compatibility tests in CI, schema evolution rules.
- Performance and reliability across unreliable networks
  - Mitigation: Caching, asynchronous patterns, offline queues, backpressure, QoS, CDN/edge for latency-sensitive use.
- Security and compliance constraints across jurisdictions
  - Mitigation: Data residency controls, encryption, tokenization, DLP, regional endpoints, privacy-by-design.
- Vendor lock-in and limited multi-vendor support
  - Mitigation: Select open standards, abstraction via integration layer, portability tests, multi-vendor certification profiles.
- Testing complexity with multiple partners
  - Mitigation: Contract testing, simulators, sandbox environments, staged rollout with canaries and feature flags.
- Inconsistent identifiers and master data ownership
  - Mitigation: Master data governance, unique identifier strategy, CDC-based sync, clear system of record.

## Performance Metrics
- Partner onboarding lead time and effort (person-days) to first successful transaction.
- Percentage of interfaces conforming to selected standards and passing contract/conformance tests.
- Interoperability defect rate by phase (requirements, integration test, production).
- API and event success rates, error rates, and p95/p99 latencies for cross-system calls.
- Number of breaking changes released versus total changes; deprecation cycle adherence.
- Mean time to detect and recover from integration incidents (MTTD/MTTR).
- Data quality metrics across integrations (schema validation pass rate, duplicate/invalid IDs).
- Uptime and SLO attainment for integration components (gateways, brokers, service mesh).
- Reuse rate of canonical models and shared interface patterns across products.
- Partner satisfaction/NPS for integration experience.

## Technology and Tools
- Requirements and modeling: Jira/Confluence, Azure DevOps, Jama, IBM DOORS; architecture modeling with Sparx EA, Archi, PlantUML.
- API and event design: OpenAPI/Swagger, AsyncAPI, JSON Schema, Avro/Protobuf, GraphQL SDL.
- Integration platforms: API gateways (Apigee, Kong, AWS API Gateway), ESB/iPaaS (MuleSoft, Boomi, Azure Integration Services), event streaming (Kafka, Pulsar), messaging (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, AMQP, MQTT), industrial (OPC UA).
- Identity and security: OAuth 2.0/OIDC providers (Keycloak, Okta), SAML federation, mTLS, PKI/CA, Vault/Secrets Manager, WAF.
- Data and MDM: ER/Studio, dbt, Informatica/Talend, MDM platforms, schema registry (Confluent).
- Testing and simulation: Postman, SoapUI, Pact for contract testing, WireMock/MockServer, Hoverfly, k6/JMeter for load, protocol validators (e.g., HL7/FHIR, ISO 20022).
- Observability: OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, ELK/Opensearch, Jaeger/Zipkin, synthetic monitoring.
- Delivery and environments: Git, CI/CD (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins), containers/Kubernetes, service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) with mTLS and policy enforcement.
- Network tools: Wireshark, iperf, TLS scanners, DNS/NTP infrastructure.

Process Details:
## Overview
Derive security requirements for products and services is the process of translating business, regulatory, and technical risk considerations into clear, testable security requirements for new or enhanced products and services. For consumer electronics (CE) and connected devices, this process focuses on protecting data streams end-to-end through strong authentication, encryption, and hardware-backed key protection (e.g., secure elements/smart cards), while ensuring feasibility for constrained devices and seamless user experience.

This process:
- Establishes the security objectives for device data streams (confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, availability, privacy).
- Selects appropriate cryptographic protocols (e.g., TLS 1.3, DTLS 1.3, SRTP) and device identity mechanisms (e.g., unique device certificates, mutual authentication).
- Defines hardware security controls (e.g., secure boot, key storage in a secure element/TPM, optional smart card-based access control) and lifecycle requirements (provisioning, rotation, revocation).
- Produces a Security Requirements Specification (SRS-Sec) and supporting artifacts (threat model, cryptographic profile, key management plan) that feed into architecture, design, and validation.

It is a critical sub-process within Define product/service requirements and ensures that downstream design, build, and test activities are guided by risk-informed, compliant, and implementable security controls.

## Key Activities
- Establish security context: scope data streams, trust boundaries, device personas, and usage scenarios.
- Data classification and regulatory mapping: identify data sensitivity and applicable laws/standards.
- Threat modeling: enumerate threats (e.g., eavesdropping, tampering, spoofing, replay) and abuse cases.
- Control selection: pick authentication, authorization, encryption, and hardware security mechanisms appropriate to constraints and ecosystems.
- Cryptographic profile definition: protocols, cipher suites, key sizes, modes, and deprecation policy.
- Device identity and key management design: provisioning, storage, rotation, renewal, revocation, recovery.
- Secure boot and update requirements: firmware integrity, signing, attestation, OTA safeguards.
- Secure onboarding/pairing: define out-of-band mechanisms and protections against MITM.
- Testability and compliance: define verification methods, acceptance criteria, and mappings to standards.
- Documentation and traceability: produce SRS-Sec, threat model, and a traceability matrix linking risks to requirements and tests.
- Cross-functional review and sign-off: security, product, architecture, legal/privacy, supply chain.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Business and product requirements, use cases, and user experience goals
  - Preliminary system architecture and data flow sketches
  - Data inventory and classification (PII, telemetry, media, credentials)
  - Regulatory/compliance obligations (e.g., GDPR, NIST IoT, ETSI EN 303 645, PCI if applicable)
  - Platform constraints (CPU, memory, battery, RTOS/OS, wireless protocols)
  - Threat intelligence and prior incident/defect history
  - Supplier and manufacturing capabilities (secure element availability, key injection process)
  - Ecosystem standards (Wi‑Fi, Bluetooth/BLE, Thread, Matter, Zigbee, WebRTC, SRTP)

- Prerequisites:
  - Stakeholders identified and available (security, product, architecture, firmware, cloud, legal/privacy, supply chain)
  - Access to secure development standards and corporate security policies
  - Tooling for threat modeling and requirements management
  - Initial Bill of Materials (incl. chipsets/SE/TPM options) and firmware update strategy draft

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - [2.2.3.1] Define product/service requirements (functional/non-functional context)
  - [2.2.3] Define product/service development requirements (overall technical feasibility)
  - Architecture and design processes (to realize the requirements)
  - Supplier selection and onboarding (hardware security components, PKI providers)
  - Compliance and risk management processes

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and scope
   - Confirm product scope, data streams (media, telemetry, control, firmware updates), and interfaces (device-cloud, device-mobile app, device-device, device-operator).
   - Define trust boundaries and assets; document assumptions and constraints.

2. Classify data and map obligations
   - Classify data (public, internal, confidential, regulated).
   - Map to regulations/standards (e.g., GDPR for PII, ETSI EN 303 645 for consumer IoT, NISTIR 8259, ISO/IEC 27001/27034, ISA/IEC 62443 if industrial, regional crypto/export controls).
   - Record mandatory controls and certification targets.

3. Perform threat modeling
   - Create data flow diagrams (DFDs).
   - Identify threats using STRIDE (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege) and privacy threats (LINDDUN if applicable).
   - Prioritize with a risk model (DREAD, CVSS-like, or corporate heatmap).
   - Capture abuse/misuse cases (e.g., rogue app pairing, IPTV stream hijacking, camera feed exfiltration, update channel compromise).

4. Define security objectives and control categories
   - Objectives: confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, availability, privacy/minimization, non-repudiation where needed.
   - Control categories to cover:
     - Identity and authentication (device, user, service)
     - Authorization and access control
     - Cryptographic communications (in transit)
     - Data at rest protection (local storage, logs, keys)
     - Key and certificate lifecycle management
     - Secure boot, firmware signing, attestation
     - Secure onboarding/pairing and enrollment
     - Logging, telemetry, and security monitoring
     - Privacy-by-design and data minimization
     - Resilience (rate limits, anti-replay, fail-secure)
     - Third-party and supply chain controls (SBOM, component vetting)
     - Vulnerability handling, updates, incident response

5. Select cryptographic protocols and profiles
   - Transport security:
     - TLS 1.3 with mutual authentication for TCP-based channels.
     - DTLS 1.3 or QUIC (TLS 1.3-based) for UDP/low-latency applications.
     - SRTP with DTLS-SRTP or SDES (avoid SDES unless legacy) for media streams; consider SFrame for end-to-end conference encryption.
     - BLE Secure Connections for Bluetooth; WPA3 for Wi‑Fi; Thread/802.15.4 with network key management; Matter security if applicable.
   - Algorithms and parameters:
     - AEAD ciphers: AES‑GCM or ChaCha20‑Poly1305; minimum 128-bit security; prefer 256-bit where feasible.
     - ECDH/ECDSA over P‑256/Ed25519; deprecate RSA where possible on constrained devices.
     - PRNG: NIST SP 800‑90A compliant; hardware TRNG preferred.
     - Hashing: SHA‑256/384; avoid SHA‑1/MD5.
   - Anti-replay and integrity: sequence numbers, nonces, and replay windows as per protocol.
   - Deprecations: ban SSL/TLS < 1.2, RC4, 3DES, export ciphers; document fallback policy (none).

6. Define device identity and authentication
   - Unique per-device identity (X.509 certificate with unique device ID; consider EAT/RATS endorsements for attestation).
   - Mutual authentication for device-cloud and device-app channels.
   - Certificate pinning for mobile apps; trust store management on device.
   - Smart card/secure element/TPM usage:
     - Hardware-backed key generation and storage (e.g., ATECC608A, TPM 2.0, TEE/TrustZone).
     - Optional smart card-based conditional access or operator authentication for set-top boxes/enterprise SKUs.
   - Operator/user authentication:
     - Support FIDO2/WebAuthn for user auth in companion apps/services.
     - Role-based access and least privilege for operator/service personnel.

7. Key and certificate lifecycle requirements
   - Provisioning: secure manufacturing key injection; support factory provisioning, FIDO Device Onboard (FDO), or cloud enrollment (AWS IoT Just-in-Time Registration/Provisioning, Azure DPS).
   - Storage: keys never leave hardware root of trust; forbid hard-coded/shared keys.
   - Rotation/renewal: define validity periods (e.g., 1–3 years for device certs), automated renewal flows, and time synchronization strategy (secure NTP).
   - Revocation: CRL/OCSP handling; short-lived certs to mitigate OCSP limitations on constrained devices.
   - Recovery: secure re-enrollment with attestation; anti-cloning safeguards.

8. Secure boot, firmware integrity, and OTA update security
   - Secure boot with verified chain of trust; measured boot where platform supports; rollback protection.
   - Firmware and configuration signing (ed25519/ECDSA); detached signatures and manifest per IETF SUIT.
   - OTA update transport protection (TLS 1.3/DTLS 1.3); staged rollout and fail-safe update (A/B partitions).
   - Third-party component validation; SBOM generation and verification.

9. Data stream–specific requirements
   - Media streams: enforce SRTP with strong key management; end-to-end encryption where feasible; watermarking/integrity for premium content; HDCP for HDMI paths if required.
   - Telemetry/commands: use mutually authenticated channels; define message-level signing if brokered (e.g., MQTT over TLS with per-topic ACLs).
   - Local interfaces: secure pairing (QR/NFC/Passcode OOB), proximity-based controls, anti-MITM; restrict debug ports (disable or require signed authorization).
   - Storage: encrypt sensitive buffers/logs; secure erase policy.

10. Privacy and data minimization
    - Collect only necessary telemetry; pseudonymize device identifiers; configurable data sharing.
    - Support subject rights (export/delete) where applicable; data retention policies.

11. Non-functional and UX constraints
    - Performance budgets for crypto (latency, throughput, battery).
    - Usability requirements for pairing/onboarding (time to pair, error messaging, recovery flows).

12. Verification and validation planning
    - Define test cases and acceptance criteria for each requirement.
    - Security testing: SAST/DAST, protocol fuzzing, crypto configuration scan, penetration testing, red/blue exercises.
    - Compliance verification: traceability to standards; FIPS-validated crypto modules if required.

13. Documentation and traceability
    - Produce SRS-Sec, Threat Model, Cryptographic Profile, Key/Cert Management Plan, Secure Update Requirements, Compliance Matrix, and Security Test Plan.
    - Maintain a requirements-to-controls-to-tests traceability matrix in the ALM tool.

14. Review, risk acceptance, and sign-off
    - Conduct cross-functional review; record exceptions with compensating controls and residual risk.
    - Baseline the requirements; publish to design and development teams.

15. Change management
    - Define process to update requirements on new threats, vulnerabilities (e.g., algorithm deprecation), or regulatory changes; tie to product lifecycle and PSIRT alerts.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Security Requirements Specification (SRS-Sec) for the product/service
- Threat model with DFDs and prioritized risks
- Cryptographic profile and deprecation policy
- Device identity and key management plan (provisioning, rotation, revocation)
- Secure boot and OTA update security requirements
- Onboarding/pairing requirements
- Compliance/regulatory mapping and control matrix
- Security Test Plan and acceptance criteria
- SBOM requirements and third-party component security criteria
- Traceability matrix (requirements ↔ risks ↔ tests)
- Success criteria:
  - 100% of critical data streams covered by mutually authenticated, encrypted channels
  - All secrets hardware-protected; no shared/hard-coded keys
  - Requirements are testable and mapped to threats and standards
  - Approved by security, product, architecture, and compliance stakeholders

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product Security Lead: Owns process, ensures completeness, coordinates threat modeling, approves SRS-Sec.
- Security Architect: Selects cryptographic protocols, hardware security approach, and attestation strategy.
- Systems/Device Architect: Aligns requirements with hardware/firmware capabilities and performance.
- Firmware/Software Leads: Provide feasibility input; plan implementation and testing.
- Cloud/Backend Security Engineer: Defines server-side authZ, PKI, and secure service integrations.
- Privacy Officer/Legal Counsel: Maps privacy requirements and regulatory obligations.
- Compliance/GRC Lead: Ensures alignment with standards/certifications; manages control mapping.
- Supply Chain/Manufacturing Engineering: Defines secure provisioning and key injection processes; validates secure element availability.
- QA/Security Testing: Develops and executes security test plans; tools for fuzzing and protocol testing.
- Product Manager: Prioritizes security requirements alongside features; manages trade-offs.
- PSIRT/Incident Response: Provides threat intel and feeds vulnerabilities into requirement updates.

## Best Practices
- Security-by-design and default-secure configurations; minimize attack surface.
- Mutual authentication for all device-to-service and device-to-app communications.
- Unique per-device credentials; prohibit hard-coded or shared secrets.
- Use modern, widely reviewed cryptographic protocols (TLS 1.3/DTLS 1.3, SRTP with DTLS-SRTP).
- Hardware-backed key storage (SE/TPM/TEE); disable insecure debug; secure boot and signed updates.
- Strong onboarding/pairing with OOB verification (QR/NFC) and anti-MITM protections.
- Regular key rotation; short-lived certificates; robust revocation strategy.
- Protect media streams end-to-end when feasible; watermark/integrity for premium content.
- SBOM creation and third-party component vetting; monitor for CVEs; rapid patching.
- Privacy by design: data minimization, transparency, configurable telemetry.
- Continuous compliance mapping and automated configuration validation.
- Plan for crypto agility to respond to deprecations and post-quantum transitions.

## Common Challenges
- Constrained devices limiting crypto performance
  - Solutions: choose efficient ciphers (ChaCha20-Poly1305), hardware acceleration, session resumption/0-RTT with care for replay.
- Key provisioning at scale and supply chain trust
  - Solutions: use secure key injection, FDO/Just-in-Time Provisioning, HSM-backed PKI, supplier audits, ISO/IEC 20243, NIST 800-161 controls.
- Certificate lifecycle and time sync
  - Solutions: short-lived certs, secure NTP bootstrapping, grace periods, fallback to attestation for renewal.
- Secure updates without bricking
  - Solutions: A/B partitions, robust rollback protection, staged rollouts, cryptographic manifests (SUIT).
- User experience friction during pairing
  - Solutions: QR/NFC OOB, clear guidance, retries and recovery, fallback with rate limiting and lockouts.
- Interoperability with legacy ecosystems
  - Solutions: gateways for protocol translation with security termination; risk-accepted legacy modes behind compensating controls.
- Regional crypto/export regulations
  - Solutions: maintain region-specific crypto profiles; legal review; dynamic feature flags.
- Third-party library vulnerabilities
  - Solutions: SBOM, automated dependency scanning, vendor SLAs for patches, allowlist of libraries.

## Performance Metrics
- Coverage and quality
  - Percent of data streams under mutual auth and strong encryption
  - Threat-to-requirement-to-test traceability coverage
  - Number of security requirements with clear acceptance criteria
- Effectiveness
  - High/critical pen test findings related to data streams (count and time-to-remediate)
  - Percentage of devices using hardware-backed key storage
  - Percentage of devices on latest certificate/keys; mean time to rotate/revoke
- Compliance
  - Audit pass rate against target standards (e.g., ETSI EN 303 645 controls)
  - SBOM completeness and third-party component policy adherence
- Reliability and UX
  - Onboarding/pairing success rate and time-to-pair
  - Connection establishment latency and media stream QoS with encryption enabled
- Process health
  - Cycle time from initiation to SRS-Sec sign-off
  - Number of open security exceptions and age

Process Details:
## Overview
Process name: [2.2.3.1.5] Derive regulatory compliance requirements

Purpose: Translate the regulatory landscape into clear, actionable design and development requirements for a specific product/service so that compliance is designed in from the outset. This includes determining applicability, thresholds, documentation and labeling obligations, and evidence plans related to directives/regulations such as RoHS, WEEE, ELV, REACH, and equivalent jurisdictional requirements (e.g., UKCA, China RoHS, US TSCA/Prop 65).

Role in the organization: This process connects market strategy and product definition with compliance-by-design. It feeds the product requirements specification (PRS/PRD) and verification plans, reduces late-stage rework, mitigates regulatory risk, and enables market access and certifications.

Scope: All new products/services and significant changes to existing products that could affect regulatory obligations, substances, labeling, documentation, or end-of-life responsibilities across target markets and industries (consumer electronics, industrial, medical, automotive, etc.).


## Key Activities
- Identify target markets and product classifications.
- Map applicable regulations, directives, and standards by market and industry.
- Analyze technical requirements (e.g., substance restrictions, thresholds, exemptions, labeling, documentation).
- Derive and document product-level and component-level requirements.
- Define supplier data and evidence requirements (material declarations, test reports, IMDS, IEC 62474).
- Determine verification, testing, and conformity assessment needs.
- Define labeling, markings, customer communications, and take-back/producer responsibility obligations.
- Assess feasibility, risks, and impacts on design, sourcing, cost, and schedule.
- Integrate requirements into the PRD and design controls; establish traceability.
- Establish ongoing regulatory surveillance and change-control triggers.

  
## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Product concept and intended use, features, and variants.
- Target markets and launch timeline.
- Preliminary bill of materials (BOM), materials, and components list (even if partial).
- Product classification and industry context (e.g., consumer electronics, automotive, B2B equipment).
- Applicable corporate policies (restricted substances list, sustainability goals).
- Historical compliance data of legacy products/components.
- Customer-specific compliance requirements/contractual clauses.
- Supplier list and contact info.

Prerequisites:
- Access to regulatory intelligence sources (e.g., official registers, standards, and alerts).
- Defined product classification approach and taxonomy.
- PLM/requirements management environment to capture and trace requirements.
- Supplier NDAs or frameworks to request sensitive composition data.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [2.2.3.1] Define product/service requirements (feeds and receives requirements).
- Supplier onboarding and qualification (to obtain declarations, audits).
- Risk management (identification and mitigation of compliance risks).
- Design and development planning (to align verification activities).
- Change control and configuration management (to maintain compliance over lifecycle).


## Process Steps
1. Initiate and scope
   - Confirm target markets (countries/regions) and launch dates.
   - Classify the product (e.g., EEE equipment category, automotive part, battery-containing device).
   - Identify variants, options, and market-specific configurations.

2. Build regulatory applicability map
   - For each target market, identify applicable laws/regulations:
     - Substance restrictions and chemical regulations (e.g., EU RoHS, REACH; China RoHS; US TSCA; California Prop 65; PFAS restrictions where applicable).
     - Producer responsibility and end-of-life (e.g., EU WEEE, batteries, packaging).
     - Sector-specific rules (e.g., automotive ELV; medical MDR; radio equipment, EMC/LVD for electrical).
     - Country/region-specific conformity frameworks (e.g., CE marking/UKCA, KC, PSE).
   - Record scope criteria and exclusions for each regulation.

3. Extract technical and documentation requirements
   - Substance thresholds and exemptions (e.g., EU RoHS 0.1% for Pb/Hg/Cr6+/PBB/PBDE and phthalates; 0.01% for Cd, by homogeneous material; REACH SVHC communication >0.1% w/w per article).
   - Material declaration standards and formats (e.g., IEC 62474, IPC-1752A; IMDS for automotive).
   - Technical documentation requirements (e.g., EN IEC 63000 for RoHS technical file).
   - Testing, analysis or due-diligence requirements (e.g., XRF screening, FTIR/GC-MS for phthalates, supplier third-party lab reports).
   - Labeling/marking requirements (e.g., WEEE bin symbol, battery labels, CE/UKCA if applicable, producer IDs).
   - Producer responsibility obligations (registration, take-back schemes, reporting cadence).
   - Communication obligations (e.g., REACH Article 33, SCIP notification where applicable).
   - Timing and transitional provisions; exemption expiry dates.

4. Assess product design impact and feasibility
   - Map requirements to BOM: identify impacted materials/components (solders, plastics, coatings, connectors, adhesives).
   - Identify likely noncompliant or high-risk parts; check availability of compliant alternatives.
   - Determine need for design choices (e.g., lead-free solder alloys, halogen-free resins, plating alternatives).
   - Evaluate cost/schedule impact and supply risk; propose mitigation options.

5. Define supplier data and evidence strategy
   - Specify data packages required per component category:
     - Full material declaration (FMD) via IEC 62474/IPC-1752A.
     - Certificates of compliance (RoHS/REACH), lab test reports as needed.
     - IMDS submissions for automotive; SCIP notifications for SVHC articles.
   - Define acceptable evidence quality (date validity, lot coverage, lab accreditation).
   - Draft and issue supplier requests with deadlines; embed requirements in POs/quality agreements.

6. Create the compliance requirements specification
   - Compile a structured, traceable set of requirements:
     - Product-level compliance requirements (what standards/directives and declarations are needed).
     - Component/material requirements (substance bans, thresholds, exemptions to use).
     - Documentation and labeling requirements.
     - Verification and validation (V&V) plan for compliance.
     - Data retention and audit-readiness requirements.
   - Link each requirement to source regulation, clause, and market.

7. Plan verification, conformity assessment, and labeling
   - Define test plans (screening vs. targeted testing), sampling, and acceptance criteria.
   - Define documentation content and owners (e.g., technical file per EN IEC 63000, DoC, WEEE registration).
   - Define required marks and statements on product, packaging, and manuals.

8. Review and approval
   - Cross-functional review (Regulatory Affairs, Engineering, Quality, Procurement, Legal).
   - Resolve conflicts/trade-offs; approve the specification.
   - Baseline the requirements in PLM/requirements tool; establish change control.

9. Integrate into design and sourcing
   - Embed requirements into PRD, drawings, material specs, and AVL/AML.
   - Update supplier qualification criteria and incoming inspection plans.

10. Monitor and maintain
   - Establish regulatory watch for changes (e.g., REACH SVHC updates semiannually; RoHS exemption sunsets).
   - Define triggers for reassessment (engineering changes, supplier changes, market expansion).
   - Update requirements and communicate changes via change management.

  
## Outputs and Deliverables
- Regulatory applicability map by market and product category.
- Compliance requirements specification (product-level and component-level).
- Compliance matrix mapping requirements to BOM, materials, and evidence.
- Supplier data request packages and response tracker.
- Verification and testing plan for compliance, including sampling and methods.
- Labeling/marking and documentation plan (e.g., DoC templates; WEEE registration plan).
- Risk register entries and mitigation actions for compliance risks.
- Approved baseline in PLM/requirements system with traceability to regulations.

Success criteria:
- All applicable regulations identified and documented before design freeze.
- Traceable, approved requirements integrated into PRD and design controls.
- ≥95% supplier declarations coverage for BOM at design freeze (or risk-justified gap plan).
- Verification plan defined and costed; no late-stage noncompliance discoveries.
- Audit-ready documentation exists for each applicable market.


## Roles and Responsibilities
- Regulatory Affairs/Compliance Lead: Owns regulatory mapping, interpretations, and final approval of requirements; maintains regulatory watch.
- Product Compliance Manager: Coordinates cross-functional execution; manages the compliance matrix and evidence plan.
- Design Engineering: Incorporates requirements into design choices, materials, and drawings; supports feasibility assessments.
- Materials/Component Engineering: Evaluates materials for restricted substances; selects compliant alternatives.
- Supplier Quality/Procurement: Obtains supplier declarations/evidence; embeds requirements in contracts; escalates non-responses.
- Quality Assurance: Ensures process controls, documentation control, and audit readiness; aligns with ISO 9001 design controls.
- Legal/Corporate Affairs: Reviews high-risk interpretations, customer terms, and producer responsibility obligations.
- Program/Project Manager: Ensures schedule integration, resources, and cross-functional alignment.
- PLM/Requirements Admin: Configures templates, traceability, and change control.
- EHS/Sustainability: Aligns corporate RSL/ESG goals and circularity with regulatory requirements.
- External partners (as needed): Accredited laboratories, notified bodies/certification agencies, regulatory intelligence providers.


## Best Practices
- Start early: Determine applicability during concept phase; design with compliant materials from the outset.
- Use recognized standards:
  - EN IEC 63000 for technical documentation (RoHS).
  - IEC 62474/IPC-1752A for material declarations.
  - IMDS for automotive (ELV).
- Create a harmonized corporate restricted substances list consolidating global requirements and customer specs.
- Maintain a single source of truth: Manage requirements and evidence in PLM integrated with BOM and change control.
- Risk-based evidence: Prioritize testing for high-risk parts (e.g., PVC cables, solders, soft plastics with potential phthalates).
- Manage exemptions proactively: Document justification, track expiry, and plan redesign before sunset dates.
- Set strong supplier expectations: Contractual clauses, data quality criteria, and escalation paths; audit high-risk suppliers.
- Monitor regulatory change: Subscribe to alerts (e.g., REACH SVHC updates) and conduct impact assessments within set SLAs.
- Train teams: Provide role-based training on applicable regulations, documentation, and labeling.
- Plan for market variants: Parameterize requirements by market; avoid proliferating SKUs through modular compliance strategies.
- Keep evidence current: Define validity windows for certificates and test reports; refresh on a set cadence or when changes occur.


## Common Challenges
- Incomplete or inaccurate supplier data
  - Solutions: Use standardized formats (IEC 62474), enforce data quality gates, conduct supplier training and audits, and perform targeted lab verification.
- Constantly changing regulatory landscape
  - Solutions: Regulatory watch program, periodic impact assessments, change control workflows, and design margin to accommodate foreseeable changes.
- Hidden substances in complex assemblies
  - Solutions: Risk-based BOM screening, material-level declarations (FMDs), deep-tier visibility via platform providers, and destructive testing for high-risk items.
- Exemption dependencies and expirations
  - Solutions: Central exemption register, automatic reminders, and redesign roadmaps well ahead of expiry.
- Multi-market conflicts and labeling complexity
  - Solutions: Harmonize to the strictest common denominator where feasible; maintain market-specific labeling matrices.
- Time and cost impacts late in development
  - Solutions: Integrate compliance gates before design freeze; include compliance milestones in project plans; allocate budget for verification.
- Legacy parts or obsolete documentation
  - Solutions: Requalify parts, source alternates, or update documentation through supplier engagement and testing.


## Performance Metrics
- Coverage metrics:
  - Percentage of BOM with current material declarations.
  - Percentage of applicable regulations mapped before design freeze.
- Timeliness:
  - Cycle time to produce the compliance requirements specification.
  - Time from regulatory change alert to updated requirements baseline.
- Quality:
  - Number of post-freeze design changes due to compliance gaps.
  - Audit findings related to technical documentation completeness.
  - Supplier data rejection rate due to quality issues.
- Risk:
  - Number of active exemptions and those within 12 months of expiry.
  - Compliance incident rate in market (e.g., customer returns, authority notices).
- Cost/schedule impact:
  - Cost of non-compliance (testing rework, redesign) as a percentage of project budget.
  - Delay days attributable to compliance issues.


## Technology and Tools

Process Details:
# [2.2.3.1.6] Derive requirements from industry standards (CTA)

## Overview
This process systematically translates Consumer Technology Association (CTA) industry standards into clear, testable product/service requirements. It ensures consumer electronics offerings are designed, built, and verified to comply with applicable CTA standards covering interoperability, performance measurement, accessibility, energy management, safety labeling, and user experience guidelines. The process sits within the broader product/service requirements definition and feeds engineering design, verification, and supplier specifications.

Purpose:
- Identify applicable CTA standards for the product category and target markets.
- Interpret normative requirements and derive implementation-ready, testable requirements.
- Create traceability from standards to design and verification artifacts.
- Reduce compliance risk, accelerate certification, and ensure market readiness.

Role in the organization:
- Provides a governance mechanism to satisfy industry conformance expectations.
- Enables cross-functional alignment on what “compliant” means for each product.
- Feeds downstream engineering, testing, technical documentation, and supplier contracts with authoritative requirements.

## Key Activities
- Standards discovery and applicability assessment
- Standards version control and change monitoring
- Interpretation and decomposition of normative clauses into requirements
- Gap analysis against existing specifications/design
- Creation and maintenance of a standards-to-requirements traceability matrix
- Cross-functional review and approval of derived requirements
- Supplier/ODM communication and contract flow-down
- Verification planning and compliance test case development
- Pre-compliance testing and evidence collection
- Continuous monitoring and change control for standards updates

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Product concept/charter, target markets, intended use cases and environments
- High-level system architecture and technology choices (e.g., display, audio, connectivity, power)
- Existing product requirements baseline (if any)
- Access to current CTA standards and related normative references (CTA portal/membership or licensed repository)
- Regulatory landscape summary to distinguish industry standards vs legal regulations

Prerequisites:
- Assigned Standards Compliance Lead and Systems Engineer
- Active CTA membership or licensed access to standards content
- Configured requirements management and document control tools
- Defined product classification taxonomy for standards applicability mapping
- Governance for change control and waivers

Dependencies on other processes:
- [2.2.3.1] Define product/service requirements (consumes outputs)
- Supplier selection and management (to flow down requirements)
- Verification and validation planning
- Risk management (FMEA/TRA) and design reviews
- Document management and configuration control

## Process Steps
1) Trigger and scope
- Trigger: new product, major revision, or market expansion.
- Define scope: product variants, regions, technologies, user personas, and interfaces.

2) Identify applicable CTA standards
- Search CTA standards catalog and working group publications by product category and technologies used.
- Consult prior product standards register and lessons learned.
- Review cross-referenced normative documents (e.g., CTA standards that point to ISO/IEC/IEEE).
- Build a preliminary applicability list with rationale for inclusion/exclusion.

3) Acquire authoritative versions and control access
- Obtain the latest published versions and errata.
- Record standard identifiers, titles, publication dates, and status in a Standards Register.
- Store in a controlled repository with versioning.

4) Analyze normative content
- Parse each standard into normative (“shall”) vs informative guidance.
- Extract constraints, performance metrics, interoperability profiles, labeling, documentation, accessibility, and test methods.
- Note conformance clauses, profiles/levels, and mandatory/optional features.

5) Decompose into implementable requirements
- For each applicable clause, craft a specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and testable requirement.
- Include acceptance criteria and verification method as attributes.
- Example template:
  - Requirement ID: CTA-REQ-001
  - Source: [CTA-XXX], Clause Y.Z
  - Statement: “The device shall …”
  - Rationale: Aligns with [CTA-XXX] conformance
  - Verification: Test case TC-CTA-001, method per [CTA-XXX] Annex A
  - Priority: Must/Should
  - Owner: Systems Engineering

6) Perform gap analysis
- Compare derived requirements against existing product requirements and current design.
- Identify gaps, conflicts, and impacts (cost, schedule, performance).
- Log issues, risks, and needed design changes.

7) Resolve ambiguities and conflicts
- Convene cross-functional reviews (engineering, QA, legal, PM, suppliers).
- Engage accredited test labs or CTA working groups for interpretation if needed.
- Document decisions, assumptions, and any requested clarifications.

8) Establish traceability
- Build a Standards Traceability Matrix linking:
  - Standard clause → Derived requirement(s) → Design elements → Verification cases → Evidence
- Ensure each normative clause maps to one or more testable requirements.

9) Approve and baseline
- Route derived requirements through formal review/approval.
- Baseline in the requirements management system with version and change history.

10) Flow down to suppliers/ODMs
- Update supplier requirement specifications and statements of work.
- Highlight mandatory CTA conformance elements and test evidence expectations.
- Align on compliance checkpoints and deliverables.

11) Plan and develop verification
- Create or adapt test plans and procedures aligned to CTA test methods.
- Prepare pre-compliance tests, fixtures, and simulation where applicable.
- Schedule internal/external testing and certification activities if offered/required by the market.

12) Execute pre-compliance and collect evidence
- Run tests to de-risk failures early.
- Capture test reports, logs, measurements, screenshots, and checklists.
- File in a compliance evidence repository.

13) Manage changes and monitor updates
- Subscribe to CTA updates/errata and relevant working group communications.
- Evaluate impact of changes; trigger change control for requirement updates.
- Communicate changes to engineering and suppliers; update traceability and plans.

14) Final conformance verification and release readiness
- Complete full verification against all CTA-derived requirements.
- Resolve nonconformities or obtain approved waivers/deviations with risk justification.
- Produce compliance summaries for launch gates and audits.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- CTA Standards Register with applicability and versions
- Derived, testable requirements set with attributes and IDs
- Standards Traceability Matrix

Deliverables:
- Compliance checklist mapped to CTA clauses
- Verification plans and CTA-aligned test procedures
- Pre-compliance and final test reports; evidence repository
- Supplier/ODM requirements addendum and compliance obligations
- Risk/issue log with decisions and waivers
- Compliance summary statement for release

Success criteria:
- 100% of applicable normative clauses mapped to requirements and tests
- Zero critical nonconformities at release; no surprises in external conformance testing
- Timely incorporation of standards updates with controlled changes
- Positive internal audit results; stakeholder approval at gates

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Standards Compliance Lead: Owns the process; maintains Standards Register; leads interpretation; ensures traceability and evidence completeness.
- Systems Engineer: Decomposes standards into requirements; manages baselining; ensures technical feasibility and testability.
- Product Manager: Confirms applicability based on market/portfolio strategy; approves scope and trade-offs.
- Hardware/Software Engineers: Implement requirements; contribute to interpretation; support testability.
- Test/QA Engineer: Develops CTA-aligned test plans and cases; conducts pre-compliance and formal testing; manages evidence.
- Legal/Regulatory Affairs: Reviews standards licensing, IP implications, labeling, and documentation obligations; differentiates voluntary vs mandatory.
- Supplier/ODM Manager: Flows down requirements; verifies supplier compliance; coordinates third-party test results.
- Technical Writer/UX: Implements documentation, labeling, and accessibility requirements derived from standards.
- Security/Privacy Specialist (as applicable): Interprets any CTA guidance that touches data, security, or privacy.
- Configuration/Document Control: Ensures version control and audit readiness.

## Best Practices
- Start early: Identify applicable CTA standards during concept to avoid late design churn.
- Use structured requirement attributes: source clause, rationale, verification method, priority, owner, and version.
- Focus on testability: Mirror the standard’s measurement methods in requirement acceptance criteria.
- Separate normative from informative content; do not over-constrain based on guidance text unless justified.
- Maintain a living Standards Register and subscribe to updates/errata.
- Engage accredited labs early for interpretation and pre-compliance test setup.
- Create a reusable CTA compliance checklist per product category to accelerate future programs.
- Train teams on key CTA standards and terminology (“shall/should/may”).
- Manage conflicts systematically using a decision log; obtain waivers with risk assessments.
- Ensure supplier flow-down includes evidence requirements (test reports, certificates, markings).
- Link CTA-derived requirements into overall MBSE or architecture models to maintain consistency.

## Common Challenges
- Ambiguity in clauses or conflicting interpretations
  - Solution: Document assumptions; seek clarification from CTA working groups or test labs; keep an interpretation register.
- Overlapping or conflicting requirements across multiple standards
  - Solution: Prioritize based on product scope and profiles; conduct trade-off/risk analysis; escalate to governance board.
- Standards updates mid-development
  - Solution: Use change impact assessments; apply freeze dates; plan for minor/major update policies.
- Insufficient testability or missing equipment
  - Solution: Invest early in fixtures and measurement capability; partner with labs; create simulation/bench tests.
- Supplier noncompliance or late discovery
  - Solution: Include CTA requirements in contracts; require early sample testing and reports; gate supplier deliverables on compliance evidence.
- Documentation and labeling gaps
  - Solution: Involve Technical Writers early; use checklists tied to standards clauses.

## Performance Metrics
- Coverage: % of applicable CTA normative clauses mapped to requirements and tests (target: 100%).
- Traceability completeness: % of requirements with end-to-end links (standard → req → test → evidence) (target: >95%).
- Defect leakage: # of CTA-related nonconformities found after design freeze or during external testing.
- Rework rate: # of engineering change orders caused by standards gaps.
- Time-to-interpretation: Average days from standard identification to approved derived requirements.
- Update responsiveness: Lead time to process CTA updates/errata into baselined requirements.
- First-pass yield: % of CTA conformance tests passed on first attempt.
- Supplier compliance: % of suppliers delivering complete CTA evidence on time.

## Technology and Tools
- Requirements Management: IBM DOORS Next, Jama Connect, Polarion ALM, Jira + requirement plugins.
- Test Management: Zephyr, Xray, TestRail; integration with CI where applicable.
- Document/Configuration Control: PLM/PDM (e.g., Windchill, Teamcenter), SharePoint/Confluence, Git for versioning specs and scripts.
- Standards Access and Monitoring: CTA member portal, licensed standards libraries; RSS/email alerts for updates.
- Traceability and Reporting: Built-in RM/ALM trace views, custom dashboards, BI tools for coverage metrics.
- Pre-compliance Test Equipment: Protocol analyzers, signal generators, oscilloscopes, audio/analyzer suites, power analyzers, EMI pre-compliance tools (as relevant to the product).
- Evidence Repository: Controlled file stores with metadata tagging for clause, requirement, and test linkage.
- Collaboration: Virtual whiteboards, meeting tools, and decision logs for interpretation records.

This process ensures that CTA standards are systematically converted into actionable, testable requirements, reducing compliance risk and improving product readiness and quality.
