Process Details:
## Overview
Derive ‘services-as-a-product’ offering is the process of packaging a service into a standardized, repeatable, and sellable offering with clear scope, pricing, SLAs, delivery model, and commercialization assets. It turns intangible services into tangible “products” by defining what is included, how it’s delivered, at what cost and price, to whom, and under what terms. This enables scale, predictable quality, margin control, and efficient go-to-market.

Purpose:
- Create standardized service packages (e.g., fixed-scope, tiered offerings) that are easy to sell, deliver, support, and scale.
- Ensure offerings align with strategy, meet target customer needs, and achieve target margins.
- Reduce variability and risk associated with bespoke services while preserving optionality through controlled add-ons.

Role in the organization:
- Bridges product management, service delivery, finance, legal, sales, and operations.
- Feeds the service catalog and product catalog, CPQ, ERP/PSA systems, and order-to-cash processes.
- Provides the basis for sales enablement, marketing, delivery readiness, and lifecycle improvement.

## Key Activities
- Define value proposition and target market segments/personas.
- Establish service scope, inclusions/exclusions, assumptions, and deliverables.
- Design packaging and tiers (e.g., Standard/Plus/Premium) and optional add-ons.
- Define service blueprint and operating model (processes, roles, skills, tools).
- Set SLAs/SLOs/OLAs, warranties, support levels, success criteria, and acceptance.
- Build cost model (labor, tooling, licenses, 3rd parties) and pricing strategy.
- Conduct competitive benchmarking and differentiation.
- Assess risks, compliance, and legal/contractual requirements.
- Define partner participation and agreements (if applicable).
- Prepare commercialization assets (SoW templates, datasheets, FAQs, runbooks).
- Configure systems (SKUs, catalog entries, CPQ rules, ERP/PSA, subscription/billing).
- Pilot/MVP, gather feedback, refine, and complete launch readiness.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Business strategy, target segments, and portfolio roadmap.
- Approved service concept or requirements from upstream process [2.2.3.1] Define product/service requirements.
- Market research: customer needs, jobs-to-be-done, competitor offerings, pricing benchmarks.
- Historical delivery data: effort, cycle times, quality, utilization, margins.
- Capability inventory: skills, tools, delivery capacity, partner capabilities.
- Legal/compliance requirements (privacy, security, labor, tax, revenue recognition).
- Risk assessments and quality standards.

Prerequisites:
- Executive or product council approval to proceed to productization (stage-gate).
- Access to finance/pricing support and delivery SMEs.
- Tooling and data availability for cost modeling and systems configuration.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [2.2.3.1] Define product/service requirements (upstream concept/requirements).
- Supplier/partner qualification and onboarding.
- Order-to-cash design, CPQ configuration, and product catalog management.
- Service delivery readiness, training, and support model setup.
- Legal/contract lifecycle management (templates, approvals).
- Information security and compliance reviews.

## Process Steps
1. Confirm strategic alignment and scope
   - Revalidate customer problem, outcomes, target segments, and business objectives (growth, margin).
   - Define success metrics and guardrails (e.g., max customization, target gross margin).

2. Customer and competitive validation
   - Conduct interviews or analyze existing feedback to refine value proposition.
   - Benchmark competitor offerings, SLAs, tiers, and pricing to inform positioning.

3. Define the service concept
   - Articulate the outcomes, core features, and value drivers.
   - Decide on “as-a-product” positioning (subscription, fixed-fee, milestone-based, consumption-based).

4. Define scope, inclusions/exclusions, and assumptions
   - List what is included, excluded, and optional.
   - Specify inputs required from the customer, dependencies, and constraints.
   - Define boundaries for customization via predefined options or add-ons.

5. Design packaging and tiers
   - Create standardized packages (e.g., Essentials, Advanced, Premium).
   - Define deliverables, SLA tiers, response/resolution times, support hours, and limits (e.g., number of sites/users).
   - Create add-on modules (e.g., accelerated onboarding, premium support).

6. Service blueprint and operating model
   - Map customer journey and service blueprint (frontstage/backstage activities).
   - Define delivery processes, RACI, skill profiles, capacity model, and tooling requirements.
   - Establish OLAs between internal teams and partners.

7. Define SLAs, KPIs, and acceptance criteria
   - Set measurable SLAs/SLOs (uptime, response, resolution, quality, time-to-value).
   - Define acceptance criteria, warranty terms, and remediation/credit mechanisms.

8. Cost modeling and unit economics
   - Build bottom-up cost model: labor hours, rates, licenses, infrastructure, travel, partner costs, overhead.
   - Validate with historical data; run sensitivity and scenario analyses.
   - Calculate CAC payback (if applicable), contribution margins, and capacity impacts.

9. Pricing and commercial policy
   - Select pricing model (fixed, tiered, subscription, consumption, hybrid).
   - Set list price, discount bands, uplift/renewal rules, and bundling/attach policies.
   - Define revenue recognition approach (e.g., ASC 606/IFRS 15), taxes, and billing cadence.

10. Legal, compliance, and risk review
    - Draft or adapt SoW templates, Ts&Cs, data processing addenda, and SLAs.
    - Review regulatory, privacy/security, export control, health/safety (for field services).
    - Create a risk register and mitigations (e.g., scope creep controls).

11. Partner ecosystem and sourcing (if applicable)
    - Define partner roles, margins, and certification requirements.
    - Establish agreements, NDAs, and quality/SLA obligations.

12. Create tangible artifacts and enablement content
    - Service Definition Document (SDD), delivery playbook/runbooks, checklists.
    - Customer-facing datasheet, solution brief, FAQs, case studies.
    - SoW templates, proposal language, acceptance forms.
    - Internal training, certification paths, and knowledge base articles.

13. Systems configuration and operational readiness
    - Create SKUs and catalog entries; configure CPQ rules (compatibility, pricing, approvals).
    - Set up ERP/PSA for resource planning, time/expense, and cost tracking.
    - Configure subscription/billing/entitlement (if recurring).
    - Define order-to-activate workflow; instrument provisioning automations where possible.

14. Pilot/MVP and validation
    - Select pilot customers, execute delivery, measure SLAs, costs, CSAT/NPS, and time-to-value.
    - Capture lessons learned and required adjustments to scope, pricing, or process.

15. Iterate and finalize
    - Update packaging, pricing, SLAs, templates, and tooling based on pilot results.
    - Confirm readiness checklist across functions.

16. Go/No-Go and launch
    - Obtain governance approval. Communicate launch plan and effective date.
    - Train sales, pre-sales, delivery, support; publish catalog entry and assets.
    - Monitor early deals and deliveries with heightened governance.

17. Continuous improvement
    - Establish feedback loops (sales, delivery, customers); update offer quarterly or as needed.
    - Track KPIs and adjust for margin, quality, and demand shifts.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Service Definition Document (SDD) with scope, packages, SLAs, and delivery model.
- Standardized SoW templates and proposal language.
- Service blueprint and process maps; delivery playbooks and runbooks.
- Cost model and approved price book entries (list price, discounts, renewal rules).
- SKU(s) and catalog entries configured in CPQ/ERP/PSA and subscription systems.
- Legal documents: Ts&Cs, DPAs, warranty terms, and partner agreements.
- Sales and marketing collateral: datasheets, solution briefs, case studies.
- Training and certification materials; internal knowledge base articles.
- Pilot report and readiness checklist; Go/No-Go decision record.
- Risk register and compliance checklist; measurement plan and dashboard.

Success criteria:
- Meets or exceeds target gross margin and unit economics.
- Validated customer value (pilot CSAT/NPS/time-to-value targets achieved).
- Operational readiness demonstrated (on-time delivery, SLA attainment).
- Sales enablement complete (win rate, cycle time comparable to targets).
- Catalog and systems configured with minimal order errors and rework.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Service/Product Manager: Owns offer vision, scope, packaging, pricing strategy, and lifecycle.
- Service Architect: Designs service blueprint, delivery model, SLAs, and technical components.
- Delivery/Operations Lead: Validates feasibility, capacity model, runbooks, and quality controls.
- Finance/Pricing Analyst: Builds cost model, sets price bands, evaluates profitability and revenue recognition.
- Sales Enablement Manager: Creates sales collateral, training, and plays; configures CPQ guidance.
- Marketing Manager: Positioning, messaging, launch plan, and demand generation assets.
- Legal/Compliance Counsel: Drafts/reviews Ts&Cs, DPAs, IP terms, liability, and regulatory compliance.
- Procurement/Partner Manager: Onboards partners, negotiates terms, ensures partner quality and SLAs.
- IT/Systems Admin: Configures catalog, CPQ, ERP/PSA, billing/subscription, and entitlement systems.
- Security/Privacy Officer: Reviews data flows, controls, and certifications.
- Quality/Risk Manager: Owns risk register, QA gates, and continuous improvement actions.
- PMO/Program Manager: Coordinates cross-functional work, stage-gates, and timeline.
- CX/Support Lead: Defines support tiers, escalation paths, and knowledge base.

## Best Practices
- Start with outcomes: define measurable customer outcomes and success criteria up front.
- Standardize with modularity: offer clear base packages with controlled add-ons to balance scale and flexibility.
- Tangibilize the service: specify deliverables, artifacts, milestones, acceptance tests, and success plans.
- Value-based pricing with cost guardrails: price to value and differentiate by tiers; verify with robust cost models.
- Clear inclusion/exclusion and assumptions in all materials to prevent scope creep.
- Pilot before broad launch; instrument measurement to validate SLAs, costs, and satisfaction.
- Integrate end-to-end: ensure catalog, CPQ, ERP/PSA, billing, and support systems are aligned.
- Use templates and automation: SoW templates, CPQ rules, provisioning workflows to reduce errors.
- Set governance and approval workflows for non-standard deals and discounts.
- Plan for scale: training, certifications, capacity ramp, partner enablement, and quality controls.
- Continuous improvement loop using data (margins, delivery variances, NPS, win/loss).

## Common Challenges
- Scope creep and over-customization: Mitigate with strict inclusions/exclusions, predefined options, and approval gates.
- Mispricing and margin erosion: Address with accurate cost models, discount controls, and periodic price reviews.
- Delivery inconsistency: Use playbooks, checklists, training, and QA audits; enforce OLAs.
- Sales misalignment: Provide simple packaging, clear qualification criteria, and CPQ guidance; train regularly.
- System gaps: Plan early for catalog/CPQ/ERP setup; run end-to-end test orders before launch.
- Partner risk: Vet partners, define quality metrics and SLAs, and implement performance reviews.
- Compliance and revenue recognition issues: Engage legal/finance early; standardize contract language and billing rules.
- Capacity constraints: Align launch with hiring/partner capacity; forecast demand and monitor utilization.

## Performance Metrics
Commercial:
- Bookings and revenue by package/tier; ARR/MRR (if subscription).
- Attach rate to core products; win rate; sales cycle time.
- Average discount vs. policy; deal size; churn/renewal rates.

Financial:
- Gross margin per package; contribution margin; variance vs. plan.
- Cost of delivery per unit; utilization rates; rework costs.

Operational/Quality:
- On-time delivery rate; time-to-value; SLA attainment (response/resolution).
- First-time-right rate; incident/defect rate; escalations.
- Capacity utilization and backlog; partner performance scores.

Customer:
- CSAT/NPS; adoption and engagement metrics; outcomes achieved vs. success plan.
- Support ticket volume and time-to-resolution by tier.

Governance:
- Percentage of non-standard deals; approval cycle time.
- Catalog/order error rate; quote-to-cash accuracy.

## Technology and Tools
- Service catalog and ITSM/ESM: ServiceNow, BMC Helix, Atlassian Jira Service Management.

Process Details:
## Overview
Process name: [2.3.1.1.1] Identify requirements for product/service design/development partners

Purpose:
- Define and validate the essential capabilities, compliance, and engagement requirements for external partners who will participate in the design and development of a new or revised product/service.
- Ensure downstream sourcing, evaluation, contracting, and onboarding of partners are efficient, objective, compliant, and aligned to product strategy and risk appetite.

Role in the organization:
- Sits within “Design and prototype products and services” and supports “Assign resources to product/service project.”
- Translates product/engineering needs and constraints into a Partner Requirements Specification used by Procurement/Vendor Management to identify, assess, and select qualified partners.
- Reduces delivery risk by embedding regulatory, security, quality, and IP protections up front; accelerates time-to-market by minimizing rework during RFI/RFP and contracting.

Scope:
- Applies to external collaborators such as design houses, engineering firms, software development vendors, UX research agencies, prototyping labs, testing/certification bodies, and managed service providers.
- Covers physical products, digital products, and service development, with domain-specific requirements as needed.

## Key Activities
- Elicit partner requirement needs from cross-functional stakeholders.
- Categorize and prioritize requirements (must/should/could/won’t).
- Integrate regulatory, security, privacy, quality, and IP requirements.
- Perform preliminary market scan and benchmark capabilities/standards.
- Define objective evaluation and scoring criteria for later vendor selection.
- Draft Partner Requirements Specification (PRS) and supporting annexes.
- Validate with stakeholders; obtain approvals and baseline for sourcing.
- Prepare an RFI pack and hand over to Procurement/Vendor Management.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved product concept/charter, business case, and high-level roadmap.
- Product/Service requirements or design brief (functional and non-functional).
- Budget envelope and target commercial model (e.g., fixed price vs T&M).
- Risk assessment context: risk appetite, criticality, data sensitivity classification.
- Regulatory/compliance obligations by market and domain.
- Enterprise standards: security policies, coding standards, design system, PLM/ALM tools.
- Existing preferred supplier list and vendor performance insights.
- Target timelines/milestones for design, prototype, and testing phases.

Prerequisites:
- Executive or portfolio approval to engage external partners.
- NDA templates and sourcing policy availability.
- Stakeholder identification and availability (Product, Engineering, Design, Legal, Security, Quality, Procurement, Finance, Compliance/Regulatory, Architecture/IT, ESG/Sustainability, Accessibility).

Dependencies on other processes:
- 2.3.1.1 Assign resources to product/service project (this process informs sourcing).
- 2.3.1 Design and prototype products and services (provides design objectives).
- Third-party risk management, Legal/Contracting, Information Security reviews.
- Procurement/eSourcing processes for RFI/RFP once requirements are baselined.

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and scope
- Trigger: Product team decides to use external partners for design/development.
- Appoint process lead (e.g., Product Operations or Sourcing Lead).
- Define scope: domains (HW/SW/UX/testing), phases covered, geographies, data classifications, and expected engagement model (onshore/nearshore/offshore, hybrid).

2) Assemble cross-functional working group
- Confirm participation: Product Manager, Engineering Lead, Design Lead, Procurement, Vendor Management, Legal/IP, InfoSec, Privacy, Compliance/Regulatory, Quality, Architecture/IT, Finance, Accessibility, ESG/Sustainability, Manufacturing/Operations (for physical).
- Set RACI and cadence; create a shared workspace and document repository.

3) Gather and analyze inputs
- Review product concept, design brief, risk profile, budget, and timeline.
- Identify domain-specific standards and regulations (e.g., ISO, IEC, FDA, GDPR).
- Review enterprise constraints (tools, code repos, design systems, CI/CD, PLM).
- Consider legacy learnings and supplier scorecards.

4) Define requirement categories and structure
- Capability: domain expertise, certifications, technologies, toolchain compatibility.
- Delivery: methodology (Agile/DevSecOps/Stage-gate), capacity, scalability, timezone overlap, communication.
- Quality: QMS standards, test capabilities, DfX/verification/validation practices, defect/leakage targets.
- Security & Privacy: security certifications, secure SDLC, data handling, DPAs, SBOM, SAST/DAST, data residency.
- Compliance/Regulatory: applicable regulations, notified bodies, documentation.
- IP & Legal: ownership, licensing (incl. OSS), indemnities, conflict of interest avoidance.
- Commercial: pricing models, rate cards, volume discounts, payment terms.
- ESG & Ethics: sustainability criteria, labor practices, diversity; responsible sourcing.
- Accessibility & Inclusivity: WCAG, inclusive design/research practices.
- Tooling & Integration: repo access, design tools, ticketing, artifact formats.
- Governance: SLAs/OLAs, KPIs/OKRs, reporting cadence, escalation, change control.
- Onboarding & Exit: knowledge transfer, shadowing, offboarding, data deletion.
- Geography & Language: data residency, export controls, language proficiency.

5) Prioritize requirements
- Use MoSCoW or similar. Tag regulatory and safety items as non-negotiable “Must.”
- Define measurable acceptance criteria for each requirement.
- Map requirements to risk drivers; document rationale for must-haves to avoid over-specification.

6) Define evaluation and scoring model
- Create weighted scorecard aligned to requirement categories.
- Define pass/fail gates (e.g., mandatory certifications).
- Establish evidence requirements: case studies, references, audit reports, sample deliverables, resumes, facilities lists.
- Align with Procurement on how scoring will be applied during RFI/RFP.

7) Conduct market intelligence and benchmarking
- Identify candidate partner archetypes and market standards.
- Benchmark typical capabilities, rates, and timelines to validate feasibility and budget.
- Identify any supply constraints, regional risks, or regulatory bottlenecks.

8) Draft Partner Requirements Specification (PRS)
- Compile requirements, acceptance criteria, and scoring model.
- Include annexes: Security Exhibit, Data Processing Requirements, IP & OSS policy, Regulatory checklist, Quality plan outline, Tooling and Access Requirements, Draft SLAs/KPIs, Onboarding checklist, Commercial parameters, RFI questionnaire.

9) Stakeholder review and risk/compliance checks
- Legal/IP review: ownership, background IP, OSS policy, indemnity.
- InfoSec/Privacy review: data flows, security controls, DPA needs.
- Quality/Regulatory review: standards coverage, documentation needs.
- Finance/Procurement review: commercial feasibility, sourcing policy alignment.
- Architecture/IT review: toolchain alignment and integration constraints.
- Consolidate feedback, resolve conflicts via facilitation, and update PRS.

10) Approve and baseline
- Obtain formal sign-off from accountable owner(s) and key control functions.
- Version-control the PRS; record decisions and justifications.

11) Prepare sourcing pack and handover
- Finalize RFI pack with PRS, scorecards, questionnaires, and submission instructions.
- Brief Procurement/Vendor Management for market engagement.
- Record lessons learned and any open assumptions/risks.

12) Maintain and change-control
- Establish process for controlled updates as product scope or regulations change.
- Track changes and communicate updates to Procurement and stakeholders.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Partner Requirements Specification (PRS), including:
  - Capability, delivery, quality, security/privacy, compliance, IP/legal, commercial, ESG, accessibility, tooling, governance, onboarding/exit, and geography requirements.
  - Measurable acceptance criteria and evidence requests.
- Weighted evaluation scorecard and pass/fail criteria.
- RFI questionnaire and instructions.
- Risk and compliance checklist; initial third-party risk profile.
- Draft SLAs/KPIs and governance model.
- Data Processing and Security requirements (e.g., DPA clauses, encryption, data residency).
- IP and OSS policy annex; NDA template reference.
- Budget parameters and preferred commercial models.
- Onboarding and exit checklists.

Success criteria:
- PRS approved by key stakeholders within target cycle time.
- ≥80% of responding vendors meet all “Must” requirements on first pass.
- Minimal post-RFP requirement changes (e.g., <10% critical changes).
- Identified risks have documented mitigations; no critical control gaps flagged by Legal/InfoSec/Regulatory.
- Procurement confirms readiness to launch sourcing without rework.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product Manager (A/R): Owns product objectives; co-owns requirement priorities; approves PRS.
- Engineering Lead (R): Defines technical stack, architecture constraints, verification needs.
- Design Lead/UX (R): Defines design research, accessibility, and design system compatibility.
- Procurement/Sourcing (C/R): Advises on market feasibility; prepares sourcing strategy post-PRS.
- Vendor Management/TPRM (R/C): Defines third-party risk requirements; conducts risk profiling.
- Legal and IP Counsel (C/A for legal terms): IP ownership, licensing, indemnity, NDA, DPA templates.
- Information Security (C): Security controls, certifications, secure SDLC, SBOM requirements.
- Privacy/Compliance (C): Data protection, regulatory obligations (GDPR, HIPAA, etc.).
- Quality/Regulatory Affairs (C): QMS, standards, testing/certification documentation.
- Finance (C): Budget alignment; commercial model guidance.
- Enterprise Architecture/IT (C): Tooling standards, integration, access management.
- ESG/Sustainability (C): Sustainability metrics, ethical sourcing, DEI considerations.
- Accessibility Lead (C): WCAG targets and verification approach.
- Manufacturing/Operations (C): DfX, prototyping, supply chain compatibility for physical products.
- Project/Program Manager (R): Facilitates workshops, tracks actions, manages approvals.

Note: R = Responsible, A = Accountable, C = Consulted.

## Best Practices
- Start with outcomes: tie partner requirements directly to product objectives and risks.
- Standardize templates: PRS, scorecards, security and DPA exhibits, and RFI to reduce cycle time.
- Prioritize objectively: use MoSCoW and weighted scoring; separate must-haves from preferences.
- Integrate compliance early: involve Legal, InfoSec, Privacy, and Regulatory in drafting, not just review.
- Evidence-driven evaluation: require verifiable artifacts (certificates, audits, case studies, code samples, SBOMs).
- Think lifecycle: include onboarding, knowledge transfer, and exit/transition requirements.
- Toolchain compatibility: mandate alignment with your repo, CI/CD, PLM/ALM, design tools, and ticketing systems.
- Security and privacy by design: specify secure SDLC, threat modeling, encryption, vulnerability management, data minimization, and data residency.
- IP clarity: define background/foreground IP, OSS policies, contribution licenses, and indemnity expectations up front.
- Market realism: benchmark rates, capacity, and lead times; avoid over-specifying niche requirements unless essential.
- Inclusivity and sustainability: include accessibility (WCAG), ESG metrics, ethical sourcing, and diverse supplier participation.
- Pilot first: include POC/pilot capability requirements to validate fit before full engagement.

## Common Challenges
- Ambiguous or over-engineered requirements leading to vendor confusion.
  - Solution: Facilitate structured workshops; use acceptance criteria and examples; right-size must-haves.
- Conflicting stakeholder priorities (e.g., speed vs. security).
  - Solution: Use risk-based trade-off logs and decision-making with clear accountability.
- Underestimating compliance or security controls.
  - Solution: Early control function engagement; use checklists and control libraries.
- Legacy toolchain constraints causing friction with partners.
  - Solution: Define minimum interoperability and provide sandbox access guidance.
- IP and OSS risks discovered late.
  - Solution: Mandate OSS disclosure/SBOM and IP terms in PRS; early legal review.
- Unrealistic timelines or budgets.
  - Solution: Benchmark market data; include “good/better/best” options and phased scope.
- Geographic/data residency conflicts.
  - Solution: Specify permitted geographies, subcontracting rules, and data localization requirements.

## Performance Metrics
- Cycle time to approved PRS (request-to-approval).
- Number of PRS revisions after RFI launch.
- Percentage of vendors meeting all must-have requirements in RFI responses.
- Coverage score of compliance/security controls (vs control library).
- Stakeholder satisfaction with PRS quality and completeness.
- Downstream rework due to missing requirements (e.g., contract changes attributable to PRS gaps).
- Variance between budget assumptions and qualified vendor proposals.
- Time-to-onboard selected partner (baseline: PRS finalization to first deliverable).
- Audit/assessment findings related to third-party controls post-onboarding.

## Technology and Tools
- Requirements and documentation: Confluence/Notion, Microsoft 365/Google Workspace, Jama, Doors Next, Jira.
- Collaboration and workshops: Miro/Mural, Teams/Zoom, Slack.
- Architecture and modeling: Lucidchart, draw.io, Figma for design alignment.
- PLM/ALM and DevOps: Jira/ADO, GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket, Jenkins/GitHub Actions, Polarion, Windchill, Arena.
- Vendor management and eSourcing: SAP Ariba, Coupa, Jaggaer, Ivalua.
- Third-party risk and GRC: OneTrust, Archer, ProcessUnity, ServiceNow GRC.
- Security and compliance evidence: Vanta/Drata for vendor attestations, Secure portal for NDA and DPA exchange, Docusign/Adobe Sign.
- Data classification and DLP: Microsoft Purview, classification labels for shared artifacts.
- Decision support: Weighted decision matrix tools or spreadsheets; BI dashboards for KPIs.

Domain-specific requirement examples (include as applicable):
- Physical products: ISO 9001, ISO 13485 (medical), IATF 16949 (automotive), AS9100 (aerospace), RoHS/REACH, UL/CE marking, DFM/DFx capability, environmental testing labs, PPAP, FAI.
- Digital products: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, OWASP ASVS, SLSA level, SBOM (CycloneDX/SPDX), CI/CD, IaC, accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA), privacy by design, API-first, design system adherence.
- Services/ITSM: ITIL v4, ISO 20000, defined SLAs/OLAs, incident/change/problem management maturity, 24x7 support capabilities.

Process Details:
# [2.3.1.8.1] Design for Manufacturing (DFM)

## Overview
Design for Manufacturing (DFM) is the systematic practice of engineering a product so it can be manufactured at the required quality, cost, yield, and schedule using capable processes and suppliers. It bridges product design with manufacturing by embedding process capabilities, tooling constraints, assembly methods, inspection strategies, and supplier capabilities into the product’s hardware and electrical design.

This process ensures that application requirements, mechanical and electrical designs, and production tooling (molds, dies, fixtures, stencils) are optimized together. It reduces late design changes, tooling rework, and ramp risks while improving first-pass yield and time-to-market.

DFM is a core activity under “Design products/services” and directly feeds subsequent prototyping, tooling, pilot builds, and process validation/qualification.

## Key Activities
- Define manufacturing strategy and volumes (make/buy, regionalization, automation level).
- Select manufacturing processes (e.g., injection molding, die casting, sheet metal forming, machining, PCB fabrication/assembly, cable harnessing, additive).
- Material selection aligned with process capability, reliability, and compliance.
- Tolerance and GD&T scheme with stack-up analyses tied to process capability (Cpk/Ppk).
- Design-for-Assembly (DFA): minimize part count, fasteners, handling, and assembly time.
- Design-for-Testing (DfT): test points, accessibility, built-in self-test, ICT/FT coverage.
- Domain-specific DFM:
  - Plastics/molds: draft, wall thickness, ribs, gates, vents, ejectors, knit lines, shrink.
  - Castings: draft, fillets, gating/risers, porosity, hot spots, machining stock, cores.
  - Sheet metal: bend radii, K-factor, reliefs, hole-to-bend distances, hem/clinches.
  - Machined parts: tool access, standard radii, tolerances, surface finishes, setups.
  - PCBs/PCBAs: stack-up, trace/space, pad design, panelization, fiducials, stencil design, component keep-outs, thermal relief.
  - Cables/harnesses: bend radii, strain reliefs, connector orientation, standard components.
- Tooling and fixture design input/specification (molds, dies, jigs, test fixtures, CMM fixtures).
- Simulation and analysis (Moldflow, casting/thermal/structural FEA, DFA/DFMA, tolerance analysis).
- Prototyping strategy (3D print, soft tools, quick-turn boards, EVT/DVT/PVT builds).
- Cost modeling and value engineering (DfC/VA-VE).
- Risk management (DFMEA/PFMEA, control plans).
- Supplier engagement (early DFM reviews, RFQ with DFM data, PPAP/FAI requirements).
- Documentation: drawings with GD&T, MBD, specifications, inspection plans, routings/Bill of Process (BoP).
- Change control and release (ECO/ECN, PLM handoff).

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Product requirements: Voice of Customer (VoC), CTQs, performance/reliability targets.
  - Concept design: CAD models, preliminary schematics/PCB layout, functional architecture.
  - Target cost and forecasted volumes; market launch timing.
  - Regulatory and compliance requirements (e.g., UL/IEC, RoHS/REACH, ISO 10993, ASME/ISO GD&T).
  - Environmental and sustainability goals (recycled content, end-of-life).
  - Preliminary BOM and make/buy strategy; supplier capability shortlist.
- Prerequisites:
  - Concept/design intent reviewed and baselined.
  - Access to required design guidelines and process capability data.
  - Cross-functional team mobilized (design, manufacturing, quality, sourcing, suppliers).
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Upstream: [2.3.1.8] Design products/services (requirements definition, concept design).
  - Parallel: Prototyping and evaluation activities; supplier sourcing.
  - Downstream: Tooling fabrication, pilot builds, process validation/qualification, production ramp.

## Process Steps
1. Plan DFM scope and gates
   - Define DFM objectives, metrics, milestones (e.g., DFM Review 1 at concept freeze; Review 2 before tooling kick-off; sign-off at design freeze).
   - Build a DFM checklist per domain (plastics, sheet metal, machining, PCB/PCBA, harness, assembly, test).
2. Define manufacturing strategy
   - Confirm forecast volumes, automation level, regional manufacturing strategy, and make/buy decisions.
   - Shortlist candidate processes and suppliers based on capability and capacity.
3. Select materials and processes
   - Choose materials compatible with processes (e.g., resin flow/shrink, cast alloy porosity risk, PCB Tg).
   - Validate against regulatory, environmental, and reliability requirements.
4. Apply domain-specific DFM and DFA rules
   - Plastics/molding: apply draft (typically ≥1–2°), uniform walls, ribs/bosses guidelines, avoid undercuts where possible, gate/vent/ejector planning, surface finish and knit-line placement.
   - Casting: ensure draft, proper fillets, gating/risering to avoid porosity, provide machining stock, minimize cores.
   - Sheet metal: maintain minimum bend radii, use standard hole sizes, add bend reliefs, respect hole-to-bend distances.
   - Machining: standardize hole sizes/threads, specify achievable surface finishes, ensure tool access and corner radii, minimize setups and tight tolerances.
   - PCB: set design rules (trace/space, annular ring), controlled impedance stack-up, component spacing, fiducials, panelization with breakaway tabs/rails, thermal reliefs.
   - PCBA: stencil thickness and aperture design, tombstoning risk mitigation, wave/selective solder keep-outs, test-point coverage and accessibility.
   - Cables: choose standard wire gauges/connectors, define bend radii and strain relief, design for modular assembly.
   - DFA: reduce part count, commonize fasteners, enforce assembly orientation and poka-yoke features, design for single-direction assembly where possible.
5. Define GD&T and perform tolerance analysis
   - Establish datum schemes aligned with assembly/inspection strategy.
   - Perform worst-case and statistical (Monte Carlo) stack-ups linked to process capabilities.
   - Allocate tolerances to meet function at minimum cost; avoid over-tolerancing.
6. Analyze manufacturability with simulation
   - Moldflow/casting simulations for fill, cooling, warpage, hot spots, porosity.
   - Structural/thermal FEA for critical load and thermal paths.
   - DFA/DFMA assessment for assembly time and cost.
7. Iterate with suppliers and manufacturing
   - Conduct early supplier DFM reviews; collect redlines and capability data (Cp/Cpk, yield history).
   - Update design per feedback; document trade-offs and decisions.
8. Tooling and fixture definition
   - Specify tool class, cavities, steel selection, cooling, gating, surface finishes for molds/dies.
   - Define jigs/fixtures for machining, assembly, test, and inspection; design CMM fixtures and measurement programs.
   - For PCBAs, define test fixtures (ICT/flying probe/functional) and stencils.
9. Prototype and build validation units
   - Plan EVT/DVT/PVT builds; select prototyping methods (soft tooling, CNC, additive, quick-turn PCB).
   - Execute FAIs; capture issues via structured defect tracking; feed learning back to design.
10. Risk assessment and control planning
    - Complete DFMEA and link high-risk items to PFMEA.
    - Develop control plans, special characteristics, inspection/test methods, and sampling plans.
11. Costing and value engineering
    - Perform detailed should-cost and DFMA analysis; run VA/VE workshops to reduce cost/complexity.
    - Confirm costed BOM meets target; adjust design/process if needed.
12. Finalize documentation and release
    - Update 3D models/drawings/MBD with GD&T, specifications, surface finishes, coatings.
    - Finalize BOM, BoP, routings, work instructions inputs, inspection plans, test plans.
    - Prepare supplier technical packages and PPAP/qualification requirements.
    - Obtain cross-functional DFM sign-off; release via PLM; initiate ECOs as necessary.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- DFM package:
  - DFM checklist(s) and review minutes; open-issues log with owners/dates.
  - Updated CAD/MBD and 2D drawings with GD&T and notes.
  - Tolerance stack-up reports and simulation results (Moldflow/casting/FEA).
  - Tooling and fixture specifications and drawings.
  - Inspection and test plans; CMM programs/fixturing requirements.
  - DFMEA, PFMEA linkages, and control plans.
  - Costed BOM, DFMA analysis, and VA/VE recommendations.
  - Supplier technical data package and PPAP/FAI requirements.
- Prototypes and build reports (EVT/DVT/PVT) with FAI/qualification data.
- Success criteria:
  - Meets CTQs and functional requirements with capable tolerances (Cpk≥target).
  - First-pass yield and scrap rates meet targets in pilot builds.
  - Cost within target; cycle times within takt; part count minimized.
  - DFM sign-off completed prior to tooling kick-off; PPAP/FAI passed on first submission.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product/Mechanical Design Engineer: Owns mechanical design, GD&T, DFM compliance, and change management.
- Electrical/PCB Design Engineer: Owns schematic/layout, DfM/DfT compliance, stack-up, and test coverage.
- Manufacturing Engineer: Defines processes, BoP/routings, fixtures, and assembly methods; leads DFA.
- Tooling Engineer: Specifies and oversees molds/dies/fixtures design and qualification.
- Process Engineer: Establishes process windows, parameters, and capability targets; executes PFMEA.
- Quality Engineer/Inspection: Defines inspection/test methods, control plans, MSA; leads FAI/PPAP.
- Supplier Quality Engineer (SQE): Leads supplier DFM reviews, audits, PPAP, and capability verification.
- Sourcing/Commodity Manager: Aligns suppliers, RFQ packages, and commercial agreements with technical needs.
- Test Engineer: Designs test strategy, fixtures, and coverage (ICT/functional/burn-in).
- Reliability/Compliance Engineer: Ensures design meets reliability and regulatory requirements.
- Program/Project Manager: Drives schedule, gating, risks, and cross-functional alignment.
- PLM/Configuration Manager: Controls documentation, releases, and ECO/ECN processes.
- Cost/Value Engineer: Performs should-cost, DFMA, and VA/VE analyses.

## Best Practices
- Involve manufacturing and suppliers early; hold structured DFM reviews at defined gates.
- Use standard components, materials, and processes wherever possible.
- Design to process capability; set tolerances based on data, not assumptions.
- Prioritize DFA: reduce part count, commonize fasteners, and design for one-way assembly.
- Implement DfT: adequate test access, isolation, and diagnosability.
- Apply simulation before committing to tooling; iterate to eliminate risks.
- Use model-based definition (MBD) and a digital thread through PLM to avoid drawing misinterpretation.
- Maintain living DFM checklists and lessons-learned repositories.
- Validate with representative prototypes; plan for soft-tool trials before hard tooling.
- Address sustainability: design for disassembly, recyclable materials, minimized waste.
- Manage change rigorously via ECO/ECN; freeze designs before tooling release.

## Common Challenges
- Overly tight tolerances drive cost and poor yields
  - Solution: Link tolerances to capability data; use tolerance analysis; relax where function allows.
- Late design changes after tooling release
  - Solution: Gate DFM sign-off before tooling; use soft tooling and virtual simulations to de-risk.
- Supplier capability mismatch
  - Solution: Early supplier audits and DFM reviews; specify capability targets in RFQs; dual-source critical parts.
- Warpage/porosity in molded/cast parts
  - Solution: Uniform walls, proper gating/venting/risers; run Moldflow/casting simulations; adjust materials/processes.
- PCB assembly defects (tombstoning/insufficient solder)
  - Solution: Stencil optimization, pad design rules, thermal balance, proper panelization.
- Assembly bottlenecks and high labor content
  - Solution: DFA workshops, modular subassemblies, poka-yoke features, ergonomic fixtures, selective automation.
- Inadequate test coverage leading to escapes
  - Solution: DfT rules, ICT/FT planning from the outset, boundary-scan where applicable.
- Documentation errors and revision confusion
  - Solution: PLM-driven configuration control, MBD, clear drawing practices, and release discipline.

## Performance Metrics
- DFM sign-off lead time vs plan.
- Number of DFM issues open/closed per gate; severity distribution.
- Post-release ECOs attributed to manufacturability (count and cycle time).
- First-pass yield (EVT/DVT/PVT and pilot builds); scrap/rework rates.
- Process capability (Cp/Cpk/Ppk) on critical-to-quality dimensions/features.
- Assembly time per unit; labor content; parts count reduction achieved.
- Cost variance to target (costed BOM and total manufacturing cost).
- PPAP/FAI pass rate on first submission; number of tooling iterations (T0/T1/Tn).
- Test coverage metrics (ICT/FT percentage) and defect Pareto.
- Supplier on-time delivery and quality (PPM) during NPI builds.

## Technology and Tools
- CAD/MBD: Creo, NX, SolidWorks, CATIA; GD&T advisors.
- ECAD/DFM: Altium, Cadence Allegro/OrCAD, Mentor Xpedition; Valor NPI/DFM.
- Simulation: Autodesk Moldflow, Ansys/Abaqus, MAGMASOFT/SolidCast, Altair, Simcenter; 3DCS/CETOL/VSA for tolerance analysis.
- DFMA/Costing: Boothroyd Dewhurst DFMA, should-cost tools.
- CAM/CNC: Mastercam, PowerMill, FeatureCAM; 3D printing for rapid prototypes/fixtures.
- Inspection/Metrology: CMM (PC-DMIS), laser scanners, vision systems; MSA tools.
- Test: ICT/flying probe systems, functional test development platforms; boundary-scan tools.
- PLM/ERP/MES: Teamcenter, Windchill, Arena/Agile; SAP/Oracle; MES for routing/SPC.
- Quality/Risk: APIS IQ-RM for FMEA, Minitab for SPC/DOE, eQMS (MasterControl, ETQ).
- Collaboration/Requirements: Jama, DOORS, Jira/Confluence for issues and traceability.

Process Details:
## Overview
Process [2.3.1.8.4] Review product troubleshooting methodology is a formal design review focused on evaluating and validating the approach, tools, and artifacts used to diagnose, isolate, and resolve product issues throughout the product lifecycle. It ensures the product is designed with supportability and serviceability in mind (“design for troubleshootability”), enabling rapid fault detection, accurate diagnosis, safe recovery, and efficient resolution in the field.

Purpose:
- Confirm that troubleshooting methods cover critical failure modes and user scenarios.
- Validate observability, diagnostics, error handling, and recovery design meet targets (e.g., MTTR).
- Align cross-functional teams (Design, QA, Support, Field Service, Compliance) on how issues will be handled from self-service through expert escalation.
- Reduce time-to-resolution, cost-to-serve, product returns, and customer downtime.

Role in the organization:
- Integral to Design and Prototype Products/Services, feeding requirements back into product design and documentation.
- A stage-gate quality and readiness checkpoint before pilot, beta, general availability, or major releases.
- Ensures alignment with incident/problem management processes and compliance/safety requirements.

Scope:
- Applicable to hardware, software, and service offerings.
- Covers self-service troubleshooting, Level 1–Level 3 support flows, field service procedures, remote diagnostics, built-in self-tests (BIST), and escalation/RMA criteria.

## Key Activities
- Define review scope and objectives (products, versions, components, markets).
- Collect and analyze inputs (FMEA, historical incidents, prototype test results, regulatory constraints).
- Assess observability and diagnostic coverage (logs, metrics, traces, error codes, telemetry).
- Evaluate troubleshooting workflows and decision trees across support tiers and customer self-service.
- Review fault containment, isolation, and recovery mechanisms (safe modes, rollback, resets).
- Validate security, privacy, and safety aspects of diagnostics and remote access.
- Confirm tools and access requirements (service ports, fixtures, credentials, software utilities).
- Assess documentation plans (service manuals, KB articles, quick guides).
- Define test and validation approach for troubleshooting methodology (fault injection, tabletop exercises).
- Identify gaps, create remediation actions, and update design requirements.
- Approve, conditionally approve, or reject the troubleshooting methodology with documented rationale.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Product/service design specifications and architecture diagrams.
- Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) or risk analysis; fault trees (if available).
- Historical field/service data from similar products; FRACAS/incident logs.
- Prototype and lab test results, including fault injection outcomes.
- Observability/logging/telemetry plans and error code taxonomies.
- Support model (tiering), escalation paths, RMA policy, and SLAs (e.g., MTTR targets).
- Compliance and regulatory requirements (safety, cybersecurity, data privacy).
- Serviceability requirements (DfX), access constraints, and tool availability.
- Draft troubleshooting workflows/decision trees and knowledge article outlines.

Prerequisites:
- Baseline design stability for the reviewed build/release.
- Defined customer personas and support tiers (self-service, L1, L2, L3/Engineering).
- Ownership and RACI for support and service processes.
- Access to representative test environments or prototypes for validation.
- Security review framework in place for diagnostic capabilities.

Dependencies on other processes:
- [2.3.1.8] Design products/services (feeding requirements and constraints).
- Prototype build and test processes; validation/plans for reliability and maintainability.
- Incident/Problem Management (ITIL) alignment for post-launch operations.
- Regulatory/compliance review; cybersecurity and safety engineering.
- Knowledge management and documentation processes.
- Training development for support and field service teams.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and Plan the Review
   - Define scope, objectives, success criteria (e.g., coverage of critical failure modes ≥ X%, MTTR target ≤ Y).
   - Schedule cross-functional review with Product, Engineering, Support, QA, Security, Compliance, Field Service.
   - Confirm required inputs and assign pre-work.

2. Gather and Analyze Inputs
   - Compile FMEA, historical incident data, prototype test outcomes.
   - Map critical user journeys and operational contexts.
   - Identify product constraints (hardware access, network, power, environmental conditions).

3. Assess Observability and Instrumentation
   - Evaluate logging/metrics/tracing coverage and signal quality.
   - Review error code taxonomy: clarity, consistency, localization readiness.
   - Confirm state capture for post-failure diagnosis (crash dumps, telemetry, audit logs).
   - For hardware: review BIST coverage, diagnostic ports, LEDs/display codes, sensor placement.

4. Evaluate Diagnostic and Troubleshooting Workflows
   - Review end-to-end decision trees for self-service, L1, L2, L3.
   - Check for logical flow, minimal branching complexity, and clear next-best-actions.
   - Verify preconditions and required tools/permissions at each step.
   - Validate scripts/playbooks for repeatability and alignment with SLAs.

5. Review Fault Containment, Isolation, and Recovery
   - Assess fault isolation capability (module boundaries, dependency mapping).
   - Validate safe modes, graceful degradation, feature toggles, and rollback plans.
   - Confirm automated recovery/self-healing actions and thresholds to avoid oscillations.
   - Define RMA criteria and No-Fault-Found handling to minimize unnecessary returns.

6. Validate Security, Privacy, and Safety
   - Review access control to diagnostic features (authN/authZ, least privilege).
   - Confirm secure remote access methods and auditability.
   - Verify handling of sensitive data in logs and telemetry (PII redaction, retention).
   - For safety-critical systems: confirm hazard mitigations, lockouts, and safe recovery procedures.

7. Tools, Access, and Environment Readiness
   - Confirm availability of diagnostic tools, service fixtures, and credentials.
   - Validate test/lab environments mirror field conditions sufficiently.
   - Define offline/low-connectivity troubleshooting contingencies.

8. Documentation and Knowledge Artifacts
   - Review structure and completeness of service manuals, KB templates, quick-starts.
   - Ensure screenshots, schematics, parts lists, and step visuals are planned.
   - Confirm localization strategy and accessibility considerations.

9. Training and Enablement Plan
   - Define learning objectives per role (self-service, L1, L2, field techs).
   - Plan hands-on exercises using fault injection and simulators.

10. Test and Validate the Methodology
    - Conduct tabletop run-throughs; simulate top N failure modes.
    - Execute fault injection tests; measure time to detect/diagnose/recover.
    - Record gaps, update workflows and requirements as needed.

11. Finalize and Approve
    - Consolidate findings into a Troubleshooting Methodology Review Report.
    - Document required changes, owners, and due dates; create backlog items/user stories.
    - Approve, conditional approve (with deadlines), or reject; define re-review plan.

12. Post-Review Follow-Up
    - Track remediation to closure; update FMEA and design artifacts.
    - Establish feedback loop from beta/field to continuously refine troubleshooting assets.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Troubleshooting Methodology Design Document (TMDD) including scope, assumptions, and constraints.
- Diagnostic workflows and decision trees for self-service, L1, L2, L3.
- Observability and telemetry requirements (log schemas, metrics, traces, error codes).
- BIST and serviceability requirements; tool and fixture specifications.
- RMA criteria and escalation paths; incident categorization and triage matrices.
- Test and validation plan for troubleshooting (fault injection scenarios).
- Security/privacy/safety assessment for diagnostics and remote access.
- Knowledge base article outlines and service manual content plan.
- Training plan and materials outline.
- Action log/backlog items for design changes and documentation updates.

Success criteria:
- Coverage of critical failure modes meets target (e.g., ≥ 95% of high-severity FMEs).
- Achievable MTTR targets demonstrated in test (e.g., P1 ≤ 30 min, P2 ≤ 2 hrs).
- First-time-fix/first-contact resolution rates projected to targets.
- False positive/negative alarm rates within thresholds.
- No critical security/safety/privacy issues outstanding.
- Tools and environments ready; documentation completeness ≥ agreed threshold.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product Manager: Owns scope and acceptance criteria; prioritizes remediation actions.
- Systems/Design Engineering: Ensures architecture supports diagnostics, isolation, and recovery; implements required instrumentation.
- Software/Firmware/Hardware Engineering: Implements logging, BIST, error handling; updates code/specs per review findings.
- Reliability/Quality Engineering: Provides FMEA; defines test protocols and validates MTTR and coverage; manages FRACAS.
- Support Engineering (L2/L3): Authors decision trees/playbooks; validates workflows; defines escalation criteria.
- Technical Support (L1) and Customer Success: Validates usability of troubleshooting flows; provides feedback on clarity.
- Field Service/Service Operations: Confirms tool/fixture needs; validates procedures for on-site repair; defines spare parts strategy.
- DevOps/SRE (for software/services): Designs observability; ensures telemetry pipelines; defines rollback and runbooks.
- Security/Privacy: Reviews access controls, data handling, and remote diagnostics.
- Compliance/Regulatory/Safety: Ensures methodology meets regulatory and safety requirements.
- Technical Writing/Knowledge Management: Produces service manuals and KBs; manages localization and updates.
- Training/Enablement: Develops and delivers training aligned to workflows and tools.
- Data/Analytics: Defines dashboards and metrics; monitors effectiveness post-launch.
- Process Owner (Supportability Lead): Facilitates review, tracks actions, and maintains process governance.

## Best Practices
- Shift-left supportability: Incorporate troubleshooting design from early design stages; make it a gate in each development phase.
- Design for serviceability: Modular design, accessible components, standard connectors, and clearly labeled parts.
- Standardized error taxonomy: Human-readable error messages with unique codes and actionable guidance.
- Robust observability: Structured logs, meaningful metrics, distributed tracing (for software), and event correlation.
- Built-in self-test and diagnostics: Automated health checks, loopbacks, and component isolation routines.
- Safe recovery mechanisms: Graceful degradation, safe modes, transactional rollback, and pause/resume.
- Human factors and usability: Clear, concise steps; minimal tool requirements; visuals and checklists; localization and accessibility.
- Security and privacy by design: Least-privilege access, audit logs, encrypted channels, PII minimization/redaction.
- Continuous improvement: Closed-loop with FRACAS; update KBs and workflows based on real-world incidents and analytics.
- Test with fault injection and digital twins/simulators: Validate detection, isolation, and recovery under realistic conditions.
- Align with ITIL: Ensure troubleshooting feeds incident/problem/change processes and CMDB updates where applicable.

## Common Challenges
- Late consideration of troubleshootability leading to costly redesigns.
  - Mitigation: Establish early-stage gates; include supportability requirements in design definition.
- Insufficient instrumentation/logging resulting in long diagnosis cycles.
  - Mitigation: Define observability standards; conduct log reviews; enforce schema/versioning.
- Overly complex decision trees that confuse agents/customers.
  - Mitigation: Simplify flows; use progressive disclosure; test usability; maintain version control.
- High false positive/negative rates in alerts.
  - Mitigation: Tune thresholds; implement alert deduplication and correlation; periodic recalibration.
- Security/privacy conflicts with diagnostic access.
  - Mitigation: Role-based access; temporary elevated access with approvals; data masking; secure tunnels.
- No-Fault-Found RMAs increasing costs.
  - Mitigation: Strengthen pre-RMA checks; remote diagnostics; better customer self-tests; clearer symptoms capture.
- Field constraints (tools, connectivity, environment).
  - Mitigation: Offline procedures; ruggedized kits; step alternatives; minimal tool variants.
- Documentation gaps and stale KBs.
  - Mitigation: Ownership and SLAs for updates; integrate doc changes into release process; analytics on article usage.
- Training gaps across support tiers.
  - Mitigation: Tier-specific curricula; hands-on labs; certification and refresh cycles.
- Localization and accessibility issues.
  - Mitigation: Internationalization of content; professional translation workflows; accessibility compliance checks.

## Performance Metrics
- Mean Time to Detect (MTTD), Diagnose (MTTDx), and Repair/Recover (MTTR).
- First-Time Fix Rate (field), First Contact Resolution (L1).
- Diagnostic Accuracy: percentage of correct root cause identification on first attempt.
- Self-Service Deflection Rate: percentage of issues resolved without contacting support.
- Alarm Fidelity: false positive and false negative rates for alerts/alarms.
- No-Fault-Found (NFF) Rate and RMA Avoidance Rate.
- Coverage of Critical Failure Modes: proportion with defined diagnostics and procedures.
- Knowledge Base Effectiveness: article usage, helpfulness scores, time-to-publish updates.
- Cost to Serve: average cost per incident; truck rolls per 1,000 units.
- Escalation Rate: percentage of tickets requiring L2/L3 or engineering involvement.
- Training Effectiveness: assessment pass rates; time to proficiency.
- Tool Readiness: percentage of required diagnostic tools available and deployed.

## Technology and Tools
- Observability and Telemetry: logging platforms, metrics/monitoring systems, distributed tracing tools, crash reporting.
- Diagnostics and Test: fault injection frameworks, simulators/digital twins, BIST frameworks, JTAG/service ports (hardware).
- Ticketing and ITSM: incident/problem/change management systems; CMDB.
- Knowledge Management and Documentation: KB platforms, content authoring, translation/localization tools.
- Analytics and Dashboards: BI tools, data warehouses/lakes; alert correlation engines.
- Remote Access and Device Management: secure remote support, device management/MDM, OTA update systems with rollback.
- Field Service Management: scheduling, parts management, mobile service apps, checklists.
- Security: secrets management, identity/access management, privileged access management, secure tunneling/VPN.
- Collaboration and Work Management: requirements and backlog tools; review/approval workflows and e-signature for gated reviews.
- Test Management and QA: test case repositories, automated test orchestration, defect tracking integrated with observability.

Process Details:
## Overview
Design and manage product data, design, and bill of materials (BOM) is the process of creating, controlling, and distributing all product data required to realize, manufacture, service, and sustain a product. It establishes and maintains:

- Engineering BOM (EBOM): design intent and as-designed structure from engineering.
- Manufacturing BOM (MBOM): as-built/as-manufactured structure aligned to manufacturing processes, routings, plants, and operations.
- Service BOM (SBOM): as-maintained/field-replaceable structure optimized for service, spare parts, and repair levels.

This process sits at the core of product lifecycle management (PLM), connecting design, sourcing, manufacturing, quality, compliance, and service. Its purpose is to provide a single source of truth for item masters, configurations, drawings, and multi-view BOMs, ensuring traceability, change control, and right-first-time execution in downstream ERP, MES, and service systems.

## Key Activities
- Define product structure strategy and templates (module hierarchy, 150% super-BOM, variant rules).
- Create and maintain item masters with standardized part numbering, classification, and attributes.
- Associate design data (CAD/ECAD models, drawings, specs, software/firmware) to items.
- Build and validate EBOMs from CAD/ECAD with quantities, reference designators, alternates/substitutes, and effectivities.
- Transform EBOM to MBOM, add non-design manufacturing items (consumables, packaging, tooling), and map to routings/operations.
- Create SBOM focusing on field-replaceable units (FRUs), service kits, and repair levels.
- Govern AML/AVL (approved manufacturer/vendor lists), alternates, and substitutes.
- Execute change control (ECR/ECO/MCO), including impact analysis across EBOM/MBOM/SBOM.
- Ensure regulatory and customer compliance (RoHS/REACH, safety, export controls).
- Publish controlled releases to ERP/MES/Service and maintain digital thread traceability.
- Perform ongoing data quality management, audits, and obsolescence management.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs
- Product requirements, targets, and product breakdown structure.
- CAD/ECAD outputs: assemblies, models, schematics, drawings, PCB layouts, netlists.
- Standards and policies: part numbering schema, description formatting, classification taxonomy, UoM standards.
- Design specifications: materials, finishes, tolerances, performance parameters.
- Manufacturing strategy: make/buy, plant codes, routing templates, operation libraries.
- Sourcing inputs: AML/AVL, preferred suppliers, cost targets, lead times.
- Compliance requirements: regulatory, environmental, safety, country of origin, export controls.
- Service strategy: FRU definitions, repair levels, warranty and maintenance plans.
- Prior revisions and lessons learned.

Prerequisites
- PLM/PDM system configured with item/BOM data model, workflows, and access controls.
- CAD/ECAD integrations to PLM, and PLM-ERP/MES integrations defined.
- Defined governance: change control (ECR/ECO), release states, sign-off authorities.
- Master data foundations: standardized attributes, UoM, plants, effectivity conventions.
- Trained roles with assigned responsibilities and RACI.

Dependencies on other processes
- Upstream: Product/service design ([2.3.1.8]), prototyping and validation, supplier qualification.
- Parallel: Manufacturing process design and routing creation, cost estimating, quality planning (PPAP/APQP), compliance management.
- Downstream: Procurement, production planning, MES execution, service planning and parts cataloging, configuration and order management.

## Process Steps
1) Plan product structure and rules
- Define the product breakdown structure (levels, modules, reuse strategy).
- Decide on 150% super-BOM vs. multiple 100% BOMs for variants.
- Establish effectivity types (date, serial/lot, plant) and configuration rules.

2) Create item masters
- Assign part numbers and versioning schema (intelligent vs. non-intelligent).
- Populate mandatory attributes: description, classification, UoM, material, finish, weight, RoHS/REACH flags, lifecycle state.
- Set planning/procurement attributes: make/buy, lead time, sourcing status, serialization/lotting.
- Create supplier-linked MPNs and AML/AVL entries where applicable.

3) Attach design data
- Check-in CAD/ECAD models/drawings/specs to PLM; link to item masters.
- Ensure metadata compliance (titles, revision, mass, material).
- For ECAD, capture reference designators, alternates, footprints; import netlists and BoMs.

4) Build EBOM
- Auto-generate from CAD assemblies and complete manually as needed (fasteners, adhesives, software).
- Capture quantities, reference designators, find numbers, alternates/substitutes, and effectivity.
- Flag phantoms, standard subassemblies, and library modules.
- Include non-physical items critical for product definition (firmware, licenses).

5) Validate EBOM
- Run automated validations: missing attributes, duplicate parts, UoM mismatches, invalid alternates.
- Perform DFM/DFA/DFT/DFMEC reviews; cost roll-up vs. targets.
- Check compliance (material declarations, restricted substances), safety, and IP/export control.
- Hold cross-functional design review and approve ECR/ECO for initial release.

6) Derive MBOM and map to manufacturing
- Collaborate with manufacturing engineering to map EBOM components to operations.
- Group or explode assemblies to match manufacturing sequence; create kits and phantoms as needed.
- Add non-design manufacturing items (consumables, packaging, labels, tooling) with operation-specific consumption and scrap factors.
- Create plant-specific MBOM variants and set effectivities.
- Link MBOM to routings/operations and preliminary work instructions.

7) Synchronize and release to ERP/MES
- Release item masters, EBOM, and MBOM through controlled workflow with sign-offs.
- Publish to ERP/MES with effectivity, planning parameters, and costing views.
- Trigger cost roll-ups and MRP readiness; validate integration logs and fix failures.

8) Create SBOM and service content
- Identify FRUs and define repair levels (board, module, component).
- Establish service kits, substitutes, supersession/interchangeability rules.
- Generate illustrated parts lists and service instructions; align with warranty policies.
- Release SBOM and service documentation to service systems/portals.

9) Manage configuration and variants
- Maintain 150% BOM rules and constraints; generate 100% configured BOM per order.
- Control software/firmware configuration items and compatibility matrices.
- Apply effectivity changes consistently across EBOM/MBOM/SBOM.

10) Execute change management
- Initiate ECR with problem statement; perform impact analysis across views and plants.
- Author ECO/MCO with updated items/BOMs, AML/AVL changes, and effectivity plans.
- Communicate changes to stakeholders; manage deviations/waivers and field retrofits if needed.

11) Govern data quality and obsolescence
- Monitor dashboards for attribute completeness, duplicates, orphaned items, and release SLA.
- Run periodic audits; cleanse and merge duplicates; retire obsolete items with supersession.
- Archive baselines and maintain digital thread traceability.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Released EBOMs, MBOMs (by plant), and SBOMs with baselines and effectivities.
- Item master records with complete attributes and linked design documents.
- AML/AVL and alternates/substitutes with approval status.
- Released drawings, specs, work instructions, and illustrated parts lists.
- Routings and operation mappings linked to MBOM.
- Configurable 150% BOM and variant rules; configured 100% BOMs for orders.
- Change records (ECR/ECO/MCO), deviations/waivers, and release notes.
- Compliance artifacts (CoCs, material declarations, IMDS/SCIP submissions).
- Product cost roll-ups and BOM costed views.

Success criteria
- BOMs are accurate, complete, released on time, and consumable by ERP/MES/Service without rework.
- Downstream execution sees minimal issues attributable to BOM/data (defects, line stops).
- Compliance and audit requirements are met; traceability is intact.
- Service readiness achieved with correct SBOM and parts availability.
- Cost and lead-time targets are supported by the released structures.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Product/Design Engineer: Define items, EBOM content, specs; resolve design issues; approve EBOM changes.
- CAD/ECAD Designer: Build CAD/ECAD assemblies and drawings; maintain associativity; manage reference designators.
- Manufacturing Engineer/Process Planner: Transform EBOM to MBOM; add manufacturing-only items; map to routings; author work instructions.
- Service Engineer: Define SBOM, FRUs, kits, repair levels; create service documentation and supersession rules.
- Sourcing/Procurement: Maintain AML/AVL; validate alternates; provide cost and lead-time data.
- Supplier Quality/Compliance: Validate supplier data, PPAP; ensure regulatory compliance and declarations.
- Master Data Specialist: Ensure attribute standards, description quality, classification, and data quality monitoring.
- PLM/PDM Administrator: Configure data model, workflows, access controls, integrations; manage baselines.
- ERP/MES Analyst: Ensure synchronization, data consumption, cost roll-ups, and planning parameters.
- Document Control: Manage releases, record retention, and audit trails.
- Program/Project Manager: Orchestrate timelines, cross-functional gates, and approvals.
- IT/Integration: Maintain interfaces, middleware, and error handling.

## Best Practices
- Establish a single source of truth in PLM; integrate CAD/ECAD and ERP/MES with automated validations.
- Use standardized part numbering and description dictionaries; classify all items for searchability and analytics.
- Build and maintain 150% BOM with rule-based configuration; generate 100% order-specific BOMs.
- Define clear effectivity (date/serial/plant) and use it consistently across EBOM/MBOM/SBOM.
- Govern alternates/substitutes and AML/AVL with engineering and quality approval; record interchangeability rules.
- Involve manufacturing, sourcing, quality, and service early; run joint DFM/DFA/Serviceability reviews.
- Capture non-physical items (software, licenses, adhesives, labels) in BOMs where they impact manufacturing or service.
- Keep EBOM and MBOM views separate but synchronized; avoid embedding process logic in EBOM.
- Automate data quality checks (attribute completeness, duplicates, UoM, reference designators).
- Manage obsolescence proactively; plan supersessions and last-time-buy with suppliers.
- Protect controlled data (ITAR/EAR, export controls) with role-based access and data segregation.

## Common Challenges
- Data duplication and poor descriptions: Mitigate with MDM governance, description rules, and deduplication tools.
- EBOM-to-MBOM misalignment: Use formal mapping with manufacturing involvement; maintain view separation and sync processes.
- Variant complexity and configuration errors: Adopt rule-based configuration, 150% BOMs, and automated validators.
- Integration failures to ERP/MES: Implement robust middleware, message monitoring, and error resolution playbooks.
- Supplier part changes and obsolescence: Maintain active AML/AVL monitoring, change notifications, and alternates.
- UoM and quantity errors: Standardize UoM; apply consumption per operation and validate conversions.
- Compliance gaps (RoHS/REACH, SCIP): Integrate compliance tools and require declarations at part onboarding.
- Late-stage changes causing line stops: Enforce gated reviews, ECO effectivity, and cut-in planning with buffers.
- Incomplete SBOM leading to service delays: Engage service engineering early; define FRUs and kits prior to launch.

## Performance Metrics
- BOM accuracy rate (% of BOMs with zero critical errors post-release).
- First-pass release yield (FPRY) for EBOM/MBOM/SBOM.
- ECO cycle time and average changes per product per phase.
- EBOM-to-MBOM sync lag (time from EBOM release to MBOM release).
- Attribute completeness rate (% items with all mandatory attributes).
- Duplicate item rate and time to resolution.
- Manufacturing disruptions due to BOM/data issues (incidents per 1,000 orders; line stops).
- Scrap/rework attributable to BOM errors (% of total).
- Cost variance vs. target at BOM roll-up.
- SBOM readiness lead time; service first-time-fix rate (FTF) and parts fill rate.
- Compliance coverage (% items with complete material declarations; audit findings).

## Technology and Tools
- PLM/PDM: Siemens Teamcenter, PTC Windchill, Dassault 3DEXPERIENCE/ENOVIA, Autodesk Vault/Fusion Manage, Arena PLM.
- CAD/ECAD: NX, Creo, CATIA, SolidWorks, Inventor; Altium Designer, Cadence Allegro/OrCAD, Mentor Xpedition.
- ERP: SAP S/4HANA, Oracle ERP Cloud/E-Business Suite, Microsoft Dynamics 365.
- MES/MOM: Siemens Opcenter, Rockwell FactoryTalk, Dassault DELMIA, SAP DM.
- Configuration/CPQ: SAP VC/AVC, Tacton, Configit, Oracle CPQ.
- MDM/Data Quality: Semarchy, Informatica, Ataccama; description builders and duplicate detection.
- Compliance: IMDS, SCIP tools, substance databases (IPC-1752), PLM compliance modules.
- Integration/Middleware: Mulesoft, Boomi, SAP PO/CPI, Kafka; API-based PLM-ERP connectors.
- Technical publishing: Service documentation and illustrated parts list tools; AR/VR work instruction platforms.
- Analytics/Dashboards: PLM and BI tools for data quality, change metrics, and release health.
