[8.7.3.1.3] Schedule change/release windows
Level: 5

Process Details:
## Overview
Schedule change/release windows is the structured process of defining, approving, reserving, and communicating time-bound windows for implementing planned changes and releases to IT services, infrastructure, and applications. Its purpose is to minimize business risk, avoid conflicts, ensure adequate staffing and resources, align with business cycles and SLAs, and maintain auditability and compliance. This process sits within IT service delivery control and coordinates cross-functional stakeholders (operations, development, security, business) to deliver predictable, low-risk change execution across environments (non-production and production).

Key outcomes include a single, authoritative enterprise change/release calendar; clear blackout and maintenance windows; coordinated resource plans; and timely stakeholder communications. It supports ITIL Change Enablement and Release Management while integrating with DevOps delivery cadences.

## Key Activities
- Maintain enterprise change/release calendars across environments and regions
- Define and manage maintenance windows, blackout periods, and freezes
- Intake and assess scheduling demand from change requests, release trains, vendor patches
- Validate readiness and lead-time criteria for candidate changes/releases
- Analyze dependency and conflict risk using CMDB/service maps
- Prioritize and bundle changes based on risk, impact, and business criticality
- Propose candidate windows and review with stakeholders (service owners, business reps, vendors)
- Obtain approvals via CAB/Release CAB and document exceptions
- Reserve and publish windows; update change tickets and communication plans
- Coordinate execution governance (start/stop checkpoints, bridge calls, staffing rosters)
- Monitor adherence during windows and manage deviations/escalations
- Perform post-window review and capture metrics, issues, and lessons learned
- Manage reschedules and cancellations with audit trails

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved or approvable change/release requests with scope, risk/impact, estimated duration, backout plan, validation plan, and affected CIs/services
- Release content and readiness status (test results, defect status)
- Service criticality and business priority, SLAs/OLAs, maintenance/outage tolerances
- Business calendars (financial close, product launches, peak seasons, holidays), global time zones
- Blackout/freeze policies, compliance windows (e.g., SOX, PCI DSS, HIPAA)
- CMDB/service dependency maps and environment availability
- Vendor-maintained schedules and contractual obligations
- Incident/problem trends that may inform moratoriums

Prerequisites:
- Defined Change Enablement and Release Management policies, including change types (standard/normal/emergency/major), risk scoring, lead times
- Governance bodies (CAB, eCAB, Release CAB) and charters
- Single source of truth for change calendar with access controls
- Communication channels and templates for stakeholder notifications
- Quality CMDB/service mapping coverage for in-scope services
- Defined maintenance windows and blackout criteria per service/platform
- Runbook standards and backout/rollback practices

Dependencies on other processes:
- Change Enablement (intake, risk assessment, approvals)
- Release and Deployment Management (build, test, deploy runbooks)
- Incident and Problem Management (moratoriums, post-change incident monitoring)
- Configuration Management (CMDB accuracy)
- Business Continuity/DR (freeze and risk acceptance)
- Vendor/Supplier Management (third-party schedules)
- Communications/Service Desk (customer-facing notices)

## Process Steps
1) Initiate scheduling cycle
- Set planning horizon and cadence (e.g., weekly ops scheduling, monthly production windows, quarterly major releases).
- Publish key dates, lead-time requirements, and submission cutoffs.

2) Collect and triage demand
- Pull candidate items from ITSM tool (change backlog), release trains, patch advisories, infrastructure maintenance needs, vendor notices.
- Categorize by environment, service, risk, expected downtime, and business priority.

3) Validate readiness and policy compliance
- Ensure minimum data set: scope, impact, risk score, duration, backout plan, validation plan, stakeholders, deployment runbook, test exit criteria (for releases).
- Verify lead times by change type and environment are met; assign provisional status if pending approvals.

4) Identify constraints and windows
- Apply maintenance windows, blackout periods, and moratoriums based on business calendars and compliance.
- Consider resource/staff availability, on-call coverage, timezone alignment, and capacity constraints (e.g., shared databases, network devices).

5) Analyze dependencies and conflicts
- Use CMDB/service maps to find overlapping CIs and upstream/downstream dependencies.
- Detect conflicts (same CI, same service chain, shared change windows, or incompatible changes).
- Assess blast radius and required separation between high-risk changes.

6) Propose candidate windows
- Define start/end times, environment, affected services, expected downtime or no-downtime approach, monitoring and validation checkpoints.
- Bundle compatible low-risk changes to optimize window utilization; isolate high-risk changes.

7) Stakeholder review and prioritization
- Review proposed windows with service/application owners, product/business reps, security, vendors, and operations.
- Resolve conflicts; apply prioritization rules (e.g., business criticality, regulatory deadlines, risk).

8) Approvals and exceptions
- Present schedule to CAB/Release CAB for decision; handle emergency/urgent items via eCAB with documented risk acceptance.
- Record approvals, conditions, and any exception to policy (e.g., freeze breach).

9) Reserve and publish
- Block the approved window in the enterprise change calendar; link all covered change tickets.
- Update each change with the window details, bridge coordinates, and staffing plan.
- Trigger downstream communications workflow for customer/internal notifications.

10) Pre-window readiness checkpoint (T-48 to T-4 hours)
- Confirm all pre-implementation checks complete: backups, backout rehearsals, change freeze list, runbooks validated, monitoring/alerts configured, maintenance page prepared, support rosters confirmed.
- Reassess risk if new incidents/problems emerged; defer if not ready.

11) Execute window governance
- Open bridge call; confirm go/no-go with stakeholders at window start.
- Enforce execution timeline, hold points, validation criteria; log deviations.
- Coordinate communication updates and status postings; invoke eCAB if scope or risk changes.

12) Close and validate
- Complete post-change validation and service health checks; confirm SLOs stable.
- Declare window closed; update change records with outcomes (success, partial, backout), durations, and any incidents.

13) Post-window review and continuous improvement
- Capture lessons learned, root causes for failures/delays, schedule conflicts found late, and improvement actions.
- Update calendars, policies, and dependency data as needed; publish metrics.

14) Manage reschedules/cancellations
- Follow formal reschedule workflow with justification, updated risk assessment, stakeholder re-approval, and revised communications.
- Maintain audit trail for compliance.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Enterprise change/release calendar with approved windows across environments and regions
- Published maintenance/blackout schedule and freeze periods
- Window reservation records linked to change/release tickets
- Stakeholder notifications and customer-facing advisories (planned maintenance notices)
- Execution governance artifacts: bridge logs, runbook version references, staffing rosters
- Approval and exception logs (CAB/eCAB decisions, risk acceptances)
- Post-window reports and metrics (success rate, incidents, delays, utilization)
Success criteria:
- No unplanned conflicts or policy breaches (e.g., blackout violations)
- On-time start/finish rates > target; adherence to lead times
- High change success rate with minimal change-induced incidents
- Stakeholder satisfaction for predictability and communication
- Audit-ready records of approvals, communications, and outcomes

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Change Manager: Owns scheduling process, policy enforcement, conflict resolution, CAB facilitation, calendar integrity, metrics reporting.
- Release Manager: Coordinates release content readiness, bundles releases, aligns pipelines to windows, leads release CAB.
- Service/Application Owners: Provide business impact, critical dates, maintenance windows; approve timing; ensure runbooks/validation.
- Platform/Infrastructure Owners (DB, Network, Cloud, OS): Provide platform constraints and windows; staff operations support; confirm capacity and backout.
- DevOps/Engineering Leads: Estimate duration, risk; prepare deployment automation; staff on-call; execute during windows.
- Information Security: Reviews security-impacting changes; validates patch urgency and compliance windows; approves exceptions.
- CAB/eCAB Members: Review and approve schedules; adjudicate conflicts; accept or reject freeze exceptions.
- Service Desk/Communications: Prepare and send notifications; update status pages and service portals; route inquiries.
- Incident Manager/On-Call Commander: Oversees incident response during windows; manages bridge if issues arise; coordinates rollback decisions.
- Vendor/Supplier Managers: Align third-party schedules; confirm SLAs and support availability.
- Business Relationship Manager/Product Owner: Represents business priorities and customer impact; signs off on timing for critical services.
- Configuration Manager: Ensures CMDB/service mapping accuracy to support conflict analysis.

## Best Practices
- Maintain a single authoritative enterprise change calendar integrated with ITSM and collaboration tools.
- Define clear blackout/freeze policies tied to business events; establish exception criteria and approval workflow.
- Enforce lead times by change type and environment; gate scheduling on readiness checks.
- Use risk-based scheduling: do not stack high-risk changes; separate dependent/high-impact items.
- Leverage CMDB/service mapping and automated conflict detection; continuously improve data quality.
- Align global windows with customer time zones; avoid regional peak hours; consider follow-the-sun staffing.
- Standardize deployment and validation runbooks; practice rollback/backout and rehearse major changes.
- Automate where possible (CI/CD, orchestration, approvals), but retain governance checkpoints for high-risk items.
- Employ progressive delivery (canary, blue/green, feature flags) to reduce downtime and risk.
- Instrument robust observability and synthetic checks for rapid post-change validation.
- Use templated communications and minimum notification timelines; provide clear customer impact statements.
- Conduct post-window reviews and feed findings into problem management and scheduling policy updates.

## Common Challenges
- Conflicting changes on shared components due to incomplete dependency data
  - Mitigation: Improve service mapping, require CI associations, add automated conflict checks.
- Late submissions or missing readiness artifacts
  - Mitigation: Enforce lead times with automated gate checks; reject or defer non-compliant requests.
- Vendor schedule misalignment or limited support availability
  - Mitigation: Early engagement with vendors; contractual SLAs for critical windows; contingency planning.
- Business event clashes and poorly understood blackout needs
  - Mitigation: Maintain up-to-date business calendars; quarterly alignment meetings with business owners.
- Timezone complexity and global stakeholder coordination
  - Mitigation: Regional windows; mirrored maintenance cycles; recorded briefings and clear handoffs.
- Change fatigue or too-frequent windows impacting user trust
  - Mitigation: Bundle low-risk changes; adopt progressive delivery; rationalize cadence by service criticality.
- Approval bottlenecks in CAB
  - Mitigation: Risk-based delegation; pre-approved standard changes; asynchronous approvals where appropriate.
- Inadequate observability leading to delayed detection of post-change issues
  - Mitigation: Mandatory health checks, SLO-based validation, synthetic tests as exit criteria.

## Performance Metrics
- Change success rate within scheduled windows (% without incident/backout)
- Change-induced incident rate (within 24/48 hours of window)
- On-time start/finish compliance (% of windows)
- Lead-time compliance (% changes meeting required submission lead times)
- Scheduling cycle time (request-to-window assignment)
- Conflict rate and late-stage conflict detection (pre- vs day-of detection)
- Window utilization (% scheduled capacity used; # of bundled changes per low-risk window)
- Reschedule/cancellation rate and reasons
- Blackout/freeze exceptions count and justification quality
- Stakeholder/customer satisfaction (post-window surveys)
- Mean time to recover (MTTR) for failed changes and rollback effectiveness

## Technology and Tools
- ITSM and Change Calendar: ServiceNow (Change, Change Calendar), Jira Service Management, BMC Helix/Remedy, Cherwell
- CMDB and Service Mapping: ServiceNow CMDB/Service Mapping, Device42, vRealize; application dependency mapping (e.g., Dynatrace, AppDynamics)
- Release/Deployment Orchestration: Azure DevOps, GitLab CI/CD, Jenkins, Spinnaker, Argo CD, Octopus Deploy, Ansible, Terraform
- Observability and Validation: Datadog, New Relic, Splunk, Prometheus/Grafana, synthetic monitoring (Catchpoint, Pingdom)
- Communication/Status: Atlassian Statuspage, Microsoft Teams/Slack/Zoom, PagerDuty/Opsgenie, email/SMS gateways
- Governance and Approvals: Built-in ITSM workflows, electronic approvals, risk scoring engines
- Feature Management: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagger
- Scheduling/Calendars: Integrated enterprise calendar; timezone coordination tools
- Runbook Automation: Rundeck, StackStorm; documentation in Confluence/Wiki
- GRC/Compliance: RSA Archer, MetricStream for policy, exceptions, and audit records
- AIOps/Conflict Detection: Tools that correlate changes to service health and detect window conflicts

[8.7.3.1.5] Balance operational workloads across available infrastructure components
Level: 5

Process Details:
## Overview
[8.7.3.1.5] Balance operational workloads across available infrastructure components is the process of continuously distributing and tuning workload execution across compute, storage, network, database, middleware, and cloud resources so that no component is persistently over- or under-utilized. The goal is to sustain service levels (SLAs/SLOs), optimize cost, protect resiliency and performance, and reduce operational risk by avoiding hotspots, bottlenecks, and stranded capacity.

This process sits within Plan operational activities for IT service delivery and executes through policy-driven, automated mechanisms with human oversight. It applies to hybrid environments (on-premises, private cloud, public cloud, edge) and across real-time/transactional, batch, and event-driven workloads.

Primary value:
- Performance and reliability: Prevents saturation and contention, reduces incidents.
- Cost efficiency: Rightsizes resources, scales elastically, reduces idle and waste.
- Resilience and continuity: Ensures capacity buffers, isolates blast radius, supports failover.
- Governance: Enforces placement, compliance, data residency, and license/policy constraints.

## Key Activities
- Define balancing policies and thresholds: Target utilization ranges, scaling rules, constraints (affinity/anti-affinity, data residency), and priorities by service tier.
- Monitor and analyze workload and infrastructure utilization: Real-time metrics, queue depths, throughput, latency, error rates, saturation indicators.
- Forecast demand: Short-term (intra-day) and medium-term (weekly/monthly) predictions using historical patterns, seasonality, and business calendars.
- Identify hotspots and stranded capacity: Detect components outside target ranges or violating SLOs.
- Plan rebalancing actions: Scale out/in, migrate, reschedule, throttle, cache, or shard; evaluate risks and change requirements.
- Execute rebalancing: Apply changes via orchestrators, schedulers, load balancers, auto-scaling, and job control systems.
- Validate and iterate: Post-change verification, rollback if needed, tune policies and automation.
- Communicate and document: Notify stakeholders, update CMDB/topology, record changes, and lessons learned.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Current utilization and performance telemetry: CPU, memory, I/O, network, storage latency/IOPS, DB wait events, queue depth, request latency/error rates.
- Workload profiles and SLOs: Criticality/tier, performance targets, concurrency, burst characteristics, business calendars.
- Infrastructure inventory and topology (CMDB): Components, capacities, dependencies, redundancy models, regions/AZs, network paths.
- Policies and constraints: Security zones, data residency/compliance, licensing restrictions, placement rules (affinity/anti-affinity), HA/DR requirements.
- Forecasts and limits: Demand forecasts, cloud quotas, reserved/committed capacity, budget guardrails.
- Change schedule and maintenance windows: Planned outages, release windows, blackouts.
- Runbooks/automation scripts: Approved procedures for scaling, migration, throttling, and rollback.

Prerequisites:
- Instrumentation and observability are in place and trustworthy.
- CMDB/topology and tagging are accurate to at least 90–95%.
- Baseline policies and utilization targets are defined (e.g., steady-state 50–70% utilization for compute, <60% storage capacity, network links <50% sustained).
- Access and automation credentials are secured and approved.
- Standard changes for routine rebalancing are pre-approved where possible.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Capacity and Performance Management (plan capacity, set targets).
- Service Level Management (SLA/SLO definitions).
- Configuration Management (CMDB accuracy).
- Change Enablement (approvals, risk assessment).
- Incident/Problem Management (triggered by capacity-related incidents; root cause).
- Release and Deployment (coordination with releases affecting load).
- Information Security and Compliance (placement and residency constraints).
- Financial/Cost Management (budgets, FinOps policies).

## Process Steps
1. Trigger and scope
   - Triggers: Scheduled cadence (e.g., hourly automated, daily review), threshold breaches, forecasted spikes, change events, incidents/problems, or seasonal/business events.
   - Define scope: Environments, services, regions, components to consider.

2. Collect and validate data
   - Pull real-time and trailing metrics from monitoring/APM and logs.
   - Retrieve CMDB/topology, deployment manifests, tag-based ownership.
   - Validate data completeness and timeliness; flag instrumentation gaps.

3. Assess current state
   - Identify components above/below target utilization or with degrading SLOs.
   - Map hotspots to upstream/downstream dependencies to avoid false positives.
   - Identify stranded capacity (underused nodes, storage tiers, links).

4. Forecast near-term demand
   - Predict next 24 hours/7 days using historical patterns, release plans, and business calendars (e.g., payroll, campaigns).
   - Consider DR/HA posture (active-active vs. active-passive requirements).

5. Apply policy and constraints
   - Enforce security, compliance, data residency, licensing, and affinity rules.
   - Respect change windows, maintenance plans, and freeze periods.
   - Confirm budget/quota headroom and reservation commitments.

6. Formulate rebalancing plan
   - Options include:
     - Traffic distribution: Adjust weights in load balancers, DNS/GSLB, service mesh.
     - Scale: Horizontal/vertical scale, HPA/VPA, cluster autoscaler, VMSS, ASGs.
     - Placement/migration: Reschedule pods/VMs, storage tiering, DB read replicas.
     - Scheduling/time-shifting: Move batch/ETL/reporting to off-peak windows.
     - Isolation: QoS/priorities, resource quotas, cgroups, DB resource governance.
     - Demand shaping: Rate limiting, backpressure, caching, feature flags.
   - Define expected impact, risks, and success criteria (target utilization and SLOs).

7. Determine change path and approvals
   - Classify as standard, normal, or emergency change based on risk.
   - Obtain approvals via Change Enablement; include rollback plan and test plan.

8. Prepare execution
   - Update automation/runbooks with parameters.
   - Pre-stage capacity where required (e.g., warm pools, pre-warmed containers, reserved nodes).
   - Communicate window and impact to stakeholders and NOC.

9. Execute rebalancing
   - Use orchestrators for deterministic steps; prefer canary/gradual shifts.
   - Sequence actions to minimize blast radius (e.g., one AZ/cluster at a time).
   - Monitor live metrics; pause if anomalies exceed thresholds.

10. Validate outcomes
    - Compare post-change metrics to success criteria over an observation window.
    - Functional checks: synthetic transactions, health checks, user journeys.
    - Rollback if criteria unmet; capture diagnostics.

11. Optimize and rightsize
    - Commit to smaller instance types, rightsized containers, storage tiers.
    - Decommission or hibernate idle capacity; update reservations/commitments.

12. Update records and communicate
    - Update CMDB, scaling policies, diagrams, and dashboards.
    - Record changes, results, and residual risks; notify stakeholders.

13. Continuous improvement
    - Review automation efficacy, false positives, and policy thresholds.
    - Feed learnings into capacity planning, SLO tuning, and runbook updates.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Balanced utilization across components within defined target ranges.
- Updated scaling and placement policies; scheduled batch windows.
- Executed change records with implementation and validation notes.

Deliverables:
- Rebalancing plan and risk assessment.
- Post-change validation report and before/after metrics.
- Updated CMDB/topology, dashboards, and runbooks.
- Exception log for constraints preventing optimal balance.

Success criteria:
- No SLA/SLO breaches attributable to resource contention during the period.
- Percentage of components within target utilization (e.g., >90% of nodes).
- Reduction in capacity-related incidents and paging.
- Measurable cost optimization (e.g., idle spend reduced, rightsizing savings).

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Service Delivery Manager: Owns process, prioritizes services, communicates outcomes.
- Capacity/Performance Manager: Defines targets, analyzes trends, forecasts, tunes policies.
- Site Reliability Engineer/Platform Engineer: Designs automation, implements orchestration, validates performance.
- Infrastructure Engineers (Compute/Storage/Network): Execute changes for their domains, ensure resilience and compliance.
- Cloud Engineers/FinOps: Manage quotas, reservations/commitments, cost guardrails; advise on right-sizing and pricing models.

- Vendor/MSP Partners (as applicable): Provide tool expertise, execute managed changes, support SLAs.

## Best Practices
- Policy- and intent-driven automation: Encode placement, scaling, and QoS as code; minimize manual decisions.
- SLO- and error-budget-driven actions: Prioritize critical workloads; use error budgets to guide throttling or deferral.
- Keep safe headroom: Maintain N+1 (or policy-defined) capacity; avoid >70% sustained utilization for shared compute.
- Multi-dimensional balancing: Consider CPU, memory, storage latency, IOPS, network throughput, license constraints, and IO amplification.
- Gradual shifts and canaries: Adjust traffic or placement incrementally; validate at each step.
- Separate noisy neighbors: Use resource quotas, namespaces, cgroups, and DB resource governance to prevent contention.
- Time-shift non-urgent work: Schedule batch/ETL/reporting for off-peak windows; align with business calendars.
- Test failover and scaling: Regularly exercise autoscaling, evacuation, and region/AZ failover; practice game days.
- Align with FinOps: Rightsize, use reservations/commitments, exploit spot/preemptible for non-critical/batch, enforce decommissioning.
- Maintain accurate CMDB and tagging: Ownership, environment, tier, cost center, data classification.
- Security and compliance baked in: Enforce data residency, segmentation, and license/logging constraints in placement policies.
- Observability first: Golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation), SLOs, topology-aware dashboards, and anomaly detection.

## Common Challenges
- Unpredictable spikes/flash crowds: Use rapid autoscaling, pre-warming, CDNs/caching, and feature flag rate limiting.
- Noisy neighbor effects: Apply quotas, isolation, and anti-affinity; consider dedicated nodes/pools for critical workloads.
- Hidden dependencies and data gravity: Maintain accurate dependency maps; co-locate data and compute; use read replicas/CDNs.
- Cloud service limits/quotas: Monitor quotas proactively; request increases early; diversify across AZs/regions.
- Legacy/monoliths and license constraints: Plan controlled vertical scaling, ensure license-aware placement, consider modernization roadmap.
- Misconfigured autoscaling: Validate metrics, cooldowns, and target utilization; test under load; avoid oscillation.
- Monitoring gaps or stale CMDB: Implement data quality checks, automated discovery, and ownership accountability.
- Change control delays: Pre-approve standard playbooks; automate low-risk changes with guardrails.
- Cost overruns due to conservative buffers: Use dynamic headroom based on patterns; leverage reservations and burstable classes.

- Utilization balance
  - % components within target utilization bands (compute, storage, network).
  - Variance of utilization across nodes/clusters/links.
- Service health
  - SLO attainment (availability, latency).
  - Error rate, queue wait times, throughput.
- Efficiency and cost

- Operational performance

  - Number of capacity-related incidents and change failure rate.
- Forecasting and planning
  - Forecast accuracy (MAPE) for demand and capacity.
  - Quota headroom adherence and breach count.

Process Details:
## Overview
Determine interest rate exposure for all markets is the process of identifying, quantifying, and aggregating the organization’s sensitivity to changes in interest rates across currencies, geographies, legal entities, business lines, and products. It captures both near-term cash flow impacts and long-term value impacts arising from fixed and floating rate assets and liabilities, forecasted transactions, and derivative positions.

Purpose:
- Provide a complete, accurate view of the firm’s exposure to interest rate movements (e.g., parallel shifts, twists, basis changes).
- Enable informed hedging decisions and adherence to risk appetite/limits.
- Support liquidity and funding strategies, pricing decisions, and performance management.
- Feed downstream processes such as hedge execution, hedge accounting, and regulatory reporting (e.g., IRRBB for banks).

Role in the organization:
- Core component of Treasury and Market Risk functions that underpins hedging strategy and capital preservation.
- Integrates data from Finance, FP&A, ALM, Trading, and Operations to form a unified risk picture.
- Provides management and the Risk Committee with timely analytics and reports to steer risk-taking and hedging.

## Key Activities
- Define scope and measurement assumptions (valuation date/time, markets/currencies, portfolios in scope).
- Ingest and validate positions and cash flows (assets, liabilities, leases, securities, debt, intercompany, derivatives).
- Obtain and validate market data (yield curves, forward curves, basis curves, calendars, vol surfaces for optionality).
- Generate cash flow schedules and repricing profiles per instrument.
- Calculate sensitivities and exposures (DV01/PV01, duration/convexity, earnings-at-risk, EVE).
- Identify basis risk, curve risk, optionality and prepayment risk, and cross-currency rate exposure.
- Aggregate and net exposures by currency, curve, tenor buckets, entity, and book (banking vs trading, if applicable).
- Perform scenario and stress testing (parallel shifts, twists, historical/idiosyncratic scenarios).
- Reconcile totals to source systems/GL and perform controls; resolve exceptions.
- Produce reports/dashboards and recommend hedging actions; obtain approvals.
- Archive results and maintain audit trail; capture learnings for process improvement.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Position and cash flow data:
  - Debt schedules (bank loans, bonds, notes, leases).
  - Investment/securities holdings (fixed income, MMF, deposits).
  - Derivatives (IRS, caps/floors, swaptions, futures, FRAs, cross-currency swaps).
  - Banking/ALM books (loans/deposits, mortgages, customer products).
  - Forecasted transactions (issuances, deposits, project finance drawdowns) and rolling cash forecasts.
- Market data:
  - Discounting and projection curves per currency (e.g., SOFR, SONIA, €STR).
  - Basis curves (e.g., OIS vs term, 1m vs 3m).
  - Historical rates and scenario libraries.
  - Day-count conventions, business calendars/holidays.
- Reference data:
  - Product taxonomy, curve mappings, pricing conventions.
  - Legal entity hierarchies, books/portfolios, counterparty and collateral terms (CSA).
- Policies and limits:
  - Risk appetite, tenor bucket definitions, stress scenarios, model and method standards.
  - Hedge accounting designations (if applicable).

Prerequisites:
- Approved methodologies for valuation and sensitivity (e.g., OIS discounting, duration/DV01, EaR/EVE).
- Data quality controls and reconciliations in place (completeness, accuracy, timeliness thresholds).
- Segregation of duties between front office, risk, and operations.
- Access to required systems and market data entitlements.
- Defined reporting calendar and cut-off times.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 9.7.x Capture and maintain treasury positions and confirm trades.
- 9.7.x Maintain market data and curves.
- 9.7.5.1 Define interest rate risk policy, risk appetite, and limits.
- 9.x Cash and liquidity forecasting (for forecasted exposures).
- 9.7.5.3 Execute hedging transactions (downstream).
- Accounting close and reconciliation processes; hedge accounting processes.
- Model governance and validation.

## Process Steps
1. Plan and define scope
   - Set valuation timestamp, business day calendar, and markets/currencies in scope.
   - Confirm portfolios/books, legal entities, and product sets to include.
   - Confirm methods and scenarios to be used per policy.

2. Acquire market data
   - Pull current discount and projection curves, basis curves, and vol surfaces (for options).
   - Validate freshness, completeness, and curve construction checks (monotonicity, arbitrage tests).
   - Log market data version and timestamps for audit.

3. Gather positions and forecasts
   - Extract positions from TMS/ALM/trade capture systems and GL bridges.
   - Load forecasted cash flows from FP&A and pipeline systems (e.g., expected debt issuance).
   - Include collateral terms (CSA) to determine discounting curves.

4. Standardize and validate data
   - Map products to standardized taxonomy and curve conventions (index, day count, reset freq, spreads).
   - Normalize fields (currency, notional, rates, maturities, next reset dates).
   - Run data quality checks: missing fields, duplicates, stale records, and reconcile totals to prior run and GL/trial balance.

5. Generate cash flow and repricing profiles
   - Create cash flow schedules for each instrument, considering amortization, prepayments (if modeled), caps/floors, call features.
   - For floating-rate items, compute next reset, index, spread, and cash flow sensitivities to index vs spread.
   - For structured products, model expected behavior or use option-adjusted frameworks as per policy.

6. Calculate exposure metrics
   - Compute DV01/PV01 and duration/convexity per instrument and aggregated.
   - Separate:
     - Cash flow exposure (impact on interest income/expense: Earnings-at-Risk).
     - Economic value exposure (present value sensitivity: EVE/PV01).
   - For options: delta, gamma, vega; for caps/floors, rate floor impacts under low-rate regimes.
   - Identify basis exposures (e.g., SOFR vs term SOFR, 1m vs 3m) and cross-currency rate legs.

7. Bucket and aggregate exposures
   - Aggregate by: currency, curve/index, tenor buckets (e.g., 0–1m, 1–3m, 3–6m, 6–12m, 1–2y, 2–5y, 5–10y, 10y+), legal entity, business unit, product, and book.
   - Distinguish structural exposures vs trading/hedged exposures; compute net and gross measures.
   - Apply netting rules consistent with legal and accounting constraints.

8. Scenario analysis and stress testing
   - Run standardized shocks: ±100/200 bps, steepening/flattening, localized market stresses.
   - Run historical episodes (e.g., rapid hiking cycles, flight-to-quality).
   - Assess basis shocks and negative rate floors if relevant.
   - Document P&L/EaR/EVE impacts and key drivers.

9. Controls, reconciliations, and signoffs
   - Reconcile position counts and notionals to source systems; resolve breaks.
   - Validate exposure changes vs prior period with attribution (new trades, run-off, market moves).
   - Review against risk limits; flag breaches and near-breaches; propose mitigations.
   - Obtain risk and treasury signoffs per RACI.

10. Reporting and communication
    - Produce management dashboards and detailed reports: DV01 by currency/tenor, gap reports, scenario results, exceptions, commentary.
    - Highlight concentrations, sensitivities to key indices, and hedge recommendations.
    - Distribute to Treasury, Risk Committee, CFO/ALCO, and relevant BU heads.

11. Feed downstream processes
    - Provide hedging requirements to execution desk (target DV01 by bucket/currency, instruments to consider).
    - Provide data sets to hedge accounting and performance measurement teams.

12. Archive and continuous improvement
    - Store datasets, reports, market data versions, and approvals in the risk repository.
    - Log issues and actions; update models/assumptions and reference data mappings as needed.

## Outputs and Deliverables
Expected outputs:
- Exposure metrics: DV01/PV01, duration/convexity by currency/tenor/entity/product.
- Gap/repricing reports: time-bucketed reprice gaps; structural vs tactical exposure.
- Scenario results: EaR/EVE impacts under standard and bespoke scenarios.
- Basis and optionality exposure summaries.
- Exception logs, reconciliation reports, and limit monitoring outcomes.

Deliverables:
- Management report and dashboard pack with commentary and trend analysis.
- Hedging requirements summary for execution (target exposures, preferred instruments, timing).
- Data extracts for accounting, regulatory, and audit stakeholders.
- Audit trail: data lineage, assumptions, market data versions, approvals.

Success criteria:
- Completeness and accuracy within defined tolerances; reconciled to GL/position systems.
- Delivered within SLA timelines; exposures aligned with risk policy.
- Actionable outputs enabling hedging decisions; no unresolved critical exceptions.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Treasury/Market Risk Analyst: Perform data ingestion, calculations, aggregation, and reporting; run scenarios; investigate exceptions.
- Treasury Risk Manager/ALM Manager: Own methodology, review results, ensure compliance with limits, approve outputs, propose hedging strategies.
- Front Office (Rates/FX Desk): Consume exposure outputs to plan and execute hedges.
- Treasury Operations: Ensure trade capture integrity, confirmations, data quality; support reconciliations.
- Market Data Manager: Curate and publish curves; conduct independent price verification; manage entitlements.
- FP&A: Provide forecasted transactions and interest expense/income projections.
- Finance/Accounting (including Hedge Accounting Specialist): Reconcile to GL; assess hedge accounting implications; support valuation controls.
- IT Risk Systems/Data Engineering: Maintain risk engines, integration pipelines, data stores, access controls, and performance SLAs.
- Model Risk/Validation: Review and approve models and assumptions; periodic backtesting.
- Compliance/Internal Audit: Test controls, segregation of duties, and documentation.

## Best Practices
- Use OIS discounting and multi-curve frameworks consistent with collateral terms (CSA) and market standards.
- Standardize tenor buckets, curve naming, and product mappings across systems.
- Implement robust data quality rules and automated reconciliations with clear break resolution workflows.
- Separate cash flow risk (EaR) and value risk (EVE/PV01); measure both regularly.
- Capture basis risk explicitly (index vs funding bases; 1m/3m/6m curves; OIS vs term).
- Model optionality appropriately (caps/floors, prepayments) with documented assumptions; use option-adjusted measures when material.
- Maintain a scenario library that includes parallel and non-parallel shocks, historical crises, and idiosyncratic local market stresses.
- Ensure segregation of duties and independent price verification for market data and valuations.
- Automate end-to-end pipelines (ETL, calculations, reports) with versioning and audit trails; minimize manual adjustments.
- Align exposure measurements with hedge accounting strategies to avoid P&L volatility mismatches.
- Regularly backtest exposure estimates against realized sensitivities and update models accordingly.
- Address benchmark rate transitions and fallback language (e.g., from IBOR to RFRs) with clear mappings and spread adjustments.

## Common Challenges
- Data fragmentation and quality issues across multiple systems
  - Solution: Centralize via data lake/warehouse; enforce standardized schemas and validation rules; implement stewardship.
- Stale or inconsistent curves and conventions
  - Solution: Single source of truth for curves; IPV; enforce curve construction standards and calendars.
- Modeling optionality and behavioral assumptions (e.g., prepayments, early redemptions)
  - Solution: Calibrate models with historical data; sensitivity testing; governance and periodic validation.
- Basis risk underappreciated or unmeasured
  - Solution: Measure and report basis DV01 separately; include basis scenarios; align hedges to index mix.
- Negative rates and floors
  - Solution: Explicitly model floors and convexity effects; ensure systems support negative rates.
- Cross-currency exposures intertwined with rate risk
  - Solution: Separate pure rate vs FX basis components; use cross-currency risk decomposition.
- Forecast uncertainty for planned issuances/transactions
  - Solution: Use scenario ranges and confidence weights; link to FP&A updates; track forecast error.
- Reconciliation and auditability gaps
  - Solution: Implement end-to-end lineage, control checklists, sign-offs, and retention policies.
- Performance and timeliness in large portfolios
  - Solution: Scalable compute (grid/cloud), incremental processing, caching of static schedules, parallelization.

## Performance Metrics
- Timeliness: Cycle time from market close/cut-off to final report (e.g., T+0 by 10:00).
- Coverage: Percentage of positions and forecasted exposures included vs total eligible (>99%).
- Data quality: Exception rate per run; number of unresolved critical data issues.
- Reconciliation accuracy: Difference between exposure position totals and GL/source systems (<0.5% threshold).
- Exposure stability/attribution: Portion explained by known drivers (new trades, market moves) vs unexplained.
- Limit management: Number and severity of limit breaches; time to remediate.
- Backtesting accuracy: Variance between predicted and realized P&L/EaR under small rate moves.
- Manual touchpoints: Count of manual overrides; trend over time.
- Stakeholder satisfaction: Survey score on usefulness and clarity of reports.
- System performance: Job runtimes, failure rates, and SLA adherence.

## Technology and Tools
- Treasury and risk systems: Murex, Adenza/Calypso, Bloomberg MARS, MSCI RiskMetrics, QRM, Moody’s ALM, SAP TRM, Kyriba.
- Market data: Bloomberg, Refinitiv, ICE; internal curve libraries and IPV tools.
- Data integration and storage: ETL/ELT tools, data lakes/warehouses (e.g., Snowflake, BigQuery), APIs, message buses (Kafka).
- Calculation engines: In-house or vendor risk engines supporting multi-curve, scenario, and sensitivity analytics; scalable compute (cloud/grid).
- BI and reporting: Power BI, Tableau, embedded dashboards; workflow/orchestration (Airflow, Control-M).
- Governance and controls: Metadata and lineage tools, access management (RBAC), audit logging, document repositories.
- DevOps/MLOps for models: Version control (Git), CI/CD for analytics, model catalog/validation tooling.

# [9.7.5.2.3] Determine interest rate hedge requirements in accordance with risk policy

## Overview
This process defines and quantifies the organization’s interest rate hedge requirements to align exposure to changes in interest rates with the approved risk policy. It translates risk appetite, limits, and hedging principles into actionable hedge targets (e.g., hedge ratios, notional amounts, tenors, and instrument types) for execution by the treasury front office.

Purpose:
- Protect forecast cash flows, earnings, and balance sheet values from adverse interest rate movements.
- Align the portfolio’s interest rate profile (duration, DV01/PV01, EaR/CfVaR) with policy-defined targets and limits.
- Select cost-effective and accounting-compliant hedge strategies (e.g., swaps, futures, options) that meet liquidity and counterparty constraints.

Role in the organization:
- Central to treasury’s asset-liability management and liquidity optimization.
- Provides a controlled, auditable bridge from risk measurement to trade execution.
- Informs budgeting, financial planning, and compliance with accounting standards.

## Key Activities
- Consolidate interest rate–sensitive exposures (debt, investments, leases, cash balances, forecast issuances/placements).
- Measure risk using standardized metrics (DV01, duration gap, Earnings-at-Risk, Cashflow-at-Risk, Value-at-Risk).
- Map exposures into time buckets and benchmark curves (e.g., SOFR, Treasury, swap curves).
- Define hedging objectives (cash flow vs. fair value hedges) based on policy and accounting implications.
- Run scenarios and stress tests to assess resilience and confirm hedging need.
- Determine hedge amounts, tenor distribution, and instrument mix to achieve policy targets.
- Validate compliance with policy limits, counterparty constraints, collateral/liquidity capacity, and hedge accounting eligibility.
- Prepare and obtain approval for a Hedge Requirements Memo and trade mandates.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved Treasury Risk Policy: risk appetite, hedge objectives, allowable instruments, limits by tenor and hedge ratio bands, approvals.
- Exposure inventory: current and forecast interest rate–sensitive items (variable/fixed-rate debt, planned issuances, investments, leases, cash balances).
- Market data: curves (risk-free, swap), basis curves, vol surfaces (caps/floors/swaptions), historical data for backtesting.
- Current hedge portfolio: outstanding derivatives, their sensitivities, maturities, designations.
- Constraints: counterparty credit limits, collateral/CSA terms, liquidity buffers, budget for hedging costs.
- Accounting and tax requirements: hedge accounting eligibility criteria (IFRS 9/ASC 815), documentation templates, desired P&L/OCI impacts.
- Systems and models: TMS, risk engine, valuation libraries, data quality validation reports.

Prerequisites:
- Up-to-date, approved risk policy and hedge governance framework.
- Accurate exposure forecasts and reconciled balances.
- Validated market data in production systems.
- Segregation of duties in place (front, middle, back office).
- Defined approval matrix and delegated authorities.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 9.7.5.2.1 Identify and measure interest rate exposure.
- 9.7.5.2.2 Assess interest rate risk against policy (limits, metrics).
- 9.7.5.2.4 Execute interest rate hedges (downstream).
- 9.7.x Manage counterparty risk and collateral.
- 9.7.x Hedge accounting and reporting setup.
- 9.1 Planning and forecasting (cash flow, debt plans).

## Process Steps
1. Trigger and scope
   - Initiate on periodic cycle (e.g., monthly/quarterly) or on trigger events: large rate moves, issuance/refinancing, policy changes, breaches.
   - Confirm scope (entities, currencies, books), hedge horizon, and reporting date.

2. Consolidate exposures and data
   - Aggregate interest rate–sensitive items into a standardized exposure file.
   - Map each item to benchmark curves, reset frequencies, and time buckets.
   - Validate data completeness and reconcile to GL/position systems.

3. Measure current risk position
   - Compute DV01/PV01, duration gap, EaR/CfVaR/MVaR, and sensitivity by tenor bucket (e.g., 0–6m, 6–12m, 1–3y, 3–5y, 5–10y).
   - Attribute risk by source (debt vs. investments vs. existing hedges).

4. Align with policy targets
   - Retrieve policy hedge ratios/bands per tenor (e.g., 50–80% next 12 months, 30–60% 1–3 years).
   - Confirm eligible instruments, counterparty and netting constraints, maximum optionality usage, and duration targets.

5. Define hedging objective(s)
   - Determine for each exposure whether the objective is cash flow stabilization (cash flow hedge) or fair value stabilization (fair value hedge).
   - Consider hedge accounting preferences and feasibility.

6. Scenario and stress testing
   - Apply parallel shifts, twists, and volatility shocks to evaluate downside risk and test the sufficiency of current hedges.
   - Identify buckets where limits or risk appetite are breached or close to breach.

7. Determine hedge requirement by bucket
   - Calculate incremental hedge DV01 or notional required per tenor to reach target ranges while avoiding over-hedging.
   - Consider layering (staggered) approach to reduce timing risk and roll risk.

8. Select instrument strategy
   - Evaluate swaps, futures, FRAs, caps/floors/collars, and swaptions against:
     - Cost (carry, premium), liquidity, accounting treatment, operational complexity, and basis risk.
   - Propose instrument mix and tenors to meet the required hedge DV01 by bucket.

9. Check constraints and feasibility
   - Counterparty credit utilization and WWR considerations.
   - Collateral and liquidity impact (initial/variation margin, CSA thresholds).
   - Product eligibility under policy and regulatory constraints.

10. Pre-trade accounting and tax assessment
   - Confirm prospective hedge effectiveness approach, designation feasibility, and documentation requirements.
   - Estimate P&L/OCI impacts and potential basis ineffectiveness.

11. Optimization and trade sizing
   - Optimize hedge portfolio to minimize expected cost/volatility subject to:
     - Meeting target ranges, limit constraints, accounting eligibility, and liquidity bounds.
   - Round notionals to market conventions and standard contract sizes.

12. Compile Hedge Requirements Memo
   - Include objectives, exposures, metrics before/after, required hedge amounts by bucket, instrument mix, scenarios, constraints, accounting assessment, and risks.
   - Attach compliance checklist and data lineage.

13. Review and approval
   - Middle office risk review for policy alignment and metrics.
   - Accounting review for hedge accounting implications.
   - Obtain approvals per authority matrix (e.g., Treasurer/CFO, Risk Committee for large programs).

14. Issue trade mandates
   - Translate requirements into execution mandates for front office: instruments, tenors, notional ranges, timing, target execution strategy.
   - Load mandates into TMS and execution workflows with pre-trade controls.

15. Recordkeeping and monitoring setup
   - Store documents, approvals, and assumptions in the TMS/EDMS.
   - Set monitoring alerts for hedge ratios, DV01 drift, and trigger thresholds.
   - Schedule periodic re-assessment/rebalancing.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Hedge Requirements Memo (HRM) with detailed analysis and recommendations.
- Hedge Allocation Matrix: required notional/DV01 by tenor bucket and instrument.
- Pre-trade accounting assessment and draft hedge designation templates.
- Compliance checklist: policy alignment, counterparty and product eligibility, collateral impact.
- Approval records and trade execution mandates.
- Updated risk dashboards showing metrics pre- and post-hedge plan.

Success criteria:
- Resulting hedge profile keeps exposures within policy bands and limits.
- Approved HRM with clear, executable mandates and no outstanding compliance exceptions.
- Hedge accounting feasibility confirmed for intended designations.
- Complete, auditable documentation and data lineage.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Treasurer / Head of Treasury: Owns process, approves hedge requirements, escalates exceptions.
- ALM/Risk Manager (Middle Office): Measures risk, validates methodology, ensures policy compliance, runs scenarios and optimization.
- Treasury Front Office: Advises on market conditions/liquidity, provides input on instrument selection, executes trades after approval.
- Hedge Accounting/Controllership: Assesses accounting eligibility, prepares designation and effectiveness testing approach.
- Treasury Operations/Back Office: Ensures static data accuracy, confirms settlement/collateral implications, records mandates in systems.
- Risk Committee/CFO: Approves large or off-policy hedging programs, sets strategic hedging direction.
- Legal/Tax: Reviews documentation standards, confirms regulatory and tax considerations.
- IT/Data Management: Manages TMS, risk systems, market data feeds, and data quality controls.

## Best Practices
- Use a layering strategy to distribute hedge inception across time and reduce timing risk.
- Define hedge ratios by tenor buckets with bands to avoid frequent rebalancing.
- Measure and manage basis risk explicitly (e.g., SOFR vs. internal benchmark) and consider basis hedges when material.
- Standardize metrics (DV01, EaR/CfVaR) and reporting across entities and currencies.
- Integrate collateral and liquidity impacts into hedge decisions, not post-trade.
- Maintain strict segregation of duties and independent model validation.
- Pre-wire hedge accounting documentation to avoid last-minute designation issues.
- Employ scenario and stress testing using both historical and hypothetical shocks.
- Implement clear exception management with quantified justification and time-bound remediation.
- Continuously backtest and refine forecasting and risk models.

## Common Challenges
- Forecast uncertainty leading to over-hedging or missed protection.
  - Mitigation: Use conservative hedge bands, options for uncertain exposures, rolling forecasts, and sensitivity overlays.
- Data quality gaps and inconsistent curve mapping.
  - Mitigation: Centralize market data, enforce validation rules, and maintain a curve governance framework.
- Basis risk undermining hedge effectiveness.
  - Mitigation: Align hedged items and instruments to the same benchmarks; apply basis hedges if needed.
- Collateral and liquidity strain from cleared/OTC derivatives.
  - Mitigation: Pre-trade liquidity assessment, set collateral limits, and diversify instruments (e.g., use futures where appropriate).
- Accounting qualification issues causing P&L volatility.
  - Mitigation: Early accounting review, align objectives with hedge accounting rules, choose instruments that fit designation.
- Counterparty concentration and WWR.
  - Mitigation: Enforce counterparty limits, diversify dealers, and utilize central clearing when feasible.
- Delayed approvals missing market windows.
  - Mitigation: Pre-approved hedging programs with mandates, clear authority thresholds, and standing instructions within policy.

## Performance Metrics
- Hedge ratio by tenor bucket vs. policy band (% within range).
- Unhedged DV01 or duration gap vs. limit (absolute and %).
- Earnings-at-Risk/Cashflow-at-Risk reduction achieved vs. target.
- Cost of hedging (bp per year, premium amortization) vs. budget/benchmark.
- Hedge effectiveness metrics (prospective/retrospective) and accounting qualification rate.
- Policy breaches or exceptions count and time-to-remediate.
- Time-to-approve Hedge Requirements Memo and trade mandates.
- Counterparty concentration index and collateral utilization vs. limits.
- Forecast accuracy for hedged exposures (variance vs. actual).
- Documentation completeness and audit findings.

## Technology and Tools
- Treasury Management System (e.g., Kyriba, GTreasury, FIS Quantum): positions, workflows, approvals, documentation.
- Risk analytics/ALM platforms (e.g., Murex, Calypso/Adenza, Quantifi): DV01, duration, VaR, scenario analysis, optimization.
- Market data and pricing (e.g., Bloomberg, Refinitiv): curves, vol surfaces, valuations.
- Valuation libraries and effectiveness testing tools: IFRS 9/ASC 815 support.
- Collateral management systems: margin simulation and monitoring.
- Data integration/quality tools: ETL, data warehouse, controls dashboards.
- Collaboration and document management: EDMS with versioning and approvals.
- Automation/monitoring: APIs/RPA for data loads, alerts for limit breaches and trigger events.

Process Details:
# [9.7.5.5.5] Monitor credit

## Overview
Monitor credit is the ongoing review of internal and external credit information to ensure accuracy, detect anomalies or potentially fraudulent activity, and protect the organization’s ability to execute hedging transactions safely. In treasury operations, this process safeguards against counterparty default risk, business identity theft, erroneous bureau data, and unexpected changes in credit standing that could impact collateral requirements, trading capacity, pricing, and liquidity.

This process supports:
- Execution of hedging transactions by validating counterparties’ creditworthiness and ensuring our organization’s credit data is accurate.
- Early-warning detection of credit deterioration (e.g., ratings downgrades, CDS spread widening, margin increases).
- Compliance and auditability through documented reviews, exception handling, and control effectiveness.

## Key Activities
- Define monitoring cadence and triggers (daily, weekly, monthly; event-driven alerts).
- Acquire and reconcile credit data for the organization and its hedging counterparties.
- Validate accuracy of credit reports (ratings, bureau files, tradelines, collateral terms).
- Detect anomalies and potential fraud (unauthorized inquiries, new accounts, rapid score/rating changes).
- Assess exposure and limit utilization against approved credit limits and risk appetite.
- Investigate exceptions and resolve discrepancies or suspected fraud with bureaus/providers.
- Recommend and implement actions (adjust limits, collateral calls, trading blocks, dispute filings).
- Maintain audit trail, dashboards, and governance reporting.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Counterparty master list with legal identifiers (LEI, tax IDs), netting sets, and agreement details (ISDA/CSA, GMRA/GMSLA).
  - Current and historical credit reports:
    - Rating agency data (S&P, Moody’s, Fitch).
    - Market-implied credit data (CDS spreads, bond OAS).
    - Business credit bureau files (Dun & Bradstreet, Experian Business, Equifax Commercial) and bank credit opinions.
  - Internal exposure data: current exposure (CE), potential future exposure (PFE), limit framework, collateral balances, margin calls.
  - Policy thresholds and risk appetite: rating floors, limit triggers, watchlist criteria, fraud indicators.
  - Prior period monitoring logs and unresolved exceptions.
- Prerequisites:
  - Executed data subscriptions and access to rating/bureau feeds.
  - Entity resolution and data mapping in place (e.g., LEI hierarchy mapping).
  - Documented credit monitoring policy, SLAs, and escalation matrix.
  - Segregation of duties and approvals workflow (four-eyes control).
- Dependencies on other processes:
  - Develop risk management/hedging strategy (defines limits, hedging mandates).
  - Execute hedging transactions (dependency for trade approval and ongoing eligibility).
  - Counterparty onboarding/KYC and maintain counterparty master data.
  - Maintain credit limits and collateral management.
  - Market data management and data quality governance.

## Process Steps
1. Plan cadence and scope
   - Define daily/weekly/monthly review scope by counterparty tiering, exposure, and criticality.
   - Confirm event-driven triggers (rating actions, CDS widening above x bps, abnormal inquiries).

2. Acquire data
   - Pull latest internal exposure, limit, collateral, and margin data from TMS/ETRM.
   - Ingest external credit data (ratings, outlooks, watchlists, CDS, business bureau reports).
   - Retrieve change logs since last review.

3. Normalize and reconcile entities
   - Match data to canonical legal entities using LEI and internal master data.
   - Aggregate at netting set level for limit assessment; flag unmatched records.

4. Validate completeness and accuracy
   - Check coverage completeness: all active counterparties and the organization’s entities have current data.
   - Compare key attributes versus prior period to detect unusual changes (score drops, new tradelines, UCC filings, inquiries).

5. Calculate exposure and limits
   - Compute CE/PFE and limit utilization by counterparty and netting set.
   - Incorporate collateral/margin and CSA thresholds; compute unsecured exposure.

6. Run anomaly and fraud detection rules
   - Automated rules: sudden rating downgrades, CDS jump > threshold, new credit inquiries on the organization, address/beneficial owner changes, unexpected new credit accounts, discrepancies across data sources.
   - Statistical/ML signals where available (outlier detection on exposure and bureau attributes).

7. Review exceptions
   - Prioritize by materiality and risk (e.g., high exposure + deterioration).
   - Perform triage: cross-verify across sources; validate with front office and counterparty managers; confirm internal system feeds.

8. Determine actions
   - For inaccuracies: submit disputes to bureaus/providers; request corrections; document evidence.
   - For deterioration: propose limit adjustments, tighten CSA terms where feasible, increase collateral frequency, place trading blocks, or require pre-trade approval.
   - For suspected fraud/identity theft: initiate incident response, freeze impacted accounts, inform Legal/Compliance, notify bureaus and affected banks.

9. Approvals and escalation
   - Route recommended actions through defined approval tiers (Credit Committee/Treasury Risk Head).
   - Log decisions with rationale and effective dates.

10. Execute actions
   - Update limits and watchlists in TMS/limit systems.
   - Trigger collateral calls/margin adjustments.
   - Communicate trading restrictions to front office and middle office.
   - Submit formal disputes to bureaus; track ticket numbers and timelines.

11. Document and report
   - Update monitoring log, exception register, and case management records.
   - Refresh dashboards with key changes, exposures, and status.
   - Distribute periodic reports to stakeholders (Treasury, Risk, Compliance, Executive).

12. Post-review controls and continuous improvement
   - Perform quality check (four-eyes) on a sample of reviews.
   - Analyze root causes of exceptions; refine rules/thresholds and data mapping.
   - Close-the-loop on disputes and control effectiveness.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Outputs:
  - Updated credit monitoring log and exception register.
  - Updated counterparty credit limits, watchlists, and trading eligibility.
  - Margin/collateral action records and confirmations.
  - Dispute submissions and outcomes with bureaus/providers.
  - Alerts/communications to trading, risk, and management.
- Deliverables:
  - Periodic credit monitoring report (KPIs, exceptions, actions, residual risk).
  - Audit-ready documentation (evidence, approvals, timestamps).
  - Updated risk dashboards (exposure vs limits, rating/score trends, CDS movements).
- Success criteria:
  - 100% of in-scope entities reviewed per cadence.
  - Material inaccuracies corrected within SLA.
  - No unauthorized trades with restricted counterparties.
  - Timely detection and mitigation of deteriorating credit/fraud events.
  - Clean internal/external audit results with effective controls.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Treasury Risk Manager (Process Owner)
  - Owns policy, cadence, thresholds, and escalations; approves material actions.
- Credit Risk Analyst
  - Performs data acquisition, analysis, exception triage, and prepares action recommendations.
- Middle Office
  - Validates exposure calculations, enforces trading restrictions, and supports collateral actions.
- Trading Desk
  - Adheres to limits/restrictions; provides counterparty intelligence; supports rapid mitigations.
- Collateral Management
  - Executes margin calls, monitors CSA compliance, reconciles collateral.
- Legal/Compliance
  - Manages disputes, regulatory notifications, reviews contractual implications; oversees fraud response.
- Data Management/IT
  - Maintains integrations, data quality, entity resolution, and alerting workflows.
- Internal Audit
  - Tests control design and operating effectiveness; reviews documentation and evidence.

## Best Practices
- Use dual-source verification for critical credit attributes (ratings, CDS, bureau data).
- Implement near real-time alerts for rating changes and CDS spikes.
- Maintain robust entity resolution using LEI and hierarchy mapping to avoid misattribution.
- Apply materiality thresholds and risk tiering to focus effort on high-impact exposures.
- Enforce segregation of duties and four-eyes review for limit changes and trading blocks.
- Automate anomaly detection with configurable rules and ML where appropriate.
- Regularly backtest thresholds and stress test credit deterioration scenarios.
- Maintain comprehensive audit trails with immutable logs.
- Establish SLAs with data providers and internal teams for timely corrections.
- Periodically simulate “red team” identity theft scenarios to test response readiness.

## Common Challenges
- Data fragmentation and inconsistent identifiers
  - Mitigation: Master data management, LEI adoption, golden record stewardship.
- Latency and stale data during volatile markets
  - Mitigation: Event-driven feeds, prioritized refresh for high-exposure names, vendor SLAs.
- False positives in anomaly detection
  - Mitigation: Calibrate thresholds, use ensemble signals, feedback loop from analyst outcomes.
- Discrepancies across data providers
  - Mitigation: Source hierarchy rules, reconciliation workflows, exception governance.
- Limited transparency for private or offshore counterparties
  - Mitigation: Supplemental financial statement collection, bank references, enhanced due diligence.
- Operational load during market stress
  - Mitigation: Predefined playbooks, surge resourcing, automation/RPA for repetitive checks.

## Performance Metrics
- Coverage and timeliness
  - % of in-scope entities reviewed on schedule.
  - Average time to review and close exceptions (MTTR).
- Data quality and accuracy
  - Exception rate per 100 entities; % resolved within SLA.
  - Dispute success rate with bureaus/providers.
- Risk posture
  - Exposure vs limit utilization distribution.
  - Number of rating downgrades/CDS alerts addressed within target time.
  - Weighted average external rating of counterparties; watchlist count and trend.
- Control effectiveness
  - Number of trades blocked due to credit restrictions (and policy adherence rate).
  - Audit findings and remediation cycle time.
- Fraud/identity protection
  - Number of unauthorized inquiries/new accounts detected.
  - Time to containment for suspected fraud events.

## Technology and Tools
- Treasury and risk platforms: Kyriba, GTreasury, FIS Integrity, Murex, Calypso.
- Market and credit data: Bloomberg, Refinitiv, S&P/Moody’s/Fitch ratings feeds, Markit for CDS, D&B/Experian/Equifax commercial reports.
- Exposure and collateral systems: TMS/ETRM, collateral management modules, tri-party platforms.
- Data integration and quality: ETL/ELT tools, MDM solutions, entity resolution (LEI, GLEIF).
- Analytics and alerting: BI dashboards (Power BI/Tableau), rules engines, ML anomaly detection, real-time alerting (email/ChatOps).
- Case and document management: ServiceNow/Jira for exceptions; secure repositories for evidence and disputes.
- Security and fraud monitoring: IAM logs, UEBA, vendor risk management tools; business identity monitoring services.
- Audit and compliance: GRC platforms for control testing and evidence retention.

## Overview
Identify specific IT requirements is the process of translating project objectives and business needs into clear, testable, and feasible technology requirements. It defines what hardware, software, telecom, data, integrations, environments, security, and operational capabilities are required across project phases and timelines. This process ensures:

- Alignment to enterprise architecture, security, data governance, and compliance standards
- Feasible delivery within budget, scope, and schedule constraints
- A solid basis for solution design, procurement, build, testing, deployment, and operations

It is a critical component of project planning and underpins downstream activities such as solution architecture, vendor selection/RFPs, cost estimation, environment provisioning, and implementation planning.

- Elicit requirements from stakeholders (business, IT, security, operations)

- Define application and platform requirements (COTS/custom, SaaS/PaaS/IaaS)

    - Support model, SLAs/OLAs, service catalog entries.
11. Tooling and delivery pipeline
    - CI/CD, artifact repositories, testing tools (performance, security), code quality.
    - Release mgmt, feature flags, environment promotion and approvals.
12. Costing and procurement
    - Bill of materials (hardware/software/licenses), cloud cost estimates and pricing tiers.
    - Vendor shortlist, RFI/RFP needs, evaluation criteria, renewal/exit terms.
    - Lead times for network circuits, hardware, licenses; budget phasing by project milestones.
13. Risk, constraints, and assumptions
    - Identify and log technology risks; propose mitigations.
    - Document regulatory constraints, technical debt, and legacy limitations.
14. Prioritization and traceability
    - Prioritize using MoSCoW or WSJF; mark MVP vs later phases.
    - Build a requirements traceability matrix (RTM) linking business objectives → IT requirements → design → test cases → deployment.
15. Review and validation
    - Architecture review board and security/privacy impact assessment.
    - Data governance and compliance review.
    - Cross-functional walkthrough; resolve comments; update drafts.
16. Baseline and change control
    - Obtain formal approval/sign-off; version requirements baseline.
    - Integrate with change control to manage requirement changes post-baseline.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- IT Requirements Specification (functional + NFRs) with acceptance criteria
- Architecture and design artifacts: context/system diagrams, logical/physical architecture, data models, integration/interface catalog, data flow diagrams
- Environment and deployment strategy; capacity sizing; network/security ruleset requirements
- Security/privacy impact assessment; compliance checklist
- Operations requirements: monitoring/alerting, backup/DR, support model, SLAs/SLOs
- Tooling/CI-CD and ITSM integration requirements
- Bill of materials and cost/TCO estimates; procurement requests; vendor shortlist or RFP package
- Risk/assumptions/constraints log
- Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)
- Success criteria:
  - Approved baseline of complete, testable, and feasible requirements
  - Alignment with enterprise/security/data standards
  - Cost and capacity estimates within budget and schedule
  - Stakeholder sign-off with no critical open risks or policy violations

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Project Manager: plan, schedule, facilitate, manage approvals and change control
- Business Analyst/Product Owner: elicit needs, document functional requirements, prioritize
- Solution/Enterprise Architect: define solution options, ensure standards alignment, approve architecture
- Security/Privacy Architect: define security controls, conduct privacy impact assessment, approve security posture
- Data Architect/Steward: define data model, quality, retention, governance, residency
- Infrastructure/Cloud Architect: define compute/storage/platform, environments, DR/HA
- Network/Telecom Engineer: define connectivity, routing, firewall, VPN, voice/UC needs
- DevOps/Platform Engineer: define CI/CD, IaC, observability, runtime platform
- Application Owner/SME: validate application-specific requirements and integrations
- QA/Test Lead: define testability and NFR test plans
- IT Operations/Service Desk Lead: define support, monitoring, SLAs/OLAs, runbooks
- Procurement/Vendor Management: coordinate quotes, RFPs, contracts, licensing
- Finance: validate budget alignment and TCO
- Compliance/Legal: validate regulatory and contractual requirements
- Change Manager: align with release calendar and change governance

## Best Practices
- Start with business outcomes; tie every requirement to a measurable objective
- Use standard templates and maintain a single source of truth in a version-controlled repository
- Capture complete NFRs early; they drive architecture, cost, and risk
- Reuse reference architectures, patterns, and standards; align with cloud/EA roadmaps
- Engage security, data, and operations from day one (“shift left”)
- Validate assumptions via PoCs/spikes for high-risk items
- Quantify capacity with data (benchmarks, logs); plan for peak and growth
- Design for resilience and observability; define SLOs and error budgets
- Consider total lifecycle: support, upgrades, end-of-life, exit strategies, vendor lock-in
- Prioritize with MoSCoW; define MVP, phased delivery, and feature toggles
- Ensure accessibility and localization where applicable
- Maintain traceability from requirements to tests; enforce change control after baseline
- Factor lead times (circuits, hardware, licensing) into the schedule
- Document constraints and decisions; record rationale

## Common Challenges
- Vague or shifting requirements
  - Solution: timebox discovery, use prototypes, baseline and control changes, maintain a prioritized backlog
- Under-specified NFRs leading to rework or outages
  - Solution: adopt NFR checklists, require measurable targets, include NFR testing in plans
- Integration complexity and hidden dependencies
  - Solution: build an interface catalog; conduct dependency mapping; run early integration tests
- Security/compliance gaps discovered late
  - Solution: early security/privacy assessments; include security sign-off gates
- Capacity/cost overruns
  - Solution: benchmark loads; scenario-based cost modeling; implement cost guards in cloud
- Vendor lock-in and unfavorable terms
  - Solution: evaluate exit strategies; negotiate portability; use open standards where feasible
- Procurement and provisioning lead-time delays
  - Solution: initiate procurement early; maintain approved product catalogs and forecasts
- Data quality and migration risks
  - Solution: data profiling, DQ rules, migration runbooks, reconciliation plans
- Network constraints impacting performance
  - Solution: pre-change network assessments, synthetic tests, QoS planning
- Misalignment with operations/support
  - Solution: involve IT ops early; define runbooks/SLAs; ensure monitoring requirements are complete

## Performance Metrics
- Cycle time: days from kickoff to requirements baseline approval
- Requirements quality: % requirements with clear acceptance criteria; NFR coverage score
- Traceability: % of IT requirements traced to business objectives and to test cases
- Change rate: # and % of requirements changes post-baseline
- Rework: defects or design changes attributable to missing/poor requirements
- Review effectiveness: # critical issues found in architecture/security reviews
- Cost accuracy: variance between estimated and actual cost (capex/opex)
- Lead-time readiness: % environments/procured items ready by scheduled need date
- Stakeholder satisfaction: survey score post-baseline
- Operational outcomes: incidents attributable to requirement gaps in first 90 days after go-live

## Technology and Tools
- Requirements and work management: Jira/Confluence, Azure DevOps, Jama, IBM DOORS
- Architecture and modeling: Sparx EA, Archi, Visio/Lucidchart/diagrams.net; BPMN, UML, ArchiMate
- Data modeling and integration: ER/Studio, ERwin, dbt, Informatica/Talend, MuleSoft/Boomi, Kafka
- Cloud and infrastructure: AWS/Azure/GCP services; Terraform/CloudFormation; Ansible/Chef; Kubernetes/Docker
- Network/telecom: SD-WAN controllers, firewall managers, IPAM/DNS tools, call center/UC platforms
- Security and identity: Okta/Azure AD, Vault/KMS, Qualys/Nessus, Prisma/Defender, SIEM (Splunk/QRadar), SAST/DAST
- Observability and ops: Prometheus/Grafana, Datadog/New Relic, Splunk/ELK, PagerDuty/Opsgenie; ITSM (ServiceNow)
- Testing: JMeter/Gatling, Selenium/Cypress, Burp/ZAP, chaos engineering tools
- Procurement and finance: SAP Ariba/Coupa, contract repositories, cloud cost tools (CloudHealth/Cloudability), vendor calculators
- Collaboration and documentation: SharePoint, Miro/Mural, Teams/Slack
