Process Details:
## Overview
Create training and communication plans is the process of designing how the project will equip people with the knowledge, skills, and motivation to adopt the change and perform their roles, and how the project will communicate timely, consistent, and targeted information throughout the lifecycle. It converts project scope and change impacts into pragmatic learning and communication strategies, schedules, materials plans, roles, budgets, and metrics.

Purpose:
- Ensure the right people receive the right training at the right time and can demonstrate proficiency.
- Build awareness, understanding, and commitment via clear, consistent, two-way communications.
- Reduce adoption risk, accelerate time to proficiency, and improve project outcomes.

Role in the organization:
- Integral to project planning under the overall program/change strategy.
- Interfaces with resource planning, IT enablement, launch planning, and reward approaches.
- Provides the baseline for execution of training and communications during project delivery and rollout.

## Key Activities
- Analyze audiences: roles, locations, languages, constraints, and change impacts.
- Define learning and communication objectives aligned to business outcomes and KPIs.
- Select delivery strategies: training modalities, comms channels, frequency, and sequencing.
- Build training curriculum and communication architecture at high level (courses, modules, message themes).
- Plan logistics: schedules, capacity, trainers, tools, environments, content development timelines.
- Define governance: approvals, version control, brand compliance, data privacy, and accessibility.
- Develop measurement plans: Kirkpatrick evaluations, adoption metrics, comms engagement metrics.
- Build risk and contingency plans (e.g., alternate channels, make-up sessions).
- Produce and baseline the Training Plan and Communication Plan.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Project charter, scope, milestones, and deployment approach (e.g., pilot, waves, big bang).
- Change impact assessment and stakeholder analysis/personas.
- Resource plan and roles/responsibilities (RACI).
- Skills inventory and initial training needs analysis (TNA) inputs if available.
- IT requirements and tool landscape (LMS, collaboration tools, intranet).
- Organizational policies: branding, tone of voice, accessibility (e.g., WCAG), data privacy, compliance.
- Budget constraints and approval guidelines.
- Risk register and issue log.
- Lessons learned from prior initiatives.

Prerequisites:
- Approved high-level project plan and release timeline.
- Identification of Training Lead and Communications Lead.
- Agreement on success measures and reporting cadence.
- Availability of SMEs and business owners for content input and approvals.

Dependencies on other processes:
- 13.2.3.3.1 Define resources and roles (feeds staffing and responsibilities).
- 13.2.3.3.2 Identify IT requirements (environments, tools, access).
- 13.2.3.3.3 Create communication strategy may inform positioning; if not separate, align here.
- 13.2.3.3.5 Design reward approaches (link recognition/incentives to adoption milestones).
- 13.2.3.3.6 Plan project launch (synchronizes comms and training cutover waves).

## Process Steps
1) Initiate and set governance
- Confirm scope, objectives, budget, timeline, and constraints for training/comms.
- Establish working team, RACI, approval workflow, and document templates.
- Align with change management strategy (e.g., ADKAR) and PMO standards.

2) Segment audiences and stakeholders
- Create audience segments by role, location, language, function, seniority, and change impact.
- Identify change champions, pilot groups, and managers who must be enabled first.

3) Conduct training needs analysis (TNA) and readiness baseline
- Define required competencies by role; compare to current state to identify gaps.
- Determine prerequisites (systems access, data, policies) and constraints (shift work, peak periods).
- Prioritize critical roles and high-impact gaps.

4) Define learning and communication objectives
- Translate business outcomes into SMART objectives by audience.
- Tie to measurable KPIs (e.g., reduce processing errors by X%, reach 90% completion).

5) Select delivery strategies
- Training: blend modalities (eLearning, VILT, ILT, microlearning, job aids, coaching, sandbox practice).
- Communications: choose channels (email, intranet, Teams/Slack, town halls, posters, video), cadence, and two-way feedback mechanisms.
- Decide on pilot vs. full rollout, Train-the-Trainer, and champion networks.

6) Design high-level curriculum and message map
- Define course/module list per role, duration, prerequisites, and sequence relative to go-live.
- Create key messages, narratives, FAQs, and benefit statements aligned to stakeholder needs.
- Map messages to project milestones (announce, why/change story, prepare, how-to, go-live, reinforce).

7) Plan logistics and resourcing
- Identify trainers, facilitators, content developers, translators, and approvers.
- Reserve environments (LMS, VILT platforms, training instances), rooms, and schedules.
- Determine class sizes, number of sessions, time zones, and make-up options.
- Estimate and allocate budget; define procurement needs (vendors, captions, translations).

8) Define content standards and governance
- Set templates, style guide, accessibility standards, and localization rules.
- Establish content repository, version control, and retention policy.
- Define legal/compliance review, brand checks, and data handling for participant records.

9) Create detailed plans and calendars
- Training Plan: curriculum map, delivery plan, schedule, resource plan, development backlog, risk log, budget, contingency plan.
- Communication Plan: stakeholder matrix, channel strategy, editorial calendar, content owners, approval workflow, feedback channels, crisis/escalation paths.

10) Measurement and feedback plan
- Define metrics (Kirkpatrick L1–L3, time-to-proficiency, adoption), data sources, baselines, and targets.
- Plan data collection instruments (surveys, quizzes, simulations, sentiment analysis).
- Set reporting cadence and dashboards.

11) Risk assessment and mitigation
- Identify risks (low attendance, tool outages, message fatigue, language barriers).
- Define mitigations (manager nudges, backups, multi-channel, translations, office hours).

12) Review, iterate, and baseline plans
- Conduct walkthroughs with sponsors, PMO, HR/L&D, Legal, and regional reps.
- Incorporate feedback; secure formal approval.
- Baseline version and publish to the project repository.

13) Prepare for execution handoff
- Brief trainers, comms owners, and managers.
- Finalize initial assets needed to start (e.g., save-the-dates, initial announcements, course outlines).
- Confirm readiness checklist (tools configured, access granted, calendars published).

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Training Plan document (version-controlled and approved).
- Communication Plan document (with editorial calendar).
- Audience segmentation and stakeholder matrix.
- Curriculum map and course catalog by role.
- Message framework: key messages, FAQs, and talking points.
- Governance and standards (templates, style/accessibility guide).
- Measurement plan and dashboard specifications.
- Risk register specific to training/comms with mitigations.
- Initial communications assets and training schedule.
Success criteria:
- Plans approved by sponsor/PMO and aligned to budget and schedule.
- Coverage of all impacted roles and stakeholders with clear objectives and timelines.
- Measurable KPIs defined with feasible data collection methods.
- Accessibility, localization, and compliance requirements addressed.
- Resourcing and logistics confirmed and feasible.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Sponsor/Executive: Approves plans; champions messages; removes obstacles.
- Project Manager: Integrates plans into master schedule and budget; tracks risks; ensures alignment with deployment.
- Change Manager: Orchestrates change strategy; ensures integration of training and communications; monitors adoption readiness.
- Training Lead/L&D: Owns TNA, curriculum design, delivery strategy, schedule, and training KPIs; manages trainers and content.
- Communications Lead: Owns stakeholder messaging, channels, editorial calendar, and comms KPIs; ensures brand/legal compliance.
- SMEs/Process Owners: Provide content; validate accuracy; support creation of job aids and scenarios.
- People Managers: Reinforce messages; enable staff attendance; coach post-training; provide feedback.
- Champion/Super-User Network: Advocate locally; provide peer coaching; relay sentiment and issues.
- HR/Learning Operations: Manage LMS, enrollments, records; coordinate logistics and vendors.
- IT/Systems: Provision training environments; ensure tool availability; support digital adoption platforms.
- Legal/Compliance/Privacy: Review content for regulatory compliance and data handling.
- PMO: Governance, standards, audit trail, and gate approvals.

## Best Practices
- Anchor to change outcomes: link learning and communications objectives to business KPIs.
- Start early; iterate: draft skeletal plans at initiation and progressively elaborate.
- Design for adults: apply adult learning principles, practice, scenarios, and spaced reinforcement.
- Blended learning: mix modalities; prioritize performance support (job aids, in-app guidance) for just-in-time needs.
- Manager enablement: give leaders toolkits, talking points, and checklists to cascade messages and coach teams.
- Two-way communications: enable Q&A, office hours, and feedback channels; act on feedback visibly.
- Accessibility and inclusion: conform to WCAG, offer captions, screen-reader friendly docs, multiple languages where needed.
- Localization: adapt not only language but examples, policies, and scheduling to local context.
- Right channel, right cadence: prevent message fatigue; use channel governance and editorial calendars.
- Pilot and refine: test training and comms with a representative group; adjust based on results.
- Governance and versioning: use a single source of truth for materials; track versions and approvals.
- Data-driven: define baselines and targets; use dashboards to steer.

## Common Challenges
- Low attendance or completion
  - Solutions: manager commitments, automated reminders, scheduling flexibility, incentives, integrate into performance goals.
- Message fatigue and low engagement
  - Solutions: streamline cadence, personalize content, use storytelling and visuals, rotate channels, segment audiences.
- Inconsistent or conflicting messages
  - Solutions: central message map, approval workflow, spokesperson training, PMO governance.
- Time zone and shift constraints
  - Solutions: asynchronous options, multiple cohorts, recordings, regional champions.
- Skills gaps underestimated
  - Solutions: rigorous TNA, pilot assessments, adjust curriculum depth, add coaching and practice labs.
- Tool or environment unavailability
  - Solutions: early environment planning, backups, sandbox alternatives, contingency calendar.
- Language and cultural barriers
  - Solutions: professional translation, local review, cultural adaptation, terminology glossaries.
- Compliance and privacy concerns
  - Solutions: early Legal/Privacy involvement, data minimization, secure LMS and survey tools, consent notices.
- Budget overruns
  - Solutions: prioritize high-impact roles, reuse content, leverage internal trainers, phased rollout.

## Performance Metrics
Training KPIs:
- Enrollment rate and on-time completion by role.
- Assessment scores and pass rates; pre/post competency delta.
- Time to proficiency; reduction in errors or rework post go-live.
- Training attendance, no-show rate, and make-up completion.
- Level 1–3 Kirkpatrick results (reaction, learning, behavior).

Communication KPIs:
- Reach by audience segment; open and click-through rates.
- Engagement (event attendance, intranet views, comments, Q&A participation).
- Sentiment and awareness scores from pulse surveys.
- FAQ resolution time; reduction in support tickets post-comms.
- Manager cascade confirmation rates.

Plan/process KPIs:
- Plan approval lead time; number of review cycles.
- Schedule adherence for content development and campaign launches.
- Risk closure rate; variance to training/comms budget.
- Audit compliance to accessibility, branding, and privacy standards.

## Technology and Tools
- Learning Management System (LMS): enrollment, tracking, reporting.
- Learning Content Management/authoring: Articulate 360, Adobe Captivate, Camtasia.
- Virtual training platforms: Microsoft Teams, Zoom, Webex.
- Digital adoption platforms: WalkMe, Whatfix, Pendo for in-app guidance.
- Collaboration and comms: Outlook/Exchange, Microsoft Teams/Slack, SharePoint/Confluence, intranet/CMS.
- Survey and analytics: Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey, Forms; analytics via Power BI/Tableau.
- Scheduling and resource management: Outlook/Calendars, Smartsheet, MS Project, Asana/Jira.
- Translation and accessibility: professional localization services, captioning tools, accessibility checkers.
- Knowledge base and DAM: SharePoint, Confluence, enterprise DAM for versioning and asset reuse.

Process Details:
# [13.2.3.3.6] Design and plan launch of project

## Overview
This process creates the comprehensive, cross-functional plan for when and how the project will be introduced to its target audience and transitioned into live operations. It aligns timing, scope, communications, training, technical cutover, operational readiness, support, and risk management so the launch achieves business objectives with minimal disruption. The output is an integrated, approved Launch Plan with clear milestones, roles, and go/no-go criteria that guides execution during go-live and the initial stabilization (“hypercare”) period.

This process is critical because it:
- Translates project objectives into an executable roll-out strategy (pilot, phased, or “big bang”).
- Ensures all enabling components (people, process, technology, data, legal, vendors) are ready at the same time.
- Reduces launch risk via structured readiness checks, contingency and rollback plans.
- Drives adoption through targeted communications and training.
- Establishes governance, decision rights, and a unified timeline across functions.

## Key Activities
- Confirm launch objectives, scope, and success metrics tied to business outcomes.
- Select launch approach (pilot/phased/big-bang) and target audiences/segments.
- Build the integrated launch timeline and critical path with dependencies.
- Define roles, responsibilities, decision rights, and escalation paths.
- Plan communications and stakeholder engagement.
- Plan training and change enablement for end users and support teams.
- Plan technical cutover, data migration, environment readiness, and integrations.
- Plan operational readiness (SOPs, service model, capacity, logistics).
- Define risk mitigations, contingency and rollback strategies.
- Establish go/no-go criteria, quality gates, and approval workflow.
- Budget and resource planning for launch and hypercare.
- Dress rehearsal(s) and readiness assessments.
- Final plan review, approvals, and baselining; socialize and distribute.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved project charter, scope, and baseline schedule/budget.
- Defined target audience, benefits, and business case metrics.
- Stakeholder map and change impact assessment (from OCM).
- Current risk/issues/assumptions/dependencies (RAID) log.
- Requirements traceability, UAT plan and acceptance criteria, test status.
- Technical architecture and deployment strategy; integration/data migration inventories.
- Operational model draft: process changes, SOPs, org impacts, support tiers.
- Compliance, security, privacy, and legal requirements.
- Vendor/partner statements of work and delivery schedules.
- Communication strategy and training needs analysis (drafts).
- Procurement status for launch-critical items (licenses, equipment, logistics).
- Monitoring/telemetry requirements and incident management procedures.

Prerequisites:
- Project plan baselined; key designs and build substantially complete.
- High-level change management plan in place.
- Environments available and stable for dress rehearsals.
- UAT acceptance criteria defined; defect triage process established.
- PMO governance and change control process defined.

Dependencies on other processes:
- Develop project plans (scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources).
- Risk and issue management; change control.
- Release/change management and CAB approvals (for IT).
- Training development and content creation.
- Communications planning and brand/legal review.
- Procurement, vendor management, and logistics.
- Security, privacy, regulatory compliance, and data governance.
- Business continuity/disaster recovery planning.

## Process Steps
1. Align on launch objectives and metrics
   - Confirm desired outcomes (e.g., adoption, revenue, cycle time reduction) and define measurable KPIs and target thresholds.
   - Document constraints (blackout dates, compliance windows, peak seasons).

2. Define launch scope and approach
   - Select pilot/phased/big-bang; determine cutover windows and geographic/functional sequencing.
   - Identify eligibility criteria for pilots and expansion gates.

3. Segment target audiences and impacts
   - Finalize stakeholder groups; map impacts by role/location.
   - Determine tailored comms and training needs per segment.

4. Build integrated launch timeline
   - Develop milestone plan from T–8+ weeks to T+4 weeks hypercare (or appropriate time horizon).
   - Identify critical path, inter-team dependencies, and lead times.

5. Establish governance and decision rights
   - Define RACI for launch; set cadence for stand-ups, risk reviews, go/no-go checkpoints.
   - Confirm escalation paths, war-room logistics, and incident severity definitions.

6. Resource and budget planning
   - Allocate resources for cutover, comms, training, hypercare, and monitoring.
   - Secure funding for overtime, travel, tools, and contingency.

7. Technical readiness and cutover planning
   - Define deployment method, change windows, freeze periods, back-out procedures.
   - Create cutover runbook with minute-by-minute tasks, owners, pre-/post-checks, and validation scripts.
   - Plan data migration steps, reconciliation, and verification; define performance and security readiness tests.

8. Operational readiness planning
   - Finalize SOPs, job aids, handoffs, SLAs/OLAs, capacity plans, and service desk scripts.
   - Validate supplier/logistics readiness; confirm spare/rollback inventory if physical components are involved.

9. Risk, contingency, and rollback planning
   - Update risk register; define mitigations and triggers for contingency execution.
   - Design and test rollback plan; document decision thresholds timed within the cutover window.

10. Communication planning
    - Define key messages, channels, cadence, and localized content.
    - Prepare executive briefings, stakeholder updates, FAQs, and customer-facing notices as needed.
    - Obtain legal/compliance approvals.

11. Training planning
    - Determine modalities (ILT, e-learning, job aids), schedules, trainers, and certification needs.
    - Build readiness assessments and track completion and proficiency.

12. Quality gates and go/no-go criteria
    - Define entry/exit criteria for each stage (e.g., UAT pass rate, defects by severity, performance benchmarks).
    - Prepare go/no-go checklist; align approval authorities.

13. Monitoring and support planning
    - Define telemetry/monitoring dashboards, alerts, and thresholds.
    - Plan hypercare (duration, staffing, hours, channels, triage, reporting).

14. Compliance, security, and legal approvals
    - Complete privacy impact assessments, security reviews, and regulatory filings.
    - Obtain CAB approval (IT), and any required executive sign-offs.

15. Dress rehearsal(s)
    - Execute end-to-end mock cutover, data migration, and validation in a non-prod environment.
    - Record timings, issues, and refine runbooks and estimates.

16. Final readiness assessment
    - Conduct readiness reviews across workstreams (tech, ops, comms, training, support).
    - Resolve gaps; if gaps remain, apply risk acceptance or adjust launch scope/timing.

17. Finalize and baseline the Launch Plan
    - Compile all sub-plans into a single, version-controlled document.
    - Secure formal approvals; communicate the plan to all stakeholders.

18. Pre-launch checkpoints (T–2 weeks to T–24 hours)
    - Reconfirm resource rosters, contact lists, access, and logistics.
    - Validate environment and data snapshots; re-run critical pre-checks.

19. Handover and execution preparedness
    - Ensure war-room communication channels and reporting templates are ready.
    - Publish daily launch/hypercare status cadence and dashboards.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Integrated Launch Plan (master document).
- Cutover runbook and back-out plan.
- Data migration plan and reconciliation procedures.
- Communications plan and content (FAQs, email templates, scripts).
- Training plan, materials, schedules, and completion tracking.
- Operational readiness package (SOPs, SLAs/OLAs, support scripts).
- Monitoring/telemetry dashboard specifications.
- Risk register updates and contingency mappings.
- Go/no-go criteria and approval matrix; quality gates.
- Readiness assessment reports and dress rehearsal results.
- Resource roster, contact lists, escalation matrix, war-room plan.
- Formal approvals and CAB/change records (as applicable).

Success criteria:
- All go/no-go criteria met and approvals obtained before launch.
- Readiness assessment score meets threshold with no unmitigated critical risks.
- Dress rehearsal completed within time bounds with acceptable issue rate.
- Communications and training coverage targets met (e.g., >95% completion for impacted users).
- Operational and technical monitoring configured and validated pre-launch.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Sponsor/Business Owner: Approves launch scope, timing, and risk acceptance; resolves cross-functional conflicts.
- Project/Program Manager: Orchestrates planning activities, maintains integrated timeline and RAID log, secures approvals.
- Product Owner/Business Lead: Confirms business readiness, acceptance criteria, and adoption targets; owns value realization plan.
- Release/Deployment Manager (IT): Owns cutover strategy, runbooks, change tickets, and technical go/no-go recommendations.
- Change Manager (OCM): Leads stakeholder engagement, comms, training strategy, and readiness assessments.
- QA/Test Lead: Validates quality gates, UAT outcomes, and defect disposition; supports rehearsal.
- Training Lead: Develops training materials, schedules delivery, and tracks completion/proficiency.
- Communications Lead: Crafts and coordinates messaging, approvals, and distribution.
- Operations Lead/Service Owner: Ensures SOPs, capacity, support model, and SLAs are in place; leads hypercare operations.
- Security/Compliance/Legal: Reviews and approves security, privacy, regulatory requirements and materials.
- Data Migration Lead: Designs and executes migration, reconciliation, and rollback scenarios.
- Architecture/Engineering Leads: Validate environment readiness, performance, integrations, and monitoring.
- Vendor/Partner Manager: Coordinates third-party readiness and contractual deliverables.
- PMO: Ensures adherence to governance, templates, and reporting standards.

## Best Practices
- Start launch planning early; run in parallel with build and test to reduce last-minute gaps.
- Choose rollout strategy based on risk and impact (pilot where uncertainty is high).
- Use a single, version-controlled Launch Plan; maintain a living RAID log.
- Define clear, objective go/no-go criteria with decision owners identified in advance.
- Conduct at least one timed dress rehearsal; refine estimates and back-out steps.
- Implement freeze windows (code/content/data) before launch to reduce change risk.
- Prepare and test rollback; ensure data consistency strategies are clear.
- Over-communicate to impacted users; tailor content by role and channel; brief leaders early.
- Track training completion and proficiency, not just attendance; certify critical roles.
- Establish a war-room with defined communication protocols and real-time dashboards.
- Align incident management and major incident processes specifically for launch window.
- Plan hypercare explicitly with enhanced staffing and reporting.
- Coordinate across time zones and regions; validate local regulatory/holiday constraints.
- Measure and learn; incorporate post-launch retrospectives into the template.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Unrealistic timelines: Use evidence from dress rehearsals; re-baseline with leadership buy-in; de-scope if needed.
- Incomplete readiness across functions: Enforce readiness gates per workstream; do not advance with critical gaps.
- Stakeholder resistance: Engage early champions; provide targeted benefits messaging and leader-led communications.
- Insufficient training: Prioritize high-impact roles; use just-in-time job aids and sandbox practice; certify critical users.
- Data migration issues: Profile and cleanse data early; pilot migrations; build reconciliation and fallback.
- Environment instability/performance: Run non-functional tests at production-like scale; enforce freeze and change control.
- Vendor delays: Add contractual readiness criteria; set escalation paths; build contingency options.
- Compliance or legal blockers: Involve teams early; use pre-approved templates; schedule reviews with buffer.
- Fragmented ownership: Define RACI and escalation; daily cross-functional stand-ups during T–2 weeks to T+2 weeks.
- Communication gaps: Use multi-channel approach; track reach and engagement; reinforce messages via managers.

## Performance Metrics
- Launch readiness index: % of readiness criteria met across workstreams.
- Go-live on-time rate: Actual vs planned launch date/time.
- Go/no-go compliance: % criteria met at decision gate; number of risk acceptances.
- Training coverage and proficiency: % completion by role; assessment scores.
- Communication reach/engagement: Open/click rates, acknowledgment rates, townhall attendance.
- Defect/incident metrics: Critical issues at/after go-live; incident rate per 100 users; MTTR during hypercare.
- Rollback occurrence: Y/N and root cause; time to rollback if triggered.
- Cutover execution variance: Actual vs planned duration; % steps completed on time.
- Adoption/usage: Active users, feature utilization, process compliance (early indicators).
- SLA attainment during hypercare: % tickets within SLA; backlog aging.
- Budget adherence: Actual launch/hypercare spend vs plan.

## Technology and Tools
- Project and portfolio management: MS Project, Smartsheet, Planview, Clarity.
- Agile/DevOps: Jira, Azure DevOps, GitLab; CI/CD pipelines; feature flags (LaunchDarkly).
- Release/change management: ServiceNow, BMC Remedy; CAB workflows.
- Collaboration and knowledge: Confluence, SharePoint, Teams, Slack; runbook repositories.
- Testing and quality: Zephyr/Xray, Selenium, Postman, JMeter; defect tracking.
- Data migration: Fivetran, Informatica, Azure Data Factory; reconciliation scripts.
- Monitoring/observability: Datadog, New Relic, Splunk, AppDynamics; custom dashboards.
- ITSM/Support: ServiceNow, Zendesk, Freshservice; major incident management modules.
- Training and comms: LMS (Cornerstone, SuccessFactors), Viva Learning; email/marketing tools (Marketo, Mailchimp); survey tools (Qualtrics).
- Compliance/GRC: Archer, OneTrust; e-sign approvals (DocuSign/Adobe Sign).
- Scheduling and war-room: PagerDuty, Opsgenie; Zoom/Teams bridges.

Process Details:
## Overview
This process evaluates how project management practices influence project measures and outcomes during execution. It aims to determine whether the way projects are planned, governed, staffed, and controlled is driving the desired results, and to identify actionable improvements. It spans defining measurement objectives, collecting and analyzing data, interpreting causal impact, and driving corrective actions at the project and program/portfolio levels.

Its role in the organization is to:
- Ensure transparency on whether project management is effective and aligned to strategy.
- Provide timely, evidence-based insights to guide interventions and optimize delivery performance.
- Support continuous improvement of the project management capability and methodology.
- Inform governance, risk decisions, and resource prioritization across the portfolio.

Typical scope includes both financial and non-financial measures such as schedule predictability, quality, risk exposure, stakeholder satisfaction, benefits realization progress, and compliance to methodology.

## Key Activities
- Define evaluation objectives, questions, and hypotheses linking PM practices to outcomes.
- Select a balanced set of metrics (leading and lagging) and determine frequency and thresholds.
- Establish baselines, targets, and control limits; agree on benchmarks.
- Design the measurement plan and data model; operationalize definitions in a metric dictionary.
- Configure tools and automate data capture from project systems.
- Collect, validate, and cleanse data; ensure data lineage and quality controls.
- Analyze performance and impact (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and causal).
- Synthesize insights and recommendations; quantify benefits and risks of proposed actions.
- Facilitate reviews; agree on and track corrective and preventive actions (CAPA).
- Update forecasts and plans; feed lessons learned into methodology and training.
- Govern and audit the evaluation process for consistency and compliance.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Project charter, scope statement, WBS, schedule baseline, cost baseline, resource plan.
  - Project Management Plan and subsidiary plans (risk, quality, communications, change, benefits).
  - Current and historical performance data (e.g., SPI/CPI, backlog metrics, defects, change logs).
  - Risk and issue registers, decision logs, RAID logs.
  - Stakeholder maps and satisfaction survey results.
  - PM methodology standards, governance requirements, maturity assessments.
  - Tool data from PMIS/PPM, agile boards, CI/CD, testing, and quality systems.
  - Prior lessons learned and benchmarks.

- Prerequisites:
  - Defined metric dictionary with clear operational definitions and ownership.
  - Established baselines, targets, and thresholds for each metric.
  - Data access agreements, privacy/compliance approvals, and required integrations.
  - Assigned roles for analysis, governance, and action ownership.
  - Training on data entry standards and metric interpretation.

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - 13.2.3 Manage projects: planning, executing, controlling, and reporting data.
  - Risk, quality, and change control processes for accurate source data.
  - Portfolio/program governance for reviews, decisions, and escalations.
  - Benefits realization management to connect delivery with outcomes.
  - Enterprise data governance and analytics for data quality and tooling.

## Process Steps
1. Initiate and scope the evaluation
   - Confirm objectives (e.g., “Does early risk identification reduce schedule variance?”).
   - Identify stakeholders and decision forums (project board, PMO, executives).
   - Determine cadence (e.g., weekly operational, monthly management, gate reviews).

2. Define metrics and targets
   - Select a balanced set of metrics across schedule, cost, scope, quality, risk, stakeholder, team health, compliance, and benefits.
   - Document operational definitions, sources, frequency, targets, and thresholds.
   - Establish baselines and control limits; secure stakeholder buy-in.

3. Design the measurement plan
   - Map data sources and integrations; define data model and transformations.
   - Define sampling methods for surveys and qualitative inputs.
   - Set data quality criteria and validation checks.

4. Configure tools and automate
   - Configure dashboards and reports; implement ETL/ELT pipelines.
   - Set alerts and thresholds for exceptions.
   - Ensure role-based access and data protection.

5. Collect and validate data
   - Pull data on cadence from PMIS/PPM, agile tools, quality systems, and surveys.
   - Run data quality checks; reconcile discrepancies with data owners.
   - Log data issues and corrective actions.

6. Analyze performance
   - Descriptive: trend lines, control charts, EVM variances, backlog flow metrics.
   - Diagnostic: root cause analyses (5 Whys, fishbone), cohort comparisons.
   - Predictive: forecast EAC/ETC, schedule risk (Monte Carlo), benefits projections.
   - Causal/impact: compare outcomes across practice adoption levels, pre/post changes, difference-in-differences, or matched cohorts.

7. Interpret and synthesize insights
   - Assess whether PM practices are driving observed outcomes; separate signal from noise.
   - Quantify impact magnitudes and confidence (where feasible).
   - Identify quick wins and structural improvements; assess cost, risk, and feasibility.

8. Recommend and agree actions
   - Develop CAPA plans with owners, timelines, and success measures.
   - Update project management plans, stage-gate criteria, and governance as needed.
   - Submit change requests where scope/schedule/cost baselines must be adjusted.

9. Communicate and review
   - Issue concise executive summaries and dashboards highlighting exceptions, trends, and actions.
   - Facilitate reviews at project stand-ups, weekly controls, monthly management, and gate reviews.
   - Capture decisions and track action status.

10. Implement and monitor improvements
   - Execute actions (e.g., additional risk reviews, backlog refinement cadence, training).
   - Monitor post-action metrics; validate effectiveness and adjust as needed.

11. Institutionalize learning
   - Update methodology guidance, playbooks, templates, and training.
   - Refresh benchmarks and targets; update metric dictionary.
   - Feed insights into portfolio prioritization and capability development.

12. Assurance and audit
   - Periodically audit metric definitions, data quality, and adherence to cadence.
   - Calibrate models and assumptions; retire vanity metrics and add new ones as needed.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Performance dashboards and scorecards with agreed cadence and thresholds.
- Impact assessment reports linking PM practices to outcomes, with quantified effects where possible.
- Variance, trend, and forecast analyses (EVM, schedule risk, quality, benefits).
- CAPA plans with owners and timelines; change requests as required.
- Updated project management plans, governance checklists, and stage-gate artifacts.
- Lessons learned and updated metric dictionary.
- Executive summaries for steering committees and portfolio reviews.

- Success criteria:
  - Reports delivered on time with agreed data quality.
  - Clear, actionable recommendations adopted by owners.
  - Measurable improvement in targeted metrics post-intervention.
  - Reduced decision latency and fewer late surprises.
  - Positive stakeholder feedback on usefulness and clarity of insights.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Project Manager: Provides data, context, and owns project-level actions and plan updates.
- PMO/Portfolio Analyst: Designs measurement plan, builds dashboards, performs analysis, synthesizes insights.
- Program/Portfolio Manager: Prioritizes interventions, arbitrates trade-offs, escalates systemic issues.
- Sponsor/Business Owner: Sets outcome expectations, approves actions and changes, removes obstacles.
- Data/BI Analyst: Integrates data, ensures quality, conducts advanced analytics and forecasting.
- Quality Manager: Defines quality metrics, audits process compliance, supports root cause analysis.
- Risk Manager: Ensures risk metrics are captured and interpreted; leads risk-related actions.
- Scrum Master/Agile Coach: Implements practice changes within teams; monitors agile health metrics.
- Product Owner: Provides value realization context; aligns backlog to outcomes.
- Finance Analyst: Validates cost/benefit impacts and EVM metrics; updates forecasts.
- Tool Administrator: Configures PMIS/PPM, integrations, access, and alerts.
- Change Manager: Plans communications and training; supports adoption of new practices.
- Governance/Audit: Periodically reviews adherence, definitions, and process integrity.

## Best Practices
- Align metrics with strategy and expected benefits; use a balanced scorecard approach.
- Focus on a small set of critical metrics with clear operational definitions to avoid noise.
- Mix leading and lagging indicators (e.g., risk review cadence vs. late rework).
- Automate data capture from source systems; minimize manual entry and duplication.
- Establish baselines early; use control charts and tolerance bands rather than point targets alone.
- Separate output, outcome, and capability metrics to clarify attribution.
- Triangulate quantitative data with qualitative feedback (surveys, retros, interviews).
- Use appropriate causal methods; avoid inferring causation from simple correlations.
- Publish a metric dictionary and provide training to prevent inconsistent interpretation.
- Build psychological safety: avoid punitive use of metrics; prevent gaming (Goodhart’s Law).
- Review and retire vanity metrics regularly; evolve targets as maturity grows.
- Embed evaluation into governance (stage gates, monthly reviews) with clear decision rights.
- Close the loop: track actions to completion and measure their effectiveness.

## Common Challenges
- Data quality and consistency issues across tools
  - Solution: Standardize definitions; implement validation rules; establish data stewardship and training.
- Attribution and confounding factors
  - Solution: Use controlled comparisons, pre/post analysis, and triangulation; document assumptions.
- Metric overload and analysis paralysis
  - Solution: Prioritize metrics tied to key decisions; limit to a focused set with clear owners.
- Tool fragmentation and siloed data
  - Solution: Integrate systems via ETL/iPaaS; adopt a common PPM platform or data lake.
- Resistance to measurement or fear of misuse
  - Solution: Communicate purpose; ensure transparency and non-punitive use; involve teams in metric design.
- Time lag between practice changes and outcomes
  - Solution: Track leading indicators and interim milestones; set realistic evaluation windows.
- Survey fatigue and bias
  - Solution: Keep surveys short, targeted, and periodic; use sampling; supplement with observational data.
- Small sample sizes for causal inference
  - Solution: Aggregate across cohorts or time; use Bayesian methods; emphasize qualitative insights where necessary.
- Inconsistent methodologies across teams
  - Solution: Provide crosswalks and normalization; measure at capability level as well as at team level.

## Performance Metrics
Consider a balanced set; select those that directly inform decisions:
- Schedule and cost
  - Schedule Predictability Index; Milestone adherence rate.
  - SPI/CPI trends; Estimate accuracy (MAPE for effort/cost/schedule).
  - Variance at Completion and forecast stability.
- Scope and change
  - Scope change rate; Requirement volatility; Change request cycle time.
- Quality
  - Defect density and escape rate; Rework rate; First-pass yield; Test coverage.
- Risk and issue management
  - Risk exposure trend; % risks mitigated before realization; Issue aging; Surprise index.
- Delivery flow (for agile/iterative)
  - Lead time and cycle time; Throughput stability (coefficient of variation); Flow efficiency; Work-in-process.
- Stakeholder and team health
  - Sponsor/stakeholder satisfaction; NPS; Team engagement/health index; Turnover rate.
- Benefits and value
  - Benefits realized to date; Forecast accuracy for benefits; Time-to-value.
- Governance and capability
  - Compliance to methodology checkpoints; Audit findings closure time.
  - Corrective action closure rate and timeliness.
  - Data quality score; Dashboard adoption rate; Decision latency from report to decision.

## Technology and Tools
- PPM/PMIS: Microsoft Project/Project Online, Planview, Clarity PPM, Primavera, Smartsheet.
- Agile/DevOps: Jira, Azure DevOps, Rally; GitHub/GitLab; Jenkins/Azure Pipelines; SonarQube.
- Quality and testing: TestRail, Zephyr, qTest; defect tracking in Jira/Azure DevOps.
- Risk and issue management: Integrated PPM modules; Risk Register tools.
- BI and analytics: Power BI, Tableau, Qlik; Python/R; Minitab for statistical analysis.
- Simulation and forecasting: @RISK, Primavera Risk Analysis, Monte Carlo add-ins.
- Data integration: Azure Data Factory, Informatica, MuleSoft; data lakes/warehouses.
- Survey and feedback: Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey, CultureAmp; forms integrated with collaboration tools.
- Documentation and collaboration: SharePoint, Confluence, Teams/Slack.
- OKR/strategy alignment: WorkBoard, Perdoo, Ally.io to connect project metrics to strategic outcomes.
- Data governance: Data catalogs and metric dictionaries; access control and audit logging.

Process Details:
## Overview
Manage project scope is the disciplined process of defining, baselining, and controlling what is and is not included in a project. It ensures the project team and stakeholders share a clear, validated understanding of goals, deliverables, boundaries, acceptance criteria, and responsibilities. It also establishes the mechanisms to evaluate and approve changes. Effective scope management prevents scope creep, improves predictability of schedule and cost, and increases the likelihood of delivering outcomes that meet stakeholder needs and business objectives.

This process sits within Execute Projects and interacts continuously with planning, scheduling, cost control, quality, change control, risk, procurement, and stakeholder engagement. It produces and maintains the scope baseline (project scope statement, Work Breakdown Structure, and WBS dictionary) and the requirements traceability that links business needs to delivered outputs.

## Key Activities
- Elicit and consolidate requirements from stakeholders.
- Define project and product scope, including explicit in-scope and out-of-scope items.
- Create the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) and WBS dictionary.
- Establish acceptance criteria for deliverables and completion.
- Baseline the scope and obtain formal approval.
- Maintain a Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM).
- Validate deliverables with stakeholders and record acceptance.
- Manage scope changes through an established change control process.
- Monitor scope performance and control scope creep.
- Communicate scope status, variances, and changes.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
- Required inputs:
  - Approved business case and project charter (objectives, high-level scope, constraints).
  - Product vision, epics/user stories or high-level requirements, and success metrics.
  - Organizational process assets (templates, policies, lessons learned, historical WBS/RTM).
  - Enterprise environmental factors (regulations, standards, technology constraints).
  - Contractual documents and statements of work (if vendors involved).
  - Initial risk register and assumptions/constraints log.
  - Program/portfolio roadmaps and architectural guidelines.

- Prerequisites:
  - Sponsor identified with decision authority.
  - Key stakeholders identified and engaged.
  - Project manager assigned; core team resourced.
  - Change control governance defined (e.g., CCB composition, thresholds).
  - Requirements management approach agreed (Agile, Hybrid, Predictive).

- Dependencies on other processes:
  - 13.2.3.1 Plan projects: feeds planning context and management plans.
  - 13.2.3.2 Initiate projects: charter and stakeholder mapping.
  - 13.2.3.4 Execute projects (overall): integration with schedule and cost execution.
  - Manage project schedule/cost/quality: alignment of baselines and changes.
  - Manage project risks/issues: scope-related risks and mitigation.
  - Manage changes: formal change control workflow and approvals.
  - Procurement/vendor management: SOW alignment and change orders.
  - Stakeholder engagement and communications.

## Process Steps
1. Prepare scope management approach
   - Confirm methodology (predictive/agile/hybrid), level of decomposition, acceptance gates, and documentation standards.
   - Define thresholds for variance and change escalation routes (e.g., what requires CCB vs PM approval).

2. Collect and analyze requirements
   - Conduct workshops, interviews, document analysis, prototyping, and/or backlog refinement.
   - Classify requirements (business, stakeholder, solution, transition, non-functional, compliance).
   - Prioritize using agreed techniques (MoSCoW, WSJF, Kano).
   - Document in a requirements repository and establish traceability to objectives.

3. Define scope boundaries and acceptance criteria
   - Draft the project and product scope statement: objectives, in-scope, out-of-scope, assumptions, constraints, success measures, deliverables list, and acceptance criteria.
   - Identify completion/definition-of-done (DoD) and, where applicable, definition-of-ready (DoR).

4. Create the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) and WBS dictionary
   - Decompose deliverables into manageable work packages (2–80 hour guideline or as appropriate).
   - Assign unique IDs; describe each work package’s scope, deliverables, acceptance criteria, and owner in the WBS dictionary.
   - Validate decomposition with technical leads and stakeholders.

5. Establish the scope baseline and obtain approval
   - Compile the scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary as the scope baseline.
   - Review with sponsor, key stakeholders, architects, QA, and governance bodies.
   - Address feedback, finalize, and obtain formal approval/sign-off.

6. Plan scope validation and control
   - Define cadence for formal scope validation (e.g., sprint reviews, stage gates, deliverable inspections).
   - Configure the change control process, forms, tooling, and SLAs for turnaround.
   - Link RTM to test cases and acceptance criteria.

7. Execute and validate scope
   - Build/produce deliverables according to the WBS and backlog.
   - Conduct incremental demonstrations, walkthroughs, and tests.
   - Record acceptance or defects; update RTM and deliverable status.

8. Monitor and control scope
   - Track variance against baseline (approved vs delivered) and requirement volatility.
   - Identify scope creep and gold plating; stop non-approved work.
   - Log change requests with impact analysis (schedule, cost, risk, quality, benefits).

9. Evaluate and approve/reject changes
   - Present change analysis to the appropriate authority (PM, Sponsor, CCB) per thresholds.
   - Update baselines upon approval; communicate changes and implement change orders with vendors.
   - Update plans (schedule, cost, resources), RTM, and configuration records.

10. Report and communicate
    - Provide transparent, periodic scope status: changes, variances, acceptance rates, and risks.
    - Maintain a visible in-scope/out-of-scope list and a change log for stakeholder reference.

11. Close scope for phases and project
    - Ensure all deliverables are accepted or dispositioned.
    - Reconcile RTM to confirm full coverage.
    - Archive scope artifacts and capture lessons learned for continuous improvement.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Outputs and artifacts:
  - Scope management approach/plan.
  - Approved project scope statement.
  - Work Breakdown Structure and WBS dictionary.
  - Requirements documentation and Requirements Traceability Matrix.
  - Scope baseline (scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary).
  - Accepted deliverables and acceptance records.
  - Change requests, change log, and approved scope changes.
  - Scope performance reports and variance analyses.
  - Updated assumptions/constraints, risk register, and lessons learned.

- Success criteria:
  - Scope baseline approved and controlled with no unauthorized changes.
  - Deliverables accepted against defined criteria within tolerance.
  - Requirement coverage = 100% in RTM; minimal rework due to scope defects.
  - Scope-related variance within thresholds; stakeholder satisfaction targets met.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Sponsor/Business Owner
  - Approves scope baseline and major changes; clarifies business outcomes; accepts final deliverables.
- Project Manager
  - Leads scope definition, baselining, and control; chairs/coordinates change control; reports scope status.
- Product Owner (Agile/Hybrid)
  - Owns and prioritizes backlog; defines acceptance criteria; accepts increments.
- Business Analyst
  - Elicits and documents requirements; maintains RTM; supports validation and change impact analysis.
- Technical Lead/Architect
  - Validates technical feasibility; informs decomposition; evaluates impact of scope changes.
- Quality Assurance/Test Lead
  - Aligns test cases with acceptance criteria; validates deliverables; tracks defects to requirements.
- Project Controls/PMO
  - Ensures adherence to standards; manages templates; tracks KPIs; facilitates governance (CCB).
- Change Control Board (CCB)
  - Reviews and approves/rejects significant scope changes.
- Procurement/Vendor Manager
  - Aligns SOW/contract scope; manages change orders; ensures vendor compliance.
- Stakeholders/End Users
  - Provide requirements; participate in validation; approve acceptance where applicable.

## Best Practices
- Define both in-scope and out-of-scope explicitly; publish a scope boundary list early.
- Use a structured WBS as the single source of truth for scope; avoid mixing tasks with deliverables at higher levels.
- Maintain a live Requirements Traceability Matrix linking needs to deliverables, tests, and benefits.
- Establish clear acceptance criteria and DoD/DoR; tie them to test cases.
- Adopt right-size decomposition and documentation for project complexity and delivery approach.
- Implement rigorous but lean change control with turnaround SLAs and thresholds.
- Validate scope frequently with demos, prototypes, or pilots to reduce ambiguity.
- Guard against gold plating; align team incentives and quality criteria to defined scope.
- Integrate scope control with schedule, cost, risk, and configuration management.
- Reuse organizational assets and lessons learned; leverage reference WBS and templates.

## Common Challenges
- Ambiguous or evolving requirements
  - Solution: early stakeholder workshops, prototyping, progressive elaboration, backlog grooming.
- Scope creep and gold plating
  - Solution: enforce change control; educate team; monitor variance; celebrate saying “no” to unapproved work.
- Stakeholder misalignment
  - Solution: clear RACI, formal approvals, visual scope boundary artifacts, frequent reviews.
- Vendor scope gaps or interpretation differences
  - Solution: precise SOW with measurable deliverables and acceptance criteria; structured change order process.
- Over/under decomposition in WBS
  - Solution: adopt decomposition guidelines; peer reviews; align to deliverable-based WBS.
- Regulatory or standards changes mid-project
  - Solution: active environmental scanning; maintain a compliance requirements set; contingency reserves.
- Traceability gaps leading to rework
  - Solution: mandatory RTM updates as part of definition-of-done; QA gates.

## Performance Metrics
- Scope change rate: number of approved changes per period.
- Requirement volatility index: percentage of requirements added/changed/removed over time.
- Scope creep percentage: effort/cost delivered without approval versus baseline.
- Acceptance rate: percent of deliverables accepted on first submission.
- Rework due to scope defects: hours or cost attributed to unclear/missing requirements.
- RTM coverage: percentage of requirements linked to design, build, and test artifacts.
- Cycle time for change approvals: average time from submission to decision.
- Impact of changes: cumulative schedule/cost variance attributable to scope changes.
- Defect leakage related to requirements: defects found post-acceptance tied to scope gaps.
- Stakeholder satisfaction score with scope clarity and outcomes.

Target thresholds should be tailored by project type and organizational maturity and embedded in the scope management plan.

## Technology and Tools
- PPM and planning: Microsoft Project, Smartsheet, Planisware, Clarity PPM.
- Agile delivery and backlog management: Jira, Azure DevOps, Rally.
- Requirements and traceability: Jama Connect, IBM DOORS Next, Helix ALM, Confluence.
- Diagramming and modeling: Visio, Lucidchart, Enterprise Architect (UML/BPMN).
- Document and configuration management: SharePoint, Confluence, Git for versioning of artifacts.
- Test management and validation: Zephyr, Xray, qTest; link to RTM.
- Change control and workflow: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, custom CCB portals.
- E-signature/approvals: DocuSign, Adobe Sign.
- Reporting and dashboards: Power BI, Tableau, built-in PPM analytics.

These tools should be integrated where possible to maintain single sources of truth for scope, requirements, and changes, and to automate traceability and reporting.

Process Details:
## Overview
Promote and sustain activity and involvement is a core project execution process focused on keeping stakeholders, teams, and sponsors actively engaged throughout delivery. It ensures project tasks are visible, understood, and supported; fosters two-way communication; removes participation barriers; and maintains momentum to achieve scope, schedule, quality, and adoption outcomes. This process complements monitoring and control by addressing the human and behavioral components of execution, aligning people with goals, and cultivating ownership, collaboration, and continuous improvement.

Primary objectives:
- Maintain consistent participation of all necessary parties to keep execution on track.
- Drive awareness, understanding, and buy-in for project deliverables and changes.
- Encourage timely decision-making and risk/issue escalation.
- Support readiness, capability building, and adoption of project outputs.
- Protect morale and prevent engagement decay or change fatigue.

## Key Activities
- Engagement strategy and planning: Define objectives, audiences, messages, channels, cadence, and metrics.
- Stakeholder analysis and segmentation: Map stakeholders by influence, impact, needs, and preferred communication modes.
- Communications management: Create and distribute updates, progress stories, demos, FAQs, and calls-to-action.
- Governance and cadence: Operate stand-ups, reviews, showcases, steering, and community forums.
- Change enablement: Readiness assessments, training plans, job aids, coaching, and hypercare.
- Feedback loops and sentiment monitoring: Surveys, polls, retro insights, and “voice of employee” mechanisms.
- Recognition and reinforcement: Celebrate contributions, milestones, and behaviors that support project values.
- Impediment removal and escalation: Identify and clear blockers impacting participation or momentum.
- Champion network management: Enable local advocates to amplify messages and surface ground realities.
- Onboarding and continuity: Rapid onboarding for new joiners; knowledge capture to reduce attrition risk.
- Adaptive improvement: Use metrics to adjust tactics, cadence, and content.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Approved project charter, scope, objectives, and success criteria
- Project plan and schedule; resource plan and team roster
- Stakeholder register and RACI/responsibility model
- Initial communication plan and change impact assessment
- Budget for training, events, and engagement tools
- Access to collaboration platforms and repositories
- Governance calendar (ceremonies, steering, decision forums)

Prerequisites:
- Sponsor commitment and visible support
- Defined escalation path and decision rights
- Baseline project metrics and reporting mechanisms
- Content owners for training and communications
- Compliance guidance for internal communications and data privacy

Dependencies on other processes:
- Manage project scope, schedule, and risks/issues
- Change management and training development
- PMO reporting and governance
- HR policies for recognition and performance alignment
- IT/InfoSec for access controls and tool provisioning

## Process Steps
1. Confirm objectives and scope of engagement
   - Align on the engagement goals, success metrics, and boundaries (what this process will and won’t cover).
2. Analyze stakeholder landscape
   - Segment by role, influence, change impact, and preferred channels; identify champions and potential resistors.
3. Define engagement strategy and metrics
   - Set participation targets (attendance, contributions), sentiment targets, and adoption outcomes; select measurement methods.
4. Establish governance and cadence
   - Calendarize stand-ups, demos/reviews, retrospectives, backlog refinement, community forums, and steering meetings.
5. Prepare infrastructure and content plan
   - Configure collaboration spaces, dashboards, mailing lists, and content repositories; create a content calendar.
6. Onboard the team and champions
   - Provide project overview, ways of working, engagement expectations, tool access, etiquette, and escalation rules.
7. Launch communications
   - Kickoff announcement with purpose, expected benefits, timelines, roles, and how to participate; share a roadmap and FAQs.
8. Facilitate ongoing ceremonies and touchpoints
   - Run predictable, time-boxed sessions; ensure inclusive participation; rotate presenters; capture and publish outcomes.
9. Execute change enablement
   - Deliver targeted training, clinics, office hours, and job aids; schedule pilots and demos; run hypercare post-release.
10. Monitor engagement and sentiment
    - Track attendance, participation quality, action closure, training completion, survey scores, and qualitative feedback.
11. Recognize and reinforce
    - Publicly acknowledge contributions and milestones; provide badges, shout-outs, and alignment with performance goals.
12. Identify and remove impediments
    - Triage blockers; escalate per the path; adjust workload or priorities; resolve cross-team conflicts quickly.
13. Adapt based on feedback and data
    - A/B test message formats, adjust cadence, refine targeting, and address root causes of low engagement.
14. Sustain and transition
    - Develop a sustainment plan with BAU owners; hand over ongoing comms, communities of practice, and knowledge bases.
15. Capture lessons learned
    - Document what worked/what didn’t in engagement, update playbooks, and feed insights to PMO standards.

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Engagement plan and content calendar
- Stakeholder map and champion network roster
- Communication artifacts: newsletters, updates, demos, FAQs, decks, videos
- Training materials, schedules, and completion records
- Engagement dashboards: participation, sentiment, adoption metrics
- Meeting records: notes, decisions, action logs, retrospectives
- Impediment log with resolutions and escalations
- Recognition records and incentives issued
- Sustainment and transition plan to operations
- Lessons learned and updated engagement playbook

Success criteria:
- Participation meets/exceeds targets across key forums
- Stakeholders report clarity and confidence (positive sentiment)
- Training completion and proficiency targets achieved
- Adoption of deliverables meets plan; reduced resistance signals
- Fewer engagement-related delays/defects; steady milestone attainment

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Project Sponsor: Champion the initiative; set tone; remove high-level blockers; visible communications.
- Project Manager: Own engagement process; integrate with schedule/risk; ensure cadence; report metrics; escalate issues.
- PMO: Provide standards, templates, dashboards; coach teams; audit adherence; aggregate metrics.
- Change Manager: Lead stakeholder analysis, readiness, and adoption tactics; align training and communications.
- Communications Lead: Develop and execute content plan; maintain channels; ensure message quality and consistency.
- Team Leads/Workstream Owners: Encourage team participation; present progress; surface risks; support training.
- Scrum Master/Delivery Manager: Facilitate ceremonies; remove impediments; coach on collaboration practices.
- Product Owner/Business Lead: Prioritize work; engage users; sponsor demos; validate value delivery.
- Champions/Change Agents: Amplify messages; gather local feedback; support adoption and peer training.
- HR/People Partner: Align recognition and performance incentives; advise on engagement practices.
- Data/Analytics Lead: Build engagement dashboards; analyze sentiment and behavior signals; recommend improvements.
- IT/Tool Admins: Provision and support collaboration and analytics tools; ensure access and governance.
- Legal/Compliance: Review materials and processes for compliance with policies, privacy, and works council rules.

## Best Practices
- Anchor engagement to clear “why” and expected benefits; tailor to audience personas.
- Use multi-channel, multi-format communications (short-form, visual, interactive) with consistent cadence.
- Make it two-way: prioritize Q&A, office hours, polls, and AMAs; close the loop on feedback.
- Showcase progress early and often: demos and quick wins build momentum and credibility.
- Foster psychological safety: encourage questions, admit unknowns, and normalize learning from mistakes.
- Design for inclusivity: time zones, accessibility, language, and varying digital literacy.
- Measure and adapt: track leading indicators (participation) and lagging (adoption); iterate monthly.
- Empower champions and line managers: equip them with toolkits and talking points.
- Minimize cognitive load: consolidate channels, standardize formats, and keep messages concise.
- Link recognition to desired behaviors; celebrate both outcomes and collaborative practices.
- Maintain a single source of truth: up-to-date hub for plans, decisions, and materials.

## Common Challenges
- Change fatigue and overload
  - Solutions: prioritize initiatives, reduce noise, coordinate calendars, emphasize benefits and sequencing.
- Low sponsor visibility
  - Solutions: schedule sponsor touchpoints; prepare concise briefs; capture short video messages.
- Inconsistent participation across teams
  - Solutions: align with managers on expectations; adjust timings; use hybrid formats; track and follow-up on attendance.
- Poor message relevance
  - Solutions: segment audiences; use role-specific content; A/B test; include “what this means for you.”
- Tool sprawl and access issues
  - Solutions: standardize platforms; provide onboarding guides; ensure timely access provisioning.
- Remote/hybrid engagement difficulties
  - Solutions: invest in virtual facilitation; interactive tools; recordings; asynchronous options.
- Resistance to change
  - Solutions: identify root causes; involve resistors in solutioning; show evidence and user testimonials; provide coaching.
- Knowledge loss due to turnover
  - Solutions: document decisions; maintain playbooks; cross-train; structured handovers.
- Decision latency
  - Solutions: clear decision rights; SLAs for approvals; escalation ladders; pre-read discipline.

## Performance Metrics
Activity and reach:
- Forum attendance rate by role and team
- Content reach and engagement (open/click rates, views, reactions)
- Training enrollment and completion rates; assessment scores

Engagement quality and sentiment:
- Participation quality (speakers per session, questions asked, backlog items contributed)
- Pulse survey scores (clarity, confidence, support) and eNPS related to the project
- Champion activity (events hosted, issues surfaced/resolved)

Execution impact:
- Cycle time adherence before/after engagement initiatives
- Issue/risk discovery lead time and time-to-resolution
- Rework/defect rates linked to miscommunication or readiness gaps
- Adoption metrics (feature utilization, process compliance) vs. targets

Efficiency and sustainment:
- Time to onboard new team members to full participation
- Cadence adherence (sessions held as planned; timely publication of notes/actions)
- Cost per engaged participant; cost per training completion

Targets should be set per project context; review metrics at least monthly and after key milestones.

## Technology and Tools
- Project and portfolio management: Jira, Azure DevOps, Asana, Trello, MS Project
- Collaboration and communication: Microsoft Teams, Slack, Zoom, Google Workspace
- Knowledge and intranet: Confluence, SharePoint, Notion, Wikis
- Email/newsletters and campaign tools: Outlook/Exchange, Mailchimp, internal bulletin systems
- Survey and pulse tools: Microsoft Forms, Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey, CultureAmp
- Analytics and dashboards: Power BI, Tableau, Looker; sentiment analysis add-ons
- Training/LMS: Workday Learning, Cornerstone, Docebo; webinar platforms
- Recognition tools: Bonusly, Kudos, internal shout-out channels
- Event and scheduling: Calendly, Teams/Google Calendar, webinar registration
- Feedback and Q&A: Slido, Mentimeter, Miro/Mural for interactive workshops
- Access/governance: Identity management for provisioning; data retention and compliance tools

This process should be embedded in the project execution plan, governed by the PM/PMO, and integrated with change management to ensure that human factors receive the same rigor as scope, schedule, and budget.

Process Details:
# [13.2.3.4.5] Conduct Project Reviews with Program Managers and Other Stakeholders

## Overview
This process establishes a consistent, organization-wide approach to conduct post-project reviews, Lessons Learned sessions, and After Action Reviews (AARs) at the end of each project or major phase. Its purpose is to:
- Identify what worked well, what did not, and why.
- Translate insights into actionable improvements for future projects, programs, and enterprise standards.
- Strengthen cross-project learning within a program and across the portfolio.
- Close the loop by tracking improvement actions to completion and updating organizational assets (methods, templates, training).

This process supports project closure and continuous improvement, feeds program and portfolio governance with evidence-based recommendations, and enhances delivery predictability, quality, and stakeholder satisfaction.

## Key Activities
- Plan the review (objectives, scope, agenda, participants, logistics).
- Gather and analyze project performance data and stakeholder feedback.
- Facilitate a blameless, data-driven review session with project and program stakeholders.
- Perform root-cause analysis on key issues and success factors.
- Prioritize and assign improvement actions (project-, program-, and enterprise-level).
- Document lessons learned, decisions, and recommendations.
- Publish to the knowledge repository and communicate outcomes.
- Track action item completion and embed improvements into standards and ways of working.
- Schedule and conduct follow-up benefits realization reviews where applicable.

## Inputs and Prerequisites
Required inputs:
- Project baseline and performance data: schedule, cost, scope changes, quality metrics, EVM (if used), KPIs.
- Risk, issue, and change logs; decision and assumption logs.
- Test results, defect logs, production incident/problem records (if applicable).
- Stakeholder feedback: customer surveys, support tickets, UAT feedback, NPS/CSAT.
- Vendor performance reports, SLAs, contract milestones (if third parties involved).
- Deliverable acceptance records and closure readiness checklist.
- Compliance, audit, and security findings (if any).
- Program objectives, interdependencies, and benefit realization plan.

Prerequisites:
- Major deliverables accepted or conditionally accepted.
- Core participants identified and available (including Program Manager).
- Neutral facilitator assigned; agenda, ground rules, and pre-work defined.
- Performance data compiled and validated.
- Safe environment established for candid discussion (leadership sponsorship).

Dependencies on other processes:
- [13.2.3.4] Execute projects: provides performance data and outcomes.
- [13.2.3.3] Monitor and control projects: source of logs, KPIs, and corrective actions.
- [13.2.3.5] Close projects: consumes review outputs for closure and archiving.
- Portfolio/program governance: receives cross-project recommendations.
- Knowledge management/change management: updates standards and training.

## Process Steps
1. Trigger and Scope
   - Trigger: project completion, major phase completion, or critical incident warranting review.
   - Define scope: end-to-end or specific phases; include program-level dependencies and outcomes.

2. Plan the Review
   - Set objectives and success criteria for the session.
   - Identify participants: Project Manager, Program Manager, Sponsor, key team leads, Product Owner/Business Owner, QA, Operations/Support, Vendors, PMO, Risk/Compliance, Change Manager.
   - Choose format: single workshop (2–4 hours), multiple short sessions, or hybrid with asynchronous inputs.
   - Prepare agenda and ground rules (blameless, evidence-first, focus on learning and actions).

3. Collect and Package Evidence
   - Compile quantitative metrics (schedule/cost variance, throughput, defect density, rework, change volume, test pass rates, stakeholder sentiment).
   - Summarize major risks/issues, changes, decisions, and outcomes.
   - Solicit pre-session feedback via survey to capture candid inputs and themes.

4. Pre-Work and Logistics
   - Distribute agenda, data pack, and pre-read.
   - Provide pre-work questions: what to start/stop/continue, surprises, systemic blockers, enablers, vendor performance.
   - Set up collaboration tools (whiteboards, polling, breakout rooms); ensure accessibility for remote participants.

5. Facilitate the Review Session
   - Opening: reiterate objectives, ground rules, and psychological safety.
   - Timeline exercise: “planned vs actual” milestones and key events.
   - What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why? What can we learn?
   - Identify successes and practices to repeat.
   - Deep-dive on top themes using root-cause techniques (5 Whys, fishbone diagram, fault tree).
   - Categorize learnings: people, process, technology, governance, vendor/contract, external factors.
   - Draft concrete actions: define owners, due dates, required resources; classify as project closure tasks, program improvements, enterprise improvements.

6. Validate and Prioritize Actions
   - Apply prioritization criteria (impact, feasibility, urgency, risk reduction).
   - Confirm ownership and funding/sponsorship for non-trivial improvements.
   - Capture potential change requests to standards, templates, or tooling.

7. Document and Approve Outputs
   - Produce a concise Review Report: executive summary, data highlights, key insights, root causes, decisions, action log, recommendations for program/portfolio.
   - Update lessons learned database with searchable metadata (project type, domain, tech stack, methodology, phase, tags).
   - Obtain Program Manager and Sponsor acknowledgment of key actions and recommendations.

8. Communicate and Publish
   - Share highlights with stakeholders, PMO, communities of practice.
   - Publish artifacts to the knowledge repository (with appropriate access controls).
   - Create digestible guidance (checklists, playbook updates) if relevant.

9. Integrate and Implement Improvements
   - Raise formal change requests to methods/templates/training.
   - Feed vendor-related insights to procurement/vendor management.
   - Update risk libraries and estimations for future planning.
   - Align with change management to drive adoption where behavior change is needed.

10. Track and Close Actions
    - PMO/Program Manager monitors action completion.
    - Report progress in program governance meetings until closure.
    - Escalate blockers; adjust timelines/resources as needed.

11. Follow-up Review (optional but recommended)
    - Schedule Post-Implementation or Benefits Realization Review (e.g., 3–6 months post go-live) to assess outcomes vs. business case and capture additional lessons.

12. Archive and Compliance
    - Archive all records per retention policy; ensure auditability.
    - Update project close-out checklist and mark review complete.

Sample agenda (2.5 hours):
- 10 min: Objectives, ground rules
- 25 min: Project story and data walk-through
- 60 min: Thematic breakouts and root-cause analysis
- 35 min: Action planning and prioritization
- 10 min: Approvals, next steps, owners, due dates

## Outputs and Deliverables
- Project Review Report and slide summary.
- Lessons Learned entries with tags/taxonomy for retrieval and reuse.
- Action Log with owners, due dates, and status.
- Root-cause analysis artifacts and decision records.
- Recommendations to program/portfolio governance and process owners.
- Updates to standards, templates, checklists, and training content.
- Communications summary to stakeholders and communities of practice.

Success criteria:
- Review completed within agreed timeframe (e.g., 10 business days of project completion).
- Representation from key stakeholder groups; high participation and sentiment of psychological safety.
- Actionable, prioritized improvements with assigned owners and agreed funding where needed.
- Actions tracked to completion; evidence of reuse of lessons on subsequent projects.
- Measurable reduction in repeat issues and improved delivery performance over time.

## Roles and Responsibilities
- Project Manager: Triggers review, compiles data, coordinates logistics, drafts report, supports action follow-through.
- Program Manager: Ensures cross-project learning, approves program-level actions, secures resources, monitors completion.
- Executive Sponsor/Business Owner: Endorses recommendations, removes blockers, funds improvements.
- PMO/Portfolio Office: Facilitates/coordinates reviews, maintains lessons repository, updates standards, tracks metrics and actions.
- Facilitator (can be PMO or independent): Ensures psychological safety, runs the session, drives root-cause and action clarity.
- Team Leads/Engineers/Analysts/QA: Provide inputs, participate in analysis, own specific actions.
- Product Owner/Customer Representative: Provide business outcome feedback and adoption insights.
- Operations/Support Lead: Bring production and support perspective; own handover and operability actions.
- Risk/Compliance/Audit: Validate controls and compliance learnings; suggest risk mitigations.
- Vendor/Supplier Representative (as applicable): Provide third-party performance insight and accept relevant actions.
- Knowledge/Change Management: Codify and disseminate lessons; drive adoption of process/tool changes.
- Finance/Benefits Owner: Validate cost/benefit outcomes and support benefits realization review.

## Best Practices
- Schedule the review in advance and hold it within 1–2 weeks of completion; add a benefits realization review after stabilization.
- Use a neutral facilitator and explicit ground rules to create a blameless environment.
- Be data-driven but human-centered: combine quantitative metrics with qualitative narratives.
- Time-box discussions; focus on a few high-impact themes rather than exhaustive lists.
- Apply structured root-cause analysis; avoid jumping to solutions.
- Produce tangible artifacts: concise executive summary and a clear action plan.
- Tag lessons using a consistent taxonomy; make them easy to search and reuse.
- Include customers, operations, and vendors to capture end-to-end perspectives.
- Encourage psychological safety and anonymity for sensitive feedback (pre-surveys).
- Close the loop: track actions to completion and update standards/training; celebrate implemented improvements.
- Integrate lessons into planning and risk estimation for new projects (pre-mortems informed by prior lessons).
- For Agile teams, align with sprint/PI retrospectives and add a formal end-of-project review to roll up program-wide insights.

## Common Challenges and Solutions
- Low attendance or engagement: Secure Sponsor/Program Manager mandate; schedule early; keep it concise; use interactive tools.
- Blame culture and defensiveness: Use neutral facilitation, anonymized pre-surveys, and focus on systems over individuals.
- Vague, non-actionable lessons: Enforce SMART actions; ask “who will do what by when” and define expected outcomes.
- Lack of reliable data: Define minimum data set during execution; automate metric collection via tooling.
- Actions not implemented: Assign owners, due dates, and governance oversight; report progress in program meetings.
- Vendor reluctance: Include participation and data-sharing clauses in contracts; offer joint learning framing.
- Repetition of known issues: Use a searchable lessons database; require teams to review relevant lessons during planning.
- Distributed teams and time zones: Offer hybrid/asynchronous options; record sessions; provide translated materials if needed.
- Confidentiality concerns: Classify content, control access, and redact sensitive details while preserving learnings.

## Performance Metrics (KPIs)
- Coverage: percentage of completed projects with a documented review.
- Timeliness: average days from completion to review publication.
- Participation: attendance rate and representation across stakeholder groups.
- Actionability: average number of prioritized actions per project; percentage with clear owners/dates.
- Action completion rate: percentage of actions completed on time.
- Reuse rate: number of projects referencing and applying prior lessons.
- Recurrence reduction: decrease in frequency/severity of repeat issues across projects.
- Improvement impact: trend improvements in schedule adherence, budget variance, quality/defects, and customer satisfaction on subsequent projects.
- Knowledge velocity: time from lesson capture to incorporation into standards/templates/training.
- Psychological safety index: aggregated, anonymized survey score post-session.

## Technology and Tools
- PPM/ALM: Microsoft Project, Planview, Clarity, Jira/Jira Align, Azure DevOps for performance data and governance.
- Collaboration/Workshopping: Miro, Mural, FigJam, Microsoft Whiteboard, Zoom/Teams for facilitation.
- Surveys/Feedback: Microsoft Forms, Google Forms, Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey for pre/post-session inputs.
- Knowledge Repositories: Confluence, SharePoint, Notion, internal wiki for publishing lessons and reports.
- Issue/Risk/Action Tracking: Jira, Azure DevOps, ServiceNow, Asana, Trello for ongoing action management.
- BI/Analytics: Power BI, Tableau, Looker for dashboards and trend analysis across projects/programs.
- RCA Aids: Cause-and-effect diagramming tools, 5 Whys templates, fault tree tools.
- Document Management and e-Signature: SharePoint, DocuSign/Adobe Sign for approvals and controlled archiving.
- Security/Compliance: DLP and access controls to protect sensitive content in artifacts.
